shelves.title: Prevention: stopping disease before it starts
shelves.question: What can be prevented — heart attacks, strokes, diabetes, cancer, fractures, infections — and what does the evidence say actually works?
shelves.balance: Prevention is where this library’s evidence is strongest and strangest. Some of it is medicine’s greatest hits: folic acid prevents neural tube defects; statins and blood-pressure treatment prevent heart attacks and strokes; HPV vaccination prevents cervical cancer. Some of it failed its trials: vitamin E did not prevent prostate cancer, beta-carotene caused lung cancer in smokers, and annual vitamin D mega-doses caused falls. This shelf lists every prevention question in the library, grouped by what you are trying to prevent — the wins, the nulls, and the backfires alike — and points to the shelf where each one’s evidence lives.

shelves.title: HIV pre-exposure prophylaxis: pills work when taken — injections work when pills don’t get taken
shelves.question: In people at high risk of acquiring HIV, how well does pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) prevent infection — daily pills, long-acting injections, and twice-yearly lenacapavir?
shelves.mesh: HIV Infections · Pre-Exposure Prophylaxis · Anti-HIV Agents · Tenofovir · Emtricitabine · Humans
shelves.balance: Every positive trial on this shelf carries the same asterisk: the drug works in proportion to its presence in the body. Daily oral tenofovir-based PrEP cut HIV incidence by 44% relative in iPrEx and by 67–75% relative in Partners PrEP — and by over 90% in participants with detectable drug levels — while the FEM-PrEP and VOICE trials in African women found no protection at all, because adherence was too low for drug to be present. The long-acting era is the adherence answer: injectable cabotegravir every 8 weeks beat daily pills head-to-head in HPTN 083 (hazard ratio 0.34) and HPTN 084 (hazard ratio 0.12), and twice-yearly lenacapavir recorded zero infections among 2,134 women in PURPOSE 1 and an incidence of 0.10 per 100 person-years in PURPOSE 2. All efficacy figures on this shelf are relative reductions; absolute incidences are printed on every card. Tier C — prevention-of-infection claims; developer verdict given personally. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026.

cards.headline: iPrEx (Grant 2010): daily oral FTC-TDF cut HIV incidence by 44% relative — and by 92% when drug was actually detectable
cards.summary: HIV infections during follow-up: 36 on daily emtricitabine-tenofovir DF vs 64 on placebo — a 44% relative reduction in incidence (95% CI 15 to 63) over 3,324 person-years; among participants with detectable drug, protection was about 92% relative — 2,499 men and transgender women who have sex with men.
cards.type: Randomized, placebo-controlled trial (iPrEx), N Engl J Med 2010
cards.people: 2,499 HIV-seronegative men or transgender women who have sex with men, followed for 3,324 person-years (median 1.2 years). (The abstract record does not print mean age.) All received HIV testing, risk-reduction counseling, condoms, and STI management.
cards.result: 100 participants became infected during follow-up: 36 in the FTC-TDF group and 64 in the placebo group — a 44% relative reduction in HIV incidence (95% CI, 15 to 63; P=0.005). The study drug was detected in 51% of seronegative participants sampled but in only 9% of those who became infected, and protection among participants with detectable drug levels was about 92% relative. Nausea was more frequent in the first 4 weeks on FTC-TDF; serious adverse event rates were similar (P=0.57).
cards.watchOut: This is the trial that defined the field's central lesson: PrEP is an adherence intervention wearing a drug label. The 44% figure is the intention-to-treat average across everyone assigned pills, including many who took few; the biology, when drug was present, was near-complete protection. Resistance was seen mainly in participants already infected at enrollment.
cards.source: Grant RM et al. Preexposure Chemoprophylaxis for HIV Prevention in Men Who Have Sex with Men. N Engl J Med. 2010;363:2587-99. PMID 21091279 · NCT00458393. DOI 10.1056/NEJMoa1011205

cards.headline: Partners PrEP (Baeten 2012): in serodiscordant couples, tenofovir cut incidence by 67% relative and FTC-tenofovir by 75% relative
cards.summary: HIV incidence: 0.65 per 100 person-years on tenofovir alone and 0.50 on tenofovir-emtricitabine vs 1.99 on placebo — 67% and 75% relative reductions (both P<0.001); with detectable drug, protection rose to about 86–90% relative — 4,758 serodiscordant heterosexual couples in Kenya and Uganda.
cards.type: Randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (Partners PrEP), N Engl J Med 2012
cards.people: 4,758 HIV-1-serodiscordant heterosexual couples from Kenya and Uganda (4,747 followed: 1,584 assigned TDF, 1,579 TDF-FTC, 1,584 placebo); in 62% of couples the HIV-negative partner was male. The HIV-positive partners had a median CD4 count of 495 cells/mm³ and were not yet eligible for antiretroviral therapy under national guidelines. Follow-up was monthly for up to 36 months.
cards.result: 82 HIV-1 infections occurred in seronegative partners: 17 on TDF (incidence 0.65 per 100 person-years), 13 on TDF-FTC (0.50 per 100 person-years), and 52 on placebo (1.99 per 100 person-years) — a 67% relative reduction with TDF (95% CI, 44 to 81; P<0.001) and a 75% relative reduction with TDF-FTC (95% CI, 55 to 87; P<0.001). Protection did not differ significantly between the two active regimens (P=0.23) and held in both men and women; in substudies with detectable drug levels, protection was about 86–90% relative. Serious adverse events were similar across groups; antiretroviral resistance developed in 2 of 8 participants found to have been infected at baseline.
cards.watchOut: The couples design is why adherence was high enough to show the drug's true effect — partners knew exactly what they were preventing. Read beside FEM-PrEP and VOICE, which tested the same pills in young African women and found no protection because drug levels showed most pills were never taken: same pharmacology, different adherence, opposite headlines.
cards.source: Baeten JM et al. Antiretroviral Prophylaxis for HIV Prevention in Heterosexual Men and Women. N Engl J Med. 2012;367:399-410. PMID 22784037 · NCT00557245. DOI 10.1056/NEJMoa1108524

cards.headline: HPTN 083 (Landovitz 2021): injectable cabotegravir every 8 weeks beat daily pills — incidence 0.41 vs 1.22 per 100 person-years (HR 0.34)
cards.summary: Incident HIV infection: 13 on long-acting cabotegravir (incidence 0.41 per 100 person-years ) vs 39 on daily oral TDF-FTC ( 1.22 per 100 person-years ) — hazard ratio 0.34 (95% CI 0.18 to 0.62), a 66% relative reduction against an active comparator; the trial was stopped early for efficacy — 4,566 participants.
cards.type: Randomized, double-blind, double-dummy, noninferiority trial (HPTN 083), N Engl J Med 2021
cards.people: 4,566 participants underwent randomization; 570 (12.5%) identified as transgender women; median age 26 years (interquartile range 22 to 32). Among 1,698 US participants, 49.8% identified as Black. Follow-up was planned for 153 weeks; the trial was stopped early at the first preplanned interim analysis.
cards.result: Incident HIV infection occurred in 52 participants: 13 in the cabotegravir group (incidence 0.41 per 100 person-years) and 39 in the TDF-FTC group (1.22 per 100 person-years) — hazard ratio 0.34 (95% CI, 0.18 to 0.62), i.e. a 66% relative reduction against daily oral PrEP, not against placebo. The effect was consistent across prespecified subgroups. Injection-site reactions were reported by 81.4% of the cabotegravir group vs 31.3% of the TDF-FTC group (who received placebo injections). No safety concerns were identified.
cards.watchOut: Both arms received an effective drug — the gap between arms is mostly an adherence gap the injection erased. The caution is real and printed in the paper: in participants who acquired HIV after cabotegravir exposure, integrase-inhibitor resistance was seen and HIV detection was delayed, because the drug can blunt early test signals. Testing strategy matters on long-acting PrEP.
cards.source: Landovitz RJ et al. Cabotegravir for HIV Prevention in Cisgender Men and Transgender Women. N Engl J Med. 2021;385:595-608. PMID 34379922 · NCT02720094. DOI 10.1056/NEJMoa2101016

cards.headline: HPTN 084 (Delany-Moretlwe 2022): in African women, cabotegravir injections cut incidence by 88% relative vs daily pills — 0.2 vs 1.85 per 100 person-years
cards.summary: Incident infections: 4 on cabotegravir (incidence 0.2 per 100 person-years ) vs 36 on daily TDF-FTC ( 1.85 per 100 person-years ) — hazard ratio 0.12 (95% CI 0.05 to 0.31), an 88% relative reduction; only 42% of sampled pill-group specimens showed daily-use drug levels — 3,224 women in seven sub-Saharan African countries.
cards.type: Phase 3, randomized, double-blind, double-dummy, active-controlled superiority trial (HPTN 084), Lancet 2022
cards.people: 3,224 women aged 18–45 years at 20 sites in seven sub-Saharan African countries (1,614 cabotegravir, 1,610 TDF-FTC); median age 25 years (interquartile range 22–30); 54.7% reported two or more partners in the preceding month. All agreed to use long-acting reversible contraception.
cards.result: 40 incident infections occurred over 3,898 person-years: 4 in the cabotegravir group (incidence 0.2 per 100 person-years) and 36 in the TDF-FTC group (1.85 per 100 person-years) — hazard ratio 0.12 (95% CI, 0.05 to 0.31; P<0.0001), an 88% relative reduction; absolute risk difference −1.6 percentage points. In a random subset of the pill group, only 42.1% of plasma samples had tenofovir levels consistent with daily use; injection coverage was 93% of person-years. Injection-site reactions were more frequent with cabotegravir (38.0% vs 10.7%) but caused no discontinuations. Pregnancy incidence was 1.3 per 100 person-years with no congenital anomalies reported.
cards.watchOut: This is the population in which daily-pill PrEP trials (FEM-PrEP, VOICE) had failed outright on adherence. The trial does not show a stronger drug so much as a delivery system that survives real life — which is precisely the clinical point. Contraception was required and provided, so pregnancy outcomes data remain thin by design.
cards.source: Delany-Moretlwe S et al. Cabotegravir for the prevention of HIV-1 in women: results from HPTN 084, a phase 3, randomised clinical trial. Lancet. 2022;399:1779-1789. PMID 35378077 · NCT03164564. DOI 10.1016/S0140-6736(22)00538-4

cards.headline: PURPOSE 1 (Bekker 2024): twice-yearly lenacapavir — zero infections in 2,134 women; incidence 0 vs 1.69 per 100 person-years on daily F/TDF
cards.summary: Incident HIV infections: 0 of 2,134 on twice-yearly subcutaneous lenacapavir ( 0 per 100 person-years ) vs 16 of 1,068 on daily F/TDF ( 1.69 per 100 person-years ) and a background screened incidence of 2.41 — incidence rate ratio 0.00 vs both background and F/TDF (P<0.001 for both) — 5,338 young women in South Africa and Uganda.
cards.type: Phase 3, double-blind, randomized, controlled trial (PURPOSE 1), N Engl J Med 2024
cards.people: 5,338 initially HIV-negative adolescent girls and young women in South Africa and Uganda, assigned 2:2:1 to lenacapavir every 26 weeks (2,134), daily oral F/TAF (2,136), or daily oral F/TDF (1,068, active control), each with matching placebos. (The abstract record does not print mean age.) Background HIV incidence was estimated in the screened population of 8,094.
cards.result: 55 incident infections were observed: 0 among 2,134 lenacapavir participants (0 per 100 person-years; 95% CI, 0.00 to 0.19), 39 among 2,136 on F/TAF (2.02 per 100 person-years), and 16 among 1,068 on F/TDF (1.69 per 100 person-years), against a background incidence of 2.41 per 100 person-years. Lenacapavir incidence was significantly lower than background (incidence rate ratio 0.00; 95% CI, 0.00 to 0.04; P<0.001) and than F/TDF (rate ratio 0.00; 0.00 to 0.10; P<0.001). F/TAF did not differ significantly from background (rate ratio 0.84; P=0.21) — adherence to both oral regimens was low. Injection-site reactions were more common with lenacapavir (68.8%) than placebo injection (34.9%); 0.2% discontinued for them.
cards.watchOut: Zero infections is the strongest result on this shelf — and the comparison structure deserves a careful read: there was no placebo pill arm, so efficacy is anchored to a screened-population background incidence and to the active oral control, whose own adherence failed again in this trial. The finding is real, but it is a finding about a twice-yearly injection versus pills largely not taken, in young women — the group every daily-pill trial had failed.
cards.source: Bekker LG et al. Twice-Yearly Lenacapavir or Daily F/TAF for HIV Prevention in Cisgender Women. N Engl J Med. 2024;391:1179-1192. PMID 39046157 · NCT04994509. DOI 10.1056/NEJMoa2407001

cards.headline: PURPOSE 2 (Kelley 2024): lenacapavir in men and gender-diverse persons — incidence 0.10 vs 0.93 per 100 person-years on daily F/TDF
cards.summary: HIV infections: 2 on twice-yearly lenacapavir (incidence 0.10 per 100 person-years ) vs 9 on daily F/TDF ( 0.93 per 100 person-years ), against a background incidence of 2.37 — rate ratio 0.11 vs F/TDF (P=0.002) and 0.04 vs background (P<0.001) — 3,265 participants in the primary analysis.
cards.type: Phase 3, double-blind, randomized, active-controlled trial (PURPOSE 2), N Engl J Med 2025
cards.people: 3,265 participants in the modified intention-to-treat analysis (2,183 lenacapavir, 1,088 F/TDF), assigned 2:1. Background HIV incidence was estimated in a screened population of 4,634. (The abstract record does not print mean age or sex mix beyond the eligible gender groups.)
cards.result: HIV infections occurred in 2 participants on lenacapavir (0.10 per 100 person-years; 95% CI, 0.01 to 0.37) and 9 on F/TDF (0.93 per 100 person-years; 95% CI, 0.43 to 1.77), against a background incidence of 2.37 per 100 person-years. Incidence on lenacapavir was significantly lower than background (incidence rate ratio 0.04; 95% CI, 0.01 to 0.18; P<0.001) and than on F/TDF (rate ratio 0.11; 0.02 to 0.51; P=0.002) — an 89% relative reduction versus the active oral control. No safety concerns were identified; discontinuations for injection-site reactions were 1.2% on lenacapavir vs 0.3% on F/TDF.
cards.watchOut: The event counts are small — 2 versus 9 — so the relative figures sit on wide intervals even though both comparisons cleared significance. As in PURPOSE 1, there is no placebo arm; the background-incidence anchor comes from the screened population. Two injections a year is the adherence story again: the delivery system is the intervention.

shelves.title: Early antiretroviral therapy: start at diagnosis — for the patient, and for the partner
shelves.question: In people with HIV who feel well and have high CD4 counts, does starting antiretroviral therapy immediately — rather than waiting for the CD4 count to fall — prevent illness, death, and transmission?
shelves.mesh: HIV Infections · Anti-Retroviral Agents · CD4 Lymphocyte Count · Disease Transmission, Infectious · Humans
shelves.balance: START settled the timing question for the patient's own health: starting ART at a CD4 count above 500 rather than waiting for 350 cut the composite of serious AIDS events, serious non-AIDS events, and death by 57% relative (hazard ratio 0.43) — and the absolute difference is printed beside it on the card, because it is the honest size of the prize: 1.8% versus 4.1% over about 3 years, an absolute difference of about 2.3 percentage points, a number-needed-to-treat of about 43. TEMPRANO, run in Côte d'Ivoire, found the same direction independently for early ART (hazard ratio 0.56) and added a second, separate win for six months of isoniazid preventive therapy (0.65). HPTN 052 answers the second question — the partner's: early ART cut genetically linked transmission by 93% relative, and no linked infection occurred while the index partner's virus was stably suppressed. Tier C — mortality and transmission claims; developer verdict given personally. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026.

cards.headline: START (2015): starting ART above CD4 500 vs waiting for 350 — composite events 1.8% vs 4.1% (HR 0.43; absolute difference ≈2.3 points, NNT ≈43)
cards.summary: Primary composite (serious AIDS event, serious non-AIDS event, or death): 1.8% with immediate ART vs 4.1% with deferred ART — hazard ratio 0.43 (95% CI 0.30 to 0.62), a 57% relative reduction; the absolute difference is ≈2.3 percentage points over a mean of 3 years (NNT ≈43) — 4,685 adults with CD4 counts above 500.
cards.type: Randomized controlled trial (START — Strategic Timing of Antiretroviral Therapy), N Engl J Med 2015
cards.people: 4,685 HIV-positive adults with CD4+ counts above 500 cells/mm³ (median CD4 at entry 651; median viral load 12,759 copies/mL), followed for a mean of 3.0 years. (The abstract record does not print mean age or sex mix.) The trial was stopped on May 15, 2015, after an interim analysis showed the question answered, and deferred-group patients were offered ART.
cards.result: The primary end point occurred in 42 patients (1.8%; 0.60 events per 100 person-years) in the immediate-initiation group versus 96 (4.1%; 1.38 per 100 person-years) in the deferred group — hazard ratio 0.43 (95% CI, 0.30 to 0.62; P<0.001), a 57% relative reduction and an absolute difference of about 2.3 percentage points (NNT ≈43 over ~3 years). Hazard ratios were 0.28 for serious AIDS-related events (0.15 to 0.50) and 0.61 for serious non-AIDS-related events (0.38 to 0.97); 68% of primary end points occurred while CD4 counts were still above 500. Grade 4 events and unscheduled hospital admissions were similar between groups.
cards.watchOut: Read the relative and absolute figures together — that is this library's rule for this shelf. A 57% relative reduction on a low absolute event rate means most deferred patients also did well over 3 years; the case for immediate start rests on the composite direction, the cancer and AIDS components, and the transmission benefit on Card 3 — not on any single dramatic number. The deferred strategy tested (start at 350) is also far more conservative than the pre-START practice in many settings.
cards.source: INSIGHT START Study Group. Initiation of Antiretroviral Therapy in Early Asymptomatic HIV Infection. N Engl J Med. 2015;373:795-807. PMID 26192873 · NCT00867048. DOI 10.1056/NEJMoa1506816

cards.headline: TEMPRANO (2015): in Côte d'Ivoire, early ART cut severe illness by 44% relative (HR 0.56) — and isoniazid prophylaxis helped independently (HR 0.65)
cards.summary: Risk of death or severe HIV-related illness: lower with early ART than deferred ART — adjusted hazard ratio 0.56 (95% CI 0.41 to 0.76), a 44% relative reduction — and independently lower with 6 months of isoniazid preventive therapy vs none — adjusted HR 0.65 (0.48 to 0.88) — 2,056 adults in Côte d'Ivoire, followed for 4,757 patient-years.
cards.type: Randomized 2-by-2 factorial trial (TEMPRANO ANRS 12136), N Engl J Med 2015
cards.people: 2,056 HIV-1-infected adults in Côte d'Ivoire with CD4 counts below 800 cells/mm³ (41% had a baseline count of 500 or above) who met no WHO criteria for ART initiation, followed for 4,757 patient-years; the primary end point was assessed at 30 months. (The abstract record does not print mean age or sex mix.)
cards.result: 204 primary end-point events occurred (3.8 per 100 person-years) — death, AIDS-defining disease, non-AIDS cancer, or invasive bacterial disease; tuberculosis (42%) and invasive bacterial disease (27%) accounted for most events. Early ART lowered the risk of death or severe illness versus deferred ART (adjusted hazard ratio 0.56; 95% CI, 0.41 to 0.76; among those with CD4 500 or above, 0.56; 0.33 to 0.94), and isoniazid preventive therapy lowered it independently (adjusted HR 0.65; 0.48 to 0.88). Grade 3 or 4 adverse events at 30 months did not differ significantly among the strategies.
cards.watchOut: TEMPRANO is the African confirmation of START with a different event mix — here the events prevented were mostly tuberculosis and bacterial disease, which is why this trial, not START, carries the isoniazid result. 'Early' in TEMPRANO meant immediate versus WHO-criteria initiation in a high-TB-burden setting; the trial predates universal test-and-treat.
cards.source: TEMPRANO ANRS 12136 Study Group (Danel C et al.). A Trial of Early Antiretrovirals and Isoniazid Preventive Therapy in Africa. N Engl J Med. 2015;373:808-22. PMID 26193126 · NCT00495651. DOI 10.1056/NEJMoa1507198

cards.headline: HPTN 052 (Cohen 2016): early ART cut genetically linked partner infections by 93% relative — and there were zero linked infections while the index partner was suppressed
cards.summary: Genetically linked partner infections: 3 in the early-ART group vs 43 in the delayed-ART group — hazard ratio 0.07 (95% CI 0.02 to 0.22), a 93% relative reduction ; no linked infection occurred while the index participant's virus was stably suppressed — 1,763 serodiscordant couples, over 10,031 person-years of index follow-up.
cards.type: Randomized controlled trial, final analysis (HPTN 052), N Engl J Med 2016 (interim analysis 2011)
cards.people: 1,763 index participants with HIV-1 infection (CD4 350–550 cells/mm³ at entry) and their HIV-negative partners: 886 started ART at enrollment (early group) and 877 started after two consecutive CD4 counts below 250 or an AIDS-defining illness (delayed group). Index participants were followed for 10,031 person-years and partners for 8,509 person-years. (The abstract record does not print mean age or sex mix.)
cards.result: 78 HIV-1 infections were observed in partners (annual incidence 0.9%); linkage was determined for 72, of which 46 were genetically linked — 3 in the early-ART group and 43 in the delayed-ART group (incidence 0.5% overall for linked infections). Early ART was associated with a 93% relative reduction in linked partner infection (hazard ratio 0.07; 95% CI, 0.02 to 0.22). No linked infections were observed when HIV-1 was stably suppressed by ART in the index participant. The 2011 interim analysis (PMID 21767103) had shown a 96% relative reduction and triggered ART being offered to all index participants.
cards.watchOut: The 'zero under suppression' line is an observation within the trial, not a randomized comparison — linked infections in the early group occurred before suppression was achieved or after virologic failure. It is nonetheless the trial foundation of 'undetectable = untransmittable' as a prevention strategy, and the reason early ART is also a public-health intervention, not only treatment.

shelves.title: The dengue vaccine serostatus lesson: protection for the previously infected, harm for the never-infected
shelves.question: Does the dengue vaccine CYD-TDV (Dengvaxia) protect against dengue — and in whom can it cause harm?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Antibodies, Viral · Child · Dengue · Dengue Vaccines · Hospitalization · Humans · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: One reanalysis, two opposite truths. Pooling the CYD-TDV trials by baseline serostatus (Sridhar 2018): in previously infected children the vaccine cut hospitalisation for dengue by about two-thirds (HR 0.32 [0.23–0.45]) — and in never-infected children it raised hospitalisation risk (HR 1.75 [1.14–2.70]), the antibody-dependent-enhancement pattern made real. The trials’ original pooled efficacy was the average of a benefit and a harm. POSSIBLE grades the knowledge, not the product: the benefit and the harm are each credible within their subgroup, and the shelf’s claim is the split itself. Proposed stamp POSSIBLE — proposed, pending the developer’s review.

cards.headline: The benefit half (Sridhar 2018, NEJM): in children who had already had dengue, CYD-TDV cut hospitalisation by two-thirds (HR 0.32)
cards.summary: The phase 3 trials’ pooled data, reanalysed by baseline dengue serostatus: among seropositive participants aged 2–16, the cumulative five-year incidence of hospitalisation for virologically confirmed dengue was 0.75% in vaccine recipients vs 2.47% in controls — HR 0.32 [0.23–0.45] ; at ages 9–16 the hazard ratio was 0.21 [0.14–0.31] (0.38% vs 1.88%). The risk of severe dengue was also lower in seropositive vaccine recipients. In the population the vaccine was designed for — children in endemic areas, most of them previously infected — the protection was large and durable over five years.
cards.type: Case-cohort reanalysis of three randomised efficacy trials, by baseline serostatus, N Engl J Med 2018. Registry IDs from the record’s own text: NCT00842530, NCT01983553, NCT01373281, NCT01374516 (the underlying trials).
cards.people: Participants aged 2–16 years in the CYD-TDV phase 2b/3 efficacy trials in Asia and Latin America, classified dengue-seropositive at baseline by measured or imputed neutralisation titres.
cards.result: Among dengue-seropositive participants 2 to 16 years of age and those 9 to 16 years of age, the cumulative incidence of hospitalization for virologically confirmed dengue was 0.75% and 0.38%, respectively, among vaccine recipients and 2.47% and 1.88% among controls, with hazard ratios of 0.32 (95% CI, 0.23 to 0.45) and 0.21 (95% CI, 0.14 to 0.31). The risk of severe virologically confirmed dengue was also lower among seropositive vaccine recipients than among seropositive controls.
cards.watchOut: This half of the record is why the vaccine was licensed and celebrated before the other half was known. Two fences: serostatus at baseline was partly imputed (from month-13 anti-NS1 results and covariates) rather than measured in everyone, and the analysis was funded by the vaccine’s maker, Sanofi Pasteur — printed on the record. Neither fence erases a hazard ratio of 0.21–0.32; both belong beside it.
cards.source: Sridhar S et al. Effect of dengue serostatus on dengue vaccine safety and efficacy. N Engl J Med. 2018;379(4):327–340. PMID 29897841. DOI 10.1056/NEJMoa1800820

cards.headline: The harm half (Sridhar 2018, NEJM): in children who had never had dengue, the same vaccine raised hospitalisation risk (HR 1.75)
cards.summary: In seronegative participants aged 2–16, the cumulative five-year incidence of hospitalisation for virologically confirmed dengue was 3.06% among vaccine recipients vs 1.87% among controls — HR 1.75 [1.14–2.70] . At ages 9–16 the hazard ratio was 1.41 [0.74–2.68], and similar trends toward higher risk were found for severe dengue. The interpretation the record supports: a first natural dengue infection is usually mild, and second infections carry the severe-disease risk; in a never-infected child the vaccine appears to act immunologically like a silent first infection, so the first natural infection that follows behaves like a second — the antibody-dependent-enhancement pattern the field had feared in theory, here measured in a trial population.
cards.type: Case-cohort reanalysis of three randomised efficacy trials, by baseline serostatus, N Engl J Med 2018. Registry IDs from the record’s own text: NCT00842530, NCT01983553, NCT01373281, NCT01374516 (the underlying trials).
cards.people: Participants aged 2–16 years in the CYD-TDV efficacy trials, classified dengue-seronegative at baseline by measured or imputed neutralisation titres.
cards.result: Among dengue-seronegative participants 2 to 16 years of age, the cumulative 5-year incidence of hospitalization for virologically confirmed dengue was 3.06% among vaccine recipients and 1.87% among controls, with a hazard ratio (vaccine vs. control) through data cutoff of 1.75 (95% CI, 1.14 to 2.70). Among seronegative participants 9 to 16 years of age, the cumulative incidence was 1.57% among vaccine recipients and 1.09% among controls, with a hazard ratio of 1.41 (95% CI, 0.74 to 2.68). Similar trends toward a higher risk among seronegative vaccine recipients than among seronegative controls were also found for severe dengue.
cards.watchOut: The harm signal rests on the same imputed-serostatus reanalysis as the benefit — a post hoc reconstruction, not a prespecified comparison, and its confidence interval (1.14–2.70) is wide. What makes it credible rather than dismissible: it is biologically predicted (enhancement), it is direction-consistent across age bands and severity, and it emerged from the sponsor’s own reanalysis of its own trials. The card prints the numbers, not a verdict on any individual’s past vaccination.

cards.headline: The serostatus lesson: the first vaccine whose effect flips sign on a blood test
cards.summary: Read whole, this shelf is the modern era’s defining vaccine-safety lesson. One vaccine, one trial programme, two opposite effects, sorted entirely by a pre-vaccination blood test most recipients never had: hazard ratio 0.32 for hospitalisation in the previously infected, 1.75 in the never-infected. The aggregate efficacy the trials originally reported was the average of a benefit and a harm — correct arithmetic, wrong answer for both groups. The practical consequence reshaped the product’s use worldwide toward documented prior infection. For this library the lesson generalises: whenever a vaccine (or any intervention) acts on an immune system whose history varies, a pooled effect can conceal a subgroup being harmed, and ‘who was immune before?’ is a first-order question, not a subgroup afterthought.
cards.type: Synthesis card — no new study. This card reads Cards 1 and 2 (a single reanalysis) together and states the lesson and its limits.
cards.people: The population of Cards 1 and 2: children and adolescents aged 2–16 in the CYD-TDV trials in dengue-endemic Asia and Latin America, split by baseline serostatus.
cards.result: The reanalysis establishes that CYD-TDV’s effect on hospitalised and severe dengue depends on prior dengue infection: substantial protection in seropositive recipients, increased risk in seronegative recipients, over five years of follow-up. It does not establish individual-level predictions (serostatus was partly imputed at group level), nor does it speak to the newer dengue vaccines with different constructs, whose serostatus profiles are separate questions.
cards.watchOut: Do not quote either hazard ratio without its serostatus label attached — that is precisely the error this shelf exists to prevent. And do not transfer the harm finding mechanically to other dengue vaccines: the lesson is to demand the serostatus split, not to presume its answer.
cards.source: Synthesis of Cards 1–2 on this shelf (PMID 29897841).

shelves.title: Xylitol for cavities
shelves.question: Does xylitol, in toothpaste, gum, lozenges, syrup or other products, prevent dental caries in children or adults compared with no xylitol or a control product?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Candy · Cariostatic Agents · Child · Child, Preschool · Dental Caries · Dentition, Permanent · Female · Fluorides · Humans · Infant · Male
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence): the Cochrane review found only low- to very-low-quality evidence, with a possible benefit confined to xylitol fluoride toothpaste in children from two studies by the same authors in the same population. The large adult X-ACT lozenge trial was null, and a single high-caries-risk adult gum trial reported a smaller caries increment. Overall benefit for xylitol products in general is unproven. Proposed stamp MAYBE (weak evidence) — proposed, pending the developer’s review.

cards.headline: Cochrane review: evidence insufficient except a possible toothpaste signal in children
cards.summary: Cochrane 2015 (10 studies, 5,903 participants): evidence low to very low quality — only 1 of 10 studies at low risk of bias. The one signal: fluoride toothpaste with 10% xylitol may reduce caries by a relative 13% in children, from two studies by the same authors in the same population. Every other product’s interval covered both benefit and harm.
cards.people: 10 studies, 5,903 participants, children and adults; abstract does not state mean age or sex breakdown
cards.result: Fluoride toothpaste containing 10% xylitol over 2.5 to 3 years may reduce caries by 13% relative (prevented fraction -0.13, 95% CI -0.18 to -0.08; 4,216 children analysed, low-quality evidence). Xylitol syrup 8 g/day reduced caries by 58% relative (95% CI 33% to 83%; 94 infants, low-quality evidence) versus low-dose syrup. All other product comparisons had 95% CIs compatible with both a reduction and an increase in caries.
cards.watchOut: Only 1 of 10 studies was at low risk of bias and 7 were at high risk of bias; the toothpaste result came from two studies by the same authors in the same population. Adverse effects included mouth sores, cramps, bloating, constipation, flatulence and loose stool or diarrhoea.
cards.source: Riley P et al. Cochrane Database Syst Rev. 2015;(3):CD010743. PMID 25809586. Registry ID: none in the PubMed record (systematic review).

cards.summary: X-ACT (691 at-risk adults, 33 months): xylitol lozenges cut the caries increment by a relative 10% — not statistically significant , less than a third of a surface per year, no dose-response. The large adult trial is null.

shelves.title: Latent tuberculosis: short rifamycin regimens match nine months of isoniazid — and people actually finish them
shelves.question: For latent tuberculosis infection, can short rifamycin-based regimens — 3 months of weekly rifapentine plus isoniazid, 1 month of daily rifapentine plus isoniazid, or 4 months of daily rifampin — prevent active tuberculosis as well as 9 months of isoniazid, with better completion and safety?
shelves.mesh: Latent Tuberculosis · Tuberculosis · Isoniazid · Rifampin · Antitubercular Agents · Drug Therapy, Combination · Directly Observed Therapy · Humans
shelves.balance: Three large randomized trials, in three populations, all found a short rifamycin regimen noninferior to 9 months of isoniazid for preventing active tuberculosis — with completion rates 7 to 15 percentage points higher and less hepatotoxicity. PREVENT TB (7,731 in the modified intention-to-treat analysis): tuberculosis in 0.19% on 3 months of weekly rifapentine–isoniazid vs 0.43% on 9 months of isoniazid; completion 82.1% vs 69.0%; hepatotoxicity 0.4% vs 2.7%, though permanent discontinuation for adverse events was slightly higher on the combination (4.9% vs 3.7%). BRIEF TB (3,000 people with HIV): the primary endpoint occurred in 2% in both arms on 1 month of daily rifapentine–isoniazid vs 9 months of isoniazid, with 97% vs 90% completion. Menzies 2018: 4 months of rifampin matched 9 months of isoniazid (confirmed tuberculosis 4 vs 4 cases) with fewer grade 3–5 and hepatotoxic adverse events. The event rates are low everywhere — prevention trials measure rare outcomes — so noninferiority is the honest verb. Proposed stamp LIKELY — proposed, pending the developer's review.

cards.headline: PREVENT TB 2011: 3 months of weekly rifapentine plus isoniazid was as effective as 9 months of isoniazid — completion 82.1% vs 69.0%, hepatotoxicity 0.4% vs 2.7%
cards.summary: PREVENT TB: 3 months of weekly rifapentine + isoniazid matched 9 months of isoniazid (TB in 0.19% vs 0.43% ), with far better completion ( 82.1% vs 69.0% ) and less hepatotoxicity (0.4% vs 2.7%).
cards.type: Open-label, randomized noninferiority trial, N Engl J Med 2011; combination therapy directly observed, isoniazid self-administered
cards.people: Subjects at high risk for tuberculosis enrolled in the United States, Canada, Brazil, and Spain, followed for 33 months; the modified intention-to-treat analysis included 3,986 in the combination group and 3,745 in the isoniazid-only group. (The abstract does not print mean age or sex mix.)
cards.result: Confirmed tuberculosis developed in 7/3,986 (cumulative rate 0.19%) on 3 months of once-weekly rifapentine (900 mg) plus isoniazid (900 mg) vs 15/3,745 (0.43%) on 9 months of daily isoniazid (300 mg) — a difference of 0.24 percentage points, inside the 0.75% noninferiority margin. Treatment completion: 82.1% vs 69.0% (P<0.001). Permanent discontinuation because of an adverse event: 4.9% vs 3.7% (P=0.009). Investigator-assessed drug-related hepatotoxicity: 0.4% vs 2.7% (P<0.001).
cards.watchOut: The comparison bundles two changes at once — shorter regimen and directly observed therapy vs self-administration — so part of the completion advantage may be the observation, not the calendar. Event rates under half a percent mean tiny absolute differences carry the noninferiority verdict.
cards.source: Sterling TR et al. Three months of rifapentine and isoniazid for latent tuberculosis infection. N Engl J Med. 2011;365(23):2155-66. PMID 22150035 · NCT00023452.

cards.headline: BRIEF TB 2019: in people with HIV, 1 month of daily rifapentine plus isoniazid was noninferior to 9 months of isoniazid — completion 97% vs 90%
cards.summary: BRIEF TB: in people with HIV, 1 month of daily rifapentine + isoniazid was noninferior to 9 months of isoniazid — completion 97% vs 90% .
cards.type: Randomized, open-label, phase 3 noninferiority trial (BRIEF TB/A5279), N Engl J Med 2019
cards.people: 3,000 HIV-infected patients living in areas of high tuberculosis prevalence or with evidence of latent tuberculosis infection, followed a median of 3.3 years; 54% were women, the median CD4+ count was 470 cells/mm³, and half were receiving antiretroviral therapy. (The abstract does not print median or mean age.)
cards.result: The primary endpoint (first diagnosis of tuberculosis, or death from tuberculosis or an unknown cause) occurred in 32/1,488 (2%) on the 1-month regimen vs 33/1,498 (2%) on 9 months of isoniazid — incidence 0.65 vs 0.67 per 100 person-years (rate difference −0.02 per 100 person-years; upper limit of the 95% CI 0.30, below the 1.25 noninferiority margin). Serious adverse events: 6% vs 7% (P=0.07). Treatment completion: 97% vs 90% (P<0.001).
cards.watchOut: This is an HIV-population result, in high-prevalence settings or with documented latent infection — it does not by itself license the 1-month regimen in the general non-HIV population, where PREVENT TB's 3-month weekly regimen is the tested one. A 2024 randomized trial (PMID 38996972, found in this shelf's currency sweep) has since compared the 1-month and 3-month rifapentine regimens in a non-HIV population on completion and safety.
cards.source: Swindells S et al. One Month of Rifapentine plus Isoniazid to Prevent HIV-Related Tuberculosis. N Engl J Med. 2019;380(11):1001-1011. PMID 30865794 · NCT01404312.

cards.headline: Menzies 2018: 4 months of daily rifampin was not inferior to 9 months of isoniazid — with fewer serious and liver adverse events
cards.summary: Menzies: 4 months of daily rifampin was not inferior to 9 months of isoniazid (4 confirmed TB cases in each group), with fewer serious and liver adverse events.
cards.type: Open-label, phase 3 randomized trial in nine countries, N Engl J Med 2018; outcomes adjudicated by independent panels
cards.people: 6,859 adults with latent tuberculosis infection (3,443 assigned 4 months of rifampin, 3,416 assigned 9 months of isoniazid), followed for 28 months after randomization (7,732 and 7,652 person-years). (The abstract does not print mean age or sex mix.)
cards.result: Confirmed active tuberculosis developed in 4 patients in each group; clinically diagnosed tuberculosis in 4 (rifampin) vs 5 (isoniazid). Rate differences (rifampin minus isoniazid) were <0.01 cases per 100 person-years for confirmed tuberculosis (95% CI −0.14 to 0.16), with the upper confidence bound below the prespecified noninferiority margin; the rifampin regimen was not superior. The treatment-completion difference was 15.1 percentage points (95% CI 12.7 to 17.4) in rifampin's favor. Grade 3–5 adverse events within the assessment window were fewer on rifampin (rate difference −1.1 points; 95% CI −1.9 to −0.4), as were hepatotoxic events (−1.2 points; 95% CI −1.7 to −0.7).
cards.watchOut: Carded as the rifampin companion to the rifapentine trials: it shows the short-course advantage is a rifamycin-class pattern, not one product's accident. With 4 confirmed cases per arm, the trial proves 'not worse within a wide margin,' which is all prevention trials at this event rate can prove.
cards.source: Menzies D et al. Four Months of Rifampin or Nine Months of Isoniazid for Latent Tuberculosis in Adults. N Engl J Med. 2018;379(5):440-453. PMID 30067931 · NCT00931736.

cards.headline: Reading the latent-TB regimen trials together
cards.summary: Three large trials converge: short rifamycin regimens prevent tuberculosis no worse than 9 months of isoniazid — and people actually finish them — LIKELY.
cards.people: People with latent tuberculosis infection: high-risk non-HIV populations (PREVENT TB), people with HIV (BRIEF TB), and adults across nine countries (Menzies).
cards.result: The fence: three large randomized trials converge — short rifamycin regimens prevent active tuberculosis no worse than 9 months of isoniazid (absolute event rates 0.19–2% depending on population risk), are finished far more often (+7 to +15 percentage points completion), and injure fewer livers. The residual uncertainties are structural: open-label designs, noninferiority margins wide relative to rare events, and (in PREVENT TB) directly observed vs self-administered delivery bundled with duration. None of the three shows superiority for preventing tuberculosis; the win is completion and safety at equal protection. Trials that could extend the shelf — 1-month regimens in non-HIV populations — are appearing (PMID 38996972, 2024) and are noted in the currency sweep.
cards.watchOut: Nine months of isoniazid was never beaten on efficacy in these trials — it was matched by regimens people complete. Where completion support for isoniazid is strong, the practical gap narrows; where it is weak, the short regimens' advantage is the point.
cards.source: Synthesis of PMID 22150035 (PREVENT TB/Sterling 2011), PMID 30865794 (BRIEF TB/Swindells 2019), and PMID 30067931 (Menzies 2018), all carded on this shelf.

shelves.title: Cambodia’s CAMELIA trial: ART at 2 weeks, not 8, in HIV with tuberculosis — deaths 18% vs 27% (country 42)
shelves.question: In adults with HIV and newly diagnosed tuberculosis and CD4 counts of 200 or lower, does starting ART at 2 weeks rather than 8 weeks after TB treatment improve survival?
shelves.mesh: AIDS-Related Opportunistic Infections · Anti-Retroviral Agents · Antitubercular Agents · CD4 Lymphocyte Count · HIV Infections · Humans · Tuberculosis · Viral Load
shelves.balance: One Cambodian trial, a mortality primary endpoint, and a result with no ambiguity of direction: deferring ART from week 2 to week 8 of TB treatment cost roughly one life in eleven among profoundly immunosuppressed patients (deaths 18% vs 27%; HR 0.62 [0.44–0.86]). The cost side is on the same record — TB-IRIS at 2.51 times the hazard with the early start — and the survival benefit survived it. Cambodia is a not-yet-covered country, so the country exception applies; LIKELY, not the top tier, because a single trial with a stavudine-era regimen and a median CD4 of 25 cannot price other strata. Proposed stamp LIKELY — proposed, pending the developer’s review.

cards.headline: CAMELIA trial (Blanc 2011, NEJM): starting ART at 2 weeks rather than 8 in HIV with tuberculosis cut deaths from 27% to 18%
cards.summary: 661 adults with newly diagnosed smear-positive tuberculosis and CD4 counts ≤200 (median just 25 ) at five hospitals in Cambodia, randomised to start ART (stavudine, lamivudine, efavirenz) at 2 weeks or 8 weeks after starting standard 6-month TB therapy. Median follow-up 25 months. Deaths: 59 of 332 (18%) early vs 90 of 329 (27%) later — HR 0.62 [0.44–0.86], P=0.006 , a 38% relative reduction (9 percentage points absolute). The price: tuberculosis-associated immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS) was significantly more frequent with earlier ART ( HR 2.51 [1.78–3.59] ). By week 50, viral load was undetectable in 96.5% of patients in both groups.
cards.type: Prospective, randomised, open-label superiority trial, N Engl J Med 2011. Registry ID from the record’s own databank: NCT01300481.
cards.people: 661 ART-naive adults in Cambodia (two hospitals in Phnom Penh, three provincial) with newly diagnosed smear-positive tuberculosis and CD4+ counts ≤200 per cubic millimeter; the median CD4 count was 25 and median viral load 5.64 log10 copies/mL — a profoundly immunosuppressed cohort. The record’s abstract does not print a mean age or sex mix, so none is stated here.
cards.result: The risk of death was significantly reduced with earlier ART: 59 deaths among 332 patients (18%) in the earlier group vs 90 among 329 (27%) in the later group (hazard ratio 0.62; 95% CI, 0.44 to 0.86; P=0.006). TB-associated IRIS was significantly increased in the earlier group (hazard ratio 2.51; 95% CI, 1.78 to 3.59; P<0.001). Irrespective of group, the median gain in CD4 count was 114 per cubic millimeter, and viral load was undetectable at week 50 in 96.5% of patients. The authors concluded that initiating ART 2 weeks after starting TB treatment significantly improved survival in adults with CD4 counts of 200 or lower.
cards.watchOut: The fence is the CD4 count: CAMELIA’s median was 25 — this is a verdict about the sickest stratum, the patients for whom waiting is deadliest. It does not by itself set the start time for a patient with a CD4 of 350, and its ART regimen (stavudine-based) belongs to its era; modern integrase-based therapy changes the side-effect ledger, not the timing question’s shape. Open-label design is the other caution — though the endpoint, death, is the one least bendable by knowing the assignment.

cards.headline: The trade CAMELIA priced: earlier ART bought survival with IRIS — 2.5 times the inflammatory syndrome, in the patients least able to shrug it off
cards.summary: CAMELIA is not a ‘earlier is simply better’ card. Restarting immunity while tuberculosis is still being killed predictably unmasks inflammatory reactions — TB-IRIS struck the early-ART group at 2.51 times the hazard [1.78–3.59]. In this cohort the trade was worth it: the IRIS excess did not translate into a mortality penalty — the group with more IRIS still buried fewer patients (18% vs 27%). But the card’s lesson travels with that arithmetic attached: the setting must be able to recognise and manage IRIS, because the sicker the patients (median CD4 25), the more of both effects — benefit and inflammation — the early start produces.
cards.type: Context card — the trial’s own secondary outcome, from the CAMELIA record (PMID 22010913). No new study.
cards.people: The same 661 Cambodian adults as Card 1: HIV with newly diagnosed tuberculosis, CD4 ≤200 (median 25), randomised to ART at 2 vs 8 weeks of TB therapy.
cards.result: Tuberculosis-associated immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome was significantly more frequent in the earlier-ART group (hazard ratio 2.51; 95% CI, 1.78 to 3.59; P<0.001), while mortality — the primary endpoint — was significantly lower in the same group (HR 0.62). CD4 recovery and viral suppression by week 50 were essentially identical between groups (median gain 114 cells; 96.5% undetectable), so the survival difference was made in the early weeks, not by better long-term HIV control.
cards.watchOut: A reader who takes only ‘start at 2 weeks’ from this shelf, into a setting without IRIS recognition or steroid access, has taken the benefit’s instruction and left its conditions behind. The trial ran in hospitals that could watch for the syndrome they were provoking; the grade belongs to that pairing of intervention and surveillance.
cards.source: Context from the CAMELIA record (PMID 22010913): TB-IRIS hazard ratio and week-50 virological outcomes.

cards.headline: Reading CAMELIA alone: one Cambodian trial, a hard endpoint, and the anchor under the two-week rule
cards.summary: Cambodia enters this library the same way Zambia did: one single-country randomised trial, mortality as the primary endpoint, an effect too large to be a mirage ( HR 0.62 [0.44–0.86] , 149 deaths), conducted in the exact population the clinical question is about. CAMELIA’s result became the anchor trial behind the WHO guidance to start ART within two weeks of TB treatment when CD4 counts are very low. Under the developer’s country exception the shelf cards on this one trial; the grade is LIKELY rather than the top tier because one trial, however clean, is one trial — and because its regimen and its median CD4 of 25 fence how far the number travels.
cards.type: Synthesis card — no new study. This card reads Cards 1 and 2 together and states the fence.
cards.people: The population of Cards 1 and 2: 661 ART-naive adults with HIV and smear-positive tuberculosis at five Cambodian hospitals, CD4 ≤200 (median 25), followed a median of 25 months.
cards.result: The trial establishes that, in profoundly immunosuppressed HIV/TB co-infection, six weeks of ART delay cost lives: roughly one extra death for every eleven patients whose start was deferred from week 2 to week 8 (27% vs 18%). It also establishes the cost of the rescue — more than double the IRIS. Questions it does not answer: timing at higher CD4 counts, timing with modern integrase regimens, and timing in TB meningitis, where the inflammatory risk is of a different order and other trials govern.
cards.watchOut: Cite this shelf for the question it answered — profound immunosuppression, ordinary pulmonary TB, 2 vs 8 weeks — and not as a universal ‘earlier is always better’ licence: the same biology that saved lives here is the reason other co-infection settings deliberately wait.
cards.source: Synthesis of Cards 1–2 on this shelf (PMID 22010913; NCT01300481).

shelves.title: COVID-19 mRNA vaccines: the pivotal efficacy trials
shelves.question: Did the BNT162b2 and mRNA-1273 vaccines prevent symptomatic and severe COVID-19 in their pivotal trials?
shelves.mesh: BNT162 Vaccine · COVID-19/immunology/prevention & control · COVID-19 Vaccines/administration & dosage/adverse effects/immunology · Fatigue/etiology · Headache/etiology · Immunization, Secondary · SARS-CoV-2/genetics
shelves.balance: LIKELY — proposed pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C, slow lane): In their pivotal placebo-controlled trials, two doses of BNT162b2 were 95% effective in relative terms against symptomatic COVID-19 (8 cases among 21,720 vaccine recipients, 0.04%, versus 162 among 21,728 placebo recipients, 0.75%) and two doses of mRNA-1273 were 94.1% effective in relative terms (11 cases among 15,210 vaccine recipients, 0.07%, versus 185 among 15,210 placebo recipients, 1.22%). Severe disease was uncommon and mostly in placebo groups (BNT162b2: 9 of 10 severe cases on placebo; mRNA-1273: all 30 severe cases on placebo, with the trial's one fatality in the placebo group) — the trials prove prevention of symptomatic and severe illness, not a measured reduction in death, for which events were too few. This shelf cards vaccine efficacy only; COVID-19 treatment trials live on their own shelves (#185 dexamethasone, #522 baricitinib). Tier C — built Nov 8, 2026 and held for the developer’s personal verdict; no approval stamp is claimed for this shelf.

cards.headline: BNT162b2 was 95% effective in relative terms against symptomatic COVID-19 (0.04% versus 0.75%)
cards.summary: BNT162b2: 8 vs 162 cases — 95% relative efficacy against symptomatic COVID-19, at absolute rates of about 0.04% vs 0.75% ; 9 of 10 severe cases were on placebo.
cards.people: 43,548 participants aged 16 years or older underwent randomisation; 43,448 received injections (21,720 BNT162b2 and 21,728 placebo). The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: There were 8 cases of COVID-19 with onset at least 7 days after the second dose among BNT162b2 recipients and 162 cases among placebo recipients; BNT162b2 was 95% effective in preventing COVID-19 in relative terms (95% credible interval, 90.3 to 97.6), corresponding to absolute rates of about 0.04% (8/21,720) versus 0.75% (162/21,728) over the trial follow-up. Similar vaccine efficacy (generally 90 to 100%) was observed across subgroups defined by age, sex, race, ethnicity, baseline body-mass index, and coexisting conditions. Among 10 cases of severe COVID-19 with onset after the first dose, 9 occurred in placebo recipients and 1 in a BNT162b2 recipient. Short-term mild-to-moderate pain at the injection site, fatigue, and headache characterised the safety profile, and serious adverse events were low and similar in both groups.
cards.watchOut: Severe cases numbered only 10 and the abstract reports no deaths, so this trial does not by itself measure a mortality benefit; follow-up for safety was a median of 2 months, in a pre-variant, largely infection-naive population.
cards.source: Polack FP et al. Safety and Efficacy of the BNT162b2 mRNA Covid-19 Vaccine. N Engl J Med. 2020 Dec 31;383(27):2603-2615. PMID: 33301246. Registry ID: NCT04368728 (ClinicalTrials.gov, from the record's databank fields).

cards.headline: mRNA-1273 was 94.1% effective in relative terms against symptomatic COVID-19 (0.07% versus 1.22%); all 30 severe cases were on placebo
cards.summary: mRNA-1273: 11 vs 185 cases — 94.1% relative efficacy (3.3 vs 56.5 per 1,000 person-years); all 30 severe cases occurred on placebo .
cards.people: 30,420 volunteers at high risk for SARS-CoV-2 infection or its complications, randomised 1:1 (15,210 mRNA-1273 and 15,210 placebo) at 99 centres in the United States; 2.2% had evidence of SARS-CoV-2 infection at baseline. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Symptomatic COVID-19 was confirmed in 11 participants in the mRNA-1273 group (3.3 per 1000 person-years) and 185 in the placebo group (56.5 per 1000 person-years); vaccine efficacy was 94.1% in relative terms (95% CI, 89.3 to 96.8; P<0.001), corresponding to absolute rates of about 0.07% (11/15,210) versus 1.22% (185/15,210). Efficacy was similar in participants 65 years of age or older and in other key secondary analyses. Severe COVID-19 occurred in 30 participants, with one fatality; all 30 were in the placebo group. Moderate, transient reactogenicity was more frequent in the mRNA-1273 group; serious adverse events were rare and similar in the two groups.
cards.watchOut: Only one death occurred in the whole trial (in the placebo group), so no mortality rate or mortality benefit can be calculated from this record; efficacy is against symptomatic illness, with severe disease a secondary, low-event outcome.
cards.source: Baden LR et al. Efficacy and Safety of the mRNA-1273 SARS-CoV-2 Vaccine. N Engl J Med. 2021 Feb 4;384(5):403-416. PMID: 33378609. Registry ID: NCT04470427 (ClinicalTrials.gov, from the record's databank fields).

cards.summary: Both mRNA vaccines prevented symptomatic COVID-19 at ~94–95% relative efficacy with absolute rates under 1.3% — efficacy only; Tier C, proposed LIKELY.

shelves.title: Insecticide-treated bed nets for malaria prevention
shelves.question: Do insecticide-treated nets reduce malaria illness and child death where malaria is endemic?
shelves.mesh: Insecticide Resistance · Insecticide-Treated Bednets · Malaria/mortality/prevention & control · Malaria, Falciparum/mortality/prevention & control · Malaria, Vivax/mortality/prevention & control · Mosquito Control/methods · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic
shelves.balance: LIKELY — proposed pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C, slow lane): Across 23 randomised trials enrolling more than 275,793 adults and children, insecticide-treated nets reduced child mortality from all causes versus no nets by 17% in relative terms (rate ratio 0.83, 95% CI 0.77 to 0.89; 5 trials, 200,833 participants, high-certainty evidence) — an absolute saving of 5.6 lives (95% CI 3.6 to 7.6) each year for every 1,000 children protected. The mortality figure printed here is all-cause mortality, as the standing rule requires. Nets also reduced uncomplicated Plasmodium falciparum episodes by almost a half in relative terms (rate ratio 0.55) and severe malaria episodes by 44% in relative terms (rate ratio 0.56). The trials were conducted between 1987 and 2001, before widespread pyrethroid resistance — the review judged the resistance data insufficient to downgrade the mortality evidence, but present-day effect sizes may differ. Tier C — built Nov 8, 2026 and held for the developer’s personal verdict; no approval stamp is claimed for this shelf.

cards.headline: Insecticide-treated nets reduced all-cause child mortality by 17% in relative terms — 5.6 lives saved per 1,000 children per year
cards.summary: Cochrane (23 trials, >275,000 participants): insecticide-treated nets cut all-cause child mortality by 17% in relative terms (rate ratio 0.83 [0.77 to 0.89]) — 5.6 lives saved per 1,000 children per year .
cards.type: Cochrane systematic review of randomised controlled trials
cards.people: 23 trials met the inclusion criteria, enrolling more than 275,793 adults and children; the included studies were conducted between 1987 and 2001. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Versus no nets, insecticide-treated nets reduced child mortality from all causes by 17% in relative terms (rate ratio 0.83, 95% CI 0.77 to 0.89; 5 trials, 200,833 participants, high-certainty evidence), corresponding to a saving of 5.6 lives (95% CI 3.6 to 7.6) each year for every 1,000 children protected. Nets reduced the incidence of uncomplicated P. falciparum malaria episodes by almost a half in relative terms (rate ratio 0.55, 95% CI 0.48 to 0.64; 5 trials, 35,551 participants, high-certainty evidence) and probably reduced uncomplicated P. vivax episodes (risk ratio 0.61, 95% CI 0.48 to 0.77; moderate-certainty evidence). Severe malaria episodes fell by 44% in relative terms (rate ratio 0.56, 95% CI 0.38 to 0.82; 2 trials, 31,173 participants, high-certainty evidence), and mean packed cell volume was higher with nets (mean difference 1.29, 95% CI 0.42 to 2.16). Versus untreated nets, nets probably reduced all-cause child mortality by a third in relative terms, but imprecisely (rate ratio 0.67, 95% CI 0.36 to 1.23; 2 trials, 25,389 participants, moderate-certainty evidence), corresponding to 3.5 lives saved per 1,000 children per year with a confidence interval crossing zero (-2.4 to 6.8).
cards.watchOut: All included trials predate widespread pyrethroid resistance (conducted 1987-2001, searched to 18 April 2018); the review found some evidence that resistance affects mosquito mortality but judged it insufficient to downgrade the mortality and illness evidence — present-day absolute benefits may be smaller. The versus-untreated-nets mortality estimate is imprecise and its interval includes no effect.
cards.source: Pryce J et al. Insecticide-treated nets for preventing malaria. Cochrane Database Syst Rev. 2018 Nov 6;11(11):CD000363. PMID: 30398672. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields — this is a systematic review, not a single trial.

shelves.balance: Split — LIKELY in men who have sex with men and transgender women: in the DoxyPEP trial, a bacterial STI was diagnosed at 10.7% of quarterly visits on doxycycline PEP versus 31.9% on standard care in the PrEP cohort (relative risk 0.34) and 11.8% versus 30.5% in the cohort living with HIV (relative risk 0.38), and the earlier IPERGAY substudy also found fewer first STIs (hazard ratio 0.53, a ratio inside the 0.5-2.0 band, carried by its chlamydia and syphilis components). MAYBE (weak evidence) in cisgender women: the Kenyan women's trial found no significant difference (relative risk 0.88, 95% CI 0.60 to 1.29), with doxycycline detected in only 29.0% of hair samples from the treatment group — a null that may reflect low use rather than no biological effect, and is printed as such. Gonorrhoea is the weakest component throughout, and tetracycline resistance is the standing watch-out.

cards.headline: DoxyPEP: STIs at 10.7% versus 31.9% of quarterly visits (PrEP cohort) and 11.8% versus 30.5% (cohort living with HIV)
cards.summary: DoxyPEP trial: an STI at 10.7% vs 31.9% of quarterly visits (PrEP cohort, relative risk 0.34) and 11.8% vs 30.5% (cohort living with HIV, 0.38).
cards.people: 501 participants (327 in the HIV PrEP cohort and 174 in the cohort of persons living with HIV) — men who have sex with men and transgender women who had had gonorrhoea, chlamydia, or syphilis in the past year; 67% were White, 7% Black, 11% Asian or Pacific Islander, and 30% Hispanic or Latino. The abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: In the PrEP cohort, an STI was diagnosed in 61 of 570 quarterly visits (10.7%) in the doxycycline group and 82 of 257 quarterly visits (31.9%) in the standard-care group (absolute difference -21.2 percentage points; relative risk 0.34, 95% CI 0.24 to 0.46; P<0.001). In the cohort living with HIV, an STI was diagnosed in 36 of 305 visits (11.8%) versus 39 of 128 visits (30.5%) (absolute difference -18.7 percentage points; relative risk 0.38, 95% CI 0.24 to 0.60; P<0.001). By infection in the PrEP cohort, relative risks were 0.45 for gonorrhoea, 0.12 for chlamydia, and 0.13 for syphilis. Five grade 3 adverse events and no serious adverse events were attributed to doxycycline. Among participants with gonorrhoea culture available, tetracycline-resistant gonorrhoea occurred in 5 of 13 in the doxycycline groups and 2 of 16 in the standard-care groups.
cards.watchOut: Open-label trial in a selected high-incidence population (recent bacterial STI required); gonorrhoea was reduced least, and the resistance numbers, though small, point the wrong way — population-level antimicrobial resistance is not measured by this trial.
cards.source: Luetkemeyer AF et al. Postexposure Doxycycline to Prevent Bacterial Sexually Transmitted Infections. N Engl J Med. 2023 Apr 6;388(14):1296-1306. PMID: 37018493. Registry ID: NCT03980223 (ClinicalTrials.gov, from the record's databank fields).

cards.headline: IPERGAY substudy: first STI in 22% versus 42% at 9 months on doxycycline PEP — driven by chlamydia and syphilis, not gonorrhoea
cards.summary: IPERGAY substudy: first STI 22% vs 42% at 9 months (hazard ratio 0.53) — driven by chlamydia and syphilis, not gonorrhoea .
cards.people: 232 men aged 18 years or older having condomless sex with men and using HIV PrEP in the ANRS IPERGAY trial in France (116 doxycycline PEP and 116 no PEP), followed for a median of 8.7 months. The abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: 73 participants presented with a new STI during follow-up: 28 in the PEP group (9-month probability 22%, 95% CI 15-32) and 45 in the no-PEP group (42%, 33-53; p=0.007). The hazard ratio for a first STI was 0.53 (95% CI 0.33-0.85; p=0.008) — a ratio inside the 0.5-2.0 band, printed here as supportive rather than solid on its own. First-episode results were stronger for chlamydia (HR 0.30; 95% CI 0.13-0.70) and syphilis (HR 0.27; 0.07-0.98) but did not differ significantly for gonorrhoea (HR 0.83; 0.47-1.47; p=0.52). Participants used a median of 680 mg doxycycline per month; 72 (71%) of all 102 STIs were asymptomatic, no HIV seroconversion was observed, and gastrointestinal adverse events were reported in 62 (53%) on PEP versus 47 (41%) without (p=0.05).
cards.watchOut: Open-label substudy of a PrEP trial, with a single 200 mg dose within 24 hours (DoxyPEP allowed 72 hours); the gonorrhoea component was null here as well.
cards.source: Molina JM et al. Post-exposure prophylaxis with doxycycline to prevent sexually transmitted infections in men who have sex with men: an open-label randomised substudy of the ANRS IPERGAY trial. Lancet Infect Dis. 2018 Mar;18(3):308-317. PMID: 29229440. Registry ID: NCT01473472 (ClinicalTrials.gov, from the record's databank fields — the parent IPERGAY trial registration, as carried on this record).

cards.headline: In Kenyan women on HIV PrEP, doxycycline PEP did not significantly reduce STIs — and hair samples showed it was often not taken
cards.summary: Kenyan women on PrEP: relative risk 0.88 , not significant — and hair samples showed the drug was often not taken.
cards.people: 449 Kenyan women 18 to 30 years of age receiving HIV PrEP (224 doxycycline PEP and 225 standard care), followed quarterly over 12 months.
cards.result: A total of 109 incident STIs occurred (50 in the doxycycline-PEP group, 25.1 per 100 person-years, and 59 in the standard-care group, 29.0 per 100 person-years), with no significant between-group difference (relative risk 0.88, 95% CI 0.60 to 1.29; P=0.51). Chlamydia accounted for 85 of the 109 STIs (35 versus 50; relative risk 0.73, 95% CI 0.47 to 1.13). No serious adverse events were considered related to doxycycline, and there were no incident HIV infections. Among 50 randomly selected participants in the doxycycline-PEP group, doxycycline was detected in only 58 of 200 hair samples (29.0%). All N. gonorrhoeae-positive isolates were resistant to doxycycline.
cards.watchOut: The null cannot be read as proof of no biological effect: objective hair testing showed low use of the assigned prophylaxis, and all gonorrhoea isolates were doxycycline-resistant in this setting. It is equally not evidence of benefit — in women, the claim stays MAYBE (weak evidence).
cards.source: Stewart J et al. Doxycycline Prophylaxis to Prevent Sexually Transmitted Infections in Women. N Engl J Med. 2023 Dec 21;389(25):2331-2340. PMID: 38118022. Registry ID: NCT04050540 (ClinicalTrials.gov, from the record's databank fields).

cards.headline: Synthesis: doxycycline PEP works in the MSM trials (LIKELY) and is unproven in cisgender women (MAYBE (weak evidence))
cards.summary: Works in the MSM and transgender-women trials (LIKELY); unproven in cisgender women (MAYBE (weak evidence)) — split as proposed.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: 501 participants in DoxyPEP, 232 in the IPERGAY substudy, and 449 cisgender women in the Kenyan dPEP trial — all open-label, all in people at high STI incidence, most on HIV PrEP.
cards.result: In men who have sex with men and transgender women, two randomised trials point the same way, with the larger showing STIs at roughly one-third the visit rate on doxycycline PEP (relative risks 0.34 and 0.38 by cohort, beside absolute differences of about -21 and -19 percentage points), strongest for chlamydia and syphilis and weakest for gonorrhoea. In cisgender women the one trial was null (relative risk 0.88, CI 0.60 to 1.29) with objectively low adherence. Hence the split stamp: LIKELY for the MSM/transgender-women population, MAYBE (weak evidence) for cisgender women. HIV PrEP itself is a different question and lives at #317; nothing from that shelf is carded here.
cards.watchOut: All three trials are open-label; none measures the population-level cost in antimicrobial resistance, and gonorrhoea tetracycline/doxycycline resistance signals appear on two of the three cards.
cards.source: Synthesis of Luetkemeyer AF et al. N Engl J Med. 2023;388(14):1296-1306. PMID: 37018493; Molina JM et al. Lancet Infect Dis. 2018;18(3):308-317. PMID: 29229440; Stewart J et al. N Engl J Med. 2023;389(25):2331-2340. PMID: 38118022. Registry IDs as on the individual cards.

shelves.title: Screening for oral cancer by visual inspection (the Kerala trial)
shelves.question: Does repeated visual inspection of the mouth by trained health workers reduce oral-cancer mortality in a high-risk (tobacco/alcohol-using) population — the Kerala cluster-randomised trial and its 15-year follow-up?
shelves.mesh: Alcohol Drinking · Areca · Cluster Analysis · India/epidemiology · Mass Screening · Mastication · Mouth Neoplasms/diagnosis,mortality
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C: this shelf carries an oral-cancer mortality claim from a single cluster-randomised trial). The Kerala trial (13 clusters, ~192,000 eligible adults aged 35+) found oral-cancer mortality was not significantly lower overall with three rounds of visual inspection (mortality rate ratio 0.79 [95% CI 0.51–1.22]); in users of tobacco or alcohol — the high-risk group the programme targets — the ratio was 0.66 (0.45–0.95). At 15 years, after four rounds, the overall relative reduction remained non-significant (12%), while tobacco/alcohol users had a significant 24% relative reduction (95% CI 3–40%). One trial, one country, a significant result only in the high-risk subgroup: POSSIBLE, and Tier C.

cards.headline: Sankaranarayanan 2005: visual oral screening did not significantly reduce oral-cancer mortality overall (rate ratio 0.79), but did in tobacco and alcohol users (0.66)
cards.summary: Kerala trial (2005): visual oral screening did not significantly reduce oral-cancer mortality overall (rate ratio 0.79 ), but did in tobacco and alcohol users.
cards.type: Cluster-randomised controlled trial (13 clusters), three screening rounds, 1996–2004
cards.people: 96,517 eligible participants in the intervention group and 95,356 in the control group — healthy adults aged 35 years and older in 13 clusters in Trivandrum district, Kerala, India; seven clusters were randomised to three rounds of oral visual inspection by trained health workers at 3-year intervals (1996–2004) and six to a control group. 87,655 (91%) of the intervention group were screened at least once; of 5145 screen-positive individuals, 3218 (63%) complied with referral.
cards.result: 205 oral cancer cases and 77 oral cancer deaths were recorded in the intervention group, against 158 cases and 87 deaths in the control group (mortality rate ratio 0.79 [95% CI 0.51–1.22] — a relative figure, not statistically significant). Among users of tobacco or alcohol, 70 oral cancer deaths occurred in the intervention group versus 85 in controls (0.66 [0.45–0.95]); the ratio was 0.57 (0.35–0.93) in male users and 0.78 (0.43–1.42) in female users. The abstract does not print absolute mortality rates.
cards.watchOut: Only 13 clusters, and the headline result is a non-significant overall effect with a significant subgroup: the trial supports screening targeted at tobacco/alcohol users in high-incidence settings — it does not demonstrate a population-wide mortality benefit, and referral compliance was only 63%.
cards.source: Sankaranarayanan R et al. Effect of screening on oral cancer mortality in Kerala, India: a cluster-randomised controlled trial. Lancet. 2005;365(9475):1927-1933. PMID: 15936419. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields — a pre-registration-era trial (1996–2004) whose record carries no databank registration field.

cards.headline: Sankaranarayanan 2013: at 15 years, the mortality reduction remained non-significant overall (12% relative) but was 24% relative in tobacco/alcohol users
cards.summary: Kerala trial at 15 years (2013): the mortality reduction remained non-significant overall (12% relative) but was 24% relative in tobacco and alcohol users.
cards.type: 15-year follow-up report of a cluster-randomized controlled trial
cards.people: The same Kerala trial population over 15 years of follow-up: 96,517 eligible subjects in the intervention arm (25,144 [26.1%] had one screening round, 22,382 [23.2%] two, 22,008 [22.8%] three, 19,288 [20.0%] four) and 95,356 in the control arm, of whom 43,992 (46.1%) received one round of screening during 2006–2009 after the control period ended.
cards.result: The 12% relative reduction in oral cancer mortality in all individuals did not reach statistical significance. In users of tobacco and/or alcohol there was a 24% relative reduction in oral cancer mortality (95% CI 3–40%) after four rounds of screening. Among tobacco/alcohol users adhering to four screening rounds, there was a 38% relative reduction in oral cancer incidence (95% CI 8–59%) and an 81% relative reduction in oral cancer mortality (95% CI 69–89%) — the adherence figures are per-protocol-style comparisons of compliers, not randomised comparisons, and the abstract prints no absolute rates for any of these endpoints.
cards.watchOut: Pinned at build as the topic file's long-term follow-up report. The control group itself was screened once in 2006–2009, diluting later contrasts, and the largest figures (81% relative mortality reduction) describe the self-selected minority who attended all four rounds — the weakest form of evidence on this shelf, printed here with that label attached.
cards.source: Sankaranarayanan R et al. Long term effect of visual screening on oral cancer incidence and mortality in a randomized trial in Kerala, India. Oral Oncol. 2013;49(4):314-321. PMID: 23265945. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields — a follow-up report of the pre-registration-era Kerala trial.

cards.headline: Synthesis: the only oral-cancer screening trial points to benefit concentrated in high-risk users — POSSIBLE, Tier C
cards.summary: The only oral-cancer screening trial points to benefit concentrated in high-risk users — POSSIBLE, Tier C, proposed only.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: the Kerala cluster trial (13 clusters, ~192,000 eligible adults) and its 15-year follow-up — one trial programme, counted once as evidence.
cards.result: Across both reports the pattern is consistent: no significant overall mortality reduction (rate ratio 0.79; later 12% relative, non-significant), and a significant reduction among tobacco/alcohol users (0.66; later 24% relative [3–40%]). This is a mortality claim resting on a single cluster trial with a subgroup-driven result — precisely the combination this library sends to the developer personally. The stamp is therefore PROPOSED at POSSIBLE, pending the developer's verdict. Other cancer-screening shelves (#158, #164, #212–#215) cover different organs and tests and are not re-carded here.
cards.watchOut: Kerala has among the world's highest oral-cancer incidence, driven by chewing tobacco and alcohol: exporting this programme's economics or yields to low-incidence populations is not supported by anything on this shelf.
cards.source: Synthesis of Sankaranarayanan R et al. Lancet. 2005;365(9475):1927-1933. PMID: 15936419; Sankaranarayanan R et al. Oral Oncol. 2013;49(4):314-321. PMID: 23265945. Registry IDs as on the individual cards.

shelves.title: Text-message support for smoking cessation: txt2stop and Text2Quit
shelves.question: Do automated text-message programmes double quit rates versus control messages — txt2stop in the UK, Text2Quit in the US?
shelves.mesh: Behavior Therapy · Cell Phone · Educational Status · Employment · Motivation · Smoking Cessation/methods · Saliva/chemistry
shelves.balance: LIKELY: Two randomised trials on two continents found automated text-message programmes roughly doubled biochemically verified quit rates at 6 months. txt2stop (UK, 5800 smokers): continuous abstinence 10.7% versus 4.9% (relative risk 2.20). Text2Quit (US, 503 smokers recruited online): repeated point-prevalence abstinence 11.1% versus 5.0% (relative risk 2.22). The relative doubling is real; the absolute quit rates (~11% vs ~5%) are the figures to quote — most smokers in both arms were still smoking at 6 months.

cards.headline: txt2stop 2011: text-message support doubled biochemically verified continuous abstinence at 6 months (10.7% vs 4.9%)
cards.summary: txt2stop (2011): text-message support doubled biochemically verified continuous abstinence at 6 months ( 10.7% vs 4.9% ; relative risk 2.20).
cards.people: 5800 smokers willing to make a quit attempt in the UK, randomly allocated to the txt2stop automated text programme (2915) — motivational messages and behavioural-change support — or control texts unrelated to quitting (2885); primary outcome data were available for 5524 (95%); the abstract does not state mean age or the sex mix.
cards.result: Biochemically verified self-reported continuous abstinence at 6 months was 10.7% on txt2stop versus 4.9% on control (relative risk 2.20 [95% CI 1.80–2.68]; p<0.0001 — a relative figure, with the absolute rates beside it). Results were similar when participants lost to follow-up were treated as smokers (268 [9%] of 2911 vs 124 [4%] of 2881; relative risk 2.14 [1.74–2.63]) and when they were excluded (2.20 [1.79–2.71]). No significant heterogeneity appeared in any prespecified subgroup.
cards.watchOut: Control participants received unrelated texts, so the comparison isolates message content rather than attention — a strength — but 2011-era texting habits and quit-service context date the absolute rates, if not the relative effect.
cards.source: Free C et al. Smoking cessation support delivered via mobile phone text messaging (txt2stop): a single-blind, randomised trial. Lancet. 2011;378(9785):49-55. PMID: 21722952. Registry ID: ISRCTN80978588, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: Text2Quit 2014: the US text programme also doubled verified abstinence (11.1% vs 5.0%), in 503 internet-recruited smokers
cards.summary: Text2Quit (2014): the US text programme also doubled verified abstinence ( 11.1% vs 5.0% ).
cards.type: Randomized trial with 6-month follow-up, intention-to-treat with losses counted as smokers
cards.people: 503 US smokers recruited on the internet and randomized to the automated, personalised, interactive Text2Quit programme or self-help material, surveyed at 1, 3 and 6 months (2011–2013), with saliva samples collected from those reporting 7-day abstinence at 6 months; the abstract does not state mean age or the sex mix.
cards.result: Biochemically confirmed repeated point-prevalence abstinence favoured the intervention: 11.1% abstinent versus 5.0% of controls (relative risk 2.22 [95% CI 1.16–4.26]; p<0.05 — a relative figure, with absolute rates beside it). Self-reported repeated point-prevalence abstinence was 19.9% versus 10.0% (p<0.01). Effects were uniform across the demographic subgroups analysed, with a suggestion of a larger effect for non-whites than whites.
cards.watchOut: Ten times smaller than txt2stop, with a correspondingly wide interval (1.16–4.26): Text2Quit confirms direction and rough size in a US online population; it cannot refine the estimate.

cards.headline: Synthesis: automated texts double quit rates — from about 1 in 20 to about 1 in 9 or 10 — LIKELY
cards.summary: Automated texts double quit rates — from about 1 in 20 to about 1 in 9 or 10 — LIKELY.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: txt2stop (5800 UK smokers) and Text2Quit (503 US smokers).
cards.result: Two independent programmes, two health systems, near-identical results: relative risks of 2.20 and 2.22 on biochemically verified abstinence at 6 months, on absolute rates of 10.7% vs 4.9% and 11.1% vs 5.0%. That replication is what carries LIKELY. Text programmes for cardiometabolic adherence and risk-factor nudges live on Shelf #439 and e-cigarettes for cessation are drafted as Shelf #531; neither is re-carded here.
cards.watchOut: Both trials predate widespread smartphone-app cessation products and modern nicotine vaping: the shelf supports automated texting as a cheap adjunct, and says nothing about app-based or vaping-based quitting.
