shelves.title: Financial incentives for smoking cessation in the general population
shelves.question: Do employer-offered financial incentives raise long-term quit rates — alone against information (Volpp), and combined with workplace group training in a European cluster trial (van den Brand)?
shelves.mesh: Health Promotion/economics · Motivation · Occupational Health · Smoking Cessation/economics,methods,statistics & numerical data · United States · Group Processes · Netherlands
shelves.balance: LIKELY: Two randomised trials in working populations found financial incentives roughly tripled long-term quit rates. Volpp 2009 (878 employees of one US multinational; up to $750 in staged incentives): cessation at 9–12 months was 14.7% versus 5.0% on information alone, and the advantage persisted at 15–18 months (9.4% vs 3.6%) after the money stopped. Van den Brand 2018 (61 Dutch companies, 604 smokers): adding up to €350 in vouchers to workplace group training raised 12-month continuous abstinence to 41% versus 26% (adjusted odds ratio 1.93 — inside the 0.5–2.0 caution band on its own, but printed beside absolute rates and consistent with Volpp). The claim is about quitting while incentives run and shortly after; neither trial shows lifetime abstinence.

cards.summary: Incentives trial (2009): staged financial incentives tripled quit rates ( 14.7% vs 5.0% ), and the gap persisted after payments ended (9.4% vs 3.6%).
cards.type: Randomized, controlled trial in employees of a single multinational company
cards.people: 878 employees of a US-based multinational company who smoked, randomly assigned to information about smoking-cessation programmes (442) or information plus financial incentives (436): $100 for completing a cessation programme, $250 for biochemically confirmed cessation within 6 months, and $400 for confirmed abstinence for a further 6 months; the abstract does not state mean age or the sex mix.
cards.result: The incentive group had significantly higher cessation 9 or 12 months after enrollment (14.7% vs 5.0%, P<0.001) and 15 or 18 months after enrollment (9.4% vs 3.6%, P<0.001) — after the final payments. Incentive participants also enrolled in a cessation programme more often (15.4% vs 5.4%, P<0.001), completed one more often (10.8% vs 2.5%, P<0.001), and quit within the first 6 months more often (20.9% vs 11.8%, P<0.001).
cards.watchOut: One employer, a self-selected workforce of smokers who enrolled in a study, and an information-only control with a low 5.0% quit rate: the tripling is against a weak baseline offer, and most incentive-group participants (85.3%) still had not quit at the primary endpoint.

shelves.title: Single-dose HPV vaccination: KEN SHE, DoRIS and ESCUDDO
shelves.question: Is one dose of HPV vaccine enough — the KEN SHE randomised efficacy trial in Kenyan women, the DoRIS immunobridging trial in Tanzanian girls, and the ESCUDDO one-versus-two-dose noninferiority trial?
shelves.mesh: Human papillomavirus 16 · Human papillomavirus 18 · Kenya/epidemiology · Papillomaviridae · Papillomavirus Infections/prevention & control · Papillomavirus Vaccines/adverse effects · Persistent Infection
shelves.balance: LIKELY: Three randomised data sets now support one dose. KEN SHE (2275 Kenyan women aged 15–20) found single-dose vaccine efficacy against persistent HPV16/18 infection of 97.5% (bivalent) and 98.8% (nonavalent) at 3 years. DoRIS immunobridging showed antibody responses in girls aged 9–14 — the actual target age — were non-inferior to those in the KEN SHE women in whom efficacy was proven. And the ESCUDDO trial (20,330 girls aged 12–16), found by this shelf's currency sweep, showed one dose was noninferior to two doses against HPV16/18 infection for both vaccines, with vaccine effectiveness of at least 97% in every group. What one dose has not yet shown in a trial is prevention of cervical cancer itself — that endpoint belongs to the multi-dose registry evidence on Shelves #216 and #446.

cards.headline: KEN SHE 2023: a single HPV vaccine dose was 97.5–98.8% efficacious against persistent HPV16/18 infection at 3 years
cards.summary: KEN SHE (2023): a single HPV vaccine dose was 97.5–98.8% efficacious against persistent HPV16/18 infection at 3 years.
cards.type: Multicentre, randomised, double-blind, controlled trial, 3-year results
cards.people: 2275 healthy Kenyan women aged 15–20 years, randomly assigned to a single dose of bivalent vaccine (760), nonavalent vaccine (758) or control vaccine (757); the primary outcome was incident persistent vaccine-type cervical HPV infection in the modified intention-to-treat cohorts.
cards.result: In the HPV16/18 cohort, 75 incident persistent infections were detected: 2 in the bivalent group, 1 in the nonavalent group and 72 in the control group. Vaccine efficacy was 97.5% (95% CI 90.0–99.4%, P < 0.0001) for the bivalent vaccine and 98.8% (91.3–99.8%, P < 0.0001) for the nonavalent vaccine. In the HPV16/18/31/33/45/52/58 cohort, 89 persistent infections were detected (5 nonavalent, 84 control); nonavalent efficacy was 95.5% (89.0–98.2%, P < 0.0001). There were no vaccine-related severe adverse events.
cards.watchOut: The endpoint is persistent infection, a validated surrogate — not precancer or cancer — and follow-up is 3 years in women vaccinated at 15–20, older than the routine target age; durability beyond 3 years in this trial is still being accrued.
cards.source: Barnabas RV et al. Durability of single-dose HPV vaccination in young Kenyan women: randomized controlled trial 3-year results. Nat Med. 2023;29(12):3224-3232. PMID: 38049621. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03675256, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: DoRIS/KEN SHE immunobridging 2024: one dose in girls aged 9–14 produced antibody responses non-inferior to one dose in the women KEN SHE proved efficacy in
cards.summary: DoRIS/KEN SHE immunobridging (2024): one dose in girls aged 9–14 produced antibody responses non-inferior to one dose in the women KEN SHE proved efficacy in.
cards.type: Immunobridging analysis of two randomised controlled trials (DoRIS and KEN SHE), month 24
cards.people: 930 girls aged 9–14 years in Tanzania (DoRIS), randomly assigned to one, two or three doses of the 2-valent or 9-valent vaccine, whose month-24 antibody responses after one dose were compared with those of women aged 15–20 years randomly assigned to one dose of the same vaccines in KEN SHE; samples were batch-tested together by ELISA. (The record's first author is Baisley; the topic file's 'Watson-Jones' is the programme's senior author.)
cards.result: Month-24 HPV16 and HPV18 antibody geometric mean concentrations in DoRIS were similar or higher than in KEN SHE. 2-valent GMC ratios (DoRIS:KEN SHE) were 0.90 (95% CI 0.72–1.14) for HPV16 and 1.02 (0.78–1.33) for HPV18; 9-valent ratios were 1.44 (1.14–1.82) and 1.47 (1.13–1.90). Non-inferiority of antibody GMCs and seropositivity was met for HPV16 and HPV18 for both vaccines. The predefined non-inferiority criterion was a lower 95% CI bound above 0.50 for the GMC ratio.
cards.watchOut: Immunobridging infers efficacy in 9–14-year-olds from antibody levels: it is only as strong as the assumption — supported, but an assumption — that the antibody response is the mechanism of the protection KEN SHE measured.
cards.source: Baisley K et al. Comparing one dose of HPV vaccine in girls aged 9-14 years in Tanzania (DoRIS) with one dose in young women aged 15-20 years in Kenya (KEN SHE): an immunobridging analysis of randomised controlled trials. Lancet Glob Health. 2024;12(3):e491-e499. PMID: 38365419. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields — this is an immunobridging analysis of two trials and its record carries no databank registration field.

cards.headline: ESCUDDO 2025: in 20,330 girls, one dose was noninferior to two doses against HPV16/18 infection for both vaccines
cards.summary: ESCUDDO (2025): in 20,330 girls, one dose was noninferior to two doses against HPV16/18 infection for both vaccines.
cards.type: Randomised noninferiority trial (ESCUDDO), four arms, with a nonrandomised survey comparison for effectiveness
cards.people: 20,330 girls aged 12 to 16 years, randomly assigned in a 1:1:1:1 ratio to one or two doses of a bivalent HPV vaccine or one or two doses of a nonavalent HPV vaccine; the primary endpoint was new HPV16 or HPV18 infection occurring from month 12 to month 60 and persisting at least 6 months; a further 3005 unvaccinated participants were enrolled in a nonrandomised survey comparison.
cards.result: One dose was noninferior to two doses in preventing HPV16 or HPV18 infection: the rate difference between one and two doses was −0.13 infections per 100 participants (95% CI, −0.45 to 0.15; P<0.001 for noninferiority) for the bivalent vaccine and 0.21 per 100 (−0.09 to 0.51; P<0.001 for noninferiority) for the nonavalent vaccine, against a prespecified noninferiority margin of 1.25 per 100. Vaccine effectiveness versus the survey comparison was at least 97% in each of the four trial groups. No safety concerns were identified.
cards.watchOut: Found by this shelf's currency sweep and carded after fetch-verification. Follow-up for the primary endpoint runs to month 60 with the analysis as reported; the ≥97% effectiveness figures rest partly on the nonrandomised survey comparison, while the randomised one-versus-two-dose noninferiority is the trial's own hard result.

cards.headline: Synthesis: one dose is enough against infection — LIKELY; cancer prevention by one dose remains an inference
cards.summary: One dose is enough against infection — LIKELY; cancer prevention by one dose remains an inference.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: KEN SHE (2275 women, efficacy vs control), DoRIS/KEN SHE immunobridging (930 girls, antibody comparison), ESCUDDO (20,330 girls, one vs two doses).
cards.result: The three randomised data sets interlock: efficacy of one dose versus no vaccine (97.5–98.8% against persistent HPV16/18 at 3 years), antibody non-inferiority at the target age of 9–14, and direct randomised noninferiority of one dose versus two in 20,330 girls. That is the evidence chain behind single-dose schedules. Five-year DoRIS extension data (PMID 39890232, found by the sweep and fenced here) show single-dose seropositivity above 99% for HPV16 at month 60, though HPV18 non-inferiority criteria were not met at that horizon — a durability caveat, not a reversal. Multi-dose vaccine efficacy and registry cancer outcomes live on Shelves #216 and #446 and are not re-carded here.
cards.watchOut: No trial anywhere on this shelf has a cervical-cancer endpoint for the single-dose regimen: programmes adopting one dose are betting, on strong surrogate evidence, that infection prevention converts into cancer prevention as it did for multi-dose schedules.
cards.source: Synthesis of Barnabas RV et al. Nat Med. 2023;29(12):3224-3232. PMID: 38049621; Baisley K et al. Lancet Glob Health. 2024;12(3):e491-e499. PMID: 38365419; Kreimer AR et al. N Engl J Med. 2025;393(24):2421-2433. PMID: 41337735. Registry IDs as on the individual cards.

shelves.title: Seasonal malaria chemoprevention in children: combinations and additions
shelves.question: In the Sahel's rainy season, does seasonal malaria chemoprevention still add protection when combined with RTS,S vaccination — and does adding azithromycin to chemoprevention reduce deaths or admissions?
shelves.mesh: Amodiaquine/therapeutic use · Antimalarials/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Burkina Faso/epidemiology · Chemoprevention · Combined Modality Therapy · Drug Combinations · Drug Therapy, Combination
shelves.balance: Split: LIKELY — vaccine + chemoprevention beats either alone · LIKELY — adding azithromycin does not reduce death or admission (the treatment made no difference). PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C: the combination card carries a death-from-malaria benefit claim). Chandramohan 2021 (6861 children in Burkina Faso and Mali): seasonal RTS,S vaccination was noninferior to seasonal chemoprevention for clinical malaria, and the combination cut clinical malaria by a further 62.8% (relative) versus chemoprevention alone, with protective efficacy of 72.9% against death from malaria (95% CI 2.9–92.4 — a very wide interval on few deaths). Chandramohan 2019 (19,578 children): adding azithromycin to chemoprevention did not reduce the primary composite of death or hospital admission (incidence rate ratio 1.1 [0.88–1.3]), although several non-malarial infection outcomes were less frequent. Topic file flagged Tier C: no; this build rules Tier C: YES because the carded 2021 trial carries a mortality benefit claim, which the pack brief sends to the developer — see summary.md.

cards.headline: Chandramohan 2021: vaccine plus chemoprevention beat either alone — 62.8% relative efficacy against clinical malaria, 72.9% against death from malaria (wide interval)
cards.summary: Vaccine plus chemoprevention (2021): beat either alone on clinical malaria (combination incidence 113 vs 305 per 1000 person-years against chemoprevention alone), with a relative efficacy against death from malaria of 72.9% printed beside the trial's absolute rates on the card.
cards.type: Individually randomized, controlled three-arm trial, 3 years
cards.people: 6861 children aged 5 to 17 months in Burkina Faso and Mali, individually randomised to seasonal chemoprevention alone (sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine plus amodiaquine; 2287), seasonal RTS,S/AS01E vaccination alone (2288), or the combination (2286); 1965, 1988 and 1967 children respectively received the first dose and were followed for 3 years.
cards.result: Uncomplicated clinical malaria occurred at 305 events per 1000 person-years in the chemoprevention group, 278 in the vaccine group, and 113 in the combination group. The hazard ratio for vaccination versus chemoprevention was 0.92 (95% CI, 0.84 to 1.01), excluding the prespecified noninferiority margin of 1.20. Protective efficacy of the combination versus chemoprevention alone was 62.8% (58.4 to 66.8) against clinical malaria, 70.5% (41.9 to 85.0) against hospital admission with severe malaria, and 72.9% (2.9 to 92.4) against death from malaria — all relative efficacy figures; the abstract does not print absolute death counts. Versus vaccine alone, combination efficacy was 59.6% (54.7 to 64.0), 70.6% (42.3 to 85.0) and 75.3% (12.5 to 93.0) respectively. Febrile seizure developed in 5 children the day after vaccination; all recovered without sequelae.
cards.watchOut: The malaria-episode results are precise; the death-from-malaria result is not (95% CI 2.9–92.4% efficacy) — it rests on few deaths and is printed here as the trial reported it, paired with the episode data, under a Tier C flag. Efficacy is seasonal and Sahel-specific: transmission intensity and drug resistance elsewhere differ.
cards.source: Chandramohan D et al. Seasonal Malaria Vaccination with or without Seasonal Malaria Chemoprevention. N Engl J Med. 2021;385(11):1005-1017. PMID: 34432975. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03143218, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: Chandramohan 2019: adding azithromycin to chemoprevention did not reduce death or hospital admission (rate ratio 1.1)
cards.summary: Adding azithromycin (2019): did not reduce death or hospital admission (rate ratio 1.1 ).
cards.type: Randomized, placebo-controlled trial (randomisation by household), three transmission seasons
cards.people: 19,578 children aged 3 to 59 months in Burkina Faso and Mali, randomly assigned by household to seasonal chemoprevention (sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine plus amodiaquine) plus azithromycin (9735) or plus placebo (9843), in four 3-day cycles at monthly intervals over three successive seasons; children aged out at 5 years and new children were enrolled each year.
cards.result: The primary endpoint — death or hospital admission for at least 24 hours not due to trauma or elective surgery — occurred 250 times in the azithromycin group and 238 times in the placebo group (24.8 vs 23.5 events per 1000 child-years; incidence rate ratio 1.1 [95% CI, 0.88 to 1.3]); per-protocol results were similar. Some outcomes were less frequent with azithromycin: gastrointestinal infections (1647 vs 1985 episodes; rate ratio 0.85 [0.79 to 0.91]), upper respiratory infections (4893 vs 5763; 0.85 [0.81 to 0.90]) and nonmalarial febrile illnesses (1122 vs 1424; 0.79 [0.73 to 0.87]) — relative figures, all inside or at the edge of the 0.5–2.0 caution band. Malaria parasitaemia prevalence and adverse-event incidence were similar in the two groups.
cards.watchOut: A very large null on the endpoint that motivated the trial (the Ethiopian mass-azithromycin mortality signal): the secondary infection reductions are real but modest, sit in the caution band, and do not rescue the primary claim — mass azithromycin also carries antibiotic-resistance costs this trial was not designed to weigh.
cards.source: Chandramohan D et al. Effect of Adding Azithromycin to Seasonal Malaria Chemoprevention. N Engl J Med. 2019;380(23):2197-2206. PMID: 30699301. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02211729, from the record's databank fields.

cards.summary: Stack the vaccine on chemoprevention; do not stack azithromycin — Split: LIKELY · LIKELY (the treatment made no difference), Tier C.

cards.result: Chemoprevention is the platform both trials build on. shelves.title: Ring vaccination for Ebola: the Guinea Ebola Ça Suffit trial
shelves.question: Does immediate ring vaccination with single-dose rVSV-ZEBOV prevent Ebola virus disease in contacts and contacts-of-contacts versus delayed vaccination?

shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C candidate ruled Tier C at build; a prevention claim against a usually fatal disease, from a single open-label cluster trial conducted inside an epidemic): In the randomised rings, no Ebola cases with onset 10 days or more after randomisation occurred among immediately vaccinated contacts and contacts-of-contacts, vs 16 cases among eligible individuals in delayed-vaccination rings — a vaccine efficacy estimate of 100% (95% CI 68.9 to 100.0; p=0.0045); across all 117 clusters (including non-randomised rings) the estimate was likewise 100% (79.3 to 100.0), with 23 cases in the comparison groups. Of 5,837 vaccinees, 53.9% reported at least one adverse event in 14 days (mostly mild; headache 25.4%, fatigue 18.9%, muscle pain 13.1% of events); 80 serious adverse events included two judged vaccine-related and one possibly related, all recovering. The Liberian PREVAIL I cluster-vaccination experience (650 contacts identified, only 32% consenting) is carded as the implementation companion: the strategy's weak point is uptake, not the point estimate. A single epidemic-era cluster trial caps the stamp at POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: Ebola Ça Suffit 2017 (final): immediate ring vaccination with rVSV-ZEBOV — zero Ebola cases from day 10 in immediate rings vs 16 cases in delayed rings (efficacy 100%, 95% CI 68.9 to 100.0)
cards.summary: Ebola Ça Suffit 2017: immediate ring vaccination — zero cases from day 10 in immediate rings vs 16 cases in delayed rings.
cards.type: Open-label, cluster-randomised ring-vaccination trial conducted during the West African epidemic
cards.people: Contacts and contacts-of-contacts of confirmed Ebola cases in Guinea (Conakry and eight surrounding prefectures) and Sierra Leone (Tonkolili, Bombali): 98 randomised rings — 51 assigned to immediate vaccination (4,539 people enumerated; 3,232 eligible; 2,119 immediately vaccinated) and 47 to vaccination delayed by 21 days (4,557 enumerated; 3,096 eligible; 2,041 vaccinated) — plus 19 non-randomised rings (2,745 enumerated; 1,677 vaccinated, including 194 children); 5,837 people received vaccine in total. Eligible individuals were aged 18 or older and not pregnant, breastfeeding or severely ill (children 6–17 were added after a DSMB recommendation).
cards.result: No cases of Ebola virus disease with onset 10 days or more after randomisation occurred among vaccinated contacts and contacts-of-contacts in immediate rings, vs 16 cases (in 7 clusters) among all eligible individuals in delayed rings: vaccine efficacy 100% (95% CI 68.9 to 100.0; p=0.0045) — a relative measure on a zero-event arm. Across all 117 clusters, no cases occurred among the immediately vaccinated vs 23 cases (11 clusters) among eligible delayed or never-vaccinated individuals (efficacy 100%, 79.3 to 100.0; p=0.0033). Vaccination also protected unvaccinated people within immediate rings. Adverse events within 14 days were reported by 3,149 of 5,837 vaccinees (53.9%), 87.5% of events mild; 80 serious adverse events were identified, two judged related to vaccination (a febrile reaction and anaphylaxis) and one possibly related, all recovering without sequelae.
cards.watchOut: Open-label, epidemic-run, with a delayed-vaccination (21-day) comparator rather than placebo, a zero-event vaccinated arm (so the confidence interval, 68.9 to 100.0, is the honest precision), and randomisation stopped early on DSMB advice: the effect is very unlikely to be zero, but '100%' is a point estimate from 16–23 comparison cases, and the design cannot separate direct protection from ring-level herd effects.
cards.source: Henao-Restrepo AM et al. Efficacy and effectiveness of an rVSV-vectored vaccine in preventing Ebola virus disease: final results from the Guinea ring vaccination, open-label, cluster-randomised trial (Ebola Ça Suffit!). Lancet. 2017;389(10068):505-518. PMID: 28017403. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields — the abstract states Pan African Clinical Trials Registry number PACTR201503001057193.

cards.headline: PREVAIL I cluster vaccination 2019 (Liberia): rVSV-ZEBOV was safe and immunogenic in a real outbreak response — but only 210 of 650 identified contacts (32%) consented
cards.summary: PREVAIL I 2019: safe and immunogenic in a real outbreak response, but only 210 of 650 identified contacts were vaccinated — an implementation companion, no efficacy claim.
cards.type: Single-arm cluster (ring) vaccination study nested in a public-health response, amended from a phase 2 trial protocol
cards.people: 650 close contacts and contacts of close contacts of three Ebola cases in Monrovia, Liberia, in November 2015, identified for ring vaccination with rVSVΔG-ZEBOV-GP; 210 (32%) consented and were vaccinated, with follow-up at 1 and 6 months (189 and 166 attending).
cards.result: No serious adverse events were reported. Among 88 participants without an elevated antibody level at baseline, 77.3% (95% CI 68.5 to 86.1) had an antibody response at 1 month. The authors' emphasis is implementation: fewer than one third of eligible individuals consented, and these data are offered to guide cluster-vaccination programme decisions in small outbreak responses.
cards.watchOut: Not an efficacy study — no comparator and no Ebola cases to prevent in a three-case flare: it is carded as the feasibility companion to the Guinea trial, and its 32% consent figure, not its immunogenicity, is the number programmes should plan around.
cards.source: Bolay FK et al. PREVAIL I Cluster Vaccination Study With rVSVΔG-ZEBOV-GP as Part of a Public Health Response in Liberia. J Infect Dis. 2019;219(10):1634-1641. PMID: 30561672. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields — a response-nested study report.

cards.headline: Synthesis: complete protection in the rings that were vaccinated, in one epidemic trial — POSSIBLE, Tier C
cards.summary: Complete protection in the rings that were vaccinated, in one epidemic trial — POSSIBLE, Tier C, proposed only.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: Ebola Ça Suffit (98 randomised rings, 5,837 vaccinated) and the PREVAIL I Liberian cluster-vaccination experience (210 vaccinated of 650 identified).
cards.result: The Guinea trial's result is as strong as a single trial can look — zero cases from day 10 among the immediately vaccinated, against 16 (randomised comparison) to 23 (all clusters) cases in delayed/never-vaccinated eligibles — and its limits are equally plain: open-label, one epidemic, one vaccine, a 21-day-delay comparator, and an interval that runs from 68.9% to 100%. The Liberian experience adds the operational caveat (32% uptake). Stamp: POSSIBLE, proposed pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C).
cards.watchOut: Do not quote '100% efficacy' without the confidence interval and the ring design; and do not treat the PREVAIL I report as efficacy evidence — it has no comparator.

shelves.title: The VITAL factorial: vitamin D and marine omega-3 for cancer and cardiovascular outcomes
shelves.question: In generally healthy adults, does vitamin D3 (2,000 IU/day), marine omega-3 (1 g/day), both, or neither lower the incidence of invasive cancer or major cardiovascular events (VITAL, n=25,871, two-by-two factorial design)?
shelves.mesh: Cardiovascular Diseases/epidemiology,mortality,prevention & control · Dietary Supplements · Incidence · Neoplasms/epidemiology,mortality,prevention & control · Treatment Failure · Vitamin D/adverse effects,analogs & derivatives,therapeutic use · Vitamins/adverse effects,therapeutic use
shelves.balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C; the outcomes tested are invasive cancer and major cardiovascular events): In VITAL's 25,871 participants (median follow-up 5.3 years), vitamin D did not lower invasive cancer (793 versus 824 cases; hazard ratio 0.96, 95% CI 0.88 to 1.06 — relative) or major cardiovascular events (396 versus 409; HR 0.97, 0.85 to 1.12), and marine omega-3 did not lower major cardiovascular events (386 versus 419; HR 0.92, 0.80 to 1.06) or invasive cancer (820 versus 797; HR 1.03, 0.93 to 1.13). All-cause mortality was also null for both (vitamin D HR 0.99; omega-3 HR 1.02). This is one very large factorial trial answering two intervention questions in one cohort — not two independent trials — and the word 'prevention' appears on this shelf only because it is the trial's own stated question; the answer the trial returned was no. The omega-3 secondary finding of fewer total myocardial infarctions (HR 0.72, 0.59 to 0.90) is a secondary endpoint inside a null-primary trial and is not a benefit claim. Fish oil and atrial fibrillation (a harm question) lives on Shelf #41 and is not re-carded here.

cards.headline: VITAL vitamin D report 2019: 2,000 IU/day did not lower invasive cancer (HR 0.96) or major cardiovascular events (HR 0.97) over 5.3 years
cards.summary: VITAL vitamin D report 2019: 2,000 IU/day did not lower invasive cancer (HR 0.96) or major cardiovascular events (HR 0.97) over 5.3 years.
cards.type: Nationwide, randomised, placebo-controlled, two-by-two factorial trial
cards.people: 25,871 participants (men 50 years or older and women 55 years or older in the United States), including 5,106 Black participants, randomised to vitamin D3 2,000 IU/day and/or marine n-3 fatty acids 1 g/day or placebos, followed for a median of 5.3 years. The abstract does not state mean age or the overall sex mix.
cards.result: Invasive cancer was diagnosed in 1,617 participants (793 vitamin D versus 824 placebo; hazard ratio 0.96, 95% CI 0.88 to 1.06; P=0.47 — a relative measure). A major cardiovascular event (myocardial infarction, stroke, or cardiovascular death) occurred in 805 participants (396 versus 409; HR 0.97, 0.85 to 1.12; P=0.69). Secondary hazard ratios included death from cancer 0.83 (0.67 to 1.02), myocardial infarction 0.96 (0.78 to 1.19), stroke 0.95 (0.76 to 1.20), death from cardiovascular causes 1.11 (0.88 to 1.40), and death from any cause 0.99 (0.87 to 1.12; 978 deaths). No excess risks of hypercalcemia or other adverse events were identified.
cards.watchOut: One factorial trial, not two trials: the vitamin D and omega-3 comparisons share the same cohort. The cancer-death hazard ratio of 0.83 is a secondary endpoint whose confidence interval crosses 1.0 inside a null-primary trial — it is not a mortality benefit, and per Tier C rules it goes to the developer personally. The record names no specific product or brand — products sold today may differ in safety and effectiveness.
cards.source: Manson JE et al. Vitamin D Supplements and Prevention of Cancer and Cardiovascular Disease. N Engl J Med. 2019;380(1):33-44. PMID: 30415629. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT01169259, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: VITAL omega-3 report 2019: 1 g/day marine n-3 did not lower major cardiovascular events (HR 0.92) or invasive cancer (HR 1.03)
cards.summary: VITAL omega-3 report 2019: 1 g/day marine n-3 did not lower major cardiovascular events (HR 0.92) or invasive cancer (HR 1.03).
cards.type: Nationwide, randomised, placebo-controlled, two-by-two factorial trial (same cohort as the vitamin D report)
cards.people: The same 25,871 VITAL participants (men 50 years or older, women 55 years or older; 5,106 Black participants), median follow-up 5.3 years. The abstract does not state mean age or the overall sex mix.
cards.result: A major cardiovascular event occurred in 386 participants in the n-3 group and 419 in the placebo group (hazard ratio 0.92, 95% CI 0.80 to 1.06; P=0.24 — a relative measure). Invasive cancer was diagnosed in 820 (n-3) versus 797 (placebo) participants (HR 1.03, 0.93 to 1.13; P=0.56). Secondary hazard ratios: expanded cardiovascular composite 0.93 (0.82 to 1.04); total myocardial infarction 0.72 (0.59 to 0.90); total stroke 1.04 (0.83 to 1.31); death from cardiovascular causes 0.96 (0.76 to 1.21); death from cancer 0.97 (0.79 to 1.20); death from any cause 1.02 (0.90 to 1.15; 978 deaths overall). No excess risks of bleeding or other serious adverse events were observed.
cards.watchOut: The total-myocardial-infarction hazard ratio of 0.72 is the one secondary signal in this report; with both primary endpoints null and many secondary comparisons, it is hypothesis-generating only and is explicitly not carded as a benefit claim (Tier C). Prescription-dose icosapent ethyl (REDUCE-IT) is a different question, already carded elsewhere, and is not this shelf. The record names no specific product or brand — products sold today may differ in safety and effectiveness.

cards.headline: Synthesis: two supplements, two null primaries, one cohort — LIKELY (the treatment made no difference), Tier C
cards.summary: Two supplements, two null primaries, one cohort — LIKELY the null, Tier C, proposed only. The two secondary signals are NOT carded as benefit claims.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: VITAL (25,871 participants; vitamin D report and omega-3 report are two comparisons within one factorial trial).
cards.result: Neither intervention lowered its primary endpoints: cancer HR 0.96 and cardiovascular events HR 0.97 for vitamin D; cardiovascular events HR 0.92 and cancer HR 1.03 for omega-3 — all relative measures with confidence intervals spanning 1.0, over a median 5.3 years. A single mega-trial of this size and duration may carry LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) under this library's rule for a very large null trial. The stamp is PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict, because the outcomes are cancer and cardiovascular events (Tier C). Ancillary VITAL findings (fractures, atrial fibrillation, autoimmune disease) are separate questions on their own shelves and are not imported here.
cards.watchOut: Do not rescue either supplement with a secondary endpoint: the omega-3/MI and vitamin D/cancer-death signals live inside null primaries and stay labelled as such wherever this shelf is summarised.

shelves.title: A single-shot live-attenuated chikungunya vaccine (VLA1553)
shelves.question: Does one dose of the live-attenuated chikungunya vaccine VLA1553 (IXCHIQ) produce a seroprotective antibody response in healthy adults versus placebo, and how long do antibodies persist?
shelves.mesh: Chikungunya Fever/prevention & control · Vaccines, Attenuated · Antibodies, Viral · Chikungunya virus · Vaccination · Antibodies, Neutralizing/blood,immunology · Antibodies, Viral/blood,immunology
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: The pivotal phase 3 trial (4,128 randomised adults) found seroprotective neutralising antibody levels 28 days after a single dose in 98.9% of vaccinees versus the placebo-defined baseline population, with serious adverse events in 1.5% versus 0.8% and two vaccine-related serious events, both resolving. The durability follow-up pinned at build (a phase 3b single-arm extension of the same programme) found a seroresponse rate of 94.5% at year 4. Every endpoint here is immunogenicity against a regulator-accepted surrogate threshold (μPRNT50 at least 150) — protection against actual chikungunya disease is inferred, never trialled — so the shelf caps at POSSIBLE and says so.

cards.headline: Schneider 2023: a single dose of VLA1553 produced seroprotective antibody levels in 98.9% of adults at day 28
cards.summary: Schneider (2023): one dose of VLA1553 produced seroprotective antibody levels in 98.9% of adults at day 28.
cards.type: Double-blind, multicentre, randomised, placebo-controlled phase 3 trial (43 sites, USA)
cards.people: 4,128 healthy volunteers aged 18 years and older randomised (3:1) to VLA1553 (3,093) or placebo (1,035) between September 2020 and April 2021; the per-protocol immunogenicity population comprised 362 participants (266 vaccine, 96 placebo) at 12 pre-selected sites. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: After a single vaccination, seroprotective chikungunya neutralising antibody levels (μPRNT50 titre at least 150) were induced in 263 (98.9%) of 266 participants in the VLA1553 group (95% CI 96.7 to 99.8; p<0.0001) 28 days post-vaccination, independent of age. Serious adverse events were reported in 46 (1.5%) of 3,082 participants exposed to VLA1553 and 8 (0.8%) of 1,033 in the placebo arm; only two serious adverse events were considered related to VLA1553 (one mild myalgia and one syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion), and both participants recovered fully.
cards.watchOut: An immunogenicity licence: the endpoint is an antibody threshold regulators accepted as reasonably likely to predict benefit because chikungunya outbreaks are unpredictable — no participant was followed for actual disease prevention, and the immunogenicity estimate rests on a 362-person subset of the 4,128 randomised.
cards.source: Schneider M et al. Safety and immunogenicity of a single-shot live-attenuated chikungunya vaccine: a double-blind, multicentre, randomised, placebo-controlled, phase 3 trial. Lancet. 2023 Jun 24;401(10394):2138-2147. PMID: 37321235. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT04546724, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: Sattler 2026: neutralising antibodies persisted above the seroresponse threshold in 94.5% of vaccinees at year 4 (single-arm follow-up of the pivotal programme)
cards.summary: Sattler (2026): neutralising antibodies persisted above the seroresponse threshold in 94.5% at year 4 (single-arm follow-up).
cards.type: Phase 3b, open-label, single-arm long-term follow-up of pivotal-trial vaccinees
cards.people: A subset of 363 VLA1553 vaccinees from the pivotal phase 3 trial entered long-term follow-up; 254 remained at year 4, with slightly more females than males and a predominantly White population without Hispanic or Latino background, as stated in the abstract. The abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: The seroresponse rate at year 4 was 94.5% (240 of 254, 95% CI 90.9% to 97.0%). Geometric mean titres fell from 3,542 at day 29 to 1,056 at year 1, 785 at year 2, 737 at year 3 and 589 at year 4 — remaining considerably above the seroresponse threshold of 150. In adults aged 65 years or older, antibody persistence was similar to younger adults throughout follow-up.
cards.watchOut: Single-arm with attrition (363 entering, 254 remaining at year 4) and no comparator: persistence of a surrogate antibody level is not persistence of proven clinical protection, and survivors who stay in follow-up may not represent all vaccinees.
cards.source: Sattler N et al. Chikungunya virus-neutralizing antibody persistence four years after single-dose vaccination with VLA1553 (IXCHIQ®). Vaccine. 2026 Aug 13;88:128787. PMID: 42250475. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields — a follow-up report of the pivotal programme (NCT04546724 on the parent trial's card).

cards.headline: Synthesis: near-universal seroprotection after one dose, durable to 4 years — against a surrogate, not against disease — POSSIBLE
cards.summary: Synthesis: near-universal seroprotection after one dose, durable to 4 years — against a surrogate, not against disease — POSSIBLE.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: Schneider 2023 (4,128 randomised adults; 362 in the immunogenicity analysis) and Sattler 2026 (254 vaccinees remaining at year 4).
cards.result: The programme shows a strong, age-independent antibody response (98.9% seroprotected at day 28) that decays slowly (94.5% still above threshold at year 4, geometric mean titre 589 against a threshold of 150). The currency sweep found an adolescent phase 3 trial of VLA1553 in endemic Brazil and a phase 3 trial of a virus-like-particle chikungunya vaccine — fenced here, not carded; they extend the field without changing this shelf's adult single-shot question. The dengue (Shelves #448, #981) and yellow fever (#1086) vaccine shelves cover different viruses and are not re-carded here.
cards.watchOut: Live-attenuated vaccine in healthy adults is the tested frame; the abstract-level record says nothing here about use in pregnancy, immunodeficiency, or endemic-population effectiveness.

shelves.title: Single-dose rifampicin post-exposure prophylaxis for leprosy contacts (COLEP)
shelves.question: Does a single dose of rifampicin given to close contacts of newly diagnosed leprosy patients reduce their incidence of leprosy over the following years?
shelves.mesh: Leprostatic Agents/administration & dosage · Leprosy/prevention & control · Rifampin/administration & dosage
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: One large double-blind cluster-randomised trial (COLEP, 21,711 eligible contacts in Bangladesh) found single-dose rifampicin reduced leprosy incidence over the first two years by 57% relative (95% CI 33% to 72%) — in absolute terms 59 of 9,417 contacts (0.63%) versus 91 of 9,452 (0.96%) developed leprosy over four years of follow-up, a number needed to treat of 297 — with no additional difference between years two and four. A single (cluster) trial with a time-limited effect caps at POSSIBLE. This is post-exposure prophylaxis of an infection; no diabetes-onset wording is involved.

cards.headline: COLEP 2008: single-dose rifampicin cut leprosy incidence in close contacts by 57% relative in the first two years (absolute rates 0.63% vs 0.96% over four years; NNT 297)
cards.summary: COLEP (2008): single-dose rifampicin cut leprosy incidence in close contacts by 57% relative in the first two years (absolute rates 0.63% vs 0.96%).
cards.type: Single-centre, double-blind, cluster-randomised, placebo-controlled trial (two districts of northwest Bangladesh)
cards.people: 28,092 close contacts of 1,037 patients with newly diagnosed leprosy, of whom 21,711 fulfilled study requirements; a single dose of rifampicin or placebo was given in the second month after the index patient started treatment, with four years of follow-up; 18,869 contacts (86.9%) were followed up at four years. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Ninety-one of 9,452 contacts in the placebo group and 59 of 9,417 in the rifampicin group developed leprosy. The overall reduction in incidence with single-dose rifampicin in the first two years was 57% relative (95% CI 33% to 72%). The groups did not differ between two and four years. The overall number needed to treat to prevent a single case of leprosy among contacts was 297 (95% CI 176 to 537), with subgroup differences in both incidence reduction and NNT at two years.
cards.watchOut: Cluster randomisation around index patients in one country's programme, an effect confined to the first two years, and a low absolute event rate (about 1% of contacts) — the intervention prevents roughly one case per 300 contacts treated, which is a programme decision, not an individual guarantee.

shelves.title: Fractional-dose yellow fever vaccination: one-fifth of a dose, the same antibodies?
shelves.question: Do fractional (one-fifth) doses of 17D yellow fever vaccines produce seroconversion non-inferior to full doses, in adults and in young children?
shelves.mesh: Antibodies, Neutralizing/immunology,isolation & purification · Kenya · Off-Label Use · Seroconversion · Uganda · Yellow Fever/prevention & control · Yellow Fever Vaccine/administration & dosage,adverse effects,immunology
shelves.balance: LIKELY: In adults, a randomised double-blind non-inferiority trial of all four WHO-prequalified vaccines (960 enrolled; 900 in the per-protocol analysis) found fractional doses met non-inferiority for day-28 seroconversion for every vaccine (absolute differences from −0.90% to +1.82%). In young children, the YEFE substudy of the same programme (420 children aged 9–59 months) also met non-inferiority at day 28 (97% vs 100% seroconversion; difference −2 percentage points, 95% CI −5 to 1), although fewer children had seroconverted by day 10. These are immunogenicity endpoints for an outbreak dose-sparing strategy — labelled as such — and the consistency across products, substrains and ages supports LIKELY.

cards.headline: Juan-Giner 2021: one-fifth doses of all four WHO-prequalified yellow fever vaccines were non-inferior to full doses for seroconversion in adults
cards.summary: Juan-Giner (2021): one-fifth doses of all four WHO-prequalified yellow fever vaccines were non-inferior to full doses for seroconversion in adults.
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, non-inferiority trial (Mbarara, Uganda, and Kilifi, Kenya)
cards.people: 960 adults aged 18–59 years with no contraindications, no pregnancy or lactation, and no history of yellow fever vaccination or infection, randomised across four WHO-prequalified vaccines from three substrains (120 per vaccine-and-dose group) to standard or one-fifth fractional dose; 900 were included in the per-protocol analysis and 959 in the safety analysis.
cards.result: The absolute difference in seroconversion (neutralising antibody titres at least 4 times baseline by PRNT50 at 28 days) between fractional and standard doses was 1.71% (95% CI −2.60 to 5.28) for Bio-Manguinhos-Fiocruz, −0.90% (−4.24 to 3.13) for Chumakov Institute, 1.82% (−2.75 to 5.39) for Institut Pasteur Dakar and 0.0% (−3.32 to 3.29) for Sanofi Pasteur; fractional doses of all four vaccines met the non-inferiority criterion (less than a 10% decrease). The most common treatment-related adverse events were headache (22.2%), fatigue (13.7%), myalgia (13.3%) and self-reported fever (9.0%); there were no vaccine-related serious adverse events.
cards.watchOut: Seroconversion is a surrogate for protection, and the trial population specifically excluded people who required vaccination for travel and anyone previously vaccinated or infected — the dose-sparing conclusion is framed by the authors for outbreak response in the general adult population during shortages.

cards.result: Fractional dosing met its non-inferiority margin in every comparison at day 28 — the evidence base WHO dose-sparing recommendations rest on. The currency sweep found newer fractional-dose trials in Ugandan children (one-fifth and one-half doses) and in African adults pointing the same way; they are fenced here, not carded, and strengthen rather than supersede this shelf. shelves.title: BCG vaccination against COVID-19 in healthcare workers (BRACE)
shelves.question: Does BCG vaccination reduce symptomatic and severe COVID-19 in healthcare workers — the largest randomised test of the trained-immunity hypothesis — and what did its 12-month outcomes show?
shelves.mesh: BCG Vaccine/therapeutic use · COVID-19/prevention & control · COVID-19 Vaccines/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Health Personnel · SARS-CoV-2 · Adjuvants, Immunologic/therapeutic use · BCG Vaccine/administration & dosage,immunology
shelves.balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference): BRACE randomised 3,988 healthcare workers to BCG-Denmark or saline placebo. At 6 months, symptomatic COVID-19 was 14.7% on BCG versus 12.3% on placebo (risk difference +2.4 points, 95% CI −0.7 to 5.5) and severe COVID-19 was 7.6% versus 6.5% — numerically worse, not better. The 12-month report of the same trial (counted once) found symptomatic COVID-19 significantly HIGHER with BCG (22.6% vs 19.6%; adjusted difference +3.0 points, 95% CI 0.2 to 5.8; p=0.04), with hospitalisations 11 versus 7. A large blinded trial whose follow-up moves against the hypothesis carries LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) for BCG as COVID-19 protection.

cards.headline: BRACE 2023: BCG did not protect healthcare workers against COVID-19 at 6 months — symptomatic COVID-19 was numerically higher (14.7% vs 12.3%)
cards.summary: BRACE (2023): BCG did not protect healthcare workers against COVID-19 at 6 months (symptomatic COVID-19 14.7% vs 12.3% ).
cards.people: 3,988 healthcare workers randomised to BCG-Denmark vaccine or saline placebo and followed for 12 months; recruitment stopped before the planned sample size because COVID-19 vaccines became available. The modified intention-to-treat population (negative baseline SARS-CoV-2 test) included 1,703 in the BCG group and 1,683 in the placebo group. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: The estimated risk of symptomatic COVID-19 by 6 months was 14.7% in the BCG group and 12.3% in the placebo group (risk difference 2.4 percentage points, 95% CI −0.7 to 5.5; P=0.13). Severe COVID-19 risk was 7.6% versus 6.5% (risk difference 1.1 points, 95% CI −1.2 to 3.5; P=0.34); most participants meeting the severe definition were not hospitalised but were unable to work for at least 3 consecutive days. There were five COVID-19 hospitalisations in each group (including one death in the placebo group). The hazard ratio for any COVID-19 episode was 1.23 relative (95% CI 0.96 to 1.59) — above 1, against BCG. No safety concerns were identified.
cards.watchOut: Recruitment was truncated by the arrival of specific COVID-19 vaccines, censoring complicates the estimates (the authors' less conservative sensitivity analyses narrowed the intervals without changing direction), and the 'severe' endpoint was mostly work absence, not hospitalisation — none of which rescues a benefit that never appeared.

shelves.title: Universal HIV testing and treatment for a whole population: PopART and SEARCH
shelves.question: Does a community-wide package of home-based HIV testing, linkage support and immediate antiretroviral therapy for all who test positive reduce population HIV incidence versus standard care?
shelves.mesh: Anti-Retroviral Agents/therapeutic use · HIV Infections/diagnosis,drug therapy,epidemiology,prevention & control · Incidence · Mass Drug Administration · Mass Screening · Prevalence · South Africa/epidemiology
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: Two giant community-randomised trials point in different directions on incidence. PopART (21 communities, about 1 million people) found incidence 30% lower in relative terms where the prevention package was paired with ART per local guidelines (adjusted rate ratio 0.70, 95% CI 0.55 to 0.88) but not where it was paired with universal ART from the start (0.93, 0.74 to 1.18) — an internal inconsistency the authors call unanticipated. SEARCH (32 communities, 150,395 people) raised viral suppression (79% vs 68%) yet found 3-year cumulative incidence essentially identical (0.77% vs 0.81%; relative risk 0.95), while death among HIV-infected persons was lower with the intervention (relative risk 0.77) — a mortality-adjacent finding reported here for context, with no mortality claim built on it. Cluster-randomised by community and unblindable by nature. Mixed incidence evidence across two mega-trials earns POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: PopART / HPTN 071 (Hayes 2019): incidence fell with the package plus guideline ART (relative rate ratio 0.70) but not with the package plus universal ART (0.93)
cards.summary: PopART / HPTN 071 (2019): incidence fell with the package plus guideline ART (rate ratio 0.70 relative) but not with the package plus universal ART (0.93).
cards.type: Community-randomised trial (21 communities in Zambia and South Africa, 2013–2018)
cards.people: 21 communities (total population approximately 1 million) assigned to group A (combination prevention intervention with universal ART), group B (prevention intervention with ART per local guidelines, universal from 2016), or group C (standard care); the prevention intervention was home-based HIV testing with linkage and adherence support; primary outcome HIV incidence between months 12 and 36 in a population cohort of 48,301 randomly sampled adults aged 18–44; baseline HIV prevalence 21–22% per group.
cards.result: Between months 12 and 36 there were 553 new infections over 39,702 person-years (1.4 per 100 person-years). Adjusted rate ratio for group A versus C was 0.93 (95% CI 0.74 to 1.18; P=0.51) and for group B versus C was 0.70 (0.55 to 0.88; P=0.006) — relative figures. Viral suppression (<400 copies/ml) at 24 months among HIV-positive participants was 71.9% (A), 67.5% (B) and 60.2% (C); estimated ART coverage at 36 months was 81% (A) and 80% (B). The authors note the lack of effect with universal ART was unanticipated and inconsistent with the viral-suppression data.
cards.watchOut: When the 'more intensive' arm (universal ART from day one) does worse than the guideline arm, secular change (guidelines themselves went universal in 2016) and chance are live explanations — this trial supports the package, not a clean dose-response for immediacy. Both ratios sit inside or at the edge of the 0.5–2.0 caution band.

cards.headline: SEARCH (Havlir 2019): viral suppression rose (79% versus 68%) but cumulative HIV incidence did not fall (0.77% versus 0.81%; relative risk 0.95)
cards.summary: SEARCH (2019): viral suppression rose ( 79% vs 68% ) but cumulative HIV incidence did not fall (0.77% vs 0.81%).
cards.type: Community-randomised trial (32 rural communities in Uganda and Kenya)
cards.people: 150,395 persons in 32 communities assigned to baseline HIV and multidisease testing with guideline-restricted ART (control) or baseline plus annual testing, universal ART eligibility and patient-centred streamlined care (intervention); primary endpoint cumulative HIV incidence at 3 years; 15,399 HIV-infected persons contributed viral-suppression data.
cards.result: Three-year cumulative incidence: 0.77% intervention versus 0.81% control (704 incident infections; relative risk 0.95, 95% CI 0.77 to 1.17 — a relative figure, absolute rates beside it). Population viral suppression among HIV-infected persons rose from 42% at baseline to 79% versus 68% at 3 years (relative prevalence 1.15). Annual incidence within the intervention group fell 32% in relative terms over 3 years. Among HIV-infected persons, death by year 3 was 3% versus 4% (0.99 vs 1.29 deaths per 100 person-years; relative risk 0.77, 0.64 to 0.93), and HIV-associated tuberculosis or death was also lower (relative risk 0.79); hypertension control was better (47% vs 37%). Mortality is printed here for context beside the incidence result; this shelf makes no mortality-benefit claim.
cards.watchOut: The control group received comprehensive baseline testing and rapidly expanding ART eligibility — a moving comparator that shrank the contrast the trial was designed to detect, as its authors state. YaTsie (Botswana, PMID 31314967) is a third member of this trial family, noted here but not carded, to keep one home per question.

shelves.question: Does promoting surgical masks at village scale reduce symptomatic COVID-19 — and how does that sit beside DANMASK-19, the individually randomised trial of a mask recommendation, which was inconclusive?
shelves.mesh: Age Factors · Bangladesh/epidemiology · COVID-19/epidemiology,prevention & control · Cluster Analysis · Communicable Disease Control · Health Promotion · Masks
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: The Bangladesh cluster-randomised promotion trial (600 villages, 342,183 adults) tripled proper mask-wearing (13.3% to 42.3%) and reduced symptomatic seroprevalence modestly (adjusted prevalence ratio 0.91, 95% CI 0.82 to 1.00 — a relative figure inside the 0.5–2.0 caution band), with a larger effect in surgical-mask villages among adults over 60 (0.65, 0.45 to 0.85, a subgroup). DANMASK-19 (6,024 adults individually randomised to a mask recommendation plus supply, in a low-incidence, masks-uncommon setting) found infection in 1.8% versus 2.1% (odds ratio 0.82, CI includes 1) and was explicitly inconclusive. The design difference is the lesson: promoting masks to a community and recommending them to individuals are different interventions. Both trials are unblindable by nature.

cards.headline: Bangladesh (Abaluck 2022): mask promotion tripled wearing (13.3% to 42.3%) and cut symptomatic seroprevalence modestly (relative adjusted prevalence ratio 0.91)
cards.summary: Bangladesh (2022): mask promotion tripled wearing (13.3% to 42.3%) and cut symptomatic seroprevalence modestly (relative adjusted reduction about 9%).
cards.type: Cluster-randomised trial (600 villages, cross-randomised by mask type and promotion strategy)
cards.people: 342,183 adults in 600 villages in rural Bangladesh, November 2020 to April 2021, randomised by village to mask distribution and promotion (cloth or surgical, with village- and household-level promotion strategies) or control. Sex mix is not stated in the abstract.
cards.result: Proper mask-wearing rose from 13.3% in control villages to 42.3% in intervention villages (adjusted difference 29 percentage points, 95% CI 26 to 31). Symptomatic seroprevalence was lower with the intervention (adjusted prevalence ratio 0.91, 95% CI 0.82 to 1.00 — a relative figure whose interval touches 1), especially among adults aged 60 or older in surgical-mask villages (adjusted prevalence ratio 0.65, 0.45 to 0.85). Absolute seroprevalence rates are not stated in the abstract and are not printed here.
cards.watchOut: The headline ratio (0.91) is small and its interval touches 1 — squarely inside the caution band on its own; the trial's strength is its scale and its measured behaviour change, and its most-quoted figure (0.65) is an age-by-mask-type subgroup. Pre-vaccine, pre-Omicron setting.
cards.source: Abaluck J et al. Impact of community masking on COVID-19: A cluster-randomized trial in Bangladesh. Science. 2022;375(6577):eabi9069. PMID: 34855513. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov: NCT04630054.

cards.headline: DANMASK-19 (Bundgaard 2021): a mask recommendation did not significantly reduce wearers' infection (1.8% versus 2.1%; odds ratio 0.82, CI includes 1)
cards.summary: DANMASK-19 (2021): a mask recommendation did not significantly reduce wearers' infection ( 1.8% vs 2.1% ; OR 0.82 relative).
cards.people: 6,024 adults spending more than 3 hours per day outside the home without occupational mask use, randomised to social-distancing encouragement plus a recommendation to wear surgical masks outside the home with a supply of 50 masks (3,030), or distancing encouragement alone (2,994), in a setting where masks were uncommon and not publicly recommended; 4,862 completed the study.
cards.result: SARS-CoV-2 infection at 1 month (antibody, PCR or hospital diagnosis) occurred in 42 mask-recommended participants (1.8%) versus 53 controls (2.1%) (difference −0.3 percentage points, 95% CI −1.2 to 0.4; odds ratio 0.82, 0.54 to 1.23 — a relative figure, absolute rates beside it). The authors state the confidence intervals are compatible with effects from a 46% relative reduction to a 23% relative increase, and list inconclusive results, missing data, variable adherence and no assessment of source control among the limitations. The trial's design/protocol record (PMID 32829745) is not carded.
cards.watchOut: DANMASK-19 tested wearer protection from a recommendation, at low community incidence — it was not designed to measure source control (protecting others), which is the mechanism community promotion chiefly targets. Comparing its null with Bangladesh's positive without naming that difference misreads both.
cards.source: Bundgaard H et al. Effectiveness of Adding a Mask Recommendation to Other Public Health Measures to Prevent SARS-CoV-2 Infection in Danish Mask Wearers : A Randomized Controlled Trial. Ann Intern Med. 2021;174(3):335-343. PMID: 33205991. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov: NCT04337541.

cards.headline: Synthesis: promotion at community scale showed a small effect; a recommendation to individuals showed none conclusively — POSSIBLE
cards.summary: Synthesis: promotion at community scale showed a small effect; a recommendation to individuals showed none conclusively — POSSIBLE.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: Bangladesh (342,183 adults, cluster-randomised) and DANMASK-19 (6,024 adults, individually randomised).
cards.result: These trials are complements, not contradictions: one changed a whole community's behaviour and found a modest reduction in symptomatic infection; the other handed individuals masks and advice in a low-incidence setting and could not resolve effects smaller than a halving. COVID-19 vaccine and antiviral shelves (#579, #580, #1089) are different interventions and are not re-carded here.
cards.watchOut: Neither trial supports certainty in either direction about masks in the abstract; the shelf's POSSIBLE is a statement about a small, setting-bound promotion effect.

shelves.title: HPV vaccination in males: the quadrivalent efficacy trial and its long-term extension
shelves.question: Does quadrivalent HPV vaccination prevent external genital lesions and vaccine-type HPV infection in young men — and does the protection last?
shelves.mesh: Alphapapillomavirus · Genital Diseases, Male/epidemiology,prevention & control,virology · Human Papillomavirus Recombinant Vaccine Quadrivalent, Types 6, 11, 16, 18 · Incidence · Injections/adverse effects · Intention to Treat Analysis · Papillomavirus Infections/epidemiology,prevention & control,virology
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: In the single pivotal placebo-controlled trial (4,065 boys and men aged 16–26 from 18 countries), quadrivalent HPV vaccine efficacy against external genital lesions related to HPV 6, 11, 16 or 18 was 65.5% in relative terms in the intention-to-treat population and 90.4% per protocol, with intention-to-treat efficacy of 60.2% against all external genital lesions. The open-label long-term extension (1,803 participants, median 9.5 years of follow-up in the early-vaccination group) found no cases of vaccine-type external genital warts or lesions arising during long-term follow-up, supporting durability. A single pivotal trial caps the stamp at POSSIBLE under the library's rules, extension notwithstanding. Lesion and infection outcomes only; no cancer claim is made from these trials. Female-programme shelves (#216, #446, #967) are not re-carded here.

cards.headline: Giuliano 2011: vaccine efficacy against vaccine-type external genital lesions was 65.5% relative (intention-to-treat) and 90.4% (per protocol)
cards.summary: Giuliano (2011): vaccine efficacy against vaccine-type external genital lesions was 65.5% relative (intention-to-treat) and 90.4% (per protocol).
cards.people: 4,065 healthy boys and men aged 16 to 26 years, enrolled in a trial of quadrivalent HPV vaccine (types 6, 11, 16, 18) versus placebo, three doses; efficacy analysed per protocol (all three doses, negative for the relevant HPV types at enrolment) and by intention to treat.
cards.result: In the intention-to-treat population, 36 external genital lesions occurred in the vaccine group versus 89 with placebo (observed efficacy 60.2%, 95% CI 40.8 to 73.8 — a relative figure, case counts beside it); efficacy for lesions related to HPV 6, 11, 16 or 18 was 65.5% (45.8 to 78.6) intention-to-treat and 90.4% (69.2 to 98.1) per protocol. Efficacy against persistent infection with HPV 6, 11, 16 or 18 was 47.8% (intention-to-treat) and 85.6% (per protocol); against DNA detection at any time, 27.1% and 44.7% respectively. Injection-site pain was more frequent with vaccine (57% vs 51%, P<0.001).
cards.watchOut: Efficacy percentages are relative measures — the absolute lesion counts (36 vs 89) are printed for scale. Per-protocol figures describe the HPV-naive vaccinated; the intention-to-treat figures, in a population with prior exposure, are the programme-relevant ones. Lesions and infection are surrogates for the cancers vaccination ultimately targets, which these trials did not measure.
cards.source: Giuliano AR et al. Efficacy of quadrivalent HPV vaccine against HPV Infection and disease in males. N Engl J Med. 2011;364(5):401-11. PMID: 21288094. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov: NCT00090285.

cards.headline: Long-term extension (Goldstone 2022): no vaccine-type genital warts or lesions arose over a median 9.5 years in the early-vaccination group
cards.summary: Long-term extension (2022): no vaccine-type genital warts or lesions arose over a median 9.5 years in the early-vaccination group.
cards.type: Open-label, long-term follow-up extension (7 years) of the randomised, placebo-controlled, phase 3 trial (46 centres, 16 countries)
cards.people: 1,803 men enrolled into long-term follow-up from the base trial: 936 in the early vaccination group (827 heterosexual men aged 16–23 and 109 men who have sex with men aged 16–26 at base) followed a median of 9.5 years after dose 3, and 867 in the catch-up vaccination group (former placebo recipients vaccinated at base-study end) followed a median of 4.7 years after dose 3.
cards.result: In the early vaccination group during long-term follow-up, incidence per 10,000 person-years was 0.0 for external genital warts related to HPV 6 or 11 (versus 137.3 in the base-study placebo group) and 0.0 for external genital lesions related to HPV 6, 11, 16 or 18 (versus 140.4); anal intraepithelial neoplasia or anal cancer related to vaccine types in men who have sex with men was 20.5 per 10,000 person-years (versus 906.2). In the catch-up group, no new vaccine-type warts or lesions were reported during follow-up, versus rates of 149.6 and 155.1 per 10,000 person-years before vaccination. No vaccine-related serious adverse events were reported.
cards.watchOut: An open-label extension comparing against base-study placebo rates, not a continuing randomised comparison — durability evidence of the observational kind layered on the pivotal trial, which is why it supports but cannot raise the stamp.
cards.source: Goldstone SE et al. Efficacy, immunogenicity, and safety of a quadrivalent HPV vaccine in men: results of an open-label, long-term extension of a randomised, placebo-controlled, phase 3 trial. Lancet Infect Dis. 2022;22(3):413-425. PMID: 34780705. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov: NCT00090285.

cards.summary: Synthesis: strong lesion prevention in one pivotal trial, durable in its extension — POSSIBLE by the single-trial ceiling.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: Giuliano 2011 (4,065 young men) and its long-term extension (1,803 men).
cards.result: The male programme rests on one well-run trial: vaccine-type lesions cut by about two-thirds in all comers and nine-tenths in the HPV-naive, with a decade of follow-up showing no late emergence of vaccine-type disease. shelves.title: Oral cholera vaccine where cholera lives: two-dose efficacy in Kolkata and a single dose in Bangladesh
shelves.question: Does a killed whole-cell oral cholera vaccine protect people who actually face cholera — over five years in Kolkata, and as a single dose in Bangladesh, including in young children?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Oral · Cholera/epidemiology,microbiology,prevention & control · Cholera Vaccines/administration & dosage · Cluster Analysis · Diarrhea/microbiology,prevention & control · India/epidemiology · Placebos
shelves.balance: LIKELY: Two randomised efficacy trials in endemic settings agree the vaccine works: two doses gave 65% cumulative protective efficacy over 5 years in Kolkata (incidence 2.2 vs 6.3 per 1000), and a single dose gave 40% efficacy against all cholera and 63% against severely dehydrating cholera over 6 months in Bangladesh — but single-dose efficacy in children aged 1 to 4 years was only 16% and not significant, the age band that needs protection most. Cholera-incidence outcomes only; no mortality claim is made.

cards.headline: Kolkata 2013: two doses of killed whole-cell oral cholera vaccine gave 65% protective efficacy sustained over 5 years (incidence 2.2 vs 6.3 per 1000)
cards.summary: Kolkata (2013): two doses of killed whole-cell oral cholera vaccine gave 65% protective efficacy (relative) sustained over 5 years (incidence 2.2 vs 6.3 per 1000).
cards.type: Double-blind, cluster-randomised, placebo-controlled trial (clusters = dwellings; 5-year follow-up)
cards.people: Residents older than 1 year in 3,933 dwellings in a Kolkata slum area; per-protocol analysis of 31,932 vaccine recipients and 34,968 placebo recipients who fully ingested two doses 14 days apart. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Culture-confirmed cholera over 5 years occurred in 69 vaccine recipients and 219 placebo recipients (incidence 2.2 per 1000 in the vaccine group and 6.3 per 1000 in the placebo group). Cumulative protective efficacy at 5 years was 65% (95% CI 52 to 74; p<0.0001) — a relative measure with the absolute incidences beside it — and yearly point estimates suggested no decline in efficacy. (The record carries a published erratum, PMID 24140391; not a retraction.)
cards.watchOut: Cluster-randomised by dwelling in one endemic urban slum, per-protocol: efficacy in fully-dosed residents of a high-exposure setting, not a measure of population (herd) impact or of one-dose campaigns.
cards.source: Bhattacharya SK et al. 5 year efficacy of a bivalent killed whole-cell oral cholera vaccine in Kolkata, India: a cluster-randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial. The Lancet. Infectious diseases. 2013;13(12):1050-6. PMID: 24140390. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields — no registry reason is stated in the record.

cards.headline: Bangladesh 2016: a single dose protected older children and adults (40% efficacy overall; 63% against severe cholera) but not children under 5 (16%, not significant)
cards.summary: Bangladesh (2016): a single dose protected older children and adults ( 40% efficacy overall; 63% against severe cholera) but not children under 5.
cards.type: Randomised, placebo-controlled efficacy trial (single dose; outcomes 7 to 180 days after dosing)
cards.people: 204,700 nonpregnant residents aged 1 year or older in an urban area of Dhaka where cholera is highly endemic, randomised to a single dose of killed oral cholera vaccine (Shanchol) or placebo. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: A total of 101 cholera episodes were detected, 37 with severe dehydration. Protective efficacy of a single dose was 40% (95% CI 11 to 60%; 0.37 vs 0.62 cases per 1000 recipients) against all cholera and 63% (24 to 82%; 0.10 vs 0.26 per 1000) against severely dehydrating cholera — relative measures with absolute rates beside them. By age at vaccination, efficacy against all cholera was 63% (-39 to 90%) at ages 5 to 14, 56% (16 to 77%) at 15 or older, and 16% (-49% to 53%) at ages 1 to 4; the age differences were not significant (P=0.25). Adverse events were similar in the two groups.
cards.watchOut: Six months of follow-up only, and the under-5 estimate (16%, CI -49% to 53%) is compatible with no protection: a single-dose campaign cannot be assumed to cover the youngest children, who carry much of the cholera burden.
cards.source: Qadri F et al. Efficacy of a Single-Dose, Inactivated Oral Cholera Vaccine in Bangladesh. The New England journal of medicine. 2016;374(18):1723-32. PMID: 27144848. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02027207, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: Synthesis: the vaccine works for years in endemic settings; the single dose fails the youngest — LIKELY
cards.summary: Synthesis: the vaccine works for years in endemic settings; the single dose fails the youngest — LIKELY.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: Kolkata (66,900 per-protocol participants, two doses, 5 years) and Bangladesh (204,700 participants, one dose, 6 months).
cards.result: Killed whole-cell oral cholera vaccine is genuinely efficacious where cholera lives: 65% relative protection sustained 5 years after two doses, and useful single-dose protection (40% overall, 63% against severe disease) for at least 6 months in people aged 5 and over. The honest gap is the under-5s after one dose (16%, not significant). No cholera-vaccine shelf existed in the library; typhoid conjugate vaccine on Shelf #726 is a different enteric vaccine and is not re-carded here.
cards.watchOut: Efficacy against culture-confirmed, treatment-seeking cholera is not efficacy against death — neither trial was powered for mortality and the shelf claims none.

shelves.title: Radical cure of vivax malaria: tafenoquine (DETECTIVE, GATHER) and short-course primaquine
shelves.question: Can a single dose of tafenoquine, or a 7-day high-dose primaquine course, replace the standard 14-day primaquine course to stop Plasmodium vivax relapsing, and what does the haemolysis risk in G6PD deficiency do to that convenience?
shelves.mesh: Aminoquinolines/administration & dosage,adverse effects · Antimalarials/administration & dosage,adverse effects · Chloroquine/administration & dosage · Cytochrome P-450 CYP2D6/metabolism · Disease-Free Survival · Drug Therapy, Combination · Glucosephosphate Dehydrogenase/metabolism
shelves.balance: Split: LIKELY — tafenoquine beats placebo for relapse prevention (freedom from recurrence at 6 months 62.4% vs 27.7% in DETECTIVE) · POSSIBLE — as a replacement for primaquine, because GATHER did not show tafenoquine noninferior to primaquine on recurrence (odds ratio for recurrence 1.81, CI 0.82 to 3.96). A third randomised option is verified at build: 7-day high-dose primaquine was noninferior to the 14-day course (Taylor 2019). All trials required normal (or, in GATHER, at worst moderately deficient in women) G6PD activity — the single dose's convenience is fenced by the haemolysis risk that makes G6PD testing mandatory. Relapse outcomes only; no mortality claim is made. Gate note: the topic file paired the author names to the two tafenoquine PMIDs in reverse; the records govern — PMID 30650322 (DETECTIVE design) is Lacerda et al. and PMID 30650326 (GATHER) is Llanos-Cuentas et al. — and the cards follow the records.

cards.headline: DETECTIVE 2019: single-dose tafenoquine cut vivax recurrence versus placebo — free from recurrence at 6 months 62.4% vs 27.7% (relative hazard ratio for recurrence 0.30)
cards.summary: DETECTIVE (2019): single-dose tafenoquine cut vivax recurrence vs placebo — free from recurrence at 6 months 62.4% vs 27.7% .
cards.type: Multicentre, double-blind, double-dummy, randomised, placebo-controlled trial (all patients also received 3 days of chloroquine)
cards.people: 522 patients with microscopically confirmed P. vivax infection and phenotypically normal G6PD activity, in Ethiopia, Peru, Brazil, Cambodia, Thailand and the Philippines; single 300-mg tafenoquine (260), placebo (133), or primaquine 15 mg daily for 14 days (129). The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: The Kaplan-Meier percentage free from recurrence at 6 months was 62.4% (95% CI 54.9 to 69.0) with tafenoquine, 27.7% (19.6 to 36.6) with placebo, and 69.6% (60.2 to 77.1) with primaquine. The hazard ratio for recurrence was 0.30 (0.22 to 0.40) with tafenoquine vs placebo (P<0.001) and 0.26 (0.18 to 0.39) with primaquine vs placebo — relative measures with the absolute recurrence-free proportions beside them. Tafenoquine was associated with asymptomatic declines in haemoglobin that resolved without intervention.
cards.watchOut: Only G6PD-normal patients were enrolled: the trial says nothing about safety in G6PD deficiency, where a single irreversible dose is precisely the danger. Recurrence mixes relapse, reinfection and recrudescence in endemic settings.
cards.source: Lacerda MVG et al. Single-Dose Tafenoquine to Prevent Relapse of Plasmodium vivax Malaria. The New England journal of medicine. 2019;380(3):215-228. PMID: 30650322. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT01376167, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: GATHER 2019: tafenoquine was NOT shown noninferior to primaquine — recurrence-free 67.0% vs 72.8% in the pooled analysis; haemoglobin drops were similar (2.4% vs 1.2%)
cards.summary: GATHER (2019): tafenoquine was NOT shown noninferior to primaquine — recurrence-free 67.0% vs 72.8% in the pooled analysis.
cards.type: Phase 3, double-blind, double-dummy, randomised, controlled trial (all patients also received 3 days of chloroquine; 180 days' follow-up)
cards.people: Patients with confirmed P. vivax parasitaemia and normal G6PD activity (women with moderate deficiency also eligible), at seven hospitals or clinics in Peru, Brazil, Colombia, Vietnam and Thailand, randomised 2:1 to single-dose tafenoquine 300 mg or primaquine 15 mg daily for 14 days (supervised). The abstract does not state the total sample size, mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: A protocol-defined decrease in haemoglobin (primary safety outcome) occurred in 4 of 166 patients (2.4%; 95% CI 0.9 to 6.0) on tafenoquine and 1 of 85 (1.2%, 0.2 to 6.4) on primaquine (difference 1.2 percentage points, -4.2 to 5.0). In the planned patient-level meta-analysis of this trial and the sister phase 3 trial (per-protocol populations), freedom from recurrence at 6 months was 67.0% (61.0 to 72.3) among 426 tafenoquine patients and 72.8% (65.6 to 78.8) among 214 primaquine patients; the odds ratio for recurrence was 1.81 (0.82 to 3.96), so noninferiority of tafenoquine to primaquine (margin: odds ratio 1.45) was NOT shown.

cards.summary: Taylor (2019): 7 days of high-dose primaquine was noninferior to 14 days — recurrence 0.18 vs 0.16 episodes per person-year; placebo 0.96.
cards.type: Multicentre, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled noninferiority trial (noninferiority margin 0.07 recurrences per person-year)
cards.people: 2,336 patients aged 6 months or older with normal G6PD and uncomplicated vivax malaria, at eight clinics in Afghanistan, Ethiopia, Indonesia and Vietnam; 7-day primaquine 1.0 mg/kg/day (935), 14-day primaquine 0.5 mg/kg/day (937), or placebo (464), all supervised, on top of standard blood schizontocidal treatment. shelves.title: Three drugs at once to clear lymphatic filariasis: the IDA trials
shelves.question: Does adding ivermectin to diethylcarbamazine and albendazole (IDA) clear microfilariae faster and more completely than the standard two-drug regimen, in an individually randomised trial and in a cluster-randomised mass-drug-administration programme?
shelves.mesh: Albendazole/administration & dosage,adverse effects · Animals · Diethylcarbamazine/administration & dosage,adverse effects · Drug Administration Schedule · Drug Therapy, Combination · Elephantiasis, Filarial/drug therapy,parasitology · Filaricides/administration & dosage,adverse effects
shelves.balance: LIKELY: Two randomised designs agree: a single IDA dose cleared microfilaraemia in 96% of participants at 12, 24 and 36 months vs 32%/56%/83% after a single two-drug dose (King 2018), and village-level mass administration of IDA drove microfilariae prevalence to 0.4% at 12 months and 0.2% at 24 months, below the 1% transmission target a year ahead of the two-drug programme (Laman 2022) — though circulating antigen prevalence did not reach its <2% target in either arm. Parasite-clearance and programme outcomes only; no mortality claim is made.

cards.headline: King 2018: one IDA dose cleared microfilaraemia in 96% at 36 months, superior to one two-drug dose (83%) and noninferior to three yearly two-drug doses (98%)
cards.summary: King (2018): one IDA dose cleared microfilaraemia in 96% at 36 months, superior to one two-drug dose (83%).
cards.people: 182 adults from Papua New Guinea with Wuchereria bancrofti microfilaraemia, assigned to a single dose of the three-drug regimen (60), a single dose of the two-drug regimen (61), or the two-drug regimen once a year for 3 years (61). The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Clearance of microfilariae from blood with one IDA dose was 96% at 12 months (55 of 57), 96% at 24 months (52 of 54) and 96% at 36 months (55 of 57). A single two-drug dose cleared 32% at 12 months (18 of 56), 56% at 24 months (31 of 55) and 83% at 36 months (43 of 52) (P=0.02, IDA vs single two-drug dose at 36 months); three yearly two-drug doses cleared 34%, 75% and 98% (51 of 52) (P=0.004 for noninferiority of IDA vs the 3-year regimen). Moderate adverse events were more common with IDA than with the combined two-drug groups (27% vs 5%, P<0.001); there were no serious adverse events.
cards.watchOut: Small (182 participants), single-blind, one country: a proof of biological efficacy in microfilaraemic adults, not by itself a programme-effectiveness result — that is the second card's job.
cards.source: King CL et al. A Trial of a Triple-Drug Treatment for Lymphatic Filariasis. The New England journal of medicine. 2018;379(19):1801-1810. PMID: 30403937. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT01975441, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: Laman 2022 (Papua New Guinea MDA): IDA mass administration cut microfilariae prevalence to 0.4% at 12 months vs 1.5% with two drugs; antigen prevalence missed its target in both arms
cards.summary: Laman (2022, Papua New Guinea MDA): IDA mass administration cut microfilariae prevalence to 0.4% at 12 months vs 1.5% with two drugs.
cards.type: Open-label, cluster-randomised trial (24 villages; mass administration at baseline and 12 months)
cards.people: 4,563 individuals enrolled in 24 villages in a lymphatic-filariasis-endemic district of Papua New Guinea (12 clusters, 2,382 participants, triple-drug; 12 clusters, 2,181 participants, two-drug); all residents aged 5 years or older and non-pregnant women were invited. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Microfilariae prevalence with IDA fell from 4.4% (105 of 2,382) at baseline to 0.4% (9 of 2,319) at 12 months and 0.2% (4 of 2,086) at 24 months, vs 4.3% to 1.5% (29 of 1,963) and 0.4% (8 of 1,844) with two drugs (adjusted estimated risk ratio 4.5, 95% CI 1.4 to 13.8, p=0.0087 at 12 months — a relative measure for the comparator's higher prevalence; 2.9, 1.0 to 8.8, p=0.058 at 24 months). Circulating filarial antigen prevalence fell to 7.5% (IDA) vs 10.0% (two-drug) at 24 months, with adjusted between-group differences not significant — neither arm reached the <2% antigen target. Drug ingestion rates were about 55-66%.
cards.watchOut: Open-label programme trial with incomplete ingestion (~two-thirds): the microfilariae target was met, the antigen target was not, and antigen persists after worm death — programme success on one marker is not elimination.
cards.source: Laman M et al.
