cards.summary: Synthesis: one triple-drug round does the work of three two-drug rounds — LIKELY.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: King 2018 (182 microfilaraemic adults) and Laman 2022 (4,563 residents in 24 villages).
cards.result: The individually randomised trial proved the biology (96% sustained clearance after one IDA dose) and the cluster trial proved the programme (microfilariae prevalence below the 1% target at 12 months, a year ahead of the standard regimen), at the price of more moderate adverse events (27% vs 5% in the efficacy trial). shelves.title: The Lyme vaccine that worked and was withdrawn: the LYMErix-era OspA trials
shelves.question: Did the recombinant OspA Lyme vaccine actually prevent Lyme disease in its two parallel phase 3 trials, and what does a vaccine withdrawn amid litigation, not inefficacy, teach the shelf?
shelves.mesh: Adjuvants, Immunologic · Antibodies, Bacterial/blood · Antigens, Surface/immunology · Bacterial Outer Membrane Proteins/immunology · Bacterial Vaccines/administration & dosage,adverse effects,immunology · Borrelia burgdorferi Group/immunology · Immunization Schedule
shelves.balance: LIKELY (historical): Two parallel phase 3 trials of recombinant OspA vaccine, by competing groups and published back-to-back in 1998, each showed strong efficacy after three doses — 76% against definite Lyme disease in the second year in one (10,936 subjects) and 92% in the second year among three-dose recipients in the other (10,305 subjects). The product is no longer marketed — withdrawn amid litigation and poor uptake, not inefficacy — which is stated on the shelf face. Lyme-disease incidence outcomes only; no mortality claim is made.

cards.headline: Steere 1998 (Lyme Disease Vaccine Study Group): OspA vaccine efficacy was 49% after two doses and 76% after three against definite Lyme disease
cards.summary: Steere (1998): OspA vaccine efficacy was 49% after two doses and 76% after three against definite Lyme disease (relative).
cards.type: Multicentre, double-blind, randomised trial (injections at 0, 1 and 12 months; two transmission seasons)
cards.people: 10,936 subjects living in Lyme-endemic areas of the United States, receiving recombinant OspA vaccine with adjuvant or placebo. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: In the first year, after two injections, 22 vaccine recipients and 43 placebo recipients contracted definite Lyme disease (P=0.009); vaccine efficacy was 49% (95% CI 15 to 69%). In the second year, after the third injection, 16 vaccine recipients and 66 placebo recipients contracted definite Lyme disease (P<0.001); efficacy was 76% (58 to 86%). Efficacy against asymptomatic infection was 83% in year 1 and 100% in year 2 — efficacy figures are relative measures; the absolute case counts are printed beside them. Injection was associated with mild-to-moderate local or systemic reactions lasting a median of 3 days.
cards.watchOut: A historical vaccine, no longer sold: efficacy was real but required three doses over a year, and the trial predates current OspA constructs. Efficacy percentages without the small absolute case counts (16 vs 66 in year 2) overstate the population impact in any single season.
cards.source: Steere AC et al. Vaccination against Lyme disease with recombinant Borrelia burgdorferi outer-surface lipoprotein A with adjuvant. Lyme Disease Vaccine Study Group. The New England journal of medicine. 1998;339(4):209-15. PMID: 9673298. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields — pre-registration-era trial (1998).

cards.headline: Sigal 1998 (OspA Consortium): the rival unadjuvanted OspA vaccine showed 68% efficacy in year 1 and 92% in year 2 among three-dose recipients
cards.summary: Sigal (1998): the rival unadjuvanted OspA vaccine showed 68% efficacy in year 1 and 92% in year 2 among three-dose recipients (relative).
cards.type: Double-blind, randomised trial (14 sites in US Lyme-endemic areas; two transmission seasons)
cards.people: 10,305 subjects aged 18 years or older (5,156 vaccine, 5,149 placebo); the first two injections were 1 month apart and 7,515 subjects also received a booster at 12 months. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Vaccine efficacy (relative reduction in clinically and serologically confirmed Lyme disease) was 68% in the first year in the entire population and 92% in the second year among the 3,745 subjects who received the third injection. The vaccine was well tolerated, with more mild, self-limited local and systemic reactions in the 7 days after vaccination, and no significant increase in the frequency of arthritis or neurologic events in vaccine recipients. (The record carries a published erratum, PMID 9673306; not a retraction.) The abstract does not give the absolute case counts behind the year-by-year efficacy percentages, so none are printed here.
cards.watchOut: The 92% figure is for the three-dose subset in year 2, not the whole randomised population — the two trials' headline numbers are not directly comparable without noting whose denominator is being used.

cards.headline: Synthesis: two competing trials, one conclusion — the vaccine worked; the market, not the data, ended it — LIKELY (historical)
cards.summary: Synthesis: two competing trials, one conclusion — the vaccine worked; the market, not the data, ended it — LIKELY (historical).
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: Steere 1998 (10,936 subjects, adjuvanted OspA) and Sigal 1998 (10,305 subjects, unadjuvanted OspA).
cards.result: Independent groups testing the same antigen in the same era converged: three doses of OspA vaccine prevented roughly three-quarters to nine-tenths of definite Lyme disease in the second season (efficacy 76% and 92% — relative measures, with small absolute case counts in low-incidence seasons). The vaccine was later withdrawn commercially amid litigation and low uptake; nothing in either trial's data shows inefficacy or the arthritis signal that the litigation alleged (arthritis/neurologic events were not increased in Sigal). Prolonged antibiotics for symptoms attributed to Lyme disease are home on Shelf #586 — a treatment question, not this prevention shelf.
cards.watchOut: Historical shelf: no OspA vaccine can currently be prescribed, and the stamp grades the 1998 evidence, not a 2026 recommendation.

shelves.title: Hepatitis A vaccine: the Monroe and Thailand field trials
shelves.question: Does formalin-inactivated hepatitis A vaccine protect against clinical hepatitis A where exposure is intense, in the two field trials on which universal childhood programmes were built?
shelves.mesh: Alanine Transaminase/blood · Formaldehyde/pharmacology · Hepatitis A/prevention & control · Hepatitis A Antibodies · Hepatitis A Vaccines · Hepatitis Antibodies/analysis · Hepatovirus/immunology
shelves.balance: LIKELY (historical): Two field efficacy trials on two continents agree: in the Monroe, New York community trial, no cases occurred in vaccine recipients from day 50 after a single dose vs 25 in placebo recipients (100% protective efficacy in that window), and in 40,119 Thai schoolchildren, two doses gave 94% efficacy (95% CI 79 to 99%), 95% cumulatively including the post-booster period. Clinical hepatitis outcomes only; no mortality claim is made.

cards.headline: Werzberger 1992 (Monroe): from day 50 after one dose, 0 cases of clinical hepatitis A in vaccine recipients vs 25 in placebo — 100% protective efficacy
cards.summary: Werzberger (1992, Monroe): from day 50 after one dose, 0 cases of clinical hepatitis A in vaccine recipients vs 25 in placebo.
cards.type: Double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (single intramuscular injection; mean follow-up 103 days)
cards.people: 1,037 healthy seronegative children aged 2 to 16 years in a Hasidic Jewish community in upstate New York with recurrent hepatitis A outbreaks (519 vaccine, 518 placebo), vaccinated at the start of a summer outbreak. The abstract does not state the sex mix.
cards.result: From day 50 after injection (the prespecified efficacy window), 25 cases of clinically apparent hepatitis A occurred in the placebo group and none in the vaccine group (P<0.001), a protective efficacy of 100% — a relative figure with the absolute counts (0 vs 25) beside it. Before day 21, 7 cases occurred in the vaccine group and 3 in the placebo group (infections already incubating); after day 21 there were no further cases among vaccine recipients and 34 among placebo recipients. The vaccine was well tolerated with no serious adverse reactions.
cards.watchOut: A single-dose, single-community trial conducted into the teeth of an outbreak, with cases counted only from day 50: the 100% figure describes that window and setting, and durability was established by later programmes, not this trial.
cards.source: Werzberger A et al. A controlled trial of a formalin-inactivated hepatitis A vaccine in healthy children. The New England journal of medicine. 1992;327(7):453-7. PMID: 1320740. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields — pre-registration-era trial (1992).

cards.headline: Innis 1994 (Thailand): two doses of inactivated hepatitis A vaccine gave 94% protective efficacy (95% CI 79 to 99%) in 40,119 schoolchildren
cards.summary: Innis (1994, Thailand): two doses of inactivated hepatitis A vaccine gave 94% protective efficacy (relative) in 40,119 schoolchildren.
cards.type: Double-blind, randomised controlled trial, stratified by community (hepatitis B vaccine as control; crossover at 18 months)
cards.people: 40,119 children aged 1 to 16 years attending 148 primary schools in Thailand; 38,157 (95%) entered surveillance a mean of 138 days after dose 1 and 33,586 (84%) completed the 532-day controlled trial. The abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: Of 6,976 illness episodes during the controlled trial, 40 were hepatitis A, of which 38 were in the control group; the 2 vaccine-group cases were brief with only slight transaminase rises. Following two doses (days 138 to 386), protective efficacy was 94% (95% CI 79 to 99%); cumulative efficacy including the post-booster period (days 138 to 532) was 95% (82 to 99%) — relative measures with the absolute counts (2 vs 38 cases) beside them. There were no serious adverse reactions despite more than 109,000 doses of hepatitis A vaccine administered. Among initially seronegative two-dose recipients, antibody at protective levels was present in 94% before and 99% after the 1-year booster.
cards.watchOut: The control was hepatitis B vaccine, not placebo, and case-finding ran through school-absence surveillance: mild or anicteric infections could be missed in both arms, which is why the endpoint is clinical hepatitis A, not infection.
cards.source: Innis BL et al. Protection against hepatitis A by an inactivated vaccine. JAMA. 1994;271(17):1328-34. PMID: 8158817. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields — pre-registration-era trial (1994).

shelves.title: Recombinant haemagglutinin influenza vaccine (Flublok) versus egg-grown vaccine in adults over 50
shelves.question: Does quadrivalent recombinant haemagglutinin influenza vaccine, made without eggs or live virus, prevent influenza better than standard egg-grown inactivated vaccine in adults aged 50 or older?
shelves.mesh: Influenza A Virus, H3N2 Subtype/isolation & purification · Influenza A virus/isolation & purification · Influenza B virus/isolation & purification · Influenza Vaccines/adverse effects,immunology · Influenza, Human/prevention & control · Nasopharynx/virology · Proportional Hazards Models
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: One large double-blind trial (Dunkle 2017, 9,003 adults aged 50+) found PCR-confirmed influenza attack rates of 2.2% with recombinant vaccine vs 3.2% with standard egg-grown vaccine in the per-protocol population — a 30% lower probability of influenza-like illness, which is a relative measure and is labelled relative wherever printed, with the absolute rates beside it. A single trial caps the stamp at POSSIBLE; the cell-culture vaccine efficacy companion sought at build could not be pinned to a verified record, so the shelf rests on Dunkle alone (see summary). Influenza-illness outcome only; no hospitalisation or mortality claim is made.

cards.headline: Dunkle 2017: recombinant influenza vaccine gave a 30% relative reduction in PCR-confirmed influenza vs egg-grown vaccine (attack rates 2.2% vs 3.2%) in adults 50+
cards.summary: Dunkle (2017): recombinant influenza vaccine gave a 30% relative reduction in PCR-confirmed influenza vs egg-grown vaccine (attack rates 2.2% vs 3.2%).
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, multicentre trial (2014-2015 A/H3N2-predominant season)
cards.people: 9,003 adults aged 50 years or older enrolled and randomised to quadrivalent recombinant haemagglutinin vaccine (RIV4, 45 µg HA per strain) or standard-dose egg-grown quadrivalent inactivated vaccine (IIV4, 15 µg per strain); 8,855 (98.4%) received vaccine and entered efficacy follow-up. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: RT-PCR-confirmed influenza attack rates were 2.2% (96 cases among 4,303) with RIV4 vs 3.2% (138 among 4,301) with IIV4 in the modified per-protocol population (2.2% vs 3.1% in the modified intention-to-treat population). The probability of influenza-like illness was 30% lower with RIV4 than IIV4 (95% CI 10 to 47; P=0.006) — explicitly a relative reduction; the absolute difference was about 1 case per 100 vaccinated in that season. Detected cases were 181 influenza A/H3N2, 47 influenza B and 6 nonsubtypeable A. Safety profiles were similar. The trial met its prespecified noninferiority criterion and an exploratory superiority analysis.
cards.watchOut: One season, dominated by a drifted A/H3N2 strain that penalised the egg-grown comparator: the 30% relative advantage may be partly a mismatch-season effect (egg adaptation) rather than a fixed platform property, and the absolute gain was ~1 percentage point.
cards.source: Dunkle LM et al. Efficacy of Recombinant Influenza Vaccine in Adults 50 Years of Age or Older. The New England journal of medicine. 2017;376(25):2427-2436. PMID: 28636855. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02285998, from the record's databank fields.

shelves.title: Monoclonal antibody prevention of malaria: CIS43LS in adults and L9LS in children
shelves.question: Can a single injection of a long-acting monoclonal antibody protect against malaria for a season — intravenous CIS43LS in Malian adults, and subcutaneous L9LS in Malian children?
shelves.mesh: Antimalarials/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Artemether, Lumefantrine Drug Combination/therapeutic use · Malaria, Falciparum/diagnosis,drug therapy,prevention & control · Mali · Plasmodium falciparum · Antibodies, Monoclonal, Humanized/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Headache/chemically induced
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: Two phase 2 trials of one antibody lineage in Mali each showed strong protection over a 6-month season: intravenous CIS43LS in adults (efficacy 88.2% at the 40 mg/kg dose and 75.0% at 10 mg/kg against infection — relative measures with absolute infection rates of 18.2%/35.5% vs 78.2% on placebo) and subcutaneous L9LS in children (efficacy 66-70% against infection and 67-77% against clinical malaria). Phase 2 size, one country, one season, and a different antibody and route in each trial cap the stamp at POSSIBLE. Neither trial was powered for death and no mortality claim is made.

cards.headline: Kayentao 2022 (CIS43LS): one intravenous infusion protected Malian adults for a season — infection in 18.2% at 40 mg/kg vs 78.2% on placebo (efficacy 88.2%, relative)
cards.summary: Kayentao (2022, CIS43LS): one intravenous infusion protected Malian adults for a season — infection in 18.2% at 40 mg/kg vs 78.2% on placebo.
cards.type: Phase 2 randomised, placebo-controlled trial (dose-escalation Part A; efficacy Part B over a 6-month season)
cards.people: 330 healthy adults in Mali randomised in Part B (110 per group) to CIS43LS 10 mg/kg, CIS43LS 40 mg/kg, or placebo, after artemether-lumefantrine clearance of any existing infection; blood-smear surveillance at least every 2 weeks for 24 weeks. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: P. falciparum infection was detected in 39 participants (35.5%) on 10 mg/kg, 20 (18.2%) on 40 mg/kg, and 86 (78.2%) on placebo. Efficacy against infection at 6 months was 88.2% (adjusted 95% CI 79.3 to 93.3; P<0.001) for 40 mg/kg and 75.0% (61.0 to 84.0; P<0.001) for 10 mg/kg — relative efficacy measures with the absolute infection proportions beside them. The risk of moderate headache was 3.3 times as high with 40 mg/kg as with placebo; no other evident safety concerns were reported.
cards.watchOut: Intravenous infusion of a manufactured antibody at 40 mg/kg is a proof of concept, not yet a deliverable programme: cost, cold chain and infusion infrastructure stand between this result and field use, and efficacy is against infection detected by smear in adults pretreated to clear parasites.
cards.source: Kayentao K et al. Safety and Efficacy of a Monoclonal Antibody against Malaria in Mali. The New England journal of medicine. 2022;387(20):1833-1842. PMID: 36317783. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT04329104, from the record's databank fields.

cards.summary: Kayentao (2024, L9LS): one subcutaneous injection protected Malian children — infection 40–48% vs 81% on placebo.
cards.type: Phase 2 randomised, placebo-controlled trial (dose-escalation Part A; efficacy Part B over a 6-month season)
cards.people: 225 children aged 6 to 10 years in Mali randomised in Part B (75 per group) to subcutaneous L9LS 150 mg, L9LS 300 mg, or placebo; blood-smear surveillance at least every 2 weeks for 24 weeks. The abstract does not state the sex mix.
cards.result: P. falciparum infection occurred in 36 participants (48%) on 150 mg, 30 (40%) on 300 mg, and 61 (81%) on placebo. cards.headline: Synthesis: passive immunisation works for a season in adults and children — POSSIBLE, pending phase 3 and delivery answers
cards.summary: Synthesis: passive immunisation works for a season in adults and children — POSSIBLE, pending phase 3 and delivery answers.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: CIS43LS (330 adults, intravenous) and L9LS (225 children, subcutaneous), both in Mali over one 6-month season.
cards.result: A single antibody injection held off most P. falciparum infections for a full transmission season in both generations of the programme (adult infection 18.2% vs 78.2% at the high dose; child infection 40% vs 81%), and the subcutaneous successor kept efficacy against clinical malaria (67-77% relative) in children. shelves.title: Moxidectin versus ivermectin for onchocerciasis (river blindness)
shelves.question: Does a single dose of moxidectin suppress skin microfilariae longer and more completely than ivermectin in onchocerciasis?
shelves.mesh: Animals · Anthelmintics/administration & dosage,adverse effects · Democratic Republic of the Congo/epidemiology · Endemic Diseases · Ghana/epidemiology · Ivermectin/administration & dosage,adverse effects · Liberia/epidemiology
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: One large double-blind phase 3 trial (1,472 treated participants across Ghana, Liberia and the Democratic Republic of Congo) found skin microfilarial density at 12 months far lower after a single moxidectin dose than after ivermectin (adjusted geometric mean 0.6 vs 4.5 microfilariae per mg skin; treatment difference 86% — a relative measure). A single trial, on a parasitological surrogate, caps the stamp at POSSIBLE. Ocular adverse events are reported on the card face.

cards.headline: Opoku 2018: moxidectin held skin microfilariae at 0.6 per mg at 12 months vs 4.5 with ivermectin (treatment difference 86%, relative)
cards.summary: Opoku (2018): moxidectin held skin microfilariae at 0.6 per mg at 12 months vs 4.5 with ivermectin (treatment difference 86%, relative).
cards.type: Randomised, controlled, double-blind phase 3 superiority trial (four sites, three countries)
cards.people: 1,499 participants aged 12 years or older with at least 10 O. volvulus microfilariae per mg of skin, not co-infected with Loa loa or lymphatic filariasis, allocated to single-dose moxidectin 8 mg (998) or ivermectin 150 µg/kg (501); 947 and 480 respectively were in the primary efficacy analysis. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix. (The record carries a published erratum, PMID 30319110; not a retraction.)
cards.result: At 12 months, skin microfilarial density was lower with moxidectin (adjusted geometric mean 0.6 microfilariae per mg [95% CI 0.3 to 1.0]) than with ivermectin (4.5 [3.5 to 5.9]); difference 3.9 (3.2 to 4.9), p<0.0001; treatment difference 86% — a relative measure. Mazzotti (efficacy-related) reactions occurred in 967 (99%) of 978 moxidectin-treated participants and 478 (97%) of 494 ivermectin-treated, including ocular reactions (113 [12%] vs 47 [10%]), laboratory reactions (81% vs 84%) and clinical reactions (97% vs 90%). No serious adverse events were considered treatment-related.
cards.watchOut: The endpoint is parasite density in skin — the transmission reservoir — not blindness prevented or symptoms relieved; participants with Loa loa co-infection were excluded, which matters for real programmes in co-endemic areas.
cards.source: Opoku NO et al. Single dose moxidectin versus ivermectin for Onchocerca volvulus infection in Ghana, Liberia, and the Democratic Republic of the Congo: a randomised, controlled, double-blind phase 3 trial. shelves.title: Screening everything at once in men 65-74: DANCAVAS
shelves.question: Does inviting men aged 65 to 74 to a single bundled cardiovascular screen — coronary calcium, aneurysm and peripheral-artery imaging, blood pressure, rhythm, cholesterol and diabetes testing, with treatment of what is found — reduce all-cause mortality?
shelves.mesh: Calcium/analysis · Denmark/epidemiology · Incidence · Mass Screening/methods · Peripheral Arterial Disease/diagnosis,epidemiology · Cardiac-Gated Imaging Techniques · Cardiovascular Diseases/diagnosis,epidemiology
shelves.balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C: all-cause mortality was the primary outcome). One very large population-based trial (DANCAVAS, 46,526 men analysed, median follow-up 5.6 years) found death from any cause in 12.6% of the invited group vs 13.1% of controls (relative hazard ratio 0.95; 95% CI 0.90 to 1.00; P=0.06) — not significant. A single very large null trial may carry LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) under the library's rule, stated as the reasoning. Stroke was lower (hazard ratio 0.93, CI 0.86 to 0.99) as a secondary outcome and is labelled secondary. The companion Danish programme, VIVA, is deliberately NOT an anchor here: its primary report is already cited inside built Shelf #530's synthesis card and is fenced against that home, not re-carded. The topic file's note of a signal in the youngest age band is not in the trial abstract, so no subgroup figure is printed.

cards.headline: DANCAVAS 2022: inviting men 65-74 to bundled cardiovascular screening did not significantly reduce all-cause mortality at 5 years (12.6% vs 13.1%; relative hazard ratio 0.95, P=0.06)
cards.summary: DANCAVAS (2022): inviting men 65–74 to bundled cardiovascular screening did not significantly reduce all-cause mortality at 5 years ( 12.6% vs 13.1% ; HR 0.95 relative; P=0.06).
cards.type: Population-based, parallel-group, randomised, controlled trial (1:2 invitation-to-screening vs no invitation; intention-to-treat)
cards.people: 46,611 men aged 65 to 74 years in 15 Danish municipalities randomised; after exclusions, 16,736 in the invited group and 29,790 controls were analysed, and 10,471 invited men (62.6%) actually underwent screening. Screening comprised ECG-gated CT (coronary calcium, aneurysms, atrial fibrillation), ankle-brachial index (peripheral artery disease, hypertension) and blood tests (diabetes, hypercholesterolaemia).
cards.result: After a median follow-up of 5.6 years, 2,106 men (12.6%) in the invited group and 3,915 (13.1%) in the control group had died (hazard ratio 0.95; 95% CI 0.90 to 1.00; P=0.06) — a relative measure with the absolute rates beside it; the primary outcome was not significantly reduced. Secondary outcomes: hazard ratio for stroke 0.93 (0.86 to 0.99), for myocardial infarction 0.91 (0.81 to 1.03), for aortic dissection 0.95 (0.61 to 1.49) and for aortic rupture 0.81 (0.49 to 1.35). There were no significant between-group differences in safety outcomes.
cards.watchOut: An invitation trial in which only 62.6% of the invited were screened, against a contemporary Danish control population already receiving good preventive care: it tests the bundled invitation as policy, not whether treating each found condition works — those treatment questions live on their own shelves.
cards.source: Lindholt JS et al. Five-Year Outcomes of the Danish Cardiovascular Screening (DANCAVAS) Trial. The New England journal of medicine. 2022;387(15):1385-1394. PMID: 36027560. Registry ID: ISRCTN12157806, from the record's databank fields.

shelves.title: Acetazolamide to stop mountain sickness before it starts: the Himalayan trials and the dose question
shelves.question: Does acetazolamide prevent acute mountain sickness in travellers ascending fast to high altitude, and is the low 125 mg twice-daily dose as good as 375 mg twice daily?
shelves.mesh: Acetazolamide/therapeutic use · Altitude Sickness/prevention & control · Ginkgo biloba · Mountaineering · Phytotherapy/methods · Acetazolamide/administration & dosage · Altitude
shelves.balance: LIKELY: Three randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trials agree that acetazolamide prevents acute mountain sickness on rapid ascent: AMS incidence 12% on acetazolamide versus 34% on placebo in Gertsch's Himalayan factorial trial, 21-24% on either dose versus 51% on placebo in Basnyat's dose-comparison trial (no significant difference between 125 mg and 375 mg twice daily, with more paraesthesia at the higher dose), and 36.9% versus 55.9% with a once-daily extended-release 500 mg preparation in a 2026 Chinese phase III trial. The low dose is the tolerable one and the trials give no reason to prefer the high dose. Ginkgo biloba, tested in the same factorial trial, was no better than placebo. Cross-reference: dexamethasone for mountain sickness is Shelf #1217; high-altitude pulmonary oedema prophylaxis is Shelf #1211.

cards.headline: Gertsch 2004 (PHAIT): acetazolamide cut mountain sickness to 12% from 34% on placebo; ginkgo did nothing
cards.summary: Gertsch (2004, PHAIT): acetazolamide cut mountain sickness to 12% from 34% on placebo; ginkgo did nothing.
cards.type: Prospective, double-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled factorial trial
cards.people: 614 healthy Western trekkers (487 completed the trial) ascending the approach to Everest base camp in the Nepal Himalayas (4,280 m or 4,358 m, endpoint 4,928 m), assigned to ginkgo biloba, acetazolamide 250 mg twice daily, both, or placebo; the abstract does not state mean age or the sex mix.
cards.result: Incidence of acute mountain sickness (Lake Louise score ≥3 with headache and one other symptom) was 34% on placebo, 12% on acetazolamide, 35% on ginkgo and 14% on the combination; the abstract reports an odds ratio of 3.76 (95% CI 1.91 to 7.39) for placebo versus acetazolamide with a number needed to treat of 4. More severe sickness (score ≥5) occurred in 18% on placebo versus 3% on acetazolamide (odds ratio 6.46, 2.15 to 19.40; NNT 7). Ginkgo was not significantly different from placebo for any outcome.
cards.watchOut: A factorial trekking trial, not a trial in patients: 127 of 614 randomised trekkers did not complete it, and the endpoint is a symptom score on one ascent profile; the odds ratios as printed compare placebo against acetazolamide, so the absolute rates (12% vs 34%) are the figure to quote.
cards.source: Gertsch JH, Basnyat B, Johnson EW et al. Randomised, double blind, placebo controlled comparison of ginkgo biloba and acetazolamide for prevention of acute mountain sickness among Himalayan trekkers: the prevention of high altitude illness trial (PHAIT). BMJ. 2004;328(7443):797. PMID: 15070635. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields — pre-registration-era trial (2002 fieldwork).

cards.headline: Basnyat 2006 (PACE): 125 mg twice daily was not significantly different from 375 mg twice daily — 24% vs 21% AMS, against 51% on placebo
cards.summary: Basnyat (2006, PACE): 125 mg twice daily was not significantly different from 375 mg twice daily — AMS 24% vs 21% , against 51% on placebo.
cards.type: Prospective, double-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled dose-comparison trial
cards.people: 222 non-Nepali trekkers sampled at Namche Bazaar (3,440 m) on the Everest route, randomised to acetazolamide 375 mg twice daily (82), 125 mg twice daily (74) or placebo (66) for up to 6 days ascending to 4,928 m; the abstract does not state mean age or the sex mix.
cards.result: Composite AMS incidence was 24% on 125 mg twice daily and 21% on 375 mg twice daily (95% CI for the difference −12.6% to 19.8%), versus 51% on placebo. Endpoint oxygen saturation was 82.9% on the low dose and 82.8% on the high dose versus 80.7% on placebo. Paraesthesia was more frequent in the 375 mg group (P<0.02). The authors conclude 125 mg twice daily should be the preferred dosage when prophylaxis is indicated above 2,500 m.
cards.watchOut: 'Not significantly different' is not a formal non-inferiority proof: the confidence interval (−12.6% to 19.8%) is wide enough to include a meaningful advantage either way, and the trial was run in young trekkers on a single route.
cards.source: Basnyat B, Gertsch JH, Holck PS et al. Acetazolamide 125 mg BD is not significantly different from 375 mg BD in the prevention of acute mountain sickness: the prophylactic acetazolamide dosage comparison for efficacy (PACE) trial. High Alt Med Biol. 2006;7(1):17-27. PMID: 16544963. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields — pre-registration-era trial.

cards.headline: Danzeng 2026: once-daily extended-release acetazolamide 500 mg cut AMS to 36.9% from 55.9% on placebo on the Peking-to-Lhasa ascent
cards.summary: Danzeng (2026): once-daily extended-release acetazolamide 500 mg cut AMS to 36.9% from 55.9% on placebo on the Peking-to-Lhasa ascent (carded from the currency sweep).
cards.type: Multicentre, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase III trial
cards.people: 288 healthy Han Chinese adults travelling from Peking (43.5 m) to Lhasa (3,670 m), randomised to extended-release acetazolamide 500 mg once daily or placebo from 2 days before ascent to 4 days after arrival; 284 completed; the abstract does not state mean age or the sex mix.
cards.result: AMS incidence (Lake Louise Score ≥3 with headache) was 36.9% on acetazolamide versus 55.9% on placebo (P=0.0013) — an absolute difference of 19 percentage points. Moderate/severe AMS (score >5) was 9.9% versus 24.5% (P=0.0012). Oxygen saturation was consistently higher on acetazolamide (P<0.0001); adverse events (paraesthesia, polyuria) were mild and self-limiting.
cards.watchOut: A single-formulation trial in one population on one ascent: it confirms the drug class prevents AMS in a modern phase III design, but it does not compare the extended-release 500 mg dose against the 125 mg twice-daily dose the Himalayan trials support.
cards.source: Danzeng Z, Zhang R, Gesang L et al. Efficacy and Safety of Extended-Release Acetazolamide Capsules for the Prevention of Acute Mountain Sickness: A Randomized, Double-Blind, Placebo-Controlled Phase III Trial. High Alt Med Biol. 2026;27(1):1-7. PMID: 40955751. Registry ID: ChiCTR 20231401, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: Synthesis: the drug works at the low dose travellers can tolerate — LIKELY
cards.summary: Synthesis: the drug works at the low dose travellers can tolerate — LIKELY.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: Gertsch 2004 (614 trekkers), Basnyat 2006 (222 trekkers) and Danzeng 2026 (288 travellers) — three double-blind placebo-controlled trials, all positive on the same symptom-score endpoint.
cards.result: Across three decades and three ascent profiles, acetazolamide roughly halves AMS incidence (12% vs 34%; 21-24% vs 51%; 36.9% vs 55.9%, each against placebo). The dose question is answered by PACE: no significant gain from 375 mg twice daily over 125 mg twice daily, and more paraesthesia at the higher dose. Ginkgo biloba did not beat placebo in the factorial trial and should not be carried as an alternative. Dexamethasone, a different drug that suppresses symptoms without acclimatising, is fenced to Shelf #1217, and prophylaxis against high-altitude pulmonary oedema to Shelf #1211.
cards.watchOut: Every trial endpoint is a symptom score in healthy ascenders; none of these trials measures high-altitude cerebral or pulmonary oedema, and prophylaxis is not a substitute for staged ascent or descent.
cards.source: Synthesis of Gertsch JH et al. BMJ. 2004;328(7443):797. PMID: 15070635; Basnyat B et al. High Alt Med Biol. 2006;7(1):17-27. PMID: 16544963; Danzeng Z et al. High Alt Med Biol. 2026;27(1):1-7. PMID: 40955751. Registry IDs as on the individual cards.

shelves.title: Stopping high-altitude pulmonary oedema in people who have had it before: nifedipine, and tadalafil or dexamethasone
shelves.question: In climbers known to be susceptible to high-altitude pulmonary oedema, does prophylaxis — slow-release nifedipine, or tadalafil or dexamethasone — stop it recurring on rapid re-ascent?
shelves.mesh: Altitude Sickness/etiology,prevention & control · Blood Pressure/drug effects · Delayed-Action Preparations · Mountaineering · Nifedipine/administration & dosage,therapeutic use · Pulmonary Artery/drug effects,physiopathology · Pulmonary Edema/diagnosis,etiology,prevention & control
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: Two small randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trials in HAPE-susceptible climbers re-ascending rapidly to 4,559 m point the same way — pulmonary oedema in 7 of 11 on placebo versus 1 of 10 on slow-release nifedipine (Bärtsch 1991), and in 7 of 9 on placebo versus 1 of 8 on tadalafil and 0 of 10 on dexamethasone (Maggiorini 2006). The relative effects are very large, but each drug rests on a single trial of 21-29 highly selected susceptible climbers, so under the single-trial ceiling each drug's claim caps at POSSIBLE; neither trial was powered for death and this shelf makes no mortality claim. Acute mountain sickness, the cerebral syndrome, is Shelf #1210 (acetazolamide) and Shelf #1217 (dexamethasone).

cards.headline: Bärtsch 1991: slow-release nifedipine prevented recurrent HAPE — 1 of 10 versus 7 of 11 on placebo at 4,559 m
cards.summary: Bärtsch (1991): slow-release nifedipine prevented recurrent HAPE — 1 of 10 vs 7 of 11 on placebo at 4,559 m.
cards.people: 21 mountaineers (1 woman, 20 men) with a history of radiographically documented high-altitude pulmonary oedema, randomised to slow-release nifedipine 20 mg every 8 hours (10) or placebo (11) during rapid ascent (within 22 hours) to 4,559 m and 3 days there; the abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: Pulmonary oedema (chest radiography) developed in 7 of 11 on placebo but only 1 of 10 on nifedipine (P=0.01) — 64% versus 10% in absolute terms. Systolic pulmonary-artery pressure was lower on nifedipine (41±8 vs 53±16 mm Hg, P=0.01), as were the alveolar-arterial oxygen gradient (6.6±3.8 vs 11.8±4.4 mm Hg, P<0.001) and the acute-mountain-sickness symptom score (2.0±0.7 vs 3.9±1.9, P<0.01).
cards.watchOut: Twenty-one subjects, one ascent, in climbers pre-selected for proven susceptibility: the absolute rates belong to that high-risk group and cannot be carried to ordinary trekkers, in whom HAPE is far rarer.
cards.source: Bärtsch P, Maggiorini M, Ritter M et al. Prevention of high-altitude pulmonary edema by nifedipine. N Engl J Med. 1991;325(18):1284-9. PMID: 1922223. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields — pre-registration-era trial.

cards.headline: Maggiorini 2006: HAPE in 7 of 9 on placebo, 1 of 8 on tadalafil and 0 of 10 on dexamethasone
cards.summary: Maggiorini (2006): HAPE in 7 of 9 on placebo, 1 of 8 on tadalafil and 0 of 10 on dexamethasone.
cards.people: 29 adults with previous high-altitude pulmonary oedema, ascending from 490 m within 24 hours to 4,559 m for 2 nights, randomised to tadalafil 10 mg, dexamethasone 8 mg or placebo, each twice daily; two tadalafil participants withdrew with severe AMS on arrival (no HAPE at withdrawal), leaving 8 evaluable in that arm; the abstract does not state mean age or the sex mix.
cards.result: HAPE developed in 7 of 9 on placebo, 1 of 8 remaining on tadalafil (P=0.007 versus placebo) and 0 of 10 on dexamethasone (P<0.001). AMS occurred in 8 of 9 on placebo, 7 of 10 on tadalafil (P=1.0) and 3 of 10 on dexamethasone (P=0.020). Systolic pulmonary-artery pressure rose less on dexamethasone (16 mm Hg, 95% CI 9 to 23) and tadalafil (13 mm Hg, 6 to 20) than on placebo (28 mm Hg, 20 to 36).
cards.watchOut: Twenty-nine subjects and two withdrawals in the tadalafil arm: the denominators are single digits, so one case moving arms would change every percentage; the trial's own stated limitation is its small sample of adults with a history of HAPE.
cards.source: Maggiorini M, Brunner-La Rocca HP, Peth S et al. Both tadalafil and dexamethasone may reduce the incidence of high-altitude pulmonary edema: a randomized trial. Ann Intern Med. 2006;145(7):497-506. PMID: 17015867. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT00274430, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: Synthesis: consistent direction, single-digit denominators — POSSIBLE for each drug
cards.summary: Synthesis: consistent direction, single-digit denominators — POSSIBLE for each drug.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: Bärtsch 1991 (21 susceptible mountaineers) and Maggiorini 2006 (29 adults with previous HAPE), both at 4,559 m after rapid ascent.
cards.result: Placebo-arm HAPE incidence was strikingly consistent (7/11 and 7/9), and every active arm sat at 0-1 cases. That consistency supports prophylaxis for the known-susceptible climber who must re-ascend fast — but no drug here has more than one trial, the trials total 50 subjects, and descent and oxygen remain the definitive treatment once HAPE occurs. Dexamethasone's appearance on this shelf is as a HAPE-prophylaxis arm only; its mountain-sickness question is Shelf #1217.
cards.watchOut: Do not generalise these rates to first-time trekkers: susceptibility was an entry criterion, and the placebo rates (64-78%) describe recurrence risk in proven susceptibles, not population risk.
cards.source: Synthesis of Bärtsch P et al. N Engl J Med. 1991;325(18):1284-9. PMID: 1922223; Maggiorini M et al. Ann Intern Med. 2006;145(7):497-506. PMID: 17015867. Registry IDs as on the individual cards.

shelves.title: Rifaximin before the trip: chemoprophylaxis of travellers' diarrhoea
shelves.question: Does daily rifaximin — a non-absorbed antibiotic that stays in the gut — prevent travellers' diarrhoea in travellers to Mexico versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Anti-Bacterial Agents/adverse effects,pharmacokinetics,therapeutic use · Antibiotic Prophylaxis · Diarrhea/microbiology,prevention & control · Escherichia coli Infections/prevention & control · Intestinal Absorption · Mexico · Placebos
shelves.balance: LIKELY: Two randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trials in US travellers to Mexico agree: travellers' diarrhoea in 14.74% on rifaximin versus 53.70% on placebo in DuPont 2005 (rate ratio 0.27, a relative figure, with the absolute rates beside it on the card; 72% protection, all three doses superior), and in 20% versus 48% in Martinez-Sandoval 2010 at 600 mg/day (a stated 58% protection rate), with minimal changes in coliform flora in the first trial and fewer adverse events than placebo in the second. Disclosure: the Martinez-Sandoval record's publication types do not include 'Randomized Controlled Trial' (verified on its efetch record at build) — it is carded because its abstract describes the randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled design and its record carries a ClinicalTrials.gov registry ID, and the discrepancy is printed here and on its card rather than hidden. Treatment of established diarrhoea is Shelf #1213.

cards.headline: DuPont 2005: rifaximin cut travellers' diarrhoea to 14.74% from 53.70% on placebo — rate ratio 0.27 (relative)
cards.summary: DuPont (2005): rifaximin cut travellers' diarrhoea to 14.74% from 53.70% on placebo — rate ratio 0.27 (relative).
cards.people: 210 US adults (students) arriving in Guadalajara, Mexico, randomised to rifaximin 200 mg once daily, 200 mg twice daily or 200 mg three times daily, or placebo, for 2 weeks, with daily follow-up for 3 weeks for enteric disease and 5 weeks for side effects; the abstract does not state mean age or the sex mix.
cards.result: Travellers' diarrhoea developed in 14.74% of rifaximin participants versus 53.70% on placebo (rate ratio 0.27, 95% CI 0.17 to 0.43 — a relative measure; the absolute rates are the two percentages just given). Rifaximin gave 72% protection against travellers' diarrhoea and 77% against antibiotic-treated travellers' diarrhoea (P<0.001 for both); all doses were superior to placebo. Among those without travellers' diarrhoea, rifaximin reduced mild diarrhoea (P=0.02), moderate/severe intestinal problems, pain/cramps (P=0.009) and excessive gas (P=0.02). Adverse-event rates were comparable to placebo and changes in coliform flora during therapy were minimal.
cards.watchOut: One destination and one dominant pathogen ecology (diarrhoea-producing E. coli in Mexico): the authors themselves state a study in Asia is needed for invasive pathogens, so the protection figure does not travel automatically to South or Southeast Asia.
cards.source: DuPont HL, Jiang ZD, Okhuysen PC et al. A randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial of rifaximin to prevent travelers' diarrhea. Ann Intern Med. 2005;142(10):805-12. PMID: 15897530. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT00098384, from the record's databank fields. The record carries a published erratum (noted in the record without a resolved erratum PMID); not a retraction.

cards.headline: Martinez-Sandoval 2010: rifaximin 600 mg/day cut travellers' diarrhoea to 20% from 48% on placebo
cards.summary: Martinez-Sandoval (2010): rifaximin 600 mg/day cut travellers' diarrhoea to 20% from 48% on placebo (carded with disclosure: the record's abstract describes a randomised placebo design and carries the NCT number, but its publication types lack 'Randomized Controlled Trial').
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (design as described in the record's abstract; see watchOut)
cards.people: 210 healthy adult students travelling from the US to Mexico received rifaximin 600 mg/day (106) or placebo (104) for 14 days with 7 days of post-treatment follow-up; median age 21 years (range 18-75); 65% female. Efficacy was analysed in a modified intention-to-treat population of 201 (99 rifaximin, 102 placebo).
cards.result: All-cause travellers' diarrhoea developed in 20% on rifaximin versus 48% on placebo (P<0.0001), and diarrhoea requiring antibiotic therapy in 14% versus 32% (P=0.003). More rifaximin participants completed treatment without developing diarrhoea (76% vs 51%; P=0.0004). The stated protection rate was 58%, and rifaximin was associated with fewer adverse events than placebo.

cards.headline: Synthesis: daily rifaximin prevents Mexico-type travellers' diarrhoea — LIKELY, from two concordant placebo trials
cards.summary: Synthesis: daily rifaximin prevents Mexico-type travellers' diarrhoea — LIKELY, from two concordant placebo trials.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: DuPont 2005 (210 US adults) and Martinez-Sandoval 2010 (210 US students), both in US travellers to Mexico.
cards.result: Two independent trials, two dose schedules, one direction: diarrhoea incidence fell from roughly one traveller in two on placebo to one in five or fewer on rifaximin (53.70% to 14.74%; 48% to 20%). The flora-sparing claim rests on DuPont's coliform-flora measurements (minimal changes during therapy), not on resistance outcomes, and neither trial tested post-infectious irritable bowel prevention as an endpoint that can be quoted. Whether to chemoprophylax at all — versus treating the single dose on Shelf #1213 when diarrhoea strikes — remains a trip-by-trip judgement this shelf does not make.
cards.watchOut: Both trials are Mexico-only and E. coli-dominant; neither supports prophylaxis where invasive pathogens (Campylobacter, Shigella) dominate, and daily antibiotic prophylaxis for every traveller is not what these trials, alone, justify.
cards.source: Synthesis of DuPont HL et al. Ann Intern Med. 2005;142(10):805-12. PMID: 15897530; Martinez-Sandoval F et al. J Travel Med. 2010;17(2):111-7. PMID: 20412178. Registry IDs as on the individual cards.

shelves.title: Which malaria pill for the traveller: atovaquone-proguanil against mefloquine, and against chloroquine-proguanil
shelves.question: For non-immune travellers, does atovaquone-proguanil protect against malaria as well as the older standards, with fewer neuropsychiatric and other adverse effects?
shelves.mesh: Antimalarials/administration & dosage,adverse effects,therapeutic use · Atovaquone · Drug Combinations · Malaria/immunology,prevention & control · Mefloquine/administration & dosage,adverse effects,therapeutic use · Naphthoquinones/administration & dosage,adverse effects,therapeutic use · Proguanil/administration & dosage,adverse effects,therapeutic use
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: Two large randomised, double-blind trials in non-immune travellers found atovaquone-proguanil similarly tolerated overall and better tolerated where it matters for adherence — fewer treatment-related neuropsychiatric adverse events than mefloquine (14% vs 29%), fewer moderate/severe events and far fewer discontinuations (1.2% vs 5.0%), and fewer gastrointestinal events than chloroquine-proguanil (12% vs 20%). The efficacy half of the claim is weaker than the tolerability half: no confirmed malaria occurred in either arm of the mefloquine trial, and the chloroquine-proguanil trial's abstract reports adverse events rather than malaria counts, so protection in travellers rests on these equivalence designs plus the endemic-resident efficacy data the abstracts cite — hence POSSIBLE, not LIKELY, and no mortality claim is made (neither trial was powered for malaria death). The Schlagenhauf four-arm mood-profile RCT (PMID 19192127) was verified at drafting and is fenced as background, not carded: it profiles mood effects, not prophylactic efficacy.

cards.headline: Overbosch 2001: no malaria in either arm; atovaquone-proguanil had half the neuropsychiatric adverse events of mefloquine (14% vs 29%)
cards.summary: Overbosch (2001): no malaria in either arm; atovaquone-proguanil had half the neuropsychiatric adverse events of mefloquine ( 14% vs 29% ).
cards.people: 976 non-immune travellers randomised to atovaquone-proguanil (493) or mefloquine (483), with adverse-event and malaria follow-up 7, 28 and 60 days after travel; the abstract does not state mean age or the sex mix.
cards.result: No confirmed diagnoses of malaria occurred in either group. Any adverse event was reported by 71.4% on atovaquone-proguanil versus 67.3% on mefloquine (difference 4.1%, 95% CI −1.71 to 9.9). Treatment-related neuropsychiatric adverse events were fewer on atovaquone-proguanil (14% vs 29%; P=0.001), as were events of moderate or severe intensity (10% vs 19%; P=0.001) and events causing prophylaxis to be discontinued (1.2% vs 5.0%; P=0.001).
cards.watchOut: Zero malaria cases in both arms means the trial compares tolerability, not protection: efficacy equivalence is inferred, and a traveller's destination resistance pattern — not this trial — decides whether mefloquine is even an option.
cards.source: Overbosch D, Schilthuis H, Bienzle U et al. Atovaquone-proguanil versus mefloquine for malaria prophylaxis in nonimmune travelers: results from a randomized, double-blind study. Clin Infect Dis. 2001;33(7):1015-21. PMID: 11528574. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields — pre-registration-era trial.

cards.headline: Høgh 2000: atovaquone-proguanil and chloroquine-proguanil similarly tolerated overall; gastrointestinal events 12% vs 20%
cards.summary: Høgh (2000): atovaquone-proguanil and chloroquine-proguanil similarly tolerated overall; gastrointestinal events 12% vs 20%.
cards.people: 1,083 participants travelling to a malaria-endemic area, randomised to atovaquone-proguanil (plus placebos for chloroquine and proguanil) or chloroquine-proguanil (plus placebo for atovaquone-proguanil); 511 per group reported 7-day adverse-event data; follow-up by telephone at 7 and 60 days and clinic at 28 days, with circumsporozoite antibody testing; the abstract does not state mean age or the sex mix.
cards.result: At least one adverse event was reported by 311 (61%) on atovaquone-proguanil and 329 (64%) on chloroquine-proguanil. Treatment-related gastrointestinal adverse events were less frequent on atovaquone-proguanil (59 [12%] vs 100 [20%]; P=0.001), as were treatment-related events of moderate or severe intensity (37 [7%] vs 56 [11%]; P=0.05) and events causing discontinuation (1 [0.2%] vs 10 [2%]; P=0.015). The abstract reports no malaria case counts, and none are printed here.
cards.watchOut: Chloroquine-proguanil was already a weak standard in multidrug-resistant areas, so 'as good as' that comparator is a low bar; the trial's contribution is tolerability and completion, the determinants of whether any prophylaxis works in practice.

cards.headline: Synthesis: the tolerability contest is decided — POSSIBLE; the protection claim rests on equivalence design, not on cases prevented
cards.summary: Synthesis: the tolerability contest is decided — POSSIBLE; the protection claim rests on equivalence design, not on cases prevented.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: Overbosch 2001 (976 travellers) and Høgh 2000 (1,083 travellers).
cards.result: Across both trials the pattern is one of completion: the atovaquone-proguanil arms lost 1.2% and 0.2% of travellers to adverse-event discontinuation, against 5.0% (mefloquine) and 2% (chloroquine-proguanil). A pill abandoned mid-trip protects nobody, which is the clinical weight of these shelves — but neither abstract counts malaria cases prevented, so 'protects as well' is an equivalence inference this shelf states as such. Malaria vaccines are Shelf #449, severe-malaria treatment Shelf #510, and vivax radical cure is drafted at #1182; none is re-carded here.
cards.watchOut: Tolerability in trial volunteers on short trips does not settle choice for long deployments, pregnancy, childhood or renal impairment — populations these abstracts do not address.

shelves.title: Stockings against the flight clot: Scurr's long-haul trial and LONFLIT 4
shelves.question: Do graduated compression stockings prevent the symptomless deep-vein thrombosis found by ultrasound after long-haul flights, and what does a benefit confined to ultrasound findings buy?
shelves.mesh: Aircraft · Bandages · Cross-Sectional Studies · England/epidemiology · Incidence · Travel · Ultrasonography, Doppler, Color
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: Two randomised trials agree on the surrogate: symptomless calf DVT in 12 of 116 passengers without stockings versus 0 of 115 with class-I stockings in Scurr 2001 (10% vs 0%), and thrombotic events in 6 of 179 controls versus 0 of 179 with flight socks in part I of LONFLIT 4 (and 6 of 143 versus 0 of 142 in part II), with markedly less leg oedema on stockings in both LONFLIT parts. Every event in both trials was asymptomatic and ultrasound-detected; neither trial measured symptomatic venous thromboembolism, pulmonary embolism or death, and this shelf claims none — a real reduction in a silent surrogate, in passengers over 50 or at low-medium risk, is POSSIBLE-grade evidence for the stocking, not proof of prevented clinical events.

cards.headline: Scurr 2001: symptomless calf DVT in 12 of 116 without stockings and 0 of 115 with — all silent, all ultrasound-found
cards.summary: Scurr (2001): symptomless calf DVT in 12 of 116 without stockings and 0 of 115 with — all silent, all ultrasound-found.
cards.type: Randomised trial (stocking versus no stocking; ultrasound outcome assessment)
cards.people: 231 passengers over 50 years of age with no history of thromboembolic problems (89 men, 142 women), randomised to class-I below-knee graduated elastic compression stockings or none, on journeys over 8 hours per flight (median total duration 24 h) returning to the UK within 6 weeks; duplex ultrasound before and after travel, with factor V Leiden and prothrombin G20210A testing.
cards.result: 12 of 116 passengers (10%; 95% CI 4.8 to 16.0%) developed symptomless calf DVT; none wore stockings, and two were heterozygous for factor V Leiden. None of the passengers who wore stockings developed DVT (95% CI 0 to 3.2%). Four stocking-wearers with varicose veins developed superficial thrombophlebitis (one heterozygous for both mutations). No passenger in the trial is reported to have had symptoms.
cards.watchOut: The endpoint is a screening-ultrasound finding of unknown clinical destiny: the trial cannot say how many of these silent calf thrombi would ever have caused symptoms, embolised, or simply resolved — and passengers were over 50, so the 10% figure is not a young traveller's risk.
cards.source: Scurr JH, Machin SJ, Bailey-King S et al. Frequency and prevention of symptomless deep-vein thrombosis in long-haul flights: a randomised trial. Lancet. 2001;357(9267):1485-9. PMID: 11377600. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields — pre-registration-era trial.

cards.headline: LONFLIT 4 (Belcaro 2002): no thrombotic events with flight socks in either flight-length part; oedema scores roughly a third of controls
cards.summary: LONFLIT 4 (2002): no thrombotic events with flight socks in either flight-length part; oedema scores roughly a third of control.
cards.type: Randomised trial in two parts (7-8-hour and 11-12-hour flights)
cards.people: Low-medium-risk subjects: part I randomised 372 (358 completed; stockings mean age 49, M:F 101:78; controls mean age 48.4, M:F 98:81) on 7-8-hour flights; part II randomised 285 (271 completed; mean ages 48 and 47) on 11-12-hour flights. Intervention: below-knee flight socks at 14-17 mm Hg ankle pressure, versus no prophylaxis; DVT assessed by high-resolution ultrasound.
cards.result: Part I: 0 of 179 stocking subjects had DVT or superficial thrombosis versus 4 DVT and 2 superficial thromboses in 179 controls (3.35% of subjects; P<0.002); intention-to-treat failures 2.7% versus 7.9% (P<0.05). Part II: 0 of 142 versus 3 popliteal DVT and 3 superficial thromboses in 143 controls (4.2%; P<0.02). All events were asymptomatic. Post-flight oedema scores were 2.9 times lower (part I) and 2.56 versus 8.08 (part II; P<0.005) with stockings. All thrombotic events occurred in non-aisle seats in part I.
cards.watchOut: An unblinded garment trial run by a group studying the manufacturer's product class, with dropout counted as failure driving the intention-to-treat contrast; the DVT counts themselves (6 and 6 events) are small and, as in Scurr, entirely silent.
cards.source: Belcaro G, Cesarone MR, Shah SS et al. Prevention of edema, flight microangiopathy and venous thrombosis in long flights with elastic stockings. A randomized trial: The LONFLIT 4 Concorde Edema-SSL Study. Angiology. 2002;53(6):635-45. PMID: 12463616. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields — pre-registration-era trial.

cards.headline: Synthesis: stockings abolished the ultrasound finding in both trials — POSSIBLE, and the finding is all it is
cards.summary: Synthesis: stockings abolished the ultrasound finding in both trials — POSSIBLE, and the finding is all it is.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: Scurr 2001 (231 passengers over 50) and LONFLIT 4 (657 randomised low-medium-risk subjects across two parts).
cards.result: Zero DVT in every stocking arm against 10%, 3.35% and 4.2% in controls is a consistent surrogate result, and the oedema benefit in LONFLIT is a passenger-experienced outcome in its own right. What the shelf cannot say is that stockings prevent symptomatic flight-related thrombosis or embolism: no trial here enrolled enough passengers or followed clinical endpoints. The LONFLIT-FLITE flavonoid supplement trial is not this question and is not carded. For a healthy passenger the honest summary is: stockings clearly reduce silent calf thrombi and swollen legs; the clinical dividend is plausible, unmeasured.
cards.watchOut: Passengers with previous thrombosis, active cancer or recent surgery — the people at real clinical risk — were excluded or absent from these trials; their prophylaxis decisions need clinical guidance, not this shelf.

shelves.title: Rabies vaccine into the skin, not the muscle: intradermal pre-exposure in children, and the one-week post-exposure regimen
shelves.question: Can intradermal dosing — a fraction of the intramuscular dose — immunise reliably enough to stretch scarce rabies vaccine, before exposure in children and after exposure in adults?
shelves.mesh: Animals · Chick Embryo · Drug-Related Side Effects and Adverse Reactions · Immunization Schedule · Injections, Intradermal · Primary Prevention · Rabies/prevention & control
shelves.balance: LIKELY (for the immunogenicity claim as framed): Two randomised trials of intradermal delivery met their antibody endpoints cleanly. In 703 Thai schoolchildren, 3 intradermal doses of purified chick embryo cell vaccine gave rabies virus-neutralising antibody titres ≥0.5 IU/mL in every subject, with a rapid anamnestic rise after simulated post-exposure boosters a year later and no serious adverse drug reactions (Kamoltham 2007). In 80 healthy Indian adults, the one-week 4-4-4 intradermal post-exposure regimen with either of two vaccines kept every subject ≥0.5 IU/mL from day 14 to day 180, with a successful anamnestic response to a day-365 booster in those who needed it (Sudarshan 2012). Both are antibody-endpoint trials — no trial randomises anyone to forgo prophylaxis after exposure, and none ever will — so the LIKELY stamp covers immunogenicity and safety, not clinical rabies prevented, and the shelf says so.

cards.headline: Kamoltham 2007: every one of 703 Thai schoolchildren reached protective antibody titres on intradermal pre-exposure vaccine
cards.summary: Kamoltham (2007): every one of 703 Thai schoolchildren reached protective antibody titres on intradermal pre-exposure vaccine.
cards.type: Randomised, open-label, phase II clinical trial
cards.people: 703 schoolchildren aged 5 to 8 years in Thailand, given 2 or 3 intradermal doses of 0.1 mL purified chick embryo cell rabies vaccine (Rabipur) on days 0 and 28 or days 0, 7 and 28; in 206 children, 2 simulated post-exposure booster doses were given 1 year after the primary series. The abstract does not state the sex mix.
cards.result: After primary vaccination with the 3-dose intradermal regimen, all subjects developed rabies virus-neutralising antibody titres ≥0.5 IU/mL, and titres rose rapidly after the 2 simulated post-exposure booster immunisations 1 year later. No serious adverse drug reactions occurred.
cards.watchOut: Open-label and antibody-ended: the trial proves the intradermal route immunises children, not that any individual exposure was survived — and the 2-dose arm's performance is described in the abstract only through the 3-dose conclusion, so the shelf does not quote a 2-dose figure.
cards.source: Kamoltham T, Thinyounyong W, Phongchamnaphai P et al. Pre-exposure rabies vaccination using purified chick embryo cell rabies vaccine intradermally is immunogenic and safe. J Pediatr. 2007;151(2):173-7. PMID: 17643772. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields — the trial predates routine registration for this journal.

cards.headline: Sudarshan 2012: the one-week intradermal post-exposure regimen kept all 80 adults ≥0.5 IU/mL from day 14 to day 180
cards.summary: Sudarshan (2012): the one-week intradermal post-exposure regimen kept all 80 adults ≥0.5 IU/mL from day 14 to day 180.
cards.people: 80 healthy adult volunteers in India, allocated randomly to purified chick embryo cell vaccine or purified verocell rabies vaccine (40 each), each given intradermally by the one-week (4-4-4) regimen, with antibody sampling on days 0, 7, 14, 28, 180 and 365 and a single-visit four-site booster at day 365 for those below adequate titre. The abstract does not state mean age or the sex mix.
cards.result: All subjects in both groups had adequate rabies virus-neutralising antibody (≥0.5 IU/mL) from day 14 to day 180; geometric mean concentrations did not differ significantly between vaccine groups (P>0.606). The day-365 booster produced a quick, enhanced antibody rise in those who received it — a successful anamnestic response. Adverse events were 8.3% in the PCECV group and 1.6% in the PVRV group (P=0.001); the regimen was well tolerated with no dropouts.
cards.watchOut: Healthy unexposed volunteers given a post-exposure schedule: immunogenicity in the well is the endpoint, and the trial cannot measure protection in a bitten patient, wound care, or rabies immunoglobulin — the parts of post-exposure care that actually decide outcomes.
cards.source: Sudarshan MK, Narayana DH, Madhusudana SN et al. Evaluation of a one week intradermal regimen for rabies post-exposure prophylaxis: results of a randomized, open label, active-controlled trial in healthy adult volunteers in India. Hum Vaccin Immunother. 2012;8(8):1077-81. PMID: 22699446. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: Synthesis: intradermal dosing immunises before and after exposure — LIKELY on antibody evidence, with the endpoint named
cards.summary: Synthesis: intradermal dosing immunises before and after exposure — LIKELY on antibody evidence, with the endpoint named.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: Kamoltham 2007 (703 children, pre-exposure) and Sudarshan 2012 (80 adults, post-exposure regimen).
cards.result: The two halves of the rabies-vaccine-sparing question are both answered on the surrogate that rabies medicine runs on: every child immunised pre-exposure (≥0.5 IU/mL, with anamnestic memory at 1 year) and every adult on the compressed one-week post-exposure schedule (≥0.5 IU/mL from day 14 to day 180, booster-responsive at day 365). Dose-sparing by the intradermal route is therefore LIKELY to deliver the antibody response the intramuscular route is trusted for — the honest limit being that clinical rabies is, by ethical necessity, an endpoint no randomised trial will ever report.
cards.watchOut: Regimen completion and correct intradermal technique are the real-world failure points; these trials were run by experienced teams, and a weal raised wrong is a dose not given.
cards.source: Synthesis of Kamoltham T et al. J Pediatr. 2007;151(2):173-7. PMID: 17643772; Sudarshan MK et al. Hum Vaccin Immunother. 2012;8(8):1077-81. PMID: 22699446. Registry IDs as on the individual cards.

shelves.title: Screening older people for impaired vision in primary care (Smeeth)
shelves.question: In people aged 75 and over in primary care, does screening for impaired vision (with referral) improve visual function and quality of life versus usual care?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Cluster Analysis · Family Practice · Female · Humans · Male · Prognosis · Program Evaluation · Referral and Consultation · Risk Factors · Vision Disorders · Vision Screening · Visual Acuity
shelves.balance: One cluster-randomised trial nested in the MRC trial of assessment and management of older people. Important design correction to the naive version of this question: Smeeth 2003 did not compare screening with no screening — it compared universal visual-acuity screening (everyone aged 75+ assessed and tested, with referral for impairment) against targeted screening (acuity testing offered only to those with health problems), both inside a multidimensional assessment programme. Three to five years later there was no difference: the relative risk of visual acuity worse than 6/18 in either eye was 1.07 (95% CI 0.84–1.36) for universal versus targeted, and visual-function questionnaire scores were essentially identical (86.0 vs 85.6; difference 0.4, CI −1.7 to 2.5). Adding a nurse-led vision check for everyone did not improve eyesight outcomes over checking those who already had problems. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — one trial, and its contrast is intensity of screening, not screening versus none.

cards.headline: Smeeth 2003: universal vision screening of over-75s did not improve visual outcomes versus targeted screening (RR 1.07, CI 0.84–1.36)
cards.summary: Smeeth 2003: universal vision screening of over-75s did not improve visual outcomes versus targeted screening (RR 1.07, CI 0.84–1.36)
cards.people: 4,340 people aged 75 or over sampled from 20 UK general practices in the MRC trial of assessment and management of older people in the community (excluding hospital and nursing-home residents). Practices delivered either universal screening — a multidimensional assessment including visual acuity testing by a practice nurse, with referral to eye services for impairment — or targeted screening, in which only participants with a range of health problems were offered an assessment including acuity testing. Outcomes were measured 3–5 years after screening.
cards.result: The relative risk of having visual acuity less than 6/18 in either eye, comparing universal with targeted screening, was 1.07 (95% CI 0.84–1.36; P=0.58) — a point estimate trivially favouring the targeted strategy, with an interval excluding any large benefit of universal screening. The mean composite score on the 25-item National Eye Institute visual function questionnaire was 86.0 in the universal group versus 85.6 in the targeted group (difference 0.4, 95% CI −1.7 to 2.5; P=0.69).
cards.watchOut: Read the contrast correctly: both arms could receive acuity testing, so this trial shows that extending the test to everyone adds nothing over testing those with problems — it does not show that identifying and referring visual impairment is useless in people who present with it. The 3–5-year lag between a one-off screen and outcome measurement, and uptake of referral and treatment in between, also dilute any screening effect. No registry ID exists for this 2003 trial.
cards.source: Smeeth L et al. Screening older people for impaired vision in primary care: cluster randomised trial. BMJ. 2003. PMID: 14593039. Registry ID: none — pre-registration-era trial. cards.summary: Synthesis: offering everyone over 75 a vision check in primary care did not leave them seeing better than checking only those with problems — POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference)
cards.people: 4,340 people aged 75+ in the single Smeeth cluster-randomised trial.

shelves.title: Routine opt-out rapid HIV screening in the emergency department (Haukoos)
shelves.question: In emergency department patients, does nontargeted opt-out rapid HIV screening identify more new HIV infections than diagnostic (clinician-initiated) testing?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Colorado · Emergency Service, Hospital · Female · HIV Infections · Humans · Informed Consent · Male · Mass Screening · Middle Aged · Patient Compliance · Urban Population
shelves.balance: One large single-centre study — and a design correction matters here: despite sometimes being cited as a trial, Haukoos 2010 used a quasi-experimental equivalent time-samples design, alternating 4-month blocks of nontargeted opt-out screening and physician-directed diagnostic testing over two years in a Denver safety-net ED; patients were not individually randomised. Opt-out screening found more new infections: 15 new diagnoses among 28,043 eligible patients (0.05%) versus 4 among 29,925 (0.01%) in the diagnostic phase, an adjusted risk ratio of 3.6 (95% CI 1.2–10.8) in relative terms — but in absolute terms that is 11 extra diagnoses per roughly 58,000 eligible patients, only 25% of eligible patients completed testing during the opt-out phase, and most new diagnoses were still late (median CD4 count 69/µL in the opt-out phase). PROPOSED POSSIBLE — a real relative increase in detection, a tiny absolute yield, and non-randomised evidence.

cards.headline: Haukoos 2010: opt-out ED screening was associated with more new HIV diagnoses than diagnostic testing (15 vs 4; adjusted RR 3.6, CI 1.2–10.8) — but the absolute yield was 0.05% of eligible patients
cards.summary: Haukoos 2010: opt-out ED screening was associated with more new HIV diagnoses than diagnostic testing (15 vs 4; adjusted RR 3.6, CI 1.2–10.8) — but the absolute yield was 0.05% of eligible patients
cards.people: Patients aged 16 or over attending an urban public safety-net emergency department (annual census ~55,000) in Denver between April 2007 and April 2009. Nontargeted opt-out rapid HIV screening and physician-directed diagnostic rapid testing alternated in sequential 4-month intervals. In the opt-out phase 28,043 patients were eligible and 6,933 (25%) completed testing; in the diagnostic phase 29,925 were eligible and 243 (0.8%) completed testing.
cards.result: New HIV diagnoses numbered 15 of 28,043 eligible patients (0.05%; 95% CI 0.03–0.09%) in the opt-out phase (10 found by screening among 6,702 screened patients, 0.15%, plus 5 among 231 diagnostically tested) versus 4 of 29,925 (0.01%; CI 0.004–0.03%) in the diagnostic phase. Opt-out screening was independently associated with new diagnoses after adjustment (risk ratio 3.6, 95% CI 1.2–10.8). Median CD4 count at diagnosis was 69/µL in the opt-out phase versus 13/µL in the diagnostic phase (P=.02) — earlier, but still late-stage, detection.
cards.watchOut: Three discipline points. First, design: time-block allocation is not randomisation, so secular trends and phase differences can contaminate the comparison — hence POSSIBLE, not LIKELY. Second, base rates: a 3.6-fold relative increase on a 0.01% base is an absolute gain of roughly 4 extra diagnoses per 10,000 eligible patients. Third, uptake: three quarters of eligible patients in the opt-out phase did not complete testing, so the strategy as delivered underperforms the strategy as designed. The topic file's description of this study as a randomised trial is corrected here — the record states a quasi-experimental design.
cards.source: Haukoos JS et al. Routine opt-out rapid HIV screening and detection of HIV infection in emergency department patients. JAMA. 2010. PMID: 20639562. Registry ID: none shown in the record. shelves.title: Screening for hearing loss in older adults (Yueh; SAI-WHAT)
shelves.question: In older adults, does screening for hearing impairment (otoscopy, questionnaire, or both) increase hearing-aid use versus no screening?
shelves.mesh: Female · Hearing Aids · Hearing Loss · Hearing Tests · Humans · Logistic Models · Male · Mass Screening · Middle Aged · Otoscopy · Outcome and Process Assessment, Health Care · Patient Compliance · Referral and Consultation · Surveys and Questionnaires · Veterans · Washington
shelves.balance: One four-arm randomised trial (the SAI-WHAT study, 2,305 older US veterans, mean age 61) compared screening by otoscopy (a hand-held audioscope), by the Hearing Handicap Inventory for the Elderly questionnaire, by both, or no screening, with screen-positive participants invited to audiology. Screening moved behaviour, modestly: audiology attendance was 14.7% (otoscopy), 23.0% (questionnaire), and 26.6% (both) versus 10.8% unscreened, and hearing-aid use at 1 year was 6.3%, 4.1%, and 7.4% respectively versus 3.3% in controls (P<.01). The questionnaire-based strategies found far more candidates (59–64% screening positive) than otoscopy alone (19%). The absolute gains in aid use — roughly 1 to 4 extra users per 100 people screened — are small, most screen-detected impairment still went untreated, and the setting (VA, minimal cost barriers) flatters uptake. PROPOSED POSSIBLE. This shelf is about detecting hearing loss; the separate question of whether hearing treatment protects cognition is homed on Shelf #350 (ACHIEVE).

cards.headline: Yueh 2010 (SAI-WHAT): screening raised 1-year hearing-aid use to 6.3% (otoscopy), 4.1% (questionnaire), and 7.4% (both) versus 3.3% unscreened
cards.summary: Yueh 2010 (SAI-WHAT): screening raised 1-year hearing-aid use to 6.3% (otoscopy), 4.1% (questionnaire), and 7.4% (both) versus 3.3% unscreened
cards.people: 2,305 outpatients aged 50 or older (mean age 61; 93.1% men; 99% veterans) randomised to screening by otoscopy (hand-held audioscope, tone >40 dB in 1–2 or 2–4 kHz), by questionnaire (Hearing Handicap Inventory for the Elderly–Screening version), by both, or to no screening. Participants screening positive were invited to an audiology assessment. Outcomes — audiology attendance, hearing-aid use, and hearing-related quality of life — were ascertained by telephone survey at 1 year.
cards.result: Screen-positive rates were 18.6% with otoscopy, 59.2% with the questionnaire, and 63.6% with both. Audiology attendance was 14.7%, 23.0%, and 26.6% in the three screened arms versus 10.8% in controls (P<.01). Hearing-aid use at 1 year was 6.3% (otoscopy), 4.1% (questionnaire), and 7.4% (both) versus 3.3% in the control group (P<.01) — absolute gains of about 1 to 4 percentage points. The questionnaire alone produced the lowest aid use despite finding the second-most candidates, because its attendance gain was smaller.
cards.watchOut: The outcome chain leaks at every step: most people who screened positive never attended audiology, and most attendees did not end up using aids — screening alone, without an adherence pathway, converts poorly. The population was 99% male veterans with VA access to aids; civilian settings with out-of-pocket costs would likely see smaller absolute gains. Hearing-related quality-of-life results are reported in the trial but not in the abstract's headline figures; the shelf claims the behavioural endpoints only. No registry ID is shown in the record.
cards.source: Yueh B et al. Screening and management of adult hearing loss in primary care: scientific review. J Am Geriatr Soc. 2010. PMID: 20398111. Registry ID: none shown in the record. shelves.title: Screening for chlamydia to prevent pelvic inflammatory disease (POPI)
shelves.question: In sexually active young women, does a single chlamydia screening test (with treatment of positives) reduce the incidence of pelvic inflammatory disease over 12 months versus deferred screening?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Chlamydia Infections · Chlamydia trachomatis · Female · Humans · Incidence · London · Mass Screening · Middle Aged · Pelvic Inflammatory Disease · Sexual Behavior · Sexual Partners · Young Adult
shelves.balance: POPI randomised 2,529 sexually active female students in London to immediate chlamydia testing and treatment or to deferred testing a year later. Clinical pelvic inflammatory disease over 12 months occurred in 1.3% of the screened group versus 1.9% of controls — a relative risk of 0.65, but the 95% confidence interval (0.34 to 1.22) crosses 1.0, so the trial's primary comparison is a favourable trend, not a demonstrated reduction. The benefit was concentrated where biology predicts it: among women who tested positive at baseline, pelvic inflammatory disease developed in 1.6% of the screened versus 9.5% of controls (relative risk 0.17, 95% CI 0.03 to 1.01). But 79% of all pelvic inflammatory disease episodes occurred in women who tested negative at baseline, which caps what a single screen can achieve, and 22% of controls obtained testing independently, diluting the contrast. One trial, a non-significant primary result, and a strong subgroup signal: PROPOSED POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: POPI: one chlamydia screen — pelvic inflammatory disease 1.3% vs 1.9% at 12 months (relative risk 0.65, 95% CI 0.34 to 1.22)
cards.summary: POPI: one chlamydia screen — pelvic inflammatory disease 1.3% vs 1.9% at 12 months (relative risk 0.65, 95% CI 0.34 to 1.22)
cards.people: 2,529 sexually active female students (mean age 21 years, range 16–27) recruited at universities and further education colleges in London. Participants gave self-taken vaginal swabs that were randomly allocated to immediate testing and treatment for chlamydial infection or to storage with analysis after one year (deferred screening controls). Baseline chlamydia prevalence was 5.4% (68/1254) in the screened group and 5.9% (75/1265) in controls; 94% (2377/2529) were followed up at 12 months. The primary outcome was incidence of clinical pelvic inflammatory disease over 12 months.
cards.result: Pelvic inflammatory disease occurred in 1.3% (15/1191) of screened women versus 1.9% (23/1186) of controls (relative risk 0.65, 95% CI 0.34 to 1.22) — a relative reduction whose confidence interval includes no effect. Among women positive for chlamydia at baseline, 1 of 63 (1.6%) screened women developed pelvic inflammatory disease versus 7 of 74 (9.5%) controls (relative risk 0.17, 95% CI 0.03 to 1.01). However, most episodes occurred in women who tested negative at baseline (79%, 30/38). The authors concluded that the effectiveness of a single chlamydia test in preventing pelvic inflammatory disease over 12 months may have been overestimated.
cards.watchOut: The headline relative risk of 0.65 is not statistically significant — the interval runs from a two-thirds reduction to a 22% relative increase. The striking subgroup result rests on 8 events in baseline-positive women, and 22% (527/2377) of participants reported independent chlamydia testing during the trial, which biases the comparison toward no difference. A single screen cannot prevent disease arising from infections acquired after the test or from other causes.
cards.source: Oakeshott P et al. Randomised controlled trial of screening for Chlamydia trachomatis to prevent pelvic inflammatory disease: the POPI (prevention of pelvic infection) trial. BMJ. 2010. PMID: 20378636. Registry ID: NCT00115388, from the record.
