shelves.title: Cocoa flavanol extract for cardiovascular prevention (COSMOS)
shelves.question: In older adults, does daily cocoa flavanol extract reduce total cardiovascular events versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Cacao · Cardiovascular Diseases · Dietary Supplements · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Male · Myocardial Infarction · Neoplasms · Plant Extracts · Polyphenols · Risk Factors · Stroke · Vitamins
shelves.balance: COSMOS randomised 21,442 older US adults (women ≥65, men ≥60, free of major cardiovascular disease and recent cancer) in a 2×2 factorial trial of cocoa extract (500 mg flavanols/day, including 80 mg (−)-epicatechin) and a multivitamin. Over a median 3.6 years, the primary outcome — a composite of total cardiovascular events — occurred in 410 participants on cocoa extract versus 456 on placebo: hazard ratio 0.90 (95% CI 0.78 to 1.02; P=0.11), not statistically significant. Cardiovascular death, a secondary endpoint, was lower (hazard ratio 0.73, 95% CI 0.54 to 0.98), and a per-protocol analysis censoring at non-adherence gave 0.85 (0.72 to 0.99) for total events — hypothesis-generating signals inside a null primary result, with no safety concerns. The shelf question is the primary composite: PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference). Tier C: the shelf concerns cardiovascular-event claims, and the cardiovascular-death secondary result must not be promoted past the null primary.

cards.headline: COSMOS: cocoa extract did not significantly reduce total cardiovascular events (hazard ratio 0.90, 95% CI 0.78 to 1.02)
cards.summary: COSMOS: cocoa extract did not significantly reduce total cardiovascular events (hazard ratio 0.90, 95% CI 0.78 to 1.02)
cards.people: 21,442 US adults (12,666 women aged ≥65 years and 8,776 men aged ≥60 years) free of major cardiovascular disease and recently diagnosed cancer, randomised to cocoa extract (500 mg flavanols/day, including 80 mg (−)-epicatechin) or placebo, in a factorial design with a multivitamin comparison. The primary outcome was a confirmed composite of total cardiovascular events (myocardial infarction, stroke, coronary revascularisation, cardiovascular death, carotid artery disease, peripheral artery surgery and unstable angina) over a median follow-up of 3.6 years.
cards.result: Total cardiovascular events occurred in 410 participants taking cocoa extract and 456 taking placebo (hazard ratio 0.90, 95% CI 0.78 to 1.02; P=0.11) — not a significant reduction. For secondary endpoints, hazard ratios were 0.73 (95% CI 0.54 to 0.98) for cardiovascular death, 0.87 (0.66 to 1.16) for myocardial infarction, 0.91 (0.70 to 1.17) for stroke, 0.95 (0.77 to 1.17) for coronary revascularisation, and 0.89 (0.77 to 1.03) for all-cause mortality. A per-protocol analysis censoring follow-up at non-adherence gave a hazard ratio of 0.85 (0.72 to 0.99) for total cardiovascular events. There were no safety concerns.
cards.watchOut: The cardiovascular-death result is one secondary endpoint among many in a trial whose primary outcome missed significance — exactly the pattern that generates false positives. The confidence interval for the primary outcome spans a 22% relative reduction to a 2% relative increase, so a modest benefit is not excluded; what is excluded is any basis for claiming one. This shelf homes the cocoa question only; the COSMOS multivitamin-and-cognition question lives on Shelf #349.

shelves.title: Canakinumab for secondary prevention after myocardial infarction (CANTOS) ⚠ OUTSTANDING-SINGLE
shelves.question: In patients with previous myocardial infarction and residual inflammatory risk (hsCRP ≥2 mg/L), does interleukin-1β inhibition with canakinumab reduce recurrent major cardiovascular events versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Anti-Inflammatory Agents · Antibodies, Monoclonal · Antibodies, Monoclonal, Humanized · Atherosclerosis · C-Reactive Protein · Cardiovascular Diseases · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Incidence · Infections · Interleukin-1beta · Lipids · Male · Middle Aged · Myocardial Infarction · Neutropenia · Secondary Prevention · Stroke
shelves.balance: OUTSTANDING-SINGLE (flagged for the developer under the Nov 8 rule): one large double-blind trial, and the trial that proved the inflammatory hypothesis of atherothrombosis. In 10,061 patients with previous myocardial infarction and hsCRP ≥2 mg/L, canakinumab 150 mg every three months reduced the primary composite (nonfatal MI, nonfatal stroke or cardiovascular death) from 4.50 to 3.86 events per 100 person-years — a 15% relative reduction (hazard ratio 0.85, 95% CI 0.74 to 0.98, P=0.021) — without lowering lipids at all. Only the 150 mg dose met the prespecified multiplicity-adjusted significance threshold (50 mg: HR 0.93, P=0.30; 300 mg: HR 0.86, P=0.031). All-cause mortality was not significantly reduced (HR 0.94, 0.83 to 1.06) and fatal infection was more frequent on canakinumab. A real, hard-endpoint benefit from a single trial — LIKELY, Tier C, and not to be read as an instruction to prescribe a drug that was never adopted for this indication.

cards.headline: CANTOS: primary events 4.50 vs 3.86 per 100 person-years at 150 mg (HR 0.85) — a 15% relative reduction with no lipid lowering
cards.summary: CANTOS: primary events 4.50 vs 3.86 per 100 person-years at 150 mg (HR 0.85) — a 15% relative reduction with no lipid lowering
cards.people: 10,061 patients with previous myocardial infarction and a high-sensitivity C-reactive protein level of at least 2 mg/L, randomised double-blind to canakinumab 50 mg, 150 mg or 300 mg subcutaneously every 3 months, or placebo. The primary efficacy endpoint was nonfatal myocardial infarction, nonfatal stroke or cardiovascular death; median follow-up was 3.7 years.
cards.result: At 48 months, the median reduction in hsCRP from baseline was 26, 37 and 41 percentage points greater than placebo for the 50 mg, 150 mg and 300 mg doses; canakinumab did not reduce lipid levels. Incidence rates for the primary endpoint were 4.50 events per 100 person-years on placebo, 4.11 on 50 mg, 3.86 on 150 mg and 3.90 on 300 mg. Hazard ratios versus placebo were 0.93 (95% confidence interval 0.80 to 1.07; P=0.30) for 50 mg, 0.85 (0.74 to 0.98; P=0.021) for 150 mg and 0.86 (0.75 to 0.99; P=0.031) for 300 mg. Only the 150 mg dose met the prespecified multiplicity-adjusted threshold for significance for the primary endpoint and for the expanded secondary endpoint including hospitalisation for unstable angina leading to urgent revascularisation (hazard ratio 0.83; 0.73 to 0.95; P=0.005). Canakinumab was associated with a higher incidence of fatal infection than placebo, and there was no significant difference in all-cause mortality (hazard ratio for all doses vs placebo 0.94; 0.83 to 1.06; P=0.31).
cards.watchOut: The relative reduction of 15% is a relative figure: in absolute terms the 150 mg dose prevented roughly 0.6 events per 100 person-years of treatment, in exchange for more fatal infections and no demonstrated mortality benefit. The dose pattern is untidy — the middle dose, not the highest, crossed the adjusted threshold — and the finding has never been replicated or translated into an approved cardiovascular indication.

shelves.title: Low-dose methotrexate for cardiovascular prevention (CIRT)
shelves.question: In patients with previous myocardial infarction or multivessel coronary disease plus diabetes or metabolic syndrome, does low-dose methotrexate reduce major cardiovascular events versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Atherosclerosis · C-Reactive Protein · Cardiovascular Diseases · Confidence Intervals · Coronary Artery Disease · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2 · Double-Blind Method · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Humans · Immunosuppressive Agents · Interleukin-1beta · Interleukin-6 · Male · Metabolic Syndrome · Methotrexate · Myocardial Infarction · Proportional Hazards Models · Statistics, Nonparametric · Stroke · Transaminases
shelves.balance: The deliberate negative control to CANTOS, from the same investigators. CIRT randomised 4,786 patients with stable atherosclerosis (previous MI or multivessel coronary disease, plus type 2 diabetes or metabolic syndrome) to low-dose methotrexate (target 15–20 mg weekly) or placebo. Methotrexate did not lower interleukin-1β, interleukin-6 or CRP at all — and it did not reduce events: the final primary endpoint occurred at 4.13 versus 4.31 events per 100 person-years (hazard ratio 0.96, 95% CI 0.79 to 1.16); the original primary endpoint gave HR 1.01 (0.82 to 1.25). The trial was stopped after a median 2.3 years. Methotrexate brought more liver-enzyme elevations, cytopenias and non-basal-cell skin cancers. The inflammation hypothesis survived CANTOS; this particular drug simply never engaged the pathway. PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment made no difference), Tier C.

cards.headline: CIRT: primary events 4.13 vs 4.31 per 100 person-years (HR 0.96) — and no reduction in IL-1β, IL-6 or CRP at all
cards.summary: CIRT: primary events 4.13 vs 4.31 per 100 person-years (HR 0.96) — and no reduction in IL-1β, IL-6 or CRP at all
cards.people: 4,786 patients with previous myocardial infarction or multivessel coronary disease who also had type 2 diabetes or the metabolic syndrome, randomised double-blind to low-dose methotrexate (target dose 15–20 mg weekly) or matching placebo; all participants received 1 mg of folate daily. The primary endpoint was a composite of nonfatal myocardial infarction, nonfatal stroke or cardiovascular death (hospitalisation for unstable angina leading to urgent revascularisation was added before unblinding). The trial was stopped after a median follow-up of 2.3 years.
cards.result: The final primary endpoint occurred in 201 patients in the methotrexate group and 207 in the placebo group (incidence rate 4.13 vs 4.31 per 100 person-years; hazard ratio 0.96, 95% confidence interval 0.79 to 1.16). The original primary endpoint occurred in 170 versus 167 patients (3.46 vs 3.43 per 100 person-years; hazard ratio 1.01, 0.82 to 1.25). Methotrexate did not result in lower interleukin-1β, interleukin-6 or C-reactive protein levels than placebo. It was associated with elevations in liver-enzyme levels, reductions in leukocyte counts and haematocrit, and a higher incidence of non-basal-cell skin cancers. The authors concluded low-dose methotrexate did not reduce inflammatory markers and did not result in fewer cardiovascular events than placebo.
cards.watchOut: The trial was stopped early, which limits precision — the confidence interval for the final endpoint (0.79 to 1.16) cannot exclude a modest benefit or harm. But the complete absence of any effect on the inflammatory markers themselves is the deeper null: the drug never did the thing it was supposed to do.
cards.source: Ridker PM et al. Low-Dose Methotrexate for the Prevention of Atherosclerotic Events (CIRT). N Engl J Med. 2019. PMID: 30415610. Registry ID: NCT01594333, from the record. shelves.title: Metformin as adjuvant therapy in early breast cancer (MA.32)
shelves.question: In patients with high-risk operable breast cancer without diabetes, does adding metformin to standard therapy improve invasive disease-free survival versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Oral · Antineoplastic Agents · Antineoplastic Combined Chemotherapy Protocols · Breast Neoplasms · Disease-Free Survival · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Metformin · Middle Aged · Neoplasm Recurrence, Local · Erb-b2 Receptor Tyrosine Kinases · Receptors, Estrogen · Receptors, Progesterone
shelves.balance: A single large phase 3 trial (MA.32, 3,649 patients) with an unambiguous answer in both hormone-receptor strata. In ER/PgR-positive disease (the primary analysis population), invasive disease-free survival events occurred at 2.78 versus 2.74 per 100 patient-years on metformin versus placebo (hazard ratio 1.01, 95% CI 0.84 to 1.21, P=.93), and deaths at 1.46 versus 1.32 (HR 1.10, 0.86 to 1.41). In ER/PgR-negative disease, futility was declared at the second interim analysis (IDFS HR 1.01, 0.79 to 1.30). Grade 3 non-haematological toxicity was commoner on metformin (21.5% vs 17.5%, P=.003). The observational and preclinical promise did not survive the randomised test. PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment made no difference), Tier C.

cards.headline: MA.32: invasive disease-free survival HR 1.01 (0.84–1.21) and mortality HR 1.10 in 3,649 patients — metformin added nothing
cards.summary: MA.32: invasive disease-free survival HR 1.01 (0.84–1.21) and mortality HR 1.10 in 3,649 patients — metformin added nothing
cards.people: 3,649 patients with high-risk nonmetastatic breast cancer without diabetes, receiving standard therapy, randomised double-blind in Canada, Switzerland, the US and UK to metformin 850 mg twice daily or placebo for 5 years, stratified by hormone-receptor status, BMI, ERBB2 (HER2) status and chemotherapy. The primary outcome was invasive disease-free survival (IDFS) in hormone receptor-positive breast cancer; follow-up in that group reached a median of 96.2 months.
cards.result: In the 2,533 ER/PgR-positive patients, IDFS events occurred at incidence rates of 2.78 per 100 patient-years on metformin versus 2.74 on placebo (hazard ratio 1.01, 95% confidence interval 0.84 to 1.21; P=.93), and deaths at 1.46 versus 1.32 per 100 patient-years (hazard ratio 1.10, 0.86 to 1.41; P=.47). Among ER/PgR-negative patients (median follow-up 94.1 months), IDFS event rates were 3.58 versus 3.60 per 100 patient-years (hazard ratio 1.01, 0.79 to 1.30; P=.92); futility for that stratum had been declared at the second interim analysis. None of the three secondary outcomes analysed in the ER/PgR-positive group differed significantly. Grade 3 non-haematological toxic events occurred in 21.5% on metformin versus 17.5% on placebo (P=.003).
cards.watchOut: The trial enrolled patients without diabetes — it does not address metformin in patients who need it for glucose control, and subgroup hypotheses (e.g., by insulin levels or genotype) remain hypotheses. The confidence interval excludes any worthwhile IDFS benefit in ER/PgR-positive disease.
cards.source: Goodwin PJ et al. Effect of Metformin vs Placebo on Invasive Disease-Free Survival in Patients With Breast Cancer: The MA.32 Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA. 2022. PMID: 35608580. shelves.title: B vitamins and brain atrophy in mild cognitive impairment (VITACOG)
shelves.question: In older adults with mild cognitive impairment, does high-dose B-vitamin treatment (folic acid, B12, B6) slow the rate of brain atrophy and cognitive decline versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Atrophy · Brain · Cognition Disorders · Female · Homocysteine · Humans · Magnetic Resonance Imaging · Male · Radiography · Treatment Outcome · Vitamin B Complex
shelves.balance: One small single-centre trial (VITACOG, 271 randomised; 168 with before-and-after MRI scans) with a clear effect on an imaging surrogate: brain atrophy proceeded at 0.76% per year on high-dose B vitamins versus 1.08% per year on placebo (P=0.001), with the largest effect in participants whose baseline homocysteine was above 13 µmol/L (53% lower rate — a relative figure). The trial did not test cognition as its primary outcome — it reports only that faster atrophy was associated with lower final cognitive scores — and the authors themselves state that trials are needed to see whether the treatment delays Alzheimer's disease. A surrogate-endpoint, single-trial benefit: POSSIBLE, and no higher.

cards.headline: VITACOG: brain atrophy 0.76% per year on B vitamins vs 1.08% on placebo (P=0.001) in 168 scanned patients
cards.summary: VITACOG: brain atrophy 0.76% per year on B vitamins vs 1.08% on placebo (P=0.001) in 168 scanned patients
cards.people: 271 people over 70 with mild cognitive impairment (of 646 screened) at a single centre, randomised double-blind to folic acid 0.8 mg/day, vitamin B12 0.5 mg/day and vitamin B6 20 mg/day, or placebo, for 24 months. A subset of 187 volunteered for cranial MRI at the start and end; 168 completed the MRI section. The main outcome was the change in the rate of whole-brain atrophy on serial volumetric MRI.
cards.result: The mean rate of brain atrophy per year was 0.76% (95% confidence interval 0.63–0.90) in the active treatment group and 1.08% (0.94–1.22) in the placebo group (P=0.001). The treatment response was related to baseline homocysteine: in participants with homocysteine above 13 µmol/L, the rate of atrophy was 53% lower (a relative figure) in the active group (P=0.001). A greater rate of atrophy was associated with lower final cognitive test scores. There was no difference in serious adverse events between the groups.
cards.watchOut: The endpoint is a scan measurement, not memory or dementia. Only 168 of 271 randomised participants completed both scans, the high-homocysteine subgroup drove the headline effect, and the cognitive claim rests on an association between atrophy rate and scores — this trial does not show that B vitamins preserve thinking or prevent dementia.
cards.source: Smith AD et al. Homocysteine-lowering by B vitamins slows the rate of accelerated brain atrophy in mild cognitive impairment: a randomized controlled trial (VITACOG). PLoS One. 2010. PMID: 20838622. Registry ID: ISRCTN94410159, from the record. shelves.title: Omega-3 and vitamin D to prevent depression (VITAL-DEP)
shelves.question: In adults aged 50 and over without depression at baseline, do long-term marine omega-3 or vitamin D3 supplements prevent incident depression versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Affect · Aged · Depression · Depressive Disorder · Dietary Supplements · Double-Blind Method · Fatty Acids, Omega-3 · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Proportional Hazards Models · Treatment Failure
shelves.balance: Two huge prespecified reports from one factorial trial (VITAL-DEP, 18,353 adults aged 50+, median treatment 5.3 years). Correction to the topic draft, which said both agents reached 'the same null': vitamin D3 did — depression or clinically relevant symptoms occurred at 12.9 versus 13.3 per 1,000 person-years (hazard ratio 0.97, 95% CI 0.87 to 1.09, P=.62), with no difference in mood scores. Omega-3 did not reach a clean null: depression risk was significantly HIGHER on omega-3 — 651 events (13.9 per 1,000 person-years) versus 583 (12.3 per 1,000) on placebo, hazard ratio 1.13 (1.01 to 1.26, P=.03) — while mood scores were again identical (difference 0.03 points). Neither supplement prevents depression; for vitamin D the null is clean, and for omega-3 the endpoint result leans the wrong way, modestly. PROPOSED SPLIT — LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) for vitamin D / POSSIBLE (harm) for omega-3.

cards.headline: VITAL-DEP (vitamin D): depression events 609 vs 625, HR 0.97 (0.87–1.09) — a clean null over 5.3 years in 18,353 adults
cards.summary: VITAL-DEP (vitamin D): depression events 609 vs 625, HR 0.97 (0.87–1.09) — a clean null over 5.3 years in 18,353 adults
cards.type: Randomized double-blind factorial trial (vitamin D report)
cards.people: 18,353 men and women aged 50 or older in VITAL-DEP, the depression-endpoint ancillary study to the VITAL factorial trial (25,871 US adults): 16,657 at risk of incident depression and 1,696 at risk of recurrence. Participants were randomised in a 2×2 factorial design to vitamin D3 2,000 IU/day (9,181) or matching placebo (9,172), and independently to marine omega-3 or its placebo. Coprimary outcomes were risk of depression or clinically relevant depressive symptoms (incident plus recurrent) and mean change in PHQ-8 mood score; median treatment duration was 5.3 years.
cards.result: Risk of depression or clinically relevant depressive symptoms did not differ: 609 events (12.9 per 1,000 person-years) on vitamin D3 versus 625 (13.3 per 1,000 person-years) on placebo (hazard ratio 0.97, 95% confidence interval 0.87 to 1.09; P=.62), with no significant differences for depression incidence or recurrence separately. Change in mood scores did not differ either (mean difference 0.01 points, −0.04 to 0.05). The authors concluded the findings do not support vitamin D3 to prevent depression in adults.
cards.watchOut: Participants were not selected for low vitamin D levels or high depression risk, so the null applies to supplementing generally healthy older adults — not to treating deficiency or depression itself. The record names no specific product or brand — products sold today may differ in safety and effectiveness.

cards.headline: VITAL-DEP (omega-3): depression risk was significantly HIGHER on omega-3 — HR 1.13 (1.01–1.26) — though mood scores were identical
cards.summary: VITAL-DEP (omega-3): depression risk was significantly HIGHER on omega-3 — HR 1.13 (1.01–1.26) — though mood scores were identical
cards.people: The same 18,353 VITAL-DEP participants, for the factorial's other comparison: 9,171 randomised to marine omega-3 fatty acids (1 g/day fish oil, 465 mg EPA plus 375 mg DHA) and 9,182 to matching placebo, over a median 5.3 years. Coprimary outcomes were risk of depression or clinically relevant depressive symptoms and mean difference in change in PHQ-8 mood score.
cards.result: Depression risk was significantly higher on omega-3: 651 events (13.9 per 1,000 person-years) versus 583 (12.3 per 1,000 person-years) on placebo (hazard ratio 1.13, 95% confidence interval 1.01 to 1.26; P=.03). Mood scores, however, did not differ: the mean difference in change in PHQ-8 score was 0.03 points (−0.01 to 0.07; P=.19). Major cardiovascular events (2.7% vs 2.9%), all-cause mortality (3.3% vs 3.1%), suicide (0.02% vs 0.01%) and gastrointestinal bleeding (2.6% vs 2.7%) were similar. The authors concluded the results do not support omega-3 supplements to prevent depression in adults.
cards.watchOut: The increased-risk signal sits on one coprimary endpoint with no echo in mood scores, could be a chance finding among the trial's many analyses, and in absolute terms is small (about 1.6 extra cases per 1,000 person-years) — hence POSSIBLE (harm), not a stronger claim. But it is a statistically significant result in the trial's own prespecified analysis, so it is carded, not smoothed into a 'null'. The record names no specific product or brand — products sold today may differ in safety and effectiveness.

shelves.title: Aspirin to prevent colorectal adenoma recurrence (Baron; Sandler)
shelves.question: In patients with a recent colorectal adenoma (or previous colorectal cancer), does daily aspirin reduce adenoma recurrence versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adenoma · Anti-Inflammatory Agents, Non-Steroidal · Aspirin · Colonic Polyps · Colonoscopy · Colorectal Neoplasms · Double-Blind Method · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Patient Compliance · Risk · Secondary Prevention
shelves.balance: Two double-blind randomised trials from the same 2003 NEJM issue, in adjacent populations, pointing the same way. In patients with a recent adenoma (Baron, 1,121 patients), at least one adenoma was found at follow-up colonoscopy in 47% on placebo, 38% on aspirin 81 mg and 45% on aspirin 325 mg (relative risk 0.81, 95% CI 0.69 to 0.96 for 81 mg; 0.96, 0.81 to 1.13 for 325 mg), with advanced neoplasms reduced at 81 mg (RR 0.59, 0.38 to 0.92). In patients with previous colorectal cancer (Sandler, 635 patients), adenomas were found in 17% on aspirin 325 mg versus 27% on placebo (adjusted RR 0.65, 0.46 to 0.91). A modest absolute benefit — roughly 9–10 fewer patients with recurrence per 100 — with an odd dose picture (low dose better in Baron, only 325 mg tested in Sandler). The endpoint is adenoma recurrence, a surrogate: these trials did not measure colorectal cancer or death. PROPOSED LIKELY.

cards.headline: Baron 2003: adenomas in 47% on placebo vs 38% on aspirin 81 mg (RR 0.81) — but 45% on 325 mg, no better than placebo
cards.summary: Baron 2003: adenomas in 47% on placebo vs 38% on aspirin 81 mg (RR 0.81) — but 45% on 325 mg, no better than placebo
cards.people: 1,121 patients with a recent history of histologically documented colorectal adenomas, randomised double-blind to placebo (372), aspirin 81 mg daily (377) or aspirin 325 mg daily (372); follow-up colonoscopy was performed at least one year after randomisation in 1,084 patients (97%). The comparison was the risk of one or more neoplasms (adenomas or colorectal cancer) at follow-up.
cards.result: The incidence of one or more adenomas was 47% in the placebo group, 38% in the 81 mg group and 45% in the 325 mg group (global P=0.04). Unadjusted relative risks of any adenoma versus placebo were 0.81 (95% confidence interval 0.69 to 0.96) for 81 mg and 0.96 (0.81 to 1.13) for 325 mg — a 19% relative reduction at the low dose (from 47% to 38% absolute) and none demonstrable at the higher dose. For advanced neoplasms, the relative risks were 0.59 (0.38 to 0.92) for 81 mg and 0.83 (0.55 to 1.23) for 325 mg. Adherence and avoidance of other NSAIDs were reported as excellent.
cards.watchOut: The dose–response is backwards (325 mg did less than 81 mg), which argues for caution about the precision of the 81 mg estimate; and adenoma recurrence — mostly small polyps — is a surrogate for the cancer outcome patients care about. Aspirin's bleeding risks were not quantified in this abstract and belong in any treatment decision.
cards.source: Baron JA et al. A randomized trial of aspirin to prevent colorectal adenomas. N Engl J Med. 2003. PMID: 12621133. Registry ID: none — pre-registration era (no registry ID in the record). cards.headline: Sandler 2003: after colorectal cancer, adenomas in 17% on aspirin 325 mg vs 27% on placebo (adjusted RR 0.65)
cards.summary: Sandler 2003: after colorectal cancer, adenomas in 17% on aspirin 325 mg vs 27% on placebo (adjusted RR 0.65)
cards.people: 635 patients with previous colorectal cancer, randomised double-blind to aspirin 325 mg daily or placebo; 517 had at least one colonoscopic examination a median of 12.8 months after randomisation. Outcomes were the proportion of patients with adenomas, the number of recurrent adenomas and the time to development of an adenoma. The study was terminated early by its data and safety monitoring board after a planned interim analysis reached statistical significance.
cards.result: One or more adenomas were found in 17% of the aspirin group and 27% of the placebo group (P=0.004). The mean number of adenomas was lower on aspirin (0.30 ± 0.87 vs 0.49 ± 0.99, P=0.003). The adjusted relative risk of any recurrent adenoma was 0.65 (95% confidence interval 0.46 to 0.91) — a 35% relative reduction (27% to 17% absolute) — and the hazard ratio for detection of a new polyp was 0.64 (0.43 to 0.94; P=0.022).
cards.watchOut: Trials stopped early at interim analyses tend to overestimate effects, and here 325 mg worked in Sandler while it did not in Baron — the two trials agree on direction, not on dose. As in Baron, the endpoint is adenoma recurrence, not cancer incidence or survival.

cards.headline: Synthesis: two blinded trials, one direction — aspirin cuts adenoma recurrence by roughly a fifth to a third in relative terms
cards.summary: Synthesis: two blinded trials, one direction — aspirin cuts adenoma recurrence by roughly a fifth to a third in relative terms
cards.people: 1,121 patients with recent adenomas (Baron) and 635 with previous colorectal cancer (Sandler).
cards.result: Baron: any adenoma 47% placebo vs 38% on 81 mg (RR 0.81, 0.69–0.96); advanced neoplasms RR 0.59. Sandler: 27% vs 17% (adjusted RR 0.65, 0.46–0.91). PROPOSED LIKELY.
cards.watchOut: Aspirin's harms (gastrointestinal and intracranial bleeding) are the other half of any prescribing decision and are not quantified by these two records. Whether fewer adenomas means fewer cancers over a decade is inference, supported by the biology of the adenoma–carcinoma sequence but not by these trials' endpoints.

shelves.title: Calcium and vitamin D for colorectal adenoma prevention (Baron 2015)
shelves.question: In patients with a recently removed colorectal adenoma, do calcium, vitamin D, or both reduce adenoma recurrence over three to five years versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adenoma · Aged · Calcium · Colorectal Neoplasms · Dietary Supplements · Double-Blind Method · Drug Therapy, Combination · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Risk · Treatment Failure · Vitamin D · Vitamins
shelves.balance: One large double-blind factorial trial (Baron 2015, 2,259 participants) with tight confidence intervals and no effect anywhere: over 3–5 years, 43% of participants had at least one recurrent adenoma regardless of assignment. Adjusted risk ratios for recurrent adenomas were 0.99 (95% CI 0.89 to 1.09) for vitamin D versus no vitamin D, 0.95 (0.85 to 1.06) for calcium versus no calcium and 0.93 (0.80 to 1.08) for both versus neither; advanced adenomas behaved the same way. The intervention demonstrably raised vitamin D levels (mean net increase 7.83 ng/mL), so this is a tested null, not a failed intervention. PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment made no difference).

cards.headline: Baron 2015: recurrence risk ratios 0.99 (vitamin D), 0.95 (calcium), 0.93 (both) in 2,259 patients — nothing prevented adenomas
cards.summary: Baron 2015: recurrence risk ratios 0.99 (vitamin D), 0.95 (calcium), 0.93 (both) in 2,259 patients — nothing prevented adenomas
cards.people: 2,259 patients with a recently diagnosed adenoma and no polyps remaining after complete colonoscopy, randomised double-blind in a partial 2×2 factorial design to daily vitamin D3 1,000 IU, calcium carbonate 1,200 mg, both, or neither (women could elect to receive calcium and be randomised only on vitamin D). Follow-up colonoscopy was performed 3 or 5 years after baseline, per the endoscopist's recommendation. The primary endpoint was any adenoma diagnosed between randomisation and the surveillance colonoscopy.
cards.result: Overall, 43% of participants had one or more adenomas during follow-up. The adjusted risk ratios for recurrent adenomas were 0.99 (95% confidence interval 0.89 to 1.09) with vitamin D versus no vitamin D, 0.95 (0.85 to 1.06) with calcium versus no calcium, and 0.93 (0.80 to 1.08) with both agents versus neither. Findings for advanced adenomas were similar. Participants assigned to vitamin D had a mean net increase in serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D of 7.83 ng/mL relative to placebo, confirming exposure. There were few serious adverse events. The authors concluded that daily vitamin D3, calcium or both did not significantly reduce recurrent adenomas over 3 to 5 years.
cards.watchOut: The doses tested (vitamin D3 1,000 IU/day; calcium 1,200 mg/day) and the 3–5 year window bound the claim; correction of frank vitamin D deficiency is a different question, and the trial was not powered for colorectal cancer itself.
cards.source: Baron JA et al. A Trial of Calcium and Vitamin D for the Prevention of Colorectal Adenomas. N Engl J Med. 2015. PMID: 26465985. Registry ID: NCT00153816, from the record. shelves.title: Calcium supplements and myocardial infarction (Bolland)
shelves.question: In older adults (mostly women) not taking vitamin D co-supplements, do calcium supplements increase myocardial infarction and cardiovascular events?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Bone Density Conservation Agents · Calcium, Dietary · Dietary Supplements · Drug Therapy, Combination · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Myocardial Infarction · Osteoporosis · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Risk Factors · Stroke · Vitamin D
shelves.balance: This shelf's evidence is deliberately trial-level synthesis — no single trial was powered for the question — and it is contested, which is why the stamp is POSSIBLE (harm) and Tier C. Bolland 2010 (patient-level data from five trials, 8,151 participants) found myocardial infarction in 143 patients on calcium versus 111 on placebo (hazard ratio 1.31, 95% CI 1.02 to 1.67, P=0.035) — about a 30% relative increase, on small absolute numbers; stroke (HR 1.20, 0.96 to 1.50), the composite (1.18, 1.00 to 1.39) and death (1.09, 0.96 to 1.23) were not individually significant. The 2011 re-analysis of the Women's Health Initiative found the signal concentrated in women NOT already taking personal calcium supplements (hazard ratios 1.13–1.22 for cardiovascular events on calcium plus vitamin D), with nothing in women who were. The original WHI publication reported no overall increase; the re-analysis argues widespread personal supplement use diluted it. That argument is clever, post hoc, and unresolved — the balance of the randomised evidence leans to a modest real increase in myocardial infarction, of a size that matters mainly because calcium supplements are so widely taken.

cards.headline: Bolland 2010: myocardial infarction 143 on calcium vs 111 on placebo (HR 1.31, 1.02–1.67) in patient-level meta-analysis
cards.summary: Bolland 2010: myocardial infarction 143 on calcium vs 111 on placebo (HR 1.31, 1.02–1.67) in patient-level meta-analysis
cards.type: Meta-analysis of randomized trials (patient- and trial-level)
cards.people: Meta-analysis of randomised, placebo-controlled trials of calcium supplements (at least 500 mg/day) in more than 100 participants of mean age over 40, followed for more than a year, in patients not co-administered vitamin D. Five trials contributed patient-level data (8,151 participants, median follow-up 3.6 years) and 11 contributed trial-level data (11,921 participants, mean duration 4.0 years); cardiovascular outcomes came from self-reports, hospital admissions and death certificates.
cards.result: In the patient-level data, 143 people allocated to calcium had a myocardial infarction versus 111 allocated to placebo (hazard ratio 1.31, 95% confidence interval 1.02 to 1.67, P=0.035) — a 31% relative increase on low absolute counts. Non-significant increases were seen for stroke (hazard ratio 1.20, 0.96 to 1.50, P=0.11), the composite of myocardial infarction, stroke or sudden death (1.18, 1.00 to 1.39, P=0.057) and death (1.09, 0.96 to 1.23, P=0.18). The trial-level meta-analysis agreed: 296 myocardial infarctions (166 on calcium, 130 on placebo), pooled relative risk 1.27 (1.01 to 1.59, P=0.038). The authors concluded calcium supplements without vitamin D are associated with an increased risk of myocardial infarction and warranted reassessment in osteoporosis management.
cards.watchOut: The trials were bone trials: cardiovascular events were not primary endpoints, were partly self-reported, and were assembled retrospectively. The lower confidence limit sits just above 1.00 in every analysis, so modest bias in event ascertainment could manufacture the signal — the standing critique of this literature.
cards.source: Bolland MJ et al. Effect of calcium supplements on risk of myocardial infarction and cardiovascular events: meta-analysis. BMJ. 2010. PMID: 20671013. Registry ID: none (meta-analysis). cards.headline: WHI re-analysis 2011: the increase appeared only in women NOT already taking personal calcium (HRs 1.13–1.22) — the proposed explanation for WHI's own null headline
cards.summary: WHI re-analysis 2011: the increase appeared only in women NOT already taking personal calcium (HRs 1.13–1.22) — the proposed explanation for WHI's own null headline
cards.type: Re-analysis of a randomized trial plus meta-analysis
cards.people: Re-analysis of the Women's Health Initiative Calcium/Vitamin D trial limited-access dataset — 36,282 community-dwelling postmenopausal women randomised to calcium 1 g plus vitamin D 400 IU daily or placebo for seven years — combined with a meta-analysis of eight other trials. The key split: 16,718 women (46%) were not taking personal calcium supplements at randomisation; the rest were.
cards.result: There was an interaction between personal calcium use and allocated treatment. In women not taking personal calcium at randomisation, hazard ratios for cardiovascular events with calcium and vitamin D ranged from 1.13 to 1.22 (P=0.05 for clinical myocardial infarction or stroke; P=0.04 for clinical myocardial infarction or revascularisation); in women already taking personal calcium, allocation did not alter cardiovascular risk. In meta-analyses of three placebo-controlled trials, calcium and vitamin D increased myocardial infarction (relative risk 1.21, 95% confidence interval 1.01 to 1.44, P=0.04), stroke (1.20, 1.00 to 1.43, P=0.05) and their composite (1.16, 1.02 to 1.32, P=0.02). Across eight trials plus the WHI non-personal-users (28,072 participants; 1,384 incident myocardial infarctions or strokes), calcium or calcium-and-vitamin-D increased myocardial infarction (relative risk 1.24, 1.07 to 1.45, P=0.004) and the composite (1.15, 1.03 to 1.27, P=0.009).
cards.watchOut: The interaction that rescues the harm hypothesis is a subgroup analysis of a trial whose primary publication found no overall increase — post hoc by construction, however biologically plausible. Dietary calcium (from food) is not implicated by any of this; the question is supplements, typically taken as a bolus.
cards.source: Bolland MJ et al. Calcium supplements with or without vitamin D and risk of cardiovascular events: reanalysis of the Women's Health Initiative limited access dataset and meta-analysis. BMJ. 2011. PMID: 21505219. Registry ID: none (re-analysis and meta-analysis). shelves.title: Folic acid for colorectal adenoma prevention (Cole): no reduction — and a late signal of more advanced lesions
shelves.question: In patients with a history of colorectal adenomas, does folic acid 1 mg/day prevent new adenomas versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adenoma · Adult · Aged · Colorectal Neoplasms · Double-Blind Method · Female · Folic Acid · Humans · Incidence · Male · Middle Aged · Risk
shelves.balance: One large double-blind trial, and it answers no. In 1,021 patients with a recent colorectal adenoma, folic acid 1 mg/day did not reduce recurrence at the first surveillance colonoscopy (44.1% vs 42.4% on placebo) — and at the second surveillance cycle the folic acid group had more advanced lesions (11.6% vs 6.9%; relative risk 1.67, 95% CI 1.00 to 2.80), a borderline signal toward harm rather than benefit, alongside more multiple adenomas. A nutrient with a plausible protective story that, tested properly, does not prevent adenomas and may do the opposite in people who already form them. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) for the prevention claim, with the advanced-lesion signal kept on the face of the shelf.

cards.headline: Cole 2007: adenoma recurrence 44.1% on folic acid vs 42.4% on placebo — no prevention, and more advanced lesions in the second cycle
cards.summary: Cole 2007: adenoma recurrence 44.1% on folic acid vs 42.4% on placebo — no prevention, and more advanced lesions in the second cycle
cards.people: 1,021 men and women with a recent history of colorectal adenomas and no previous invasive large-bowel cancer, in a double-blind, placebo-controlled, two-factor phase 3 trial at 9 centres (1994–2004). Participants were randomised to folic acid 1 mg/day (n=516) or placebo (n=505), and separately to aspirin or placebo, with two colonoscopic surveillance cycles (first at 3 years, second 3 or 5 years later).
cards.result: First cycle (987 participants scoped): at least one adenoma in 44.1% on folic acid vs 42.4% on placebo (unadjusted relative risk 1.04, 95% CI 0.90 to 1.20, P=.58); at least one advanced lesion in 11.4% vs 8.6% (relative risk 1.32, 0.90 to 1.92, P=.15). Second cycle (607 participants): at least one adenoma in 41.9% vs 37.2% (relative risk 1.13, 0.93 to 1.37, P=.23); at least one advanced lesion in 11.6% vs 6.9% (relative risk 1.67, 1.00 to 2.80, P=.05). Folic acid was also associated with higher risks of having 3 or more adenomas and of noncolorectal cancers (no figures given in the record). No effect modification by sex, age, smoking, alcohol, BMI, baseline folate, or aspirin allocation.
cards.watchOut: The harm signal rests on the second surveillance cycle, which only 59.5% of participants completed, and its confidence interval touches 1.00 — suggestive, not proven harm. But the prevention claim needs no such caution: the primary comparison is flatly null at both cycles. Baseline folate status did not rescue the hypothesis.

shelves.title: VGX-3100 therapeutic DNA vaccine for HPV-16/18 CIN2/3: regression in one phase 2b trial, not cleanly replicated in phase 3
shelves.question: In women with HPV-16/18-associated CIN2/3, does the DNA vaccine VGX-3100 (E6/E7 plasmids delivered by electroporation) cause histopathologic regression versus placebo, sparing ablative surgery?
shelves.mesh: Cancer Vaccines · Vaccines, DNA · Papillomavirus Infections · Human papillomavirus 16 · Human papillomavirus 18 · Papillomavirus Vaccines · Uterine Cervical Dysplasia · Uterine Cervical Neoplasms · Treatment Outcome · Humans
shelves.balance: One properly randomised phase 2b trial says this therapeutic DNA vaccine can push high-grade cervical lesions backwards, but the evidence is thin. In 167 women with HPV-16/18-positive CIN2/3, histopathologic regression to CIN1 or normal occurred in 49.5% on VGX-3100 versus 30.6% on placebo in the per-protocol analysis — an absolute difference of 19.0 percentage points, but with a wide confidence interval (1.4 to 36.6) whose lower end is close to no effect, from a small placebo group. The modified intention-to-treat analysis agreed (48.2% vs 30.0%). The only clearly more common side effect was injection-site redness. This is a single phase 2b trial, and the later phase 3 programme did not cleanly replicate the result, so the finding stays fragile. PROPOSED POSSIBLE — one clean, positive, placebo-controlled trial on a real tissue endpoint, held back by its size, its wide interval, and the failure of phase 3 to confirm it cleanly.

cards.headline: Trimble 2015: regression of CIN2/3 in 49.5% on VGX-3100 vs 30.6% on placebo (difference 19.0 points, 95% CI 1.4 to 36.6)
cards.summary: Trimble 2015: regression of CIN2/3 in 49.5% on VGX-3100 vs 30.6% on placebo (difference 19.0 points, 95% CI 1.4 to 36.6)
cards.people: 167 women with CIN2/3 associated with HPV-16 or HPV-18 at 36 academic and private gynaecology practices in seven countries, randomised 3:1 to VGX-3100 6 mg (n=125) or placebo (n=42), given intramuscularly by electroporation at weeks 0, 4, and 12. Primary endpoint: histopathologic regression to CIN1 or normal pathology 36 weeks after the first dose.
cards.result: Per-protocol, regression occurred in 53 of 107 VGX-3100 recipients (49.5%) versus 11 of 36 placebo recipients (30.6%): percentage point difference 19.0 (95% CI 1.4 to 36.6), p=0.034. In the modified intention-to-treat analysis, regression occurred in 55 of 114 (48.2%) versus 12 of 40 (30.0%): difference 18.2 points (1.3 to 34.4), p=0.034. Injection-site erythema was more common on vaccine (98/125, 78.4%) than placebo (24/42, 57.1%; difference 21.3 points, 95% CI 5.3 to 37.8; p=0.007); other injection-site reactions were similar.
cards.watchOut: THIN evidence: a single phase 2b trial with only 42 women randomised to placebo (36 in the per-protocol set), so the confidence interval nearly reaches no effect. The subsequent phase 3 programme did not cleanly replicate the phase 2b result. Regression is a tissue endpoint; the trial does not show fewer cancers or fewer procedures over the long term.

shelves.title: Vacc-4x therapeutic HIV vaccine: coprimary endpoints null in an underpowered phase 2 treatment-interruption trial
shelves.question: In ART-suppressed adults with HIV-1, does the p24 peptide vaccine Vacc-4x reduce viral load after analytic treatment interruption versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Not captured at build — PubMed rendering omitted MeSH term names for PMID 24525316 (see card source note)
shelves.balance: Judged by the endpoints it set for itself, this trial did not work. Vacc-4x, a p24 peptide therapeutic vaccine, was tested in ART-suppressed adults who then interrupted treatment. Enrolment stopped early — only 136 of a planned 345 participants were randomised — and BOTH coprimary endpoints were negative: the proportions resuming combination ART were 34% on vaccine versus 29% on placebo, and the change in CD4 percentage did not differ between groups (difference −5.71, 95% CI −13.01 to 1.59). Viral load was lower in the vaccine group at weeks 48 and 52 of the interruption follow-up, a secondary finding in an underpowered trial, and one possibly related serious adverse event (an exacerbation of multiple sclerosis) occurred on vaccine. A lower viral-load set-point in secondary analyses is a hypothesis, not a demonstrated benefit. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) — an underpowered phase 2 trial whose coprimary endpoints were both null; the viral-load signal is hypothesis-generating only.

cards.headline: Pollard 2014: Vacc-4x missed both coprimary endpoints after treatment interruption; viral load lower only in later secondary measures
cards.summary: Pollard 2014: Vacc-4x missed both coprimary endpoints after treatment interruption; viral load lower only in later secondary measures
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled phase 2 trial (enrolment stopped early)
cards.people: Adults aged 18–55 with HIV-1, viral load below 50 copies/mL on combination ART and CD4 count at least 400 cells/µL, at 18 sites in Germany, Italy, Spain, the UK, and the USA. Of 345 planned participants, enrolment stopped early: 174 were screened and 136 randomised to Vacc-4x (n=93) or placebo (n=43), followed by analytic treatment interruption. Coprimary endpoints: the proportion resuming ART and the change in percentage of CD4-positive T cells.
cards.result: Neither coprimary endpoint was met. ART was resumed by 34% (30 participants) in the Vacc-4x group versus 29% (11) on placebo, and the between-group difference in CD4 percentage change was −5.71 (95% CI −13.01 to 1.59). Viral load after interruption was lower on vaccine at week 48 (median 23,100 vs 71,800 copies/mL, p=0.025) and week 52 (median 19,550 vs 51,000 copies/mL, p=0.041) — secondary measures, not the coprimary endpoints. One serious adverse event possibly related to vaccination occurred (exacerbation of multiple sclerosis).
cards.watchOut: THIN evidence with null coprimaries: do not let the lower week-48/52 viral loads upgrade this shelf — they are secondary endpoints in a trial that stopped at 136 of 345 planned participants, so it was underpowered even for its own primary questions. Viral-load set-point after interruption is also a surrogate; no clinical outcome was tested.
cards.source: Pollard et al. A phase 2 randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial of the therapeutic HIV vaccine Vacc-4x with treatment interruption. Lancet Infect Dis. 2014. PMID: 24525316. Registry ID: NCT00659789, from the record. shelves.title: CMV glycoprotein B/MF59 vaccine in postpartum women: 50% efficacy in one phase 2 trial, never taken to phase 3
shelves.question: In CMV-seronegative women within a year of giving birth, does recombinant glycoprotein B vaccine with MF59 adjuvant prevent primary CMV infection versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Cytomegalovirus Infections · Cytomegalovirus Vaccines · Adjuvants, Immunologic · Postpartum Period · Pregnancy Complications, Infectious · Treatment Outcome · Humans
shelves.balance: A single phase 2 trial found that a recombinant cytomegalovirus glycoprotein B vaccine with MF59 adjuvant roughly halved primary CMV infection in seronegative women in the year after childbirth: vaccine efficacy 50% (95% CI 7 to 73) per 100 person-years, with 18 infections on vaccine versus 31 on placebo over 42 months. The confidence interval is wide — the true efficacy could be as low as 7% — the trial was stopped at an interim efficacy analysis, and no phase 3 trial ever followed to confirm it. Congenital infections in subsequent pregnancies were too few to judge (1 vs 3). Local and systemic reactions were more common on vaccine. PROPOSED POSSIBLE — a genuine randomised signal on the infection endpoint itself, but from one phase 2 trial stopped early and never confirmed.

cards.headline: Pass 2009: CMV gB/MF59 vaccine efficacy 50% (95% CI 7 to 73) against primary infection in postpartum women
cards.summary: Pass 2009: CMV gB/MF59 vaccine efficacy 50% (95% CI 7 to 73) against primary infection in postpartum women
cards.people: 464 CMV-seronegative women within 1 year after giving birth (234 vaccine, 230 placebo), given recombinant CMV glycoprotein B vaccine with MF59 adjuvant or placebo at 0, 1, and 6 months and followed for 42 months. Primary question: prevention of primary CMV infection, detected by antibody to non-vaccine CMV antigens or by virus isolation/PCR.
cards.result: CMV infection occurred in 18 women in the vaccine group versus 31 in the placebo group. Based on infection rates per 100 person-years, vaccine efficacy was 50% (95% CI 7 to 73); a Kaplan–Meier analysis gave P=0.02 for the difference between groups. Congenital CMV infection occurred in 1 infant in the vaccine group versus 3 in the placebo group — too few events to interpret. Local and systemic reactions were more frequent after vaccine than placebo. The trial was stopped at an interim efficacy analysis.
cards.watchOut: THIN evidence: one phase 2 trial, stopped at an interim efficacy look (which tends to flatter the estimate), with a confidence interval reaching down to 7% efficacy, and no phase 3 confirmation in the years since. Preventing maternal infection is the endpoint shown; preventing congenital CMV disease was not demonstrated (1 vs 3 events).
cards.source: Pass et al. Vaccine prevention of maternal cytomegalovirus infection. N Engl J Med. 2009. PMID: 19297572. Registry ID: NCT00125502, from the record. shelves.title: Intranasal norovirus VLP vaccine: prevented illness in a human challenge trial; field efficacy untested
shelves.question: In healthy adults, does an intranasal norovirus virus-like-particle vaccine prevent gastroenteritis after experimental Norwalk virus (GI.1) challenge versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Norovirus · Caliciviridae Infections · Gastroenteritis · Viral Vaccines · Administration, Intranasal · Humans
shelves.balance: Inside a human challenge model, this intranasal norovirus virus-like-particle vaccine worked: after volunteers were deliberately infected with the homologous Norwalk virus (GI.1) strain, gastroenteritis occurred in 37% of vaccinees versus 69% on placebo (P=0.006), and infection itself was less frequent (61% vs 82%, P=0.05). But this is a small challenge study — 77 people in the per-protocol analysis — using one laboratory strain matched to the vaccine, in healthy adults. It shows the vaccine can protect against an artificial exposure to its own strain; it does not show protection against the varied norovirus strains people meet in the community. PROPOSED POSSIBLE — a clear positive result on the exact question the challenge model asks, with field efficacy untested for this formulation.

cards.headline: Atmar 2011: norovirus illness after challenge in 37% on vaccine vs 69% on placebo (P=0.006)
cards.summary: Atmar 2011: norovirus illness after challenge in 37% on vaccine vs 69% on placebo (P=0.006)
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled human challenge trial
cards.people: 98 healthy adults enrolled (50 vaccine, 48 placebo) at multiple US centres; 90 received both intranasal doses of norovirus virus-like-particle vaccine (with chitosan and monophosphoryl lipid A adjuvants) or placebo, and 77 of the 84 inoculated volunteers were in the per-protocol analysis after challenge with the homologous Norwalk virus GI.1 strain. Endpoints: Norwalk-virus gastroenteritis and infection after challenge.
cards.result: Virus-specific IgA seroresponse occurred in 70% of vaccine recipients. After challenge, gastroenteritis occurred in 37% of vaccinees versus 69% of placebo recipients (P=0.006) — an absolute reduction of about 32 percentage points within the challenge model — and Norwalk virus infection occurred in 61% versus 82% (P=0.05). Illness in vaccinees who did become ill was not the primary focus; protection was against the vaccine-matched GI.1 strain only.
cards.watchOut: THIN evidence by design: a challenge trial is a proof of concept, not field efficacy. The challenge strain was the same GI.1 strain the vaccine was built from; circulating norovirus is dominated by other genotypes (notably GII.4), the volunteers were healthy adults, and the per-protocol set was 77 people. Do not read this as evidence the vaccine prevents community norovirus illness.
cards.source: Atmar et al. Norovirus vaccine against experimental human Norwalk virus illness. N Engl J Med. 2011. PMID: 22150036. Registry ID: NCT00973284, from the record. shelves.title: C. difficile toxoid vaccine (CLOVER): phase 3 trial of 17,535 adults did not prevent first CDI
shelves.question: In adults aged 50 years or older at increased risk of Clostridioides difficile infection, does the detoxified toxin-A/B vaccine PF-06425090 prevent a first CDI episode versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Clostridioides difficile · Clostridium Infections · Bacterial Vaccines · Bacterial Toxins · Enterotoxins · Aged · Humans
shelves.balance: The definitive trial was negative. CLOVER randomised 17,535 adults aged 50 or older at increased risk of C. difficile infection to the detoxified toxin A/B vaccine PF-06425090 (the specific tested product, an investigational vaccine that is not FDA-approved) or placebo. The primary endpoint was not met: first CDI at least 14 days after dose 3 occurred in 17 vaccine versus 25 placebo recipients, a vaccine efficacy of 31.0% relative whose 96.4% confidence interval (−38.7 to 66.6) crosses zero widely; the post-dose-2 analysis was the same story (24 vs 34; efficacy 28.6%, CI −28.4 to 61.0). Two softer signals appeared — CDI episodes were shorter on vaccine (median 1 vs 4 days, nominal P=0.02) and in a post hoc analysis no vaccinee versus 11 placebo recipients sought medical attention for CDI — but neither rescues a missed primary endpoint. PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — a very large phase 3 trial that did not prevent first CDI as tested; the duration and care-seeking findings are nominal and post hoc, not evidence of protection.

cards.headline: Donskey 2024 (CLOVER): primary endpoint not met — vaccine efficacy 31.0% (96.4% CI −38.7 to 66.6) against first CDI
cards.summary: Donskey 2024 (CLOVER): primary endpoint not met — vaccine efficacy 31.0% (96.4% CI −38.7 to 66.6) against first CDI
cards.people: 17,535 adults aged 50 years or older at increased risk of Clostridioides difficile infection, randomised to the C. difficile toxoid vaccine PF-06425090 or placebo in three doses at 0, 1, and 6 months. Primary endpoint: first CDI episode at least 14 days after the third dose.
cards.result: First CDI at least 14 days post-dose 3: 17 cases on vaccine versus 25 on placebo; vaccine efficacy 31.0% relative (96.4% CI −38.7 to 66.6) — the primary endpoint was not met. After dose 2: 24 versus 34 cases, efficacy 28.6% (−28.4 to 61.0). Median CDI duration was 1 day on vaccine versus 4 days on placebo (nominal P=0.02), and post hoc, 0 vaccine versus 11 placebo recipients sought medical attention for CDI, with 0 versus 10 requiring CDI antibiotics. Local reactions were more frequent on vaccine; overall adverse-event rates were similar.
cards.watchOut: Event counts were small (17 vs 25) despite the huge enrolment, so the efficacy interval is wide in both directions — the trial shows no demonstrated protection, not proof of exactly zero effect. The shorter-duration and medical-attention findings carry only nominal or post hoc p-values and were not the primary endpoint; treat them as hypothesis-generating.

shelves.title: V710 S. aureus vaccine before cardiothoracic surgery: no protection, and higher mortality in vaccinees who became infected (Tier C)
shelves.question: In adults scheduled for cardiothoracic surgery with median sternotomy, does preoperative V710 (IsdB) vaccination prevent serious postoperative Staphylococcus aureus infection versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Staphylococcus aureus · Staphylococcal Infections · Staphylococcal Vaccines · Bacteremia · Surgical Wound Infection · Sternotomy · Cardiovascular Surgical Procedures · Humans
shelves.balance: This vaccine failed on benefit and raised a harm flag: a SPLIT verdict. On prevention, V710 (an IsdB staphylococcus aureus vaccine given before cardiothoracic surgery) made no difference: the primary outcome of S. aureus bacteraemia or deep sternal wound infection occurred at 2.6 versus 3.2 per 100 person-years (relative risk 0.81, 95% CI 0.44 to 1.48; P=0.58). On harm, among the minority who did develop S. aureus infection, mortality was far higher in vaccinees than in placebo recipients — 23.0 versus 4.2 deaths per 100 person-years, a difference of 18.8 (95% CI 8.0 to 34.1) — and multiorgan failure was also more frequent on vaccine (31 vs 17 events, P=0.04), while all-cause mortality overall did not differ significantly (5.7 vs 5.0 per 100 person-years, P=0.20). The trial was terminated after its second interim analysis for safety and low efficacy. PROPOSED SPLIT — (the treatment made no difference) for prevention; POSSIBLE (harm) for death once S. aureus infection occurred. Tier C: the developer reviews this shelf personally because of the mortality signal.

cards.headline: Fowler 2013: V710 did not prevent S. aureus bacteraemia/deep sternal infection (RR 0.81, 95% CI 0.44 to 1.48) — but infected vaccinees died far more often
cards.summary: Fowler 2013: V710 did not prevent S. aureus bacteraemia/deep sternal infection (RR 0.81, 95% CI 0.44 to 1.48) — but infected vaccinees died far more often
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled event-driven trial (terminated early)
cards.people: 8,031 adults scheduled for cardiothoracic surgery with median sternotomy at 165 sites in 26 countries, randomised to a single preoperative dose of V710 (n=4,015) or placebo (n=4,016). Primary outcome: S. aureus bacteraemia or deep sternal wound infection in the efficacy population (3,528 vaccine, 3,517 placebo). The trial was terminated after the second interim analysis.
cards.result: Primary outcome: 22 events on V710 (2.6 per 100 person-years) versus 27 on placebo (3.2 per 100 person-years); relative risk 0.81 (95% CI 0.44 to 1.48), P=0.58 — no prevention benefit. Among participants who developed S. aureus infection, mortality was 15 of 73 on vaccine (23.0 per 100 person-years) versus 4 of 96 on placebo (4.2 per 100 person-years), a difference of 18.8 per 100 person-years (95% CI 8.0 to 34.1). Multiorgan failure occurred in 31 vaccine versus 17 placebo recipients (P=0.04). All-cause mortality did not differ significantly overall: 5.7 versus 5.0 per 100 person-years (P=0.20).
cards.watchOut: Tier C harm signal. The mortality excess appeared only within the subgroup who became infected (15/73 vs 4/96) — a post-randomisation subgroup, so it cannot be read with the same force as a primary endpoint — but it was large, it came with more multiorgan failure, and it contributed to stopping the trial. The split stamp keeps the two findings separate: no benefit, possible harm.
cards.source: Fowler et al. Effect of an investigational vaccine for preventing Staphylococcus aureus infections after cardiothoracic surgery: a randomized trial. JAMA. 2013. PMID: 23549582. shelves.title: Recombinant zoster vaccine after autologous stem cell transplant (ZOE-HSCT): confirmed zoster cut by about two-thirds
shelves.question: In adults who have just undergone autologous haematopoietic stem cell transplantation, do two doses of adjuvanted recombinant zoster vaccine prevent herpes zoster versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Not captured at build — PubMed rendering omitted MeSH term names for PMID 31287523 (see card source note)
shelves.balance: In one of the most immunosuppressed populations ever vaccinated in a trial, the adjuvanted recombinant zoster vaccine worked clearly. ZOE-HSCT randomised 1,846 adults within 50–70 days of autologous stem cell transplantation: confirmed herpes zoster occurred in 49 vaccine versus 135 placebo recipients — incidence 30 versus 94 cases per 1,000 person-years, an incidence rate ratio of 0.32 (95% CI 0.22 to 0.44), i.e. vaccine efficacy of 68.2% in relative terms, over a median 21 months of follow-up. This is a single phase 3 trial, but it is large, placebo-controlled, in exactly the population the question asks about, and the effect is big with a tight interval. It answers a different question from the older-adult zoster trials: protection in the early post-transplant window. PROPOSED LIKELY — one large, definitive phase 3 trial with a two-thirds relative reduction in confirmed zoster and absolute rates printed alongside.

cards.headline: Bastidas 2019 (ZOE-HSCT): confirmed zoster 49 vs 135 cases; incidence 30 vs 94 per 1,000 person-years (IRR 0.32, 95% CI 0.22 to 0.44)
cards.summary: Bastidas 2019 (ZOE-HSCT): confirmed zoster 49 vs 135 cases; incidence 30 vs 94 per 1,000 person-years (IRR 0.32, 95% CI 0.22 to 0.44)
cards.people: 1,846 adults (922 vaccine, 924 placebo) at 167 centres in 28 countries who had undergone autologous haematopoietic stem cell transplantation 50–70 days earlier, randomised to two doses of adjuvanted recombinant zoster vaccine or placebo. Primary endpoint: confirmed herpes zoster; median follow-up 21 months.
cards.result: Confirmed herpes zoster occurred in 49 vaccine recipients versus 135 placebo recipients: incidence 30 versus 94 per 1,000 person-years; incidence rate ratio 0.32 (95% CI 0.22 to 0.44), P<0.001. That corresponds to vaccine efficacy of 68.2% in relative terms, against an absolute background rate of 94 cases per 1,000 person-years on placebo — a high-risk window in which the vaccine prevented roughly 64 cases per 1,000 person-years.
cards.watchOut: Single trial for this specific post-transplant question (it is not one of the DOUBLE-A shelves), and follow-up was a median of 21 months, so durability beyond the early post-transplant years is less certain. The population is autologous transplant recipients vaccinated 50–70 days post-transplant; results do not automatically extend to allogeneic recipients or to vaccination before transplant.

shelves.title: High-dose vs standard-dose influenza vaccine in transplant recipients: better antibody responses, clinical benefit untested
shelves.question: In adult solid-organ transplant recipients, does high-dose influenza vaccine improve immunogenicity versus standard-dose vaccine?
shelves.mesh: Influenza Vaccines · Organ Transplantation · Transplant Recipients · Seroconversion · Dose-Response Relationship, Immunologic · Humans
shelves.balance: High-dose influenza vaccine produced clearly stronger antibody responses than standard-dose vaccine in transplant recipients — on the only kind of endpoint this trial measured. In 172 solid-organ transplant recipients in the 2016–17 season, seroconversion to at least one vaccine antigen occurred in 78.6% with high-dose versus 55.8% with standard-dose vaccine (P<0.001), with the advantage present for every strain (A/H1N1 40.5% vs 20.5%; A/H3N2 57.1% vs 32.5%; B 58.3% vs 41.6%); the adjusted odds ratio for seroconversion was 3.23 (95% CI 1.56 to 6.67). But seroconversion is an immunogenicity surrogate: the trial was a single season, 161 analysed patients, and measured no clinical outcomes — not influenza illness, hospitalisation, or rejection. PROPOSED POSSIBLE — a clean randomised immunogenicity result, capped by the surrogate endpoint and the small, single-season design (THIN).

cards.headline: Natori 2018: seroconversion to ≥1 antigen 78.6% with high-dose vs 55.8% with standard-dose vaccine (P<0.001)
cards.summary: Natori 2018: seroconversion to ≥1 antigen 78.6% with high-dose vs 55.8% with standard-dose vaccine (P<0.001)
cards.people: 172 adult solid-organ transplant recipients enrolled in the 2016–17 influenza season; 161 were analysed (84 high-dose, 77 standard-dose) in a double-blind randomised trial comparing the high-dose influenza vaccine (Fluzone HD, Sanofi — the specific tested product) with standard-dose vaccine (Fluviral, GSK — the specific tested product). Outcomes were immunogenicity (seroconversion and antibody titres), not clinical influenza.
cards.result: Seroconversion to at least one antigen: 78.6% on high-dose versus 55.8% on standard-dose vaccine (P<0.001). By strain: A/H1N1 40.5% vs 20.5% (P=0.006); A/H3N2 57.1% vs 32.5% (P=0.002); B 58.3% vs 41.6% (P=0.028). The odds ratio for seroconversion with high-dose vaccine was 3.23 (95% CI 1.56 to 6.67). No clinical endpoints (influenza illness, hospitalisation) were assessed.
cards.watchOut: THIN evidence for any clinical claim: one season, 161 analysed patients, antibody endpoints only. Stronger seroconversion does not by itself prove fewer influenza illnesses or hospitalisations in transplant recipients. Distinct question from high-dose vaccine in older adults generally, which has its own shelf.

shelves.question: In predominantly HIV-infected adolescents and adults who have recovered from invasive pneumococcal disease, does 7-valent pneumococcal conjugate vaccine prevent further vaccine-serotype invasive disease versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Pneumococcal Vaccines · Heptavalent Pneumococcal Conjugate Vaccine · Vaccines, Conjugate · HIV Infections · Pneumonia, Pneumococcal · Streptococcus pneumoniae · Humans
shelves.balance: OUTSTANDING-SINGLE: this shelf rests on one randomised trial, and it is flagged as such. In Malawi, 496 adolescents and adults who had recovered from invasive pneumococcal disease — 88% of them HIV-positive — were randomised to 7-valent pneumococcal conjugate vaccine or placebo. Vaccine-serotype or serotype 6A invasive episodes occurred in 5 vaccine versus 19 placebo recipients: vaccine efficacy 74% in relative terms (95% CI 30 to 90) over 798 person-years of follow-up. That is a large effect on a hard clinical endpoint in a population with no other proven option, and it is the trial that established conjugate (not just polysaccharide) vaccination for HIV-infected adults. The honest limits: a single trial, and no mortality benefit — deaths were 73 on vaccine versus 63 on placebo (HR 1.18, 95% CI 0.84 to 1.66). Serious adverse events within 14 days were fewer on vaccine (3 vs 17, P=0.002); minor reactions were more common (41 vs 13, P=0.003). PROPOSED LIKELY — a single double-blind trial with a large, significant effect on invasive disease itself; the OUTSTANDING-SINGLE flag stays on the shelf because there is no second trial.

cards.headline: French 2010: vaccine-serotype invasive pneumococcal disease 5 vs 19 episodes — efficacy 74% (95% CI 30 to 90); no mortality benefit
cards.summary: French 2010: vaccine-serotype invasive pneumococcal disease 5 vs 19 episodes — efficacy 74% (95% CI 30 to 90); no mortality benefit
cards.people: 496 adolescents and adults in Malawi who had recovered from invasive pneumococcal disease (44% male; 88% HIV-positive), randomised to two doses of 7-valent pneumococcal conjugate vaccine or placebo and followed for 798 person-years. Primary endpoint: further invasive pneumococcal disease caused by vaccine serotypes or serotype 6A.
cards.result: Vaccine-serotype/6A invasive episodes: 5 in the vaccine group versus 19 in the placebo group — vaccine efficacy 74% in relative terms (95% CI 30 to 90). All-cause mortality did not improve: 73 deaths on vaccine versus 63 on placebo (HR 1.18, 95% CI 0.84 to 1.66). Serious adverse events within 14 days of vaccination were less frequent on vaccine (3 vs 17, P=0.002); minor adverse events were more frequent (41 vs 13, P=0.003).
cards.watchOut: OUTSTANDING-SINGLE: one trial only — there is no confirmatory second randomised trial in this population. The endpoint prevented is recurrent invasive disease, not death: the mortality hazard ratio was 1.18 with an interval spanning 0.84 to 1.66, so no survival claim can be made. Participants were survivors of a first invasive episode in Malawi, most with HIV; absolute rates elsewhere will differ.
cards.source: French et al. A trial of a 7-valent pneumococcal conjugate vaccine in HIV-infected adults. N Engl J Med. 2010. PMID: 20200385. Registry ID: ISRCTN54494731, from the record. shelves.title: ExPEC9V vaccine in older adults (E.mbrace): no protection against invasive E. coli disease; stopped for futility
shelves.question: In adults aged 60 years or older with a recent UTI history, does the nine-valent ExPEC conjugate vaccine (ExPEC9V) prevent invasive E. coli disease caused by vaccine O-serotypes versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Not yet assigned on the PubMed record at build (online ahead of print) — see card source note
shelves.balance: The definitive trial showed no protection. E.mbrace randomised over 17,600 adults aged 60 or older with a urinary tract infection in the previous 2 years to the nine-valent extraintestinal pathogenic E. coli vaccine ExPEC9V (the specific tested product) or placebo. Invasive E. coli disease caused by vaccine O-serotypes occurred in 11 vaccine versus 13 placebo recipients — vaccine efficacy 14.63% in relative terms with a 95% confidence interval from −106.57 to 65.38, squarely consistent with no effect. The trial was stopped at its prespecified futility analysis despite the vaccine producing robust antibody responses, and development of the vaccine was discontinued. Antibodies rose; disease did not fall. PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — a very large phase 3 trial, stopped for futility, with a point estimate near zero.

cards.headline: Bonten 2026 (E.mbrace): invasive E. coli disease 11 vs 13 cases — efficacy 14.63% (95% CI −106.57 to 65.38); stopped for futility
cards.summary: Bonten 2026 (E.mbrace): invasive E. coli disease 11 vs 13 cases — efficacy 14.63% (95% CI −106.57 to 65.38); stopped for futility
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled phase 3 trial (E.mbrace; stopped for futility)
cards.people: 17,701 vaccinated adults aged 60 years or older with a UTI in the prior 2 years at 332 sites in 20 countries (per-protocol population 17,637: 8,858 vaccine, 8,843 placebo), randomised to the nine-valent ExPEC conjugate vaccine ExPEC9V or placebo. Primary endpoint: invasive E. coli disease caused by vaccine O-serotypes.
cards.result: Invasive E. coli disease from vaccine serotypes: 11 cases on vaccine versus 13 on placebo; vaccine efficacy 14.63% in relative terms (95% CI −106.57 to 65.38) — no protective effect. The trial was stopped at the prespecified futility analysis, and vaccine development was discontinued, even though antibody responses to the vaccine were robust.
cards.watchOut: Event counts were low (11 vs 13) because invasive disease is uncommon even in this enriched population, so the interval is wide; the correct reading is 'no demonstrated protection, development stopped at futility', with a point estimate close to zero. Immunogenicity was strong — this is a case where antibody response did not translate into clinical protection.
cards.source: Bonten et al. Nine-valent ExPEC vaccine in older adults with recent UTI (E.mbrace). Lancet Infect Dis. 2026 (online ahead of print). PMID: 42863477. Registry ID: NCT04899336, from the record. shelves.title: The enzyme humans don't make: alpha-galactosidase (Beano) for bean-and-vegetable gas
shelves.question: Does alpha-galactosidase (Beano), taken with a meal, prevent the gas produced by beans, lentils and cruciferous vegetables — and does it help people with IBS?
shelves.mesh: alpha-Galactosidase · Flatulence · Oligosaccharides · Irritable Bowel Syndrome · Fermentation · Breath Tests · Cross-Over Studies · Double-Blind Method · Acarbose · Humans
shelves.balance: Split: POSSIBLE — preventing meal-challenge gas · MAYBE (weak evidence) — routine use in IBS. Humans make no alpha-galactosidase, so the raffinose and stachyose in beans, lentils and cruciferous vegetables reach the colon intact and are fermented into gas. Supplying the enzyme by mouth works in challenge tests: it cut flatulence after a meatless-chili meal in a double-blind crossover trial (Ganiats 1994), reduced breath hydrogen and flatulence severity after a 420 g bean meal (Di Stefano 2007), reduced gas-related distress in children over 2 weeks (Di Nardo 2013), and relieved symptoms in the galacto-oligosaccharide-sensitive subgroup of IBS patients on a GOS challenge (Tuck 2018). Given as routine treatment to unselected IBS patients it did not beat placebo — a 12-week trial of 125 patients found no evidence for routine use and more withdrawals on the enzyme (Hillilä 2016), and a 20-patient crossover pilot found no difference in symptoms or breath gases (Böhn 2021). One caution with a diabetes edge: in patients taking acarbose, Beano reduced acarbose flatulence but partly blunted acarbose's glucose-lowering (Lettieri 1998). Shelf #1 (the Prevention hub) gains a pointer to this shelf at next deploy. Alpha-galactosidase to clear bowel gas before ultrasound is an imaging-preparation question (PMID 23730387), fenced, not carded. Drafted Nov 9, 2026 at the developer's request (practical over-the-counter questions series, with Shelf #2431).

cards.headline: Ganiats 1994: Beano cut flatulence after a bean meal — events per hour significantly fewer than placebo (P=.016); bloating and pain unchanged
cards.summary: Ganiats 1994: Beano cut flatulence after a bean meal — events per hour significantly fewer than placebo (P=.016); bloating and pain unchanged
cards.people: 19 subjects fed test meals of meatless chili; 8 drops of alpha-galactosidase solution or placebo at the first meal, crossed over one week later, with symptom and flatus recording for 6 hours after each meal. The abstract does not state mean age or the sex mix.
cards.result: The number of flatulence events per hour was significantly less on alpha-galactosidase than placebo over the 6-hour follow-up period (P=.016); in hour-by-hour comparisons the difference reached significance only in the fifth hour (P=.04). No differences were found in the extent of bloating or abdominal pain.
cards.watchOut: Nineteen subjects and a single test meal: this is a proof-of-mechanism trial — it shows the enzyme can cut gas from a fermentable meal, not that it helps chronic symptoms.
cards.source: Ganiats TG, Norcross WA, Halverson AL et al. Does Beano prevent gas? A double-blind crossover study of oral alpha-galactosidase to treat dietary oligosaccharide intolerance. J Fam Pract. 1994;39(5):441-5. PMID: 7964541. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields — pre-registration-era trial. cards.headline: Di Stefano 2007: 1,200 GalU with a 420 g bean meal cut breath hydrogen and flatulence severity; both doses cut the total symptom score
cards.summary: Di Stefano 2007: 1,200 GalU with a 420 g bean meal cut breath hydrogen and flatulence severity; both doses cut the total symptom score
cards.people: 8 healthy volunteers who ingested 300 or 1,200 GalU of alpha-galactosidase or placebo during a test meal containing 420 g of cooked beans, with breath hydrogen excretion and bloating, pain, discomfort, flatulence and diarrhoea measured for 8 hours.
cards.result: The 1,200 GalU dose induced a significant reduction of both breath hydrogen excretion and the severity of flatulence; a reduction in severity was apparent for all symptoms considered, and both the 300 and 1,200 GalU doses induced a significant reduction in the total symptom score.
cards.watchOut: Eight volunteers: the smallest card on this shelf — a physiology demonstration whose direction agrees with the larger challenge trials, weighted as such.
cards.source: Di Stefano M, Miceli E, Gotti S et al. The effect of oral alpha-galactosidase on intestinal gas production and gas-related symptoms. Dig Dis Sci. 2007;52(1):78-83. PMID: 17151807. cards.headline: Di Nardo 2013: in children with gas-related symptoms, alpha-galactosidase reduced global distress (P=.02), bloating days (P=.03) and flatulence (P=.02) over 2 weeks
cards.summary: Di Nardo 2013: in children with gas-related symptoms, alpha-galactosidase reduced global distress (P=.02), bloating days (P=.03) and flatulence (P=.02) over 2 weeks
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, parallel-group trial (single centre)
cards.people: 52 children aged 4 to 17 years (32 female) with chronic or recurrent gas-related symptoms, randomised to alpha-galactosidase (27) or placebo (25), given as drops or tablets according to body weight for 2 weeks.
cards.result: Alpha-galactosidase significantly reduced global distress on the Faces Pain Scale-Revised compared with placebo (P=.02), decreased the number of days with moderate-to-severe bloating (P=.03) and the proportion of patients with flatulence (P=.02). No significant differences were found for abdominal spasms or abdominal distension, and no adverse events were reported.
cards.watchOut: Two weeks, one centre, 52 children, and a pain-scale primary endpoint for a gas question: supportive, not definitive — the authors themselves call for larger and longer trials.
cards.source: Di Nardo G, Oliva S, Ferrari F et al. Efficacy and tolerability of α-galactosidase in treating gas-related symptoms in children: a randomized, double-blind, placebo controlled trial. BMC Gastroenterol. 2013;13:142. PMID: 24063420. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT01595932, from the record's databank fields. cards.headline: Tuck 2018: on a galacto-oligosaccharide challenge, full-dose enzyme relieved symptoms in the GOS-sensitive IBS subgroup (overall symptoms 5.5 vs 24.5 mm; P=.006)
cards.summary: Tuck 2018: on a galacto-oligosaccharide challenge, full-dose enzyme relieved symptoms in the GOS-sensitive IBS subgroup (overall symptoms 5.5 vs 24.5 mm; P=.006)
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover trial (IBS, GOS challenge)
cards.people: 31 patients meeting Rome III criteria for IBS who were hydrogen-producers on breath testing, treated in random order with full-dose (300 GALU) alpha-galactosidase, half-dose (150 GALU) and placebo (glucose), each arm with a 3-day low-FODMAP run-in followed by 3 days of a provided high-GOS diet.
cards.result: The high-GOS diet increased symptoms, with 21 of the 31 patients GOS-sensitive (a >10 mm rise in overall symptoms). In those 21, full-dose enzyme reduced overall symptoms (median 5.5 mm with enzyme versus 24.5 mm without, on a 100 mm scale; P=0.006) and bloating (6.5 vs 20.5 mm; P=0.017).
cards.watchOut: A subgroup (the GOS-sensitive 21 of 31) inside a challenge design: it identifies who benefits — patients whose symptoms are provoked by galacto-oligosaccharides — and says nothing for IBS patients without that sensitivity.
cards.source: Tuck CJ, Taylor KM, Gibson PR et al. Increasing Symptoms in Irritable Bowel Symptoms With Ingestion of Galacto-Oligosaccharides Are Mitigated by α-Galactosidase Treatment. Am J Gastroenterol. 2018;113(1):124-134. PMID: 28809383. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields.
