cards.headline: Hillilä 2016: 12 weeks of alpha-galactosidase did not relieve IBS — no evidence for routine use, and more patients withdrew on the enzyme
cards.summary: Hillilä 2016: 12 weeks of alpha-galactosidase did not relieve IBS — no evidence for routine use, and more patients withdrew on the enzyme
cards.people: 125 subjects with IBS and abdominal bloating or flatulence received alpha-galactosidase or placebo at meals for 12 weeks, with IBS Symptom Severity Score and quality of life assessed at baseline, during treatment and at 4-week follow-up.
cards.result: The enzyme showed only a trend toward a more prominent decrease in IBS-SSS; the responder rate at week 16 was higher in the enzyme group, but quality of life did not differ between groups. Twenty-five patients withdrew — 18 in the alpha-galactosidase group versus 7 on placebo (P=0.016) — with abdominal pain and diarrhoea more often reported as the reason for withdrawal in the enzyme group. The authors conclude they found no evidence to support routine use of alpha-galactosidase in IBS patients.
cards.watchOut: The week-16 responder signal may be an artefact of differential dropout (non-responders leaving the enzyme arm), as the authors themselves note; the trial's headline is the null.

cards.headline: Böhn 2021: in an IBS crossover pilot, alpha-galactosidase with high-oligosaccharide meals beat placebo on nothing — symptoms and breath gases identical
cards.summary: Böhn 2021: in an IBS crossover pilot, alpha-galactosidase with high-oligosaccharide meals beat placebo on nothing — symptoms and breath gases identical
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover pilot study
cards.people: 20 adults with IBS (19 women; mean age 49 years, range 22–75) given alpha-galactosidase 1,200 GaIU per meal (Nogasin) or placebo capsules with three standardised meals high in oligosaccharides, with symptom ratings and breath hydrogen and methane measured every 30 minutes over 7.5 hours.
cards.result: Neither gastrointestinal symptom ratings over time nor hydrogen and methane concentrations differed between the alpha-galactosidase and placebo days. Severity of abdominal pain and bloating was lower the following morning than at baseline, with no difference between enzyme and placebo. The authors conclude alpha-galactosidase was not superior to placebo in reducing postprandial symptoms or gas production in IBS.
cards.watchOut: A 20-patient pilot — small, but it is a direct null in exactly the population the IBS claim needs, and it aligns with the larger 12-week null on the card above.
cards.source: Böhn L, Törnblom H, Van Oudenhove L et al. cards.headline: Lettieri 1998: Beano cut acarbose flatulence (score 0.79 vs 1.09) and breath hydrogen (31.2 vs 50.5 ppm) — but partly blunted acarbose's glucose-lowering
cards.summary: Lettieri 1998: Beano cut acarbose flatulence (score 0.79 vs 1.09) and breath hydrogen (31.2 vs 50.5 ppm) — but partly blunted acarbose's glucose-lowering
cards.type: Randomised, double-masked, placebo-controlled, three-period crossover study (type 2 diabetes)
cards.people: 37 patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus (20 men, 17 women; ages 36–72) received, in random order across three 3-day periods, acarbose 100 mg, acarbose 100 mg plus Beano, or placebo, with Beano given at the beginning of each of three meals daily.
cards.result: Patients who took Beano with acarbose had a significantly lower flatulence score than on acarbose alone (0.79 vs 1.09), and breath hydrogen was lower (31.2 vs 50.5 ppm). However, postprandial serum glucose levels were higher with acarbose plus Beano than with acarbose alone — Beano appeared to diminish acarbose's activity — although both acarbose treatments still lowered postprandial glucose significantly versus placebo.
cards.watchOut: The interaction is the point for a diabetes audience: an enzyme that pre-digests carbohydrate can work against a drug whose job is to slow carbohydrate digestion. Patients on acarbose should not add Beano casually.
cards.source: Lettieri JT, Dain B. Effects of beano on the tolerability and pharmacodynamics of acarbose. Clin Ther. 1998;20(3):497-504. PMID: 9663365. cards.headline: Synthesis: the enzyme prevents challenge-meal gas — POSSIBLE; as routine IBS treatment it failed its trials — MAYBE (weak evidence)
cards.summary: Synthesis: the enzyme prevents challenge-meal gas — POSSIBLE; as routine IBS treatment it failed its trials — MAYBE (weak evidence)
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: Ganiats 1994 (19 adults, meal challenge), Di Stefano 2007 (8 healthy volunteers, bean meal), Di Nardo 2013 (52 children), Tuck 2018 (31 IBS patients, GOS challenge), Hillilä 2016 (125 IBS patients, 12 weeks), Böhn 2021 (20 IBS patients, crossover pilot) and Lettieri 1998 (37 patients with type 2 diabetes on acarbose).
cards.result: The pattern is consistent once the questions are separated. When the gas source is a defined fermentable load — beans, chili, a GOS challenge diet — the enzyme reduces gas production (breath hydrogen) and flatulence in blinded tests, including in children and in the GOS-sensitive IBS subgroup. When it is given as everyday treatment to unselected IBS patients, two trials found no benefit over placebo, and the larger one found more withdrawals on the enzyme. Practical reading: a reasonable, cheap preventive for a known bean-or-vegetable meal; not an IBS treatment. And not a casual addition for patients taking acarbose.
cards.watchOut: Every positive card is a challenge study or a provoked subgroup; no trial shows benefit for undifferentiated chronic bloating, which is a different and larger claim.
cards.source: Synthesis of Ganiats TG et al. PMID: 7964541; Di Stefano M et al. PMID: 17151807; Di Nardo G et al. PMID: 24063420; Tuck CJ et al. PMID: 28809383; Hillilä M et al. PMID: 26133538; Böhn L et al. PMID: 33619835; Lettieri JT et al. PMID: 9663365. Registry IDs as on the individual cards.

shelves.title: Ginkgo biloba to prevent dementia: two large, long trials — GEM and GuidAge — both found no protection
shelves.question: In older adults with normal cognition, mild cognitive impairment, or memory complaints, does standardised ginkgo biloba extract (EGb 761, 240 mg/day) prevent dementia or Alzheimer's disease compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Alzheimer Disease/epidemiology, prevention & control · Cognition · Dementia/epidemiology, prevention & control · Double-Blind Method · Ginkgo biloba · Humans · Incidence · Phytotherapy · Plant Extracts/administration & dosage, therapeutic use · Proportional Hazards Models · Ginkgo Extract
shelves.balance: Ginkgo biloba extract is one of the most widely bought supplements for memory, and it is one of the few ever tested at the scale the question deserves. Two large, long, double-blind trials asked whether 240 mg/day of the standardised extract EGb 761 prevents dementia. In the US GEM study (3,069 volunteers aged 75 and over, median 6.1 years), dementia developed at 3.3 per 100 person-years on ginkgo versus 2.9 on placebo (hazard ratio 1.12, 95% CI 0.94–1.33) — no protection in people with normal cognition and none in the subgroup with mild cognitive impairment. In the French GuidAge trial (2,854 adults aged 70 and over with memory complaints, 5 years), Alzheimer's disease was diagnosed in 61 people on ginkgo versus 73 on placebo (HR 0.84, 0.60–1.18; p=0.306). Neither trial showed an effect on stroke or other cardiovascular events, and adverse effects were similar. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): two adequately powered prevention trials, one answer — taking ginkgo to ward off dementia does not work.

cards.headline: GEM: ginkgo did not reduce dementia incidence over a median 6.1 years in 3,069 volunteers aged 75+ (HR 1.12, 0.94–1.33)
cards.summary: GEM: ginkgo did not reduce dementia incidence over a median 6.1 years in 3,069 volunteers aged 75+ (HR 1.12, 0.94–1.33)
cards.people: 3,069 community volunteers aged 75 years or older (2,587 with normal cognition, 482 with mild cognitive impairment) at five US academic centres, randomised to ginkgo biloba extract 120 mg twice daily or placebo and assessed every 6 months for incident dementia by expert panel consensus.
cards.result: 523 participants developed dementia (277 on ginkgo, 246 on placebo); 92% were classified as possible or probable Alzheimer's disease or Alzheimer's with vascular disease. Dementia rate 3.3 vs 2.9 per 100 person-years; HR 1.12 (95% CI 0.94–1.33; p=0.21) for all-cause dementia and 1.16 (0.97–1.39) for Alzheimer's disease. In the MCI subgroup the HR for progression was 1.13 (0.85–1.50). Dropout was low (6.3%) and adverse-effect profiles were similar.
cards.watchOut: The trial tested one standardised extract at one dose; it does not address ginkgo for treating established dementia or for other indications, and non-standardised products may differ — but for prevention, this is the definitive test and it was null. Product tested: EGb 761, the proprietary Ginkgo biloba extract of Dr Willmar Schwabe — the extract designation is the product identity; other ginkgo extracts are not this product. The record names no specific product or brand — products sold today may differ in safety and effectiveness.
cards.source: DeKosky ST et al.. Ginkgo biloba for prevention of dementia: a randomized controlled trial. JAMA. 2008. PMID: 19017911. Registry ID: NCT00010803. cards.headline: GuidAge: five years of EGb 761 did not reduce conversion to Alzheimer's disease in 2,854 older adults with memory complaints (HR 0.84, 0.60–1.18)
cards.summary: GuidAge: five years of EGb 761 did not reduce conversion to Alzheimer's disease in 2,854 older adults with memory complaints (HR 0.84, 0.60–1.18)
cards.people: 2,854 French adults aged 70 or older who had spontaneously reported memory complaints to their primary-care physician, randomised to standardised ginkgo biloba extract 120 mg twice daily or matched placebo for 5 years; primary outcome conversion to probable Alzheimer's disease.
cards.result: Probable Alzheimer's disease was diagnosed in 61 participants on ginkgo (1.2 per 100 person-years) versus 73 on placebo (1.4 per 100 person-years); HR 0.84 (95% CI 0.60–1.18; p=0.306), with a non-proportional risk pattern over time. Deaths (76 vs 82) and strokes (65 vs 60) did not differ, nor did haemorrhagic or cardiovascular events.
cards.watchOut: The point estimate leans toward ginkgo but the confidence interval spans a 40% relative reduction to an 18% relative increase — the trial cannot support a prevention claim, and read beside GEM (HR 1.12) the pair is best summarised as no demonstrated effect. Product tested: EGb 761, the proprietary Ginkgo biloba extract of Dr Willmar Schwabe.
cards.source: Vellas B et al.. Long-term use of standardised Ginkgo biloba extract for the prevention of Alzheimer's disease (GuidAge): a randomised placebo-controlled trial. The Lancet. Neurology. 2012. PMID: 22959217. Registry ID: NCT00276510. shelves.title: Nicotinamide to prevent skin cancer: fewer new cancers in high-risk immunocompetent adults (ONTRAC) — none in transplant recipients (ONTRANS)
shelves.question: In adults at high risk of keratinocyte cancer, does oral nicotinamide 500 mg twice daily for 12 months reduce new basal-cell and squamous-cell cancers — and does the answer change in organ-transplant recipients?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Basal Cell Carcinoma/epidemiology, prevention & control · Carcinoma, Squamous Cell/epidemiology, prevention & control · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Keratosis, Actinic/epidemiology, prevention & control · Male · Middle Aged · Niacinamide/adverse effects, therapeutic use · Secondary Prevention · Skin Neoplasms/epidemiology, prevention & control · Vitamin B Complex/adverse effects, therapeutic use
shelves.balance: Nicotinamide (the amide form of vitamin B3) repairs ultraviolet DNA damage in experimental work, and the ONTRAC trial tested whether that translates into fewer skin cancers. In 386 immunocompetent adults who had had at least two nonmelanoma skin cancers in the previous five years, 500 mg twice daily for 12 months lowered the rate of new nonmelanoma skin cancers by 23% relative to placebo (95% CI 4–38) and cut actinic keratoses by 11–20% at successive visits; the benefit vanished within months of stopping. The companion question — transplant recipients, whose skin-cancer risk is far higher — was answered by ONTRANS: 158 recipients, 207 new keratinocyte cancers on nicotinamide versus 210 on placebo (rate ratio 1.0, 0.8–1.3). Same drug, same dose, opposite answer by population. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), for immunocompetent high-risk adults only, and only while it is taken. Tier C: the benefit rests on a single positive trial.

cards.headline: ONTRAC: new nonmelanoma skin cancers 23% relatively lower on nicotinamide over 12 months in high-risk immunocompetent adults
cards.summary: ONTRAC: new nonmelanoma skin cancers 23% relatively lower on nicotinamide over 12 months in high-risk immunocompetent adults
cards.type: Phase 3 randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (Chen 2015, ONTRAC)
cards.people: 386 participants with at least two nonmelanoma skin cancers in the previous 5 years, randomised to nicotinamide 500 mg twice daily or placebo for 12 months, with dermatologist skin checks every 3 months for 18 months.
cards.result: Rate of new nonmelanoma skin cancers was 23% lower in relative terms (95% CI 4 to 38; p=0.02) on nicotinamide. New basal-cell carcinomas were 20% relatively lower (−6 to 39; p=0.12) and new squamous-cell carcinomas 30% relatively lower (0 to 51; p=0.05). Actinic keratoses were 11% fewer at 3 months, 14% at 6, 20% at 9 and 13% at 12 months. Adverse events did not differ, and there was no evidence of benefit in the 6 months after the tablets stopped.
cards.watchOut: The 23% figure is a relative rate reduction over one year in a very high-risk group; the trial does not show prevention of melanoma, of skin-cancer death, or any benefit that outlasts taking the tablets.
cards.source: Chen AC et al.. A Phase 3 Randomized Trial of Nicotinamide for Skin-Cancer Chemoprevention. The New England journal of medicine. 2015. PMID: 26488693. cards.headline: ONTRANS: no reduction in keratinocyte cancers in organ-transplant recipients (207 vs 210 new cancers; rate ratio 1.0)
cards.summary: ONTRANS: no reduction in keratinocyte cancers in organ-transplant recipients (207 vs 210 new cancers; rate ratio 1.0)
cards.type: Phase 3 randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (Allen 2023, ONTRANS)
cards.people: 158 solid-organ transplant recipients with at least two keratinocyte cancers in the past 5 years, randomised to nicotinamide 500 mg twice daily or placebo for 12 months; the trial was stopped early because of poor recruitment.
cards.result: At 12 months there were 207 new keratinocyte cancers in the nicotinamide group and 210 in the placebo group (rate ratio 1.0, 95% CI 0.8 to 1.3; p=0.96). No significant differences in squamous-cell or basal-cell carcinoma counts, actinic keratoses, quality of life, adverse events, or laboratory variables.
cards.watchOut: Early stopping for poor recruitment left the trial smaller than planned; even so, the point estimate is exactly 1.0, so underpowering does not explain the null — immunosuppression appears to override nicotinamide's mechanism.
cards.source: Allen NC et al.. Nicotinamide for Skin-Cancer Chemoprevention in Transplant Recipients. The New England journal of medicine. 2023. PMID: 36856616. Registry ID: ACTRN12617000599370 (Australian New Zealand Clinical Trials Registry, as recorded in the record). shelves.title: Vitamin D to delay type 2 diabetes in prediabetes: D2d and the Tromsø trial both missed — supplementation does not hold back the diagnosis
shelves.question: In adults with prediabetes, does vitamin D3 supplementation delay progression to type 2 diabetes compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Oral · Aged · Cholecalciferol/administration & dosage, therapeutic use · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2/prevention & control · Dietary Supplements · Disease-Free Survival · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Male · Middle Aged · Prediabetic State/blood, drug therapy · Risk Factors · Treatment Failure · Vitamin D/analogs & derivatives, blood · Vitamins/administration & dosage, therapeutic use
shelves.balance: Low blood vitamin D tracks with higher diabetes risk in observational studies, which made supplementation an attractive candidate for delaying diabetes. The two randomised tests agree that it does not delay onset in people who are not frankly deficient. In D2d (2,423 adults meeting at least two of three prediabetes criteria), vitamin D3 4,000 IU/day produced diabetes in 293 participants versus 323 on placebo over a median 2.5 years — 9.39 vs 10.66 events per 100 person-years, HR 0.88 (95% CI 0.75–1.04; p=0.12). In the Tromsø trial (511 people with prediabetes), five years of 20,000 IU/week gave progression in 103 versus 112 (HR 0.90, 0.69–1.18). Both point estimates lean the same way and neither is significant; a small effect is not excluded, but no trial shows supplementation delays the formal diagnosis. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference). This shelf is about vitamin D only; lifestyle and medicines to delay diagnosis live on Shelves #111 and #112.

cards.headline: D2d: diabetes developed in 293 on vitamin D vs 323 on placebo (HR 0.88, 0.75–1.04; p=0.12)
cards.summary: D2d: diabetes developed in 293 on vitamin D vs 323 on placebo (HR 0.88, 0.75–1.04; p=0.12)
cards.people: 2,423 adults meeting at least two of three glycaemic criteria for prediabetes and no criterion for diabetes, randomised to vitamin D3 4,000 IU/day or placebo regardless of baseline 25-hydroxyvitamin D; event-driven design targeting 508 diabetes events.
cards.result: By month 24 mean 25-hydroxyvitamin D was 54.3 ng/mL on vitamin D (from 27.7) versus 28.8 on placebo (from 28.2), so the exposure contrast was real. After median 2.5 years, new diabetes occurred in 293 vs 323 participants (9.39 vs 10.66 per 100 person-years); HR 0.88 (95% CI 0.75–1.04; p=0.12). Adverse events did not differ significantly.
cards.watchOut: Participants were not selected for vitamin D insufficiency; the trial cannot exclude a benefit confined to frankly deficient people, nor a small effect — its confidence interval runs from a 25% relative reduction to a 4% relative increase.
cards.source: Pittas AG et al.. Vitamin D Supplementation and Prevention of Type 2 Diabetes. The New England journal of medicine. 2019. PMID: 31173679. Registry ID: NCT01942694. cards.headline: Tromsø: five years of weekly vitamin D did not delay progression from prediabetes (103 vs 112 cases; HR 0.90, 0.69–1.18)
cards.summary: Tromsø: five years of weekly vitamin D did not delay progression from prediabetes (103 vs 112 cases; HR 0.90, 0.69–1.18)
cards.people: 511 subjects with prediabetes on oral glucose tolerance testing in the Tromsø Study (mean age 62; mean baseline 25-hydroxyvitamin D 60 nmol/L), randomised to cholecalciferol 20,000 IU/week or placebo for 5 years with annual glucose tolerance tests.
cards.result: Type 2 diabetes developed in 103 participants on vitamin D and 112 on placebo (HR 0.90, 95% CI 0.69–1.18; p=0.45, intention-to-treat). No consistent significant effects on glucose levels, insulin resistance, lipids, or blood pressure; subgroup analyses by baseline vitamin D level were similar; no serious intervention-related side effects.
cards.watchOut: A Norwegian population with relatively replete baseline vitamin D (60 nmol/L) — the authors note that showing any effect in deficient subjects would need very large studies; as tested, supplementation did not delay diabetes.
cards.source: Jorde R et al.. Vitamin D 20,000 IU per Week for Five Years Does Not Prevent Progression From Prediabetes to Diabetes. The Journal of clinical endocrinology and metabolism. 2016. PMID: 26829443. Registry ID: NCT00685594. shelves.title: Berberine after polypectomy: adenomas recurred in 36% on berberine vs 47% on placebo over up to 2 years — one large trial, no cancers in either arm
shelves.question: In adults who have had colorectal adenomas completely removed, does berberine (0.3 g twice daily) prevent adenoma recurrence at follow-up colonoscopy compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adenoma/pathology, prevention & control, surgery · Adolescent · Adult · Aftercare · Aged · Antineoplastic Agents, Phytogenic/administration & dosage, adverse effects, therapeutic use · Berberine/administration & dosage, adverse effects, therapeutic use · Chemoprevention/methods · China/epidemiology · Colonoscopy/methods, statistics & numerical data · Colorectal Neoplasms/epidemiology, pathology · Double-Blind Method · Humans · Intention to Treat Analysis/methods · Middle Aged · Placebos/administration & dosage · Plants, Medicinal/adverse effects · Recurrence · Safety · Young Adult
shelves.balance: Berberine, a plant alkaloid long used in Chinese medicine and now sold widely as a supplement, has one genuinely large chemoprevention trial. In seven Chinese centres, 1,108 adults aged 18–75 who had one to six histologically confirmed adenomas completely removed within the previous 6 months were randomised to berberine 0.3 g twice daily or placebo, with colonoscopy at 1 year and again at 2 years if clear. In the full analysis set (891 participants), adenomas recurred in 155 of 429 (36%) on berberine versus 216 of 462 (47%) on placebo — an unadjusted relative risk of 0.77 (95% CI 0.66–0.91; p=0.001): a 23% relative reduction, 11 percentage points absolute. No colorectal cancers were detected in either arm, and the commonest adverse event was constipation (1% vs <0.5%), with no serious adverse events reported. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit). Tier C: a single trial carries a cancer-prevention-adjacent claim — and the claim is adenoma recurrence only, since no cancers occurred to be prevented. (Berberine for blood glucose and lipids is Shelf #548's question and is not duplicated.)

cards.headline: Adenoma recurrence 36% on berberine vs 47% on placebo (relative risk 0.77, 0.66–0.91; p=0.001); no cancers detected in either arm
cards.summary: Adenoma recurrence 36% on berberine vs 47% on placebo (relative risk 0.77, 0.66–0.91; p=0.001); no cancers detected in either arm
cards.people: 1,108 adults aged 18–75 at seven hospital centres in six Chinese provinces who had 1–6 histologically confirmed colorectal adenomas completely removed within the previous 6 months, randomised to berberine 0.3 g twice daily (n=553) or placebo (n=555), with follow-up colonoscopy at 1 year and, if clear, at 2 years; primary endpoint adenoma recurrence at any follow-up colonoscopy, analysed in the full analysis set (429 berberine, 462 placebo).
cards.result: Recurrent adenoma: 155/429 (36%) on berberine vs 216/462 (47%) on placebo (unadjusted relative risk 0.77, 95% CI 0.66–0.91; p=0.001). No colorectal cancers were detected during follow-up in either group. Constipation was the commonest adverse event (1% vs <0.5%); no serious adverse events were reported.
cards.watchOut: About one in five randomised participants contributed no efficacy data to the full analysis set, follow-up ended at 2 years, and a single-country trial of a supplement-grade compound needs independent replication before the claim can rise above POSSIBLE. The endpoint is adenoma recurrence — a cancer claim would require cancers, and there were none in either arm. The publication names no commercial brand; the tested substance was berberine 0.3 g twice daily. Supplement berberine products are not regulated to this trial's standard. The record names no specific product or brand — products sold today may differ in safety and effectiveness.
cards.source: Chen YX et al.. Berberine versus placebo for the prevention of recurrence of colorectal adenoma: a multicentre, double-blinded, randomised controlled study. The lancet. Gastroenterology & hepatology. 2020. PMID: 31926918. Registry ID: NCT02226185. shelves.title: Shingrix for shingles prevention: 97% efficacy at 50+, about 90% at 70+ — with a genuinely rough two days after each dose
shelves.question: In adults aged 50 and over, does the adjuvanted recombinant zoster vaccine (Shingrix) prevent shingles and postherpetic neuralgia compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adjuvants, Immunologic · Aged · Double-Blind Method · Female · Herpes Zoster/immunology/*prevention & control · Herpes Zoster Vaccine/administration & dosage/adverse effects/*immunology · Humans · Injections, Intramuscular/adverse effects · Male · Middle Aged · Treatment Outcome · Vaccines, Subunit/immunology
shelves.balance: The recombinant zoster vaccine (Shingrix) is one of the most effective vaccines ever tested in older adults — a population in which vaccines usually work least well. In ZOE-50 (15,411 adults aged 50 and over evaluated), shingles occurred in 6 people on vaccine versus 210 on placebo — 0.3 versus 9.1 cases per 1,000 person-years, a vaccine efficacy of 97.2% (95% CI 93.7–99.0). In ZOE-70 (13,900 adults aged 70 and over), efficacy was 89.8% (84.2–93.7), and pooled efficacy against postherpetic neuralgia in the over-70s was 88.8%. The price is reactogenicity: grade-3 symptoms (severe enough to stop normal activity) occurred in 17.0% of vaccinees versus 3.2% on placebo in ZOE-50 — a sore, rough two days is common, and worth warning about. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): two very large trials with near-total protection against a disease whose main burden is chronic nerve pain.

cards.headline: ZOE-50: vaccine efficacy 97.2% against shingles in 15,411 adults aged 50+ (6 cases versus 210)
cards.summary: ZOE-50: vaccine efficacy 97.2% against shingles in 15,411 adults aged 50+ (6 cases versus 210)
cards.people: 15,411 adults aged 50 years or older evaluated in a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial of two doses of the adjuvanted recombinant zoster vaccine (Shingrix) versus placebo (ZOE-50).
cards.result: Herpes zoster occurred in 6 vaccinated versus 210 placebo recipients — 0.3 versus 9.1 per 1,000 person-years; vaccine efficacy 97.2% (95% CI 93.7–99.0). Grade-3 solicited symptoms occurred in 17.0% of vaccinees versus 3.2% on placebo. Registry ID: NCT01165177 (verified in the record).
cards.watchOut: Efficacy is against shingles, not against the rare disseminated disease of the severely immunosuppressed (a different shelf, #2206, covers vaccination after stem-cell transplant). Reactogenicity is substantial — plan both doses.

cards.summary: ZOE-70: efficacy 89.8% in adults 70+, and 88.8% against postherpetic neuralgia in the pooled over-70 analysis
cards.people: 13,900 adults aged 70 years or older evaluated in the companion randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (ZOE-70), with a pre-specified pooled analysis of both ZOE trials for the over-70 population.
cards.result: Vaccine efficacy against herpes zoster was 89.8% (95% CI 84.2–93.7); pooled efficacy in adults 70+ was 91.3% against shingles and 88.8% (68.7–97.1) against postherpetic neuralgia. Registry ID: NCT01165229 (verified in the record, which also lists the ZOE-50 registration).
cards.watchOut: Protection persisted across all older age bands in the pooled analysis — the usual age-related fall-off of vaccine response was not seen within the trial horizon. Distinct from shelf #442, which asks a different question (zoster vaccination and dementia risk).

shelves.title: Text-message support to quit smoking
shelves.question: Do automated text-message programmes help smokers quit?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Cell Phone · Confidence Intervals · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Health Education · Humans · Income · Male · Patient Selection · Smoking Cessation · Smoking Prevention
shelves.balance: LIKELY — two large trials in different countries each found a relative risk of 2.20, the UK one on biochemically verified six-month abstinence (10.7% vs 4.9%), and the Cochrane pooling of 26 trials (33,849 smokers) confirms a real but smaller average effect (RR 1.54). Consistent, replicated and verified — LIKELY.

cards.headline: A personalised texting programme doubled quit rates at six weeks in 1,705 smokers
cards.summary: A personalised texting programme doubled quit rates at six weeks in 1,705 smokers
cards.people: 1,705 smokers across New Zealand who wanted to quit and owned a mobile phone; personalised cessation texts from quit day vs a control group whose free texts were deferred to six months
cards.result: Not smoking in the past week at six weeks: 239 (28%) in the intervention group vs 109 (13%) in controls — relative risk 2.20 (95% CI 1.79–2.70; P < 0.0001), consistent across age, sex, income and region. Reported quit rates remained higher at six months, though follow-up by then was incomplete (74%).
cards.watchOut: The six-week outcome was self-reported (sensitivity analyses using salivary cotinine agreed); the six-month between-group difference is less certain because of missing follow-up.
cards.source: Rodgers A et al.. Do u smoke after txt? Results of a randomised trial of smoking cessation using mobile phone text messaging. Tob Control. 2005. PMID: 16046689. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Txt2stop doubled biochemically verified abstinence at six months in 5,800 smokers
cards.summary: Txt2stop doubled biochemically verified abstinence at six months in 5,800 smokers
cards.people: 5,800 UK smokers willing to make a quit attempt; automated motivational and behavioural-support text programme (txt2stop) vs text messages unrelated to quitting; outcome assessors masked
cards.result: Self-reported continuous abstinence at six months, biochemically verified: 10.7% with txt2stop vs 4.9% with control texts — relative risk 2.20 (95% CI 1.80–2.68; P < 0.0001), an absolute gain of about 6 quitters per 100 smokers. Results held when missing participants were counted as smokers.
cards.watchOut: Even in the winning group, about nine of ten smokers had not quit at six months — the programme helps modestly, at very low cost per person.
cards.source: Free C et al.. Smoking cessation support delivered via mobile phone text messaging (txt2stop): a single-blind, randomised trial. Lancet. 2011. PMID: 21722952. cards.headline: Cochrane review of 26 studies: texting raises quit rates by about half over minimal support
cards.summary: Cochrane review of 26 studies: texting raises quit rates by about half over minimal support
cards.people: 26 randomised studies, 33,849 smokers, mostly in high-income countries; outcomes at six months or longer
cards.result: Automated text messaging vs minimal smoking-cessation support: relative risk 1.54 (95% CI 1.19–2.00) — moderate-certainty evidence. Text messaging added to other cessation support vs that support alone: RR 1.59 (95% CI 1.09–2.33) — also moderate certainty. Smartphone apps showed no clear benefit (RR 1.00; very low-certainty evidence).
cards.watchOut: The record carries no MeSH terms. Effects vary between programmes (heterogeneity I² = 71%), so the pooled 1.54 — not the 2.20 of the two showcase trials — is the safer expectation for a new programme.
cards.source: Whittaker R et al.. Mobile phone text messaging and app-based interventions for smoking cessation. Cochrane Database Syst Rev. 2019. PMID: 31638271. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: the record carries no MeSH terms

cards.headline: What this means
cards.summary: What this means
cards.result: Automated text-message programmes are among the best-proven cheap aids to quitting: expect roughly five to six extra verified quitters per 100 smokers at six months from a good programme, used alongside — not instead of — standard stop-smoking medicines where those are indicated.
cards.watchOut: The trials tested structured multi-week programmes, not occasional reminder texts.
cards.source: Synthesis of the references on this shelf.

shelves.title: Probiotics to prevent colds: about a quarter fewer people caught at least one in relative terms — modest, and strain-specific
shelves.question: Do probiotic supplements prevent ordinary upper respiratory tract infections (colds and similar illnesses) in children and adults?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Anti-Bacterial Agents · Child · Humans · Influenza Vaccines · Influenza, Human · Probiotics · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Respiratory Tract Infections
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — across 24 randomised trials (6,950 participants), probiotics reduced the chance of at least one upper respiratory infection (RR 0.76) and shortened episodes by about 1.2 days, and one well-run trial of Lactobacillus GG in day-care children agrees (RR 0.66). Certainty is low to moderate, strains and doses vary between trials, and the effect is a modest reduction in colds — not prevention of influenza or pneumonia.

cards.headline: Cochrane 2022: probiotics reduced the risk of at least one cold (RR 0.76) and shortened episodes by ~1.2 days
cards.summary: Cochrane 2022: probiotics reduced the risk of at least one cold (RR 0.76) and shortened episodes by ~1.2 days
cards.people: 24 randomised trials (23 in the meta-analyses), 6,950 participants — children, adults (mean age 37) and older people (mean age 85); mostly one or two Lactobacillus strains at 10^9–10^11 colony-forming units/day for more than three months vs placebo or no treatment
cards.result: At least one URTI: RR 0.76 (95% CI 0.67–0.87; 16 studies, 4,798 participants; low-certainty evidence). At least three URTIs: RR 0.59 (0.38–0.91; moderate certainty). Incidence rate ratio 0.82 (0.73–0.92). Mean episode duration 1.22 days shorter (95% CI −2.12 to −0.33). Antibiotic prescriptions for URTIs: RR 0.58 (0.42–0.81). Adverse events no more frequent (RR 1.02) and mostly minor gastrointestinal symptoms.
cards.watchOut: Most pooled estimates are low-certainty, and 'probiotics' here is a family of different strains and doses — the result does not transfer to any particular product on a shelf.
cards.source: Zhao Y et al.. Probiotics for preventing acute upper respiratory tract infections. Cochrane Database Syst Rev. 2022. PMID: 36001877. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Lactobacillus GG in day-care children: upper respiratory infections RR 0.66, NNT 5 over one winter term
cards.summary: Lactobacillus GG in day-care children: upper respiratory infections RR 0.66, NNT 5 over one winter term
cards.people: 281 children attending day-care centres in Croatia; Lactobacillus GG 10^9 colony-forming units in 100 mL fermented milk daily vs the same pasteurised fermented milk without LGG, for 3 months, double-blind
cards.result: Upper respiratory tract infections: RR 0.66 (95% CI 0.52–0.82; NNT 5). Respiratory infections lasting more than 3 days: RR 0.57 (0.41–0.78). Days with respiratory symptoms fewer (P < 0.001). Lower respiratory infections not reduced (RR 0.82, 0.24–2.76), and gastrointestinal infections were not significantly reduced (RR 0.63, 0.38–1.06).
cards.watchOut: One strain, one dose, one delivery food, one country — a clean trial whose result belongs to LGG in fermented milk, not to probiotic products generally.

shelves.title: Sauna bathing and the heart: frequent bathers die less in Finnish cohort data — association, dose-graded, never trial-tested for hard outcomes
shelves.question: Does regular sauna bathing protect against cardiovascular disease and early death?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Cardiovascular Diseases · Cause of Death · Coronary Disease · Finland · Follow-Up Studies · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Mortality · Odds Ratio · Prospective Studies · Risk Factors · Risk Reduction Behavior · Steam Bath
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE, Tier C — the mortality evidence is one large Finnish cohort: men bathing 4–7 times a week had roughly half the fatal cardiovascular rate of once-a-week bathers (12.0% vs 22.3% over ~21 years), with a clean dose gradient — but it is observational, and men who sauna often differ in fitness, wealth and habits in ways adjustment cannot fully remove. The one randomised trial (n = 47) shows sauna added to exercise lowered systolic pressure by 8 mmHg more than exercise alone. No trial has tested sauna against death or heart attack, so the hard-outcome claim stays Tier C.

cards.headline: Finnish cohort: fatal cardiovascular disease in 12.0% of men sauna bathing 4–7 times weekly vs 22.3% at once weekly
cards.summary: Finnish cohort: fatal cardiovascular disease in 12.0% of men sauna bathing 4–7 times weekly vs 22.3% at once weekly
cards.people: 2,315 middle-aged men (42–60 years) from eastern Finland in the Kuopio Ischemic Heart Disease cohort, followed a median of 20.7 years; sauna frequency and session length recorded at baseline
cards.result: Sudden cardiac death occurred in 10.1% (1 session/week), 7.8% (2–3/week) and 5.0% (4–7/week); adjusted hazard ratio for 4–7 vs 1 session/week 0.37 (95% CI 0.18–0.75). Fatal coronary disease: 14.9%, 11.5%, 8.5%. Fatal cardiovascular disease: 22.3%, 16.4%, 12.0%. All-cause mortality: 49.1%, 37.8%, 30.8%. Sessions longer than 19 minutes carried an adjusted sudden-death hazard ratio of 0.48 (0.31–0.75) vs under 11 minutes.
cards.watchOut: Observational: sauna frequency was self-chosen, and frequent bathers were fitter and healthier at baseline in ways statistics can only partly correct. This card is the reason the shelf is Tier C.
cards.source: Laukkanen T et al.. Association between sauna bathing and fatal cardiovascular and all-cause mortality events. JAMA Intern Med. 2015. PMID: 25705824. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Randomised trial: adding 15 minutes of sauna after exercise lowered systolic pressure 8 mmHg more than exercise alone
cards.summary: Randomised trial: adding 15 minutes of sauna after exercise lowered systolic pressure 8 mmHg more than exercise alone
cards.people: 47 sedentary adults (mean age 49) with at least one cardiovascular risk factor, randomised for 8 weeks to guideline exercise plus 15-minute post-exercise sauna, exercise alone, or control
cards.result: Exercise plus sauna vs exercise alone: systolic blood pressure fell 8.0 mmHg more (95% CI −14.6 to −1.4), cardiorespiratory fitness improved by an additional 2.7 mL/kg/min (0.2 to 5.3), and total cholesterol was lower. Exercise alone improved fitness (+6.2 mL/kg/min vs control) and fat mass but did not change blood pressure vs control.
cards.watchOut: 47 people, 8 weeks, surrogate outcomes — it shows sauna can move blood pressure, not that it prevents deaths.

cards.headline: Synthesis: enjoy the sauna; don't prescribe it as cardiology yet
cards.summary: Synthesis: enjoy the sauna; don't prescribe it as cardiology yet
cards.people: 2,315 Finnish men followed for two decades; 47 adults in the only randomised trial carded
cards.result: Frequent sauna bathing is associated with substantially lower cardiovascular and all-cause mortality in a dose-graded way, and a small trial supports a real blood-pressure effect on top of exercise. Causation for hard outcomes is unproven. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), Tier C.
cards.watchOut: The cohort is Finnish men in a sauna culture; women, other populations and people with unstable heart disease are barely represented. Alcohol plus sauna, and sauna with unstable angina or severe aortic stenosis, are recognised hazards outside this evidence.
cards.source: Synthesis of Laukkanen T et al. JAMA Intern Med. 2015 (PMID: 25705824); Lee E et al. Am J Physiol Regul Integr Comp Physiol. 2022 (PMID: 35785965).

shelves.title: Nicotine vaccines for smoking cessation: no trial beat placebo — the two phase III NicVAX trials quit at about 11% in both arms
shelves.question: Can a vaccine against nicotine help smokers quit — or stop recent quitters from relapsing?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Secondary Prevention · Smoking/*immunology · Smoking Cessation/*methods · Smoking Prevention · Vaccines/adverse effects/*therapeutic use
shelves.balance: No. Every nicotine vaccine tested in a randomised trial failed to beat placebo on long-term abstinence. The Cochrane review (Hartmann-Boyce 2012) found four eligible trials covering 2,642 smokers and no statistically significant cessation benefit for any vaccine; the two phase III NicVAX trials, reported only in summary form, quit at approximately 11% in both the vaccine and placebo arms. The best individual results are no better: NicVAX added to varenicline and counselling quit at 27.7% versus 30.0% on placebo (Hoogsteder 2014), and the Niccine vaccine, tested for relapse prevention, left fewer people relapse-free than placebo at one year (43.3% versus 51.1%; Tonstad 2013). The one positive signal in the whole record is a subgroup: in the phase II Nicotine-Qbeta trial (Cornuz 2008), the third of vaccinees with the highest antibody levels had higher continuous abstinence than placebo (56.6% versus 31.3%) — but the trial's intention-to-treat result was null, and no later trial turned that subgroup signal into a treatment effect, including in pre-planned top-responder analyses. No nicotine vaccine is licensed. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): the null is consistent across three vaccine products, four-plus trials and a Cochrane review; what remains unproven is not whether these vaccines worked — they did not — but whether any future vaccine achieving much higher antibody levels could.

cards.headline: Hartmann-Boyce 2012 (Cochrane): four trials, 2,642 smokers — no nicotine vaccine significantly improved long-term cessation; phase III NicVAX quit rates were about 11% in both arms
cards.summary: Hartmann-Boyce 2012 (Cochrane): four trials, 2,642 smokers — no nicotine vaccine significantly improved long-term cessation; phase III NicVAX quit rates were about 11% in both arms
cards.type: Cochrane systematic review of randomised trials of nicotine vaccines (Hartmann-Boyce 2012)
cards.people: Four randomised trials at phase II or III met the review's criteria: three of the nicotine conjugate vaccine NicVAX against placebo and one of NIC002 (Nicotine-Qbeta) against placebo, all industry-run smoking-cessation trials in adult smokers or recent ex-smokers. Total participation across the included studies was 2,642 smokers.
cards.result: None of the four included studies detected a statistically significant difference in long-term cessation between vaccine and placebo. The risk ratio for 12-month cessation was 1.35 (95% CI 0.82 to 2.22) in the NIC002 trial and 1.74 (95% CI 0.73 to 4.18) in one NicVAX trial — both relative measures whose intervals span no effect. Two phase III NicVAX trials, for which full results were not available to the reviewers, reported similar quit rates of approximately 11% in both groups. The reviewers did not pool the trials because the vaccines and regimens differed, and they judged every trial at high or unclear risk of bias in at least one domain.
cards.watchOut: The review's search closed in April 2012, so it predates the published Hoogsteder 2014 and Tonstad 2013 trials carded below — both null, so the conclusion stands — and the two phase III NicVAX results were available to the reviewers only as summaries, not full reports. Risk ratios are relative measures; the absolute quit rates behind them were low in both arms.
cards.source: Hartmann-Boyce J et al. Nicotine vaccines for smoking cessation. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2012. PMID: 22895958. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Cornuz 2008: Nicotine-Qbeta missed its intention-to-treat endpoint — only the highest-antibody third quit more than placebo (56.6% vs 31.3%)
cards.summary: Cornuz 2008: Nicotine-Qbeta missed its intention-to-treat endpoint — only the highest-antibody third quit more than placebo (56.6% vs 31.3%)
cards.type: Phase II randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial (Cornuz 2008)
cards.people: 341 smokers randomised to five monthly intramuscular injections of the nicotine vaccine Nicotine-Qbeta (NIC002; 229 subjects) or placebo (112), all with individual behavioural cessation counselling, treated for 6 months and followed for a further 6 months. The vaccine induced a 100% antibody responder rate after the first injection.
cards.result: Point prevalence of abstinence at month 2 favoured the vaccine (47.2% versus 35.1%; P = 0.036), but continuous abstinence between months 2 and 6 — the outcome that matters — was not significantly different in the intention-to-treat population. In a per-protocol subgroup analysis, the third of vaccinees with the highest antibody levels had higher continuous abstinence from month 2 to month 6 than placebo (56.6% versus 31.3%; odds ratio 2.9; P = 0.004 — a relative measure), while medium and low antibody levels did not increase abstinence; the high-responder advantage persisted at 12 months (difference 20.2 percentage points; P = 0.012). The vaccine was safe and generally well tolerated.
cards.watchOut: The positive finding is a subgroup defined by a post-randomisation measurement (antibody level), analysed per protocol: people who mount high antibody responses may differ from those who do not in ways that themselves predict quitting, so this cannot be read as the vaccine's effect. The trial's own primary reading is the null intention-to-treat result.
cards.source: Cornuz J et al. A vaccine against nicotine for smoking cessation: a randomized controlled trial. PLoS One. 2008. PMID: 18575629. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT00369616, from the record's databank fields. cards.headline: Hoogsteder 2014: adding NicVAX to varenicline and counselling changed nothing — prolonged abstinence 27.7% vs 30.0% on placebo
cards.summary: Hoogsteder 2014: adding NicVAX to varenicline and counselling changed nothing — prolonged abstinence 27.7% vs 30.0% on placebo
cards.type: Randomised placebo-controlled trial of NicVAX added to varenicline (Hoogsteder 2014)
cards.people: 558 smokers at two Dutch centres randomised to six injections of the nicotine vaccine 3'-AmNic-rEPA (NicVAX; n = 278) or placebo (n = 280), both co-administered with open-label varenicline and behavioural support. The primary outcome was carbon-monoxide-validated prolonged abstinence from weeks 9 to 52.
cards.result: There was no difference in abstinence between NicVAX and placebo from weeks 9 to 52 (27.7% versus 30.0%; odds ratio 0.89, 95% CI 0.62 to 1.29 — a relative measure) or from weeks 37 to 52 (33.8% versus 33.2%; odds ratio 1.03, 95% CI 0.73 to 1.46). The pre-planned subgroup analysis in the top 30% of antibody responders showed only a non-significant tendency toward higher late abstinence (42.2% versus 33.2%; odds ratio 1.47, 95% CI 0.89 to 2.42). The authors conclude that NicVAX does not appear to improve the chances of stopping smoking when added to varenicline and behavioural support.
cards.watchOut: Because every participant received varenicline — itself an effective cessation drug — this trial tests the vaccine as an add-on, not as a stand-alone treatment; but the Cochrane review's placebo-controlled NicVAX trials were also null, so the add-on design does not rescue the vaccine. The trial's protocol was published separately (BMC Public Health 2012) and is not carded as evidence.
cards.source: Hoogsteder PH et al. cards.headline: Tonstad 2013: Niccine for relapse prevention — nonrelapse at one year was lower on vaccine than placebo (43.3% vs 51.1%)
cards.summary: Tonstad 2013: Niccine for relapse prevention — nonrelapse at one year was lower on vaccine than placebo (43.3% vs 51.1%)
cards.type: Phase II randomised double-blind placebo-controlled multicentre trial (Tonstad 2013)
cards.people: 355 smokers aged 25–50 in a 1-year relapse-prevention trial: Niccine (a nicotine hapten–tetanus toxoid conjugate vaccine, 40 µg) or placebo on days 0, 28, 56, 90, 150 and 210, with varenicline given between days 56 and 98 to help participants quit; only those abstinent at days 90–98 continued to the 1-year relapse phase (219 of the 265 who reached that point).
cards.result: At 1 year, nonrelapse was 43.3% in the Niccine group versus 51.1% in the placebo group (difference −7.9 percentage points; 95% CI −20.6 to 4.9) — the vaccine arm did numerically worse, and the difference was not significant. There was no benefit of Niccine on smoking status at 6 or 9 months, exhaled carbon monoxide, time to relapse, abstinence, withdrawal symptoms or smoking reinforcement. Antibody levels rose on vaccine but were unrelated to relapse. Adverse events other than hypersensitivity and compensatory smoking did not differ between groups.
cards.watchOut: A relapse-prevention design in people who had already quit with varenicline's help: it answers the relapse question, not the cessation question, and its confidence interval is wide enough to include a small benefit as well as harm. The authors' own reading is that antibody levels achieved may simply have been too low — the recurring explanation across this whole shelf, never yet converted into a working product.
cards.source: Tonstad S et al. Niccine®, a nicotine vaccine, for relapse prevention: a phase II, randomized, placebo-controlled, multicenter clinical trial. Nicotine & Tobacco Research. 2013. cards.headline: Synthesis: three nicotine vaccines, every controlled comparison null — the antibody-responder subgroup is the only signal, and it has never survived a confirmatory test — POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference)
cards.summary: Synthesis: three nicotine vaccines, every controlled comparison null — the antibody-responder subgroup is the only signal, and it has never survived a confirmatory test — POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference)
cards.people: One Cochrane review (4 trials, 2,642 smokers), one phase II cessation trial (341 smokers), one randomised add-on trial (558 smokers) and one phase II relapse-prevention trial (355 smokers), covering three distinct vaccine products (NicVAX, Nicotine-Qbeta/NIC002, Niccine).
cards.result: No trial found a significant long-term abstinence benefit: pooled qualitatively by Cochrane (risk ratios 1.35 and 1.74, both with intervals spanning 1; phase III quit rates about 11% in both arms), NicVAX plus varenicline 27.7% versus 30.0%, and Niccine relapse prevention numerically favouring placebo (43.3% versus 51.1% nonrelapse). The single positive result is the high-antibody subgroup of one phase II trial (56.6% versus 31.3% continuous abstinence), a post-randomisation subgroup that later pre-planned responder analyses did not confirm. The smoking-cessation pharmacotherapies that do work — varenicline, nicotine replacement, cytisine — live on their own shelves (for example #410 for cytisine and #531 for nicotine e-cigarettes); this shelf is the vaccine concept only.
cards.watchOut: All carded trials were industry development-programme studies, several judged at high or unclear risk of bias in the Cochrane review, and the phase III NicVAX results were never published in full — the shelf relies on the Cochrane summary for them. The verdict is about the vaccines as tested: antibody levels achieved were modest, and a future vaccine producing far higher titres is a hypothesis, not a finding.
cards.source: Synthesis of Hartmann-Boyce J et al. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2012 (PMID: 22895958); Cornuz J et al. PLoS One. 2008 (PMID: 18575629); Hoogsteder PH et al. Addiction. 2014 (PMID: 24894625); Tonstad S et al. Nicotine & Tobacco Research. 2013 (PMID: 23471101).

shelves.title: VILPA: in device-measured cohorts of non-exercisers, three or four minutes a day of vigorous everyday movement was associated with roughly a quarter to a half lower mortality — striking numbers from a single observational cohort, with no trial yet
shelves.question: In adults who do no formal exercise, do brief vigorous bursts of everyday activity — a minute or two of fast walking, stairs or carrying, a few times a day — reduce the risks of death, cardiovascular disease and cancer?
shelves.mesh: Male · Humans · Female · Middle Aged · Exercise · Leisure Activities · *Cardiovascular Diseases/etiology · Life Style · *Neoplasms/complications · Mortality
shelves.balance: Wearable accelerometers made a previously invisible exposure measurable: vigorous intermittent lifestyle physical activity (VILPA) — the 1–2 minute bursts of fast walking, stair climbing and load-carrying embedded in ordinary days, done by people who never 'exercise'. In the UK Biobank accelerometry cohort of 25,241 self-reported non-exercisers (Stamatakis 2022, PMID: 36482104), participants accruing the median frequency of 3 length-standardised bouts a day showed 38–40% lower all-cause and cancer mortality risk and 48–49% lower cardiovascular mortality risk than those with no VILPA (relative reductions as reported); the median total duration of 4.4 minutes a day was associated with 26–30% lower all-cause and cancer mortality and 32–34% lower cardiovascular mortality. The companion cancer-incidence analysis (Stamatakis 2023, PMID: 37498576) found 4.5 minutes a day associated with a hazard ratio of 0.80 for total cancer and 0.69 for the composite of physical-activity-related cancers, with a minimal dose around 3.4–3.7 minutes a day. And in the joint sedentary-behaviour analysis (Koemel 2025, PMID: 39325719), high sedentary time carried no excess major cardiovascular event risk in participants with medium-to-high incidental vigorous activity — about 4.1 minutes a day appeared to offset it. Now the discipline: all three papers draw on the same UK Biobank accelerometry subsample with overlapping participants, the design is observational, and the obvious confounder runs hard — people who are already ill move less, so some of the gradient is sickness causing stillness rather than stillness causing sickness. No randomised trial of VILPA exists. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (Tier C: observational, single-cohort).

cards.headline: Stamatakis 2022: among 25,241 non-exercisers, the median 3 vigorous bouts a day was associated with 38–40% lower all-cause and cancer mortality and 48–49% lower cardiovascular mortality than no VILPA (relative reductions)
cards.summary: Stamatakis 2022: among 25,241 non-exercisers, the median 3 vigorous bouts a day was associated with 38–40% lower all-cause and cancer mortality and 48–49% lower cardiovascular mortality than no VILPA (relative reductions)
cards.people: Prospective analysis of the UK Biobank wearable-accelerometry subsample: 25,241 self-reported non-exercisers (mean age 61.8 years; 14,178 women, 11,063 men), with vigorous intermittent lifestyle physical activity measured by wrist-worn devices. Over an average 6.9 years of follow-up, 852 deaths occurred. VILPA bouts were length-standardised (lasting 1 or 2 minutes).
cards.result: VILPA was inversely associated with all-cause, cardiovascular and cancer mortality in a near-linear fashion. Compared with participants who engaged in no VILPA, those at the sample median frequency of 3 bouts per day showed a 38%–40% reduction in all-cause and cancer mortality risk and a 48%–49% reduction in cardiovascular mortality risk; the sample median duration of 4.4 minutes per day was associated with a 26%–30% reduction in all-cause and cancer mortality risk and a 32%–34% reduction in cardiovascular mortality risk (all relative reductions as reported by the authors). Similar associations were seen for vigorous physical activity in a parallel analysis of 62,344 exercisers.
cards.watchOut: Effect sizes of 40–50% from minutes of activity should trigger the reverse-causation alarm: undiagnosed illness suppresses vigorous movement years before death, and adjustment cannot fully remove that. The ranges (e.g. 38–40%) reflect the authors' parallel bout definitions, and every figure is a relative association from one cohort — there is no randomised confirmation that prescribing VILPA reproduces any of it.
cards.source: Stamatakis E et al. Association of wearable device-measured vigorous intermittent lifestyle physical activity with mortality. Nature Medicine. 2022. PMID: 36482104. cards.headline: Stamatakis 2023: 4.5 minutes of VILPA a day was associated with lower cancer incidence (hazard ratio 0.80 for total cancer, 0.69 for physical-activity-related cancers); the minimal dose was about 3.4 minutes a day
cards.summary: Stamatakis 2023: 4.5 minutes of VILPA a day was associated with lower cancer incidence (hazard ratio 0.80 for total cancer, 0.69 for physical-activity-related cancers); the minimal dose was about 3.4 minutes a day
cards.people: Prospective cohort analysis of 22,398 self-reported non-exercising adults in the UK Biobank accelerometry subsample (mean age 62.0 years), followed a mean of 6.7 years (149,650 person-years), during which 2,356 total incident cancers occurred, 1,084 of them at the 13 sites pre-classified as physical-activity-related. 92.3% of VILPA was accrued in bouts of up to 1 minute. Hazard ratios were estimated with cubic splines adjusted for demographic, lifestyle and other activity variables.
cards.result: Daily VILPA duration was associated with cancer incidence in a near-linear manner, with steeper curves for physical-activity-related cancer than for total cancer. Compared with no VILPA, the median daily duration of 4.5 minutes (bouts up to 1 minute) was associated with a hazard ratio of 0.80 (95% CI 0.69 to 0.92) for total cancer and 0.69 (0.55 to 0.86) for physical-activity-related cancer. The minimal dose — the dose at which 50% of the maximum risk reduction occurred — was 3.4 minutes per day for total cancer (HR 0.83; 0.73 to 0.93) and 3.7 minutes for physical-activity-related cancer (HR 0.72; 0.59 to 0.88). Findings were similar for bouts of up to 2 minutes.
cards.watchOut: Substantially the same people as the mortality paper — an overlapping subsample of one biobank, 96% White, healthier than the general population — so this is a second outcome read on one cohort, not independent replication. Cancer latency dwarfs the 6.7-year follow-up: associations over this horizon are more plausibly detection and progression effects, or residual confounding, than prevention of cancers not yet initiated.

cards.headline: Koemel 2025: high sedentary time (>11.4 hours/day) carried no excess cardiovascular-event risk in non-exercisers with medium-to-high incidental vigorous activity; about 4.1 minutes a day appeared to offset it
cards.summary: Koemel 2025: high sedentary time (>11.4 hours/day) carried no excess cardiovascular-event risk in non-exercisers with medium-to-high incidental vigorous activity; about 4.1 minutes a day appeared to offset it
cards.people: Joint-association analysis of 22,368 non-exercising adults from the UK Biobank accelerometry sub-study (median age 62.9 years; 41.8% male), with physical activity and sedentary behaviour classified by a machine-learning intensity and posture schema. Over a median 8.0 years, 819 major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) occurred.
cards.result: Compared with the highest-activity, lowest-sedentary group, high sedentary behaviour (>11.4 h/day) combined with low incidental vigorous activity (<2.1 min/day) carried a hazard ratio of 1.34 for MACE (95% CI 0.98 to 1.84), and with low incidental moderate-to-vigorous activity (<21.8 min/day) a hazard ratio of 1.89 (1.42 to 2.52). Sedentary behaviour was not associated with MACE at medium and high levels of vigorous activity or VILPA; the authors estimate that completing 4.1 minutes per day of vigorous activity or VILPA may offset the MACE risk of high sedentary behaviour, while 31–65 minutes of incidental moderate-to-vigorous activity (or 26–52 minutes of moderate-to-vigorous intermittent lifestyle activity) largely attenuated it.
cards.watchOut: Again the same UK Biobank accelerometry resource — the third read of one cohort on this shelf. The key vigorous-activity contrast (HR 1.34) has a confidence interval crossing 1.0, and 'offset' is the authors' modelling language for an interaction pattern in observational data, not a demonstrated exchange rate between sitting and stair-climbing.
cards.source: Koemel NA et al. Can incidental physical activity offset the deleterious associations of sedentary behaviour with major adverse cardiovascular events? European Journal of Preventive Cardiology. 2025. PMID: 39325719. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: minutes of daily vigorous everyday movement track with substantially lower death, cancer and cardiovascular risk in non-exercisers — MAYBE (weak evidence), because one cohort and no trial is all there is
cards.summary: Synthesis: minutes of daily vigorous everyday movement track with substantially lower death, cancer and cardiovascular risk in non-exercisers — MAYBE (weak evidence), because one cohort and no trial is all there is
cards.people: Three analyses of the UK Biobank accelerometry subsample (22,368–25,241 non-exercising adults per analysis, overlapping participants), with 852 deaths, 2,356 incident cancers and 819 major cardiovascular events across the reports.
cards.result: At median exposures of about 3 bouts or 4.4–4.5 minutes of VILPA per day versus none: all-cause and cancer mortality lower by roughly a quarter to two-fifths in relative terms, cardiovascular mortality by roughly a third to a half; total cancer incidence HR 0.80 and physical-activity-related cancer HR 0.69; and no excess MACE risk from high sedentary time among those with medium-to-high incidental vigorous activity. Dose-response is near-linear from zero upward, with a minimal dose around 3.4 minutes a day for cancer incidence.
cards.watchOut: One cohort, one measurement week of accelerometry per person, self-reported non-exerciser status, and a healthy-volunteer biobank population: the shelf's three cards are corroboration of an association's robustness across outcomes, not three independent confirmations. Until a randomised trial assigns brief vigorous activity and measures events, VILPA is a promising, low-cost, low-risk hypothesis — reasonable to encourage, not reasonable to promise.
cards.source: Synthesis of Stamatakis E et al. Nature Medicine. 2022 (PMID: 36482104); Stamatakis E et al. JAMA Oncology. 2023 (PMID: 37498576); Koemel NA et al. European Journal of Preventive Cardiology. 2025 (PMID: 39325719).

shelves.title: JYNNEOS vaccine against mpox: two doses protect substantially, one dose less — and all the evidence is observational
shelves.question: In adults at risk during the 2022–2023 outbreak, how well did the JYNNEOS (MVA-BN) vaccine prevent mpox — one dose versus two?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Humans · Male · Case-Control Studies · HIV Infections/epidemiology, prevention & control · Homosexuality, Male · Mpox, Monkeypox*/epidemiology, prevention & control · Sexual and Gender Minorities/statistics & numerical data · United States/epidemiology · Vaccine Efficacy*/statistics & numerical data · Smallpox Vaccine · Vaccines, Attenuated
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — consistent observational protection, no trial. Three case-control studies from the 2022–2023 United States outbreak point the same way: adjusted effectiveness of two JYNNEOS doses against diagnosed mpox was 66.0% (95% CI 47.4 to 78.1) in a national electronic-health-record study (Deputy 2023, PMID: 37199451), 85.9% (73.8 to 92.4) in a 12-jurisdiction matched study (Dalton 2023, PMID: 37200229), and 88.5% in New York State (Rosenberg 2023, PMID: 37339074). One dose was consistently weaker and far less precise (35.8%, 75.2% and 68.1%). The dose-sparing intradermal route performed similarly to subcutaneous injection where both were measured. What this literature does not establish matters as much: there is no randomised trial, protection in immunocompromised patients is essentially unmeasured (70.2%, CI −37.9 to 93.6), and none of the studies could address severe disease, death, duration of protection, or other mpox clades. Tier C: the shelf rests entirely on observational evidence for a preventive claim, so it is flagged for the developer's personal verdict.

cards.headline: Deputy 2023 (Epic Cosmos case-control): two JYNNEOS doses 66% effective against diagnosed mpox, one dose 36% — adjusted estimates, no randomised trial exists
cards.summary: Deputy 2023 (Epic Cosmos case-control): two JYNNEOS doses 66% effective against diagnosed mpox, one dose 36% — adjusted estimates, no randomised trial exists
cards.type: Case-control study (Deputy 2023, New England Journal of Medicine)
cards.people: Case-control study in the Cosmos nationwide Epic electronic health record database, United States, during the 2022–2023 outbreak: 2,193 case patients with an mpox diagnosis code or positive orthopoxvirus/mpox laboratory result, and 8,319 control patients with an incident HIV diagnosis or a new or refill order for HIV preexposure prophylaxis — a control group drawn from the population at risk. The vaccine is JYNNEOS (Modified Vaccinia Ankara vaccine, Bavarian Nordic), given subcutaneously or by the dose-sparing intradermal route authorised in August 2022.
cards.result: Adjusted vaccine effectiveness against medically attended, diagnosed mpox was 66.0% (95% CI 47.4 to 78.1) for full vaccination (2 doses) and 35.8% (95% CI 22.1 to 47.1) for partial vaccination (1 dose). Effectiveness is (1 − adjusted odds ratio) × 100, as reported.
cards.watchOut: Observational EHR data: people who sought vaccination differ from those who did not in exposure and health-seeking behaviour, and adjustment cannot remove that completely. The estimate is for diagnosed, medically attended mpox — not for infection without symptoms, and not for severe disease or death, which were too rare to measure.
cards.source: Deputy NP et al. Vaccine Effectiveness of JYNNEOS against Mpox Disease in the United States. New England Journal of Medicine. 2023. PMID: 37199451. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Dalton 2023 (12-jurisdiction matched case-control): two doses 85.9% effective; route made little difference; the immunocompromised estimate is very imprecise
cards.summary: Dalton 2023 (12-jurisdiction matched case-control): two doses 85.9% effective; route made little difference; the immunocompromised estimate is very imprecise
cards.people: Matched case-control study across 12 United States jurisdictions during the 2022 outbreak: 309 mpox case patients and 608 controls. JYNNEOS (Modified Vaccinia Ankara vaccine, Bavarian Nordic) was given as a 2-dose series, subcutaneously (0.5 mL) or, under the emergency authorisation, intradermally (0.1 mL).
cards.result: Vaccine effectiveness was 75.2% (95% CI 61.2 to 84.2) for 1 dose and 85.9% (95% CI 73.8 to 92.4) for 2 doses. For 2 doses, effectiveness was similar by route: 88.9% subcutaneous, 80.3% intradermal, 86.9% mixed routes. In immunocompromised patients the 2-dose estimate was 70.2% but with a very wide interval (95% CI −37.9 to 93.6) — compatible with anything from no effect to near-complete protection.
cards.watchOut: The point estimates here are higher than in the national EHR study (Deputy 2023) — different designs, populations and calendar windows, not a contradiction to average away. The immunocompromised subgroup is the clinically important one and the one this literature measures worst.
cards.source: Dalton AF et al. Estimated Effectiveness of JYNNEOS Vaccine in Preventing Mpox: A Multijurisdictional Case-Control Study - United States, August 19, 2022-March 31, 2023. cards.headline: Rosenberg 2023 (New York State case-control): combined effectiveness 75.7%; two doses 88.5%, one dose 68.1%
cards.summary: Rosenberg 2023 (New York State case-control): combined effectiveness 75.7%; two doses 88.5%, one dose 68.1%
cards.people: Case-control study by the New York State Department of Health among men aged 18 years or older residing in New York State outside New York City, during the outbreak window July 24 to October 31, 2022: 252 case patients with diagnosed mpox and 255 contemporaneous controls, using surveillance reporting data. The vaccine deployed was JYNNEOS (Modified Vaccinia Ankara vaccine, Bavarian Nordic), a 2-dose series 4 weeks apart.
cards.result: Estimated vaccine effectiveness against diagnosed mpox was 75.7% (95% CI 48.5 to 88.5) for vaccination overall, 68.1% for 1 dose and 88.5% for 2 doses, as reported by the authors.
cards.watchOut: A small, single-state, early-outbreak study: its 1-dose estimate (68.1%) sits well above the national EHR estimate (35.8%), a reminder that one-dose protection is the least precisely measured number in this literature. All three carded studies measure diagnosed mpox in the 2022 clade IIb outbreak; none speaks to other clades or to post-exposure use.
cards.source: Rosenberg ES et al. Effectiveness of JYNNEOS Vaccine Against Diagnosed Mpox Infection - New York, 2022. MMWR Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report. 2023. PMID: 37339074. cards.headline: Synthesis: three case-control studies agree two doses protect substantially and one dose protects less — POSSIBLE, observational only
cards.summary: Synthesis: three case-control studies agree two doses protect substantially and one dose protects less — POSSIBLE, observational only
cards.people: Three case-control studies from the 2022–2023 United States outbreak: a national EHR study (2,193 cases / 8,319 controls), a 12-jurisdiction matched study (309 / 608), and a New York State study (252 / 255). No randomised trial of JYNNEOS against mpox exists; before the outbreak, effectiveness rested on immunology and animal challenge data.
cards.result: Two doses: adjusted effectiveness 66.0%, 85.9% and 88.5% across the three studies. One dose: 35.8%, 75.2% and 68.1% — consistently lower and much less precisely estimated. Route (subcutaneous vs dose-sparing intradermal) did not materially change effectiveness where it was measured. Effectiveness in immunocompromised patients — the group at highest risk of severe mpox — is essentially unmeasured (70.2%, CI −37.9 to 93.6).
cards.watchOut: This shelf cannot answer how long protection lasts, whether vaccination prevents severe disease or death (too few such outcomes), or how the vaccine performs against other mpox clades. Case-control effectiveness from an outbreak is real evidence, but it is not trial evidence, and the stamp is set accordingly.
cards.source: Synthesis of Deputy NP et al. New England Journal of Medicine. 2023 (PMID: 37199451); Dalton AF et al. MMWR Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report. 2023 (PMID: 37200229); Rosenberg ES et al. MMWR Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report. 2023 (PMID: 37339074).

shelves.title: MenACWY in adolescents: programme data show group W and Y disease falling fast after vaccination, and a randomised trial shows carriage of vaccine serogroups cut by about a third
shelves.question: In adolescents, does quadrivalent meningococcal conjugate vaccine (MenACWY) prevent invasive meningococcal disease and reduce nasopharyngeal carriage?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Carrier State/prevention & control · Female · Humans · Male · Meningococcal Infections/prevention & control · Meningococcal Vaccines/therapeutic use · Neisseria meningitidis · Neisseria meningitidis, Serogroup B · Single-Blind Method · Young Adult
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — the disease evidence is observational and the carriage evidence is a randomised trial of a surrogate. No trial of MenACWY has invasive disease as an endpoint, and none is now feasible. What exists: in a phase 3 observer-blind randomised trial of 2,954 English university students, one dose of MenACWY-CRM reduced carriage of capsular group CWY meningococci by 36.2% relative and of serogroup Y by 39.0% relative versus control over 12 months, though there was no difference at 1 month (Read 2014, PMID: 25145775). England's emergency adolescent MenACWY programme, introduced in 2015 against a group W outbreak, was followed by incidence rate ratios of 0.35 for MenW and 0.21 for MenY disease in 14–18-year-olds, with an estimated overall vaccine effectiveness of 94% (95% CI 80 to 99) against MenCWY disease and most prevented cases attributed to indirect (herd) effects (Campbell 2022, PMID: 34883094). The mechanism is not speculative: when the serogroup C conjugate vaccine was introduced in the UK, serogroup C carriage fell by 81% relative (rate ratio 0.19), vaccine efficacy against carriage was 75%, and there was no serogroup replacement (Maiden 2008, PMID: 18271745). The honest limits: the disease numbers come from surveillance and modelling of an outbreak that might have waned anyway — the estimate of MenW cases prevented through herd effects ranges from 205 to 1,193 depending on the assumed counterfactual — and the carriage trial enrolled 18–24-year-olds, not the 13–18-year-olds programmes target. Whether the 4CMenB vaccine reduces carriage is a separate question, answered at shelf #2593; the recombinant and live zoster vaccines sit at shelves #2483 and #2596.

cards.headline: Read 2014: in 2,954 English university students, MenACWY-CRM cut carriage of serogroup CWY meningococci by 36% relative and serogroup Y by 39% relative over 12 months — with no effect at 1 month
cards.summary: Read 2014: in 2,954 English university students, MenACWY-CRM cut carriage of serogroup CWY meningococci by 36% relative and serogroup Y by 39% relative over 12 months — with no effect at 1 month
cards.people: 2,954 university students aged 18–24 at ten English sites, randomised 1:1:1 to Japanese encephalitis vaccine (control), 4CMenB (two doses), or MenACWY-CRM (one dose, then placebo). Oropharyngeal swabs before vaccination and at five intervals over 1 year; 31–34% carried meningococci at entry. Primary outcome: cross-sectional carriage 1 month after the vaccine course.
cards.result: At 1 month there was no significant carriage difference for MenACWY-CRM versus control (odds ratio 0.9, 95% CI 0.6 to 1.3). Across the later timepoints, carriage was significantly lower with MenACWY-CRM than control for serogroup Y (39.0% relative carriage reduction, 95% CI 17.3 to 55.0) and for capsular groups CWY combined (36.2% relative reduction, 95% CI 15.6 to 51.7). (The 4CMenB arm's carriage results are summarised at shelf #2593.) Vaccines were generally well tolerated; no safety concerns were identified.
cards.watchOut: Carriage is a surrogate for transmission, not disease: the trial could not and did not measure invasive meningococcal disease, the effect took months to appear, and university students aged 18–24 carry meningococci at higher rates than the 13–18-year-olds routine programmes vaccinate — the size of the carriage effect in younger adolescents is inferred, not measured.
cards.source: Read RC et al. PMID: 25145775. Registry ID: NCT01214850. cards.headline: Campbell 2022: England's adolescent MenACWY programme was followed by incidence rate ratios of 0.35 (MenW) and 0.21 (MenY) in 14–18-year-olds, and 94% estimated effectiveness against MenCWY disease
cards.summary: Campbell 2022: England's adolescent MenACWY programme was followed by incidence rate ratios of 0.35 (MenW) and 0.21 (MenY) in 14–18-year-olds, and 94% estimated effectiveness against MenCWY disease
cards.people: National surveillance and modelling study of laboratory-confirmed invasive meningococcal disease in England, academic years 2010–11 to 2018–19. The emergency MenACWY programme began in August 2015, targeting 13–18-year-olds against a hypervirulent group W ST-11 outbreak strain; uptake by 2019 was 71–86% in school-vaccinated younger teenagers and 37–41% in 18-year-olds vaccinated in primary care.
cards.result: MenW and MenY cases plateaued within 12 months of the programme and then declined. In adolescents aged 14–18, the incidence rate ratio was 0.35 (95% CI 0.17 to 0.76) for MenW and 0.21 (0.07 to 0.59) for MenY; MenC cases remained low throughout. Depending on whether the counterfactual assumed cases would plateau or keep rising, an estimated 205–1,193 MenW cases were prevented through indirect (herd) effects of the programme versus 25 through direct protection, and 60–106 MenY cases indirectly versus 19 directly. Overall vaccine effectiveness against MenCWY disease combined, by the screening method, was 94% (95% CI 80 to 99).
cards.watchOut: An outbreak evaluation, not a controlled comparison: the number of cases 'prevented' depends entirely on the modelled counterfactual (plateau versus continued rise), which is why the MenW range spans 205 to 1,193. The attribution of most benefit to herd effects is likewise modelled from who was vaccinated and who stopped falling ill, not directly observed.
cards.source: Campbell H et al. Impact of an adolescent meningococcal ACWY immunisation programme to control a national outbreak of group W meningococcal disease in England: a national surveillance and modelling study. The Lancet. Child & adolescent health. 2022. PMID: 34883094. Registry ID: none — observational programme evaluation. cards.headline: Maiden 2008: after the UK MenC conjugate programme, serogroup C carriage fell by 81% relative (rate ratio 0.19), carriage efficacy was 75%, and there was no serogroup replacement
cards.summary: Maiden 2008: after the UK MenC conjugate programme, serogroup C carriage fell by 81% relative (rate ratio 0.19), carriage efficacy was 75%, and there was no serogroup replacement
cards.people: Multicentre serial cross-sectional carriage surveys conducted during the introduction of meningococcal serogroup C conjugate (MCC) vaccine in the UK in 1999 and over the two following years: 48,309 pharyngeal samples, from which 8,599 meningococci were isolated and characterised by genotyping and phenotyping.
cards.result: Serogroup C carriage fell with a rate ratio of 0.19, an effect lasting at least 2 years, with no evidence of serogroup replacement. Vaccine efficacy against carriage was 75%. The impact was greatest on the ST-11 complex serogroup C meningococci that cause most invasive disease (rate ratio 0.06), which also showed high rates of capsule expression. The pattern was consistent with herd immunity protecting young children whose own vaccine protection was short-lived.
cards.watchOut: This is the serogroup C conjugate vaccine, not the quadrivalent ACWY product: it is carded here as the proof of principle that a conjugate meningococcal vaccine can suppress carriage and generate herd protection. The size of the effect for the A, W and Y components of MenACWY rests on Read 2014 and Campbell 2022, not on this study.
cards.source: Maiden MC et al. Impact of meningococcal serogroup C conjugate vaccines on carriage and herd immunity. The Journal of infectious diseases. 2008. PMID: 18271745. Registry ID: none in the record.
