cards.headline: Synthesis: carriage falls by about a third in the trial, disease fell fastest where carriage was targeted — POSSIBLE
cards.summary: Synthesis: carriage falls by about a third in the trial, disease fell fastest where carriage was targeted — POSSIBLE
cards.people: One randomised carriage trial (2,954 students), one national programme evaluation (England, 2015–2019), and the MenC carriage surveys (48,309 samples) that established the mechanism.
cards.result: MenACWY-CRM reduced carriage of the serogroups it covers by roughly a third relative over 12 months (CWY 36.2%, Y 39.0%), with no effect in the first month. After England vaccinated its adolescents, MenW disease in 14–18-year-olds fell to an incidence rate ratio of 0.35 and MenY to 0.21, with screening-method effectiveness of 94% (80–99) against MenCWY disease — most of the benefit modelled as herd protection of the unvaccinated. The MenC experience (carriage rate ratio 0.19, no replacement) shows the mechanism is real. No randomised trial with a disease endpoint exists.
cards.watchOut: The stamp is POSSIBLE, not higher, because every disease number is observational: an outbreak strain can wane on its own, and the programme evaluation cannot fully separate vaccine effect from the outbreak's natural course. The carriage effect, though randomised, is a surrogate measured in young adults rather than in the early adolescents programmes actually vaccinate.
cards.source: Synthesis of Read RC et al. Lancet. 2014 (PMID: 25145775); Campbell H et al. The Lancet. Child & adolescent health. 2022 (PMID: 34883094); Maiden MC et al. The Journal of infectious diseases. 2008 (PMID: 18271745).

shelves.title: 4CMenB in infants: England's programme was followed by group B disease falling by half, then by three quarters, in eligible cohorts — though the per-child effectiveness estimate is imprecise
shelves.question: In infants, does the 4CMenB meningococcal B vaccine prevent invasive meningococcal disease?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Immunization Programs · Immunization Schedule · Infant · Meningococcal Infections/epidemiology/microbiology/prevention & control · Meningococcal Vaccines/administration & dosage · Public Health · Treatment Outcome · United Kingdom/epidemiology
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — a large, consistent programme effect, but every number is observational and the direct effectiveness estimate is imprecise. England introduced 4CMenB (Bexsero) in September 2015 at a reduced two-dose infant priming schedule (2 and 4 months) with a 12-month booster. In the first 10 months, two-dose vaccine effectiveness against all MenB cases was 82.9% (95% CI 24.1 to 95.2) by the screening method, and MenB cases in vaccine-eligible infants halved compared with the previous 4 years (37 versus an average of 74; incidence rate ratio 0.50, 95% CI 0.36 to 0.71), regardless of each infant's own vaccination status (Parikh 2016, PMID: 28100432). Over the first 3 years, 63 cases were observed in eligible cohorts versus 253 expected (incidence rate ratio 0.25, 95% CI 0.19 to 0.36) — a 75% relative reduction in fully eligible age groups — with an estimated 277 cases prevented (Ladhani 2020, PMID: 31971676). The tension a reader should see: in that 3-year analysis the adjusted per-child effectiveness was 52.7% for the two-dose schedule and 59.1% with the booster, but both confidence intervals cross zero (−33.5 to 83.2 and −31.1 to 87.2), because disease became so rare that the screening method lost precision. The programme-level fall is the stronger evidence; the per-child number is the weaker one. There is no randomised trial with a disease endpoint, and none is feasible at this incidence. Whether 4CMenB reduces adolescent carriage — the herd-protection question — is answered separately at shelf #2593, and its cross-protection against gonorrhoea at shelf #2594.

cards.headline: Parikh 2016: in the programme's first 10 months, two-dose 4CMenB effectiveness was 82.9% and MenB cases in eligible infants halved (37 versus an average of 74)
cards.summary: Parikh 2016: in the programme's first 10 months, two-dose 4CMenB effectiveness was 82.9% and MenB cases in eligible infants halved (37 versus an average of 74)
cards.people: National observational cohort study using Public Health England enhanced surveillance of laboratory-confirmed meningococcal disease in England, cases diagnosed 1 September 2015 to 30 June 2016. The UK programme offered a reduced two-dose 4CMenB priming schedule at 2 and 4 months, with catch-up for 3- and 4-month-olds; coverage reached 95.5% for one dose and 88.6% for two doses by 6 months of age. The vaccine was predicted to cover 73–88% of MenB strains.
cards.result: Two-dose vaccine effectiveness against all MenB cases was 82.9% (95% CI 24.1 to 95.2) by the screening method — equivalent to 94.2% effectiveness against the highest predicted strain coverage of 88%. Compared with the prevaccine period, MenB cases in the vaccine-eligible cohort fell by half (37 cases versus an average of 74; incidence rate ratio 0.50, 95% CI 0.36 to 0.71; p=0.0001), irrespective of the infants' own vaccination status or predicted strain coverage, and the reduction persisted after adjustment for disease trends in eligible and ineligible children.
cards.watchOut: The screening method estimates effectiveness from the vaccination status of cases versus population coverage — it is not a controlled comparison, and the confidence interval (24.1 to 95.2) is wide because only 37 eligible cases occurred. Part of the halving of cases may reflect herd effects and secular trends in MenB incidence, which was already falling in England before 2015.
cards.source: Parikh SR et al. Effectiveness and impact of a reduced infant schedule of 4CMenB vaccine against group B meningococcal disease in England: a national observational cohort study. Lancet. 2016. PMID: 28100432. Registry ID: none — observational programme evaluation. cards.headline: Ladhani 2020: over 3 years, 63 MenB cases were observed in eligible cohorts versus 253 expected (rate ratio 0.25) — but adjusted effectiveness of 52.7–59.1% had confidence intervals crossing zero
cards.summary: Ladhani 2020: over 3 years, 63 MenB cases were observed in eligible cohorts versus 253 expected (rate ratio 0.25) — but adjusted effectiveness of 52.7–59.1% had confidence intervals crossing zero
cards.people: Enhanced national surveillance of invasive meningococcal disease in England, September 2015 to August 2018 (average annual birth cohort about 650,000 infants). Uptake stayed high: 92.5% had completed primary immunisations by their first birthday and 87.9% had received all three doses by age 2 in early 2018 data.
cards.result: Incidence of meningococcal group B disease in vaccine-eligible cohorts was significantly lower than expected from the 4-year prevaccination period (63 observed versus 253 expected cases; incidence rate ratio 0.25, 95% CI 0.19 to 0.36), a 75% relative reduction in age groups fully eligible for vaccination. Adjusted vaccine effectiveness by the indirect screening method was 52.7% (95% CI −33.5 to 83.2) for the two-dose priming schedule and 59.1% (−31.1 to 87.2) with the 12-month booster. An estimated 277 cases (95% CI 236 to 323) were prevented over the 3 years, and protection after three doses was sustained for at least 2 years.
cards.watchOut: Hold the two findings separately: the fall in cases (63 versus 253 expected) is large and consistent, but the screening-method effectiveness estimate is statistically fragile — its confidence interval includes no effect — precisely because the vaccine era produced so few cases. Expected cases are modelled from prevaccination incidence and trends in ineligible cohorts, so any error in that counterfactual flows straight into the headline ratio.
cards.source: Ladhani SN et al. Vaccination of Infants with Meningococcal Group B Vaccine (4CMenB) in England. The New England journal of medicine. 2020. PMID: 31971676. cards.people: Two evaluations of the same English national programme: the first 10 months (Parikh 2016) and the first 3 years (Ladhani 2020), covering several million infant-years of surveillance.
cards.result: MenB cases in vaccine-eligible infants: 37 versus an average of 74 in the first 10 months (rate ratio 0.50), and 63 versus 253 expected over 3 years (rate ratio 0.25), with an estimated 277 cases prevented. Screening-method effectiveness: 82.9% (24.1–95.2) for two doses early on; 52.7% (−33.5 to 83.2) and 59.1% (−31.1 to 87.2) in the 3-year analysis. No randomised disease-endpoint trial exists for this vaccine in infants.
cards.watchOut: Both cards evaluate one country's programme with overlapping surveillance data — they are two looks at the same natural experiment, not two independent confirmations. Secular decline in MenB disease and possible herd effects from the infant programme itself both push the observed fall upward relative to the vaccine's direct effect on a vaccinated child.
cards.source: Synthesis of Parikh SR et al. Lancet. 2016 (PMID: 28100432); Ladhani SN et al. The New England journal of medicine. 2020 (PMID: 31971676).

shelves.title: 4CMenB does not stop adolescents carrying meningococci: in a 24,000-student cluster trial, carriage of disease-causing strains was 2.55% in vaccinated schools and 2.52% in controls
shelves.question: In adolescents and young adults, does MenB vaccination (4CMenB) reduce meningococcal carriage?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Australia/epidemiology · Carrier State/epidemiology/prevention & control · Female · Humans · Male · Meningococcal Infections/prevention & control · Meningococcal Vaccines/immunology · Neisseria meningitidis/genetics/isolation & purification · Neisseria meningitidis, Serogroup B/isolation & purification · Odds Ratio · Prevalence · Risk Factors · Serogroup · Single-Blind Method
shelves.balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — for the outcome that matters, carriage of disease-causing meningococci. The definitive test is the South Australian 'B Part of It' cluster-randomised trial: 237 schools, 24,269 students aged 15–18, randomised by school to 4CMenB at baseline or at 12 months. At 12 months, carriage of disease-causing Neisseria meningitidis was 2.55% in the vaccination group and 2.52% in controls (adjusted odds ratio 1.02, 95% CI 0.80 to 1.31; P = 0.85), with no significant differences in any secondary carriage outcome (Marshall 2020, PMID: 31971677). A substudy of the same trial found no difference in carriage density either (3.80 versus 3.73 log CFU/mL, P = 0.51), although students who were already carriers at baseline were less likely to still be carrying at 12 months if vaccinated (31% versus 43%; odds ratio 0.60, 95% CI 0.40 to 0.90) — a clearance signal that did not translate into lower carriage prevalence (McMillan 2021, PMID: 32447370). One tension to state plainly: the smaller English student trial (Read 2014, homed at shelf #2591) found 4CMenB reduced carriage of capsular groups BCWY by 26.6% relative from 3 months — but its outcome counted all capsular-group carriage, not specifically disease-causing genogroups, in a population with much higher baseline carriage. The practical consequence: unlike the conjugate vaccines (shelf #2591), 4CMenB should not be expected to generate herd protection; its value is direct protection of the vaccinated person (shelves #2592 and #2594).

cards.headline: Marshall 2020 (B Part of It): carriage of disease-causing meningococci at 12 months was 2.55% with 4CMenB versus 2.52% in controls — adjusted odds ratio 1.02
cards.summary: Marshall 2020 (B Part of It): carriage of disease-causing meningococci at 12 months was 2.55% with 4CMenB versus 2.52% in controls — adjusted odds ratio 1.02
cards.type: Cluster-randomised controlled trial (Marshall 2020, B Part of It)
cards.people: Cluster-randomised trial in South Australia: 237 schools randomised to 4CMenB at baseline (intervention) or at 12 months (control); 24,269 students in years 10–11 (aged 15–18) and 10,220 in year 12 enrolled in 2017. Primary outcome: oropharyngeal carriage of disease-causing N. meningitidis (genogroups A, B, C, W, X, Y) at 12 months in years 10–11, by PCR.
cards.result: There was no difference in carriage of disease-causing meningococci between the vaccination group (2.55%; 326 of 12,746) and the control group (2.52%; 291 of 11,523): adjusted odds ratio 1.02 (95% CI 0.80 to 1.31; P = 0.85). No secondary carriage outcome differed significantly, including carriage of all N. meningitidis and of individual genogroups. Baseline carriage risk factors included older school year, current upper respiratory infection, cigarette and water-pipe smoking, attending pubs or clubs, and intimate kissing. No vaccine safety concerns were identified.
cards.watchOut: Baseline carriage of disease-causing strains was low (about 2.5%), so the trial best excludes a large effect on the strains that matter; it does not exclude small effects on carriage of any meningococcus, and South Australian adolescents are not English university students — the population in which Read 2014 (shelf #2591) found a modest delayed reduction in capsular-group carriage.
cards.source: Marshall HS et al. Meningococcal B Vaccine and Meningococcal Carriage in Adolescents in Australia. The New England journal of medicine. 2020. PMID: 31971677. Registry ID: NCT03089086. cards.headline: McMillan 2021: 4CMenB did not reduce carriage density (3.80 versus 3.73 log CFU/mL) — but baseline carriers who were vaccinated were less likely to still carry at 12 months (31% versus 43%)
cards.summary: McMillan 2021: 4CMenB did not reduce carriage density (3.80 versus 3.73 log CFU/mL) — but baseline carriers who were vaccinated were less likely to still carry at 12 months (31% versus 43%)
cards.type: Cluster-randomised trial substudy (McMillan 2021, B Part of It)
cards.people: Substudy of the B Part of It cluster-randomised trial: 913 South Australian students aged about 15–18 who had N. meningitidis carriage detected at 12 months, plus 504 students with carriage at baseline followed for persistence. Carriage density estimated from quantitative PCR cycle thresholds calibrated against colony-forming units.
cards.result: Among the 913 carriers at 12 months, mean carriage density did not differ between vaccinated (3.80 log CFU/mL, SD 1.29) and control students (3.73 log CFU/mL, SD 1.30; P = 0.51). Higher baseline density predicted persistent carriage (odds ratio 1.36 per 1.0 log CFU/mL increase, 95% CI 1.17 to 1.58). Among baseline carriers, persistent carriage at 12 months was less common in the vaccinated (81 of 260, 31%) than in controls (105 of 244, 43%): odds ratio 0.60 (95% CI 0.40 to 0.90; P = 0.01).
cards.watchOut: The persistence finding is a secondary, subgroup analysis of the same trial as Marshall 2020 — it is not independent confirmation of a carriage effect, and it sits alongside null results for the trial's primary outcome and for carriage density. Faster clearance in existing carriers, if real, was not enough to lower carriage prevalence in the vaccinated schools.
cards.source: McMillan M et al. Impact of Meningococcal B (4CMenB) Vaccine on Pharyngeal Neisseria meningitidis Carriage Density and Persistence in Adolescents. Clinical infectious diseases. 2021. cards.headline: Synthesis: no effect on carriage prevalence or density in the one large randomised test — LIKELY (no difference)
cards.summary: Synthesis: no effect on carriage prevalence or density in the one large randomised test — LIKELY (no difference)
cards.people: One cluster-randomised trial programme (24,269 students in the main trial; 913 carriers in the density substudy), South Australia, 2017–2018.
cards.result: Carriage of disease-causing meningococci at 12 months: 2.55% vaccinated versus 2.52% control (adjusted OR 1.02, 0.80–1.31). Carriage density among carriers: 3.80 versus 3.73 log CFU/mL (P = 0.51). The single positive signal — less persistent carriage among baseline carriers (OR 0.60, 0.40–0.90) — did not change prevalence. Programmes should not count on 4CMenB for herd protection.
cards.watchOut: Both cards report the same trial programme (NCT03089086), so this shelf rests on one randomised experiment, conducted where disease-causing carriage was uncommon. Read 2014's capsular-group carriage reduction with 4CMenB (26.6% relative for BCWY from 3 months), homed at shelf #2591, is the contrary data point; the difference in outcome definition — any capsular group versus disease-causing genogroups — is the most likely reconciliation.
cards.source: Synthesis of Marshall HS et al. The New England journal of medicine. 2020 (PMID: 31971677); McMillan M et al. Clinical infectious diseases. 2021 (PMID: 32447370).

shelves.title: An accidental gonorrhoea vaccine: meningococcal B vaccination is associated with roughly a quarter to two fifths fewer gonorrhoea infections across three observational studies
shelves.question: In adults, does MenB vaccination protect against gonorrhoea?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Case-Control Studies · Chlamydia Infections/epidemiology/prevention & control · Comorbidity · Cross-Sectional Studies · Female · Gonorrhea/epidemiology/prevention & control · Humans · Male · Meningococcal Vaccines/administration & dosage/adverse effects · New Zealand · Retrospective Studies · Treatment Outcome · Vaccines, Conjugate/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Young Adult
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — three observational studies, two related vaccines, a consistent direction, and no randomised trial. The signal first came from New Zealand's MeNZB campaign vaccine (an outer-membrane-vesicle MenB vaccine, later withdrawn): in a retrospective case-control study of 14,730 sexual-health clinic attendees aged 15–30, vaccinated people were less likely to have gonorrhoea than chlamydia-only controls, giving an adjusted effectiveness of 31% (95% CI 21 to 39) against gonorrhoea diagnosis (Petousis-Harris 2017, PMID: 28705462). A New Zealand cohort study of 935,496 people estimated effectiveness of 24% (95% CI 1 to 42) against hospitalisation from gonorrhoea (Paynter 2019, PMID: 30621260). With the current 4CMenB vaccine, a US study linking STI surveillance to immunisation registries in New York City and Philadelphia found complete two-dose vaccination 40% effective (95% CI 23 to 53) and a single dose 26% effective (12 to 37) against gonorrhoea in 16–23-year-olds (Abara 2022, PMID: 35427490). The biology is plausible — the gonococcus and meningococcus are close relatives and share outer-membrane antigens — but every estimate is vulnerable to confounding: people who got these vaccines differ from those who did not in healthcare contact and sexual-health service use, and the 'healthy vaccinee' problem has been raised specifically for this literature. Effect sizes of 24–40% relative are worth having for a disease with rising antibiotic resistance, but they are not trial-grade numbers, and no guideline should quote them as if they were. Trials of 4CMenB for gonorrhoea prevention are the missing evidence. Treatment of gonorrhoea itself is homed at shelves #1635 and #2190–#2193; post-exposure doxycycline at shelf #582.

cards.headline: Petousis-Harris 2017: MeNZB-vaccinated young New Zealanders were less likely to have gonorrhoea — adjusted vaccine effectiveness 31% (21 to 39)
cards.summary: Petousis-Harris 2017: MeNZB-vaccinated young New Zealanders were less likely to have gonorrhoea — adjusted vaccine effectiveness 31% (21 to 39)
cards.people: Retrospective case-control study linking sexual-health clinic records to the National Immunisation Register: 14,730 cases and controls aged 15–30, born 1984–1998 and eligible for the MeNZB campaign — 1,241 gonorrhoea cases, 12,487 chlamydia-only controls, and 1,002 co-infections, from 11 of 24 clinics nationally.
cards.result: Vaccinated individuals were significantly less likely to be gonorrhoea cases than controls (511 of 1,241 cases [41%] versus 6,424 of 12,487 controls [51%] vaccinated; adjusted odds ratio 0.69, 95% CI 0.61 to 0.79; p<0.0001). Adjusted vaccine effectiveness of MeNZB against gonorrhoea was 31% (95% CI 21 to 39), after adjustment for ethnicity, deprivation, geographical area and sex. This was the first demonstration that any vaccine could protect against gonorrhoea.
cards.watchOut: The vaccine studied, MeNZB, is a campaign vaccine no longer in use; the result transfers to 4CMenB only by shared outer-membrane-vesicle biology, which Abara 2022 tests directly. The chlamydia-control design assumes vaccination does not affect chlamydia risk and that clinic attendees who test for one STI are comparable for the other — reasonable, but an assumption, and residual confounding by sexual behaviour cannot be excluded.
cards.source: Petousis-Harris H et al. Effectiveness of a group B outer membrane vesicle meningococcal vaccine against gonorrhoea in New Zealand: a retrospective case-control study. Lancet. 2017. PMID: 28705462. Registry ID: none — observational study. cards.headline: Paynter 2019: in a cohort of 935,496 New Zealanders, MeNZB effectiveness against hospitalisation from gonorrhoea was 24% (1 to 42)
cards.summary: Paynter 2019: in a cohort of 935,496 New Zealanders, MeNZB effectiveness against hospitalisation from gonorrhoea was 24% (1 to 42)
cards.people: Retrospective cohort study using linked national administrative data (demographics, hospitalisation, immunisation) for people born 1984–1999 who were eligible for MeNZB vaccination in 2004–2008; 935,496 cohort members were included in the analysis after exclusions for missing data. Outcome: hospitalisation with a primary diagnosis of gonorrhoea.
cards.result: After adjustment for gender, ethnicity and deprivation, vaccine effectiveness of MeNZB against hospitalisation caused by gonorrhoea was 24% (95% CI 1 to 42), estimated from Cox proportional-hazards models with Firth correction for the rare outcome. The direction matched the earlier case-control finding for gonorrhoea diagnosis, extending it to the severe end of the disease spectrum.
cards.watchOut: Gonorrhoea hospitalisation is rare and is a proxy for severe or complicated disease, not for infection itself; the confidence interval (1 to 42) only just excludes no effect. Nearly 200,000 otherwise eligible people were excluded for missing deprivation data, and adjustment covered only gender, ethnicity and deprivation — not sexual behaviour or healthcare use.
cards.source: Paynter J et al. Effectiveness of a Group B Outer Membrane Vesicle Meningococcal Vaccine in Preventing Hospitalization from Gonorrhea in New Zealand: A Retrospective Cohort Study. Vaccines. 2019. PMID: 30621260. Registry ID: none — observational study. MeSH: none in the record.

cards.headline: Abara 2022: in US surveillance data, a complete 4CMenB series was 40% effective (23 to 53) against gonorrhoea and one dose 26% effective (12 to 37)
cards.summary: Abara 2022: in US surveillance data, a complete 4CMenB series was 40% effective (23 to 53) against gonorrhoea and one dose 26% effective (12 to 37)
cards.people: Retrospective observational study linking STI surveillance records to immunisation registries in New York City and Philadelphia, 2016–2018: 167,706 infections (18,099 gonococcal, 124,876 chlamydial, 24,731 co-infections) among 109,737 individuals aged 16–23; 7,692 individuals had received MenB-4C (4CMenB), 52.4% one dose and 46.7% two doses.
cards.result: Compared with no vaccination, complete 4CMenB vaccination was associated with an adjusted prevalence ratio of 0.60 (95% CI 0.47 to 0.77) for gonorrhoea — 40% effectiveness (95% CI 23 to 53) — and partial (single-dose) vaccination with a ratio of 0.74 (0.63 to 0.88), 26% effectiveness (12 to 37). The dose-response pattern (two doses better than one) strengthens a causal reading of the association.
cards.watchOut: Adolescents who received MenB vaccine in the US in 2016–2018 were a selected group (vaccination was by shared clinical decision-making, often in outbreak or high-contact settings), and the comparison cannot fully adjust for differences in sexual behaviour, testing frequency or care access. A later analysis by the same group documented healthy-vaccinee bias in MenB effectiveness studies — the bias runs in the direction of overstating protection.
cards.source: Abara WE et al. Effectiveness of a serogroup B outer membrane vesicle meningococcal vaccine against gonorrhoea: a retrospective observational study. The Lancet. Infectious diseases. 2022. PMID: 35427490. Registry ID: none — observational study. cards.headline: Synthesis: three observational studies, two vaccines, one direction — about a quarter to two fifths relative protection — POSSIBLE
cards.summary: Synthesis: three observational studies, two vaccines, one direction — about a quarter to two fifths relative protection — POSSIBLE
cards.people: A New Zealand case-control study (14,730 clinic attendees) and cohort study (935,496 people) of MeNZB, and a US registry-linkage study (109,737 individuals) of 4CMenB. No randomised trial exists.
cards.result: Effectiveness against gonorrhoea: 31% (21–39) for MeNZB against diagnosis; 24% (1–42) for MeNZB against hospitalisation; 40% (23–53) for a complete 4CMenB series and 26% (12–37) for one dose. All relative measures from observational data. The consistency across designs, countries and both OMV-containing vaccines is the strength of this shelf; the absence of randomisation is its ceiling.
cards.watchOut: Every estimate could shrink toward zero under better confounding control — vaccinated and unvaccinated people differ in ways registries do not capture, and publication of a striking positive first result (2017) may have encouraged confirmatory analyses. Until a randomised trial reports, this is a reason to offer MenB vaccine where it is already indicated, not a standalone indication for vaccinating against gonorrhoea.

shelves.title: Two doses beat one: over ten years the varicella vaccine was 98.3% effective with two doses versus 94.4% with one, and breakthrough disease climbs steeply as the years since a single dose pass
shelves.question: In children, do two doses of varicella vaccine prevent chickenpox and breakthrough disease better than one dose?
shelves.mesh: Age Distribution · Antibodies, Viral/analysis · Chickenpox/epidemiology/immunology/prevention & control · Chickenpox Vaccine/administration & dosage · Child · Child, Preschool · Enzyme-Linked Immunosorbent Assay · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Herpes Zoster/epidemiology/immunology/prevention & control · Herpesvirus 3, Human/immunology · Humans · Immunity/physiology · Immunization Schedule · Incidence · Infant · Male · Probability · Risk Assessment · Sex Distribution · Time Factors · Vaccination/methods · Vaccines, Attenuated/administration & dosage
shelves.balance: LIKELY — three different designs point the same way. In the randomised comparison with 10-year active follow-up of about 2,000 children, estimated efficacy of varicella vaccine (Oka/Merck, VARIVAX) was 94.4% for one injection and 98.3% for two (P < 0.001); the cumulative risk of varicella was 7.3% after one dose versus 2.2% after two — a 3.3-fold lower risk with two doses — and most breakthrough cases in both groups were mild (Kuter 2004, PMID: 14872179). The reason a second dose matters is visible in US surveillance: among one-dose recipients, the annual breakthrough rate rose from 1.6 per 1,000 person-years in the first year after vaccination to 9.0 at 5 years and 58.2 at 9 years, and children vaccinated 5 or more years earlier were more likely to have moderate or severe breakthrough disease (risk ratio 2.6, 95% CI 1.2 to 5.8) (Chaves 2007, PMID: 17360990). After the routine second dose was introduced, a matched case-control study with PCR-confirmed cases found 2-dose effectiveness of 98.3% (95% CI 83.5 to 100) and odds of varicella 95% lower with two doses than with one (odds ratio 0.053, 95% CI 0.002 to 0.320) (Shapiro 2011, PMID: 21208922). The residual questions are about the second dose's own durability — the case-control data cover only the first 2.5 years after the recommendation — and about herpes zoster in vaccinated cohorts as they age, which none of these studies answers. This shelf is about dose number; the live attenuated zoster vaccine given to older adults is shelf #2596.

cards.headline: Kuter 2004: over 10 years, efficacy was 94.4% after one injection versus 98.3% after two — breakthrough varicella in 7.3% versus 2.2% of children
cards.summary: Kuter 2004: over 10 years, efficacy was 94.4% after one injection versus 98.3% after two — breakthrough varicella in 7.3% versus 2.2% of children
cards.people: About 2,000 healthy children aged 12 months to 12 years with a negative varicella history, randomised in 1991–1993 to one or two injections of varicella virus vaccine live (Oka/Merck, VARIVAX) given 3 months apart, with active yearly follow-up for varicella, varicella-like illness, zoster and exposures for 10 years; antibody persistence measured yearly for 9 years.
cards.result: The risk of developing varicella more than 42 days after vaccination during the 10-year period was 3.3-fold lower (P < 0.001) in children who received two injections than in those who received one (2.2% versus 7.3% cumulative incidence). Estimated vaccine efficacy over the 10 years was 94.4% for one injection and 98.3% for two injections (P < 0.001). Most cases in both groups were mild, and measurable serum antibody persisted for 9 years in all subjects.
cards.watchOut: The two injections in this trial were given 3 months apart in toddlers and young children — not the modern schedule of a first dose at 12–15 months and a second at 4–6 years — and the trial was conducted before wild-type varicella circulation fell, so its absolute breakthrough rates (7.3% and 2.2% over a decade) come from an era of intense natural exposure and boosting that no longer exists in high-coverage countries.
cards.source: Kuter B et al. Ten year follow-up of healthy children who received one or two injections of varicella vaccine. The Pediatric infectious disease journal. 2004. PMID: 14872179. cards.headline: Chaves 2007: breakthrough varicella after one dose rose from 1.6 per 1,000 person-years at 1 year to 58.2 at 9 years after vaccination
cards.summary: Chaves 2007: breakthrough varicella after one dose rose from 1.6 per 1,000 person-years at 1 year to 58.2 at 9 years after vaccination
cards.people: Ten years (1995–2004) of active surveillance in a US sentinel population of 350,000: 11,356 varicella cases, of whom 1,080 (9.5%) were breakthrough disease (rash onset more than 42 days after vaccination). Analysis adjusted for calendar year and age at onset and at vaccination.
cards.result: The annual rate of breakthrough varicella increased significantly with time since vaccination: 1.6 cases per 1,000 person-years (95% CI 1.2 to 2.0) within 1 year of vaccination, 9.0 per 1,000 (6.9 to 11.7) at 5 years, and 58.2 per 1,000 (36.0 to 94.0) at 9 years. Children aged 8–12 who had been vaccinated at least 5 years earlier were significantly more likely to have moderate or severe disease than those vaccinated less than 5 years earlier (risk ratio 2.6, 95% CI 1.2 to 5.8).
cards.watchOut: A rising breakthrough rate with time since vaccination mixes true waning with ageing: children vaccinated longest ago are also the oldest, with different exposure patterns, and the analysis cannot fully separate the two. The 9-year rate (58.2 per 1,000 person-years) rests on small numbers, as its wide confidence interval shows.
cards.source: Chaves SS et al. Loss of vaccine-induced immunity to varicella over time. The New England journal of medicine. 2007. PMID: 17360990. Registry ID: none — observational surveillance study. cards.headline: Shapiro 2011: two-dose effectiveness was 98.3% (83.5 to 100) — no case child had received two doses, versus 15.7% of controls
cards.summary: Shapiro 2011: two-dose effectiveness was 98.3% (83.5 to 100) — no case child had received two doses, versus 15.7% of controls
cards.people: Matched case-control study, July 2006 to January 2010 (after the routine second dose was recommended in the US): 71 children aged 4 years or older with PCR-confirmed varicella and 140 controls matched by age and paediatric practice.
cards.result: No case (0%) had received two doses of varicella vaccine, versus 22 controls (15.7%); 93.0% of cases and 83.6% of controls had received one dose. Effectiveness of two doses was 98.3% (95% confidence level 83.5% to 100%; P < .001). The matched odds ratio for two doses versus one dose was 0.053 (95% CI 0.002 to 0.320; P < .001) — the odds of varicella were about 95% lower with two doses than with one.
cards.watchOut: Small numbers drive the estimate: zero two-dose cases among 71 is what produces the striking odds ratio, and its confidence interval is correspondingly wide (0.002 to 0.320). Follow-up covered only the first 2.5 years after the second-dose recommendation, so this study says nothing about how long two-dose protection lasts into adolescence.
cards.source: Shapiro ED et al. Effectiveness of 2 doses of varicella vaccine in children. The Journal of infectious diseases. 2011. PMID: 21208922. Registry ID: none — observational study. cards.headline: Synthesis: two doses are better than one by every design that has tested it — LIKELY
cards.summary: Synthesis: two doses are better than one by every design that has tested it — LIKELY
cards.people: One randomised 1-versus-2-dose trial with 10-year follow-up (about 2,000 children), one 10-year surveillance analysis (11,356 cases), and one PCR-confirmed matched case-control study (71 cases, 140 controls).
cards.result: Efficacy/effectiveness: 94.4% (one dose) versus 98.3% (two doses) over 10 years in the trial; breakthrough risk 7.3% versus 2.2% cumulative. One-dose protection visibly erodes with time (breakthrough 1.6 → 58.2 per 1,000 person-years from year 1 to year 9). Case-control: two-dose effectiveness 98.3% (83.5–100), odds ratio 0.053 for two versus one dose. The second dose answers both primary vaccine failure and waning.
cards.watchOut: None of these studies follows two-dose recipients into late adolescence or adulthood, and none measures herpes zoster in vaccinated cohorts — the two open questions about the two-dose programme. Most breakthrough disease in every study was mild; the argument for the second dose is about preventing cases and their complications at population scale, not about severe disease in the typical breakthrough case.
cards.source: Synthesis of Kuter B et al. The Pediatric infectious disease journal. 2004 (PMID: 14872179); Chaves SS et al. The New England journal of medicine. 2007 (PMID: 17360990); Shapiro ED et al. The Journal of infectious diseases. 2011 (PMID: 21208922).

shelves.title: The live zoster vaccine halved shingles in its one big trial — but protection faded to about a fifth by years 7–11, which is why the recombinant vaccine has replaced it
shelves.question: In adults aged 60 and over, does the live attenuated zoster vaccine prevent shingles, and how fast does protection wane?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Chickenpox Vaccine/adverse effects/immunology · Cost of Illness · Double-Blind Method · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Herpes Zoster/complications/epidemiology/prevention & control · Herpesvirus 3, Human/immunology · Humans · Immunologic Memory · Incidence · Male · Middle Aged · Neuralgia/prevention & control/virology · Vaccines, Attenuated/adverse effects/immunology · Virus Activation
shelves.balance: LIKELY — one very large randomised trial, a consistent field cohort, and a clear waning curve. In the Shingles Prevention Study, 38,546 adults aged 60 and over were randomised to live attenuated Oka/Merck zoster vaccine or placebo: over a median 3.12 years there were 315 confirmed herpes zoster cases in vaccine recipients versus 642 in placebo recipients — efficacy 51.3% against incidence, 66.5% against postherpetic neuralgia (27 versus 80 cases), and 61.1% against the burden-of-illness measure (Oxman 2005, PMID: 15930418). In routine practice (Kaiser Permanente Southern California), vaccinated adults had a zoster incidence of 6.4 versus 13.0 per 1,000 person-years in matched unvaccinated adults (adjusted hazard ratio 0.45, 95% CI 0.42 to 0.48) (Tseng 2011, PMID: 21224457). The catch is durability: in the long-term persistence substudy, which followed 6,867 original vaccine recipients for up to 11 years against modelled placebo rates, estimated efficacy against zoster incidence fell from 51.3% to 21.1%, remained significantly above zero only through year 8 for incidence (year 10 for burden of illness), and declined across every outcome from years 7 to 11 (Morrison 2015, PMID: 25416754). So the live vaccine worked, briefly by vaccine standards — a profile that explains why the adjuvanted recombinant vaccine, with higher and more durable efficacy, has displaced it where available (that vaccine is shelf #2483; whether zoster vaccination affects dementia risk is a different question, at shelf #442). Being live, this vaccine was also contraindicated in significant immunosuppression, a restriction the recombinant product does not share.

cards.headline: Oxman 2005 (Shingles Prevention Study): 315 zoster cases on vaccine versus 642 on placebo — efficacy 51.3% for incidence, 66.5% for postherpetic neuralgia
cards.summary: Oxman 2005 (Shingles Prevention Study): 315 zoster cases on vaccine versus 642 on placebo — efficacy 51.3% for incidence, 66.5% for postherpetic neuralgia
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial (Oxman 2005, Shingles Prevention Study)
cards.people: 38,546 adults aged 60 years or older in a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial of live attenuated Oka/Merck varicella-zoster vaccine; more than 95% completed the study, with median surveillance of 3.12 years. Primary endpoint: burden of illness from herpes zoster (incidence, severity and duration of pain); secondary endpoint: incidence of postherpetic neuralgia.
cards.result: Confirmed herpes zoster occurred in 315 vaccine recipients and 642 placebo recipients; postherpetic neuralgia in 27 and 80 respectively. The vaccine reduced the burden of illness from zoster by 61.1% (P < 0.001), the incidence of postherpetic neuralgia by 66.5% (P < 0.001), and the incidence of herpes zoster by 51.3% (P < 0.001) — all relative reductions. Injection-site reactions were more frequent with vaccine but generally mild.
cards.watchOut: One trial carries the whole efficacy claim for this vaccine, in immunocompetent volunteers healthier than the general over-60 population; efficacy was lower in the oldest participants in the trial's age-stratified results. Median follow-up was only about 3 years — the trial itself cannot speak to the waning that the persistence substudy later documented.
cards.source: Oxman MN et al. A vaccine to prevent herpes zoster and postherpetic neuralgia in older adults. The New England journal of medicine. 2005. PMID: 15930418. cards.headline: Tseng 2011: in routine practice, zoster incidence was 6.4 per 1,000 person-years in vaccinated adults versus 13.0 in unvaccinated — adjusted hazard ratio 0.45
cards.summary: Tseng 2011: in routine practice, zoster incidence was 6.4 per 1,000 person-years in vaccinated adults versus 13.0 in unvaccinated — adjusted hazard ratio 0.45
cards.people: Retrospective cohort study in Kaiser Permanente Southern California, 2007–2009: 75,761 vaccinated immunocompetent community-dwelling adults aged 60 or older, age-matched 1:3 to 227,283 unvaccinated members.
cards.result: Herpes zoster occurred at 6.4 per 1,000 person-years (828 cases in 130,415 person-years) in the vaccinated cohort versus 13.0 per 1,000 person-years (4,606 cases in 355,659 person-years) in the unvaccinated — an adjusted hazard ratio of 0.45 (95% CI 0.42 to 0.48), consistent across age strata and in people with chronic diseases. Ophthalmic zoster (HR 0.37, 95% CI 0.23 to 0.61) and zoster hospitalisations (HR 0.35, 0.24 to 0.51) were also less likely in vaccine recipients.
cards.watchOut: Observational: vaccinated members were whiter, more often women, had more outpatient visits and fewer chronic diseases than the unvaccinated — the authors' check against unrelated acute conditions argues the zoster result is not pure bias, but healthy-vaccinee confounding cannot be fully excluded. Follow-up was short (2007–2009), so this study measures early effectiveness, close to the trial's time window.
cards.source: Tseng HF et al. Herpes zoster vaccine in older adults and the risk of subsequent herpes zoster disease. JAMA. 2011. PMID: 21224457. Registry ID: none — observational study. cards.headline: Morrison 2015: by years 7–11, estimated efficacy against zoster incidence had fallen from 51.3% to 21.1% — significant only through year 8
cards.summary: Morrison 2015: by years 7–11, estimated efficacy against zoster incidence had fallen from 51.3% to 21.1% — significant only through year 8
cards.type: Long-term persistence substudy with modelled controls (Morrison 2015)
cards.people: Long-Term Persistence Substudy of the Shingles Prevention Study: 6,867 original vaccine recipients followed for up to 11 years after vaccination, with surveillance and case determination as in the parent trial. Because original placebo recipients had been offered vaccine, there was no concurrent control group; efficacy was estimated against placebo rates modelled from the original trial and its short-term substudy.
cards.result: Estimated vaccine efficacy declined over the long-term period for all outcomes: from 61.1% to 37.3% for burden of illness, from 66.5% to 35.4% for postherpetic neuralgia incidence, and from 51.3% to 21.1% for herpes zoster incidence. Efficacy for burden of illness remained significantly greater than zero through year 10; efficacy for zoster incidence only through year 8. Efficacy declined year by year across years 7 to 11 for every measure.
cards.watchOut: The comparison group is a statistical model, not randomised contemporaneous controls, and substudy volunteers are survivors of the original trial cohort — both features soften the precision of the year-by-year efficacy estimates. The direction and rough pace of waning, however, are consistent across all three outcomes and with the immunology of a single live-virus boost in older adults.

cards.headline: Synthesis: real protection that halves shingles for a few years, then fades — LIKELY benefit, with waning as part of the answer
cards.summary: Synthesis: real protection that halves shingles for a few years, then fades — LIKELY benefit, with waning as part of the answer
cards.people: One randomised trial (38,546 adults), one matched field cohort (303,044 adults), and an 11-year persistence substudy (6,867 vaccine recipients) of the same vaccine.
cards.result: Efficacy against zoster incidence 51.3% and against postherpetic neuralgia 66.5% over about 3 years in the trial; field hazard ratio 0.45 (0.42–0.48). By years 7–11, estimated incidence efficacy had fallen to 21.1%, statistically distinguishable from zero only through year 8. The recombinant vaccine at shelf #2483 exists precisely because of this profile.
cards.watchOut: Do not quote the 51.3% figure without its time window: it describes the first few years after vaccination in trial volunteers. Anyone vaccinated with the live product a decade ago should be assumed to retain little protection, which is the practical question this shelf most often answers now.

shelves.title: Tick-borne encephalitis vaccination in Austria: field effectiveness of about 99% in people vaccinated on schedule, and national incidence down to roughly a sixth of the pre-vaccine era
shelves.question: In endemic regions, does tick-borne encephalitis vaccination prevent TBE at population level?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Animals · Austria/epidemiology · Child · Child, Preschool · Encephalitis Viruses, Tick-Borne/immunology · Encephalitis, Tick-Borne/epidemiology/immunology/prevention & control · Humans · Immunization Programs/legislation & jurisprudence/organization & administration · Immunization Schedule · Infant · Infant, Newborn · Middle Aged · Treatment Outcome · Vaccination/methods · Vaccines, Inactivated/administration & dosage/immunology · Viral Vaccines/administration & dosage/immunology
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — the effect size is very large and internally consistent, but the evidence is field epidemiology from essentially one country's programme and one research group, with no randomised trial. Austria is the natural experiment: by the 2000s, 88% of its population had a history of TBE vaccination and 58% were vaccinated within the recommended schedule. Comparing hospitalised cases in vaccinated and unvaccinated people against population denominators for 2000–2006, field effectiveness in regularly vaccinated persons was about 99%, with no significant difference between age groups; it was at least as high after the first two doses, but significantly lower — about 95% — in people with irregular vaccination histories. An estimated 2,800 cases were prevented in 2000–2006 (Heinz 2007, PMID: 17869389). Over 40 years, Austrian TBE incidence fell to about 16% of the prevaccination era while incidence in the unvaccinated population remained high, and incidence stayed high in the Czech Republic and Slovenia, where coverage was lower; about 4,000 cases were estimated prevented in Austria in 2000–2011 (Heinz 2013, PMID: 23259984). The caveats are structural: TBE incidence fluctuates strongly year to year with tick ecology and human exposure, case ascertainment and denominators come from surveys, and the comparison between countries is ecological. Even so, a fall confined to the vaccinated population, sustained over decades, at 99% estimated effectiveness, is not plausibly an artefact of weather. Both cards come from the Austrian reference-laboratory group that also advises the programme — independent replication in other high-coverage settings would strengthen this shelf.

cards.headline: Heinz 2007: Austrian field effectiveness of TBE vaccination was about 99% in regularly vaccinated people and about 95% with irregular vaccination; roughly 2,800 cases prevented in 2000–2006
cards.summary: Heinz 2007: Austrian field effectiveness of TBE vaccination was about 99% in regularly vaccinated people and about 95% with irregular vaccination; roughly 2,800 cases prevented in 2000–2006
cards.people: Field-effectiveness analysis for Austria, 2000–2006, based on documented numbers of hospitalised TBE cases in unvaccinated and vaccinated people and the sizes of those population groups from representative surveys. Vaccination coverage in Austria: 88% of the total population had a history of TBE vaccination; 58% were regularly vaccinated within the recommended schedule.
cards.result: Overall field effectiveness in regularly vaccinated persons was about 99%, with no statistically significant difference between age groups. Effectiveness was at least as high after the first two vaccinations — before completion of the basic three-dose scheme — but significantly lower, at about 95%, in those with a record of irregular vaccination. The authors estimate that about 2,800 TBE cases were prevented by vaccination in Austria during 2000–2006.
cards.watchOut: Effectiveness this high is computed, not randomised: it divides hospitalised cases by survey-estimated vaccinated and unvaccinated population sizes, so errors in either the case vaccination histories or the denominators move the estimate. Breakthrough cases in fully vaccinated people do occur and are documented in the Austrian literature — 99% is a population average, not a guarantee for an individual.
cards.source: Heinz FX et al. Field effectiveness of vaccination against tick-borne encephalitis. Vaccine. 2007. PMID: 17869389. Registry ID: none — observational field-effectiveness analysis. cards.headline: Heinz 2013: over 40 years, Austria's TBE incidence fell to about 16% of the pre-vaccination era while rates stayed high in the unvaccinated and in lower-coverage neighbours
cards.summary: Heinz 2013: over 40 years, Austria's TBE incidence fell to about 16% of the pre-vaccination era while rates stayed high in the unvaccinated and in lower-coverage neighbours
cards.people: Forty-year comparison of TBE incidence in three highly endemic central European countries — Austria (mass vaccination), the Czech Republic and Slovenia (lower coverage) — including age-distribution shifts and, within Austria, incidence in vaccinated versus non-vaccinated populations.
cards.result: All three countries showed extensive annual and longer-range fluctuations and shifts in patient age distribution. The distinctive finding was Austria's: mass vaccination decreased incidence to approximately 16% of that of the prevaccination era, while incidence rates remained high for the non-vaccinated population, and the vaccine was effective in all age groups. During 2000–2011, approximately 4,000 cases of TBE were estimated to have been prevented by vaccination in Austria.
cards.watchOut: An ecological comparison across countries that differ in tick ecology, surveillance and leisure patterns as well as vaccine coverage — the between-country contrast is supportive, not decisive. The within-Austria contrast (incidence high in the unvaccinated, low overall) is the stronger evidence, and it shares the same data systems as the 2007 analysis rather than independently replicating it.
cards.source: Heinz FX et al. Vaccination and tick-borne encephalitis, central Europe. Emerging infectious diseases. 2013. PMID: 23259984. Registry ID: none — observational analysis. shelves.title: Japanese encephalitis vaccines work: 91% efficacy in a 65,000-child randomised trial of the inactivated vaccine, and 97.5% effectiveness for two doses of the live SA14-14-2 vaccine
shelves.question: In children and travellers in endemic Asia, do Japanese encephalitis vaccines prevent JE?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Child · Child, Preschool · Clinical Trials as Topic · Dengue/prevention & control · Encephalitis Virus, Japanese/immunology · Encephalitis, Japanese/prevention & control/transmission · Humans · Immunization Schedule · Infant · Thailand · Vaccination · Vaccines, Attenuated/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Viral Vaccines/administration & dosage/adverse effects
shelves.balance: LIKELY — a large randomised trial with a clinical endpoint for one vaccine, a strong case-control estimate for the other, and an immunogenicity bridge to the modern product. In northern Thailand, 65,224 children were randomised to two doses of inactivated mouse-brain-derived JE vaccine (monovalent or bivalent) or tetanus toxoid placebo: the cumulative attack rate for JE was 51 per 100,000 on placebo versus 5 per 100,000 in each vaccine group — efficacy 91% (95% CI 70 to 97) (Hoke 1988, PMID: 2842677). For the inexpensive live attenuated SA14-14-2 vaccine used across China, a case-control study in Sichuan (56 serologically confirmed cases, 1,299 matched controls) estimated effectiveness of 80% (95% CI 44 to 93) for one dose and 97.5% (86 to 99.6) for two doses given a year apart (Hennessy 1996, PMID: 8667866). The modern Vero-cell inactivated vaccine (Ixiaro) was never trialled against disease; its licence rests on a non-inferiority immunogenicity trial in 867 adults, in which seroconversion was 98% versus 95% for the older mouse-brain vaccine and geometric mean titres were 2.3-fold higher (Tauber 2007, PMID: 18061060). That bridge is reasonable — neutralising antibody is the accepted correlate — but it is a bridge: the 91% figure belongs to a discontinued mouse-brain product, and travellers receiving the Vero-cell vaccine are protected by inference from antibody levels, not by a disease-endpoint trial of their vaccine. (The slate that proposed this shelf described the Hoke trial as a live SA14-14-2 trial; the fetched record shows it tested inactivated vaccines — the live vaccine's evidence is Hennessy 1996.)

cards.headline: Hoke 1988: in 65,224 Thai children, JE attack rates were 51 per 100,000 on placebo versus 5 per 100,000 on inactivated vaccine — efficacy 91% (70 to 97)
cards.summary: Hoke 1988: in 65,224 Thai children, JE attack rates were 51 per 100,000 on placebo versus 5 per 100,000 on inactivated vaccine — efficacy 91% (70 to 97)
cards.people: Placebo-controlled, blinded, randomised trial in a northern Thai province, 1984–1985: 65,224 children received two doses of monovalent (Nakayama strain; n = 21,628) or bivalent (Nakayama plus Beijing; n = 22,080) inactivated purified mouse-brain-derived JE vaccine, or tetanus toxoid placebo (n = 21,516). Outcomes: incidence and severity of JE and of dengue haemorrhagic fever.
cards.result: The cumulative attack rate for JE was 51 per 100,000 in the placebo group and 5 per 100,000 in each vaccine group. Efficacy in both vaccine groups combined was 91% (95% confidence interval 70 to 97%). Attack rates for dengue haemorrhagic fever declined but not significantly, though dengue severity was also reduced. Side effects of vaccination were minor.
cards.watchOut: The vaccine that earned the 91% figure — mouse-brain-derived inactivated vaccine — has been withdrawn in most countries over production and safety concerns, and this trial's MeSH indexing (which includes 'Vaccines, Attenuated') does not match the inactivated products actually tested; the MeSH above is reproduced as the record carries it. The efficacy transfers to modern vaccines only through the antibody correlate, tested for the Vero-cell vaccine by Tauber 2007.
cards.source: Hoke CH et al. Protection against Japanese encephalitis by inactivated vaccines. The New England journal of medicine. 1988. PMID: 2842677. Registry ID: none — pre-registration era. cards.headline: Hennessy 1996: two doses of live SA14-14-2 vaccine were 97.5% effective (86 to 99.6) against JE in Sichuan children; one dose 80% (44 to 93)
cards.summary: Hennessy 1996: two doses of live SA14-14-2 vaccine were 97.5% effective (86 to 99.6) against JE in Sichuan children; one dose 80% (44 to 93)
cards.people: Case-control study in rural Sichuan Province, China: 56 children admitted to hospital with serologically confirmed acute JE, and 1,299 village- and age-matched controls, with vaccination histories taken from pre-existing written records. The vaccine is the live attenuated SA14-14-2 strain, licensed in China in 1988 and given inexpensively at population scale.
cards.result: Effectiveness was 80% (95% CI 44 to 93) for one dose and 97.5% (95% CI 86 to 99.6) for two doses administered 1 year apart. Controlling for multiple potential confounders did not alter the results. The authors concluded that a two-dose regimen of the live attenuated vaccine is effective in preventing clinically important disease, while noting that further safety study was needed.
cards.watchOut: Only 56 cases: the one-dose estimate (80%) has a wide interval (44 to 93), and case-control vaccination histories, even from written records, can misclassify. This is the pivotal effectiveness evidence for the vaccine most widely used in Asia — strong in effect size, thin in case numbers, and observational by necessity.
cards.source: Hennessy S et al. Effectiveness of live-attenuated Japanese encephalitis vaccine (SA14-14-2): a case-control study. Lancet. 1996. PMID: 8667866. Registry ID: none — observational study. cards.headline: Tauber 2007: the Vero-cell inactivated vaccine (Ixiaro) was non-inferior to the mouse-brain vaccine — seroconversion 98% versus 95%, titres 2.3-fold higher
cards.summary: Tauber 2007: the Vero-cell inactivated vaccine (Ixiaro) was non-inferior to the mouse-brain vaccine — seroconversion 98% versus 95%, titres 2.3-fold higher
cards.people: Multicentre, multinational, observer-blinded, randomised phase III non-inferiority trial in 867 adults (sites in the USA, Germany and Austria): the Vero-cell-derived inactivated JE vaccine intramuscularly on days 0 and 28 (n = 430) versus the licensed mouse-brain-derived vaccine subcutaneously on days 0, 7 and 28 (n = 437). Primary endpoint: neutralising antibody (plaque-reduction neutralisation test) at day 56, assessable in 725 per-protocol participants.
cards.result: Seroconversion was 98% with the test vaccine versus 95% with the licensed vaccine (95% CI for the difference −1.33 to 3.43), meeting non-inferiority. Geometric mean titre was 244 with the test vaccine versus 102 with the licensed vaccine (ratio 2.3, 95% CI 1.967 to 2.75). Adverse-event frequency was similar between groups, vaccine-related events were generally mild, and local tolerability favoured the test vaccine.
cards.watchOut: An antibody trial in non-endemic-country adults, not a disease trial in the children who bear JE's burden: protection of travellers by this vaccine is inferred from the neutralising-antibody correlate and from the older vaccine's clinical efficacy. It also says nothing about duration of protection or booster timing, which rest on separate immunogenicity follow-up studies.
cards.source: Tauber E et al. Safety and immunogenicity of a Vero-cell-derived, inactivated Japanese encephalitis vaccine: a non-inferiority, phase III, randomised controlled trial. Lancet. 2007. PMID: 18061060. Registry ID: EudraCT 2004-002474-36. randomised non-inferiority immunogenicity trial (tauber 2007) multicentre, multinational, observer-blinded, randomised phase iii non-inferiority trial in 867 adults (sites in the usa, germany and austria): the vero-cell-derived inactivated je vaccine intramuscularly on days 0 and 28 (n = 430) versus the licensed mouse-brain-derived vaccine subcutaneously on days 0, 7 and 28 (n = 437). primary endpoint: neutralising antibody (plaque-reduction neutralisation test) at day 56, assessable in 725 per-protocol participants. seroconversion was 98% with the test vaccine versus 95% with the licensed vaccine (95% ci for the difference −1.33 to 3.43), meeting non-inferiority. geometric mean titre was 244 with the test vaccine versus 102 with the licensed vaccine (ratio 2.3, 95% ci 1.967 to 2.75). adverse-event frequency was similar between groups, vaccine-related events were generally mild, and local tolerability favoured the test vaccine. an antibody trial in non-endemic-country adults, not a disease trial in the children who bear je's burden: protection of travellers by this vaccine is inferred from the neutralising-antibody correlate and from the older vaccine's clinical efficacy. it also says nothing about duration of protection or booster timing, which rest on separate immunogenicity follow-up studies. tauber e et al. safety and immunogenicity of a vero-cell-derived, inactivated japanese encephalitis vaccine: a non-inferiority, phase iii, randomised controlled trial. lancet. 2007. pmid: 18061060. registry id: eudract 2004-002474-36. mesh: adolescent · adult · aged · aged, 80 and over · analysis of variance · animals · antibodies, viral/blood · chlorocebus aethiops · encephalitis, japanese/immunology/prevention & control · female · humans · immunization schedule · japanese encephalitis vaccines/administration & dosage/adverse effects/immunology · male · middle aged · vero cells

cards.headline: Synthesis: two different vaccines, two disease-endpoint studies, one conclusion — LIKELY
cards.summary: Synthesis: two different vaccines, two disease-endpoint studies, one conclusion — LIKELY
cards.people: One randomised trial of inactivated vaccine (65,224 children), one case-control study of the live vaccine (56 cases, 1,299 controls), and one immunogenicity non-inferiority trial of the modern Vero-cell vaccine (867 adults).
cards.result: Inactivated vaccine efficacy 91% (70–97) against clinical JE (attack rates 5 versus 51 per 100,000). Live SA14-14-2 effectiveness 80% (44–93) for one dose and 97.5% (86–99.6) for two. The Vero-cell successor is immunologically non-inferior to the vaccine class with proven clinical efficacy, with 2.3-fold higher geometric mean titres.
cards.watchOut: The chain has one inferential link: no modern traveller vaccine has a disease-endpoint trial, so its protection is extrapolated from antibody levels benchmarked against a discontinued product. The direct disease evidence is also old (1988, 1996) and from high-transmission settings; effectiveness where exposure is brief and seasonal, as for most travellers, is assumed rather than measured.
cards.source: Synthesis of Hoke CH et al. The New England journal of medicine. 1988 (PMID: 2842677); Hennessy S et al. Lancet. 1996 (PMID: 8667866); Tauber E et al. Lancet. 2007 (PMID: 18061060).

shelves.title: Hepatitis A vaccine after exposure: it prevented secondary cases in a randomised household trial and met non-inferiority against immune globulin — with a hint it may be slightly less effective
shelves.question: After exposure to hepatitis A, does hepatitis A vaccine prevent illness as well as immune globulin?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Child · Child, Preschool · Double-Blind Method · Female · Hepatitis A/immunology/prevention & control · Hepatitis A Vaccines · Hepatitis A Virus, Human/immunology · Hepatitis Antibodies/blood · Humans · Immunoglobulin M/blood · Immunoglobulins/therapeutic use · Infant · Male · Middle Aged
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — one head-to-head trial that met its non-inferiority criterion while pointing slightly the wrong way, plus one randomised trial showing the vaccine works as post-exposure prophylaxis at all. In Almaty, Kazakhstan, 1,090 susceptible household and day-care contacts aged 2–40 were randomised within 14 days of exposure to one dose of hepatitis A vaccine or to immune globulin: symptomatic laboratory-confirmed hepatitis A occurred in 4.4% of vaccine recipients (25 of 568) versus 3.3% of immune globulin recipients (17 of 522) — relative risk 1.35 (95% CI 0.70 to 2.67). The prespecified non-inferiority criterion was met, and both groups' rates were low, but the point estimate favours immune globulin and the authors themselves note the difference might be clinically meaningful in some settings (Victor 2007, PMID: 17947390). That the vaccine is active after exposure is independently supported by an Italian randomised trial in household contacts of sporadic cases: secondary infection occurred in 1.0% of vaccinated contacts (2 of 197) versus 5.8% of unvaccinated contacts (12 of 207) — protective efficacy 79% (95% CI 7 to 95), with 18 contacts needing vaccination to prevent one secondary infection (Sagliocca 1999, PMID: 10209977). The vaccine's practical advantages are real: it also confers long-term protection, is more available than immune globulin, and avoids a blood product. The honest summary for a clinician choosing today: vaccine is a reasonable, evidence-backed alternative to immune globulin for post-exposure prophylaxis in healthy younger contacts; where the exposure is high-risk or the contact is older or immunocompromised, the trial evidence does not exclude a modest advantage for immune globulin, and this shelf takes no position beyond the data.

cards.headline: Victor 2007: symptomatic hepatitis A in 4.4% after vaccine versus 3.3% after immune globulin (relative risk 1.35, 0.70 to 2.67) — non-inferiority met, point estimate favouring immune globulin
cards.summary: Victor 2007: symptomatic hepatitis A in 4.4% after vaccine versus 3.3% after immune globulin (relative risk 1.35, 0.70 to 2.67) — non-inferiority met, point estimate favouring immune globulin
cards.people: Randomised double-blind trial in Almaty, Kazakhstan: 4,524 household and day-care contacts aged 2–40 underwent randomisation; 1,414 (31%) were susceptible to hepatitis A virus and 1,090 were eligible for the per-protocol analysis (568 vaccine, 522 immune globulin). Prophylaxis was given within 14 days of exposure (average interval 10 days); most contacts were children (average age 12). Outcome: laboratory-confirmed symptomatic hepatitis A between days 15 and 56 after exposure.
cards.result: Symptomatic confirmed hepatitis A occurred in 25 contacts receiving vaccine (4.4%) and 17 receiving immune globulin (3.3%): relative risk 1.35 (95% CI 0.70 to 2.67). The study's prespecified criterion for non-inferiority was met, and absolute rates in both groups were low, indicating both interventions provided good protection after exposure. The authors note the slightly higher rate with vaccine may indicate a true modest difference in efficacy.
cards.watchOut: Most participants were children treated in the second week after exposure in a high-incidence setting; the trial does not directly answer PEP for older adults, immunocompromised contacts, or exposures treated in the first days, and its confidence interval is compatible with the vaccine being up to about two thirds worse in relative terms (upper bound 2.67) — 'non-inferior by the prespecified margin' is not 'identical'.
cards.source: Victor JC et al. Hepatitis A vaccine versus immune globulin for postexposure prophylaxis. The New England journal of medicine. 2007. PMID: 17947390. Registry ID: NCT00139139. cards.headline: Sagliocca 1999: secondary hepatitis A infection in 1.0% of vaccinated household contacts versus 5.8% of unvaccinated — protective efficacy 79% (7 to 95)
cards.summary: Sagliocca 1999: secondary hepatitis A infection in 1.0% of vaccinated household contacts versus 5.8% of unvaccinated — protective efficacy 79% (7 to 95)
cards.people: Randomised controlled trial in Italy among household contacts of people with sporadic hepatitis A (index cases): households were randomised by week of enrolment to vaccination of all contacts at entry or to no vaccination, with 45 days of follow-up. 404 contacts were analysed (197 vaccinated, 207 unvaccinated) in 146 households.
cards.result: Secondary infection occurred in 2 of 197 vaccinated contacts (1.0%) versus 12 of 207 unvaccinated contacts (5.8%); at household level, 2 of 71 vaccine-group households (2.8%) versus 10 of 75 untreated households (13.3%) had a secondary case. Protective efficacy of the vaccine was 79% (95% CI 7 to 95). Eighteen individuals needed to be vaccinated to prevent one secondary infection.
cards.watchOut: The comparator is no treatment, not immune globulin — this trial proves the vaccine works after exposure, not how it compares with the standard it would replace. Event numbers are small (14 secondary infections in total), the efficacy interval is very wide (7 to 95), and household-level randomisation by enrolment week is a weaker design than individual randomisation.
cards.source: Sagliocca L et al. Efficacy of hepatitis A vaccine in prevention of secondary hepatitis A infection: a randomised trial. Lancet. 1999. PMID: 10209977. Registry ID: none — pre-registration era. cards.headline: Synthesis: vaccine works after exposure and met non-inferiority against immune globulin — but the only direct comparison leans toward immune globulin — POSSIBLE
cards.summary: Synthesis: vaccine works after exposure and met non-inferiority against immune globulin — but the only direct comparison leans toward immune globulin — POSSIBLE
cards.people: One randomised head-to-head non-inferiority trial (1,090 susceptible contacts) and one randomised trial against no treatment (404 household contacts).
cards.result: Versus immune globulin: 4.4% versus 3.3% symptomatic confirmed hepatitis A (RR 1.35, 0.70–2.67), non-inferiority criterion met. Versus nothing: secondary infection 1.0% versus 5.8%, protective efficacy 79% (7–95), number needed to vaccinate 18. Both interventions leave absolute post-exposure risk low; the vaccine additionally leaves the contact immune for the future.
cards.watchOut: The stamp is POSSIBLE rather than LIKELY because the comparative claim — 'as well as immune globulin' — rests on a single trial whose point estimate favours the comparator. For contacts at highest risk of severe hepatitis A, this evidence base does not justify displacing immune globulin where guidelines still prefer it; for routine healthy contacts, it supports the vaccine as a reasonable alternative.
cards.source: Synthesis of Victor JC et al. The New England journal of medicine. 2007 (PMID: 17947390); Sagliocca L et al. Lancet. 1999 (PMID: 10209977).

shelves.title: Assisted partner services for HIV: partners tested 67% versus 13% and five times the new diagnoses in the Kenyan cluster trial, with a smaller but consistent pooled effect
shelves.question: In people newly diagnosed with HIV, does assisted partner notification (provider-supported partner services) increase partner testing and new diagnoses versus passive referral?
shelves.mesh: Cluster Analysis · HIV Infections/diagnosis*/epidemiology*/virology · Health Services* · Humans · Kenya/epidemiology · Mass Screening · Sexual Partners* · Spouse Abuse · Young Adult
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — in a Kenyan cluster-randomised trial of 18 clinics, immediate assisted partner services multiplied partner testing nearly fivefold at 6 weeks: 67% of partners tested versus 13% with delayed services (incidence rate ratio 4.8, 95% CI 3.7 to 6.4), new HIV diagnoses in 23% versus 4% of partners (5.0, 3.2 to 7.9), and new enrolment in care in 15% versus 3% (4.4, 2.6 to 7.4), with one intimate-partner-violence event related to notification in each group. A WHO systematic review of the wider literature found a more modest pooled effect (partner test uptake relative risk 1.46, 95% CI 1.22 to 1.75, across three individually randomised trials) with few reports of harm — the Kenyan cluster effect is larger than the pooled average, likely reflecting its delayed-service comparator. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): provider-supported partner services find substantially more partners, diagnoses, and care enrolments than passive referral, without a demonstrated increase in partner violence in these studies. Tier C is set because the anchor is a single cluster trial.

cards.headline: Cherutich 2017: assisted partner services — partners tested 67% vs 13%, new diagnoses 23% vs 4%, enrolment in care 15% vs 3% at 6 weeks
cards.summary: Cherutich 2017: assisted partner services — partners tested 67% vs 13%, new diagnoses 23% vs 4%, enrolment in care 15% vs 3% at 6 weeks
cards.people: 1305 non-pregnant adults (at least 18 years) with newly or recently diagnosed HIV, without a recent history of intimate partner violence and not yet or only recently linked to care, enrolled at 18 HIV testing services clinics in Kenya cluster-randomised to immediate versus delayed assisted partner services (625 immediate, 680 delayed); outcomes counted partners interviewed at 6-week follow-up.
cards.result: At 6 weeks, 392 (67%) of 586 partners had tested for HIV in the immediate group versus 85 (13%) of 680 in the delayed group (incidence rate ratio 4.8, 95% CI 3.7 to 6.4). New HIV diagnoses: 136 (23%) partners versus 28 (4%) (5.0, 3.2 to 7.9). Newly enrolled in care: 88 (15%) versus 19 (3%) (4.4, 2.6 to 7.4). Assisted partner services did not increase intimate partner violence: one event related to partner notification or study procedures occurred in each group.
cards.watchOut: Index patients with a recent history of intimate partner violence were excluded, so the reassuring safety result does not cover the group at highest risk from notification. The comparator was delayed (not absent) services, and 18 clusters is a modest number for cluster-level inference.
cards.source: Cherutich P et al. Assisted partner services for HIV in Kenya: a cluster randomised controlled trial. The lancet. HIV. 2017. PMID: 27913227. Registry ID: NCT01616420. cards.headline: Dalal 2017 (WHO systematic review): assisted partner notification raised partner test uptake 1.46-fold and HIV-positive partner identification 1.47-fold across the wider literature
cards.summary: Dalal 2017 (WHO systematic review): assisted partner notification raised partner test uptake 1.46-fold and HIV-positive partner identification 1.47-fold across the wider literature
cards.people: Systematic review for WHO guidelines: four randomised controlled trials and six observational studies totalling 5150 index patients from eight countries, comparing assisted HIV partner notification services with passive or no notification; literature searched through June 2016.
cards.result: Meta-analysis of three individually randomised trials showed assisted partner notification increased HIV testing uptake among partners versus passive referral (relative risk 1.46, 95% CI 1.22 to 1.75; I²=0%). The proportion of HIV-positive partners was also higher with assisted notification (relative risk 1.47, 95% CI 1.12 to 1.92; I²=0%). Few instances of violence or harm occurred. The reviewers note WHO strongly recommends voluntary assisted HIV partner notification services as part of a comprehensive package of testing and care.
cards.watchOut: The pooled relative risks (about 1.5-fold) are much smaller than the Kenyan cluster trial's ratios (about 5-fold) — different comparators and settings explain much of the gap, and the pooled figure is the safer expectation for a new programme. Most included studies predate current treatment-as-prevention practice.
cards.source: Dalal et al. Improving HIV test uptake and case finding with assisted partner notification services. AIDS (London, England). 2017. PMID: 28590326. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.summary: Synthesis: partner testing and case-finding rise substantially with assisted services in both the Kenyan trial and the pooled literature, with few reported harms
cards.people: One Kenyan cluster trial (18 clinics, 1305 index patients) plus a WHO systematic review of 10 studies and 5150 index patients from eight countries.
cards.result: Kenyan trial at 6 weeks: testing 67% vs 13% (rate ratio 4.8), new diagnoses 23% vs 4%, care enrolment 15% vs 3%; one notification-related violence event per group. Pooled trials: test uptake relative risk 1.46 (95% CI 1.22 to 1.75); HIV-positive partners relative risk 1.47 (1.12 to 1.92). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).

shelves.title: Hepatitis B vaccine for prior nonresponders with HIV: the CpG vaccine protected 93–99% versus 81% for repeating the standard vaccine in BEe-HIVe
shelves.question: In people with HIV who previously did not respond to hepatitis B vaccination, does the 2-dose CpG-adjuvanted hepatitis B vaccine achieve seroprotection where the alum-adjuvanted vaccine failed?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Adjuvants, Immunologic*/administration & dosage · Aluminum Hydroxide/administration & dosage/immunology · Hepatitis B*/immunology/prevention & control · Hepatitis B Antibodies/blood/immunology · Hepatitis B Surface Antigens/immunology · Hepatitis B Vaccines*/administration & dosage/adverse effects/immunology · HIV Infections*/complications/drug therapy/immunology · Injections, Intramuscular · Immunization Schedule · Immunogenicity, Vaccine · Dinucleoside Phosphates
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — in BEe-HIVe, a phase 3 randomised trial of 561 people with HIV who had previously not responded to hepatitis B vaccination, the CpG-adjuvanted vaccine outperformed the conventional alum-adjuvanted vaccine on seroprotection (antibody at least 10 mIU/mL): 93.1% after 2 doses of HepB-CpG, 99.4% after 3 doses, versus 80.6% after 3 doses of HepB-alum. The 2-dose regimen beat the alum regimen by a stratified difference of 12.5% (97.5% CI 4.1% to 20.9%) — non-inferior and superior — and the 3-dose CpG regimen by 18.4% (repeated 97.5% CI 10.4% to 26.2%); over 90% of CpG recipients were protected by week 12, and 78.1% of the 3-dose CpG group exceeded 1000 mIU/mL versus 35.2% on alum. No unexpected safety issues were observed. The outcome is an antibody threshold, not prevented hepatitis B infections, and durability beyond the primary timepoints is not shown in this record. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): in prior nonresponders with HIV, HepB-CpG — especially 3 doses — achieves seroprotection in substantially more people than repeating the alum vaccine. Tier C is set because this is a single trial with a surrogate outcome.

cards.headline: Marks 2025 (BEe-HIVe): seroprotection 93.1% (2-dose CpG) and 99.4% (3-dose CpG) vs 80.6% (3-dose alum) in people with HIV who had never responded
cards.summary: Marks 2025 (BEe-HIVe): seroprotection 93.1% (2-dose CpG) and 99.4% (3-dose CpG) vs 80.6% (3-dose alum) in people with HIV who had never responded
cards.type: Phase 3 open-label randomised clinical trial (BEe-HIVe, Marks 2025)
cards.people: 561 adults with HIV on antiretroviral therapy (CD4 count at least 100 cells/μL and HIV RNA below 1000 copies/mL), with prior nonresponse to HepB-alum vaccine and no serological evidence of past hepatitis B or vaccine response, at 41 sites in 10 countries in Africa, Asia, North America, and South America (median age 46 years; 64% male). Randomised to 2 doses of HepB-CpG (weeks 0 and 4), 3 doses of HepB-CpG (weeks 0, 4, and 24), or 3 doses of HepB-alum (weeks 0, 4, and 24), all intramuscular.
cards.result: Seroprotection response (anti-HBs at least 10 mIU/mL) was achieved in 93.1% of the 2-dose HepB-CpG group (n=174), 99.4% of the 3-dose HepB-CpG group (n=169), and 80.6% of the 3-dose HepB-alum group (n=165), measured at week 12 for the 2-dose regimen and week 28 for the 3-dose regimens. The stratified difference for 2-dose CpG versus 3-dose alum was 12.5% (97.5% CI 4.1% to 20.9%), achieving noninferiority (10% margin) and indicating superiority; 3-dose CpG versus 3-dose alum differed by 18.4% (repeated 97.5% CI 10.4% to 26.2%). By week 12, more than 90% of HepB-CpG recipients had a seroprotection response. Antibody above 1000 mIU/mL: 78.1% (3-dose CpG), 26.4% (2-dose CpG), 35.2% (3-dose alum). No unexpected safety issues were observed.
cards.watchOut: Seroprotection is a laboratory threshold accepted as a vaccine correlate, not a count of prevented hepatitis B infections, and participants had CD4 counts of at least 100 and suppressed or near-suppressed HIV on treatment — results may not extend to people with uncontrolled HIV. The 2-dose and 3-dose primary timepoints differ (week 12 vs week 28), which the stratified analysis handles but casual readers miss.
