shelves.title: Oteseconazole for recurrent yeast infections: only about 4–7% recurred over 48 weeks versus about 40% on placebo, in two phase 3 trials
shelves.question: In women with recurrent vulvovaginal candidiasis, does oteseconazole reduce recurrence versus placebo over 50 weeks?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Female · Candidiasis, Vulvovaginal*/drug therapy · Antifungal Agents*/therapeutic use/adverse effects/administration & dosage · Adult · Double-Blind Method · Recurrence* · Young Adult · Treatment Outcome · Middle Aged · Adolescent
shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit) — the VIOLET programme comprises two global phase 3, double-blind, placebo-controlled trials (656 women whose screening episode had first cleared with fluconazole induction). Through week 48, the averaged proportion with one or more recurrent episodes was 6.7% and 3.9% on oteseconazole in the two trials versus 42.8% and 39.4% on placebo (P<0.001 for both) — roughly a 36–39 percentage-point absolute reduction, with hazard ratios for time to recurrence of 0.11 (95% CI 0.06 to 0.21) and 0.08 (0.04 to 0.17), an 89–92% relative reduction in recurrence hazard alongside those absolute rates. Mean time to recurrence among those who did recur was about 46–47 weeks on oteseconazole versus 28–33 weeks on placebo. Treatment-emergent adverse events were similar between groups, with no drug-related serious events and no adverse effects on pregnancy outcomes, liver function, or QT interval reported. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): oteseconazole maintenance after fluconazole induction prevents most recurrences for a year in women with recurrent vulvovaginal candidiasis.

cards.headline: Sobel 2022 (VIOLET, two trials): recurrence through week 48 in 6.7% and 3.9% on oteseconazole vs 42.8% and 39.4% on placebo
cards.summary: Sobel 2022 (VIOLET, two trials): recurrence through week 48 in 6.7% and 3.9% on oteseconazole vs 42.8% and 39.4% on placebo
cards.type: Two phase 3 randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trials (VIOLET CL-011 and CL-012, Sobel 2022)
cards.people: 656 women with three or more symptomatic acute vulvovaginal candidiasis episodes in the previous 12 months, including a screening episode that cleared with fluconazole induction therapy, randomised 2:1 in two global phase 3 trials (CL-011, 326 women; CL-012, 330 women) to oral oteseconazole 150 mg daily for 7 days then once weekly for 11 weeks, or matching placebo for 12 weeks, with 36 weeks of post-treatment follow-up.
cards.result: Through week 48, the averaged percentage of participants with one or more recurrent episodes was 6.7% (range 6.5 to 7.4%) in CL-011 and 3.9% (3.7 to 4.6%) in CL-012 in the oteseconazole groups versus 42.8% (41.3 to 45.0%) and 39.4% (38.0 to 42.6%) in the placebo groups (P<0.001). Among participants who did experience a recurrence (oteseconazole n=22; placebo n=84), mean time to recurrence was 45.7 and 47.2 weeks (oteseconazole) versus 27.8 and 33.1 weeks (placebo); hazard ratios were 0.11 (95% CI 0.06 to 0.21) for CL-011 and 0.08 (0.04 to 0.17) for CL-012 (P<0.001). Types and frequencies of treatment-emergent adverse events were similar between groups, with no drug-related serious adverse events or adverse effects on pregnancy outcomes, liver function, or QT interval.
cards.watchOut: Every participant entered the maintenance phase only after fluconazole had cleared the screening episode, so this is prevention in fluconazole-responsive disease — it says nothing about fluconazole-resistant species or episodes that never clear. Follow-up ends at week 48; what happens in year two after a 12-week course is not in this record.
cards.source: Sobel JD et al. Efficacy and Safety of Oteseconazole in Recurrent Vulvovaginal Candidiasis. NEJM evidence. 2022. PMID: 38319878. Registry ID: NCT03562156; NCT03561701. shelves.title: Weekly fluconazole for recurrent yeast infections: 91% stayed disease-free on treatment versus 36% on placebo — but the advantage largely faded within six months of stopping
shelves.question: In women with recurrent vulvovaginal candidiasis, does weekly maintenance fluconazole for 6 months keep the infection suppressed versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Oral · Adult · Antifungal Agents/adverse effects/therapeutic use* · Candida albicans/isolation & purification · Candida glabrata/isolation & purification · Candidiasis, Vulvovaginal/drug therapy*/prevention & control · Double-Blind Method · Drug Administration Schedule · Drug Resistance, Fungal · Female · Fluconazole/adverse effects/therapeutic use* · Humans · Logistic Models · Remission Induction · Secondary Prevention · Time Factors · Vagina/microbiology
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — in the single classic trial, after remission was induced with three fluconazole doses, weekly fluconazole 150 mg for 6 months kept 90.8% of women disease-free at 6 months versus 35.9% on placebo (P<0.001) — a 54.9 percentage-point absolute difference during treatment. The protection then decayed off therapy: disease-free proportions were 73.2% versus 27.8% at 9 months and 42.9% versus 21.9% at 12 months, and median time to recurrence was 10.2 versus 4.0 months (P<0.001). There was no evidence of fluconazole resistance in Candida albicans isolates or superinfection with Candida glabrata, and one patient stopped fluconazole for headache. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): weekly fluconazole suppresses recurrent vulvovaginal candidiasis while it is taken, but a long-term cure after stopping remains difficult to achieve — the trial's own conclusion. Tier C is set because this is a single trial.

cards.headline: Sobel 2004: weekly fluconazole kept 90.8% disease-free at 6 months vs 35.9% on placebo — but only 42.9% vs 21.9% by 12 months, after therapy stopped
cards.summary: Sobel 2004: weekly fluconazole kept 90.8% disease-free at 6 months vs 35.9% on placebo — but only 42.9% vs 21.9% by 12 months, after therapy stopped
cards.people: 387 women with recurrent vulvovaginal candidiasis who first achieved clinical remission with open-label fluconazole (three 150-mg doses at 72-hour intervals), then randomised to fluconazole 150 mg or placebo weekly for six months, followed by six months of observation without therapy. The primary outcome was the proportion in clinical remission at the end of the first six months.
cards.result: The proportions of women who remained disease-free at 6, 9, and 12 months in the fluconazole group were 90.8%, 73.2%, and 42.9%, compared with 35.9%, 27.8%, and 21.9% respectively in the placebo group (P<0.001). Median time to clinical recurrence was 10.2 months in the fluconazole group versus 4.0 months in the placebo group (P<0.001). There was no evidence of fluconazole resistance in isolates of Candida albicans or of superinfection with Candida glabrata. Fluconazole was discontinued in one patient because of headache.
cards.watchOut: All participants had first responded to fluconazole induction, so the trial cannot speak to fluconazole-resistant or non-albicans disease. The 12-month figures are the sobering half of the result: most of the treatment advantage erodes within six months of stopping, which is why this is suppression, not cure.
cards.source: Sobel JD et al. Maintenance fluconazole therapy for recurrent vulvovaginal candidiasis. The New England journal of medicine. 2004. PMID: 15329425. Registry ID: none in the record. shelves.title: Stopping Pneumocystis prophylaxis after CD4 recovery: zero cases in 262 patients who stopped — the upper confidence limit, not certainty, is what the cohort buys
shelves.question: In adults with HIV whose CD4 counts have recovered on antiretroviral therapy, can primary prophylaxis against Pneumocystis pneumonia be stopped safely?
shelves.mesh: AIDS-Related Opportunistic Infections/epidemiology · Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Anti-HIV Agents/therapeutic use · Anti-Infective Agents/administration & dosage · CD4 Lymphocyte Count · Cohort Studies · Drug Therapy, Combination · Female · HIV Infections/drug therapy · HIV-1* · Humans · Incidence · Male · Middle Aged · Pneumonia, Pneumocystis/epidemiology · Primary Prevention · Toxoplasmosis, Cerebral/epidemiology
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the Swiss HIV Cohort Study (Furrer H et al., PMID: 10219064) prospectively stopped primary prophylaxis in 262 adults whose CD4 counts had risen to at least 200 cells per cubic millimeter and at least 14 percent of total lymphocytes, sustained for at least 12 weeks on combination antiretroviral therapy, and followed them for a median of 11.3 months: there were no cases of Pneumocystis pneumonia and no cases of toxoplasmic encephalitis. Zero events is reassuring but not proof of zero risk — the one-sided upper 99 percent confidence limit was 1.9 cases per 100 patient-years for Pneumocystis pneumonia (238 patient-years) and 4.2 per 100 patient-years for toxoplasmic encephalitis (110 patient-years, among the 121 participants seropositive for Toxoplasma gondii). This is a prospective cohort, not a randomised trial: patients whose counts recovered may differ from those whose did not, follow-up was under a year at the median, and prophylaxis was resumed in nine patients. No systematic review or meta-analysis of prophylaxis discontinuation itself was found in-session, so the shelf rests on this cohort and the consistent discontinuation studies of its era that the miner entry cites. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): for patients meeting the CD4 and lymphocyte-percentage thresholds on effective antiretroviral therapy, stopping primary prophylaxis is a reasonable, evidence-supported step that removes drug burden and toxicity risk — with restarting if counts fall again.

cards.headline: Furrer 1999 (Swiss HIV Cohort): 262 patients stopped primary prophylaxis after CD4 recovery — zero cases of Pneumocystis pneumonia and zero of toxoplasmic encephalitis over a median 11.3 months
cards.summary: Furrer 1999 (Swiss HIV Cohort): 262 patients stopped primary prophylaxis after CD4 recovery — zero cases of Pneumocystis pneumonia and zero of toxoplasmic encephalitis over a median 11.3 months
cards.type: Prospective cohort study (Furrer 1999, Swiss HIV Cohort Study)
cards.people: 262 HIV-1-infected adults in the Swiss HIV Cohort Study whose CD4 counts had increased to at least 200 cells per cubic millimeter and at least 14 percent of total lymphocytes on combination antiretroviral therapy, sustained for at least 12 weeks; median CD4 at entry 325 per cubic millimeter (range 210 to 806), median nadir 110; 121 (46.2 percent) were IgG-positive for Toxoplasma gondii. Prophylaxis was stopped at entry and patients were examined every three months.
cards.result: During a median follow-up of 11.3 months (range 3.0 to 18.8), there were no cases of Pneumocystis carinii pneumonia (the primary end point) and no cases of toxoplasmic encephalitis (the secondary end point). The one-sided upper 99 percent confidence limit for the incidence of Pneumocystis pneumonia was 1.9 cases per 100 patient-years (based on 238 patient-years of follow-up); the corresponding figure for toxoplasmic encephalitis was 4.2 per 100 patient-years (based on 110 patient-years). Prophylaxis was resumed in nine patients and two patients died. The authors conclude that stopping primary prophylaxis appears to be safe in patients with a sustained CD4 rise to at least 200 cells per cubic millimeter and at least 14 percent of lymphocytes.
cards.watchOut: A cohort with zero events bounds risk rather than excluding it: the upper 99 percent limit of 1.9 per 100 patient-years is compatible with a small real risk, median follow-up was under a year, and there was no randomised comparison against continuing prophylaxis. The thresholds matter — this says nothing about stopping at lower CD4 counts, after shorter recovery, or in patients not on effective antiretroviral therapy.

median cd4 at entry 325 per cubic millimeter (range 210 to 806), median nadir 110; 121 (46.2 percent) were igg-positive for toxoplasma gondii. prophylaxis was stopped at entry and patients were examined every three months. during a median follow-up of 11.3 months (range 3.0 to 18.8), there were no cases of pneumocystis carinii pneumonia (the primary end point) and no cases of toxoplasmic encephalitis (the secondary end point). the one-sided upper 99 percent confidence limit for the incidence of pneumocystis pneumonia was 1.9 cases per 100 patient-years (based on 238 patient-years of follow-up); the corresponding figure for toxoplasmic encephalitis was 4.2 per 100 patient-years (based on 110 patient-years). prophylaxis was resumed in nine patients and two patients died. the authors conclude that stopping primary prophylaxis appears to be safe in patients with a sustained cd4 rise to at least 200 cells per cubic millimeter and at least 14 percent of lymphocytes. a cohort with zero events bounds risk rather than excluding it: the upper 99 percent limit of 1.9 per 100 patient-years is compatible with a small real risk, median follow-up was under a year, and there was no randomised comparison against continuing prophylaxis. the thresholds matter — this says nothing about stopping at lower cd4 counts, after shorter recovery, or in patients not on effective antiretroviral therapy. furrer h et al. discontinuation of primary prophylaxis against pneumocystis carinii pneumonia in hiv-1-infected adults treated with combination antiretroviral therapy. swiss hiv cohort study. the new england journal of medicine. 1999. pmid: 10219064. registry id: none in the record. mesh: aids-related opportunistic infections/epidemiology · adult · aged · aged, 80 and over · anti-hiv agents/therapeutic use · anti-infective agents/administration & dosage · cd4 lymphocyte count · cohort studies · drug therapy, combination · female · hiv infections/drug therapy · hiv-1* · humans · incidence · male · middle aged · pneumonia, pneumocystis/epidemiology · primary prevention · toxoplasmosis, cerebral/epidemiology

cards.people: 262 adults with HIV and sustained CD4 recovery on combination antiretroviral therapy in one prospective Swiss cohort — the anchor record for this shelf; no randomised discontinuation trial and no discontinuation-specific systematic review was verified in-session.
cards.result: Pneumocystis pneumonia after stopping: 0 cases in 238 patient-years (upper one-sided 99 percent limit 1.9 per 100 patient-years). shelves.title: TB-CHAMP: tuberculosis in 1.1% of children on levofloxacin versus 2.6% on placebo — a halving that the trial could not confirm (hazard ratio 0.44, 95% CI 0.15 to 1.25)
shelves.question: In children with household exposure to multidrug-resistant tuberculosis, does 24 weeks of levofloxacin preventive treatment prevent tuberculosis disease versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Child · Child, Preschool · Female · Humans · Infant · Male · Antitubercular Agents/administration & dosage · Double-Blind Method · HIV Infections/complications · Incidence · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Levofloxacin*/administration & dosage · Mycobacterium tuberculosis/drug effects · South Africa/epidemiology · Tuberculosis, Multidrug-Resistant*/diagnosis · Tuberculosis, Pulmonary*/diagnosis · Interferon-gamma Release Tests
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — TB-CHAMP (Hesseling AC et al., PMID: 39693542) randomised 497 South African households, enrolling 922 children with household exposure to an adult with bacteriologically confirmed multidrug-resistant pulmonary TB, to 24 weeks of daily levofloxacin or placebo. By week 48, tuberculosis had developed in 5 of 453 children (1.1 percent) on levofloxacin and 12 of 469 (2.6 percent) on placebo — hazard ratio 0.44 (95% CI 0.15 to 1.25), a difference that was not significant; sensitivity analyses agreed. Grade 3 or higher possibly-related adverse events occurred in 4 children on levofloxacin and 8 on placebo, and grade 2 tendonitis in one levofloxacin-treated child. The wider literature looks stronger than the trial: a systematic review and meta-analysis of preventive treatment for MDR-TB contacts (Zhou G et al., PMID: 37741621) pooled a relative risk of 0.34 (95% CI 0.16 to 0.72) for progression — but from 11 mostly observational studies of 1,105 contacts, not from randomised comparisons. The honest summary is that the point estimates all lean the same way while the one randomised test in children ran out of events: only 17 children developed TB in total. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): levofloxacin prophylaxis for child contacts is biologically and observationally supported and was safe in the trial, but its efficacy is not yet proven by randomised evidence. Tier C is set because this rests on a single underpowered trial.

cards.headline: TB-CHAMP 2024 (NEJM): TB by week 48 in 5 children (1.1%) on levofloxacin versus 12 (2.6%) on placebo — hazard ratio 0.44 (95% CI 0.15 to 1.25), not significant
cards.summary: TB-CHAMP 2024 (NEJM): TB by week 48 in 5 children (1.1%) on levofloxacin versus 12 (2.6%) on placebo — hazard ratio 0.44 (95% CI 0.15 to 1.25), not significant
cards.people: 922 children from 497 households in South Africa with household exposure to an adult with bacteriologically confirmed multidrug-resistant pulmonary tuberculosis; 91.0 percent were younger than 5 years (eligible regardless of interferon-gamma release assay result or HIV status), and children 5 to 17 years were eligible with a positive assay or HIV infection. Households were cluster-randomised to levofloxacin (453 children) or placebo (469) once daily for 24 weeks; at least 80 percent of doses were received by 86 percent in each group.
cards.result: By week 48, incident tuberculosis (including death from tuberculosis) had occurred in 5 participants (1.1 percent) in the levofloxacin group and 12 (2.6 percent) in the placebo group (hazard ratio 0.44; 95% CI 0.15 to 1.25); sensitivity analyses were consistent with the primary analysis. Grade 3 or higher adverse events during treatment considered at least possibly related to the regimen occurred in 4 participants on levofloxacin and 8 on placebo (hazard ratio 0.52; 95% CI 0.16 to 1.71). Grade 2 tendonitis occurred in 1 child in the levofloxacin group.
cards.watchOut: Only 17 end-point events in 922 children: the trial was powered for a higher incidence than occurred, so the confidence interval (0.15 to 1.25) cannot exclude anything from an 85 percent relative reduction to a 25 percent relative increase. Most participants were under 5; evidence for older children is thinner still. Fluoroquinolone use in children carries the tendon concern the single tendonitis case gestures at, even though serious events were numerically fewer on levofloxacin.

cards.headline: Zhou 2024 (systematic review and meta-analysis): preventive treatment of MDR-TB contacts pooled at relative risk 0.34 (95% CI 0.16 to 0.72) for progression — from 11 mostly observational studies
cards.summary: Zhou 2024 (systematic review and meta-analysis): preventive treatment of MDR-TB contacts pooled at relative risk 0.34 (95% CI 0.16 to 0.72) for progression — from 11 mostly observational studies
cards.people: Eleven studies involving 1,105 individuals comparing tuberculosis preventive treatment with no treatment in contacts of patients with multidrug-resistant tuberculosis, searched across EMBASE, PubMed, Web of Science and the Cochrane Library to 24 July 2023; random-effects meta-analysis with a modified Newcastle-Ottawa quality scale.
cards.result: The pooled relative risk for progression to TB disease in contacts receiving preventive treatment versus no treatment was 0.34 (95% CI 0.16 to 0.72). Regimens tailored to the index patient's drug-resistance profile had a lower pooled relative risk (0.22, 95% CI 0.06 to 0.84) than uniform regimens (0.49, 0.17 to 1.35), a subgroup difference that was not statistically significant. The pooled completion rate was 83.8 percent, the adverse effect rate 22.9 percent, and the discontinuation rate 6.5 percent; excluding the levofloxacin-plus-pyrazinamide study, completion rose to 88.0 percent and adverse effects and discontinuation fell to 8.0 percent and 4.0 percent.
cards.watchOut: The pooled 0.34 comes predominantly from observational comparisons, where families who accept and complete prophylaxis differ from those who do not — exactly the confounding the randomised TB-CHAMP trial was designed to escape, and TB-CHAMP's own estimate (0.44) was not significant. Read the review as supportive context, not confirmation.

cards.headline: Synthesis: every estimate points toward protection, none of the randomised ones reach significance — an underpowered-evidence problem, not a negative result
cards.summary: Synthesis: every estimate points toward protection, none of the randomised ones reach significance — an underpowered-evidence problem, not a negative result
cards.people: One cluster-randomised trial in 922 exposed children (TB-CHAMP 2024) plus an 11-study systematic review of preventive treatment in 1,105 MDR-TB contacts (Zhou 2024).
cards.result: Randomised (children): TB 1.1 percent versus 2.6 percent, hazard ratio 0.44 (95% CI 0.15 to 1.25), not significant; grade 3+ possibly-related adverse events 4 versus 8. Observational pooled: relative risk 0.34 (95% CI 0.16 to 0.72); completion 83.8 percent; adverse effects 22.9 percent across regimens. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence).
cards.watchOut: This shelf pairs with the V-QUIN shelf (adult and mixed-age contacts in Vietnam), which found the same direction and the same non-significance — two trials agreeing on a point estimate near a halving while neither excludes no effect. Policy may reasonably act on the combined picture; this shelf's stamp grades only the proof, which remains weak. Tier C is set for the single-trial randomised base.

shelves.title: V-QUIN: confirmed TB in 0.6% on levofloxacin versus 1.1% on placebo over 30 months — again a halving, again not significant (incidence rate ratio 0.55, 95% CI 0.19 to 1.62)
shelves.question: In household contacts of people with multidrug-resistant tuberculosis in Vietnam, does 6 months of daily levofloxacin prevent tuberculosis versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Child · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Young Adult · Antitubercular Agents/therapeutic use · Double-Blind Method · Levofloxacin*/administration & dosage · Mycobacterium tuberculosis*/drug effects · Rifampin/pharmacology · Tuberculosis, Multidrug-Resistant*/diagnosis · Vietnam/epidemiology · Administration, Oral · Tuberculin Test/statistics & numerical data · Placebos/administration & dosage · Child, Preschool · Aged · Aged, 80 and over
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — V-QUIN (Fox GJ et al., PMID: 39693541) randomised 2,041 household contacts of people with bacteriologically confirmed rifampicin-resistant or multidrug-resistant TB in Vietnam to 6 months of daily levofloxacin or placebo, following them for 30 months. Confirmed tuberculosis occurred in 6 participants (0.6 percent) on levofloxacin and 11 (1.1 percent) on placebo — incidence rate ratio 0.55 (95% CI 0.19 to 1.62), not significant. Tolerability is the counterweight: adverse events of any grade were reported by 306 participants (31.9 percent) taking levofloxacin versus 125 (13.0 percent) on placebo (risk difference 18.9 percentage points, 95% CI 14.2 to 23.6), although grade 3 or 4 events differed little (risk difference 1.0 percentage point, −0.3 to 2.4) and no acquired fluoroquinolone resistance was observed. The systematic review of preventive treatment for MDR-TB contacts (Zhou G et al., PMID: 37741621) pools a relative risk of 0.34 (95% CI 0.16 to 0.72), but from mostly observational studies. With only 17 confirmed cases across 2,041 contacts, V-QUIN — like its paediatric sibling TB-CHAMP — was defeated by how rare the outcome was. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): the direction of effect is consistent across both randomised trials and the observational literature, but randomised proof of efficacy is still missing, and a third of treated contacts report some adverse event. Tier C is set because this rests on a single trial for its population.

cards.headline: V-QUIN 2024 (NEJM): confirmed TB in 6 (0.6%) on levofloxacin versus 11 (1.1%) on placebo at 30 months — incidence rate ratio 0.55 (95% CI 0.19 to 1.62), not significant; any-grade adverse events 31.9% versus 13.0%
cards.summary: V-QUIN 2024 (NEJM): confirmed TB in 6 (0.6%) on levofloxacin versus 11 (1.1%) on placebo at 30 months — incidence rate ratio 0.55 (95% CI 0.19 to 1.62), not significant; any-grade adverse events 31.9% versus 13.0%
cards.people: 2,041 household contacts of any age in Vietnam of persons with bacteriologically confirmed rifampicin-resistant or multidrug-resistant tuberculosis, eligible with a positive tuberculin skin test or immunologic impairment; 3,948 people were screened (61, 1.5 percent, had coprevalent TB before randomisation) and 1,995 participants (97.7 percent) completed 30 months of follow-up, had an end-point event, or died. Treatment was 6 months of daily weight-based levofloxacin or placebo.
cards.result: Bacteriologically confirmed tuberculosis within 30 months occurred in 6 participants (0.6 percent) in the levofloxacin group and 11 (1.1 percent) in the placebo group (incidence rate ratio 0.55; 95% CI 0.19 to 1.62) — not significant. Grade 3 or 4 adverse events differed little (risk difference 1.0 percentage point; 95% CI −0.3 to 2.4), but adverse events of any grade were reported in 306 participants (31.9 percent) on levofloxacin and 125 (13.0 percent) on placebo (risk difference 18.9 percentage points; 95% CI 14.2 to 23.6). No acquired fluoroquinolone resistance was observed.
cards.watchOut: Seventeen total end-point events: the trial cannot distinguish a true halving of risk from chance. The adverse-event gap is mostly low-grade, but at population scale a preventive drug given to many healthy contacts must clear a high tolerability bar — 31.9 percent reporting any event is the number programmes will feel. Results come from one country with its own resistance patterns and contact-investigation system.

systematic review and meta-analysis (zhou 2024) eleven studies involving 1,105 individuals comparing tuberculosis preventive treatment with no treatment in contacts of patients with multidrug-resistant tuberculosis, searched across embase, pubmed, web of science and the cochrane library to 24 july 2023; random-effects meta-analysis with a modified newcastle-ottawa quality scale. the pooled relative risk for progression to tb disease in contacts receiving preventive treatment versus no treatment was 0.34 (95% ci 0.16 to 0.72). regimens tailored to the index patient's drug-resistance profile had a lower pooled relative risk (0.22, 95% ci 0.06 to 0.84) than uniform regimens (0.49, 0.17 to 1.35), a subgroup difference that was not statistically significant. the pooled completion rate was 83.8 percent, the adverse effect rate 22.9 percent, and the discontinuation rate 6.5 percent; excluding the levofloxacin-plus-pyrazinamide study, completion rose to 88.0 percent and adverse effects and discontinuation fell to 8.0 percent and 4.0 percent. the pooled estimate is dominated by non-randomised studies and predates full incorporation of the two 2024 placebo-controlled trials, both of which were non-significant. where the review and the trials disagree in certainty, the trials govern: observational prophylaxis cohorts overstate benefit when healthier, more adherent contacts are the ones treated. zhou g et al. effectiveness and safety of tuberculosis preventive treatment for contacts of patients with multidrug-resistant tuberculosis: a systematic review and meta-analysis. clinical microbiology and infection. 2024. pmid: 37741621. registry id: none in the record. mesh: humans · antitubercular agents/adverse effects · tuberculosis, multidrug-resistant*/drug therapy · pyrazinamide/therapeutic use · levofloxacin/therapeutic use · drug-related side effects and adverse reactions* · disease progression

cards.people: One randomised trial in 2,041 Vietnamese household contacts of all ages (V-QUIN 2024), its paediatric sibling trial in South Africa, and an 11-study systematic review of 1,105 MDR-TB contacts (Zhou 2024).
cards.result: Randomised (V-QUIN): confirmed TB 0.6 percent versus 1.1 percent, incidence rate ratio 0.55 (95% CI 0.19 to 1.62); any-grade adverse events 31.9 percent versus 13.0 percent; grade 3–4 events similar; no acquired fluoroquinolone resistance. Observational pooled: relative risk 0.34 (95% CI 0.16 to 0.72). PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence).
cards.watchOut: Absolute risk frames the decision: even if the relative effect is real, roughly 200 contacts were treated for 30 months per case prevented at V-QUIN's event rates, while about 1 in 5 extra treated contacts reported an adverse event. That trade may still favour treatment for high-risk contacts — but it is a judgement on unproven efficacy, and this shelf grades the proof, not the policy. Tier C is set for the single-trial base.

shelves.title: TEMPRANO long-term follow-up: 6 months of isoniazid preventive therapy cut the hazard of death by about a third (hazard ratio 0.63) — a benefit still visible at 6 years in people with high CD4 counts
shelves.question: In adults with HIV and high CD4 counts in West Africa, does 6 months of isoniazid preventive therapy reduce death or severe HIV illness when added to early antiretroviral therapy?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Africa, Western/epidemiology · Anti-Retroviral Agents/therapeutic use · Antitubercular Agents/therapeutic use · CD4 Lymphocyte Count/statistics & numerical data · Drug Therapy, Combination · Female · Follow-Up Studies · HIV Infections/drug therapy · Humans · Isoniazid/therapeutic use · Male · Risk · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit) — the long-term follow-up of the TEMPRANO ANRS 12136 factorial trial (Badje A et al., PMID: 29025631) followed 2,056 HIV-infected adults in Côte d'Ivoire (mean baseline CD4 count 477 cells per microliter) for 9,404 patient-years (median 4.9 years), comparing those randomised to 6 months of isoniazid preventive therapy (IPT) with those randomised to none, across both early and deferred antiretroviral therapy (ART) strategies. Eighty-six deaths occurred: the 6-year probability of death was 4.1 percent (95% CI 2.9 to 5.7) with IPT versus 6.9 percent (5.1 to 9.2) without — hazard ratio 0.63 (95% CI 0.41 to 0.97) adjusted for ART strategy, and 0.61 (0.39 to 0.94) after fuller adjustment, with no interaction with ART timing (p=0.77) or with time (p=0.94). The mechanism is credible: the Cochrane review of preventive therapy in HIV (Akolo C et al., PMID: 20091503; 12 trials, 8,578 participants) found preventive therapy reduced active tuberculosis (relative risk 0.68, 95% CI 0.54 to 0.85), most strongly in tuberculin-positive people (0.38, 0.25 to 0.57), with a mortality reduction for isoniazid monotherapy in that subgroup (0.74, 0.55 to 1.00). The absolute mortality gain here is modest — about 2.8 percentage points over 6 years — in a setting with TB incidence of 159 per 100,000, and one factorial trial carries the mortality claim. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): at high CD4 counts on early ART, 6 months of IPT adds a durable survival benefit beyond ART alone. Tier C is set because the mortality result rests on a single trial analysis.

cards.headline: Badje 2017 (TEMPRANO long-term follow-up): death at 6 years 4.1% with IPT versus 6.9% without — hazard ratio 0.63 (95% CI 0.41 to 0.97), no interaction with early versus deferred ART
cards.summary: Badje 2017 (TEMPRANO long-term follow-up): death at 6 years 4.1% with IPT versus 6.9% without — hazard ratio 0.63 (95% CI 0.41 to 0.97), no interaction with early versus deferred ART
cards.type: Long-term follow-up of a factorial randomised trial (TEMPRANO ANRS 12136, Badje 2017)
cards.people: 2,056 HIV-infected adults in Côte d'Ivoire (mean baseline CD4 count 477 cells per microliter) randomised in a 2x2 factorial design to deferred ART, deferred ART plus IPT, early ART, or early ART plus IPT (6 months of isoniazid preventive therapy), then followed in-trial and in a post-trial phase for 9,404 patient-years (median follow-up 4.9 years, IQR 3.3 to 5.8); the post-trial primary end point was all-cause death by intention to treat.
cards.result: 86 deaths were recorded (47 during the trial, 39 in the post-trial phase): 34 in patients assigned IPT (6-year probability of death 4.1 percent, 95% CI 2.9 to 5.7) and 52 in those assigned no IPT (6.9 percent, 5.1 to 9.2). The hazard ratio for death with IPT was 0.63 (95% CI 0.41 to 0.97) after adjusting for the ART strategy, and 0.61 (0.39 to 0.94) after adjustment for ART strategy, baseline CD4 count and other key characteristics. There was no evidence of interaction between IPT and ART (p=0.77) or between IPT and time (p=0.94) on mortality.
cards.watchOut: One trial, one country, 86 deaths: the confidence interval (0.41 to 0.97) only just excludes no effect, and the result is a secondary long-term analysis of a trial designed around 30-month severe morbidity. Côte d'Ivoire's TB incidence (159 per 100,000, as the authors note) is higher than many settings where this question arises; where TB exposure is rarer, the absolute benefit shrinks even if the relative effect holds.
cards.source: Badje A et al. cards.headline: Akolo 2010 (Cochrane, 12 trials, 8,578 participants): preventive therapy reduced active TB (relative risk 0.68, 95% CI 0.54 to 0.85), with the clearest effect in tuberculin-positive people (0.38, 0.25 to 0.57)
cards.summary: Akolo 2010 (Cochrane, 12 trials, 8,578 participants): preventive therapy reduced active TB (relative risk 0.68, 95% CI 0.54 to 0.85), with the clearest effect in tuberculin-positive people (0.38, 0.25 to 0.57)
cards.type: Systematic review of randomised trials (Akolo 2010, Cochrane)
cards.people: Twelve randomised trials including 8,578 HIV-infected participants without active tuberculosis, allocated to TB preventive therapy (any regimen) or placebo, or to alternative preventive regimens; participants could be tuberculin skin test positive or negative.
cards.result: Preventive therapy versus placebo was associated with a lower incidence of active TB (relative risk 0.68, 95% CI 0.54 to 0.85). The benefit was more pronounced with a positive tuberculin skin test (relative risk 0.38, 95% CI 0.25 to 0.57) than with a negative test (0.89, 0.64 to 1.24), and efficacy was similar across regimens. Mortality was reduced with isoniazid monotherapy versus placebo among tuberculin-positive individuals (relative risk 0.74, 95% CI 0.55 to 1.00); short-course multidrug regimens were much more likely than isoniazid monotherapy to be discontinued for adverse effects.
cards.watchOut: Most trials in this review predate universal early ART and enrolled people at lower CD4 counts than TEMPRANO's — they establish that preventive therapy prevents TB (the mechanism), not that it adds mortality benefit on top of modern early ART at high CD4 counts, which is TEMPRANO's distinct contribution. The tuberculin-negative subgroup showed no significant TB reduction.
cards.source: Akolo C et al. Treatment of latent tuberculosis infection in HIV infected persons. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2010. PMID: 20091503. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: a mortality benefit with a proven mechanism — fewer TB cases (Cochrane) translating into fewer deaths over 6 years (TEMPRANO)
cards.summary: Synthesis: a mortality benefit with a proven mechanism — fewer TB cases (Cochrane) translating into fewer deaths over 6 years (TEMPRANO)
cards.people: One factorial trial with long-term follow-up in 2,056 adults with HIV and high CD4 counts (Badje 2017) plus a Cochrane review of 12 preventive-therapy trials in 8,578 HIV-infected participants (Akolo 2010).
cards.result: Mortality: 6-year probability 4.1 percent with IPT versus 6.9 percent without; hazard ratio 0.63 (95% CI 0.41 to 0.97), durable with no time interaction. Active TB (Cochrane): relative risk 0.68 (95% CI 0.54 to 0.85) for any preventive therapy; 0.38 (0.25 to 0.57) if tuberculin-positive. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit).
cards.watchOut: Distinct from the shelved REMEMBER question (empiric TB therapy versus IPT at CD4 below 50): TEMPRANO asked the opposite end of the CD4 range, where the competing intuition was that early ART alone suffices. The absolute benefit (about 2.8 percentage points over 6 years) depends on background TB incidence and should not be transplanted to low-incidence settings without rescaling. Tier C is set because the mortality claim is single-trial.
cards.source: Synthesis of Badje A et al. The Lancet Global Health. 2017 (PMID: 29025631); Akolo C et al. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2010 (PMID: 20091503).

shelves.title: Valacyclovir in early-pregnancy CMV infection cut fetal transmission from 30% to 11% in the one randomised trial
shelves.question: In pregnant women with primary cytomegalovirus infection in early pregnancy, does valacyclovir prevent vertical transmission to the fetus?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Antiviral Agents/adverse effects+therapeutic use · Cytomegalovirus Infections/transmission · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Infectious Disease Transmission, Vertical/prevention & control · Medication Adherence · Pregnancy · Pregnancy Trimester, First · Prospective Studies · Time-to-Treatment · Valacyclovir/adverse effects+therapeutic use
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — in the single randomised trial (Shahar-Nissan K et al., PMID: 32919517), high-dose valacyclovir (8 g/day) from enrolment to amniocentesis cut positive amniocenteses from 30% (14 of 47) to 11% (5 of 45), an odds ratio of 0.29 — with the effect concentrated in first-trimester infection (11% vs 48%). An individual patient data meta-analysis including this trial (Chatzakis C et al., PMID: 37473793; 3 studies, 527 women) found the same direction for vertical transmission (adjusted OR 0.34) and neonatal infection (adjusted OR 0.30), with severe side effects in 2.1%. The evidence base is still one small per-protocol trial plus largely non-randomised data in the pooled analysis, and the endpoint is amniocentesis positivity rather than long-term infant outcome. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): valacyclovir probably reduces vertical transmission after early primary maternal CMV infection; infant-outcome proof is still indirect.

cards.headline: Shahar-Nissan 2020: valacyclovir cut vertical transmission on amniocentesis from 30% to 11% (OR 0.29); in first-trimester infection, 11% versus 48%
cards.summary: Shahar-Nissan 2020: valacyclovir cut vertical transmission on amniocentesis from 30% to 11% (OR 0.29); in first-trimester infection, 11% versus 48%
cards.people: 100 pregnant women aged 18 or older with serological evidence of primary cytomegalovirus infection acquired periconceptionally or in the first trimester, randomised double-blind at a single Israeli centre to oral valacyclovir 8 g/day or placebo until amniocentesis at 21–22 weeks; 90 women (45 per group) were included in the per-protocol analysis.
cards.result: A positive amniocentesis for cytomegalovirus occurred in 5 (11%) of 45 in the valacyclovir group versus 14 (30%) of 47 amniocenteses in the placebo group (p=0.027; odds ratio 0.29, 95% CI 0.09 to 0.90). Among first-trimester infections, positivity was 2 (11%) of 19 versus 11 (48%) of 23 (p=0.020). No clinically significant adverse events were reported. Absolute rates: 11% versus 30% overall — a 19-percentage-point absolute difference alongside the relative odds reduction.
cards.watchOut: Per-protocol analysis of 90 women at one centre, with amniocentesis positivity as a surrogate for the outcomes families ultimately care about (symptomatic congenital infection and sequelae). Ten randomised women were excluded from the analysis, five per group.

cards.headline: Chatzakis 2024: individual patient data meta-analysis (3 studies, 527 women) — valacyclovir reduced vertical transmission (adjusted OR 0.34) and neonatal infection (adjusted OR 0.30); severe side effects 2.1%
cards.summary: Chatzakis 2024: individual patient data meta-analysis (3 studies, 527 women) — valacyclovir reduced vertical transmission (adjusted OR 0.34) and neonatal infection (adjusted OR 0.30); severe side effects 2.1%
cards.people: Individual patient data meta-analysis of randomised and quasi-randomised studies of oral valacyclovir 8 g/day in pregnant women with primary cytomegalovirus infection acquired periconceptionally or in the first trimester; 3 studies, 527 women, analysed with a one-stage generalised linear mixed model clustered by trial.
cards.result: Valacyclovir reduced vertical transmission (adjusted odds ratio 0.34, 95% CI 0.18 to 0.61), apparent both for periconceptional infection (aOR 0.34, 95% CI 0.12 to 0.96) and first-trimester infection (aOR 0.35, 95% CI 0.16 to 0.76). Neonatal infection was also reduced (aOR 0.30, 95% CI 0.19 to 0.47), as was termination of pregnancy for CMV-associated severe fetal findings (aOR 0.23, 95% CI 0.22 to 0.24 as reported). Earlier treatment initiation correlated with better outcomes. The overall prevalence of severe side effects was 2.1%.
cards.watchOut: Only three studies, and not all randomised — the pooled estimate leans heavily on the single RCT plus quasi-randomised data, so it strengthens consistency more than it adds independent proof. The very narrow confidence interval reported for the termination outcome should be read as printed in the record.

cards.people: One randomised trial (90 women analysed) plus an individual patient data meta-analysis of 3 studies (527 women) — the evidence for valacyclovir to prevent vertical CMV transmission.
cards.result: Amniocentesis positivity 11% vs 30% (OR 0.29) in the trial; first-trimester subgroup 11% vs 48%. Pooled: vertical transmission aOR 0.34, neonatal infection aOR 0.30, severe side effects 2.1%. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).
cards.watchOut: This shelf is about periconceptional and first-trimester primary infection only, treated early at 8 g/day — it does not address later-pregnancy infection, reactivation, or lower doses, and long-term infant outcomes after prevented transmission are inferred, not yet trialled. Tier C is set because the randomised evidence is a single small trial.
cards.source: Synthesis of Shahar-Nissan K et al. The Lancet. 2020 (PMID: 32919517); Chatzakis C et al. American Journal of Obstetrics and Gynecology. 2024 (PMID: 37473793).

shelves.title: A maternal group B strep vaccine raised protective-looking antibodies in most infants — phase 2 only, with no disease-prevention trial yet
shelves.question: In pregnant women, does a hexavalent group B streptococcus polysaccharide-protein conjugate vaccine produce antibody responses likely to protect infants, with acceptable safety?
shelves.mesh: Female · Humans · Infant · Infant, Newborn · Pregnancy · Antibodies, Bacterial · Immunoglobulin G · Seroepidemiologic Studies · Streptococcal Infections*/epidemiology+immunology+prevention & control · Streptococcus agalactiae* · Vaccines, Combined/administration & dosage+adverse effects+immunology+therapeutic use · Vaccines, Conjugate/administration & dosage+adverse effects+immunology+therapeutic use · Streptococcal Vaccines*/administration & dosage+adverse effects+immunology+therapeutic use · Immunity, Maternally-Acquired/immunology
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — this is immunogenicity evidence, not protection evidence. In the phase 2 trial and parallel seroepidemiology study (Madhi SA et al., PMID: 37467497), the hexavalent conjugate vaccine GBS6 raised maternal antibodies to all six serotypes, transferred to infants at maternal-to-infant ratios of about 0.4 to 1.3, and 57 to 97% of infants exceeded the lowest putative protective threshold (0.184 µg/mL) with the most immunogenic formulation — thresholds themselves derived from natural-history association (IgG levels linked to 75–95% relative reductions in disease risk), not from a vaccine efficacy trial. No safety signals were seen in mothers or infants, with more local reactions in aluminium-phosphate formulations. No baby in this record was shown to be protected from group B streptococcal disease by vaccination. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): a promising maternal vaccine candidate whose clinical efficacy is untested.

cards.headline: Madhi 2023: phase 2 GBS6 trial — antibodies to all serotypes transferred to infants (ratios 0.4–1.3); 57–97% of infants above the 0.184 µg/mL threshold with the most immunogenic formulation; no safety signals
cards.summary: Madhi 2023: phase 2 GBS6 trial — antibodies to all serotypes transferred to infants (ratios 0.4–1.3); 57–97% of infants above the 0.184 µg/mL threshold with the most immunogenic formulation; no safety signals
cards.type: Phase 2 randomised trial with parallel seroepidemiologic study (Madhi 2023)
cards.people: Pregnant women in an ongoing phase 2 placebo-controlled trial received a single dose of various formulations of GBS6, a hexavalent capsular polysaccharide–CRM197 glycoconjugate vaccine; in a parallel seroepidemiologic study in the same population, serotype-specific anti-CPS IgG concentrations associated with reduced risk of invasive disease in newborns through 89 days were estimated.
cards.result: Naturally acquired anti-CPS IgG was associated with reduced disease risk; thresholds associated with 75% to 95% relative reductions in risk were 0.184 to 0.827 µg/mL. No GBS6-associated safety signals were observed in mothers or infants; adverse and serious adverse event incidences were similar across groups, with more local reactions in aluminium-phosphate-containing groups, and the commonest infant serious adverse events were minor congenital anomalies (umbilical hernia and congenital dermal melanocytosis) as reported. GBS6 induced maternal responses to all serotypes, with maternal-to-infant antibody ratios of approximately 0.4 to 1.3 by dose; the percentage of infants above 0.184 µg/mL varied by serotype and formulation, reaching 57 to 97% with the most immunogenic formulation.
cards.watchOut: Antibody thresholds are correlates derived from natural infection immunity, not validated vaccine correlates — exceeding them does not prove an infant is protected, and the wide 57–97% range means serotype and formulation matter a great deal. The trial was not powered or designed to measure disease.
cards.source: Madhi SA et al. Potential for Maternally Administered Vaccine for Infant Group B Streptococcus. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2023. PMID: 37467497. Registry ID: NCT03765073. cards.headline: Synthesis: GBS6 does what a maternal vaccine must do immunologically — whether it prevents a single case of infant disease is still unknown
cards.summary: Synthesis: GBS6 does what a maternal vaccine must do immunologically — whether it prevents a single case of infant disease is still unknown
cards.people: One phase 2 trial with a parallel seroepidemiologic study — the entire record for hexavalent group B streptococcus conjugate vaccine in pregnancy on this shelf.
cards.result: Immunogenicity: responses to all six serotypes, transfer ratios 0.4–1.3, 57–97% of infants above the lowest putative threshold with the best formulation. Safety: no signals; more local reactions with aluminium phosphate. Efficacy against invasive infant disease: not measured. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence).
cards.watchOut: Do not let antibody percentages be quoted as protection percentages — they are different claims, and only a phase 3 efficacy trial can connect them. This shelf does not address intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis, the current standard prevention strategy. Tier C is set because the evidence is phase 2 immunogenicity only.
cards.source: Synthesis of Madhi SA et al. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2023 (PMID: 37467497).

shelves.title: Liver-cancer surveillance in hepatitis B cut HCC deaths by about a third in relative terms in the one large randomised trial
shelves.question: In adults with chronic hepatitis B at high risk, does regular ultrasound plus alpha-fetoprotein surveillance reduce hepatocellular carcinoma mortality versus no screening?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Biomarkers, Tumor/blood · Carcinoma, Hepatocellular/diagnostic imaging+mortality+pathology+prevention & control · China/epidemiology · Female · Humans · Incidence · Liver Neoplasms/diagnostic imaging+mortality+pathology+prevention & control · Male · Mass Screening*/methods · Middle Aged · Neoplasm Staging · Survival Rate · Ultrasonography · Urban Population/statistics & numerical data · alpha-Fetoproteins/metabolism
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the one large randomised trial (Zhang BH et al., PMID: 15042359; 18,816 people with hepatitis B or chronic hepatitis in Shanghai) found biannual ultrasound plus alpha-fetoprotein surveillance reduced hepatocellular carcinoma mortality from 131.5 to 83.2 per 100,000 — a mortality rate ratio of 0.63, i.e. a 37% relative reduction — with far more subclinical, small and resectable cancers found in the screened group, though only 58.2% of offered screening was completed. A meta-analysis in cirrhosis (Singal AG et al., PMID: 24691105) is directionally consistent: surveillance was associated with earlier detection (OR 2.08), more curative treatment (OR 2.24) and prolonged survival (OR 1.90), but that literature is observational and lead-time bias is its known weakness. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): surveillance probably reduces HCC mortality in high-risk patients; the randomised proof is a single trial in a hepatitis B population.

cards.headline: Zhang 2004: randomised trial of 18,816 people — biannual ultrasound plus AFP cut HCC mortality to 83.2 vs 131.5 per 100,000 (rate ratio 0.63, a 37% relative reduction)
cards.summary: Zhang 2004: randomised trial of 18,816 people — biannual ultrasound plus AFP cut HCC mortality to 83.2 vs 131.5 per 100,000 (rate ratio 0.63, a 37% relative reduction)
cards.people: 18,816 people aged 35–59 with hepatitis B virus infection or a history of chronic hepatitis in urban Shanghai, randomised to screening (9,373) or control (9,443, no screening, usual care). The screening group was invited to alpha-fetoprotein testing and ultrasonography every 6 months (five to ten offers by December 1997); all participants were followed to December 1998. Primary outcome was HCC mortality.
cards.result: The screened group completed 58.2% of screening offered. HCC cases numbered 86 in the screened group versus 67 in controls, but subclinical HCC was 52 (60.5%) versus 0, small HCC 39 (45.3%) versus 0, and resection was achieved in 40 (46.5%) versus 5 (7.5%). Survival at 1, 3 and 5 years was 65.9%, 52.6% and 46.4% in the screened group versus 31.2%, 7.2% and 0% in controls. HCC deaths were 32 versus 54, and HCC mortality was 83.2 versus 131.5 per 100,000 — a mortality rate ratio of 0.63 (95% CI 0.41 to 0.98), a 37% relative reduction in HCC mortality alongside those absolute rates.
cards.watchOut: One trial, in a hepatitis B / chronic hepatitis population in 1990s Shanghai, with incomplete adherence (58.2%) — the effect in cirrhosis of other causes, and with modern imaging and treatment, is extrapolation. The confidence interval (0.41–0.98) only just excludes no effect.
cards.source: Zhang BH et al. Randomized controlled trial of screening for hepatocellular carcinoma. Journal of Cancer Research and Clinical Oncology. 2004. PMID: 15042359. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Singal 2014: meta-analysis of 47 studies in cirrhosis — surveillance associated with early detection (OR 2.08), curative treatment (OR 2.24) and prolonged survival (OR 1.90)
cards.summary: Singal 2014: meta-analysis of 47 studies in cirrhosis — surveillance associated with early detection (OR 2.08), curative treatment (OR 2.24) and prolonged survival (OR 1.90)
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of studies from 1990 to 2014 reporting early-stage detection, curative treatment receipt or survival by surveillance status in patients with cirrhosis: 47 studies, 15,158 patients, of whom 6,284 (41.4%) had HCC detected by surveillance.
cards.result: HCC surveillance was associated with improved early-stage detection (odds ratio 2.08, 95% CI 1.80 to 2.37) and curative treatment rates (OR 2.24, 95% CI 1.99 to 2.52), and with significantly prolonged survival (OR 1.90, 95% CI 1.67 to 2.17), which remained significant in the subset of studies adjusting for lead-time bias. The authors note many studies had insufficient follow-up to assess survival and most did not adjust for liver function or lead-time bias.
cards.watchOut: Observational studies throughout — people who receive surveillance differ from those who do not, and lead-time and length biases inflate survival comparisons even after adjustment. This card supports the trial; it cannot substitute for one.
cards.source: Singal AG et al. Early detection, curative treatment, and survival rates for hepatocellular carcinoma surveillance in patients with cirrhosis: a meta-analysis. PLoS Medicine. 2014. PMID: 24691105. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: surveillance finds smaller, resectable cancers and probably saves lives in high-risk liver disease — randomised proof rests on one hepatitis B trial
cards.summary: Synthesis: surveillance finds smaller, resectable cancers and probably saves lives in high-risk liver disease — randomised proof rests on one hepatitis B trial
cards.people: One randomised trial (18,816 people) plus a 47-study observational meta-analysis in cirrhosis — the evidence for ultrasound plus alpha-fetoprotein surveillance against HCC mortality.
cards.result: Mortality: 83.2 vs 131.5 per 100,000 (rate ratio 0.63, 95% CI 0.41–0.98) in the trial. Mechanism, consistently: subclinical HCC 60.5% vs 0%, resection 46.5% vs 7.5%; meta-analysis early detection OR 2.08, curative treatment OR 2.24, survival OR 1.90. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).
cards.watchOut: The trial population was hepatitis B / chronic hepatitis, not the full modern cirrhosis mix, and surveillance only helps if curative treatment follows detection — the resection gap (46.5% vs 7.5%) is the pathway, and systems that cannot deliver it should expect less benefit. Tier C is set because the mortality evidence is a single trial.
cards.source: Synthesis of Zhang BH et al. Journal of Cancer Research and Clinical Oncology. 2004 (PMID: 15042359); Singal AG et al. PLoS Medicine. 2014 (PMID: 24691105).

shelves.title: Endoscopic screening for oesophageal cancer in rural China: incidence and deaths trended lower at 9 years, but neither reduction was significant
shelves.question: In a high-incidence rural Chinese population, does endoscopic screening for oesophageal cancer reduce oesophageal cancer incidence and mortality?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Esophageal Neoplasms*/mortality+epidemiology+diagnosis · Male · China/epidemiology · Female · Incidence · Middle Aged · Aged · Early Detection of Cancer*/methods · Esophageal Squamous Cell Carcinoma/mortality+epidemiology+diagnosis · Esophagoscopy · Mass Screening/methods
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — the ESECC randomised trial's 9-year report (Liu M et al., PMID: 38457759; 33,847 residents of a high-risk region of northern China) found endoscopic screening associated with 19% and 18% relative reductions in oesophageal cancer incidence and mortality in intention-to-treat analysis — but neither estimate was statistically significant (incidence aHR 0.81, 95% CI 0.60 to 1.09; mortality aHR 0.82, 95% CI 0.53 to 1.26), and per-protocol estimates (0.78 and 0.79) were likewise non-significant. Absolute rates were 60.9 versus 72.5 per 100,000 person-years for incidence and 29.7 versus 32.4 for mortality. The authors themselves describe the reductions as modest and call for a more efficient screening and management strategy. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): a single round of chromoendoscopy in a high-incidence population may reduce incidence and mortality, but this trial did not prove it.

cards.headline: Liu 2024 (ESECC, 9 years): screening gave non-significant 19% relative lower incidence (aHR 0.81) and 18% relative lower mortality (aHR 0.82); absolute mortality 29.7 vs 32.4 per 100,000 person-years
cards.summary: Liu 2024 (ESECC, 9 years): screening gave non-significant 19% relative lower incidence (aHR 0.81) and 18% relative lower mortality (aHR 0.82); absolute mortality 29.7 vs 32.4 per 100,000 person-years
cards.people: Community-based cluster randomised trial in a high-risk region for oesophageal squamous cell carcinoma in northern China: 668 villages randomised 1:1, with 33,847 permanent residents aged 45–69 analysed — 17,104 in the screening group (15,165, 88.7%, underwent Lugol's chromoendoscopy) and 16,743 controls (no screening), followed for up to 9 years, with intention-to-treat and per-protocol analyses.
cards.result: Oesophageal cancer incidence was 60.9 per 100,000 person-years in the screening group versus 72.5 in controls, and mortality 29.7 versus 32.4 per 100,000 person-years. Intention-to-treat adjusted hazard ratios were 0.81 for incidence (95% CI 0.60 to 1.09 — a 19% relative reduction) and 0.82 for mortality (95% CI 0.53 to 1.26 — an 18% relative reduction), neither statistically significant. Per-protocol adjusted hazard ratios were 0.78 for incidence (95% CI 0.56 to 1.10 — a 22% relative reduction) and 0.79 for mortality (95% CI 0.49 to 1.30 — a 21% relative reduction), also non-significant. The authors conclude screening induces modest reductions and that a more efficient strategy is needed.
cards.watchOut: Every headline estimate crosses no-effect — this is a suggestive, underpowered-for-mortality result, not a demonstrated benefit, and the absolute mortality difference (2.7 per 100,000 person-years) is small even if real. Results from a high-incidence squamous-cell region do not transfer to low-incidence or adenocarcinoma-predominant populations.
cards.source: Liu M et al. Effectiveness of Endoscopic Screening on Esophageal Cancer Incidence and Mortality: A 9-Year Report of the Endoscopic Screening for Esophageal Cancer in China (ESECC) Randomized Trial. Journal of Clinical Oncology. 2024. PMID: 38457759. Registry ID: NCT01688908. cards.headline: Synthesis: one large screening trial, a consistent direction of effect, and confidence intervals that include no benefit at all
cards.summary: Synthesis: one large screening trial, a consistent direction of effect, and confidence intervals that include no benefit at all
cards.people: One cluster randomised trial of 33,847 people with 9-year follow-up — the randomised record for endoscopic screening against oesophageal cancer incidence and mortality on this shelf.
cards.result: Incidence 60.9 vs 72.5 per 100,000 person-years (aHR 0.81, 0.60–1.09); mortality 29.7 vs 32.4 (aHR 0.82, 0.53–1.26); per-protocol aHRs 0.78 and 0.79, all non-significant. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence).
cards.watchOut: A non-significant result is not proof of no effect — longer follow-up or a higher-risk or repeat-screening strategy could separate the curves — but policy claims should match what was shown: modest, unproven reductions in one high-risk Chinese population. Tier C is set because the evidence is a single trial programme.

shelves.title: Spraying plus nets in Tanzania: each beat standard nets alone, but together they were redundant — the second intervention added little
shelves.question: In malaria-endemic Tanzania, does adding indoor residual spraying to long-lasting insecticidal nets (including piperonyl-butoxide nets) reduce malaria infection versus nets alone?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Animals · Child · Child, Preschool · Cross-Sectional Studies · Female · Humans · Infant · Insecticide Resistance* · Insecticide-Treated Bednets* · Insecticides/therapeutic use · Malaria/epidemiology+prevention & control+transmission · Male · Mosquito Vectors/parasitology+physiology · Organothiophosphorus Compounds/therapeutic use · Pesticide Synergists/therapeutic use · Piperonyl Butoxide/therapeutic use · Pyrethrins · Tanzania/epidemiology
shelves.balance: SPLIT — the factorial cluster trial (Protopopoff N et al., PMID: 29655496) shows each intervention worked against standard nets where pyrethroid resistance was prevalent, but combining them was redundant rather than additive. At 9 months, malaria prevalence in children was lower with indoor residual spraying than without (28% vs 44%; OR 0.33) and lower with piperonyl-butoxide (PBO) nets than standard nets (29% vs 42%; OR 0.37), yet the significant interaction (OR 2.43) indicated the combination gave back part of that advantage; the PBO-net effect persisted at 21 months (45% vs 62%; OR 0.40). So adding spraying helps on top of standard nets, while a programme already deploying PBO nets should not assume spraying adds the same again. PROPOSED SPLIT: benefit depends on which net is underneath — additive with standard nets, redundant with PBO nets.

cards.headline: Protopopoff 2018: factorial cluster trial — IRS cut prevalence at 9 months (28% vs 44%, OR 0.33) and PBO nets cut it too (29% vs 42%, OR 0.37), but the interaction (OR 2.43) showed redundancy when combined
cards.summary: Protopopoff 2018: factorial cluster trial — IRS cut prevalence at 9 months (28% vs 44%, OR 0.33) and PBO nets cut it too (29% vs 42%, OR 0.37), but the interaction (OR 2.43) showed redundancy when combined
cards.people: Four-group, two-by-two factorial cluster randomised trial in 48 clusters from 40 villages in Muleba, Tanzania, where pyrethroid resistance is prevalent: standard long-lasting insecticidal nets, PBO nets, standard nets plus indoor residual spraying with pirimiphos-methyl, or PBO nets plus spraying. Nets were distributed in 2015 and spraying applied once in 2015; 15,469 (89.0%) of 17,377 eligible children aged 6 months to 14 years were included in the intention-to-treat analysis across surveys at 4, 9, 16 and 21 months; 94% of visited spraying-group households had been sprayed.
cards.result: At 9 months, malaria infection prevalence was lower in PBO-net groups than standard-net groups (531 [29%] of 1852 vs 767 [42%] of 1809; odds ratio 0.37, 95% CI 0.21 to 0.65; p=0.0011) and lower in spraying groups than non-spraying groups (508 [28%] of 1846 vs 790 [44%] of 1815; OR 0.33, 95% CI 0.19 to 0.55; p<0.0001), with a significant interaction between PBO nets and spraying (OR 2.43, 95% CI 1.19 to 4.97; p=0.0158) indicating redundancy when combined. The PBO-net effect was sustained at 21 months (865 [45%] of 1930 vs 1255 [62%] of 2034; OR 0.40, 95% CI 0.20 to 0.81; p=0.0122). Net use fell from 77.3% of residents after 1 year to 59.2% in the second year.
cards.watchOut: One spraying round in one Tanzanian district with pyrethroid-resistant vectors — the redundancy finding is about this insecticide pairing (pirimiphos-methyl spraying over PBO nets), not a universal law for all spraying-net combinations, and effects waned as net use fell.

shelves.title: CHoBI7 in Bangladesh: hygiene help triggered by a hospital diarrhoea admission cut child diarrhoea and stunting over the next year
shelves.question: In households of patients hospitalised with diarrhoea in Bangladesh, does a hospital-delivered water, sanitation and hygiene programme (CHoBI7) reduce diarrhoea and improve child growth?
shelves.mesh: Bangladesh/epidemiology · Child · Cholera*/epidemiology+prevention & control · Diarrhea/epidemiology · Hospitals · Humans · Hygiene · Sanitation · Telemedicine* · Water
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — in the CHoBI7 cluster trial (George CM et al., PMID: 32761174; 769 households, 2,626 participants in Dhaka), a hospital-delivered water, sanitation and hygiene programme with mobile-health messaging reduced 12-month diarrhoea prevalence in children under five in both delivery arms — prevalence ratio 0.73 with two home visits and 0.82 with no home visits — and reduced stunting at 12 months in children under two (about 32–33% versus 45%; odds ratios 0.54–0.55). The broader WASH meta-analysis (Wolf J et al., PMID: 29537671) supports the direction for water, sanitation and handwashing interventions generally, while warning that correcting for non-blinding shrinks the associations. This is a single trial of a specific hospital-triggered programme, with reported (not observed) diarrhoea as the primary outcome. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): CHoBI7 lowered diarrhoea and stunting in the households it targeted.

cards.headline: George 2021 (CHoBI7): under-5 diarrhoea prevalence lower in both programme arms (PR 0.73 with home visits, 0.82 without); under-2 stunting 32–33% versus 45% (OR 0.54–0.55)
cards.summary: George 2021 (CHoBI7): under-5 diarrhoea prevalence lower in both programme arms (PR 0.73 with home visits, 0.82 without); under-2 stunting 32–33% versus 45% (OR 0.54–0.55)
cards.people: Cluster-randomised trial of diarrhoea-patient households in Dhaka, Bangladesh (December 2016 to April 2018): 2,626 participants in 769 households allocated to a standard oral-rehydration message (849), facility-delivered CHoBI7 plus mobile health with no home visits (886), or CHoBI7 plus two home visits and mobile health (891). Primary outcome was reported diarrhoea in the past 2 weeks, collected monthly for 12 months; secondary outcomes were stunting, underweight and wasting at 12 months.
cards.result: Children under 5 had significantly lower 12-month diarrhoea prevalence in the home-visits arm (prevalence ratio 0.73, 95% CI 0.61 to 0.87) and the no-home-visits arm (PR 0.82, 95% CI 0.69 to 0.97) than the standard-message arm. Children under 2 were significantly less likely to be stunted in the home-visits arm (33% vs 45%; odds ratio 0.55, 95% CI 0.31 to 0.97) and the no-home-visits arm (32% vs 45%; OR 0.54, 95% CI 0.31 to 0.96). Analysis was intention-to-treat. The programme was delivered from the hospital during the patient's admission, targeting the high-risk week after discharge (the '7 days' of CHoBI7).
cards.watchOut: Diarrhoea was reported by households who knew their allocation — an unblinded, self-reported primary outcome in a hygiene trial is exactly where courtesy and recall bias operate, and the stunting confidence intervals only just exclude no effect. One city, one programme, cholera-hospital households.
cards.source: George CM et al. cards.headline: Wolf 2018: updated meta-analysis of 135 studies — point-of-use filtration cut diarrhoea risk by 61% relative (RR 0.39), sanitation by 25% relative (RR 0.75), handwashing promotion by 30% relative (RR 0.70)
cards.summary: Wolf 2018: updated meta-analysis of 135 studies — point-of-use filtration cut diarrhoea risk by 61% relative (RR 0.39), sanitation by 25% relative (RR 0.75), handwashing promotion by 30% relative (RR 0.70)
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis / meta-regression of 135 studies (1970 to February 2016) of drinking-water, sanitation and handwashing interventions against childhood diarrhoeal disease, largely in developing-country settings.
cards.result: Point-of-use filter interventions with safe storage reduced diarrhoea risk (risk ratio 0.39, 95% CI 0.32 to 0.48 — a 61% relative reduction); higher-quality continuously available piped water to premises reduced risk by 75% relative (RR 0.25, 95% CI 0.09 to 0.67) and continuous availability alone by 36% relative (RR 0.64, 95% CI 0.42 to 0.98); sanitation interventions reduced risk by 25% relative (RR 0.75, 95% CI 0.63 to 0.88), with greater reductions at high coverage; and handwashing-with-soap promotion reduced risk by 30% relative (RR 0.70, 95% CI 0.64 to 0.77). The authors caution that correcting for non-blinding would reduce the associations to some extent.
cards.watchOut: A general WASH literature, not a test of the hospital-triggered CHoBI7 model — it establishes that the components can work, while its own non-blinding warning applies with full force to CHoBI7's self-reported outcome.

cards.summary: Synthesis: a hospital-triggered hygiene programme reduced diarrhoea and stunting in patient households — consistent with the wider WASH evidence, resting on self-reported outcomes
cards.people: One cluster trial (769 households) of the CHoBI7 programme plus a 135-study WASH meta-analysis — the evidence for hospital-delivered household WASH after a diarrhoea admission.

shelves.title: One-week rabies pre-exposure vaccination primed travellers well for a later simulated exposure — but it formally missed non-inferiority
shelves.question: In people exposed to rabies risk (travellers and occupational groups), is one-week pre-exposure prophylaxis (intramuscular or intradermal) non-inferior to the standard 3-week schedule for antibody response?
shelves.mesh: Animals · Antibodies, Viral · Chlorocebus aethiops · Diploidy · Humans · Injections, Intradermal · Post-Exposure Prophylaxis · Pre-Exposure Prophylaxis* · Rabies*/prevention & control · Rabies Vaccines* · Rabies virus* · Vaccination · Vero Cells
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — the phase 3 trial (Quiambao BP et al., PMID: 35933278; 570 participants) gives a genuinely mixed answer. One-week pre-exposure regimens (two visits, intramuscular or intradermal, with either vaccine) produced seroconversion of 96.7–97.2% fourteen days after the last injection, against 100% for the classic three-week regimen — and the trial's primary objective, formal non-inferiority of one-week intramuscular versus three-week, was NOT demonstrated. Yet the priming worked in the way that matters clinically: after simulated post-exposure vaccination a year later, every group mounted rapid, robust anamnestic responses, with all but one participant seroconverting, and no safety concerns arose. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): one-week PrEP primes reliably enough to answer a simulated exposure a year later, but it did not meet its own non-inferiority bar on the primary antibody endpoint, so 'non-inferior' must not be claimed.

cards.headline: Quiambao 2022: one-week PrEP seroconverted 96.7–97.2% versus 100% for three-week — non-inferiority NOT demonstrated — but simulated PEP a year later seroconverted all but one participant in every group
cards.summary: Quiambao 2022: one-week PrEP seroconverted 96.7–97.2% versus 100% for three-week — non-inferiority NOT demonstrated — but simulated PEP a year later seroconverted all but one participant in every group
cards.people: 570 healthy participants aged 2–64 in a multicentre, open-label, randomised phase 3 trial, allocated to: one-week intramuscular human diploid cell vaccine (days 0 and 7), classic three-week intramuscular (days 0, 7, 21), one-week intradermal human diploid cell vaccine (two 0.1 mL doses per visit), or one-week Vero cell vaccine intramuscularly or intradermally. All received simulated post-exposure prophylaxis (two doses, three days apart) one year later. Seroconversion was a neutralising antibody titre of at least 0.5 IU/mL.
cards.result: Seroconversion 14 days after the last PrEP injection was 96.7% to 97.2% across the one-week groups and 100% in the three-week group; non-inferiority of one-week intramuscular versus three-week (the primary objective) was not demonstrated. After simulated post-exposure vaccination one year later, all groups showed rapid and robust immune responses, with all but one participant achieving seroconversion. There were no safety concerns, and tolerability was similar across groups. The authors conclude one-week intramuscular or intradermal PrEP with either vaccine provided efficacious priming, enabling rapid robust anamnestic responses to simulated PEP one year later across age groups.
cards.watchOut: Antibody endpoints and a simulated exposure — no participant was actually exposed to rabies, and the failed primary non-inferiority objective is part of the result, not a technicality to be waved past. Whether regulators or guidelines accept one-week PrEP on priming-plus-anamnestic grounds is a policy judgement this shelf does not make.
cards.source: Quiambao BP et al. cards.people: One phase 3 trial of 570 participants — the randomised record for one-week versus three-week rabies pre-exposure prophylaxis on this shelf.
cards.result: Primary endpoint: seroconversion 96.7–97.2% (one-week) vs 100% (three-week); non-inferiority not demonstrated. Functional endpoint: simulated PEP at one year seroconverted all but one participant across all groups; no safety concerns. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence).
cards.watchOut: Distinct from post-exposure regimen shelves: this is pre-exposure priming for travellers and occupational groups, where the payoff is a simpler, immunoglobulin-free response to a later exposure. shelves.title: Prednisolone for leprosy nerve damage: 20 weeks matched 32 in an 868-patient trial — and against placebo, benefit has never been shown
shelves.question: In leprosy patients, does prednisolone given early prevent or improve nerve function impairment and reactions versus placebo or shorter courses?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Anti-Inflammatory Agents/administration & dosage+therapeutic use · Double-Blind Method · Drug Administration Schedule · Female · Humans · Leprosy/complications+drug therapy · Male · Middle Aged · Peripheral Nervous System Diseases/drug therapy+etiology · Prednisolone/administration & dosage+therapeutic use · Young Adult
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — two facts bound what can be claimed. First, on duration, the large TENLEP clinical trial (Wagenaar I et al., PMID: 28976976; 868 patients with recent nerve function impairment) found 32 weeks of prednisolone no better than 20 weeks — improvement or restoration at 78 weeks in 77.5% versus 78.1% — with more serious adverse events on the longer course, so 20 weeks is the preferred initial duration. Second, on whether prednisolone beats nothing at all, the Cochrane review (Van Veen NH et al., PMID: 27210895) found the two placebo-controlled trials (84 and 95 participants) showed no significant difference in nerve function improvement after 12 months, on moderate-to-low quality evidence. The TENLEP programme's companion subclinical trial — prednisolone for nerve damage detected only on conduction studies, to prevent clinical impairment — was set out in the TENLEP protocols (PMID: 23249098). PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): steroids remain standard practice for recent leprosy nerve impairment, but placebo-controlled proof of benefit is lacking and longer courses add harm without benefit.

cards.headline: Wagenaar 2017 (TENLEP clinical): 32 weeks of prednisolone was no better than 20 weeks — improved/restored nerve function 77.5% versus 78.1% at 78 weeks, with more serious adverse events on the longer course
cards.summary: Wagenaar 2017 (TENLEP clinical): 32 weeks of prednisolone was no better than 20 weeks — improved/restored nerve function 77.5% versus 78.1% at 78 weeks, with more serious adverse events on the longer course
cards.people: 868 leprosy patients with recently developed clinical nerve function impairment (under 6 months) in a multicentre, triple-blind randomised trial, allocated to prednisolone for 20 weeks (429) or 32 weeks (439), starting at 45 or 60 mg/day by body weight and tapering. Nerve function was assessed by voluntary muscle testing and monofilament testing; the primary outcome was the proportion with improved or restored nerve function at week 78.
cards.result: At 78 weeks, improved or restored nerve function did not differ between groups: 78.1% in the 20-week arm and 77.5% in the 32-week arm (p=0.821). Secondary outcomes (Reaction Severity Scale, SALSA Scale, Participation Scale) also did not differ, except for a significantly higher proportion of serious adverse events in the longer treatment arm (the record does not give the two percentages). The authors conclude 20 weeks is the preferred initial treatment duration, after which likely only a minority require further individualised treatment.
cards.watchOut: A duration comparison with no untreated arm — it shows longer is not better, not that either course beats natural history, and about four in five patients improving in both arms is exactly the pattern spontaneous recovery would also produce.
cards.source: Wagenaar I et al. Effectiveness of 32 versus 20 weeks of prednisolone in leprosy patients with recent nerve function impairment: A randomized controlled trial. PLoS Neglected Tropical Diseases. 2017. PMID: 28976976. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Van Veen 2016 (Cochrane): five trials, 576 people — the two placebo trials found no significant difference in nerve function improvement at 12 months with prednisolone
cards.summary: Van Veen 2016 (Cochrane): five trials, 576 people — the two placebo trials found no significant difference in nerve function improvement at 12 months with prednisolone
cards.people: Cochrane review (updated 2016) of randomised and quasi-randomised trials of corticosteroids for nerve damage in leprosy versus no treatment, placebo, or another regimen: five trials, 576 people, largely low risk of bias but moderate-to-low quality evidence, mainly from imprecision. Two trials reported the primary outcome, improvement in nerve function after one year, both comparing prednisolone with placebo.
cards.result: There was no significant difference in nerve function improvement after 12 months between prednisolone and placebo in either placebo trial — one with 84 participants treating mild sensory impairment of less than six months, the other with 95 participants treating impairment of 6 to 24 months' duration. Adverse events were not reported significantly more often with corticosteroids than placebo in those trials. The other three trials did not report the primary outcome: one (334 participants) compared three corticosteroid regimens for severe type 1 reactions with no serious steroid side effects reported; one (21 participants) compared low- with high-dose prednisone for ulnar neuropathy; and one (42 participants) compared intravenous methylprednisolone plus oral prednisolone with saline plus oral prednisolone, with no significant difference in adverse events.
cards.watchOut: The placebo trials were small (84 and 95 participants) and treated different impairment durations and severities, so 'no significant difference' is compatible with a modest real benefit — it is the absence of demonstrated benefit, in the only designs that could show it, that drives this shelf's stamp.
cards.source: Van Veen NH et al. Corticosteroids for treating nerve damage in leprosy. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2016. PMID: 27210895. Registry ID: none in the record.
