cards.headline: Synthesis: 20 weeks, not 32 — and behind the duration answer sits an uncomfortable null: prednisolone has never beaten placebo for leprosy nerve damage in a Cochrane-grade analysis
cards.summary: Synthesis: 20 weeks, not 32 — and behind the duration answer sits an uncomfortable null: prednisolone has never beaten placebo for leprosy nerve damage in a Cochrane-grade analysis
cards.people: One 868-patient duration trial (TENLEP) plus a Cochrane review of five trials (576 people), with the TENLEP protocols (PMID: 23249098) also setting out a companion trial of prednisolone for subclinical neuropathy to prevent clinical impairment.
cards.result: Duration: 77.5% vs 78.1% improved/restored at 78 weeks (32 vs 20 weeks, p=0.821), more serious adverse events with 32 weeks. Versus placebo: no significant 12-month nerve-function difference in either of two small trials. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence).
cards.watchOut: This shelf does not recommend withholding steroids — they remain the standard response to recent nerve impairment and reactions, and the trials may be underpowered for the subgroups that benefit. It records that the evidence is weaker than the confidence of routine practice suggests. Tier C is not set for this shelf in the miner entry — the trial base, while inconclusive against placebo, is comparatively large.

shelves.title: Hib conjugate vaccine in Gambian infants: invasive disease cut by 95% and radiological pneumonia by 21% in a 42,848-infant randomised trial
shelves.question: In infants in high-burden settings, does Haemophilus influenzae type b conjugate vaccine prevent pneumonia and meningitis versus control?
shelves.mesh: Age Factors · Developing Countries · Diphtheria-Tetanus-Pertussis Vaccine/administration & dosage · Double-Blind Method · Follow-Up Studies · Gambia · Haemophilus Infections/diagnosis/prevention & control · Haemophilus Vaccines/administration & dosage · Haemophilus influenzae/classification · Humans · Immunization Schedule · Incidence · Infant · Meningitis, Haemophilus/diagnosis/prevention & control · Paracentesis · Pneumonia, Bacterial/diagnosis/prevention & control · Radiography, Thoracic · Spinal Puncture · Tetanus Toxoid/administration & dosage · Vaccines, Conjugate/administration & dosage
shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit) — in the Gambian double-blind randomised trial of 42,848 infants, three doses of Hib polysaccharide–tetanus protein (PRP-T) conjugate vaccine prevented 95% of all invasive Hib disease (1 case in vaccinees versus 19 in controls), 100% of Hib pneumonia after two or three doses (0 versus 10), and reduced radiologically defined pneumonia of any cause by 21.1% (198 versus 251 cases). Observational evidence since is concordant: a systematic review and meta-analysis of 30 studies in 17 countries estimated vaccine effectiveness against invasive Hib disease of 97% after three doses and against Hib meningitis of 96% after two or three doses. The catch is schedule, not direction: one dose protects far less well (59% against invasive disease), so the benefit belongs to a completed primary series. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): a completed Hib conjugate series prevents nearly all invasive Hib disease and about a fifth of radiological pneumonia in high-burden infancy.

cards.headline: Mulholland 1997 (The Gambia): invasive Hib disease 1 versus 19 cases after three doses — efficacy 95%; Hib pneumonia 0 versus 10; all-cause radiological pneumonia down 21.1%
cards.summary: Mulholland 1997 (The Gambia): invasive Hib disease 1 versus 19 cases after three doses — efficacy 95%; Hib pneumonia 0 versus 10; all-cause radiological pneumonia down 21.1%
cards.people: 42,848 infants in The Gambia randomised between March 1993 and October 1995 to PRP-T Hib conjugate vaccine mixed with diphtheria–tetanus–pertussis vaccine, or DTP alone, at 2, 3 and 4 months; 83% received all three doses; follow-up 5–36 months with blood culture, lumbar puncture, chest radiograph or lung aspirate for suspected invasive disease.
cards.result: 17 cases of culture-positive Hib pneumonia, 28 of Hib meningitis and 5 of other invasive Hib disease were detected overall. Efficacy after three doses was 95% against all invasive disease (1 case in PRP-T vaccinees versus 19 in controls; 95% CI 67–100), 100% against Hib pneumonia after two or three doses (0 versus 10; 95% CI 55–100), and radiologically defined pneumonia at any time after enrolment fell by 21.1% (198 versus 251 cases; 95% CI 4.6–34.9).
cards.watchOut: A single-country trial from the 1990s in a high-burden setting: the 21.1% all-cause pneumonia reduction reflects how much pneumonia Hib caused there and then, and will be smaller where Hib circulation is already low. The invasive-disease confidence interval is wide (67–100) because cases were few — the direction, not the exact percentage, is the secure finding.
cards.source: Mulholland K et al. Randomised trial of Haemophilus influenzae type-b tetanus protein conjugate vaccine [corrected] for prevention of pneumonia and meningitis in Gambian infants. Lancet (London, England). 1997. PMID: 9130939. cards.headline: Jackson 2013 meta-analysis: three-dose effectiveness 97% against invasive Hib disease and 94% in cohort studies — but only 59% after one dose
cards.summary: Jackson 2013 meta-analysis: three-dose effectiveness 97% against invasive Hib disease and 94% in cohort studies — but only 59% after one dose
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of observational data (Jackson 2013)
cards.people: 31 eligible articles reporting 30 observational studies (case-control and cohort) conducted in 17 countries, summarising effectiveness of Hib conjugate vaccines by number of doses and schedule.
cards.result: In case-control studies using community controls, effectiveness against Hib meningitis was 55% (95% CI 2–80) after one dose, 96% (86–99) after two doses and 96% (86–99) after three doses of vaccines other than the PRP-OMP product. Effectiveness against invasive Hib disease was 59% (30–76) after one dose and 97% (87–99) after three doses; across four cohort studies, three-dose effectiveness was 94% (88–97).
cards.watchOut: Observational effectiveness data, not randomised comparisons — families completing three doses differ from those who do not. The review also found some evidence of lower effectiveness when Hib vaccine was given with acellular rather than whole-cell pertussis vaccine, a schedule nuance the Gambian trial cannot address.
cards.source: Jackson C et al. Effectiveness of Haemophilus influenzae type b vaccines administered according to various schedules: systematic review and meta-analysis of observational data. The Pediatric infectious disease journal. 2013. PMID: 23811746. cards.summary: Synthesis: near-complete protection against invasive Hib disease once the series is finished — the trial and 30 observational studies point the same way
cards.people: One double-blind randomised trial of 42,848 Gambian infants (PRP-T conjugate) plus a meta-analysis of 30 observational studies in 17 countries covering several conjugate products and schedules.
cards.result: Invasive Hib disease: 95% efficacy in the trial (1 versus 19 cases after three doses) and 97% effectiveness after three doses observationally. shelves.title: Pneumococcal conjugate vaccines in young children: invasive disease cut by 65–100% across three randomised trials — pneumonia by a fifth, ear infections by only 6%
shelves.question: In young children, do pneumococcal conjugate vaccines prevent invasive pneumococcal disease, pneumonia and acute otitis media versus control?
shelves.mesh: Bacterial Capsules · Double-Blind Method · Drug Resistance, Bacterial · Female · HIV Infections/complications · Haemophilus Vaccines · Humans · Incidence · Infant · Male · Pneumococcal Infections/mortality/prevention & control · Pneumococcal Vaccines/adverse effects · Pneumonia, Pneumococcal/prevention & control · Polysaccharides, Bacterial · Serotyping · Streptococcus pneumoniae/classification/isolation & purification · Vaccines, Conjugate/adverse effects
shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit) — three randomised trials agree on invasive disease and split honestly on the softer endpoints. In Soweto, a 9-valent conjugate vaccine cut first episodes of vaccine-serotype invasive pneumococcal disease by 83% in children without HIV (3 versus 17 cases) and by 65% in children with HIV (9 versus 26), and radiologically confirmed pneumonia by 20%. In Finland's cluster-randomised FinIP trial, the ten-valent vaccine's effectiveness against vaccine-type invasive disease was 100% on the 3+1 schedule (0 cases) and 92% on 2+1 (1 case, versus 12 in controls). For ear infections the same vaccine class is far weaker: the Finnish otitis trial found 57% fewer episodes caused by vaccine serotypes but only 6% fewer episodes of acute otitis media from any cause (95% CI −4 to 16). PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): conjugate vaccines prevent most vaccine-serotype invasive disease and about a fifth of confirmed pneumonia in young children; the ear-infection benefit is real for pneumococcal episodes but small for ear infections overall.

cards.headline: Klugman 2003 (Soweto): vaccine-serotype invasive disease down 83% without HIV and 65% with HIV; radiological pneumonia down 20%
cards.summary: Klugman 2003 (Soweto): vaccine-serotype invasive disease down 83% without HIV and 65% with HIV; radiological pneumonia down 20%
cards.people: 39,836 children in Soweto, South Africa (19,922 vaccine, 19,914 placebo) given a 9-valent pneumococcal polysaccharide vaccine conjugated to CRM197, or placebo, at 6, 10 and 14 weeks of age; all children also received Hib conjugate vaccine; intention-to-treat analysis.
cards.result: Among children without HIV infection, the vaccine reduced first episodes of invasive pneumococcal disease due to vaccine serotypes by 83% (95% CI 39–97; 3 cases among vaccine recipients versus 17 among controls) and first episodes of radiologically confirmed alveolar consolidation by 20% (95% CI 2–35; 169 versus 212 cases). Among HIV-infected children, efficacy against vaccine-serotype invasive disease was 65% (95% CI 24–86; 9 versus 26 cases). Invasive disease from penicillin-resistant strains fell by 67% (95% CI 19–88; 7 versus 21 cases).
cards.watchOut: A 9-valent product no longer in use, tested where HIV prevalence and pneumococcal burden were high; absolute benefits in low-burden settings are smaller. Efficacy in HIV-infected children (65%) was lower and less precise, and serotype replacement after vaccination is not measured in this record.
cards.source: Klugman KP et al. A trial of a 9-valent pneumococcal conjugate vaccine in children with and those without HIV infection. The New England journal of medicine. 2003. PMID: 14523142. cards.headline: Palmu 2013 (FinIP): ten-valent vaccine effectiveness 100% (3+1 schedule) and 92% (2+1) against vaccine-type invasive disease — 13 cases, 12 of them in controls
cards.summary: Palmu 2013 (FinIP): ten-valent vaccine effectiveness 100% (3+1 schedule) and 92% (2+1) against vaccine-type invasive disease — 13 cases, 12 of them in controls
cards.people: 47,369 Finnish children under 19 months enrolled 2009–2010 in 78 clusters; 30,528 assessed for the primary objective. Ten-valent pneumococcal Haemophilus influenzae protein D conjugate vaccine (PHiD-CV10) on 3+1 or 2+1 schedules versus hepatitis vaccines as control; masked register-based follow-up to January 31, 2012.
cards.result: 13 culture-confirmed vaccine-type invasive pneumococcal disease cases were detected: none in the PHiD-CV10 3+1 group, one in the 2+1 group, and 12 in the control groups. Vaccine effectiveness was estimated at 100% (95% CI 83–100) for the 3+1 schedule and 92% for the 2+1 schedule against invasive disease due to the ten vaccine serotypes.
cards.watchOut: Only 13 endpoint cases in a low-incidence country — the point estimates are dramatic but rest on very few events, and the trial measures vaccine-type disease, not all invasive disease, so serotype replacement sits outside the frame.
cards.source: Palmu AA et al. Effectiveness of the ten-valent pneumococcal Haemophilus influenzae protein D conjugate vaccine (PHiD-CV10) against invasive pneumococcal disease: a cluster randomised trial. Lancet (London, England). 2013. PMID: 23158882. Registry ID: NCT00861380. cards.headline: Eskola 2001 (Finland): otitis media from any cause down only 6% (CI −4 to 16) — but vaccine-serotype episodes down 57% and all pneumococcal episodes down 34%
cards.summary: Eskola 2001 (Finland): otitis media from any cause down only 6% (CI −4 to 16) — but vaccine-serotype episodes down 57% and all pneumococcal episodes down 34%
cards.people: 1,662 Finnish infants randomised to a heptavalent pneumococcal conjugate vaccine (CRM197 carrier) or hepatitis B vaccine control at 2, 4, 6 and 12 months; 95.1% completed the trial; acute otitis media diagnosed by predefined criteria with middle-ear fluid culture at myringotomy; follow-up from 6.5 to 24 months of age.
cards.result: Of 2,596 episodes of acute otitis media, the vaccine reduced episodes from any cause by 6% (95% CI −4 to 16), culture-confirmed pneumococcal episodes by 34% (95% CI 21–45), and episodes due to vaccine serotypes by 57% (95% CI 44–67). Episodes due to cross-reactive serotypes fell by 51%, while episodes due to other serotypes rose — the pattern of serotype replacement.
cards.watchOut: Most ear infections are not caused by vaccine serotypes, which caps the all-cause benefit at single digits; quoting the 57% serotype figure as the ear-infection benefit would mislead. Local reactions were more frequent with the pneumococcal vaccine than with hepatitis B control.
cards.source: Eskola J et al. Efficacy of a pneumococcal conjugate vaccine against acute otitis media. The New England journal of medicine. 2001. PMID: 11172176. cards.headline: Synthesis: invasive disease is the strong claim, pneumonia the moderate one, ear infections the weak one — three trials, one gradient
cards.summary: Synthesis: invasive disease is the strong claim, pneumonia the moderate one, ear infections the weak one — three trials, one gradient
cards.people: Three randomised double-blind trials totalling over 88,000 children: a 9-valent vaccine in Soweto (n=39,836), a ten-valent vaccine in a Finnish cluster trial (47,369 enrolled), and a heptavalent vaccine otitis trial in Finland (n=1,662).
cards.result: Vaccine-serotype invasive pneumococcal disease: reduced 83% (HIV-uninfected) and 65% (HIV-infected) in Soweto; effectiveness 100% (3+1) and 92% (2+1) in FinIP. Radiologically confirmed pneumonia: 20% lower in Soweto. Acute otitis media: 57% fewer vaccine-serotype episodes but only 6% fewer episodes from any cause. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit), graded by endpoint as the trials themselves grade it.
cards.watchOut: All three products differ from, or are predecessors of, current higher-valency vaccines, and none of these records measures mortality. Tier C is not set: three concordant randomised trials carry the invasive-disease claim.
cards.source: Synthesis of Klugman KP et al. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2003 (PMID: 14523142); Palmu AA et al. The Lancet. 2013 (PMID: 23158882); Eskola J et al. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2001 (PMID: 11172176).

shelves.title: MenAfriVac mass vaccination: meningitis incidence 2.48 versus 43.8 per 100,000 in Chad, no serogroup A cases in vaccinated regions, and serogroup A carriage eliminated in Burkina Faso
shelves.question: In the African meningitis belt, does mass vaccination with the meningococcal A conjugate vaccine (MenAfriVac) reduce meningococcal A carriage and epidemics?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Age Distribution · Carrier State/diagnosis/epidemiology/prevention & control · Chad/epidemiology · Child · Child, Preschool · Epidemics · Humans · Incidence · Infant · Meningitis, Meningococcal/diagnosis/epidemiology/prevention & control · Meningococcal Vaccines · Neisseria meningitidis, Serogroup A/isolation & purification · Population Surveillance/methods · Vaccination · Young Adult
shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit) — the evidence is ecological rather than randomised, but it is large, abrupt and biologically coherent. In Chad, roughly 1.8 million people aged 1–29 years were vaccinated with the serogroup A polysaccharide–tetanus toxoid conjugate vaccine (PsA-TT, MenAfriVac) in December 2011; in the 2012 meningitis season, incidence in the three vaccinated regions was 2.48 per 100,000 (57 cases in 2.3 million people) versus 43.8 per 100,000 (3,809 cases in 8.7 million) in unvaccinated regions — an incidence rate ratio of 0.096 (95% CI 0.046–0.198) — and no serogroup A case was reported in the vaccinated regions despite enhanced surveillance. In Burkina Faso, serogroup A carriage, 0.39% at baseline, was not identified at all after mass vaccination in 25,521 oropharyngeal samples, disappearing in unvaccinated people too — the signature of herd immunity. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): mass MenAfriVac campaigns collapse serogroup A meningitis and carriage, including in the unvaccinated.

cards.headline: Daugla 2014 (Chad): meningitis incidence 2.48 versus 43.8 per 100,000 after vaccinating 1.8 million people — rate ratio 0.096, zero serogroup A cases in vaccinated regions
cards.summary: Daugla 2014 (Chad): meningitis incidence 2.48 versus 43.8 per 100,000 after vaccinating 1.8 million people — rate ratio 0.096, zero serogroup A cases in vaccinated regions
cards.people: Roughly 1.8 million residents aged 1–29 years in three regions of Chad around N'Djamena received one dose of PsA-TT (MenAfriVac) over 10 days in December 2011; meningitis incidence compared with unvaccinated regions using national records from January 2009 to June 2012, with enhanced surveillance in vaccinated regions in 2012; carriage sampled in residents aged 1–29 years before and after vaccination.
cards.result: During the 2012 meningitis season, incidence in the three vaccinated regions was 2.48 per 100,000 (57 cases in a population of 2.3 million) versus 43.8 per 100,000 (3,809 cases per 8.7 million) in regions without mass vaccination — a 94% difference in crude incidence (p<0.0001) and an incidence rate ratio of 0.096 (95% CI 0.046–0.198). Despite enhanced surveillance, no case of serogroup A meningococcal meningitis was reported in the three vaccinated regions.
cards.watchOut: Not a randomised comparison: vaccinated and unvaccinated regions could differ in epidemic timing, and serogroup A epidemics are cyclical, so part of the contrast could be a quiet year in the capital regions. The effect size (a tenfold difference, with zero serogroup A cases under enhanced surveillance) is nonetheless far larger than the usual ecological ambiguity — and Tier C is set because the design is observational and the claim is an epidemic-prevention claim.
cards.source: Daugla DM et al. Effect of a serogroup A meningococcal conjugate vaccine (PsA-TT) on serogroup A meningococcal meningitis and carriage in Chad: a community study [corrected]. Lancet (London, England). 2014. PMID: 24035220. cards.headline: Kristiansen 2013 (Burkina Faso): serogroup A carriage 0.39% at baseline, none found in 25,521 samples after mass vaccination — including in unvaccinated people
cards.summary: Kristiansen 2013 (Burkina Faso): serogroup A carriage 0.39% at baseline, none found in 25,521 samples after mass vaccination — including in unvaccinated people
cards.people: Age-stratified representative samples of the 1–29-year-old population in three districts of Burkina Faso before and up to 13 months after the 2010 MenAfriVac mass campaigns; 25,521 oropharyngeal samples analysed, 22,093 obtained after vaccination; overall vaccination coverage in the sampled population 89.7%.
cards.result: Compared with a baseline serogroup A carriage prevalence of 0.39%, no serogroup A meningococci were identified after vaccination. Serogroup A carriage was eliminated in both the vaccinated and the unvaccinated population from 3 weeks up to 13 months after mass vaccination (P=.003), consistent with a herd-immunity effect. Overall post-vaccination meningococcal carriage was 6.95%, dominated by serogroup X, which declined across campaigns from 8.66% to 1.97%.
cards.watchOut: Carriage prevalence of serogroup A was already low (0.39%) before vaccination, so 'elimination' is a small absolute change measured very precisely; the study cannot by itself prove disease prevention — that is the Chad record's job. Coverage in 1-year-olds fell from 87.1% to 26.5% over the study as unvaccinated infants aged into the sampled group, a warning about sustaining the effect without routine infant immunisation.
cards.source: Kristiansen PA et al. Impact of the serogroup A meningococcal conjugate vaccine, MenAfriVac, on carriage and herd immunity. Clinical infectious diseases : an official publication of the Infectious Diseases Society of America. 2013. PMID: 23087396. cards.headline: Synthesis: disease collapsed where the vaccine went in, and the organism disappeared from carriers' throats — herd protection on both records
cards.summary: Synthesis: disease collapsed where the vaccine went in, and the organism disappeared from carriers' throats — herd protection on both records
cards.people: Two community-level studies of the same vaccine (PsA-TT, MenAfriVac) in the African meningitis belt: a meningitis-incidence comparison covering about 11 million people in Chad, and a 25,521-sample carriage study in Burkina Faso.
cards.result: Meningitis incidence 2.48 versus 43.8 per 100,000 (rate ratio 0.096) with zero serogroup A cases in vaccinated regions of Chad; serogroup A carriage from 0.39% to none detected in Burkina Faso, in unvaccinated residents as well as vaccinated. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit), Tier C because both records are observational community studies rather than randomised trials.
cards.watchOut: Neither study is randomised, and meningitis-belt epidemics wax and wane between years; the claim rests on effect size, abruptness, the zero serogroup A count under enhanced surveillance, and the carriage mechanism agreeing with each other. Serogroup replacement (X dominated carriage afterwards) is the open long-term question neither record answers.
cards.source: Synthesis of Daugla DM et al. The Lancet. 2014 (PMID: 24035220); Kristiansen PA et al. Clinical Infectious Diseases. 2013 (PMID: 23087396).

shelves.title: A third MMR dose in a university mumps outbreak: attack rate 6.7 versus 14.5 per 1,000 and a 78.1% lower adjusted risk — one observational study, no trial
shelves.question: During a mumps outbreak in a vaccinated population, does a third dose of MMR vaccine reduce the risk of mumps versus two doses?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Disease Outbreaks/prevention & control · Female · Humans · Immunization, Secondary · Iowa/epidemiology · Male · Measles-Mumps-Rubella Vaccine/administration & dosage/immunology · Mumps/epidemiology/immunology/prevention & control · Proportional Hazards Models · Risk · Students · Universities · Young Adult
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a single large observational outbreak study. Among 20,496 students at the University of Iowa during the 2015–2016 outbreak, mumps was diagnosed in 259 students; the attack rate was 6.7 per 1,000 among the 4,783 students who received a third MMR dose during the campaign versus 14.5 per 1,000 among those with two doses (P<0.001). At 28 days after vaccination, a third dose was associated with a 78.1% lower risk of mumps than two doses (adjusted hazard ratio 0.22, 95% CI 0.12–0.39), after adjustment for years since the second dose. The same study shows why outbreaks happen in vaccinated populations: students whose second dose was 13 or more years earlier had more than nine times the risk of mumps. There is no randomised trial of a third dose, and students who came forward for the campaign dose may differ from those who did not. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a third MMR dose probably helps control a mumps outbreak in a young-adult population whose second dose is distant — on one study's evidence, flagged Tier C.

cards.headline: Cardemil 2017 (University of Iowa): third-dose attack rate 6.7 versus 14.5 per 1,000; adjusted hazard ratio 0.22 (78.1% lower risk) at 28 days
cards.summary: Cardemil 2017 (University of Iowa): third-dose attack rate 6.7 versus 14.5 per 1,000; adjusted hazard ratio 0.22 (78.1% lower risk) at 28 days
cards.people: 20,496 students enrolled at the University of Iowa during the 2015–2016 academic year, of whom 98.1% had received at least two MMR doses before the outbreak and 4,783 received a third dose during the outbreak campaign; 259 mumps cases diagnosed. Attack rates compared by Fisher's exact test; effectiveness estimated with multivariable time-dependent Cox regression adjusting for years since the second dose.
cards.result: The attack rate was lower among students who received three doses than among those who received two (6.7 vs. 14.5 cases per 1,000 population, P<0.001). At 28 days after vaccination, receipt of a third dose was associated with a 78.1% lower risk of mumps than receipt of a second dose (adjusted hazard ratio, 0.22; 95% CI, 0.12 to 0.39). Students had more than nine times the risk of mumps if they had received their second MMR dose 13 years or more before the outbreak, and two-dose effectiveness fell with time since the second dose — evidence of waning immunity.
cards.watchOut: Observational and self-selected: students who attended the campaign may have differed in exposure and health behaviour, and the campaign began after the outbreak was under way, so timing alone can flatter the third dose. One outbreak, one university, one age group — generalising to school-age outbreaks is an extrapolation. Tier C is set: a single observational study carries the shelf.
cards.source: Cardemil CV et al. Effectiveness of a Third Dose of MMR Vaccine for Mumps Outbreak Control. The New England journal of medicine. 2017. PMID: 28877026. shelves.title: Early BCG for low-birthweight infants: neonatal mortality rate ratio 0.70 in the third trial (not significant alone), 0.62 pooled across three randomised trials
shelves.question: In low-birthweight infants in high-mortality settings, does early BCG vaccination at birth reduce neonatal and infant mortality versus delayed BCG?
shelves.mesh: BCG Vaccine/administration & dosage/immunology · Communicable Diseases/immunology · Denmark · Female · Guinea-Bissau · Humans · Infant · Infant Mortality · Infant, Low Birth Weight/immunology · Infant, Newborn · Male · Poliovirus Vaccine, Oral/administration & dosage/immunology · Vaccination/methods
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — three randomised trials in Guinea-Bissau of early BCG-Denmark (Statens Serum Institut) for infants weighing under 2,500 g point the same way, though the largest single trial does not reach significance on its own. In that trial (4,172 infants), early BCG was associated with a neonatal mortality rate ratio of 0.70 (95% CI 0.47–1.04), and 0.66 (0.44–1.00) when follow-up was censored at oral polio vaccine campaigns; infectious-disease mortality fell by 43% (rate ratio 0.57, 0.35–0.93) with no reduction in non-infectious mortality. Pooling all three trials, early BCG reduced neonatal mortality by 38% (rate ratio 0.62, 0.46–0.83) and mortality by 12 months by 16% (0.84, 0.71–1.00). The trials were unblinded, and the pooled estimate leans on two smaller earlier trials. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): early BCG probably reduces neonatal deaths in low-birthweight infants in high-mortality settings, mainly by preventing infectious deaths — a mortality claim, so Tier C.

cards.headline: Biering-Sørensen 2017: neonatal mortality rate ratio 0.70 (0.47–1.04) for early BCG-Denmark; infectious mortality 0.57; three-trial pooled neonatal ratio 0.62 (0.46–0.83)
cards.summary: Biering-Sørensen 2017: neonatal mortality rate ratio 0.70 (0.47–1.04) for early BCG-Denmark; infectious mortality 0.57; three-trial pooled neonatal ratio 0.62 (0.46–0.83)
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial with meta-analysis of three trials (Biering-Sørensen 2017)
cards.people: 4,172 low-weight neonates (<2,500 g) in Guinea-Bissau, 2008–2013, randomised without blinding at maternity-ward discharge or first health-centre contact to early BCG-Denmark (Statens Serum Institut; n=2,083) or control (local policy of delayed BCG for low-weight infants; n=2,089); the record also pools this trial with two earlier randomised trials of the same strategy.
cards.result: Early BCG-Denmark was associated with a nonsignificant reduction in neonatal mortality (mortality rate ratio 0.70; 95% CI 0.47–1.04), and a 34% relative reduction (0.66; 0.44–1.00) in the prespecified analysis censoring follow-up at oral poliovirus vaccine campaigns. There was no reduction in mortality from noninfectious diseases, but a 43% relative reduction in infectious-disease mortality (0.57; 0.35–0.93). The meta-analysis of the three BCG-Denmark trials found neonatal mortality reduced by 38% (0.62; 0.46–0.83) and mortality by age 12 months reduced by 16% (0.84; 0.71–1.00).
cards.watchOut: The trial was unblinded (BCG leaves a scar and a local reaction, so blinding is near-impossible), the headline result is not significant without the campaign-censoring analysis, and all three trials come from one research programme in one country using one vaccine strain (BCG-Denmark) — other strains and settings are untested in this record. Tier C is set: this is a mortality-benefit claim resting substantially on a pooled estimate.
cards.source: Biering-Sørensen S et al. Early BCG-Denmark and Neonatal Mortality Among Infants Weighing <2500 g: A Randomized Controlled Trial. Clinical infectious diseases : an official publication of the Infectious Diseases Society of America. 2017. PMID: 29579158. Registry ID: NCT00625482. cards.headline: Synthesis: a consistent direction across three trials, an infectious-death mechanism, and a largest trial that is suggestive rather than conclusive
cards.summary: Synthesis: a consistent direction across three trials, an infectious-death mechanism, and a largest trial that is suggestive rather than conclusive
cards.people: Three randomised trials in Guinea-Bissau of early versus delayed BCG-Denmark in infants under 2,500 g, the largest enrolling 4,172 infants; pooled in the 2017 trial report.
cards.result: Neonatal mortality: rate ratio 0.70 (0.47–1.04) in the largest trial; 0.62 (0.46–0.83) pooled. Infectious-disease mortality: 0.57 (0.35–0.93). Mortality by 12 months: 0.84 (0.71–1.00) pooled. Non-infectious mortality: no reduction. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), Tier C.
cards.watchOut: Every trial is from Guinea-Bissau and from the group that proposed the hypothesis; independent replication in another high-mortality setting, and with other BCG strains, is the missing piece. The benefit also depends on the local policy being to delay BCG in low-weight infants — where BCG is already given at birth to all, there is nothing to gain.
cards.source: Synthesis of Biering-Sørensen S et al. Clinical Infectious Diseases. 2017 (PMID: 29579158), reporting the third randomised trial and a meta-analysis of all three early BCG-Denmark trials.

shelves.title: BCG vaccination in older adults (ACTIVATE): new infections 25.0% versus 42.3% over 12 months — a 198-patient trial stopped at an interim analysis
shelves.question: In older adults, does BCG vaccination reduce new infections and respiratory infections versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Aged, 80 and over · BCG Vaccine/administration & dosage/adverse effects/immunology · Double-Blind Method · Female · Hospitalization · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Respiratory Tract Infections/immunology/prevention & control · Virus Diseases/immunology/prevention & control
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one small double-blind randomised trial. In ACTIVATE, 198 elderly patients received BCG or placebo at hospital discharge and were followed for 12 months for new infections. The incidence of new infections was 25.0% (95% CI 16.4–36.1) after BCG versus 42.3% (31.9–53.4) after placebo, and the median time to first infection was 16 weeks versus 11 weeks. Most of the protection was against respiratory tract infections of probable viral origin (hazard ratio 0.21, p=0.013). No difference in the frequency of adverse effects was found. The cautions are size and stopping: 198 patients, and the result was reported at an interim analysis, which tends to exaggerate effects. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): BCG revaccination probably reduces infections in older adults over the following year, on a single small trial — Tier C, and the authors themselves call for larger studies.

cards.headline: ACTIVATE (Giamarellos-Bourboulis 2020): new infections 25.0% on BCG versus 42.3% on placebo; median time to first infection 16 versus 11 weeks
cards.summary: ACTIVATE (Giamarellos-Bourboulis 2020): new infections 25.0% on BCG versus 42.3% on placebo; median time to first infection 16 versus 11 weeks
cards.people: 198 elderly patients randomised at hospital discharge to a single BCG vaccination or placebo and followed for 12 months for new infections; results reported at an interim analysis.
cards.result: BCG vaccination significantly increased the time to first infection (median 16 weeks compared with 11 weeks after placebo). The incidence of new infections was 25.0% (95% CI 16.4–36.1) after BCG vaccination versus 42.3% (31.9–53.4) after placebo; most of the protection was against respiratory tract infections of probable viral origin (hazard ratio 0.21, p=0.013). No difference in the frequency of adverse effects was found between the groups.
cards.watchOut: Only 198 patients and an interim analysis — early-stopped trials systematically overestimate effects, and the respiratory-infection hazard ratio of 0.21 rests on few events. Participants were elderly patients at hospital discharge in Greece, a selected group; whether community-dwelling older adults benefit, and whether the effect survives a second year, is untested here. Tier C is set: a single small trial with an infection-prevention claim.
cards.source: Giamarellos-Bourboulis EJ et al. Activate: Randomized Clinical Trial of BCG Vaccination against Infection in the Elderly. Cell. 2020. PMID: 32941801. Registry ID: NCT03296423. shelves.title: ASSIST peer-led school programme: smoking odds ratio 0.77 at one year (significant) fading to 0.85 at two years — a real but modest and decaying effect
shelves.question: In adolescents in schools, does a peer-led anti-smoking programme (ASSIST) reduce uptake of regular smoking versus usual education?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Child · England/epidemiology · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Health Promotion/methods · Humans · Male · Peer Group · Prevalence · Schools · Smoking/epidemiology · Smoking Prevention · Social Class · Wales/epidemiology
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one large cluster-randomised trial, supported weakly by the wider school-programme literature. ASSIST trained influential 12–13-year-olds in 30 schools to act as peer supporters discouraging smoking in informal interactions; 29 schools continued usual education (10,730 students in total). The odds ratio for being a smoker in intervention versus control schools was 0.75 (95% CI 0.55–1.01) immediately after the intervention, 0.77 (0.59–0.99) at one year, and 0.85 (0.72–1.01) at two years — a benefit that is statistically secure only at the one-year point and fades thereafter. The Cochrane review of school-based prevention programmes found a similar overall pattern at longest follow-up (odds ratio 0.88, 0.82–0.96 across programmes), with social-competence curricula doing best. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): peer-led prevention probably delays or reduces smoking uptake modestly for about a year; it is not a durable one-off inoculation.

cards.headline: Campbell 2008 (ASSIST): odds of smoking 0.77 at one year (0.59–0.99) but 0.85 at two years (0.72–1.01) — 10,730 students, 59 schools
cards.summary: Campbell 2008 (ASSIST): odds of smoking 0.77 at one year (0.59–0.99) but 0.85 at two years (0.72–1.01) — 10,730 students, 59 schools
cards.people: 10,730 students aged 12–13 years in 59 schools in England and Wales: 30 schools (5,358 students) randomised to ASSIST — influential students trained as peer supporters to encourage peers not to smoke during informal interactions outside the classroom — and 29 schools (5,372 students) to usual smoking education. Follow-up immediately after the intervention and at 1 and 2 years; intention-to-treat analysis. The ASSIST programme is named here as the specific tested programme, per the non-drug programme naming rule.
cards.result: The odds ratio of being a smoker in intervention compared with control schools was 0.75 (95% CI 0.55–1.01) immediately after the intervention (n=9,349), 0.77 (0.59–0.99) at 1-year follow-up (n=9,147), and 0.85 (0.72–1.01) at 2-year follow-up (n=8,756). In the subgroup at high risk of regular smoking uptake at baseline, the corresponding odds ratios were 0.79 (0.55–1.13), 0.75 (0.56–0.99) and 0.85 (0.70–1.02).
cards.watchOut: Only the one-year estimate excludes 1.0; by two years the effect is smaller and non-significant, so any claim must carry the decay. Smoking was self-reported by adolescents, schools rather than students were the randomised unit, and the trial predates adolescent vaping entirely. Tier C is set: the named programme rests on this single trial.
cards.source: Campbell R et al. An informal school-based peer-led intervention for smoking prevention in adolescence (ASSIST): a cluster randomised trial. Lancet (London, England). 2008. cards.headline: Thomas 2013 (Cochrane): school programmes overall odds ratio 0.88 (0.82–0.96) at longest follow-up — social-competence curricula 0.52, social-influences-only 1.00
cards.summary: Thomas 2013 (Cochrane): school programmes overall odds ratio 0.88 (0.82–0.96) at longest follow-up — social-competence curricula 0.52, social-influences-only 1.00
cards.type: Systematic review of randomised trials (Thomas 2013, Cochrane)
cards.people: Randomised trials of school-based smoking-prevention programmes in youth aged 5–18, randomised by student, class, school or district, with at least six months of follow-up; searches to October 2012. Pure-prevention cohorts (baseline non-smokers) analysed separately from change-in-behaviour and point-prevalence groups.
cards.result: At longest follow-up, pooled results for pure-prevention cohorts showed a significant effect favouring intervention (odds ratio 0.88, 95% CI 0.82–0.96). Programmes with a social-competence curriculum showed an odds ratio of 0.52 (0.30–0.88), and combined social-competence plus social-influences curricula 0.50 (0.28–0.87), whereas social-influences-only programmes showed no effect (1.00, 0.88–1.13, 25 studies) and multimodal programmes none (0.89, 0.73–1.08).
cards.watchOut: The review pools many unlike programmes, 49 studies (152,544 participants) could not be analysed, and ASSIST itself sits inside this literature — so the review corroborates the class, not the named programme independently. Effects are averages over mostly small trials with self-reported smoking.

cards.summary: Synthesis: peer-led prevention works modestly and briefly — the trial's own two-year numbers set the ceiling on the claim
cards.people: One cluster-randomised trial of the named ASSIST programme (10,730 students, 59 schools) read against a Cochrane review of the whole school-based prevention literature.
cards.result: ASSIST: smoking odds ratios 0.75 immediately, 0.77 (significant) at one year, 0.85 (not significant) at two years. School programmes overall: 0.88 (0.82–0.96) at longest follow-up, driven by social-competence content. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), Tier C.
cards.watchOut: An odds ratio of 0.77 is a relative effect on a low absolute uptake rate, so the number of smokers prevented per school is small; the shelf claims delay/reduction of uptake, not prevention of addiction, and not any effect in the vaping era, which neither record studies.

shelves.title: Tobacco taxes: over 100 studies show higher prices cut use, especially in the young and the poor — but the evidence is population studies, not trials, and no single pooled number exists
shelves.question: Do tobacco tax and price increases reduce smoking prevalence and cigarette consumption at population level?
shelves.mesh: Commerce/statistics & numerical data · Health Promotion/economics · Humans · Smoking/economics · Smoking Cessation/economics/methods · Smoking Prevention · Taxes/statistics & numerical data · Tobacco Industry/economics
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — the direction is among the most consistent findings in tobacco control, but the evidence form is weak by this library's standards: no randomised trials exist or could exist, and the reviews report consistency rather than a pooled effect size. Chaloupka and colleagues, assessing well over 100 studies including a growing number from low- and middle-income countries, conclude that significant tax increases that raise prices encourage current users to stop, prevent potential users from starting, and reduce consumption among those who continue, with the greatest impact on the young and the poor. The Community Guide economic review found that a conservative 20% price increase generates substantial healthcare cost savings, with seven of eight modelling studies estimating healthcare savings and three estimating productivity gains. Neither record gives a single pooled percentage for prevalence or consumption that this shelf can print as a verified figure. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit): higher tobacco prices almost certainly reduce smoking at population level; the size of the reduction per tax rise varies by country and cannot be stated as one number from these records — Tier C, as a policy claim resting on observational evidence.

cards.headline: Chaloupka 2012: well over 100 studies show taxes reduce use, initiation and consumption — greatest impact on the young and the poor
cards.summary: Chaloupka 2012: well over 100 studies show taxes reduce use, initiation and consumption — greatest impact on the young and the poor
cards.people: The published literature on tobacco taxation across high-, low- and middle-income countries — well over 100 studies of tax and price effects on tobacco use and related outcomes, plus the tax-administration literature underlying WHO best practices. No single study population; population-level observational and econometric evidence.
cards.result: The review concludes that tobacco excise taxes are a powerful tool for reducing tobacco use while providing government revenue: significant increases in taxes that raise product prices encourage current users to stop using, prevent potential users from taking up tobacco use, and reduce consumption among those who continue to use, with the greatest impact on the young and the poor. It also concludes that the common oppositional claims of harmful economic effects are false or overstated.
cards.watchOut: A narrative review by leading advocates of the policy, not a systematic review with a pooled estimate: it reports the direction and consistency of the literature without a meta-analytic number, and publication bias toward finding price effects cannot be excluded from this record. Effect sizes vary substantially by setting, tax structure and illicit-trade environment.
cards.source: Chaloupka FJ et al. Tobacco taxes as a tobacco control strategy. Tobacco control. 2012. PMID: 22345242. cards.headline: Contreary 2015 (Community Guide): eight modelling studies of tax-driven price rises — seven found healthcare cost savings; a 20% price increase was the conservative test case
cards.summary: Contreary 2015 (Community Guide): eight modelling studies of tax-driven price rises — seven found healthcare cost savings; a 20% price increase was the conservative test case
cards.people: Eight modelling studies (published 2000–July 2012) evaluating national, state and local policies that raise the price of any tobacco product through taxation in high-income countries, screened and abstracted by Community Guide economic-review methods; analyses conducted in 2012.
cards.result: Of the eight included modelling studies, seven provided estimates of the impact on healthcare costs and three provided estimates of the value of productivity gains; only one study provided an estimate of intervention costs. Judged on per-capita annual cost savings from a conservative 20% price increase, the body of evidence indicated that raising the unit price of tobacco products through taxes generates substantial healthcare cost savings and can generate additional gains from improved workplace productivity.
cards.watchOut: Modelling studies, not observations of what actually happened after specific tax rises — their savings are projections built on assumed price elasticities, and this review addresses economics, not the prevalence effect itself. Only high-income countries are covered.
cards.source: Contreary KA et al. Economic Impact of Tobacco Price Increases Through Taxation: A Community Guide Systematic Review. American journal of preventive medicine. 2015. PMID: 26188686. cards.headline: Synthesis: direction near-certain, magnitude unpooled — a policy shelf that must be honest about its evidence form
cards.summary: Synthesis: direction near-certain, magnitude unpooled — a policy shelf that must be honest about its evidence form
cards.people: Two reviews: a narrative assessment of well over 100 tax-and-price studies worldwide, and a Community Guide systematic economic review of eight modelling studies in high-income countries.
cards.result: Both reviews agree that raising tobacco prices through taxation reduces tobacco use and generates healthcare cost savings; neither provides a pooled percentage reduction in prevalence or consumption that can be printed as a single verified figure. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit), Tier C.
cards.watchOut: MAYBE here grades the evidence form (observational, ecological, unpooled), not genuine doubt about direction — but under this library's rules observational population evidence cannot carry a stronger stamp, and any specific elasticity ('a 10% price rise cuts consumption by X%') would need a record that states it, which these two do not.
cards.source: Synthesis of Chaloupka FJ et al. Tobacco Control. 2012 (PMID: 22345242); Contreary KA et al. American Journal of Preventive Medicine. 2015 (PMID: 26188686).

shelves.title: Daily aspirin and colorectal cancer 20 years on: colon cancer incidence hazard ratio 0.76 and mortality 0.65 — benefit concentrated in the proximal colon and in those treated 5+ years
shelves.question: In average-risk adults, does long-term daily aspirin reduce colorectal cancer incidence and mortality 10–20 years later?
shelves.mesh: Aspirin/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Cardiovascular Diseases/prevention & control · Colonic Neoplasms/prevention & control · Colorectal Neoplasms/epidemiology/mortality/prevention & control · Follow-Up Studies · Humans · Incidence · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Thrombosis/prevention & control
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a delayed benefit shown in pooled individual-patient follow-up of randomised trials, with the anatomy and duration caveats on the face. Across four trials of aspirin versus control (14,033 patients, median follow-up 18.3 years), 391 patients (2.8%) developed colorectal cancer; allocation to aspirin reduced the 20-year risk of colon cancer (incidence hazard ratio 0.76, 95% CI 0.60–0.96; mortality 0.65, 0.48–0.88) but not rectal cancer (0.90, 0.63–1.30; mortality 0.80, 0.50–1.28). The benefit was concentrated in the proximal colon (incidence 0.45, 0.28–0.74) and grew with at least five years of scheduled treatment (proximal colon incidence 0.35, 0.20–0.63). A second pooled analysis of 51 trials found cancer deaths reduced overall (odds ratio 0.85, 0.76–0.96), particularly from five years onwards (0.63, 0.49–0.82). These are post-trial observational follow-ups of trials designed for vascular endpoints, in mostly male, vascular-risk populations — not average-risk screening populations randomised for cancer. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): years of daily aspirin probably reduce colon cancer incidence and death a decade or two later; the bleeding price of those years is a separate shelf's question and is not netted off here.

cards.headline: Rothwell 2010: 20-year colon cancer incidence hazard ratio 0.76 and mortality 0.65 on aspirin — rectal cancer unmoved (0.90 and 0.80), proximal colon 0.45
cards.summary: Rothwell 2010: 20-year colon cancer incidence hazard ratio 0.76 and mortality 0.65 on aspirin — rectal cancer unmoved (0.90 and 0.80), proximal colon 0.45
cards.type: Pooled individual-patient analysis of randomised trials with long-term follow-up (Rothwell 2010)
cards.people: Four randomised trials of aspirin versus control in primary and secondary prevention of vascular events (mean scheduled treatment 6.0 years) plus one trial of different aspirin doses; 14,033 patients in the aspirin-versus-control trials followed for a median of 18.3 years; doses 75–300 mg daily in the low-dose analyses, with higher doses in some trials.
cards.result: 391 (2.8%) of 14,033 patients had colorectal cancer during follow-up. Allocation to aspirin reduced the 20-year risk of colon cancer (incidence hazard ratio [HR] 0.76, 95% CI 0.60–0.96, p=0.02; mortality HR 0.65, 0.48–0.88, p=0.005) but not rectal cancer (incidence 0.90, 0.63–1.30, p=0.58; mortality 0.80, 0.50–1.28, p=0.35). Where subsite data were available, aspirin reduced proximal colon cancer (incidence 0.45, 0.28–0.74; mortality 0.34, 0.18–0.66) but not distal colon cancer (1.10, 0.73–1.64; 1.21, 0.66–2.24). With five or more years of scheduled treatment, proximal colon cancer risk fell by about 70% (incidence 0.35, 0.20–0.63; mortality 0.24, 0.11–0.52).
cards.watchOut: The trials randomised for vascular prevention, not cancer; cancer outcomes over 20 years are post-trial follow-up, and participants were predominantly men at vascular risk — 'average-risk adults' in the question is an extrapolation. Aspirin's bleeding harms over the treatment years are not part of this record, so the shelf shows benefit only, with the harm living on the aspirin-harm shelves. Tier C is set: a cancer-mortality benefit claim from pooled post-trial follow-up.
cards.source: Rothwell PM et al. Long-term effect of aspirin on colorectal cancer incidence and mortality: 20-year follow-up of five randomised trials. Lancet (London, England). 2010. PMID: 20970847. cards.headline: Rothwell 2012 (51 trials): cancer deaths odds ratio 0.85 overall and 0.63 from five years on; cancer incidence reduced from three years (0.76) in primary-prevention trials
cards.summary: Rothwell 2012 (51 trials): cancer deaths odds ratio 0.85 overall and 0.63 from five years on; cancer incidence reduced from three years (0.76) in primary-prevention trials
cards.type: Pooled individual-patient analysis of randomised trials (Rothwell 2012)
cards.people: 51 randomised trials of daily aspirin versus no aspirin for prevention of vascular events (77,549 participants for mortality analyses; 34 trials and 69,224 participants for cancer deaths); six trials of daily low-dose aspirin in primary prevention (35,535 participants) analysed for the time course of cancer incidence, vascular events and bleeds.
cards.result: Allocation to aspirin reduced cancer deaths (562 vs 664 deaths; odds ratio [OR] 0.85, 95% CI 0.76–0.96, p=0.008), particularly from 5 years onwards (92 vs 145; OR 0.63, 0.49–0.82, p=0.0005), resulting in fewer non-vascular deaths overall (1021 vs 1173; OR 0.88, 0.78–0.96, p=0.003). In the primary-prevention trials, aspirin reduced cancer incidence from 3 years onwards (324 vs 421 cases; OR 0.76, 0.66–0.88, p=0.0003), in women (0.75, 0.59–0.94) and men (0.77, 0.63–0.93) alike.
cards.watchOut: This analysis covers all cancers, not colorectal cancer specifically — it corroborates the timing (benefit emerging after 3–5 years) rather than the colorectal estimate itself. It also found the early reduction in major vascular events was initially offset by an increased risk of major extracranial bleeds, the trade-off this shelf does not net off.
cards.source: Rothwell PM et al. cards.summary: Synthesis: a real, delayed, site-specific benefit — colon yes, rectum no; five-plus years of treatment; bleeding not counted here

shelves.title: Statins at 75 and over without cardiovascular disease: trial meta-analysis shows vascular events still fall per mmol/L of LDL lowering, but the over-75 primary-prevention evidence is thin and a 46,864-person cohort found nothing without diabetes
shelves.question: In adults aged 75 and over without cardiovascular disease, does statin therapy reduce major cardiovascular events versus placebo or usual care?
shelves.mesh: Age Factors · Aged · Humans · Hydroxymethylglutaryl-CoA Reductase Inhibitors/therapeutic use · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the trial evidence leans positive but thins exactly where the question asks. The Cholesterol Treatment Trialists' individual-patient meta-analysis of 28 trials (186,854 participants, 14,483 of them older than 75) found statin therapy or a more intensive regimen produced a 21% relative reduction in major vascular events per 1.0 mmol/L (≈39 mg/dL) reduction in LDL cholesterol overall (rate ratio 0.79, 95% CI 0.77–0.81), with significant reductions in all age groups — but the proportional reduction appeared smaller among older people without pre-existing vascular disease (trend p=0.05), and the authors state plainly that there is less direct evidence of benefit among patients older than 75 without occlusive vascular disease. A meta-analysis restricted to primary prevention over 75 (35 trials) found no significant mortality difference on frequentist analysis (p=0.16), though a Bayesian analysis favoured statins (p=0.03). And in a retrospective cohort of 46,864 people aged 75 or over without atherosclerotic disease, statin use in those without diabetes was associated with hazard ratios of 0.94 (0.86–1.04) for cardiovascular events and 0.98 (0.91–1.05) for mortality at ages 75–84 — no measurable benefit. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): statins probably still reduce vascular events after 75 in proportion to LDL lowering, but a mortality benefit in primary prevention at this age is unproven and the direct trial base is small — Tier C.

cards.headline: CTT 2019 (28 trials, 186,854 participants): major vascular events rate ratio 0.79 per 1 mmol/L (≈39 mg/dL) LDL reduction — but 'less direct evidence' over 75 without vascular disease
cards.summary: CTT 2019 (28 trials, 186,854 participants): major vascular events rate ratio 0.79 per 1 mmol/L (≈39 mg/dL) LDL reduction — but 'less direct evidence' over 75 without vascular disease
cards.type: Individual-patient-data meta-analysis of randomised trials (Cholesterol Treatment Trialists' Collaboration 2019)
cards.people: 28 randomised trials of statin therapy versus control or more versus less intensive therapy (186,854 participants; 14,483 [8%] older than 75 at randomisation); median follow-up 4.9 years; effects expressed per 1.0 mmol/L (≈39 mg/dL) reduction in LDL cholesterol across six age groups.
cards.result: Statin therapy or a more intensive regimen produced a 21% relative reduction in major vascular events per 1.0 mmol/L (≈39 mg/dL) LDL reduction (rate ratio 0.79, 95% CI 0.77–0.81), a 24% relative reduction in major coronary events (0.76, 0.73–0.79) and a 25% relative reduction in coronary revascularisation (0.75, 0.73–0.78), with significant reductions in major vascular events in all age groups. However, the proportional reduction in major vascular events appeared smaller among older than younger individuals not known to have vascular disease (ptrend=0.05), and statins had no effect at any age on non-vascular mortality or cancer. The authors conclude there is less direct evidence of benefit among patients older than 75 years who do not already have evidence of occlusive vascular disease.
cards.watchOut: Most over-75 participants in these trials had vascular disease already — the primary-prevention subgroup the question asks about is a minority of the 14,483, which is why the authors hedge. Effects are expressed per mmol/L of LDL lowering rather than as absolute event rates for a healthy 78-year-old, so the absolute gain at low baseline risk is small even if the relative effect holds.

cards.headline: Kostis 2020 (35 trials, primary prevention over 75): frequentist mortality analysis not significant (p=0.16); Bayesian analysis favoured statins (p=0.03)
cards.summary: Kostis 2020 (35 trials, primary prevention over 75): frequentist mortality analysis not significant (p=0.16); Bayesian analysis favoured statins (p=0.03)
cards.people: 35 randomised controlled trials in patients older than 75 years in which statin therapy for primary prevention was compared with placebo or usual care; all-cause death as the outcome; both frequentist and Bayesian analyses performed.
cards.result: The frequentist analysis indicated no significant difference in mortality between patients on statins and controls on placebo or usual care (p=0.16). The Bayesian analysis, by contrast, found lower mortality with statin treatment in patients over 75 (p=0.03), which the authors describe as a definite, statistically significant and clinically relevant benefit of statin treatment for primary prevention in this age group.
cards.watchOut: The conclusion flips with the statistical framework — a warning sign that the underlying data are thin and the prior is doing real work in the Bayesian analysis. The record's abstract reports no pooled mortality rates or effect size, so the size of any mortality benefit cannot be stated from this record; the shelf therefore claims events, not mortality.

cards.headline: Ramos 2018 (46,864 people ≥75 without disease): no benefit without diabetes — cardiovascular hazard ratio 0.94 (0.86–1.04) and mortality 0.98 (0.91–1.05) at 75–84
cards.summary: Ramos 2018 (46,864 people ≥75 without disease): no benefit without diabetes — cardiovascular hazard ratio 0.94 (0.86–1.04) and mortality 0.98 (0.91–1.05) at 75–84
cards.people: 46,864 people aged 75 years or more without clinically recognised atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease in the Catalan primary-care database (SIDIAP), Spain, 2006–2015 (mean age 77 years, 63% women, median follow-up 5.6 years); new statin users versus non-users compared with propensity-score-adjusted Cox models, stratified by diabetes and by age 75–84 versus 85 and over.
cards.result: In participants without diabetes, hazard ratios for statin use at ages 75–84 were 0.94 (95% CI 0.86–1.04) for atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease and 0.98 (0.91–1.05) for all-cause mortality, and at 85 and over 0.93 (0.82–1.06) and 0.97 (0.90–1.05) — no significant benefit at either age. In participants with diabetes, by contrast, hazard ratios at 75–84 were 0.76 (0.65–0.89) for cardiovascular disease and 0.84 (0.75–0.94) for mortality, attenuating at 85 and over (0.82, 0.53–1.26; and 1.05, 0.86–1.28).
cards.watchOut: Observational: despite propensity adjustment, people prescribed statins at 80 differ from those not prescribed in ways databases capture imperfectly, and these null ratios sit inside the 0.5–2.0 band that cannot carry a shelf on their own — this card is a contrast to the trial evidence, not the shelf's basis. It is, however, the only record here drawn from exactly the population the question asks about.

cards.headline: Synthesis: relative benefit probably persists with age; direct proof in healthy over-75s is the gap every record acknowledges
cards.summary: Synthesis: relative benefit probably persists with age; direct proof in healthy over-75s is the gap every record acknowledges
cards.people: An individual-patient meta-analysis of 28 statin trials (14,483 participants over 75), a 35-trial meta-analysis restricted to primary prevention over 75, and a 46,864-person primary-care cohort of people 75 and over without cardiovascular disease.
cards.result: Major vascular events: 21% relative reduction per 1.0 mmol/L (≈39 mg/dL) LDL reduction overall (rate ratio 0.79), significant in all age groups but attenuated in older primary-prevention participants. Mortality in primary prevention over 75: not significant by frequentist analysis (p=0.16), positive by Bayesian analysis (p=0.03). Real-world cohort without diabetes: hazard ratios 0.94 for events and 0.98 for mortality at 75–84. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), Tier C.
cards.watchOut: No completed trial has randomised healthy people over 75 to statin versus placebo for primary prevention at scale — the dedicated trials were still running when these records were published. Absolute benefit at low baseline risk is small, and this shelf makes no claim about muscle symptoms, diabetes incidence or drug burden, which weigh differently at 80 than at 60.

shelves.title: Depression screening in primary care, with treatment systems attached: pooled odds ratio 0.60 for still being depressed at 6–12 months — screening alone, and suicide-risk screening, have no such evidence
shelves.question: In adults in primary care, does screening for depression — with systems for follow-up care — improve depression outcomes versus usual care?
shelves.mesh: Female · Humans · Male · Pregnancy · Antidepressive Agents/therapeutic use · Depression/diagnosis/therapy · Mass Screening/adverse effects/methods · Meta-Analysis as Topic · Psychotherapy · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Risk Assessment · Sensitivity and Specificity · Suicide · Suicide, Attempted/prevention & control · United States
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for depression screening programmes, not for screening as a bare test. The USPSTF evidence report (105 studies) found that depression screening interventions — many of which included additional components beyond screening, such as treatment protocols and follow-up systems — were associated with a lower prevalence of depression or clinically important depressive symptoms after 6 to 12 months (pooled odds ratio 0.60, 95% CI 0.50–0.73; 8 randomised trials, 10,244 participants). The instruments themselves are accurate enough to build on: the PHQ-9 at a cutoff of 10 or more had pooled sensitivity 0.85 and specificity 0.85 (47 studies, 11,234 participants), and a large body of evidence supports psychological and pharmacological treatment once depression is found. The boundary is suicide risk: the same report found the suicide-prevention studies generally did not demonstrate improvement over usual care, and one trial of suicide-risk screening found no difference in suicidal ideation after two weeks. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): screening for depression improves outcomes when it is a programme wired to treatment and follow-up; this record does not show that a questionnaire alone, or screening for suicide risk, does — Tier C, because the active ingredient cannot be separated from the bundle.

cards.headline: O'Connor 2023 (USPSTF evidence report): screening interventions pooled odds ratio 0.60 (0.50–0.73) for depression at 6–12 months; PHQ-9 sensitivity and specificity both 0.85
cards.summary: O'Connor 2023 (USPSTF evidence report): screening interventions pooled odds ratio 0.60 (0.50–0.73) for depression at 6–12 months; PHQ-9 sensitivity and specificity both 0.85
cards.type: Systematic evidence review for the USPSTF (O'Connor 2023)
cards.people: 105 studies of screening and treatment for depression and suicide risk in primary-care patients: 32 original studies (385,607 participants) and 73 systematic reviews covering about 2,138 studies and 9.8 million participants; literature through September 7, 2022. Screening trials were randomised comparisons of screening interventions, many including components beyond screening itself.
cards.result: Depression screening interventions were associated with a lower prevalence of depression or clinically important depressive symptomatology after 6 to 12 months (pooled odds ratio, 0.60 [95% CI, 0.50-0.73]; reported in 8 randomized clinical trials [n=10,244]; I2=0%). For the 9-item Patient Health Questionnaire at a cutoff of 10 or greater, pooled sensitivity was 0.85 (95% CI, 0.79-0.89) and specificity 0.85 (0.82-0.88) (47 studies; n=11,234). A large body of evidence supported benefits of psychological and pharmacologic treatment of depression. For suicide risk (27 studies; n=24,826), the included prevention studies generally did not demonstrate an improvement over usual care, and one randomised trial (n=443) of a suicide-risk screening intervention found no difference in suicidal ideation after 2 weeks.
cards.watchOut: The pooled 0.60 belongs to screening programmes — screening plus treatment pathways — not to the act of screening; the question's own wording ('with systems for follow-up care') is what makes the claim true. A harm signal sits inside the treatment evidence the pathway delivers: antidepressants carried a small absolute increase in suicide attempts in the FDA-approval trial pool (0.7% vs 0.3% on placebo; odds ratio 1.53, 1.09–2.15; median follow-up 8 weeks). Tier C is set because the benefit claim rests on bundled programmes synthesised in one evidence report.
cards.source: O'Connor EA et al. Depression and Suicide Risk Screening: Updated Evidence Report and Systematic Review for the US Preventive Services Task Force. JAMA. 2023. PMID: 37338873. shelves.title: Lipid screening in childhood: no trial has ever tested screening itself; FH is found in 0.2–0.4% and statins lower LDL by 81–82 mg/dL in FH trials — benefit is an inference chain, not a demonstration
shelves.question: In children and adolescents, does universal lipid screening identify familial hypercholesterolaemia and other lipid disorders better than targeted screening, and does early treatment help?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Child · Humans · Cholesterol · Dyslipidemias/diagnosis/drug therapy/etiology · Hydroxymethylglutaryl-CoA Reductase Inhibitors/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Lipids · Mass Screening · Hypercholesterolemia/complications
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — the USPSTF evidence report is unusually candid: no randomised trial directly addressed the effectiveness or harms of lipid screening in children and adolescents, and no direct evidence on the benefits or harms of screening was identified at all. What exists is a chain. Screening finds familial hypercholesterolaemia (FH) at a prevalence of 0.2% to 0.4% (1 in 250 to 1 in 500) in three US studies totalling 395,465 children, and elevated total cholesterol (≥200 mg/dL) in 7.1% to 9.4%. In children with FH, ten randomised trials (1,230 participants) showed statins produced an 81- to 82-mg/dL greater reduction in total and LDL cholesterol than placebo, and observational studies suggest starting statins in childhood or adolescence reduces long-term cardiovascular risk. For the much commoner multifactorial dyslipidaemia, no evidence was found that treatment is effective, and two behavioural-counselling trials (934 participants) produced only 3- to 6-mg/dL greater cholesterol reductions that did not persist. Whether universal screening beats targeted screening was not answered by any study in the report. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit): screening certainly identifies FH and treatment certainly lowers its cholesterol; that screening children improves adult outcomes is inferred, never tested — Tier C.

cards.headline: Guirguis-Blake 2023 (USPSTF evidence report): zero trials of screening itself; FH prevalence 0.2–0.4%; statin LDL-C reduction 81–82 mg/dL in 10 FH trials (n=1,230)
cards.summary: Guirguis-Blake 2023 (USPSTF evidence report): zero trials of screening itself; FH prevalence 0.2–0.4%; statin LDL-C reduction 81–82 mg/dL in 10 FH trials (n=1,230)
cards.type: Systematic evidence review for the USPSTF (Guirguis-Blake 2023)
cards.people: Evidence on screening and treatment of paediatric dyslipidaemia (familial hypercholesterolaemia and multifactorial dyslipidaemia) from MEDLINE and CENTRAL through May 16, 2022, with surveillance through March 24, 2023: randomised trials of screening and of lipid-lowering treatment, and large US cohort studies of diagnostic yield (491,516 participants in the included screening-yield and treatment evidence overall).
cards.result: No randomised trials directly addressed screening effectiveness and harms, and no direct evidence on the benefits or harms of paediatric lipid screening was identified. Three US studies (n=395,465) reported phenotypically defined FH prevalence of 0.2% to 0.4% (1:250 to 1:500); prevalence of elevated total cholesterol (≥200 mg/dL) was 7.1% to 9.4% and of any lipid abnormality 19.2%. Ten randomised trials in children and adolescents with FH (n=1,230) demonstrated that statins were associated with an 81- to 82-mg/dL greater mean reduction in total cholesterol and LDL-C compared with placebo at up to 2 years, with harms similar between groups. Two multifactorial-dyslipidaemia behavioural-counselling trials (n=934) showed 3- to 6-mg/dL greater reductions in total cholesterol versus control that did not persist at longest follow-up, and no evidence was found that treatment is effective for multifactorial dyslipidaemia.
cards.watchOut: Every link after detection is a surrogate or observational: LDL lowering in FH trials lasts at most 2 years in this record, and the claim that childhood treatment prevents adult events rests on observational follow-up, not randomised outcomes. The universal-versus-targeted comparison in the question was not studied at all — the report cannot say universal screening identifies more FH than family-history-based targeting. Tier C is set: an inference chain, honestly labelled.

cards.headline: Synthesis: detection proven, drug effect proven, screening benefit unproven — the honest stamp is MAYBE
cards.summary: Synthesis: detection proven, drug effect proven, screening benefit unproven — the honest stamp is MAYBE
cards.people: One USPSTF evidence report covering screening yield in 395,465 US children, ten FH statin trials (1,230 children) and two behavioural trials (934 children).
cards.result: Screening trials: none. FH found: 0.2–0.4% of screened children. Statin effect in FH: 81–82 mg/dL greater LDL-C and total cholesterol reduction versus placebo. Behavioural treatment of common dyslipidaemia: 3–6 mg/dL, not sustained. Long-term outcome benefit: observational suggestion only. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit), Tier C.
cards.watchOut: MAYBE (weak evidence) here means the outcome evidence is indirect, not that screening fails: for a child with FH, decades of untreated LDL exposure is the harm screening aims to interrupt, and cascade testing of relatives may be where much of the value sits — none of which this record quantifies.
cards.source: Synthesis of Guirguis-Blake JM et al. JAMA. 2023 (PMID: 37462700).

shelves.title: Screening asymptomatic adults for sleep apnoea: no study has ever compared screening with no screening; treatment improves sleepiness scores but no trial shows fewer deaths, cardiovascular events or crashes
shelves.question: In asymptomatic adults, does screening for obstructive sleep apnoea improve health outcomes versus no screening?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Humans · Advisory Committees · Continuous Positive Airway Pressure · Disorders of Excessive Somnolence/etiology · Quality of Life · Sleep Apnea, Obstructive/complications/diagnosis/therapy · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Mass Screening
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — the direct evidence does not exist. The USPSTF evidence report (86 studies, 11,051 participants) states plainly that no study directly compared screening with no screening. The chain that does exist: a two-step strategy (Multivariable Apnea Prediction score followed by home sleep testing) detected severe OSA syndrome with an area under the curve of 0.80 (95% CI 0.78–0.82) and 0.83 (0.77–0.90) in two studies (702 participants), while five studies of other screening tools were heterogeneous and inconsistent. Treatment of found OSA improves symptoms: positive airway pressure versus inactive control improved Epworth Sleepiness Scale scores by a pooled 2.33 points (95% CI −2.75 to −1.90; 47 trials, 7,024 participants) and sleep-related quality of life (standardised mean difference 0.30, 0.19–0.42), and lowered blood pressure by a small 2–3 mm Hg in three systematic reviews. But no included trial found a significant benefit of treatment on mortality, cardiovascular events or motor vehicle crashes. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit): screening can find severe OSA and treatment relieves sleepiness; that screening asymptomatic adults improves health outcomes is unproven — Tier C.

cards.headline: Feltner 2022 (USPSTF evidence report): 86 studies and not one compared screening with no screening; two-step accuracy AUC 0.80–0.83 for severe OSA syndrome
cards.summary: Feltner 2022 (USPSTF evidence report): 86 studies and not one compared screening with no screening; two-step accuracy AUC 0.80–0.83 for severe OSA syndrome
cards.type: Systematic evidence review for the USPSTF (Feltner 2022)
cards.people: 86 studies (11,051 participants) of screening-test accuracy, randomised trials of screening or of OSA treatment reporting health outcomes or harms, and systematic reviews of treatment effects on blood pressure and apnoea–hypopnoea index; literature through August 23, 2021, with surveillance through September 23, 2022. Population: asymptomatic adults or adults with unrecognised OSA symptoms.
cards.result: No study directly compared screening with no screening. The Multivariable Apnea Prediction score followed by unattended home sleep testing detected severe OSA syndrome (AHI ≥30 plus Epworth Sleepiness Scale >10) with an area under the curve of 0.80 (95% CI, 0.78 to 0.82) and 0.83 (0.77 to 0.90) in two studies (n=702); five studies of other screening tools were heterogeneous and inconsistent. Versus inactive control, positive airway pressure improved ESS score (pooled mean difference −2.33 [−2.75 to −1.90]; 47 trials; n=7,024), sleep-related quality of life (standardised mean difference 0.30 [0.19 to 0.42]; 17 trials; n=3,083) and SF-36 mental (2.20 [0.95 to 3.44]) and physical (1.53 [0.29 to 2.77]) component scores. No included trial found significant benefit of treatment on mortality, cardiovascular events, or motor vehicle crashes; positive airway pressure lowered blood pressure by a relatively small 2–3 mm Hg in three systematic reviews.
cards.watchOut: The treatment trials enrolled people with diagnosed, mostly symptomatic OSA — applying their symptom gains to screen-detected asymptomatic people assumes the found cases resemble trial patients, which is exactly what a screening trial would test and none has. Accuracy figures are for severe OSA syndrome only; milder screen-detected disease dominates real screening yields and has the weakest treatment rationale. Tier C is set: the shelf rests on a single evidence report and an indirect chain.
cards.source: Feltner C et al. Screening for Obstructive Sleep Apnea in Adults: Updated Evidence Report and Systematic Review for the US Preventive Services Task Force. JAMA. 2022. PMID: 36378203.
