shelves.title: Intermittent preventive malaria treatment in infancy (sulfadoxine–pyrimethamine): clinical malaria down 30.3% and anaemia down 21.3% across six pooled trials — deaths unchanged (56 versus 53)
shelves.question: In infants in malaria-endemic Africa, does perennial malaria chemoprevention (intermittent preventive treatment in infancy) with sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine reduce clinical malaria and anaemia versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Africa/epidemiology · Anemia/epidemiology · Antimalarials/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Double-Blind Method · Drug Administration Schedule · Drug Combinations · Follow-Up Studies · Humans · Immunization Schedule · Incidence · Infant · Infant Mortality · Malaria, Falciparum/epidemiology/prevention & control · Patient Admission/statistics & numerical data · Pyrimethamine/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Regression Analysis · Research Design · Risk Factors · Safety · Sulfadoxine/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a pooled analysis of six double-blind, placebo-controlled trials (7,930 infants) of intermittent preventive treatment in infancy (IPTi) with sulfadoxine–pyrimethamine, given at routine Expanded Program on Immunization vaccination visits. IPTi had a protective efficacy of 30.3% (95% CI 19.8–39.4) against clinical malaria, 21.3% (8.2–32.5) against anaemia, 38.1% (12.5–56.2) against hospital admissions associated with malaria parasitaemia, and 22.9% (10.0–34.0) against all-cause hospital admissions, up to 12 months of age. Mortality did not fall: 56 deaths in the IPTi group versus 53 in the placebo group (rate ratio 1.05, 0.72–1.54). Safety was reassuring in this record — four of 676 non-fatal admissions in the IPTi group were judged possibly treatment-related, versus five of 860 on placebo. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): IPTi with sulfadoxine–pyrimethamine prevents about a third of clinical malaria episodes and a fifth of anaemia in the first year of life in endemic Africa; it has not been shown to save lives, and sulfadoxine–pyrimethamine resistance has grown since these trials.

cards.headline: Aponte 2009 (pooled IPTi analysis): clinical malaria efficacy 30.3%, anaemia 21.3%, malaria admissions 38.1% — mortality rate ratio 1.05 (0.72–1.54)
cards.summary: Aponte 2009 (pooled IPTi analysis): clinical malaria efficacy 30.3%, anaemia 21.3%, malaria admissions 38.1% — mortality rate ratio 1.05 (0.72–1.54)
cards.type: Pooled analysis of six randomised placebo-controlled trials (Aponte 2009)
cards.people: Six double-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled trials (one each in Tanzania, Mozambique and Gabon, three in Ghana) of IPTi with sulfadoxine–pyrimethamine given at routine WHO Expanded Program on Immunization vaccination visits; 7,930 infants (IPTi n=3,958; placebo n=3,972) analysed by modified intention to treat for outcomes up to 12 months of age, using standardised outcome definitions.
cards.result: IPTi had a protective efficacy of 30.3% (95% CI 19.8-39.4, p<0.0001) against clinical malaria, 21.3% (8.2-32.5, p=0.002) against the risk of anaemia (packed-cell volume <25% or haemoglobin <80 g/L), 38.1% (12.5-56.2, p=0.007) against hospital admissions associated with malaria parasitaemia, and 22.9% (10.0-34.0, p=0.001) against all-cause hospital admissions. There were 56 deaths in the IPTi group compared with 53 in the placebo group (rate ratio 1.05, 95% CI 0.72-1.54, p=0.79). Four of 676 non-fatal hospital admissions in the IPTi group were deemed related to study treatment compared with five of 860 in the placebo group, and none of three serious dermatological adverse events in the IPTi group was judged treatment-related, versus one of 13 in the placebo group.
cards.watchOut: The trials predate the spread of high-grade sulfadoxine–pyrimethamine resistance in much of Africa, so the 30.3% figure describes what the drug could do then, in those sites — current efficacy with the same drug may be lower, and newer chemoprevention agents are outside this record. The mortality neutrality is a genuine null on 109 deaths, not a power footnote to be waved away.
cards.source: Aponte JJ et al. Efficacy and safety of intermittent preventive treatment with sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine for malaria in African infants: a pooled analysis of six randomised, placebo-controlled trials. Lancet (London, England). 2009. PMID: 19765816. cards.headline: Synthesis: a third fewer malaria episodes and a fifth less anaemia in year one — morbidity prevented, mortality untouched
cards.summary: Synthesis: a third fewer malaria episodes and a fifth less anaemia in year one — morbidity prevented, mortality untouched
cards.people: Six randomised placebo-controlled trials pooled at individual level: 7,930 African infants receiving sulfadoxine–pyrimethamine or placebo alongside routine immunisation visits, followed to 12 months.
cards.result: Clinical malaria: protective efficacy 30.3%. Anaemia: 21.3%. Malaria-associated admissions: 38.1%. All-cause admissions: 22.9%. Deaths: 56 versus 53 (rate ratio 1.05). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).
cards.watchOut: Tier C is not set: the shelf rests on a pooled analysis of six concordant placebo-controlled trials and claims morbidity, not mortality. The open questions are drug resistance and whether the effect persists where transmission has fallen — neither is answerable from this record, and both are stated rather than smoothed over.

shelves.title: Post-discharge malaria chemoprevention after severe anaemia: readmission or death hazard ratio 0.65 in the Kenyan–Ugandan trial, mortality rate ratio 0.23 during the intervention period in the three-trial pooled analysis — protection ends when the drug stops
shelves.question: In children discharged after treatment for severe malarial anaemia, does post-discharge malaria chemoprevention reduce readmission and death versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Aftercare · Anemia/drug therapy · Antimalarials/therapeutic use · Artemisinins/therapeutic use · Child, Preschool · Drug Combinations · Endemic Diseases · Female · Humans · Infant · Kenya/epidemiology · Malaria/epidemiology/prevention & control · Male · Patient Readmission/statistics & numerical data · Quinolines/therapeutic use · Uganda/epidemiology · Piperazines
shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit) — during the months the drug is given. In a multicentre placebo-controlled trial in Kenya and Uganda, 1,049 children under five discharged after severe anaemia received three monthly 3-day courses of dihydroartemisinin–piperaquine or placebo: from week 3 to week 26 there were 184 readmission-or-death events in the chemoprevention group versus 316 on placebo (hazard ratio 0.65, 95% CI 0.54–0.78), concentrated in the intervention period (weeks 3–14: hazard ratio 0.30, 0.22–0.42) and absent after it (weeks 15–26: 1.13, 0.87–1.47). The individual-patient meta-analysis of all three post-discharge trials (3,663 children) found the same shape: during the intervention period, mortality was reduced by 77% in relative terms (rate ratio 0.23, 0.08–0.70) and all-cause readmissions by 55% in relative terms (hazard ratio 0.45, 0.36–0.56), with protection not sustained after the drugs' pharmacological effect waned. No serious adverse events were attributed to dihydroartemisinin–piperaquine in the trial. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): post-discharge chemoprevention strongly protects recently discharged children with severe anaemia while it is being taken — and only while it is being taken, which is a delivery problem, not a reason to withhold it. Tier C is set because the pooled claim includes a mortality reduction.

cards.headline: Kwambai 2020 (Kenya/Uganda): 184 versus 316 readmission-or-death events on dihydroartemisinin–piperaquine versus placebo (HR 0.65); HR 0.30 while on drug, 1.13 after
cards.summary: Kwambai 2020 (Kenya/Uganda): 184 versus 316 readmission-or-death events on dihydroartemisinin–piperaquine versus placebo (HR 0.65); HR 0.30 while on drug, 1.13 after
cards.people: 1,049 children younger than 5 years admitted with severe anaemia to nine hospitals in Kenya and Uganda, all given standard in-hospital care and a 3-day course of artemether–lumefantrine at discharge, then randomised two weeks after discharge (524 chemoprevention, 525 placebo) to 3-day courses of dihydroartemisinin–piperaquine or placebo at 2, 6 and 10 weeks; followed to 26 weeks. Primary outcome: one or more hospital readmissions for any reason or death from randomisation to 6 months.
cards.result: From week 3 through week 26, 184 events of readmission or death occurred in the chemoprevention group versus 316 in the placebo group (hazard ratio, 0.65; 95% CI, 0.54 to 0.78; P<0.001). The lower incidence was restricted to the intervention period (week 3 through week 14; hazard ratio, 0.30; 95% CI, 0.22 to 0.42) and was not sustained afterwards (week 15 through week 26; hazard ratio, 1.13; 95% CI, 0.87 to 1.47). No serious adverse events were attributed to dihydroartemisinin–piperaquine.
cards.watchOut: Event counts are events, not children — recurrent-event modelling means 184 versus 316 overstates the per-child contrast slightly. The trial ran in areas of intense malaria transmission; where transmission is seasonal or low, the post-discharge risk this strategy treats is smaller. And the rebound-shaped curve (1.13 after week 14) warns that three courses postpone rather than abolish the vulnerable period.
cards.source: Kwambai TK et al. Malaria Chemoprevention in the Postdischarge Management of Severe Anemia. The New England journal of medicine. 2020. PMID: 33264546. Registry ID: NCT02671175. cards.headline: Phiri 2024 (IPD meta-analysis, 3 trials, 3,663 children): mortality rate ratio 0.23 and readmissions hazard ratio 0.45 during the intervention period — nothing sustained beyond it
cards.summary: Phiri 2024 (IPD meta-analysis, 3 trials, 3,663 children): mortality rate ratio 0.23 and readmissions hazard ratio 0.45 during the intervention period — nothing sustained beyond it
cards.people: Three double-blind, placebo-controlled trials including 3,663 children with severe anaemia in malaria-endemic Africa (3,507 in the modified intention-to-treat analysis): monthly sulfadoxine–pyrimethamine to the end of the transmission season in The Gambia (n=1,085), monthly artemether–lumefantrine at weeks 4 and 8 in Malawi (n=1,373), and monthly dihydroartemisinin–piperaquine at weeks 2, 6 and 10 in Uganda and Kenya (n=1,049); mean 3.1 courses per child in the Gambian trial.
cards.result: During the intervention period, post-discharge malaria chemoprevention was associated with a 77% relative reduction in mortality (rate ratio 0.23 [95% CI 0.08-0.70], p=0.0094, I2=0%) and a 55% relative reduction in all-cause readmissions (hazard ratio 0.45 [95% CI 0.36-0.56], p<0.0001) compared with placebo, with absolute rates as reported in the component trials. The protective effect was restricted to the intervention period and was not sustained after the direct pharmacodynamic effect of the drugs had waned.
cards.watchOut: Three trials, three different drugs and schedules — the pooled mortality estimate (0.23) rests on few deaths, hence the wide interval (0.08–0.70), and the authors note the small trial count limited assessment of heterogeneity and publication bias. Tier C is set because the shelf carries a mortality-benefit claim.

cards.headline: Synthesis: strong, consistent, and strictly temporary — chemoprevention buys protected months after discharge, not lasting immunity
cards.summary: Synthesis: strong, consistent, and strictly temporary — chemoprevention buys protected months after discharge, not lasting immunity
cards.people: One large placebo-controlled trial (1,049 children, dihydroartemisinin–piperaquine) plus the individual-patient meta-analysis of all three post-discharge chemoprevention trials (3,663 children, three different regimens).
cards.result: Readmission or death: hazard ratio 0.65 over 26 weeks in the trial (184 vs 316 events); 0.30 during treatment weeks. Pooled during-intervention effects: mortality rate ratio 0.23, readmissions hazard ratio 0.45. After the intervention: hazard ratio 1.13 in the trial — no residual protection. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit), Tier C for the mortality claim.
cards.watchOut: The strategy's value depends on delivery systems that can dose children at 2, 6 and 10 weeks after discharge — the trials achieved this with research infrastructure. Nothing here addresses non-malarial causes of post-discharge death, which the meta-analysis authors flag as the next target.
cards.source: Synthesis of Kwambai TK et al. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2020 (PMID: 33264546); Phiri KS et al. The Lancet Global Health. 2024 (PMID: 38097295).

shelves.title: HIV post-exposure prophylaxis after needlestick injury: zidovudine use associated with odds ratio 0.19 for seroconversion in the only case-control study — and full 28-day prescriptions complete better than starter packs (70% versus 53.2%)
shelves.question: After occupational exposure to HIV, does post-exposure prophylaxis reduce the risk of HIV transmission, and which regimens are completed?
shelves.mesh: Analysis of Variance · Anti-HIV Agents/therapeutic use · Blood-Borne Pathogens · Case-Control Studies · Female · HIV Infections/prevention & control/transmission · HIV Seropositivity/epidemiology · Health Personnel · Humans · Infectious Disease Transmission, Patient-to-Professional · Logistic Models · Male · Needlestick Injuries/complications · Occupational Diseases/epidemiology/prevention & control · Population Surveillance · Risk Factors · Wounds, Stab/complications · Zidovudine/therapeutic use
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the efficacy evidence is a single case-control study, because a placebo trial of PEP after occupational exposure has never been run and could not now be run. Among health-care workers with percutaneous exposure to HIV-infected blood, the 33 who seroconverted were significantly less likely to have taken zidovudine after exposure than 665 exposed controls who did not seroconvert (odds ratio 0.19, 95% CI 0.06–0.52) — against a background average transmission risk of 0.3% per percutaneous exposure. The same study defines who is at risk: deep injury (odds ratio 15, 6.0–41), a device visibly contaminated with blood (6.2, 2.2–21), a needle placed in the source patient's artery or vein (4.3, 1.7–12), and a source patient who died of AIDS within two months (5.6, 2.0–16). On completion, a systematic review of 54 studies (11,714 PEP initiations) found outcomes were better with a full 28-day prescription at first presentation than with starter packs: fewer refusals (11.4% versus 22%) and higher completion (70% versus 53.2%), with 28% of starter-pack recipients never returning for the rest of the course. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): PEP probably prevents most transmissions it could plausibly reach — an 81% relative reduction in the odds of seroconversion in the only direct study — and giving the whole course up front gets it finished; Tier C, as a single observational efficacy study.

cards.headline: Cardo 1997 (case-control, 33 cases, 665 controls): zidovudine after exposure odds ratio 0.19 (0.06–0.52); deep injury odds ratio 15
cards.summary: Cardo 1997 (case-control, 33 cases, 665 controls): zidovudine after exposure odds ratio 0.19 (0.06–0.52); deep injury odds ratio 15
cards.type: Case-control study (Cardo 1997, CDC Needlestick Surveillance Group)
cards.people: Health-care workers with occupational percutaneous exposure to HIV-infected blood: 33 case patients who seroconverted after exposure, reported by national surveillance systems in France, Italy, the United Kingdom and the United States, and 665 controls from a prospective surveillance project who were exposed but did not seroconvert; logistic-regression analysis. Background risk: the average risk of HIV infection after percutaneous exposure to HIV-infected blood is 0.3 percent.
cards.result: Case patients were significantly less likely than controls to have taken zidovudine after the exposure (odds ratio=0.19; 95 percent confidence interval, 0.06 to 0.52). Significant risk factors for seroconversion were deep injury (odds ratio=15; 6.0 to 41), injury with a device visibly contaminated with the source patient's blood (6.2; 2.2 to 21), a procedure involving a needle placed in the source patient's artery or vein (4.3; 1.7 to 12), and exposure to a source patient who died of AIDS within two months afterwards (5.6; 2.0 to 16).
cards.watchOut: Case-control, 33 cases, 1997: zidovudine monotherapy is no longer the regimen (modern PEP is a three-drug combination), source patients today are often virologically suppressed, and confounding by indication — the highest-risk exposures being most likely to receive PEP — would bias the estimate against PEP, making 0.19 if anything conservative. But it remains one observational study with wide intervals, which is why the stamp is POSSIBLE and Tier C is set.
cards.source: Cardo DM et al. A case-control study of HIV seroconversion in health care workers after percutaneous exposure. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention Needlestick Surveillance Group. The New England journal of medicine. 1997. PMID: 9366579. cards.headline: Ford 2015 (54 studies, 11,714 initiations): full 28-day prescription at first visit — refusals 11.4% versus 22%, completion 70% versus 53.2% versus starter packs
cards.summary: Ford 2015 (54 studies, 11,714 initiations): full 28-day prescription at first visit — refusals 11.4% versus 22%, completion 70% versus 53.2% versus starter packs
cards.people: 54 studies providing data on 11,714 PEP initiations (occupational and non-occupational): 37 studies (including 3 randomised trials, none specifically assessing starter packs) reporting starter-pack provision and 17 studies (2 randomised trials, 15 cohorts) reporting full prescriptions; databases searched to December 2013, updated June 2014; completion rates pooled by random-effects meta-analysis.
cards.result: Outcomes were better when participants were offered a full 28-day course of PEP at initial presentation, with fewer refusals (11.4% [95% CI, 5.3%-17.5%] vs 22% [16.7%-28.1%]) and higher completion rates (70% [56.7%-77.3%] vs 53.2% [44.4%-62.2%]) than with starter packs. More than a quarter (28% [21.4%-34.5%]) of individuals provided with a starter pack failed to return for their subsequent appointment and therefore defaulted before receiving a full course. The overall quality of the evidence was rated very low, and the authors conclude starter packs do not improve adherence and may lower completion.
cards.watchOut: Mostly observational cohorts with a 'very low' evidence rating, and starter-pack services may differ systematically from full-prescription services (setting, clientele, follow-up intensity) in ways pooling cannot remove. The comparison answers the question's second half — which prescribing approach gets regimens completed — not which drug combination works best.
cards.source: Ford N et al. Starter packs versus full prescription of antiretroviral drugs for postexposure prophylaxis: a systematic review. Clinical infectious diseases : an official publication of the Infectious Diseases Society of America. 2015. PMID: 25972501. cards.headline: Synthesis: efficacy from one case-control study, delivery from one review — prescribe the full course, immediately, to the exposures that carry risk
cards.summary: Synthesis: efficacy from one case-control study, delivery from one review — prescribe the full course, immediately, to the exposures that carry risk
cards.people: One multinational case-control study (33 seroconversions, 665 exposed controls) for efficacy, and one systematic review of 54 studies (11,714 PEP initiations) for completion.
cards.result: Zidovudine PEP: odds ratio 0.19 (0.06–0.52) for seroconversion, against a 0.3% average per-exposure risk. Highest-risk exposures: deep injury OR 15, visibly blood-contaminated device OR 6.2. Completion: 70% with full-course prescribing versus 53.2% with starter packs; refusals 11.4% versus 22%. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), Tier C.
cards.watchOut: Modern three-drug PEP has never been compared with anything in a controlled design — its use rests on this case-control result, animal data outside this record set, and the impossibility of a placebo trial. The shelf does not extend the claim to non-occupational exposure, which the efficacy study did not examine.
cards.source: Synthesis of Cardo DM et al. The New England Journal of Medicine. 1997 (PMID: 9366579); Ford N et al. Clinical Infectious Diseases. 2015 (PMID: 25972501).

shelves.title: Home safety education and equipment: safety practices clearly improve (smoke alarms odds ratio 1.81, fire escape plans 2.01) but injuries fall only in home-delivered programmes (rate ratio 0.75) — and the one large equipment trial found no injury reduction at all
shelves.question: In families with young children, do home safety education and provision of safety equipment reduce childhood injuries versus usual care?
shelves.mesh: Accident Prevention/instrumentation/methods · Accidental Falls/prevention & control · Accidents, Home/prevention & control · Adolescent · Burns/prevention & control · Burns, Electric/prevention & control · Child · Child, Preschool · Drowning/prevention & control · Humans · Infant · Infant, Newborn · Poisoning/prevention & control · Protective Devices · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Safety
shelves.balance: SPLIT — practices versus injuries. The Cochrane review (98 studies, 2,605,044 people; 54 studies in at least one meta-analysis) found home safety interventions reliably changed what families do: safe hot tap water temperatures (odds ratio 1.41, 95% CI 1.07–1.86), functional smoke alarms (1.81, 1.30–2.52), a fire escape plan (2.01, 1.45–2.77), and storing medicines (1.53, 1.27–1.84) and cleaning products (1.55, 1.22–1.96) out of reach. Injury rates were a different story: after adjusting controlled before-and-after studies for baseline rates, the pooled incidence rate ratio was 0.89 (0.78–1.01) — not significant overall — with greater reductions for interventions delivered in the home (0.75, 0.62–0.91) and, counterintuitively, for interventions not providing safety equipment (0.78, 0.66–0.92); there was a lack of evidence that interventions reduced thermal injuries or poisoning. The largest single randomised trial (3,428 families) of advice plus free fitted equipment found no reduction in medically attended injuries (odds ratio 1.14, 0.98–1.50) despite improved safety practices. PROPOSED SPLIT: home safety education improves safety behaviour and probably reduces injuries when delivered in the home; handing over equipment, by itself, has not been shown to reduce injuries — Tier C.

cards.headline: Kendrick 2012 (Cochrane, 98 studies): practices up across the board — injuries IRR 0.89 (0.78–1.01) overall, 0.75 (0.62–0.91) for home-delivered interventions
cards.summary: Kendrick 2012 (Cochrane, 98 studies): practices up across the board — injuries IRR 0.89 (0.78–1.01) overall, 0.75 (0.62–0.91) for home-delivered interventions
cards.people: 98 studies involving 2,605,044 people, of families with children and young people aged 19 years and under receiving home safety education with or without provision of safety equipment; 54 studies (812,705 people) comparable enough for at least one meta-analysis, 35 (65%) of them randomised trials and the rest controlled before-and-after studies; individual-participant data obtained for 19 studies.
cards.result: There was a lack of evidence that home safety interventions reduced rates of thermal injuries or poisoning. Interventions may reduce injury rates after adjusting controlled before-and-after studies for baseline injury rates (incidence rate ratio 0.89, 95% CI 0.78 to 1.01), with greater reductions for interventions delivered in the home (IRR 0.75, 95% CI 0.62 to 0.91) and for interventions not providing safety equipment (0.78, 0.66 to 0.92). Interventions increased the proportion of families with safe hot tap water temperatures (odds ratio 1.41, 95% CI 1.07 to 1.86), functional smoke alarms (1.81, 1.30 to 2.52), a fire escape plan (2.01, 1.45 to 2.77), storing medicines (1.53, 1.27 to 1.84) and cleaning products (1.55, 1.22 to 1.96) out of reach.
cards.watchOut: A third of the pooled studies are before-and-after designs vulnerable to secular falls in injury rates, the headline injury estimate crosses 1.0, and the 'no equipment does better' subgroup is a meta-regression finding that could reflect programme intensity rather than equipment harming anyone. Practice outcomes are self-reported or observed behaviours, not injuries.
cards.source: Kendrick D et al. Home safety education and provision of safety equipment for injury prevention. The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2012. PMID: 22972081. cards.headline: Watson 2005 (3,428 families): free fitted stair gates, fire guards, smoke alarms, cupboard and window locks — practices improved, medically attended injuries did not (OR 1.14, 0.98–1.50)
cards.summary: Watson 2005 (3,428 families): free fitted stair gates, fire guards, smoke alarms, cupboard and window locks — practices improved, medically attended injuries did not (OR 1.14, 0.98–1.50)
cards.people: 3,428 families with children under 5 years living in deprived areas, recruited from 47 general practices in Nottingham, randomised to a standardised safety consultation plus free and fitted stair gates, fire guards, smoke alarms, cupboard locks and window locks, or usual care; outcomes over two years: medically attended injuries, primary- and secondary-care attendance and hospital admission rates, plus possession of equipment and safety practices.
cards.result: No significant difference was found in the proportion of families in which a child had a medically attended injury (odds ratio 1.14, 95% confidence interval 0.98 to 1.50) or in rates of attendance in secondary care (incidence rate ratio 1.02, 0.90 to 1.13) or admission to hospital (1.02, 0.70 to 1.48). Children in the intervention arm had a significantly higher attendance rate for injuries in primary care (1.37, 1.11 to 1.70, P=0.003). At one and two years, intervention families were significantly more likely to have a range of safety practices, but absolute differences in percentages were relatively small.
cards.watchOut: One trial, in deprived areas of one English city, with equipment fitted free — the null may reflect small absolute changes in practice, as the authors note, rather than proof that equipment cannot work. The higher primary-care attendance rate (1.37) may be surveillance (families primed to attend) rather than more injuries. It is nonetheless the most direct test of the 'provide equipment' model and it found no injury benefit.
cards.source: Watson M et al. Providing child safety equipment to prevent injuries: randomised controlled trial. BMJ (Clinical research ed.). 2005. PMID: 15604156. cards.headline: Synthesis: teach in the home and behaviour changes and injuries probably fall; post equipment through the door and only behaviour changes
cards.summary: Synthesis: teach in the home and behaviour changes and injuries probably fall; post equipment through the door and only behaviour changes
cards.people: A Cochrane review of 98 studies (2,605,044 participants; 54 studies meta-analysed) and the largest single randomised trial within that literature (3,428 families, equipment provided and fitted free).
cards.result: Safety practices: odds ratios 1.41–2.01 across five behaviours in the review, and significantly improved practices in the trial. Injuries: pooled IRR 0.89 (0.78–1.01) overall; 0.75 (0.62–0.91) for home-delivered interventions; trial medically attended injuries OR 1.14 (0.98–1.50), admissions IRR 1.02. Thermal injuries and poisoning: lack of evidence of reduction. PROPOSED SPLIT, Tier C.

shelves.title: Helmet-promotion programmes roughly double children's helmet wearing — and helmets themselves cut head-injury odds by about 60% in crash studies, though no promotion trial measured injuries
shelves.question: Do interventions promoting bicycle helmet use increase helmet wearing and reduce head injuries in children?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Bicycling/legislation & jurisprudence/statistics & numerical data · Child · Child, Preschool · Craniocerebral Trauma/prevention & control · Head Protective Devices/statistics & numerical data/supply & distribution · Humans · Program Development
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — promotion works on wearing; the injury benefit is inferred, not trialled. The Cochrane review of non-legislative interventions (Owen R et al., PMID: 22071810) pooled 11 studies and found observed helmet wearing roughly doubled (OR 2.08, 95% CI 1.29 to 3.34), with the largest effects for community-based programmes (OR 4.30) and free-helmet provision (OR 4.35), and a smaller effect for education alone (OR 1.43). Whether wearing prevents injury rests on crash data, not trials: the Attewell meta-analysis of case-control studies (PMID: 11235796) found helmet use associated with lower odds of head injury (OR 0.40, 95% CI 0.29 to 0.55), brain injury (OR 0.42) and fatal injury (OR 0.27), against a possible neck-injury signal (OR 1.36, 95% CI 1.00 to 1.86). No promotion trial measured head injuries directly, and the injury evidence is observational — which is why this shelf is Tier C. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): programmes — especially community-based ones giving helmets away — increase wearing, and the observational crash evidence says wearing matters.

cards.headline: Cochrane review: promotion raised observed helmet wearing (OR 2.08) — community programmes OR 4.30, free helmets OR 4.35, education alone OR 1.43
cards.summary: Cochrane review: promotion raised observed helmet wearing (OR 2.08) — community programmes OR 4.30, free helmets OR 4.35, education alone OR 1.43
cards.people: 29 controlled studies (21 in at least one meta-analysis) of non-legislative interventions to promote cycle helmet wearing in children aged 0–18 years, including randomised and controlled before-and-after studies, searched to April 2009.
cards.result: Non-legislative interventions increased observed helmet wearing (11 studies: OR 2.08, 95% CI 1.29 to 3.34). Effects were largest for community-based interventions (4 studies: OR 4.30, 95% CI 2.24 to 8.25) and interventions providing free helmets (2 studies: OR 4.35, 95% CI 2.13 to 8.89); school-based interventions OR 1.73 (95% CI 1.03 to 2.91); education-only OR 1.43 (95% CI 1.09 to 1.88). Subsidised helmets showed no significant effect (OR 2.02, 95% CI 0.98 to 4.17).
cards.watchOut: The outcome is wearing, not injury — no included study showed a promotion programme reducing head injuries. Studies are old (searched to 2009) and heterogeneous, and effects in children under 12 may exceed those in mixed-age groups.
cards.source: Owen R et al. Non-legislative interventions for the promotion of cycle helmet wearing by children. The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2011. PMID: 22071810. cards.headline: Attewell 2001 meta-analysis: helmet use associated with head injury OR 0.40, brain injury OR 0.42, fatal injury OR 0.27 — neck injury OR 1.36
cards.summary: Attewell 2001 meta-analysis: helmet use associated with head injury OR 0.40, brain injury OR 0.42, fatal injury OR 0.27 — neck injury OR 1.36
cards.people: Peer-reviewed studies from several countries published 1987–1998 with individual injury and helmet-use data from bicycle crashes, pooled in a formal meta-analysis.
cards.result: Summary odds ratios for helmet use were 0.40 (95% CI 0.29 to 0.55) for head injury, 0.42 (0.26 to 0.67) for brain injury, 0.53 (0.39 to 0.73) for facial injury and 0.27 (0.10 to 0.71) for fatal injury. Three studies gave an unfavourable neck-injury estimate of 1.36 (1.00 to 1.86), which the authors note may not apply to lighter modern helmets.
cards.watchOut: Case-control data cannot exclude confounding — helmet wearers may ride differently and crash differently. The 0.40 ratio clears the developer's two-sided floor for observational benefit (≤0.5), but it is still not trial evidence, and the studies predate current helmet designs.
cards.source: Attewell RG et al. Bicycle helmet efficacy: a meta-analysis. Accident; analysis and prevention. 2001. PMID: 11235796. shelves.title: Giving parents a child seat plus education works — education alone does not: distribution programmes carry the strongest evidence for getting children restrained
shelves.question: Do child safety-seat distribution and education programmes increase correct seat use and reduce injuries versus usual care?
shelves.mesh: Automobile Driving · Community Health Services · Health Education · Humans · Infant · Infant Equipment/statistics & numerical data · Preventive Health Services
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for the programmes that hand over a seat, not for leaflets. The Community Preventive Services Task Force reviews (Zaza S et al., PMID: 11691560) screened 72 studies and found strong evidence of effectiveness for child safety-seat laws and for distribution-plus-education programmes, sufficient evidence for community-wide information with enhanced enforcement and for incentive-plus-education programmes, and insufficient evidence for education-only programmes. The Cochrane review of booster-seat interventions for 4–8-year-olds (Ehiri JE et al., PMID: 16437484) pooled 5 studies (3,070 children) and found interventions increased booster use (RR 1.43, 95% CI 1.05 to 1.96), with free distribution plus education strongest (RR 2.34, 95% CI 1.50 to 3.63). The injury link is background effectiveness: correctly used seats reduce hospitalisation by 69% and death by about 70% in infants and 47–54% in toddlers, as summarised in the Task Force review. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): distribution plus education reliably raises correct restraint use; education alone is unproven.

cards.headline: Task Force reviews (72 studies): strong evidence for seat laws and distribution-plus-education; insufficient evidence for education-only programmes
cards.summary: Task Force reviews (72 studies): strong evidence for seat laws and distribution-plus-education; insufficient evidence for education-only programmes
cards.type: Systematic reviews for the Community Preventive Services Task Force (Zaza 2001)
cards.people: 72 studies meeting inclusion criteria from more than 3,500 citations screened to March 1998, evaluating five intervention types to increase child safety-seat use in children, with changes in seat use or injury rates as outcomes.
cards.result: Strong evidence of effectiveness was found for child safety-seat laws and for distribution-plus-education programmes; sufficient evidence for community-wide information plus enhanced enforcement campaigns and for incentive-plus-education programmes; insufficient evidence for education-only programmes aimed at parents, young children, health professionals or law enforcement. The review's background data: correctly installed and used seats reduce the need for hospitalisation by 69% and the risk of death by approximately 70% for infants and 47% to 54% for toddlers (aged 1 to 4 years).
cards.watchOut: The underlying studies are largely non-randomised programme evaluations from before 1998, and 'use' was often observed or reported rather than verified as correct installation in every study — the gap between owning a seat and using it correctly is where these programmes can still fail.
cards.source: Zaza S et al. Reviews of evidence regarding interventions to increase use of child safety seats. American journal of preventive medicine. 2001. PMID: 11691560. cards.summary: Cochrane booster-seat review: interventions raised use (RR 1.43) — free seats plus education RR 2.34, incentives plus education RR 1.32
cards.people: 5 randomised or controlled before-and-after trials involving 3,070 individuals, testing interventions to increase acquisition and use of booster seats in children aged 4 to 8 years travelling in motor vehicles.
cards.result: All interventions showed a positive effect on booster-seat use (RR 1.43, 95% CI 1.05 to 1.96). Free booster-seat distribution combined with education: RR 2.34 (95% CI 1.50 to 3.63; n=380). Incentives combined with education: RR 1.32 (95% CI 1.12 to 1.55; n=1,898). Education-only interventions: RR 1.32 (95% CI 1.16 to 1.49; n=563). One law-enforcement study showed no marked benefit.
cards.watchOut: Only five trials, and the biggest effect (free distribution) rests on 380 children. Outcomes are acquisition and use of booster seats, not injuries, and follow-up is short — whether the seat is still used correctly a year later is largely unmeasured.

shelves.title: BARCODE1: screening only the top genetic-risk decile found cancer in 40% of men biopsied — over half needing treatment, most of whom the standard UK pathway would have missed; no outcomes data yet
shelves.question: In prostate screening, does a polygenic risk score identify a high-risk group in whom targeted PSA screening finds more clinically significant cancers?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Biopsy · Early Detection of Cancer/methods · Genetic Predisposition to Disease · Genetic Risk Score · Genome-Wide Association Study · Multifactorial Inheritance · Multiparametric Magnetic Resonance Imaging · Prostate/pathology/diagnostic imaging · Prostate-Specific Antigen/blood · Prostatic Neoplasms/blood/diagnosis/genetics/pathology · Risk Assessment/methods · Saliva/chemistry · United Kingdom · Case-Control Studies · Prospective Studies
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for finding clinically significant cancer in a pre-selected high-risk group; whether that saves lives is untested. In BARCODE1 (McHugh JK et al., PMID: 40214032), 6,393 UK men aged 55–69 had a 130-variant polygenic risk score calculated; the 745 (11.7%) in the top decile were offered MRI and biopsy regardless of PSA. Of 468 men biopsied, 187 (40.0%) had prostate cancer, and 103 (55.1%) of those cancers were intermediate-risk or higher, so treatment was indicated — 74 (71.8%) of those 103 would not have been detected by the current UK diagnostic pathway. The pilot (Benafif S et al., PMID: 34214236) showed the approach is feasible but uptake is the constraint: only 26% of invited men took part. There is no randomised comparison and no mortality, metastasis or overdiagnosis outcome — detection yield is a surrogate, and some detected cancers would never have caused harm. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): risk-targeted screening concentrates significant cancers where it looks, at the price of biopsying a group in whom 60% have no cancer found.

cards.headline: BARCODE1: 187 cancers in 468 biopsied top-decile men (40.0%); 103 treatment-indicated, 71.8% of those invisible to the current UK pathway
cards.summary: BARCODE1: 187 cancers in 468 biopsied top-decile men (40.0%); 103 treatment-indicated, 71.8% of those invisible to the current UK pathway
cards.people: UK primary-care patients aged 55–69 years: 40,292 invited, 8,953 (22.2%) expressed interest, 6,393 had a polygenic risk score from 130 variants calculated; 745 (11.7%) scored at or above the 90th percentile and were invited to MRI and transperineal biopsy irrespective of PSA; 468 (62.8%) underwent both.
cards.result: Prostate cancer was detected in 187 of 468 biopsied men (40.0%). Of these, 103 (55.1%) had intermediate-or-higher-risk cancer by 2024 NCCN criteria, so treatment was indicated; 74 (71.8%) of these 103 would not have been detected under the UK pathway then in use (high PSA and positive MRI). Forty men (21.4% of cancers) had unfavourable intermediate-risk or high/very-high-risk disease. Median age at diagnosis was 64 years.
cards.watchOut: No control group, no randomisation, and no follow-up outcomes: the study shows where cancers are found, not that finding them this way reduces deaths or that the extra cancers found are the ones that kill. Overdiagnosis cannot be quantified from this design, and only 22.2% of invitees engaged at all.
cards.source: McHugh JK et al. Assessment of a Polygenic Risk Score in Screening for Prostate Cancer. The New England journal of medicine. 2025. PMID: 40214032. Registry ID: NCT03857477. cards.headline: BARCODE1 pilot: feasible, but only 26% of invited men took part — and all 7 cancers found were low-risk, managed with surveillance
cards.summary: BARCODE1 pilot: feasible, but only 26% of invited men took part — and all 7 cancers found were low-risk, managed with surveillance
cards.people: Healthy UK men aged 55–69 invited through general practitioners; saliva DNA genotyped for 130 prostate-cancer risk SNPs; men above the 90th centile of polygenic risk were invited to prostate MRI and biopsy. Invitation letters went to 1,434 men.
cards.result: Overall uptake was 26% (375 of 1,436); 297 men had genotype data and 25 were invited for screening; 18 of 25 (72%) underwent MRI and biopsy, yielding 7 prostate-cancer diagnoses (38.9%), all low-risk and managed with active surveillance.
cards.watchOut: A pilot of feasibility, not effectiveness — and its cancer yield was entirely low-risk disease of the kind screening critics cite as overdiagnosis, in contrast to the main study's higher-risk yield. Small numbers throughout.

cards.search: barcode1 pilot: feasible, but only 26% of invited men took part — and all 7 cancers found were low-risk, managed with surveillance barcode1 pilot: feasible, but only 26% of invited men took part — and all 7 cancers found were low-risk, managed with surveillance in prostate screening, does a polygenic risk score identify a high-risk group in whom targeted psa screening finds more clinically significant cancers? feasibility study (benafif 2022, barcode1 pilot) healthy uk men aged 55–69 invited through general practitioners; saliva dna genotyped for 130 prostate-cancer risk snps; men above the 90th centile of polygenic risk were invited to prostate mri and biopsy. invitation letters went to 1,434 men. overall uptake was 26% (375 of 1,436); 297 men had genotype data and 25 were invited for screening; 18 of 25 (72%) underwent mri and biopsy, yielding 7 prostate-cancer diagnoses (38.9%), all low-risk and managed with active surveillance. a pilot of feasibility, not effectiveness — and its cancer yield was entirely low-risk disease of the kind screening critics cite as overdiagnosis, in contrast to the main study's higher-risk yield. small numbers throughout. benafif s et al. the barcode1 pilot: a feasibility study of using germline single nucleotide polymorphisms to target prostate cancer screening. bju international. 2022. pmid: 34214236. mesh: early detection of cancer/methods · feasibility studies · germ cells/pathology · humans · male · pilot projects · polymorphism, single nucleotide/genetics · prostate-specific antigen/genetics · prostatic neoplasms/diagnosis/genetics/pathology

cards.headline: Synthesis: risk-targeting works as a detection strategy in one large single-arm study; the outcome question — fewer deaths versus more overdiagnosis — is untouched
cards.summary: Synthesis: risk-targeting works as a detection strategy in one large single-arm study; the outcome question — fewer deaths versus more overdiagnosis — is untouched
cards.people: BARCODE1 main study (6,393 scored; 468 biopsied) and its pilot (1,434 invited), both UK primary-care based, using the same 130-variant score and top-decile threshold.
cards.result: Detection: 40.0% of biopsied men had cancer; 55.1% of cancers were treatment-indicated; most significant cancers would have been missed by the PSA/MRI pathway. Feasibility: 26% uptake in the pilot, 22.2% expressing interest in the main study. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) for detection yield, Tier C: a single-arm programme with no comparative or long-term outcome data.
cards.watchOut: The shelf's question says 'targeted PSA screening' — BARCODE1 in fact bypassed PSA, offering MRI and biopsy on genetic risk alone; readers should not read this as evidence about PSA-based pathways.
cards.source: Synthesis of McHugh JK et al. The New England journal of medicine. 2025 (PMID: 40214032); Benafif S et al. BJU international. 2022 (PMID: 34214236).

shelves.title: HPV vaccine and oral infection in men: no trial in men exists — vaccinated young men had no vaccine-type oral infections at all in US survey data (0.0% vs 2.13%), and the one randomised proof comes from women (93% efficacy)
shelves.question: In boys and men, does HPV vaccination prevent vaccine-type oral HPV infection, a precursor pathway to oropharyngeal cancer?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Age Distribution · Cross-Sectional Studies · Female · Humans · Incidence · Male · Mouth Diseases/diagnosis/epidemiology/prevention & control/virology · Nutrition Surveys · Papillomavirus Infections/diagnosis/epidemiology/prevention & control/virology · Papillomavirus Vaccines/administration & dosage · Patient Acceptance of Health Care · Prevalence · Sex Distribution · Time Factors · United States/epidemiology · Vaccination · Young Adult
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — strongly suggestive, never randomised in men. In US NHANES 2011–2014 data (Chaturvedi AK et al., PMID: 29182497), vaccine-type oral HPV prevalence was 0.11% in vaccinated versus 1.61% in unvaccinated young adults (an adjusted 88.2% relative reduction), and among men specifically 0.0% versus 2.13%. The biological bridge is a vaccine trial in 150 mid-adult men (Pinto LA et al., PMID: 27511896): all developed serum anti-HPV-16/18 antibodies and over 90% had detectable oral-cavity antibodies after vaccination with the quadrivalent vaccine (Gardasil, as named in the publication). The only randomised efficacy evidence against oral infection is in women: the Costa Rica trial found 93.3% efficacy against prevalent oral HPV16/18 infection four years after bivalent vaccination (Herrero R et al., PMID: 23873171). Because the male evidence is cross-sectional and immunogenicity-based, this shelf is Tier C. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): every available strand points the same way, but a male efficacy trial remains undone.

cards.headline: NHANES analysis: vaccine-type oral HPV prevalence 0.11% vaccinated vs 1.61% unvaccinated; in men 0.0% vs 2.13%
cards.summary: NHANES analysis: vaccine-type oral HPV prevalence 0.11% vaccinated vs 1.61% unvaccinated; in men 0.0% vs 2.13%
cards.people: 2,627 US men and women aged 18–33 years in a nationally representative survey; oral HPV16/18/6/11 infection compared by self-reported receipt of at least one HPV vaccine dose before age 26 (29.2% of women and 6.9% of men reported vaccination).
cards.result: Prevalence of oral HPV16/18/6/11 infection was 0.11% in vaccinated versus 1.61% in unvaccinated participants (adjusted P=.008), an estimated 88.2% relative reduction in prevalence (95% CI 5.7% to 98.5%) after adjustment for age, sex and race. In men the figures were 0.0% versus 2.13% (adjusted P=.007). Because uptake was low, the population-level effect was only 6.9% in men.
cards.watchOut: Cross-sectional and self-reported vaccination: vaccinated men differ from unvaccinated men in ways adjustment cannot fully capture, the male vaccinated group is small (zero events), and prevalence at one visit is not the same as prevented persistent infection or prevented cancer. The effect ratio (~0.07) clears the observational floor, but the design caps the stamp.
cards.source: Chaturvedi AK et al. Effect of Prophylactic Human Papillomavirus (HPV) Vaccination on Oral HPV Infections Among Young Adults in the United States. Journal of clinical oncology : official journal of the American Society of Clinical Oncology. 2018. PMID: 29182497. cards.headline: Mid-adult male vaccine trial: quadrivalent HPV vaccine induced oral-cavity antibodies in over 90% of men for HPV-16
cards.summary: Mid-adult male vaccine trial: quadrivalent HPV vaccine induced oral-cavity antibodies in over 90% of men for HPV-16
cards.people: 150 men aged 27–45 years in Tampa, Florida and Cuernavaca, Mexico, given the quadrivalent HPV vaccine (Gardasil, as named in the publication) at day 1 and months 2 and 6; serum and oral specimens (mouthwash and sponge) tested for anti-HPV-16/18 IgG at day 1 and month 7.
cards.result: All participants developed detectable serum anti-HPV-16 and anti-HPV-18 antibodies. At month 7, HPV-16 antibodies were detected in 93.2% of mouthwash and 95.7% of sponge specimens; HPV-18 in 72.1% and 65.5% respectively. Oral antibody levels were about 3 logs lower than serum levels and correlated strongly with them (ρ 0.86–0.92).
cards.watchOut: Immunogenicity only — no infection endpoint, no placebo group, and oral antibody presence is a plausible mechanism, not proof of protection. The publication names the product (Gardasil) but does not state its manufacturer in the record, so none is given here.
cards.source: Pinto LA et al. Quadrivalent Human Papillomavirus (HPV) Vaccine Induces HPV-Specific Antibodies in the Oral Cavity: Results From the Mid-Adult Male Vaccine Trial. cards.headline: Costa Rica randomised trial (women): bivalent HPV vaccine efficacy against oral HPV16/18 infection was 93.3% at four years
cards.summary: Costa Rica randomised trial (women): bivalent HPV vaccine efficacy against oral HPV16/18 infection was 93.3% at four years
cards.people: 7,466 women aged 18–25 in Costa Rica randomised to bivalent HPV16/18 vaccine or hepatitis A vaccine control; 5,840 provided oral specimens at the blinded 4-year visit. NCT00128661.
cards.result: There were 15 prevalent oral HPV16/18 infections in the control group and 1 in the vaccine group, giving estimated vaccine efficacy of 93.3% (95% CI 63% to 100%) against prevalent oral HPV16/18 infection; efficacy against cervical HPV16/18 in the same cohort was 72.0%.
cards.watchOut: Women, not men, and a bivalent vaccine — this card is the randomised proof-of-principle that HPV vaccination can prevent oral infection at all; it cannot by itself establish the effect in boys and men, and oral infection counts were small (16 events).
cards.source: Herrero R et al. Reduced prevalence of oral human papillomavirus (HPV) 4 years after bivalent HPV vaccination in a randomized clinical trial in Costa Rica. PloS one. 2013. cards.headline: Synthesis: mechanism in men, population association in men, randomised efficacy in women — three strands, one missing male trial
cards.summary: Synthesis: mechanism in men, population association in men, randomised efficacy in women — three strands, one missing male trial
cards.people: One cross-sectional US survey analysis (n=2,627), one male immunogenicity trial (n=150), and one randomised trial oral substudy in women (n=5,840 with oral specimens).
cards.result: Men: vaccine-type oral HPV prevalence 0.0% vs 2.13% by vaccination status; oral antibodies in >90% after vaccination. Women (randomised): 93.3% efficacy against oral HPV16/18. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), Tier C: the male claim rests on observational and surrogate evidence.
cards.watchOut: Oropharyngeal cancer itself — the outcome that matters — has never been a trial endpoint for HPV vaccination in either sex; every shelf on this pathway is necessarily built on infection surrogates.

shelves.title: Tirzepatide in obesity with prediabetes: diabetes diagnosed in 1.3% versus 13.3% over three years — a 93% relative reduction in onset, still evident after 17 weeks off the drug
shelves.question: In adults with obesity and prediabetes, does tirzepatide reduce progression to type 2 diabetes versus placebo over three years?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Anti-Obesity Agents/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2/epidemiology/etiology/prevention & control · Disease Progression · Double-Blind Method · Obesity/complications/diagnosis/drug therapy · Prediabetic State/drug therapy/etiology · Tirzepatide/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Weight Loss/drug effects · Glucagon-Like Peptide-1 Receptor Agonists/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Body Weight/drug effects · Gastrointestinal Diseases/chemically induced/epidemiology · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug
shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit) — one large trial, an effect too big to be fragile, on delaying the formal diagnosis. In the three-year SURMOUNT-1 analysis (Jastreboff AM et al., PMID: 39536238), among 1,032 participants with obesity and prediabetes, type 2 diabetes was diagnosed in 1.3% on tirzepatide versus 13.3% on placebo over 176 weeks (hazard ratio 0.07, 95% CI 0.0 to 0.1) — a 93% relative reduction, 12.0 percentage points absolute. After 17 weeks off treatment the gap persisted (2.4% versus 13.7%; HR 0.12). Weight fell 12.3% to 19.7% by dose versus 1.3% on placebo, consistent with the parent trial's 72-week results (PMID: 35658024). Consistent with the developer's framing, this is best described as delaying progression to a diabetes diagnosis — driven by weight loss — rather than proof of permanent prevention: what happens over a decade, or after years off the drug, is unknown. Tier C: a single trial carrying a diabetes-onset benefit claim. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): tirzepatide delays progression from prediabetes to diabetes for at least three years.

cards.headline: Three-year SURMOUNT-1 prediabetes analysis: diabetes in 1.3% on tirzepatide vs 13.3% on placebo (HR 0.07); 2.4% vs 13.7% after 17 weeks off treatment
cards.summary: Three-year SURMOUNT-1 prediabetes analysis: diabetes in 1.3% on tirzepatide vs 13.3% on placebo (HR 0.07); 2.4% vs 13.7% after 17 weeks off treatment
cards.people: 1,032 participants with obesity and prediabetes (from 2,539 randomised in SURMOUNT-1), assigned to once-weekly tirzepatide 5 mg, 10 mg or 15 mg or placebo for 176 weeks, followed by a 17-week off-treatment period. NCT04184622.
cards.result: At 176 weeks, mean weight change was −12.3% (5 mg), −18.7% (10 mg) and −19.7% (15 mg) versus −1.3% on placebo (P<0.001 for all). Type 2 diabetes was diagnosed in 1.3% of tirzepatide participants versus 13.3% on placebo (hazard ratio 0.07, 95% CI 0.0 to 0.1; P<0.001) — a 93% relative reduction with absolute rates printed here. After 17 weeks off treatment, diabetes had been diagnosed in 2.4% versus 13.7% (HR 0.12, 95% CI 0.1 to 0.2). Adverse events were mainly gastrointestinal, mostly mild to moderate during dose escalation; no new safety signals.
cards.watchOut: A pre-specified analysis of the prediabetes subset of one trial, with diabetes onset as a key secondary endpoint. Seventeen weeks off treatment is short against a lifelong disease: the data show delay of diagnosis while weight is held down, not eradication of risk, and regain after stopping (shown in other tirzepatide withdrawal data) would be expected to erode the gap.
cards.source: Jastreboff AM et al. Tirzepatide for Obesity Treatment and Diabetes Prevention. The New England journal of medicine. 2025. PMID: 39536238. Registry ID: NCT04184622. cards.headline: SURMOUNT-1 at 72 weeks: weight −15.0% to −20.9% by dose versus −3.1% on placebo — the weight loss that carries the diabetes effect
cards.summary: SURMOUNT-1 at 72 weeks: weight −15.0% to −20.9% by dose versus −3.1% on placebo — the weight loss that carries the diabetes effect
cards.people: 2,539 adults with BMI ≥30, or ≥27 with a weight-related complication, excluding diabetes, randomised 1:1:1:1 to tirzepatide 5 mg, 10 mg or 15 mg once weekly or placebo for 72 weeks including 20-week dose escalation. Mean baseline weight 104.8 kg, mean BMI 38.0. NCT04184622.
cards.result: Mean weight change at week 72 was −15.0% (5 mg), −19.5% (10 mg) and −20.9% (15 mg) versus −3.1% on placebo (P<0.001 for all). A ≥5% weight reduction was achieved by 85%, 89% and 91% versus 35%; ≥20% reduction by 50% (10 mg) and 57% (15 mg) versus 3%. Adverse events causing discontinuation occurred in 4.3%, 7.1% and 6.2% on tirzepatide versus 2.6% on placebo; most adverse events were gastrointestinal.
cards.watchOut: This is the parent trial report in the full obesity population (diabetes excluded), carded here for the weight mechanism and tolerability — it is the same trial programme as the three-year card above, not an independent replication.
cards.source: Jastreboff AM et al. Tirzepatide Once Weekly for the Treatment of Obesity. The New England journal of medicine. 2022. PMID: 35658024. Registry ID: NCT04184622. cards.headline: Synthesis: one trial programme, two reports — a very large delay in diabetes onset that tracks the weight loss, unproven beyond three years
cards.summary: Synthesis: one trial programme, two reports — a very large delay in diabetes onset that tracks the weight loss, unproven beyond three years
cards.people: SURMOUNT-1: 2,539 randomised with obesity; 1,032 with prediabetes followed for 176 weeks plus 17 weeks off treatment.
cards.result: Diabetes onset 1.3% vs 13.3% at three years (HR 0.07); 2.4% vs 13.7% after 17 weeks off drug (HR 0.12). Weight −19.7% at the top dose vs −1.3%. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit), Tier C: single trial, and the honest verb is 'delays' — durability after long-term discontinuation is unknown.
cards.watchOut: No second trial has tested tirzepatide for diabetes onset; class evidence from other agents cannot be imported onto this shelf, and cost and supply for a diabetes-delay indication are outside the trial record.
cards.source: Synthesis of Jastreboff AM et al. The New England journal of medicine. 2025 (PMID: 39536238); Jastreboff AM et al. The New England journal of medicine. 2022 (PMID: 35658024).

shelves.title: High-dose flu vaccine in nursing homes: respiratory hospital admissions 3.4% versus 3.9% over one season in an 823-home cluster trial — a real but modest edge (adjusted RR 0.87)
shelves.question: In nursing-home residents, does high-dose influenza vaccine reduce respiratory-related hospital admissions versus standard-dose vaccine?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Cluster Analysis · Comparative Effectiveness Research · Female · Hospitalization/statistics & numerical data · Humans · Influenza Vaccines/administration & dosage · Influenza, Human/prevention & control · Male · Nursing Homes/statistics & numerical data · Single-Blind Method · United States · Vaccination/methods
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a modest relative effect on a common outcome, from one very large pragmatic trial. The cluster-randomised trial across 823 US nursing homes (Gravenstein S et al., PMID: 28736045) found respiratory-related hospital admissions in 3.4% of residents in high-dose facilities versus 3.9% in standard-dose facilities over six months (0.185 versus 0.211 per 1,000 resident-days; adjusted relative risk 0.873, 95% CI 0.776 to 0.982, p=0.023) — a 13% relative reduction, 0.5 percentage points absolute. Supporting evidence in community-dwelling older adults points the same way: a meta-analysis of 15 publications over 10 seasons (Lee JKH et al., PMID: 33422382) found high-dose vaccine relatively more effective against pneumonia admissions (relative VE 27.3%) and influenza admissions (relative VE 11.7%). Tier C: the nursing-home claim rests on a single trial, and its unadjusted analysis was not significant (RR 0.888, p=0.061). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): high-dose vaccine gives nursing-home residents a small reduction in respiratory admissions.

cards.headline: Gravenstein 2017: respiratory admissions 3.4% (high-dose homes) vs 3.9% (standard-dose homes); adjusted RR 0.873, unadjusted p=0.061
cards.summary: Gravenstein 2017: respiratory admissions 3.4% (high-dose homes) vs 3.9% (standard-dose homes); adjusted RR 0.873, unadjusted p=0.061
cards.people: 823 Medicare-certified US nursing homes randomised facility-wide to high-dose or standard-dose trivalent influenza vaccine for the 2013–14 season (with a factorial staff-vaccination component); 53,008 long-stay residents aged ≥65, of whom 38,256 were matched to Medicare fee-for-service claims for the admission analysis. NCT01815268.
cards.result: Respiratory-related hospital admissions were lower in high-dose facilities: 0.185 versus 0.211 per 1,000 resident-days, i.e. 3.4% versus 3.9% of residents over 6 months. The unadjusted relative risk was 0.888 (95% CI 0.785 to 1.005, p=0.061); the adjusted relative risk was 0.873 (95% CI 0.776 to 0.982, p=0.023). Staff vaccination rates did not differ between groups.
cards.watchOut: One season (2013–14), one country, claims-based outcomes, and significance that depends on the adjusted model. The absolute gain — about 5 fewer respiratory admissions per 1,000 residents per season — is worthwhile at population scale but small per facility.
cards.source: Gravenstein S et al. Comparative effectiveness of high-dose versus standard-dose influenza vaccination on numbers of US nursing home residents admitted to hospital: a cluster-randomised trial. The Lancet. Respiratory medicine. 2017. PMID: 28736045. Registry ID: NCT01815268. cards.headline: Meta-analysis in older adults ≥65: high-dose vaccine relatively better against pneumonia admissions (rVE 27.3%) and influenza admissions (rVE 11.7%)
cards.summary: Meta-analysis in older adults ≥65: high-dose vaccine relatively better against pneumonia admissions (rVE 27.3%) and influenza admissions (rVE 11.7%)
cards.people: 15 publications covering 10 consecutive influenza seasons and more than 22 million high-dose vaccine recipients aged ≥65 years, in randomised and observational settings, comparing high-dose trivalent vaccine with standard-dose vaccines.
cards.result: High-dose vaccine showed improved protection against influenza-like illness (relative VE 15.9%, 95% CI 4.1 to 26.3), all-cause hospital admissions (rVE 8.4%, 95% CI 5.7 to 11.0), influenza admissions (rVE 11.7%, 95% CI 7.0 to 16.1), pneumonia admissions (rVE 27.3%, 95% CI 15.3 to 37.6) and pneumonia/influenza mortality (rVE 39.9%, 95% CI 18.6 to 55.6), with similar advantages in matched and mismatched seasons.
cards.watchOut: This card supports direction, not the nursing-home number: its population is older adults generally (mostly community-dwelling), it mixes randomised and observational seasons, and relative VE against standard dose is not an absolute effect. The nursing-home shelf stands or falls on the Gravenstein trial.
cards.source: Lee JKH et al. Efficacy and effectiveness of high-dose influenza vaccine in older adults by circulating strain and antigenic match: An updated systematic review and meta-analysis. Vaccine. 2021. PMID: 33422382. shelves.title: School hand-hygiene programmes: illness absence may fall a little (pooled IRR 0.82, very low certainty) — but the largest trial, 60 schools in Addis Ababa, found no effect on absence at all
shelves.question: In primary-school children, do school-based hand-hygiene programmes reduce illness-related absence versus usual practice?
shelves.mesh: Absenteeism · Adolescent · Child · Child, Preschool · Gastrointestinal Diseases/epidemiology/prevention & control · Hand Hygiene/methods · Humans · Preventive Medicine/methods · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Respiratory Tract Diseases/epidemiology/prevention & control · Schools/statistics & numerical data
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — the signal is small, the certainty very low, and the biggest trial is null on absence. The Cochrane review of rinse-free hand washing (Munn Z et al., PMID: 32270476; 19 studies, 30,747 children) found illness-related absenteeism may be reduced (IRR 0.82, 95% CI 0.69 to 0.97; 6 studies) but rated the evidence very low certainty, and found little to no difference for absenteeism for any reason (IRR 0.91, 95% CI 0.82 to 1.01). The WISE cluster trial in 60 Addis Ababa primary schools (Bick S et al., PMID: 39218883; 6,229 pupils) found no effect on roll-call absence (adjusted OR 1.07) or diarrhoea, with only a borderline reduction in reported respiratory illness (adjusted OR 0.84, 95% CI 0.71 to 1.00). A small US trial (Sandora TJ et al., PMID: 18519460) did reduce gastrointestinal-illness absence with sanitizer plus surface disinfection. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit): programmes are cheap and safe, but a dependable absence reduction is not established.

cards.headline: Cochrane rinse-free hand wash review: illness absenteeism IRR 0.82 (6 studies) but very low-certainty; any-cause absenteeism IRR 0.91
cards.summary: Cochrane rinse-free hand wash review: illness absenteeism IRR 0.82 (6 studies) but very low-certainty; any-cause absenteeism IRR 0.91
cards.people: 19 randomised trials with 30,747 participants aged 2–18 in preschool and school settings (13 in elementary/primary schools), comparing rinse-free hand wash (rub, sanitizer, gel, foam) with soap-and-water washing, education alone, or no intervention.
cards.result: For absenteeism due to any illness, the pooled incidence rate ratio was 0.82 (95% CI 0.69 to 0.97; 6 studies) — rinse-free hand washing may reduce illness absence (about 13 fewer days per the review's presentation). For absenteeism for any reason, IRR was 0.91 (95% CI 0.82 to 1.01; 2 studies), little to no difference. Every outcome was graded low or very low certainty, mainly for high risk of bias (blinding is near-impossible) and inconsistency.
cards.watchOut: Very low certainty means the true effect could be materially different; most trials are small, short, and from high-income settings, and several combine sanitizer with education or disinfection, so 'hand hygiene' here is a bundle, not a single ingredient.
cards.source: Munn Z et al. Rinse-free hand wash for reducing absenteeism among preschool and school children. The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2020. PMID: 32270476. cards.headline: WISE trial, Addis Ababa (60 schools, 6,229 pupils): no effect on absence (aOR 1.07) or diarrhoea; borderline fewer respiratory illnesses (aOR 0.84)
cards.summary: WISE trial, Addis Ababa (60 schools, 6,229 pupils): no effect on absence (aOR 1.07) or diarrhoea; borderline fewer respiratory illnesses (aOR 0.84)
cards.people: 60 public primary schools in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia, randomised to a water-and-hygiene programme (drinking-water storage and filtration, handwashing stations, behaviour-change promotion; planned sanitation improvements were not realised) or waitlist control over one academic year; 6,229 pupils aged 7–16 enrolled. NCT05024890.
cards.result: Roll-call absence: adjusted OR 1.07 (95% CI 0.83 to 1.38) — no effect. Pupil-reported diarrhoea in the past 7 days: aOR 1.15 (95% CI 0.84 to 1.59) — no effect. Pupil-reported respiratory illness: aOR 0.84 (95% CI 0.71 to 1.00, p=0.046) — a 16% relative reduction in odds, borderline. Menstrual-care self-efficacy rose slightly (+3.32 on a 0–100 scale).
cards.watchOut: The intervention as delivered lacked its sanitation component, and illness outcomes were pupil-reported. A well-run large trial finding no absence effect is the strongest single piece of evidence on this shelf and pulls against the pooled small-trial signal.
cards.source: Bick S et al. Impact of a school-based water and hygiene intervention on child health and school attendance in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia: a cluster-randomised controlled trial. BMC medicine. 2024. PMID: 39218883. Registry ID: NCT05024890. cards.headline: Sandora 2008 US trial: sanitizer plus surface disinfection reduced gastrointestinal-illness absence; respiratory absence unchanged
cards.summary: Sandora 2008 US trial: sanitizer plus surface disinfection reduced gastrointestinal-illness absence; respiratory absence unchanged
cards.people: 285 students in grades 3–5 at a single US elementary school; intervention classrooms used alcohol-based hand sanitizer at school plus daily quaternary-ammonium surface disinfection for 8 weeks; control classrooms followed usual hand-washing and cleaning. NCT00514670.
cards.result: The adjusted absenteeism rate for gastrointestinal illness was significantly lower in intervention classrooms; absenteeism for respiratory illness did not differ significantly. Norovirus — the only virus detected — was found less often on intervention-classroom surfaces (9% versus 29%).
cards.watchOut: One school, 285 children, 8 weeks: this cannot carry a general claim, and the record reports the gastrointestinal result without absolute absence rates. It shows a bundle can work in one setting, not that programmes generally reduce absence.
cards.source: Sandora TJ et al. Reducing absenteeism from gastrointestinal and respiratory illness in elementary school students: a randomized, controlled trial of an infection-control intervention. Pediatrics. 2008. PMID: 18519460. Registry ID: NCT00514670. cards.summary: Synthesis: small pooled benefit at very low certainty, one large null trial on absence, one small positive trial — the honest stamp is MAYBE

shelves.title: Screen-and-treat for malaria in pregnancy matches preventive treatment on birth outcomes in low-resistance areas — but in high-resistance Malawi it left more malaria at delivery and more fetal loss
shelves.question: In pregnant women in malaria-endemic Africa, does intermittent screening and treatment for malaria match intermittent preventive treatment for preventing placental malaria and low birthweight?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Africa · Antimalarials/therapeutic use · Birth Weight · Burkina Faso · Drug Combinations · Female · Gambia · Ghana · Hemoglobins/analysis · Humans · Malaria/drug therapy · Mali · Mass Screening · Placenta/parasitology · Pregnancy · Pregnancy Complications, Parasitic/diagnosis/drug therapy · Pregnancy Outcome · Pyrimethamine/therapeutic use · Sulfadoxine/therapeutic use · Treatment Outcome · Young Adult
shelves.balance: SPLIT — the answer depends on where the parasites stand on sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine (SP) resistance. In four West African countries with low SP resistance, the Tagbor trial (PMID: 26258474; 5,354 women) found screen-and-treat with artemether-lumefantrine non-inferior to IPTp-SP on low birthweight (15.6% versus 15.1%), anaemia and placental malaria (24.2% versus 24.5%). In Malawi, where SP resistance is high, the Madanitsa trial (PMID: 27622558; 1,873 women) found similar adverse birth outcomes (29.9% versus 28.8%) but more malaria at delivery with screen-and-treat (48.7% versus 40.8%) and more fetal loss (2.6% versus 1.3%; RR 2.06). The individual-participant meta-analysis of five trials (Gutman JR et al., PMID: 34746720; 10,821 pregnancies) found no difference in adverse pregnancy outcomes (RR 1.00) and no superiority for screening, with more subpatent infections missed by rapid tests. PROPOSED SPLIT: birth outcomes match, infection control does not — screening is not a superior replacement for preventive treatment anywhere it has been tested.

cards.headline: Tagbor 2015 (West Africa, low SP resistance): screen-and-treat non-inferior — low birthweight 15.6% vs 15.1%, placental malaria 24.2% vs 24.5%
cards.summary: Tagbor 2015 (West Africa, low SP resistance): screen-and-treat non-inferior — low birthweight 15.6% vs 15.1%, placental malaria 24.2% vs 24.5%
cards.people: 5,354 primi- or secundigravid women in The Gambia, Mali, Burkina Faso and Ghana, individually randomised to intermittent screening with a rapid diagnostic test plus artemether-lumefantrine if positive (2–3 screens), or IPTp with sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine (2–3 doses). NCT01084213.
cards.result: Low birthweight occurred in 15.6% (screen-and-treat) versus 15.1% (IPTp-SP) (OR 1.03, 95% CI 0.88 to 1.22); mean haemoglobin before delivery 10.94 versus 10.97 g/dL; active placental malaria 24.2% versus 24.5% (OR 0.95, 95% CI 0.81 to 1.12) — non-inferior on all primary endpoints. More women in the screening group presented with parasitaemia between scheduled visits (310 versus 182 episodes), though malaria admissions were similar.
cards.watchOut: Conducted where SP still works — the setting least favourable to the new strategy's rationale. Non-inferiority there does not answer the high-resistance question, and between-visit parasitaemia was visibly worse under screening.
cards.source: Tagbor H et al. A Non-Inferiority, Individually Randomized Trial of Intermittent Screening and Treatment versus Intermittent Preventive Treatment in the Control of Malaria in Pregnancy. cards.headline: Madanitsa 2016 (Malawi, high SP resistance): birth outcomes similar (29.9% vs 28.8%) but malaria at delivery 48.7% vs 40.8% and fetal loss 2.6% vs 1.3%
cards.summary: Madanitsa 2016 (Malawi, high SP resistance): birth outcomes similar (29.9% vs 28.8%) but malaria at delivery 48.7% vs 40.8% and fetal loss 2.6% vs 1.3%
cards.people: 1,873 HIV-seronegative women at three Malawian sites with high SP resistance, randomised to scheduled screening with rapid tests plus dihydroartemisinin-piperaquine if positive, or IPTp-SP, at 3–4 visits in the second and third trimesters.
cards.result: Adverse live-birth outcome (small-for-gestational-age, low birthweight or preterm) was 29.9% with screen-and-treat versus 28.8% with IPTp-SP (RR 1.04, 95% CI 0.90 to 1.20). But malaria at delivery was more common with screening (48.7% versus 40.8%; RR 1.19, 95% CI 1.07 to 1.33), and fetal loss was more common (2.6% versus 1.3%; RR 2.06, 95% CI 1.01 to 4.21), highest among screening-arm women who never received treatment because their tests were negative.
cards.watchOut: Open-label design, and the fetal-loss difference rests on small numbers with a confidence interval that just excludes 1. Even so, the direction is consistent: rapid tests miss low-grade infections that preventive treatment would have suppressed.
cards.source: Madanitsa M et al. Scheduled Intermittent Screening with Rapid Diagnostic Tests and Treatment with Dihydroartemisinin-Piperaquine versus Intermittent Preventive Therapy with Sulfadoxine-Pyrimethamine for Malaria in Pregnancy in Malawi: An Open-Label Randomized Controlled Trial. cards.headline: IPD meta-analysis of 5 trials (10,821 pregnancies): adverse pregnancy outcome RR 1.00 — screening not superior anywhere; subpatent infections more common (RR 1.31)
cards.summary: IPD meta-analysis of 5 trials (10,821 pregnancies): adverse pregnancy outcome RR 1.00 — screening not superior anywhere; subpatent infections more common (RR 1.31)
cards.people: Five randomised trials (2007–2014) comparing screen-and-treat with an artemisinin combination versus IPTp-SP — three from low-SP-resistance West Africa, two from high-resistance Kenya and Malawi; individual data for 10,362 pregnancies.
cards.result: Adverse pregnancy outcome (small-for-gestational-age, low birthweight or preterm delivery) did not differ (RR 1.00, 95% CI 0.96 to 1.05). Any malaria infection at delivery was similar (RR 1.08, 95% CI 1.00 to 1.16), but subpatent infections (PCR-positive, test-negative) were more common in screening recipients (RR 1.31, 95% CI 1.05 to 1.62), and subpatent infection was itself associated with low birthweight (adjusted RR 1.13) and preterm delivery (adjusted RR 1.35).
cards.watchOut: The pooled birth-outcome null conceals the Malawi trial's fetal-loss signal, and the analysis is explicit that current rapid tests are the weak link — a more sensitive test could change the comparison, but that is a hypothesis, not a result.
cards.source: Gutman JR et al. cards.summary: Synthesis: screening matches preventive treatment on the outcomes mothers feel, and loses on the infections tests can't see
cards.people: Two large trials in opposite resistance settings (5,354 and 1,873 women) plus an individual-participant meta-analysis of five trials (10,821 pregnancies).
cards.result: Low birthweight/adverse birth outcomes: no difference anywhere (pooled RR 1.00). Infection at delivery: worse under screening in high-resistance Malawi (48.7% vs 40.8%), with fetal loss 2.6% vs 1.3%. PROPOSED SPLIT as stamped; not Tier C — multiple randomised trials plus an IPD meta-analysis carry it.
cards.watchOut: All trials used the current generation of rapid diagnostic tests; the shelf should be revisited if point-of-care tests with substantially better sensitivity are trialled.

shelves.title: Preventive zinc in young children: diarrhoea falls modestly (RR 0.91 in 96 modern trials) — the pneumonia claim from the 1999 pooled analysis (OR 0.59) was not reproduced for respiratory morbidity (RR 1.01)
shelves.question: In young children in low-income settings, does zinc supplementation prevent diarrhoea and pneumonia versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Child · Developing Countries · Diarrhea/prevention & control · Dietary Supplements · Humans · Pneumonia/prevention & control · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Zinc/therapeutic use
shelves.balance: SPLIT — diarrhoea yes, modestly; pneumonia not on current evidence. The 1999 pooled analysis of randomised trials (Bhutta ZA et al., PMID: 10586170) found continuous zinc supplementation reduced diarrhoea incidence (OR 0.82, 95% CI 0.72 to 0.93) and pneumonia incidence (OR 0.59, 95% CI 0.41 to 0.83). The much larger 2023 Cochrane review (Imdad A et al., PMID: 36994923; 96 trials, 219,584 children) confirmed a small diarrhoea reduction (RR 0.91, 95% CI 0.90 to 0.93, moderate certainty) but found little to no difference in lower-respiratory-tract morbidity (RR 1.01, 95% CI 0.95 to 1.08, high certainty) and little to no difference in all-cause mortality (RR 0.93, 95% CI 0.84 to 1.03). Vomiting increased (RR 1.29). PROPOSED SPLIT: a real but small diarrhoea benefit; the pneumonia prevention claim rests on the older, smaller analysis and did not survive the larger one.

cards.headline: Bhutta 1999 pooled analysis: continuous zinc cut diarrhoea incidence (OR 0.82) and pneumonia incidence (OR 0.59)
cards.summary: Bhutta 1999 pooled analysis: continuous zinc cut diarrhoea incidence (OR 0.82) and pneumonia incidence (OR 0.59)
cards.type: Pooled analysis of randomised trials (Bhutta 1999, Zinc Investigators' Collaborative Group)
cards.people: Randomised trials in children under 5 in developing countries given at least half the US recommended daily allowance of zinc: 7 'continuous' trials (1–2 RDA, 5–7 times weekly throughout surveillance) and 3 'short-course' trials (2–4 RDA daily for 2 weeks, then 2–3 months of surveillance), with household-visit morbidity ascertainment.
cards.result: In continuous trials, pooled odds ratios for zinc versus control were 0.82 (95% CI 0.72 to 0.93) for diarrhoea incidence, 0.75 (0.63 to 0.88) for diarrhoea prevalence, and 0.59 (0.41 to 0.83) for pneumonia incidence. Short-course trials showed similar point estimates with wider intervals (pneumonia OR 0.74, 95% CI 0.40 to 1.37). Effects did not differ significantly by age, baseline zinc status, nutrition or sex subgroups.
cards.watchOut: Ten trials from the 1990s, with pneumonia ascertained clinically in an era of variable definitions — the estimate that later, larger evidence failed to reproduce. Small-trial pooled analyses of this vintage tend to overstate effects.
cards.source: Bhutta ZA et al. Prevention of diarrhea and pneumonia by zinc supplementation in children in developing countries: pooled analysis of randomized controlled trials. Zinc Investigators' Collaborative Group. The Journal of pediatrics. 1999. PMID: 10586170.
