cards.headline: Cochrane 2023 (96 trials, 219,584 children): diarrhoea RR 0.91, LRTI morbidity RR 1.01, all-cause mortality RR 0.93, vomiting RR 1.29
cards.summary: Cochrane 2023 (96 trials, 219,584 children): diarrhoea RR 0.91, LRTI morbidity RR 1.01, all-cause mortality RR 0.93, vomiting RR 1.29
cards.people: 96 randomised trials of preventive zinc supplementation versus placebo/no intervention in children aged 6 months to 12 years (most under 5), in 34 countries, 87 of them low- or middle-income; commonest dose 10–15 mg daily as zinc sulfate syrup; median follow-up 26 weeks.
cards.result: Preventive zinc likely reduces all-cause diarrhoea incidence (RR 0.91, 95% CI 0.90 to 0.93; 39 studies, 19,468 participants; moderate certainty) but results in little to no difference in LRTI morbidity (RR 1.01, 95% CI 0.95 to 1.08; 19 studies; high certainty) or all-cause mortality (RR 0.93, 95% CI 0.84 to 1.03). Vomiting episodes increased (RR 1.29, 95% CI 1.14 to 1.46; high certainty). Co-supplementing iron consistently reduced zinc's benefits.
cards.watchOut: The diarrhoea effect (RR 0.91) is small in relative terms — its value depends entirely on how common diarrhoea is where a child lives. The review covers prevention only; therapeutic zinc for acute diarrhoea is a different question with its own evidence.
cards.source: Imdad A et al. Zinc supplementation for preventing mortality, morbidity, and growth failure in children aged 6 months to 12 years. The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2023. PMID: 36994923. cards.summary: Synthesis: the diarrhoea benefit shrank but survived a 20-fold larger evidence base; the pneumonia benefit did not
cards.people: Pooled analysis of 10 trials (1999) versus Cochrane review of 96 trials and 219,584 children (2023).
cards.result: Diarrhoea: OR 0.82 → RR 0.91, still a reduction. Pneumonia/LRTI: OR 0.59 → RR 1.01, no difference, at high certainty. Mortality: RR 0.93, not significant. PROPOSED SPLIT as stamped; not Tier C — the base is large randomised-trial meta-evidence.

shelves.title: STROKESTOP II: NT-proBNP triage concentrated AF detection where it aimed (4.4% new AF in the high-peptide group, almost none below the cut-off) — but screening did not reduce stroke at five years (HR 0.96)
shelves.question: In asymptomatic older adults at high stroke risk, does NT-proBNP-guided systematic ECG screening detect more atrial fibrillation than standard screening invitation?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Atrial Fibrillation/diagnosis/blood · Peptide Fragments/blood · Natriuretic Peptide, Brain/blood · Aged · Electrocardiography · Female · Male · Sweden/epidemiology · Mass Screening/methods · Stroke/diagnosis/epidemiology · Biomarkers/blood
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for detection, with the outcome caveat on the face. In STROKESTOP II (Kemp Gudmundsdottir K et al., PMID: 39217615), all 75–76-year-olds in the Stockholm region were randomised to screening invitation or control (28,712 people); among participants without known AF, NT-proBNP ≥125 ng/L triggered two weeks of four-times-daily ECG recordings, while those below the cut-off had a single ECG. The stepwise report (PMID: 31790147) found new AF in 4.4% of the high-NT-proBNP group versus a single case in the low group, raising known AF prevalence from 8.1% to 10.5% among participants, with anticoagulation started in 94.5% of those newly diagnosed. Yet at a median 5.1 years there was no difference in stroke or systemic embolism between invited and control groups (HR 0.96, 95% CI 0.86 to 1.06). Tier C: a single trial, and a screening claim. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): the peptide triage demonstrably finds AF where it looks — the stroke payoff was not shown.

cards.headline: STROKESTOP II stepwise report: new AF in 4.4% of the high-NT-proBNP group; one case in the low group; anticoagulation started in 94.5% of new diagnoses
cards.summary: STROKESTOP II stepwise report: new AF in 4.4% of the high-NT-proBNP group; one case in the low group; anticoagulation started in 94.5% of new diagnoses
cards.type: Population screening study within a randomised trial (Kemp Gudmundsdottir 2020, STROKESTOP II)
cards.people: All 75/76-year-olds in the Stockholm region (28,712) randomised 1:1 to screening invitation or control; 6,868 accepted, of whom 6,315 (91.9%) had no previously known AF. Participants with NT-proBNP ≥125 ng/L (3,766; 59.6%) received extended handheld ECG screening; those below had a single index ECG.
cards.result: New AF was detected in 2.6% (95% CI 2.2 to 3.0) of participants without previous AF overall, and in 4.4% (95% CI 3.7 to 5.1) of the high-NT-proBNP group, of whom 18% already had AF on the index ECG. In the low-NT-proBNP group, one participant was diagnosed on the index ECG. Screening raised known AF prevalence among participants from 8.1% to 10.5%; oral anticoagulation was initiated in 94.5% of newly diagnosed participants.
cards.watchOut: Detection yield is not a health outcome: the low group's near-zero yield partly reflects that it received almost no screening (a single ECG by design), so the comparison shows triage efficiency, not that low-peptide people have no AF to find.

cards.headline: STROKESTOP II main results: new AF in 2.4% of the invited group — and no difference in stroke or systemic embolism at five years (HR 0.96)
cards.summary: STROKESTOP II main results: new AF in 2.4% of the invited group — and no difference in stroke or systemic embolism at five years (HR 0.96)
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial (Kemp Gudmundsdottir 2024, STROKESTOP II)
cards.people: 28,712 Stockholm residents aged 75–76 randomised to screening invitation (13,905 analysed) or control (13,884); participation in the invited group was 49.2% (6,843). Outcomes from Swedish national registries; median follow-up 5.1 years. NCT02743416.
cards.result: New AF was detected in 2.4% (165 of 6,843) of the intervention group. After 5 years there was no difference between groups in AF prevalence or anticoagulant treatment, and no difference in the primary outcome of stroke or systemic embolism (HR 0.96, 95% CI 0.86 to 1.06). The low-NT-proBNP subgroup had fewer strokes/emboli than control (HR 0.59, 95% CI 0.46 to 0.74), while the high group remained at higher risk than the low group (HR 1.57).
cards.watchOut: Half the invited group did not participate, diluting any screening effect; the low-peptide subgroup's lower event rate is a prognostic observation (a low peptide marks low risk), not evidence that withholding extended screening caused the benefit. Detection success did not convert into a population outcome difference.

shelves.title: Varenicline in adolescent smokers: two placebo-controlled trials, two null primary results — end-of-treatment abstinence 8.9% versus 8.9%, and 20–27% versus 18% at higher enrolment, neither significant
shelves.question: In adolescents who smoke, does varenicline increase abstinence versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Counseling/methods · Double-Blind Method · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Humans · Male · Retrospective Studies · Smoking Cessation/methods · Smoking Cessation Agents/administration & dosage · Tobacco Use Disorder/therapy · Treatment Outcome · Varenicline/administration & dosage · Young Adult
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — on the primary outcomes of both trials. In the US trial (Gray KM et al., PMID: 31609433; 157 smokers aged 14–21), cotinine-confirmed 7-day abstinence at end of treatment was identical: 8.9% on varenicline and 8.9% on placebo (RR 0.97, 95% CI 0.29 to 2.99). Secondary measures favoured varenicline — earlier first abstinence (HR 1.91) and higher self-reported weekly abstinence during treatment (RR 1.81) — but the pre-selected primary endpoint was flat. The larger multinational trial (Gray KM et al., PMID: 32979939; 312 smokers aged 12–19) found continuous abstinence at weeks 9–12 of 20% on high-dose and 27% on low-dose varenicline versus 18% on placebo, neither significant (OR 1.18 and 1.73). Treatment was generally well tolerated in both. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): adult efficacy does not transfer to adolescents on the evidence of these two trials.

cards.headline: Gray 2019 (US, n=157): cotinine-confirmed abstinence at end of treatment 8.9% on varenicline vs 8.9% on placebo (RR 0.97)
cards.summary: Gray 2019 (US, n=157): cotinine-confirmed abstinence at end of treatment 8.9% on varenicline vs 8.9% on placebo (RR 0.97)
cards.people: 157 treatment-seeking adolescent and young-adult smokers aged 14–21 at a Charleston, South Carolina outpatient site, randomised to 12 weeks of varenicline (n=77) or placebo (n=80), all with weekly cessation counselling. NCT01509547.
cards.result: The primary outcome — urine cotinine-confirmed 7-day abstinence at end of treatment — was 8.9% (4 of 45) in both groups (RR 0.97, 95% CI 0.29 to 2.99; P=.96). Secondary outcomes favoured varenicline: earlier first 7-day abstinence (HR 1.91, 95% CI 1.12 to 3.27), higher self-reported weekly abstinence during treatment (RR 1.81, 95% CI 1.09 to 2.99) and at follow-up (RR 1.82). The drug was generally well tolerated.
cards.watchOut: Only 45 participants per group contributed to the primary-outcome denominators — attrition shrank an already small trial, and the confidence interval (0.29 to 2.99) cannot exclude a real effect. The positive secondary outcomes were self-reported, not biochemically confirmed.
cards.source: Gray KM et al. Efficacy and Safety of Varenicline for Adolescent Smoking Cessation: A Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA pediatrics. 2019. PMID: 31609433. Registry ID: NCT01509547. cards.headline: Gray 2020 (multinational, n=312): continuous abstinence weeks 9–12 was 20% high-dose, 27% low-dose, 18% placebo — neither dose significant
cards.summary: Gray 2020 (multinational, n=312): continuous abstinence weeks 9–12 was 20% high-dose, 27% low-dose, 18% placebo — neither dose significant
cards.people: 312 treatment-seeking adolescent smokers aged 12–19 at 57 outpatient centres in the USA, Russia, South Korea, Taiwan, Canada and Georgia, randomised to 12 weeks of high-dose varenicline (n=109), low-dose varenicline (n=103) or placebo (n=100), with brief counselling at all visits and 40 weeks of follow-up. NCT01312909.
cards.result: Continuous abstinence from weeks 9 to 12 (cotinine-confirmed) was 20% (22 of 109) on high-dose, 27% (28 of 103) on low-dose and 18% (18 of 100) on placebo. Neither comparison was significant: high-dose OR 1.18 (95% CI 0.59 to 2.37; p=0.63), low-dose OR 1.73 (0.88 to 3.39; p=0.11). Treatment-emergent adverse events occurred in 60%, 53% and 53% respectively, mostly mild.
cards.watchOut: The low-dose arm numerically beat the high-dose arm — a pattern more consistent with noise around a null than with a dose response. Adolescent quit rates on placebo plus counselling (18%) were substantial, leaving less room for a drug effect than in adult trials.
cards.source: Gray KM et al. High-dose and low-dose varenicline for smoking cessation in adolescents: a randomised, placebo-controlled trial. The Lancet. Child & adolescent health. 2020. cards.summary: Synthesis: two concordant nulls on confirmed abstinence — varenicline's adult effect has not been shown in adolescents
cards.people: Two randomised placebo-controlled trials totalling 469 adolescent/young-adult smokers (ages 12–21), both with counselling in all arms and biochemical confirmation of the primary outcome.
cards.result: Primary abstinence: 8.9% vs 8.9% (RR 0.97); 20%/27% vs 18% (ORs 1.18 and 1.73, both NS). Tolerability acceptable in both trials. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference); not Tier C — two concordant randomised trials carry the null.

shelves.title: Church-based colorectal screening programmes: screening rose in intervention and comparison churches alike — the faith-based programmes themselves added nothing measurable (+6.4 vs +4.7 points, p=.25)
shelves.question: In communities, do faith-based programmes increase colorectal cancer screening among church-going adults versus control education?
shelves.mesh: Black or African American/psychology · Aged · Colonoscopy · Colorectal Neoplasms/diagnosis/prevention & control/psychology · Counseling/methods · Early Detection of Cancer/methods · Exercise/psychology · Female · Health Knowledge, Attitudes, Practice/ethnology · Health Promotion/methods · Humans · Male · Michigan · Middle Aged · Multivariate Analysis · North Carolina · Periodicals as Topic · Program Evaluation · Religion and Medicine · Social Support · Surveys and Questionnaires
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — for the faith-based programme as the active ingredient. In the ACTS of Wellness cluster trial (Leone LA et al., PMID: 26515276; 19 urban African American churches), up-to-date colorectal screening rose by 6.4 percentage points in intervention churches and 4.7 points in comparison churches (p=.25) — no significant programme effect, in a population already 74–76% screened at baseline. In the Holt trial (PMID: 23033548; 16 churches), a spiritually themed education series and an identical non-spiritual series both improved awareness and self-reported screening, with no significant group differences except fecal occult blood test uptake, which rose more in the non-spiritual arm. Screening improved more, within the ACTS intervention arm, among members who actually spoke with a peer counsellor or recalled the newsletters — engagement, not faith content, is the plausible lever. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): churches are workable venues, but the programmes tested did not beat their comparisons.

cards.headline: ACTS of Wellness cluster trial (19 churches): screening +6.4 points intervention vs +4.7 comparison (p=.25); physical activity also unchanged
cards.summary: ACTS of Wellness cluster trial (19 churches): screening +6.4 points intervention vs +4.7 comparison (p=.25); physical activity also unchanged
cards.people: 19 urban African American churches in North Carolina and Michigan randomised to intervention (10) or comparison (9); intervention members received three mailed tailored newsletters over ~6 months plus motivational calls from a peer counsellor if not up-to-date with screening. Baseline screening was already high: 75.9% (n=374) intervention, 73.7% (n=338) comparison.
cards.result: Up-to-date colorectal screening increased by 6.4 percentage points in intervention churches and 4.7 points in comparison churches (p=.25) — not significant. Physical activity did not change significantly either (−0.30 versus −0.05 MET-hours/week, p=.15). Within the intervention arm, screening improved more among members who spoke with a peer counsellor or recalled the newsletters.
cards.watchOut: A ceiling problem: with three-quarters already screened at baseline, the reachable margin was small, and church-level randomisation with 19 clusters limits power. The null is about this programme in this population, not about every church-based design.
cards.source: Leone LA et al. cards.headline: Holt 2013 (16 churches): spiritual and non-spiritual education both raised screening; the only group difference favoured the non-spiritual arm (FOBT)
cards.summary: Holt 2013 (16 churches): spiritual and non-spiritual education both raised screening; the only group difference favoured the non-spiritual arm (FOBT)
cards.people: 16 African American churches assigned to a spiritually based colorectal-cancer education series or an identical non-spiritual comparison, delivered as two group sessions by trained peer community health advisors; enrollees surveyed at baseline, 1 month and 12 months.
cards.result: Both interventions significantly improved awareness of all four screening modalities and self-reported receipt of fecal occult blood testing, flexible sigmoidoscopy and colonoscopy from baseline. There were no significant between-group differences in outcomes except fecal occult blood test utilisation, where the non-spiritual group showed significantly greater pre-post change.
cards.watchOut: Self-reported screening without verification, and a pre-post design within arms: secular trends and the education itself (present in both arms) can explain the shared gains. The trial isolates the spiritual framing — and finds it adds nothing measurable.

shelves.title: Fractional-dose IPV: one-fifth doses boost immunity as well as full doses in primed people (non-inferior in the Cuban trial) and match seroconversion by three doses — but a single fractional dose is clearly weaker (RR 0.61)
shelves.question: In outbreak response, does fractional-dose (one-fifth) intradermal inactivated poliovirus vaccine boost immunity comparably to a full intramuscular dose?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Oral · Antibodies, Viral/blood · Child, Preschool · Dose-Response Relationship, Immunologic · Humans · Immunization Schedule · Immunogenicity, Vaccine · Injections, Intradermal · Poliomyelitis/prevention & control · Poliovirus · Poliovirus Vaccine, Inactivated/administration & dosage/immunology · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Seroconversion
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for boosting and multi-dose schedules, not for a single priming dose. The systematic review and meta-analysis (Mashunye TR et al., PMID: 33939958) found seroconversion after fractional versus full-dose IPV in children diverged by dose count for poliovirus type 2: risk ratio 0.61 (95% CI 0.51 to 0.72) after one dose, 0.90 (0.82 to 1.00) after two, and 0.95 (0.91 to 1.00) after three, with antibody titres lower after fractional doses at every count. The outbreak-relevant evidence is the Cuban boosting trial (Resik S et al., PMID: 28073858): in OPV-primed adults, one-fifth intradermal doses produced immune responses in 94.8–98.0% across serotypes versus 98.0–99.2% for full intramuscular doses, meeting non-inferiority at days 7, 28 and 56. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): in an outbreak, fractional doses stretch supply fivefold and boost primed populations comparably — they are not a like-for-like substitute for a first full dose in a naive child.

cards.headline: Resik 2017 Cuba: fractional intradermal doses boosted 94.8–98.0% of primed adults vs 98.0–99.2% for full dose — non-inferior at days 7, 28 and 56
cards.summary: Resik 2017 Cuba: fractional intradermal doses boosted 94.8–98.0% of primed adults vs 98.0–99.2% for full dose — non-inferior at days 7, 28 and 56
cards.people: 534 adults in Cuba with a history of oral poliovirus vaccine receipt, randomised to fractional-dose IPV (one-fifth dose, intradermal) or full-dose IPV (intramuscular) on days 0 and 28; 503 (94.2%) completed all requirements. Seroconversion or ≥4-fold titre rise was the primary endpoint, with a 10% non-inferiority margin. ACTRN12615000305527.
cards.result: Twenty-eight days after the first dose, immune responses in the fractional group were 94.8% (type 1), 98.0% (type 2) and 98.0% (type 3), versus 98.1%, 98.0% and 99.2% in the full-dose group. Non-inferiority was achieved on days 7, 28 and 56 for all serotypes. No serious adverse events were reported.
cards.watchOut: Boosting in OPV-primed adults is the easiest test fractional dosing will ever face — memory responses are brisk. This trial says nothing about priming infants, which is where the meta-analysis below shows fractional doses lag.

cards.headline: Meta-analysis (10 completed studies): seroconversion RR for fractional vs full dose 0.61 at one dose, 0.90 at two, 0.95 at three; titres always lower
cards.summary: Meta-analysis (10 completed studies): seroconversion RR for fractional vs full dose 0.61 at one dose, 0.90 at two, 0.95 at three; titres always lower
cards.people: 14 articles (10 completed studies) comparing fractional-dose (0.1 mL) with full-dose (0.5 mL) IPV immunogenicity in healthy children aged ≤5 years, any route or dose count, with measurements at least 4 weeks after vaccination.
cards.result: For poliovirus type 2, seroconversion risk ratios (fractional versus full) were 0.61 (95% CI 0.51 to 0.72) after one dose, 0.90 (0.82 to 1.00) after two doses and 0.95 (0.91 to 1.00) after three doses, with similar patterns for types 1 and 3. Geometric mean titres were lower with fractional doses at every dose count (type 2 differences −0.49 to −0.98). Certainty was high for three-dose comparisons and moderate otherwise.
cards.watchOut: Heterogeneity was substantial in the one- and two-dose analyses, and seroconversion is an immunogenicity surrogate — population protection in an actual outbreak also depends on coverage speed, which is the fractional strategy's real argument and is not measured here.
cards.source: Mashunye TR et al. Fractional dose compared with standard dose inactivated poliovirus vaccine in children: a systematic review and meta-analysis. The Lancet. Infectious diseases. 2021. cards.headline: Synthesis: fractional IPV is a supply-stretching booster strategy with trial support — and a documented weakness as a single priming dose
cards.summary: Synthesis: fractional IPV is a supply-stretching booster strategy with trial support — and a documented weakness as a single priming dose
cards.people: One randomised boosting trial in 503 primed adults and one meta-analysis of 10 paediatric immunogenicity studies.
cards.result: Boosting: non-inferior. Priming: one fractional dose seroconverts ~39% relatively fewer children (RR 0.61); by three doses the gap closes (RR 0.95) though titres stay lower. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) for the outbreak-boost use named in the question; not Tier C — randomised and meta-analytic evidence agree on the split.
cards.watchOut: This shelf concerns immunogenicity. It does not cover fractional-dose priming schedules in infancy as a standalone policy question, which has its own trial literature and a different balance.

shelves.title: Chlorfenapyr-pyrethroid bed nets beat standard nets where mosquitoes resist pyrethroids: malaria prevalence 25.6% vs 45.8% and incidence halved in two cluster trials — pyriproxyfen nets did not
shelves.question: In areas with pyrethroid-resistant mosquitoes, do dual-active-ingredient insecticidal nets (chlorfenapyr-pyrethroid or pyriproxyfen-pyrethroid) protect against malaria better than standard pyrethroid-only nets?
shelves.mesh: Animals · Child · Cost-Benefit Analysis · Cross-Sectional Studies · Humans · Insecticide-Treated Bednets · Insecticides · Malaria/epidemiology/prevention & control · Mosquito Control · Pyrethrins/pharmacology · Tanzania/epidemiology
shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit) — for one of the two new net types, in two independent cluster-randomised trials. In Tanzania (Mosha JF et al., PMID: 35339225), malaria infection prevalence in children at 24 months was 25.6% under chlorfenapyr-pyrethroid nets versus 45.8% under pyrethroid-only nets (adjusted odds ratio 0.45, 95% CI 0.30 to 0.67). In Benin (Accrombessi M et al., PMID: 36706778), mean malaria incidence over 2 years was 0.56 cases per child-year under chlorfenapyr nets versus 1.03 under standard nets (hazard ratio 0.54, 95% CI 0.42 to 0.70). Pyriproxyfen-pyrethroid nets did not significantly beat standard nets in either trial (aOR 0.79 and HR 0.86, both non-significant), and piperonyl-butoxide nets also failed in Tanzania (aOR 0.99). Chlorfenapyr nets were cost-effective in the Tanzanian economic analysis at US$19–28 per DALY averted. Both trials were run where pyrethroid resistance is high; where mosquitoes remain susceptible, standard nets may do as well. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): two concordant cluster trials, one clear winner among the dual-ingredient nets.

cards.headline: Mosha 2022 (Tanzania): malaria prevalence at 24 months 25.6% on chlorfenapyr nets vs 45.8% on standard nets (aOR 0.45) — pyriproxyfen and PBO nets no better than standard
cards.summary: Mosha 2022 (Tanzania): malaria prevalence at 24 months 25.6% on chlorfenapyr nets vs 45.8% on standard nets (aOR 0.45) — pyriproxyfen and PBO nets no better than standard
cards.people: 84 clusters (39,307 households) in Misungwi, Tanzania, an area of pyrethroid-resistant vectors; 147,230 nets distributed (one per two people). Arms: pyrethroid-only (reference), pyriproxyfen-pyrethroid, chlorfenapyr-pyrethroid, or piperonyl-butoxide-pyrethroid nets. Primary outcome: malaria infection prevalence in children aged 6 months to 14 years at 24 months.
cards.result: Prevalence at 24 months: 45.8% (549/1199) on pyrethroid-only nets, 37.5% on pyriproxyfen nets (aOR 0.79, 95% CI 0.54 to 1.17; p=0.24), 40.7% on piperonyl-butoxide nets (aOR 0.99, 0.67 to 1.45) and 25.6% (326/1272) on chlorfenapyr nets (aOR 0.45, 0.30 to 0.67; p=0.0001). Chlorfenapyr nets cost US$19 more per DALY averted to public providers than standard nets. Net use fell from 72.1% at 3 months to 40.9% at 24 months.
cards.watchOut: Prevalence in cross-sectional surveys, not clinical episodes, is the primary outcome, and net use decayed substantially by 24 months in all arms — the comparison is of net types as actually used, in one high-resistance setting. Skin irritation or paraesthesia was the commonest side-effect in all groups.
cards.source: Mosha JF et al. cards.headline: Accrombessi 2023 (Benin): malaria incidence 0.56 vs 1.03 cases per child-year on chlorfenapyr vs standard nets (HR 0.54); pyriproxyfen nets again no significant difference
cards.summary: Accrombessi 2023 (Benin): malaria incidence 0.56 vs 1.03 cases per child-year on chlorfenapyr vs standard nets (HR 0.54); pyriproxyfen nets again no significant difference
cards.people: 60 clusters (53,854 households, 216,289 inhabitants) in Zou Department, Benin, an area of high pyrethroid resistance; 115,323 nets distributed. Primary outcome: malaria case incidence over 2 years in a cohort of children aged 6 months to 10 years.
cards.result: Mean incidence over 2 years was 1.03 cases per child-year (95% CI 0.96 to 1.09) on pyrethroid-only nets, 0.84 on pyriproxyfen-pyrethroid nets (HR 0.86, 95% CI 0.65 to 1.14; p=0.28) and 0.56 on chlorfenapyr-pyrethroid nets (HR 0.54, 95% CI 0.42 to 0.70; p<0.0001) — roughly 46% fewer cases in relative terms, an absolute difference of about 0.47 cases per child-year.
cards.watchOut: A second positive trial in a second country strengthens the chlorfenapyr claim, but both trials share the same caveat: high baseline pyrethroid resistance. The result licenses chlorfenapyr nets where resistance undermines standard nets; it does not show standard nets failing where vectors are susceptible.

cards.headline: Synthesis: the dual-ingredient idea works only for chlorfenapyr — two trials, same answer, same exception
cards.summary: Synthesis: the dual-ingredient idea works only for chlorfenapyr — two trials, same answer, same exception
cards.people: Two cluster-randomised trials in Tanzania (84 clusters) and Benin (60 clusters), each comparing dual-active-ingredient nets with pyrethroid-only nets over 2 years in pyrethroid-resistant settings.
cards.result: Chlorfenapyr-pyrethroid nets: malaria prevalence aOR 0.45 and incidence HR 0.54 versus standard nets. Pyriproxyfen-pyrethroid nets: aOR 0.79 and HR 0.86, neither significant. Piperonyl-butoxide nets (one trial): aOR 0.99. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit) for chlorfenapyr nets in resistant settings; the shelf's negative half — pyriproxyfen nets — is part of the answer, not a footnote.
cards.watchOut: Durability of the chlorfenapyr effect beyond 2 years and the evolution of chlorfenapyr resistance are open; both trial teams flag resistance management as the condition for scale-up.
cards.source: Synthesis of Mosha JF et al. Lancet. 2022 (PMID: 35339225); Accrombessi M et al. Lancet. 2023 (PMID: 36706778).

shelves.title: Handwashing promotion cuts diarrhoea episodes by about a third in day-care and by about a quarter in communities — and a behaviour-change campaign lifted actual handwashing with soap from 2% to 37%
shelves.question: Does promoting handwashing with soap prevent diarrhoea in children and adults, in day-care, school, community and hospital settings?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Bias · Child · Child Day Care Centers/statistics & numerical data · Community-Acquired Infections/prevention & control · Cross Infection/prevention & control · Developed Countries/statistics & numerical data · Developing Countries/statistics & numerical data · Diarrhea/prevention & control · Hand Disinfection/methods · Humans · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Schools/statistics & numerical data · Soaps
shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit) — one of the oldest ideas in prevention, and the randomised evidence supports it. The Cochrane review of 29 trials (Ejemot-Nwadiaro RI et al., PMID: 33539552) found handwashing promotion prevented about a third of diarrhoea episodes in child day-care and schools in high-income countries (incidence rate ratio 0.70, 95% CI 0.58 to 0.85; high-certainty) and probably about a quarter in communities in low- and middle-income countries (IRR 0.71, 0.62 to 0.81; moderate-certainty), with larger effects where soap was provided free (RR 0.66) than with education alone (RR 0.84). The SuperAmma cluster trial in India (Biran A et al., PMID: 25102847) shows the behaviour itself can be moved at scale: observed handwashing with soap at key events rose from about 1–2% at baseline to 37% in intervention villages versus 6% in controls at 6 months. No trial in the review measured diarrhoea deaths or cost-effectiveness, follow-up was short, and behaviour measurement is easily biased. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): many trials, consistent direction, honest surrogate — episodes, not deaths.

cards.headline: Cochrane 2021 (29 trials): diarrhoea episodes down by about 30% in day-care and schools and about 29% in LMIC communities; free soap beat education alone
cards.summary: Cochrane 2021 (29 trials): diarrhoea episodes down by about 30% in day-care and schools and about 29% in LMIC communities; free soap beat education alone
cards.type: Systematic review of randomised trials (Ejemot-Nwadiaro 2021, Cochrane)
cards.people: 29 RCTs: 13 in child day-care centres or schools, mainly in high-income countries (54,471 participants), 15 community-based trials in low- and middle-income countries (29,347 participants), and 1 hospital trial in people with AIDS (148 participants). All follow-up was short-term.
cards.result: Handwashing promotion prevented around one-third of diarrhoea episodes in day-care/schools in high-income countries (IRR 0.70, 95% CI 0.58 to 0.85; 9 trials, 4,664 participants, high-certainty evidence) and a similar proportion in the two LMIC school trials (IRR 0.66, 0.43 to 0.99; low-certainty). In LMIC communities it probably prevented about a quarter of episodes (IRR 0.71, 0.62 to 0.81; 9 trials, 15,950 participants, moderate-certainty); trials providing free soap averaged RR 0.66 versus RR 0.84 for education alone. The single hospital trial found 1.68 fewer diarrhoea episodes in the intervention group.
cards.watchOut: Episodes, not deaths: no included trial reported diarrhoea-related mortality or cost-effectiveness, and only four trials measured behaviour change, with methods open to bias. Six of the nine community trials were Asian, so the community estimate is geographically narrow.
cards.source: Ejemot-Nwadiaro RI et al. Hand-washing promotion for preventing diarrhoea. The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2021. PMID: 33539552. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: SuperAmma (Biran 2014): an emotion-based village campaign raised observed handwashing with soap at key events from ~2% to 37% at 6 months (vs 6% in controls)
cards.summary: SuperAmma (Biran 2014): an emotion-based village campaign raised observed handwashing with soap at key events from ~2% to 37% at 6 months (vs 6% in controls)
cards.people: 14 villages in Chittoor district, Andhra Pradesh, India, randomised to a scalable behaviour-change intervention (animated film, skits, public pledging, school and community events) or control; handwashing was measured by direct observation in 20–25 households per village at baseline and at 6 weeks, 6 months and 12 months.
cards.result: Handwashing with soap at key events (after defecation, after cleaning a child's bottom, before food preparation, before eating) was rare at baseline (1% intervention vs 2% control). At 6 weeks it was 19% versus 4% (difference 15%, p=0.005) and at 6 months 37% versus 6% (difference 31%, p=0.02). At 12 months, after control villages received a shortened intervention, both groups were at 29%.
cards.watchOut: The outcome is observed behaviour, not diarrhoea — this trial is the mechanism card for the Cochrane result, showing promotion can change the behaviour itself, durably to at least 6 months. Fourteen villages is a small cluster count, and observation can itself change behaviour despite the study's masking efforts.

shelves.title: Vaccinating children against influenza protected their unvaccinated neighbours: 3.1% vs 7.6% confirmed influenza in non-recipients in the Hutterite colony trial (61% protective effectiveness)
shelves.question: Does vaccinating children and adolescents against influenza reduce influenza illness in unvaccinated members of their communities (herd protection)?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Age Factors · Aged · Canada/epidemiology · Child · Child, Preschool · Double-Blind Method · Female · Hepatitis A Vaccines/administration & dosage · Humans · Influenza A virus/genetics/immunology · Influenza B virus/genetics/immunology · Influenza Vaccines/administration & dosage · Influenza, Human/epidemiology/prevention & control/transmission · Male · Middle Aged · Religion · Reverse Transcriptase Polymerase Chain Reaction · Rural Population · Young Adult
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one well-designed cluster trial, with a wide confidence interval. Loeb M et al. (PMID: 20215608) randomised 49 Hutterite colonies to vaccinate children aged 36 months to 15 years with inactivated influenza vaccine or hepatitis A vaccine (an active control), achieving about 83% coverage. Among community members who did not receive study vaccine, PCR-confirmed influenza occurred in 39 of 1,271 (3.1%) in influenza-vaccine colonies versus 80 of 1,055 (7.6%) in control colonies — a protective effectiveness of 61% (95% CI 8% to 83%; p=0.03); across all residents the rates were 4.5% versus 10.6% (effectiveness 59%). No serious vaccine adverse events were observed. The setting — closed, rural, communal colonies — maximises measurable herd effects and may flatter what school-based programmes achieve in open populations; the confidence interval reaches down to 8%. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), Tier C: a single cluster trial carrying a population-level claim.

cards.headline: Loeb 2010: influenza in non-recipients 3.1% (flu-vaccine colonies) vs 7.6% (control colonies) — 61% relative protective effectiveness, CI 8% to 83%
cards.summary: Loeb 2010: influenza in non-recipients 3.1% (flu-vaccine colonies) vs 7.6% (control colonies) — 61% relative protective effectiveness, CI 8% to 83%
cards.people: 49 Hutterite colonies in Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba, Canada: 947 children and adolescents aged 36 months to 15 years received study vaccine (inactivated trivalent influenza vaccine or hepatitis A vaccine as control, allocated by colony, blinded), and 2,326 community members who did not receive study vaccine were followed over the 2008–09 season. Coverage averaged 83% (influenza colonies) and 79% (control colonies).
cards.result: Among non-recipients, PCR-confirmed influenza illness occurred in 39 of 1,271 (3.1%) in influenza-vaccine colonies versus 80 of 1,055 (7.6%) in hepatitis A colonies: protective effectiveness 61% (95% CI 8% to 83%; p=0.03) in relative terms, an absolute difference of 4.5 percentage points. Among all participants, rates were 80 of 1,773 (4.5%) versus 159 of 1,500 (10.6%), effectiveness 59% (95% CI 5% to 82%). No serious vaccine adverse events were observed.
cards.watchOut: One season, one virus mix, and an unusually favourable setting for herd effects: small, stable, communal colonies with high coverage. The confidence interval is wide enough to include a small effect (8%), and the trial cannot say what coverage an open urban school programme would need.
cards.source: Loeb M et al. Effect of influenza vaccination of children on infection rates in Hutterite communities: a randomized trial. JAMA. 2010. PMID: 20215608. Registry ID: NCT00877396. shelves.title: Hepatitis B immunoglobulin plus vaccine at birth: only 6% of infants of highly infectious mothers became carriers, versus 88% of controls in the founding trial
shelves.question: In newborn infants of hepatitis B surface antigen-positive (especially e-antigen-positive) mothers, does hepatitis B immunoglobulin plus hepatitis B vaccine at birth prevent perinatal hepatitis B infection and the carrier state?
shelves.mesh: Carrier State/prevention & control · Clinical Trials as Topic · Double-Blind Method · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Hepatitis B/prevention & control/transmission · Hepatitis B Antibodies/analysis · Hepatitis B e Antigens/analysis · Hepatitis B virus/immunology · Humans · Immunization, Passive · Infant · Infant, Newborn · Maternal-Fetal Exchange · Pregnancy · Viral Vaccines
shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit) — among the most decisive prevention results in the library, from the pre-vaccine-era trial record. In the founding randomised blinded trial in Taipei (Beasley RP et al., PMID: 6138642), infants of e-antigen-positive carrier mothers received HBIG at birth plus vaccine on one of three schedules: persistent HBs antigenaemia developed in only 9 of 159 infants (6%), versus 88% of controls; the combined efficacy was 94%, compared with 71% for HBIG alone and 75% for vaccine alone in the programme's comparisons. The Cochrane review of 29 randomised trials (Lee C et al., PMID: 16625613) found vaccine plus HBIG reduced hepatitis B occurrence versus vaccine alone (relative risk 0.54, 95% CI 0.41 to 0.73, 10 trials) and versus placebo or no intervention (RR 0.08, 0.03 to 0.17, 3 trials), with vaccine alone also effective (RR 0.28). The trials are old — plasma-derived vaccine era — because the question became untestable once the answer was known; modern recombinant vaccines inherit the result. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): a near-total effect on the carrier state, consistent across the trial record.

cards.headline: Beasley 1983: persistent antigenaemia in 6% of infants given HBIG plus vaccine vs 88% of controls — combined efficacy 94%
cards.summary: Beasley 1983: persistent antigenaemia in 6% of infants given HBIG plus vaccine vs 88% of controls — combined efficacy 94%
cards.people: Infants born in Taipei to e-antigen-positive HBsAg carrier mothers (the highest-transmission group), given hepatitis B immune globulin immediately after birth plus hepatitis B vaccine on one of three schedules, compared within the programme against HBIG alone, vaccine alone and untreated controls. 159 infants received the combined prophylaxis.
cards.result: There was no difference in efficacy between the three vaccine schedules. Persistent HBs antigenaemia developed in only 9 of 159 infants (6%) receiving combined prophylaxis, but in 88% of controls. Combined efficacy was 94%, compared with 71% for HBIG alone and 75% for vaccination alone. Antibodies developed in all infants who did not become antigenaemic.
cards.watchOut: A 1983 trial with plasma-derived vaccine, in a single very-high-risk population (e-antigen-positive mothers in Taiwan); absolute risks in infants of e-antigen-negative mothers are far lower. The trial's own lesson — HBIG as soon as possible after birth, vaccine timing flexible within the first month — is operational, and modern practice gives both within 12–24 hours.
cards.source: Beasley RP et al. Prevention of perinatally transmitted hepatitis B virus infections with hepatitis B immune globulin and hepatitis B vaccine. Lancet (London, England). 1983. PMID: 6138642. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Cochrane 2006 (29 trials): vaccine plus HBIG beat vaccine alone (RR 0.54) and placebo (RR 0.08) for hepatitis B occurrence in newborns of HBsAg-positive mothers
cards.summary: Cochrane 2006 (29 trials): vaccine plus HBIG beat vaccine alone (RR 0.54) and placebo (RR 0.08) for hepatitis B occurrence in newborns of HBsAg-positive mothers
cards.type: Systematic review of randomised trials (Lee 2006, Cochrane)
cards.people: 29 randomised clinical trials (5 rated high quality) of hepatitis B vaccine and/or HBIG in newborn infants of HBsAg-positive mothers, with hepatitis B occurrence (HBsAg, HBeAg or anti-HBc positivity) as the primary outcome at maximal follow-up.
cards.result: Versus placebo or no intervention, vaccine reduced hepatitis B occurrence (RR 0.28, 95% CI 0.20 to 0.40; 4 trials), HBIG reduced it (RR 0.50, 0.41 to 0.60; 1 trial) and plasma-derived vaccine plus HBIG reduced it most (RR 0.08, 0.03 to 0.17; 3 trials). Versus vaccine alone, vaccine plus HBIG reduced occurrence (RR 0.54, 0.41 to 0.73; 10 trials). Recombinant and plasma-derived vaccines did not differ (RR 1.00). Few trials reported adverse events; the interventions seemed safe.
cards.watchOut: Most included trials predate modern trial reporting, only three trials enrolled e-antigen-negative mothers, and adverse-event reporting was thin. The review's age is a feature of the question: once efficacy reached the 90% range, placebo-controlled trials in newborns became unethical, so this record will not be refreshed.
cards.source: Lee C et al. Hepatitis B immunisation for newborn infants of hepatitis B surface antigen-positive mothers. The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2006. PMID: 16625613. cards.summary: Synthesis: perinatal hepatitis B is a solved prevention problem where the birth dose is actually delivered

shelves.title: Telephone counselling and quitlines help smokers quit: risk ratio 1.37 for call-back counselling to helpline callers and 1.27 in other settings, across 77 trials
shelves.question: Does telephone counselling — proactive call-back support from quitlines, or telephone counselling offered in other settings — help smokers stop smoking?
shelves.mesh: Counseling/methods · Hotlines · Humans · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Smoking Cessation/statistics & numerical data
shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit) — a modest relative effect, replicated at scale. The Cochrane review of 77 trials (Stead LF et al., PMID: 23934971) found that among smokers who contacted helplines, those randomised to multiple sessions of proactive call-back counselling quit at higher rates than controls (risk ratio 1.37, 95% CI 1.26 to 1.50; 9 studies, over 24,000 participants). Telephone counselling offered outside quitline settings also increased quitting (RR 1.27, 1.20 to 1.36; 51 studies, over 30,000 participants), with some evidence of a dose response — one or two brief calls are less likely to help, three or more calls increase the chances — and a smaller relative increment when counselling was added to pharmacotherapy than when the comparison was self-help material alone. Effects are relative gains on low absolute quit rates, which the review reports as risk ratios rather than percentages; at typical control quit rates of around 5–10%, an RR of 1.3 is roughly 2–3 extra quitters per 100 smokers counselled. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): many trials, consistent direction, honestly modest size.

cards.headline: Cochrane 2013 (77 trials): quitline call-back counselling RR 1.37; telephone counselling in other settings RR 1.27; more calls, more effect
cards.summary: Cochrane 2013 (77 trials): quitline call-back counselling RR 1.37; telephone counselling in other settings RR 1.27; more calls, more effect
cards.type: Systematic review of randomised trials (Stead 2013, Cochrane)
cards.people: 77 randomised or quasi-randomised trials of proactive or reactive telephone counselling for smokers or recent quitters, including 9 studies of helpline callers (over 24,000 participants) and 51 studies recruiting in other settings (over 30,000 participants); abstinence at at least 6 months, with lost-to-follow-up counted as smoking.
cards.result: Among helpline callers, multiple sessions of proactive counselling increased cessation versus control (RR 1.37, 95% CI 1.26 to 1.50). Telephone counselling not initiated by helpline calls also increased quitting (RR 1.27, 1.20 to 1.36). Meta-regression suggested slightly larger effects with more calls offered and in smokers motivated to quit; the relative benefit was smaller when counselling was added to pharmacotherapy than when controls received only self-help materials or brief advice. Two trials comparing counselling intensities both found a dose response.
cards.watchOut: These are relative effects: the review's headline numbers are risk ratios on abstinence, and absolute quit-rate gains are a few percentage points. Three single-contact counselling comparisons found no significant differences, and eight heterogeneous studies could not be pooled — the benefit belongs to structured multi-call proactive counselling, not to any phone call.
cards.source: Stead LF et al. Telephone counselling for smoking cessation. The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2013. PMID: 23934971. Registry ID: none in the record. shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — for diarrhoea, the outcome the programmes are sold on. In Mali's cluster trial of community-led total sanitation (Pickering AJ et al., PMID: 26475017), 121 villages were randomised: latrine access nearly doubled (65% vs 35% of households) and reported open defecation fell sharply, yet diarrhoea prevalence in under-5s was 22% versus 24% (prevalence ratio 0.93, 95% CI 0.76 to 1.14) — while children in CLTS villages were taller (height-for-age Z +0.18) and less often stunted (35% vs 41%). In Odisha, India (Clasen T et al., PMID: 25442689), a government sanitation campaign raised village latrine coverage from 9% to 63% of households (vs 8% to 12% in controls), but 7-day diarrhoea prevalence in under-5s was 8.8% versus 9.1% (period prevalence ratio 0.97, 0.83 to 1.12), with no clear gains in helminth infection or malnutrition. Coverage is not exposure reduction: partial uptake leaves transmission pathways open. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — for diarrhoea in these two trials; the Mali growth finding is recorded on the face of the shelf as the unexplained exception.

cards.headline: Pickering 2015 (Mali, CLTS): latrines 65% vs 35% of households, diarrhoea 22% vs 24% (PR 0.93) — but children grew taller (+0.18 height-for-age Z)
cards.summary: Pickering 2015 (Mali, CLTS): latrines 65% vs 35% of households, diarrhoea 22% vs 24% (PR 0.93) — but children grew taller (+0.18 height-for-age Z)
cards.people: 121 villages (4,532 households) in Koulikoro, Mali, randomised to a government community-led total sanitation programme or none; outcomes measured 1.5 years after delivery in children under 5 (3,140 intervention and 2,872 control children assessed for diarrhoea).
cards.result: Diarrhoea prevalence did not differ: 706 of 3,140 (22%) in CLTS villages versus 693 of 2,872 (24%) in controls (prevalence ratio 0.93, 95% CI 0.76 to 1.14). Access to a private latrine was 65% versus 35% of households, and reported open defecation fell to about 9–10% versus 33%. Children in CLTS villages were taller (height-for-age Z score +0.18, 0.03 to 0.32) and less likely to be stunted (35% vs 41%; PR 0.86, 0.74 to 1.0), with the growth benefit concentrated in children under 2 at enrolment.
cards.watchOut: An unmasked behavioural intervention with self-reported sanitation behaviour; the growth benefit without a diarrhoea benefit is biologically puzzling (environmental enteropathy pathways are the usual explanation offered) and comes from secondary outcomes. One trial, one country, one programme model.
cards.source: Pickering AJ et al. Effect of a community-led sanitation intervention on child diarrhoea and child growth in rural Mali: a cluster-randomised controlled trial. The Lancet. Global health. 2015. PMID: 26475017. Registry ID: NCT01900912. cards.headline: Clasen 2014 (Odisha): latrine coverage 9% to 63% of households — diarrhoea prevalence 8.8% vs 9.1% (ratio 0.97), no helminth or nutrition gains
cards.summary: Clasen 2014 (Odisha): latrine coverage 9% to 63% of households — diarrhoea prevalence 8.8% vs 9.1% (ratio 0.97), no helminth or nutrition gains
cards.people: 100 rural villages in Odisha, India (about 51,000 individuals), randomised to a latrine promotion and construction intervention under India's Total Sanitation Campaign or no intervention; health surveillance in about 2,900 households with children under 5 (3,835 children).
cards.result: Mean village latrine coverage rose from 9% to 63% of households in intervention villages versus 8% to 12% in controls. Seven-day diarrhoea prevalence in under-5s was 8.8% versus 9.1% (period prevalence ratio 0.97, 95% CI 0.83 to 1.12). Deaths were similar (162 vs 151 overall). The authors conclude that increased coverage cannot be assumed to deliver health gains without uptake and genuine exposure reduction.
cards.watchOut: Coverage at village level (63%) still leaves a third of households — and shared environmental contamination — in place; the trial tests a real government programme at real-world fidelity, which is both its strength and the limit on what it says about sanitation done completely.
cards.source: Clasen T et al. Effectiveness of a rural sanitation programme on diarrhoea, soil-transmitted helminth infection, and child malnutrition in Odisha, India: a cluster-randomised trial. The Lancet. Global health. 2014. PMID: 25442689. Registry ID: NCT01214785. cards.headline: Synthesis: sanitation programmes deliver infrastructure and behaviour change on paper; the diarrhoea endpoint has now failed in two large randomised tests
cards.summary: Synthesis: sanitation programmes deliver infrastructure and behaviour change on paper; the diarrhoea endpoint has now failed in two large randomised tests
cards.people: Two cluster-randomised trials (121 Malian and 100 Indian villages) of community sanitation programmes versus no programme, with child diarrhoea as a primary outcome in both.
cards.result: Diarrhoea: prevalence ratio 0.93 (Mali) and period prevalence ratio 0.97 (Odisha), both null, despite latrine coverage rising to 65% and 63% of households. Growth: improved in Mali only. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — for diarrhoea; distinct from the household WASH-hardware question on Shelf #969 and the handwashing-promotion question on Shelf #4132.
cards.watchOut: A null for these programmes at this coverage is not a null for sanitation as such — safely managed, near-universal sanitation has strong observational support. The randomised record says the campaign model, as delivered, does not reach the exposure threshold.
cards.source: Synthesis of Pickering AJ et al. The Lancet Global Health. 2015 (PMID: 26475017); Clasen T et al. The Lancet Global Health. 2014 (PMID: 25442689).

shelves.title: Screening houses against mosquitoes: indoor mosquito counts fell by about half (ratio 0.41–0.53) and childhood anaemia was less common (OR ~0.5) in the Gambian randomised trial
shelves.question: Does screening houses (full screening of doors, windows and eaves, or screened ceilings) reduce malaria mosquito entry and childhood anaemia in malaria-endemic areas?
shelves.mesh: Analysis of Variance · Anemia/blood/epidemiology/parasitology · Animals · Anopheles/parasitology/physiology · Bedding and Linens · Child · Child, Preschool · Female · Gambia/epidemiology · Hemoglobins · Housing · Humans · Insecticides · Interior Design and Furnishings/methods · Logistic Models · Malaria, Falciparum/complications/epidemiology/prevention & control/transmission · Male · Morbidity · Mosquito Control/methods · Population Surveillance · Principal Component Analysis · Residence Characteristics
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one randomised trial with an entomological primary endpoint and a supportive clinical secondary, plus observational housing evidence behind it. Kirby MJ et al. (PMID: 19732949) randomised 500 houses in The Gambia to full screening, screened ceilings, or no screening: mean Anopheles gambiae caught per trap per night were 15.2 with full screening and 19.1 with screened ceilings versus 37.5 unscreened (ratios of means 0.41, 95% CI 0.31 to 0.54, and 0.53, 0.40 to 0.70). Among 731 children, anaemia (haemoglobin <80 g/L) affected 12% in both screened groups versus 19% in control houses (adjusted OR 0.53 and 0.51), while parasitaemia did not differ. The systematic review of housing and malaria (Tusting LS et al., PMID: 26055986) found residents of modern houses had lower odds of malaria infection (adjusted OR 0.53) and clinical malaria across observational studies, at low to very low quality. No trial has yet measured clinical malaria incidence as a primary endpoint for screening alone. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), Tier C: the clinical claim rests on a secondary endpoint of one trial plus observational data.

cards.headline: Kirby 2009: mosquitoes per trap per night 15.2 (full screening) and 19.1 (ceilings) vs 37.5 (none); anaemia in children 12% vs 19% (adjusted OR 0.53 and 0.51)
cards.summary: Kirby 2009: mosquitoes per trap per night 15.2 (full screening) and 19.1 (ceilings) vs 37.5 (none); anaemia in children 12% vs 19% (adjusted OR 0.53 and 0.51)
cards.people: 500 occupied houses in and near Farafenni, The Gambia (462 in the modified intention-to-treat analysis), randomised to full screening of windows, doors and closed eaves (n=188 analysed), screened ceilings (n=178) or no screening (n=96), in an area of seasonal transmission and low bednet use. Mosquito entry was measured by fortnightly light traps; anaemia and parasitaemia were measured in 731 children aged 6 months to 10 years living in the houses.
cards.result: Mean female Anopheles gambiae per trap per night: 37.5 (95% CI 31.6 to 43.3) in unscreened houses, 15.2 with full screening (ratio of means 0.41, 0.31 to 0.54; p<0.0001) and 19.1 with screened ceilings (ratio 0.53, 0.40 to 0.70; p<0.0001). Anaemia (haemoglobin <80 g/L) affected 30 of 158 children (19%) in control houses versus 38 of 309 (12%) with full screening (adjusted OR 0.53, 0.29 to 0.97; p=0.04) and 31 of 264 (12%) with ceilings (OR 0.51, 0.27 to 0.96; p=0.04). Parasitaemia frequency did not differ between groups.
cards.watchOut: The primary endpoints were entomological; anaemia is a secondary clinical endpoint with modest numbers, and parasitaemia — the more direct malaria measure — was null. Screening was untreated (no insecticide), houses were in one Gambian town area, and durability, cost and acceptability at programme scale are untested in randomised form.
cards.source: Kirby MJ et al. Effect of two different house screening interventions on exposure to malaria vectors and on anaemia in children in The Gambia: a randomised controlled trial. Lancet (London, England). 2009. PMID: 19732949. Registry ID: ISRCTN51184253. cards.headline: Tusting 2015 meta-analysis: modern housing associated with about half the odds of malaria infection (adjusted OR 0.53) — across observational studies rated low to very low quality
cards.summary: Tusting 2015 meta-analysis: modern housing associated with about half the odds of malaria infection (adjusted OR 0.53) — across observational studies rated low to very low quality
cards.people: 90 studies in qualitative synthesis and 53 with epidemiological outcomes in meta-analysis, comparing malaria risk by house design (overall house type, screening, wall/roof/floor materials, eaves, ceilings, elevation) across malaria-endemic settings; the modern-versus-traditional comparisons were all observational.
cards.result: Residents of modern houses had 47% lower odds of malaria infection than residents of traditional houses (adjusted OR 0.53, 95% CI 0.42 to 0.67; 5 studies) and 45–65% lower odds of clinical malaria (case-control adjusted OR 0.35, 0.20 to 0.62; cohort adjusted rate ratio 0.55, 0.36 to 0.84). Of 53 studies with epidemiological outcomes, 39 (74%) trended toward lower risk with improved house features. Evidence quality was very low to low, with high risk of bias within studies.
cards.watchOut: Housing quality travels with wealth, education and every other malaria determinant; adjusted observational ratios around 0.5 sit exactly at this library's threshold for taking observational evidence seriously, and residual confounding plausibly inflates them. This card supports the trial; it cannot substitute for one.
cards.source: Tusting LS et al. The evidence for improving housing to reduce malaria: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Malaria journal. 2015. PMID: 26055986. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: screening a house keeps mosquitoes out — that much is randomised fact; the step to fewer malaria cases is still inference
cards.summary: Synthesis: screening a house keeps mosquitoes out — that much is randomised fact; the step to fewer malaria cases is still inference
cards.people: One randomised trial of 500 Gambian houses with entomological and child-health endpoints, and a 90-study systematic review of housing and malaria.
cards.result: Mosquito entry: ratios 0.41 (full screening) and 0.53 (ceilings) versus none. Childhood anaemia: OR ~0.5 in both screened groups. Parasitaemia: no difference. Modern housing and malaria infection in observational data: adjusted OR 0.53. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), Tier C.
cards.watchOut: Nets and spraying have randomised clinical-endpoint evidence (Shelf #4129 covers the newest nets); house screening does not yet. The shelf's claim is deliberately limited to entry reduction plus an anaemia signal.
cards.source: Synthesis of Kirby MJ et al. Lancet. 2009 (PMID: 19732949); Tusting LS et al. Malaria Journal. 2015 (PMID: 26055986).

shelves.title: Pictorial cigarette pack warnings beat text-only warnings: quit attempts 40% vs 34% and 7-day quitting 5.7% vs 3.8% in a 2,149-smoker randomised trial
shelves.question: Do pictorial warnings on cigarette packs change smoking behaviour — quit attempts and quitting — compared with text-only warnings?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Drug Labeling · Female · Humans · Intention · Male · Middle Aged · Outcome Assessment, Health Care · Product Labeling/methods · Risk Reduction Behavior · Smoking/psychology · Smoking Cessation/methods/psychology · Smoking Prevention
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a policy intervention with a genuine randomised trial of behaviour, which is rarer than it should be. Brewer NT et al. (PMID: 27273839) randomised 2,149 adult smokers in California and North Carolina to smoke for 4 weeks from packs bearing pictorial warnings or the existing text-only Surgeon General's warnings: smokers with pictorial warnings were more likely to attempt to quit during the trial (40% vs 34%; odds ratio 1.29, 95% CI 1.09 to 1.54) and more likely to have quit for at least 7 days at trial end (5.7% vs 3.8%; OR 1.53, 1.02 to 2.29), with more forgoing of cigarettes, quit intentions and conversations about quitting, and no demographic subgroup differences. The meta-analysis of the experimental literature (Noar SM et al., PMID: 25948713; 37 studies, 33,613 participants) found pictorial warnings outperformed text on 12 of 17 effectiveness outcomes — attention, cognitive and emotional reactions, attitudes and quit intentions — while noting that most experiments measured reactions and intentions rather than behaviour. Four weeks is short, the sample was a convenience sample, and population-level effects after real implementation are a further step. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): behaviour moved in the one large trial designed to measure it.

cards.headline: Brewer 2016: quit attempts 40% vs 34% (OR 1.29) and quit ≥7 days 5.7% vs 3.8% (OR 1.53) after 4 weeks of pictorial vs text-only packs
cards.summary: Brewer 2016: quit attempts 40% vs 34% (OR 1.29) and quit ≥7 days 5.7% vs 3.8% (OR 1.53) after 4 weeks of pictorial vs text-only packs
cards.people: 2,149 adult cigarette smokers recruited from the general population in California and North Carolina (1,901 completed; 88%), randomised to relabel their cigarette packs for 4 weeks with either pictorial warnings (a required warning text plus a picture of smoking harms, on the top half of front and back) or text-only warnings (a current Surgeon General's warning on the side). Primary outcome: attempting to quit during the study.
cards.result: In intention-to-treat analyses (n=2,149), smokers with pictorial warnings were more likely to attempt to quit (40% vs 34%; OR 1.29, 95% CI 1.09 to 1.54) and to have quit for at least the 7 days before trial end (5.7% vs 3.8%; OR 1.53, 1.02 to 2.29). Pictorial warnings also increased forgoing a cigarette, intentions to quit, negative emotional reactions, thinking about harms, and conversations about quitting. Findings did not differ across demographic groups, and no participant withdrew because of adverse events.
cards.watchOut: Four weeks of exposure, self-reported behaviour, and a convenience sample willing to relabel packs and attend visits — real-world warning policies act on all smokers for years, with wear-out of impact over time that a 4-week trial cannot see. The absolute quitting difference (1.9 percentage points) is small per smoker and large only when multiplied by a smoking population.
cards.source: Brewer NT et al. Effect of Pictorial Cigarette Pack Warnings on Changes in Smoking Behavior: A Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA internal medicine. 2016. PMID: 27273839. Registry ID: NCT02247908. cards.headline: Noar 2016 meta-analysis (37 studies, 33,613 participants): pictorial warnings beat text on 12 of 17 outcomes — attention, reactions, attitudes, quit intentions — but behaviour was rarely measured
cards.summary: Noar 2016 meta-analysis (37 studies, 33,613 participants): pictorial warnings beat text on 12 of 17 outcomes — attention, reactions, attitudes, quit intentions — but behaviour was rarely measured
cards.people: 37 experimental studies with 48 independent samples (N=33,613) comparing pictorial with text-only cigarette pack warnings, across countries; outcomes grouped as attention, cognitive/emotional reactions, attitudes, intentions and perceived effectiveness.
cards.result: Pictorial warnings were more effective than text-only warnings for 12 of 17 effectiveness outcomes (all p<0.05): they attracted and held attention better, produced stronger cognitive and emotional reactions, more negative pack and smoking attitudes, and stronger intentions not to start and to quit. Participants rated pictorial warnings as more effective on all 8 perceived-effectiveness outcomes. The authors flag the gaps: little assessment of smoking behaviour and little theory-based research on mechanisms.
cards.watchOut: Most included experiments are brief laboratory or survey exposures measuring reactions, not smoking; perceived effectiveness is not effectiveness. This card establishes the consistency of the psychological pathway that the Brewer trial then connects to behaviour — neither card alone would carry the shelf as well.
cards.source: Noar SM et al. Pictorial cigarette pack warnings: a meta-analysis of experimental studies. Tobacco control. 2016. PMID: 25948713. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: warnings that are seen are warnings that work a little — the behavioural trial and the reaction literature point the same way
cards.summary: Synthesis: warnings that are seen are warnings that work a little — the behavioural trial and the reaction literature point the same way
cards.people: One 2,149-smoker randomised trial of 4 weeks of real pack exposure, and a 37-study meta-analysis of pictorial versus text warnings (33,613 participants).
cards.result: Quit attempts 40% vs 34% (OR 1.29); ≥7-day quitting 5.7% vs 3.8% (OR 1.53); 12 of 17 experimental outcomes favour pictorial warnings. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — modest absolute effects, honestly framed as population-policy effects rather than cessation treatment.
cards.watchOut: This shelf does not compare warnings with cessation services or pharmacotherapy, and says nothing about plain packaging, which is a separate policy with its own literature.
cards.source: Synthesis of Brewer NT et al. JAMA Internal Medicine. 2016 (PMID: 27273839); Noar SM et al. Tobacco Control. 2016 (PMID: 25948713).

shelves.title: Repeated ivermectin mass administration cut malaria episodes in young children (2.00 vs 2.49 episodes per child in one season) — in a single trial of eight villages where most young children were too short to be treated
shelves.question: In malaria-endemic villages, does frequently repeated mass administration of ivermectin to the whole community reduce malaria episodes in young children?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Albendazole/therapeutic use · Antiparasitic Agents/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Burkina Faso · Child · Cluster Analysis · Drug Administration Schedule · Female · Humans · Ivermectin/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Malaria, Falciparum/drug therapy · Male · Mass Drug Administration · Treatment Outcome · Young Adult
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — an ingenious idea (make human blood lethal to the mosquitoes that bite) with exactly one cluster trial behind it. In RIMDAMAL (Foy BD et al., PMID: 30878222), eight villages in Burkina Faso were randomised: in intervention villages, eligible residents received six single doses of ivermectin at 3-week intervals across one rainy season (both groups received one combined ivermectin–albendazole dose). In the active case-detection cohort of children aged 5 and under, cumulative malaria incidence was 2.00 episodes per child (648 episodes among 327 children) versus 2.49 per child in controls (647 among 263) — a risk difference of -0.49 episodes (95% CI -0.79 to -0.21; p=0.0009). Adverse events did not differ significantly (3% vs 2% of participants) and no adverse reactions were reported. The catches are structural: eight clusters is very few, most young children were themselves ineligible for treatment (height under 90 cm), so the effect is entirely indirect, and one season in one district cannot speak to resistance, repeat seasons or other transmission settings. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit), Tier C: a single small-cluster trial of a community-level intervention.

cards.headline: RIMDAMAL (Foy 2019): malaria episodes per child 2.00 vs 2.49 over 18 weeks (difference -0.49, p=0.0009); harms 3% vs 2%, not significantly different
cards.summary: RIMDAMAL (Foy 2019): malaria episodes per child 2.00 vs 2.49 over 18 weeks (difference -0.49, p=0.0009); harms 3% vs 2%, not significantly different
cards.people: 8 villages in Burkina Faso randomised 1:1; 2,712 residents consented and enrolled (1,447 intervention, 1,265 control). All eligible participants (at least 90 cm tall) in both groups received one dose of ivermectin (150–200 µg/kg) plus albendazole (400 mg); the intervention group received five further ivermectin-only doses at 3-week intervals over the 18-week rainy-season treatment phase. Primary outcome: cumulative incidence of uncomplicated malaria in an active case-detection cohort of 590 children aged 5 years or younger.
cards.result: Cumulative malaria incidence was lower in the intervention group: 648 episodes among 327 children (estimated mean 2.00 episodes per child) versus 647 episodes among 263 children in controls (2.49 per child) — risk difference -0.49 (95% CI -0.79 to -0.21; p=0.0009, adjusted for sex and clustering), about a 20% relative reduction. Adverse events occurred in 45 of 1,447 (3%) intervention participants versus 24 of 1,265 (2%) controls (risk ratio 1.63, 1.01 to 2.67; risk difference 1.21, p=0.060), and no adverse reactions were reported.
cards.watchOut: Eight clusters is the minimum a cluster trial can have and remain a trial — village-level chance differences can masquerade as effects despite adjustment. Most children in the outcome cohort were too short to receive ivermectin themselves, so the entire effect is a herd effect through treated older residents; whether it persists across seasons, and what repeated community ivermectin does to parasite and helminth resistance, is untested.
cards.source: Foy BD et al. Efficacy and risk of harms of repeat ivermectin mass drug administrations for control of malaria (RIMDAMAL): a cluster-randomised trial. Lancet (London, England). 2019. PMID: 30878222. Registry ID: NCT02509481. cards.headline: Synthesis: a real effect in one small trial of a big idea — filed at the grade a single 8-village trial earns
cards.summary: Synthesis: a real effect in one small trial of a big idea — filed at the grade a single 8-village trial earns
cards.people: One cluster-randomised trial: 8 villages, 2,712 enrolled residents, 590 children in the outcome cohort, one transmission season.
cards.result: Child malaria episodes: 2.00 vs 2.49 per child per season (difference -0.49, 95% CI -0.79 to -0.21). Harms: no significant difference. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit), Tier C.
cards.watchOut: Larger multi-season trials of ivermectin mass administration have been designed precisely because this result is promising and fragile in equal measure; this shelf should be re-graded the moment one reports.

shelves.title: Novel oral polio vaccine type 2 (nOPV2): two doses seroprotected 92.9% of Gambian infants and 99% of Bangladeshi newborns — but giving it together with bivalent OPV blunted the type 2 response (86% alone versus 65% combined)
shelves.question: In infants and young children, does the genetically stabilised novel oral poliovirus vaccine type 2 (nOPV2) produce protective type 2 antibody responses comparable to the Sabin vaccines it replaces — and what happens when it is given together with bivalent OPV?
shelves.mesh: Child, Preschool · Humans · Infant · Antibodies, Viral · Antibody Formation · Gambia · Immunization Schedule · Poliomyelitis/epidemiology · Poliovirus · Poliovirus Vaccine, Oral
shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit) — for antibody protection, the outcome these trials can measure. In the phase 3 Gambian trial (Ochoge M et al., PMID: 38402887), two doses of nOPV2 left 92.9% of infants and 95.5% of young children seroprotected against type 2 poliovirus, with seroconversion in 85.6% of baseline-seronegative infants; in Bangladeshi newborns (Zaman K et al., PMID: 36495882), two doses at birth and 4 weeks seroconverted 90% and left 99% seroprotected. In Panama (Sáez-Llorens X et al., PMID: 33308427), the novel candidates' day-28 seroprotection in infants (91–95%) was non-inferior to Sabin monovalent OPV2 (94%). The catch is co-administration: in Dhaka (Wilkinson AL et al., PMID: 37178706), giving nOPV2 together with bivalent OPV cut the type 2 response to 65% versus 86% for nOPV2 alone — non-inferiority for type 2 was not met, though types 1 and 3 were unaffected. No trial measures paralysis prevented; the vaccine's reason to exist — greater genetic stability, hence fewer vaccine-derived outbreaks — is a design property the immunogenicity trials support only indirectly, through similar shedding and response profiles. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): nOPV2 reliably immunises infants against type 2 poliovirus at Sabin-like rates, but it should not be co-administered with bivalent OPV when the type 2 response is the point.

cards.headline: Ochoge 2024 (phase 3, Gambia): three nOPV2 lots equivalent (one-dose seroconversion 48.9–49.2%); two doses seroprotected 92.9% of infants and 95.5% of young children
cards.summary: Ochoge 2024 (phase 3, Gambia): three nOPV2 lots equivalent (one-dose seroconversion 48.9–49.2%); two doses seroprotected 92.9% of infants and 95.5% of young children
cards.people: 2,345 infants aged 18 to <52 weeks and 600 young children aged 1 to <5 years in The Gambia, randomised to one or two doses of one of three lots of nOPV2 or one lot of bivalent OPV (infants), or two doses of nOPV2 lot 1 or bivalent OPV (children); safety followed to 3 months after dosing.
cards.result: One-dose type 2 seroconversion rates were 48.9–49.2% across the three nOPV2 lots, with pairwise 95% confidence intervals inside the ±10% equivalence margin (lower bound −5.8%, upper bound 5.4%), so lot-to-lot equivalence was shown. Among baseline-seronegative participants, 143 (85.6%) of 167 infants and 54 (83.1%) of 65 young children seroconverted over the two-dose nOPV2 schedule. Post-two-dose seroprotection was 604 (92.9%) of 650 infants and 276 (95.5%) of 289 young children. No safety concerns were identified; 41.7% of sampled infants were excreting type 2 poliovirus 7 days after dose one.
cards.watchOut: The comparator was bivalent OPV, which contains no type 2 component — so this trial proves nOPV2 immunises and that its lots agree, not that it matches Sabin monovalent OPV2 head-to-head; that comparison rests on the earlier Panama phase 2 trial. Endpoints are antibodies, not paralysis prevented.
cards.source: Ochoge M et al. Safety of the novel oral poliovirus vaccine type 2 (nOPV2) in infants and young children aged 1 to <5 years and lot-to-lot consistency of the immune response to nOPV2 in infants in The Gambia: a phase 3, double-blind, randomised controlled trial. Lancet. 2024. PMID: 38402887. Registry ID: PACTR202010705577776 (as named in the record). cards.headline: Zaman 2023 (newborns, Bangladesh): two doses of nOPV2 at birth and 4 weeks — 90% seroconverted, 99% seroprotected, tolerability matching placebo
cards.summary: Zaman 2023 (newborns, Bangladesh): two doses of nOPV2 at birth and 4 weeks — 90% seroconverted, 99% seroprotected, tolerability matching placebo
cards.people: 330 healthy full-term newborn infants at Matlab, Bangladesh, randomised 2:1 to two doses of nOPV2 or placebo at age 0–3 days and 4 weeks; poliovirus vaccine-naive; antibodies measured at birth, 4 and 8 weeks.
cards.result: nOPV2 was well tolerated: solicited adverse events occurred in 154 (70%) of 220 vaccine recipients and 78 (71%) of 110 placebo recipients, all mild or moderate; severe unsolicited events (5% in each group) were judged unrelated. Although 93% of infants had seroprotective maternal antibody at birth, this fell to 56% by 8 weeks in the placebo group; in the nOPV2 group 196 (90%) of 217 infants seroconverted by week 8 after two doses, and 214 (99%) had seroprotective antibodies.
cards.watchOut: A newborn schedule is not how nOPV2 is mainly used in outbreak campaigns; the trial's value is showing the vaccine takes even under maternal antibody. Seroconversion is again a laboratory endpoint, and follow-up ends at 8 weeks.
cards.source: Zaman K et al. Evaluation of the safety, immunogenicity, and faecal shedding of novel oral polio vaccine type 2 in healthy newborn infants in Bangladesh: a randomised, controlled, phase 2 clinical trial. Lancet. 2023. PMID: 36495882. Registry ID: NCT04693286. cards.headline: Sáez-Llorens 2021 (Panama): novel OPV2 candidates non-inferior to Sabin monovalent OPV2 in infants — day-28 seroprotection 91–95% versus 94%
cards.summary: Sáez-Llorens 2021 (Panama): novel OPV2 candidates non-inferior to Sabin monovalent OPV2 in infants — day-28 seroprotection 91–95% versus 94%
cards.type: Randomised phase 2 trial with phase 4 historical control (Sáez-Llorens 2021)
cards.people: 150 children aged 1–4 years and 684 infants aged 18–22 weeks in Panama, in a phase 4 control study of monovalent Sabin OPV2 (2015–16) and a phase 2 study (2018–19) of low- and high-dose novel OPV2 candidates c1 and c2, one dose with subsets receiving a second dose 28 days later.
cards.result: Vaccines were safe and well tolerated, with no causally associated serious adverse events. In children, day-28 seroprotection after one dose was 100% for monovalent OPV2 and both novel candidates. In infants, day-28 seroprotection was 91 (94%) of 97 on monovalent OPV2, 134 (94%) of 143 on high-dose novel OPV2-c1, 122 (93%) of 131 on low-dose c1, 138 (95%) of 146 on high-dose c2 and 115 (91%) of 127 on low-dose c2; non-inferiority (10% margin) was shown for low- and high-dose c1 and high-dose c2.
cards.watchOut: The Sabin comparator comes from a historical control study run three years earlier in the same population, not a concurrent randomised arm, and monovalent recipients had higher baseline immunity — the non-inferiority reading is supportive, not definitive.
cards.source: Sáez-Llorens X et al. Safety and immunogenicity of two novel type 2 oral poliovirus vaccine candidates compared with a monovalent type 2 oral poliovirus vaccine in children and infants: two clinical trials. Lancet. 2021. PMID: 33308427. Registry ID: NCT03554798; NCT02521974. cards.headline: Wilkinson 2023 (Dhaka): giving nOPV2 together with bivalent OPV cut the type 2 response to 65% versus 86% alone — non-inferiority for type 2 not met; types 1 and 3 unaffected
cards.summary: Wilkinson 2023 (Dhaka): giving nOPV2 together with bivalent OPV cut the type 2 response to 65% versus 86% alone — non-inferiority for type 2 not met; types 1 and 3 unaffected
cards.people: 736 healthy full-term infants in Dhaka, Bangladesh, randomised to nOPV2 only, nOPV2 plus bivalent OPV, or bivalent OPV only, at 6, 10 and 14 weeks; primary outcome the cumulative immune response at 14 weeks after two doses.
cards.result: After two doses, a type 2 immune response was present in 209 (86%) of the nOPV2-only group versus 159 (65%) of the nOPV2-plus-bOPV group; co-administration was non-inferior for type 1 (92% combined versus 93% bOPV only) and type 3 (88% versus 86%) but not for type 2. Fifteen serious adverse events, including three deaths (one per group, all attributed to sudden infant death syndrome), were none of them attributed to vaccination.
cards.watchOut: This is the shelf's practical warning: the interference is specific to the type 2 response that is the entire reason for giving nOPV2, so campaign designs that mix the two vaccines in one visit would blunt exactly the immunity they are buying.
cards.source: Wilkinson AL et al. Immunogenicity of novel oral poliovirus vaccine type 2 administered concomitantly with bivalent oral poliovirus vaccine: an open-label, non-inferiority, randomised, controlled trial.
