cards.headline: Synthesis: Sabin-level antibody responses in four trials across three continents — with one clear operational exception, co-administration with bivalent OPV
cards.summary: Synthesis: Sabin-level antibody responses in four trials across three continents — with one clear operational exception, co-administration with bivalent OPV
cards.people: Four randomised trials totalling over 4,100 infants and children (Gambia phase 3; Bangladesh newborn and co-administration trials; Panama phase 2 with Sabin historical control), plus adult phase 1–2 data not carded here.
cards.result: Two-dose seroprotection: 92.9% (infants) and 95.5% (young children) in Gambia; 99% in Bangladeshi newborns. Against Sabin monovalent OPV2 in Panama, infant seroprotection was 91–95% versus 94%, non-inferior. Given together with bivalent OPV, the type 2 response fell to 65% versus 86% (Dhaka). No vaccine-attributed serious adverse events in any carded trial. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit) on immunogenicity, with the co-administration caveat on the face of the shelf.
cards.watchOut: Every endpoint is serological. The claim that nOPV2 seeds fewer vaccine-derived outbreaks rests on its engineered genetic stability and on field use under WHO emergency listing, not on any randomised comparison of outbreak rates — that evidence is programmatic and sits outside these cards.
cards.source: Synthesis of Ochoge M et al. Lancet. 2024 (PMID: 38402887); Zaman K et al. Lancet. 2023 (PMID: 36495882); Sáez-Llorens X et al. Lancet. 2021 (PMID: 33308427); Wilkinson AL et al. The Lancet Infectious Diseases. 2023 (PMID: 37178706).

shelves.title: Pentavalent meningococcal vaccine NmCV-5 (A, C, W, Y and X): non-inferior to the licensed quadrivalent vaccine for the four shared serogroups in 2-to-29-year-olds, with a 97.2% response to serogroup X — the serogroup no licensed vaccine covered
shelves.question: In children, adolescents and young adults in the African meningitis belt, does a single dose of the pentavalent meningococcal conjugate vaccine NmCV-5 produce antibody responses non-inferior to a licensed quadrivalent vaccine for serogroups A, C, W and Y — and does it immunise against serogroup X?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Gambia/epidemiology · Health Status · Mali/epidemiology · Vaccines, Conjugate/administration & dosage/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Meningococcal Vaccines/administration & dosage/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Child, Preschool · Child · Adolescent · Young Adult · Adult · Immunogenicity, Vaccine · Injections, Intramuscular · Meningitis/epidemiology/prevention & control · Epidemics/prevention & control
shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit) — on immunogenicity, the endpoint meningococcal conjugate vaccines are licensed on. In the phase 3 trial in Mali and Gambia (Haidara FC et al., PMID: 37224196), a single dose of NmCV-5 produced seroresponses of 70.5% (serogroup A) to 98.5% (W) across the shared serogroups, non-inferior to MenACWY-D on both seroresponse differences (1.2 to 20.5 percentage points in NmCV-5's favour) and geometric mean titre ratios (1.7 to 2.8), and a 97.2% seroresponse to serogroup X, which no licensed vaccine covers. In Malian toddlers (Tapia MD et al., PMID: 34077644), bactericidal titres ≥128 were reached by 99–100% for all five serogroups after two doses. In infants given the vaccine alongside routine 9- or 15-month vaccinations (Diallo F et al., PMID: 40086461), NmCV-5 was non-inferior to MenACWY-TT for all five serogroups at both ages. Systemic adverse events were similar to the licensed comparators (11.1% versus 9.2% in phase 3), with no vaccine-related serious events in the infant trial. No trial measures meningitis cases prevented; that inference rides on the bactericidal-antibody correlate every predecessor vaccine was licensed on. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): NmCV-5 matches the licensed quadrivalent vaccines serogroup for serogroup and adds X, the gap in the meningitis belt's cover.

cards.headline: Haidara 2023 (phase 3, Mali and Gambia): seroresponse 70.5–98.5% across A, C, W and Y, non-inferior to MenACWY-D — and 97.2% for serogroup X
cards.summary: Haidara 2023 (phase 3, Mali and Gambia): seroresponse 70.5–98.5% across A, C, W and Y, non-inferior to MenACWY-D — and 97.2% for serogroup X
cards.people: 1,800 healthy 2-to-29-year-olds in Mali and Gambia randomised 2:1 to a single intramuscular dose of NmCV-5 or the quadrivalent vaccine MenACWY-D; immunogenicity assessed at day 28.
cards.result: In the NmCV-5 group, seroresponse ranged from 70.5% (95% CI 67.8–73.2) for serogroup A to 98.5% (97.6–99.2) for serogroup W, and was 97.2% (96.0–98.1) for serogroup X. Differences versus MenACWY-D for the four shared serogroups ranged from 1.2 percentage points (96% CI −0.3 to 3.1) for W to 20.5 points (15.4 to 25.6) for A, all meeting non-inferiority; geometric mean titre ratios ranged from 1.7 (98.98% CI 1.5–1.9) for A to 2.8 (2.3–3.5) for C, and the X component met its prespecified criteria. Systemic adverse events occurred in 11.1% on NmCV-5 and 9.2% on MenACWY-D; no safety concerns were evident.
cards.watchOut: Serogroup A seroresponse (70.5%) is the softest number on the card — the population had high baseline immunity from earlier MenA campaigns, and the endpoint is a titre change, not disease prevented. Efficacy against epidemic meningitis is inferred from the bactericidal correlate, as it was for every licensed predecessor.
cards.source: Haidara FC et al. Meningococcal ACWYX Conjugate Vaccine in 2-to-29-Year-Olds in Mali and Gambia. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2023. PMID: 37224196. Registry ID: NCT03964012. cards.headline: Tapia 2021 (phase 2, Malian toddlers): bactericidal titres ≥128 in 99–100% for all five serogroups after two doses of NmCV-5
cards.summary: Tapia 2021 (phase 2, Malian toddlers): bactericidal titres ≥128 in 99–100% for all five serogroups after two doses of NmCV-5
cards.people: 376 Malian children aged 12–16 months randomised 2:2:1 to non-adjuvanted NmCV-5, alum-adjuvanted NmCV-5, or MenACWY-D, two intramuscular doses 12 weeks apart; 362 received both doses; safety followed for 169 days.
cards.result: Local solicited adverse events were reported by 1% (non-adjuvanted NmCV-5), 1% (adjuvanted) and 4% (MenACWY-D); systemic solicited events by 6%, 5% and 7%. At day 84 (before the second dose), an SBA titre of at least 128 was seen in 91–100% of NmCV-5 recipients for all five serogroups and in 36–99% of MenACWY-D recipients excluding X; at day 112 the figures were 99–100% for NmCV-5 (all five serogroups) and 92–100% for MenACWY-D (excluding X). Responses to the adjuvanted and non-adjuvanted formulations were similar.
cards.watchOut: A toddler immunogenicity trial with a titre threshold as its outcome; the day-84 MenACWY-D range (36–99%) shows how much the second dose matters at this age, and neither arm was followed for disease.
cards.source: Tapia MD et al. Meningococcal Serogroup ACWYX Conjugate Vaccine in Malian Toddlers. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2021. PMID: 34077644. Registry ID: NCT03295318. cards.headline: Diallo 2025 (phase 3, Mali): NmCV-5 alongside routine 9- and 15-month vaccines non-inferior to MenACWY-TT for all five serogroups at both ages
cards.summary: Diallo 2025 (phase 3, Mali): NmCV-5 alongside routine 9- and 15-month vaccines non-inferior to MenACWY-TT for all five serogroups at both ages
cards.people: 1,325 Malian infants enrolled at 9–11 months and randomised to receive a meningococcal vaccine at their 9-month (n=602) or 15-month (n=723) routine visit, then randomised again 2:1 to NmCV-5 or MenACWY-TT, co-administered with measles–rubella and (at 9 months) yellow fever vaccines; 1,200 received a meningococcal vaccine.
cards.result: In the per-protocol population, differences in seroprotection for NmCV-5 versus MenACWY-TT at 9 months were 0.0% (95% CI −1.0 to 2.0) for A, −0.5% (−2.3 to 1.9) for C, −3.0% (−6.3 to 0.8) for W and −3.0% (−5.4 to −0.4) for Y, with X assessed against the comparator's W response at +2.3% (0.3 to 4.7); at 15 months the differences were 0.8% for A, −0.8% for C, 0.3% for W, 1.4% for Y and 1.9% for X. NmCV-5 was non-inferior for all five serogroups at both ages. Six serious adverse events were recorded, none deemed related to vaccination.
cards.watchOut: This is the routine-programme question — fitting the vaccine into the infant schedule without disturbing it — answered on seroprotection proportions 28 days after one dose; durability beyond that window and any effect on the co-administered vaccines' own long-term protection sit outside the record.
cards.source: Diallo F et al. cards.headline: Synthesis: three trials, three age bands, one consistent answer — NmCV-5 matches the licensed vaccines and closes the serogroup X gap
cards.summary: Synthesis: three trials, three age bands, one consistent answer — NmCV-5 matches the licensed vaccines and closes the serogroup X gap
cards.people: Three randomised trials totalling 3,501 participants in Mali and Gambia: toddlers (phase 2, two doses), 2-to-29-year-olds (phase 3, single dose), and infants at routine 9- and 15-month visits (phase 3, co-administered).
cards.result: Non-inferiority to licensed quadrivalent conjugate vaccines was met for serogroups A, C, W and Y in every trial, and the X component produced a 97.2% seroresponse in 2-to-29-year-olds and 99–100% titre ≥128 rates in toddlers. Adverse-event rates tracked the licensed comparators throughout, with no vaccine-related serious events reported in the infant trial. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit) on the bactericidal-antibody correlate these vaccines are licensed on.
cards.watchOut: No carded trial counts meningitis cases, and none follows protection beyond the early post-vaccination window in this set; the belt's epidemic cycles, not trial follow-up, will deliver the disease-endpoint verdict. The vaccine is named as the publications name it (NmCV-5); the records carded here do not name a manufacturer, so none is stated.
cards.source: Synthesis of Haidara FC et al. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2023 (PMID: 37224196); Tapia MD et al. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2021 (PMID: 34077644); Diallo F et al. Lancet. 2025 (PMID: 40086461).

shelves.title: One 200 mg dose of doxycycline after a deer-tick bite: erythema migrans in 0.4% versus 3.2% in the one randomised trial — an 87% relative reduction built on nine events, with nausea in 15%
shelves.question: After a bite from an Ixodes scapularis tick in a Lyme-endemic area, does a single 200 mg dose of doxycycline prevent Lyme disease compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Animals · Anti-Bacterial Agents/administration & dosage · Antibiotic Prophylaxis · Bites and Stings · Borrelia burgdorferi Group/isolation & purification · Child · Double-Blind Method · Doxycycline/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Erythema Chronicum Migrans/prevention & control · Female · Humans · Ixodes/growth & development · Lyme Disease/prevention & control/transmission · Male · Middle Aged · Nymph
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a large relative effect on a small absolute risk, from one trial. In the randomised, double-blind New York trial (Nadelman RB et al., PMID: 11450675), erythema migrans developed in 1 of 235 subjects (0.4%) given a single 200 mg dose of doxycycline within 72 hours of removing an attached Ixodes scapularis tick, versus 8 of 247 (3.2%) on placebo (p<0.04) — an 87% relative reduction in efficacy terms (95% CI 25 to 98), an absolute reduction of about 2.8 percentage points, and no extracutaneous Lyme disease or asymptomatic seroconversion in anyone. The updated meta-analysis of all randomised prophylaxis trials (Zhou G et al., PMID: 34749665) pools 3,766 people: unfavourable events in 0.4% treated versus 2.2% control (pooled RR 0.38, 95% CI 0.22–0.66), with the single-dose doxycycline subgroup at RR 0.29 (0.14–0.60). The price is gastrointestinal: adverse effects in 30.1% on doxycycline versus 11.1% on placebo, nausea 15.4% versus 2.6% and vomiting 5.8% versus 1.3%. Risk concentrates in engorged nymphal ticks (erythema migrans after 9.9% of untreated bites from partially engorged nymphs, 0% after adult female bites in this trial), so the absolute case for the dose is strong after an engorged nymph and thin after a briefly attached adult tick. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): one dose very likely prevents most early Lyme disease after a high-risk bite; the trial base is a single study with nine outcome events, so the shelf is Tier C.

cards.headline: Nadelman 2001: erythema migrans in 1 of 235 (0.4%) on single-dose doxycycline versus 8 of 247 (3.2%) on placebo — efficacy 87% relative, on nine events
cards.summary: Nadelman 2001: erythema migrans in 1 of 235 (0.4%) on single-dose doxycycline versus 8 of 247 (3.2%) on placebo — efficacy 87% relative, on nine events
cards.people: 482 subjects in a Lyme-hyperendemic area of New York who had removed attached Ixodes scapularis ticks within the previous 72 hours, randomised to a single 200 mg dose of doxycycline or placebo; interviewed, examined, serologically tested and blood-cultured at baseline, 3 and 6 weeks; tick species, stage and engorgement confirmed by entomologists.
cards.result: Erythema migrans at the bite site developed in 1 of 235 (0.4%) on doxycycline versus 8 of 247 (3.2%) on placebo (p<0.04); treatment efficacy was 87% relative (95% CI 25 to 98). No subject developed objective extracutaneous Lyme disease, and there were no asymptomatic seroconversions. Adverse effects were more frequent on doxycycline (30.1% versus 11.1%, p<0.001), chiefly nausea (15.4% versus 2.6%) and vomiting (5.8% versus 1.3%). Untreated risk was concentrated in nymphal bites: erythema migrans followed 8 of 142 nymphal bites (5.6%) versus 0 of 97 adult female bites, and 8 of 81 bites (9.9%) from at least partially engorged nymphs.
cards.watchOut: Nine outcome events in total, all of them the early skin lesion — the trial cannot speak to preventing disseminated or late Lyme disease, only to the early infection that produces erythema migrans, and its confidence interval for efficacy runs from 25% to 98%. It also predates current tick ecology in much of the endemic range.

PMID: 11450675. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.search: nadelman 2001: erythema migrans in 1 of 235 (0.4%) on single-dose doxycycline versus 8 of 247 (3.2%) on placebo — efficacy 87% relative, on nine events nadelman 2001: erythema migrans in 1 of 235 (0.4%) on single-dose doxycycline versus 8 of 247 (3.2%) on placebo — efficacy 87% relative, on nine events after a bite from an ixodes scapularis tick in a lyme-endemic area, does a single 200 mg dose of doxycycline prevent lyme disease compared with placebo? randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial (nadelman 2001) 482 subjects in a lyme-hyperendemic area of new york who had removed attached ixodes scapularis ticks within the previous 72 hours, randomised to a single 200 mg dose of doxycycline or placebo; interviewed, examined, serologically tested and blood-cultured at baseline, 3 and 6 weeks; tick species, stage and engorgement confirmed by entomologists. erythema migrans at the bite site developed in 1 of 235 (0.4%) on doxycycline versus 8 of 247 (3.2%) on placebo (p<0.04); treatment efficacy was 87% relative (95% ci 25 to 98). no subject developed objective extracutaneous lyme disease, and there were no asymptomatic seroconversions. adverse effects were more frequent on doxycycline (30.1% versus 11.1%, p<0.001), chiefly nausea (15.4% versus 2.6%) and vomiting (5.8% versus 1.3%). untreated risk was concentrated in nymphal bites: erythema migrans followed 8 of 142 nymphal bites (5.6%) versus 0 of 97 adult female bites, and 8 of 81 bites (9.9%) from at least partially engorged nymphs. nine outcome events in total, all of them the early skin lesion — the trial cannot speak to preventing disseminated or late lyme disease, only to the early infection that produces erythema migrans, and its confidence interval for efficacy runs from 25% to 98%. it also predates current tick ecology in much of the endemic range. nadelman rb et al. prophylaxis with single-dose doxycycline for the prevention of lyme disease after an ixodes scapularis tick bite. the new england journal of medicine. 2001. pmid: 11450675. registry id: none in the record. mesh: adolescent · adult · aged · aged, 80 and over · animals · anti-bacterial agents/administration & dosage · antibiotic prophylaxis · bites and stings · borrelia burgdorferi group/isolation & purification · child · double-blind method · doxycycline/administration & dosage/adverse effects · erythema chronicum migrans/prevention & control · female · humans · ixodes/growth & development · lyme disease/prevention & control/transmission · male · middle aged · nymph

cards.headline: Zhou 2021 meta-analysis: six randomised trials, 3,766 people — unfavourable events 0.4% on prophylaxis versus 2.2% on control (pooled RR 0.38); single-dose doxycycline subgroup RR 0.29
cards.summary: Zhou 2021 meta-analysis: six randomised trials, 3,766 people — unfavourable events 0.4% on prophylaxis versus 2.2% on control (pooled RR 0.38); single-dose doxycycline subgroup RR 0.29
cards.people: Six randomised trials (3,766 individuals) of antibiotic prophylaxis started within 72 hours of a tick bite in people with no clinical evidence of Lyme disease at enrolment, pooled with a random-effects model; regimens included single-dose doxycycline, 10-day oral courses, and topical azithromycin.
cards.result: The pooled rate of unfavourable events was 0.4% (95% CI 0.1–1.1) in treated groups versus 2.2% (1.6–3.0) in controls, a pooled risk ratio of 0.38 (0.22–0.66). By subgroup, the pooled RR was 0.29 (0.14–0.60) for single-dose 200 mg doxycycline, 0.28 (0.05–1.67) for 10-day courses of amoxicillin, penicillin or tetracycline, and 0.73 (0.25–2.08) for topical azithromycin.
cards.watchOut: The pooled estimate leans heavily on the Nadelman trial for the single-dose claim, and the older multi-day-course trials were too small to resolve their own subgroup (confidence interval 0.05–1.67). Event rates are low everywhere, so small differences in what counted as an 'unfavourable event' move the pooled ratio.

cards.headline: Synthesis: one well-run trial and a concordant meta-analysis — real protection against early Lyme disease after high-risk bites, bought with a day of nausea for many
cards.summary: Synthesis: one well-run trial and a concordant meta-analysis — real protection against early Lyme disease after high-risk bites, bought with a day of nausea for many
cards.people: One randomised double-blind trial (482 subjects, New York) and a meta-analysis of six randomised trials (3,766 subjects) covering single-dose doxycycline, multi-day oral courses and topical prophylaxis after tick bites.
cards.result: Erythema migrans: 0.4% versus 3.2% in the anchor trial (87% relative efficacy); pooled unfavourable events 0.4% versus 2.2% across trials (RR 0.38), single-dose doxycycline subgroup RR 0.29. Harm: adverse effects 30.1% versus 11.1%, mostly nausea and vomiting. Absolute benefit tracks bite risk — about 1 case prevented per 36 unselected treated bites in the trial, and far fewer needed after an engorged nymphal bite (untreated risk 9.9%). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), Tier C: the regimen-specific claim rests on a single trial.
cards.watchOut: Nothing here addresses bites from other tick species, other Borrelia genospecies (the European trials in the pool notwithstanding), or prevention of late Lyme manifestations; and prophylaxis given later than 72 hours after tick removal is untested in this evidence.
cards.source: Synthesis of Nadelman RB et al. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2001 (PMID: 11450675); Zhou G et al. BMC Infectious Diseases. 2021 (PMID: 34749665).

shelves.title: Rabies monoclonal antibodies instead of human rabies immunoglobulin: two randomised trials met non-inferiority on day-14 antibody responders (90.2% versus 94.4% for the Twinrab cocktail; antibody levels fourfold higher with SII RMAb)
shelves.question: For people with WHO category III suspected rabies exposures, can a manufactured monoclonal antibody (or cocktail) replace scarce human rabies immunoglobulin as the passive component of post-exposure prophylaxis, alongside vaccine?
shelves.mesh: Animals · Antibodies, Monoclonal · Antibodies, Neutralizing · Antibodies, Viral · Humans · Post-Exposure Prophylaxis · Rabies/prevention & control · Rabies Vaccines · Rabies virus
shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit) — on the antibody endpoint rabies prophylaxis is judged by, since a placebo-controlled efficacy trial after a rabid bite would be unethical. In the phase 3 trial (Kansagra K et al., PMID: 32556113), 308 patients with WHO category III suspected rabies exposures received the monoclonal cocktail Twinrab (docaravimab and miromavimab, as named in the publication) or human rabies immunoglobulin (Imogam Rabies-HT, as named in the publication), each with vaccine: day-14 responders (neutralising antibody ≥0.5 IU/mL) were 90.21% on Twinrab versus 94.37% on HRIG in the per-protocol population, geometric mean titres 4.38 versus 4.85 IU/mL, non-inferiority confirmed with protection maintained to day 84, and no deaths or serious adverse events. In the earlier phase 2/3 trial (Gogtay NJ et al., PMID: 29020321), 199 participants received the single monoclonal SII RMAb (as named in the publication) or HRIG with five vaccine doses: the day-14 geometric mean concentration ratio was 4.23 (95% CI 2.59–6.94) in the monoclonal's favour (24.90 versus 5.88 IU/mL), meeting non-inferiority, with adverse reactions mostly mild to moderate in both groups. Neither publication names a manufacturer for its monoclonal product in the record, so none is stated. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): manufactured monoclonals match the blood product on the protective-antibody window — the supply, cost and safety rationale for replacing HRIG is strong, though no trial can or does count rabies cases prevented.

cards.headline: Kansagra 2021 (phase 3): Twinrab cocktail responders 90.21% versus 94.37% on HRIG at day 14 — non-inferior, no deaths or serious adverse events
cards.summary: Kansagra 2021 (phase 3): Twinrab cocktail responders 90.21% versus 94.37% on HRIG at day 14 — non-inferior, no deaths or serious adverse events
cards.people: 308 patients with WHO category III exposure to a suspected rabid animal, randomised 1:1 to the anti-rabies monoclonal antibody cocktail Twinrab (docaravimab and miromavimab) or human rabies immunoglobulin (Imogam Rabies-HT), each alongside rabies vaccine; primary endpoint the percentage with rabies virus neutralising antibody titres ≥0.5 IU/mL on day 14, assessed per-protocol.
cards.result: Responders in the per-protocol population were 90.21% in the Twinrab arm and 94.37% in the HRIG arm; day-14 geometric mean titres were 4.38 and 4.85 IU/mL respectively. The authors concluded Twinrab was non-inferior to HRIG, providing an unbroken window of protection up to day 84. No deaths or serious adverse events were reported.
cards.watchOut: Open-label, and the endpoint is an antibody threshold at day 14 — the accepted correlate, but not rabies prevented; exposures were to suspected, not confirmed, rabid animals, so most participants were never truly at risk, which is precisely why the correlate has to carry the claim.
cards.source: Kansagra K et al. A Phase 3, Randomized, Open-label, Noninferiority Trial Evaluating Anti-Rabies Monoclonal Antibody Cocktail (TwinrabTM) Against Human Rabies Immunoglobulin (HRIG). Clinical Infectious Diseases. 2021. PMID: 32556113. Registry ID: CTRI/2017/07/009038 (as named in the record). cards.headline: Gogtay 2018 (phase 2/3): SII RMAb day-14 antibody geometric mean 24.90 IU/mL versus 5.88 on HRIG — ratio 4.23, non-inferiority demonstrated
cards.summary: Gogtay 2018 (phase 2/3): SII RMAb day-14 antibody geometric mean 24.90 IU/mL versus 5.88 on HRIG — ratio 4.23, non-inferiority demonstrated
cards.people: 200 participants with WHO category III suspected rabies exposures, randomised 1:1 (single-blind) to the recombinant human monoclonal antibody SII RMAb or HRIG, infiltrated in wounds and intramuscularly if required on day 0, with five intramuscular vaccine doses on days 0, 3, 7, 14 and 28; 199 received treatment and at least one vaccine dose.
cards.result: The day-14 geometric mean concentration ratio of rabies virus neutralising activity for SII RMAb relative to HRIG was 4.23 (95% CI 2.59–6.94), with geometric means of 24.90 IU/mL (95% CI 18.94–32.74) versus 5.88 IU/mL (4.11–8.41) — non-inferiority demonstrated. The majority of local injection-site and systemic adverse reactions in both groups were mild to moderate in severity.
cards.watchOut: A single monoclonal against one epitope is a narrower shield than polyclonal immunoglobulin in theory; the trial's antibody titres were higher, not merely non-inferior, but titre height is not itself proof of equal protection against every viral variant, and follow-up is serological.

cards.headline: Synthesis: two different manufactured antibodies, one consistent answer — the passive component of rabies PEP no longer has to come from human blood
cards.summary: Synthesis: two different manufactured antibodies, one consistent answer — the passive component of rabies PEP no longer has to come from human blood
cards.people: Two randomised non-inferiority trials in India totalling 507 people with category III suspected rabies exposures: a two-antibody cocktail (308 patients) and a single monoclonal (200 participants), each against HRIG with vaccine.
cards.result: Day-14 responder rates 90.21% versus 94.37% (cocktail versus HRIG); day-14 antibody geometric mean ratio 4.23 (single monoclonal versus HRIG). No deaths or serious adverse events in the phase 3 trial; adverse reactions mostly mild to moderate in both. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit) on the neutralising-antibody correlate that rabies prophylaxis licensing rests on.
cards.watchOut: The products are named exactly as the publications name them (Twinrab — docaravimab and miromavimab; SII RMAb); neither record names a manufacturer, so none is stated, and other monoclonal products cannot borrow these results. Cost and real-world supply — the actual reasons HRIG fails patients — are programme questions outside these trials.
cards.source: Synthesis of Kansagra K et al. Clinical Infectious Diseases. 2021 (PMID: 32556113); Gogtay NJ et al. Clinical Infectious Diseases. 2018 (PMID: 29020321).

shelves.title: Male circumcision beyond HIV: HSV-2 seroconversion 7.8% versus 10.3% at two years (adjusted HR 0.72) and high-risk HPV prevalence 18.0% versus 27.9% (adjusted RR 0.65) — but no effect on syphilis (HR 1.10)
shelves.question: In adolescent boys and men, does medical male circumcision reduce acquisition of herpes simplex virus type 2, human papillomavirus and syphilis — the sexually transmitted infections beyond HIV that the circumcision trials also measured?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Circumcision, Male · Condoms/statistics & numerical data · Confounding Factors, Epidemiologic · Genotype · Herpes Genitalis/epidemiology/prevention & control · Herpesvirus 2, Human/isolation & purification · Humans · Incidence · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Male · Papillomaviridae/genetics/isolation & purification · Papillomavirus Infections/epidemiology/prevention & control · Prevalence · Sexual Behavior · Syphilis/epidemiology/prevention & control · Treponema pallidum/isolation & purification · Young Adult
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for HSV-2 and HPV, with a clean null for syphilis in the same men. The analysis pools the two Rakai, Uganda randomised trials (Tobian AAR et al., PMID: 19321868): 5,534 HIV-negative uncircumcised males aged 15–49 were randomised to immediate circumcision or circumcision deferred 24 months. Among the 3,393 who were HSV-2-seronegative at enrolment, cumulative HSV-2 seroconversion at 24 months was 7.8% in the intervention group versus 10.3% in controls (adjusted hazard ratio 0.72, 95% CI 0.56–0.92; p=0.008) — a 28% relative reduction. In the subgroup evaluated for HPV, high-risk genotype prevalence at 24 months was 18.0% versus 27.9% (adjusted risk ratio 0.65, 0.46–0.90; p=0.009), a 35% relative reduction. Syphilis incidence did not differ (adjusted HR 1.10, 0.75–1.65; p=0.44). The HPV figure is prevalence at a single 24-month sweep, not measured incidence, and both positive endpoints are secondary analyses of HIV trials — the reason this is POSSIBLE rather than LIKELY. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): circumcision modestly reduces HSV-2 acquisition and high-risk HPV carriage in men; it does not prevent syphilis.

cards.headline: Tobian 2009 (Rakai trials): HSV-2 seroconversion 7.8% versus 10.3% (adjusted HR 0.72); high-risk HPV prevalence 18.0% versus 27.9% (adjusted RR 0.65); syphilis HR 1.10, null
cards.summary: Tobian 2009 (Rakai trials): HSV-2 seroconversion 7.8% versus 10.3% (adjusted HR 0.72); high-risk HPV prevalence 18.0% versus 27.9% (adjusted RR 0.65); syphilis HR 1.10, null
cards.people: 5,534 HIV-negative uncircumcised males aged 15–49 years enrolled in two randomised trials in Rakai, Uganda, assigned to immediate circumcision or circumcision after 24 months; 3,393 (61.3%) were HSV-2-seronegative at enrolment (1,684 intervention, 1,709 control) and were tested for HSV-2, HIV and syphilis at baseline and 6, 12 and 24 months, with a subgroup evaluated for HPV at baseline and 24 months.
cards.result: At 24 months, the cumulative probability of HSV-2 seroconversion was 7.8% in the intervention group and 10.3% in the control group (adjusted hazard ratio 0.72, 95% CI 0.56–0.92; p=0.008). The prevalence of high-risk HPV genotypes was 18.0% in the intervention group and 27.9% in the control group (adjusted risk ratio 0.65, 0.46–0.90; p=0.009). No significant difference was observed in the incidence of syphilis (adjusted hazard ratio 1.10, 0.75–1.65; p=0.44).
cards.watchOut: These are secondary endpoints of HIV-prevention trials: the HPV outcome is prevalence at one 24-month measurement (a mix of acquisition and clearance), not incidence; the men are Ugandan adolescents and adults in a high-prevalence setting, and the effect sizes are relative reductions on absolute risks of a few percentage points over two years.
cards.source: Tobian AAR et al. Male circumcision for the prevention of HSV-2 and HPV infections and syphilis. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2009. PMID: 19321868. cards.headline: Synthesis: one operation, three infections, two answers — less herpes and HPV in circumcised men, syphilis untouched
cards.summary: Synthesis: one operation, three infections, two answers — less herpes and HPV in circumcised men, syphilis untouched
cards.people: Two pooled randomised trials (5,534 HIV-negative males aged 15–49, Rakai, Uganda; immediate versus 24-month-deferred circumcision), with HSV-2 assessed in 3,393 seronegative participants and HPV in a subgroup.
cards.result: HSV-2 seroconversion at 24 months: 7.8% versus 10.3% (adjusted HR 0.72). High-risk HPV prevalence: 18.0% versus 27.9% (adjusted RR 0.65). Syphilis incidence: adjusted HR 1.10 (0.75–1.65), no effect. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) for HSV-2 and HPV — trial-randomised evidence, but secondary endpoints of trials designed and powered for HIV, which has its own shelf in this library and is not re-argued here.
cards.watchOut: Nothing here measures disease in female partners, genital warts, or penile cancer — the downstream benefits are plausible extensions, not trial findings; and the syphilis null is a standing warning against treating circumcision as broad STI protection.
cards.source: Synthesis of Tobian AAR et al. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2009 (PMID: 19321868).

shelves.title: Early two-dose measles vaccination and child survival: the first Guinea-Bissau trial pointed to lower mortality (rate ratio 0.78, not significant; 0.59 without neonatal vitamin A) — the larger replication found none (HR 1.38), with a possible harmful interaction with polio campaigns
shelves.question: In high-mortality settings, does giving measles vaccine early — at about 4.5 months, with a second dose at 9 months — reduce all-cause childhood mortality compared with the standard single dose at 9 months, beyond preventing measles itself?
shelves.mesh: Age Factors · Child, Preschool · Dietary Supplements · Drug Administration Schedule · Female · Humans · Infant · Infant Mortality · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Male · Measles/mortality/prevention & control · Measles Vaccine/administration & dosage · Urban Health · Vitamin A/administration & dosage · Vitamins/administration & dosage
shelves.balance: SPLIT — two large randomised trials from the same research setting point in opposite directions, and the shelf keeps both. The first (Aaby P et al., PMID: 21118875) randomised 6,648 Guinea-Bissau children to Edmonston-Zagreb measles vaccine at 4.5 and 9 months or a single dose at 9 months: the intention-to-treat mortality rate ratio from 4.5 to 36 months was 0.78 (95% CI 0.59–1.05) — not significant overall, though significant in girls (0.64, 0.42–0.98) and in the 3,402 children who had not received neonatal vitamin A (0.59, 0.39–0.89), and 0.65 (0.43–0.99) when measles cases were censored, which is why the result was read as a non-specific (non-measles) effect. The replication (Nielsen S et al., PMID: 35747181), 6,598 children randomised 2:1 to two doses (4 and 9 months) versus one dose, found a mortality hazard ratio of 1.38 (0.92–2.06) between 4 and 60 months (90 versus 33 deaths) — no benefit, with a significant interaction: HR 0.81 (0.29–2.22) in children with no oral polio vaccine campaigns, but 4.73 (1.44–15.6) in children exposed to campaigns before and after enrolment (interaction p=0.027), while early vaccination in the presence of maternal measles antibody was associated with 50% lower mortality (20–68%). A third trial, in Burkina Faso (PMID: 29523450), found no effect of an additional early dose on hospitalisation or mortality (HR 1.00, 0.83–1.20). PROPOSED SPLIT: the early two-dose strategy's survival benefit appeared in one trial's subgroups, vanished in its replication, and may depend on the surrounding campaign environment — it is not a settled reason to move the measles schedule.

cards.headline: Aaby 2010 (Guinea-Bissau): mortality rate ratio 0.78 (0.59–1.05) for two doses versus one — significant in girls (0.64) and without neonatal vitamin A (0.59), and after censoring measles cases (0.65)
cards.summary: Aaby 2010 (Guinea-Bissau): mortality rate ratio 0.78 (0.59–1.05) for two doses versus one — significant in girls (0.64) and without neonatal vitamin A (0.59), and after censoring measles cases (0.65)
cards.people: 6,648 children aged 4.5 months in urban Guinea-Bissau (Bandim Health Project) who had received three DTP doses at least four weeks earlier, randomised to Edmonston-Zagreb measles vaccine at 4.5 and 9 months, or no vaccine at 4.5 months with Edmonston-Zagreb or Schwarz vaccine at 9 months; 80% had previously taken part in neonatal vitamin A trials; main outcome mortality rate ratio between 4.5 and 36 months.
cards.result: In intention-to-treat analysis, the mortality rate ratio for two doses versus one dose between 4.5 and 36 months was 0.78 (95% CI 0.59–1.05). Between 4.5 and 9 months it was 0.67 (0.38–1.19) and between 9 and 36 months 0.83 (0.83–1.16, as printed in the record). The effect was significant for girls (0.64, 0.42–0.98) but the sex interaction was not significant (p=0.18). Among the 3,402 children who had not received neonatal vitamin A, the rate ratio was 0.59 (0.39–0.89); with measles cases censored, 0.65 (0.43–0.99). The authors concluded the results may indicate a beneficial non-specific effect of the two-dose schedule.
cards.watchOut: The primary comparison missed significance; the persuasive numbers live in subgroups (sex, vitamin A status) the trial was not powered to separate, and the vaccine strain, setting and era are specific — this is the hypothesis-generating result the replication was built to test.
cards.source: Aaby P et al. Non-specific effects of standard measles vaccine at 4.5 and 9 months of age on childhood mortality: randomised controlled trial. BMJ. 2010. PMID: 21118875. Registry ID: NCT00168558. cards.headline: Nielsen 2022 (replication, Guinea-Bissau): mortality HR 1.38 (0.92–2.06) for two doses versus one — no benefit; HR 4.73 in children exposed to polio campaigns before and after enrolment (interaction p=0.027)
cards.summary: Nielsen 2022 (replication, Guinea-Bissau): mortality HR 1.38 (0.92–2.06) for two doses versus one — no benefit; HR 4.73 in children exposed to polio campaigns before and after enrolment (interaction p=0.027)
cards.people: 6,636 children enrolled in Guinea-Bissau (6,598 analysed), randomised 2:1 by sex-stratified blocks to measles vaccine at 4 and 9 months or at 9 months only, eligible four weeks after the third DTP-containing vaccine; maternal measles antibody measured before randomisation; primary outcome all-cause mortality between 4 and 60 months.
cards.result: The hazard ratio (2-dose/1-dose) between 4 and 60 months was 1.38 (95% CI 0.92–2.06), with 90 deaths in the 2-dose group and 33 in the 1-dose group; before the 9-month dose the HR was 0.94 (0.45–1.96). The HR was 0.81 (0.29–2.22) in children who received no oral polio vaccine campaigns and 4.73 (1.44–15.6) in children who received campaigns before and after enrolment (interaction p=0.027). Within the 2-dose group, mortality was 50% lower (20–68%) for children vaccinated at 4 months in the presence of maternal measles antibody than in its absence. The authors concluded the main result contrasts with previous findings.
cards.watchOut: Deaths are few (123 in total) and the campaign-interaction rests on small cells (27 versus 3 deaths); but as the pre-registered replication of the earlier hypothesis, its null headline cannot be waved away — the two trials together say the effect, if real, is conditional in ways nobody has prospectively pinned down.
cards.source: Nielsen S et al. Effect of early two-dose measles vaccination on childhood mortality and modification by maternal measles antibody in Guinea-Bissau, West Africa: A single-centre open-label randomised controlled trial. cards.headline: Burkina Faso trial 2018: an additional early measles dose — hospitalisation or mortality HR 1.00 (0.83–1.20) in 4,496 children
cards.summary: Burkina Faso trial 2018: an additional early measles dose — hospitalisation or mortality HR 1.00 (0.83–1.20) in 4,496 children
cards.people: 4,496 children in the Nouna health and demographic surveillance system, Burkina Faso, randomised to an additional early dose of measles vaccine four weeks after the third pentavalent (DTP-containing) dose plus the standard 9-month dose, or the standard dose alone; composite endpoint of overnight hospitalisation (with or without recovery) or death without prior hospitalisation between 4.5 and 36 months; 464 endpoint episodes observed.
cards.result: There was no difference between intervention and control groups on the composite endpoint (HR 1.00, 95% CI 0.83–1.20); per-protocol and intention-to-treat analyses were similar. The record's authors note the results suggested possible subgroup patterns but none was significant.
cards.watchOut: A composite dominated by hospitalisations rather than deaths, in a different country and vaccine environment — it constrains the size of any general benefit without directly re-testing the Guinea-Bissau mortality claim.
cards.source: Schoeps A et al. No effect of an additional early dose of measles vaccine on hospitalization or mortality in children: A randomized controlled trial. Vaccine. 2018. PMID: 29523450. Registry ID: NCT01644721. cards.headline: Synthesis: one suggestive trial, two null replications — the early-dose survival hypothesis is unproven, and the campaign interaction is a warning, not an answer
cards.summary: Synthesis: one suggestive trial, two null replications — the early-dose survival hypothesis is unproven, and the campaign interaction is a warning, not an answer
cards.people: Three randomised trials totalling about 17,700 children in Guinea-Bissau (two) and Burkina Faso: measles vaccine at ~4–4.5 plus 9 months versus 9 months alone, with all-cause mortality or hospitalisation endpoints.
cards.result: Mortality: rate ratio 0.78 (0.59–1.05) in the first trial, HR 1.38 (0.92–2.06) in its replication, HR 1.00 (0.83–1.20) for hospitalisation-or-death in the third. Subgroup signals (girls, no neonatal vitamin A, maternal antibody present, no polio campaigns) recur but were never the primary result of any trial. PROPOSED SPLIT, Tier C — mortality claims from subgroup and interaction analyses are exactly what the developer reviews personally.
cards.watchOut: Nothing on this shelf questions measles vaccination itself or the standard 9-month dose — the dispute is only about an additional early dose and non-measles mortality effects; measles prevention by the standard schedule is settled elsewhere in this library.
cards.source: Synthesis of Aaby P et al. BMJ. 2010 (PMID: 21118875); Nielsen S et al. EClinicalMedicine. 2022 (PMID: 35747181); Schoeps A et al. Vaccine. 2018 (PMID: 29523450).

shelves.title: A third mRNA COVID-19 vaccine dose in organ transplant recipients: neutralising responses against Delta in 55% versus 18% on placebo (difference 37 points) — an antibody trial, with no proven clinical endpoint
shelves.question: In organ transplant recipients who have had two doses of COVID-19 vaccine, does a third dose of mRNA-1273 vaccine raise neutralising antibody responses against SARS-CoV-2 variants compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: 2019-nCoV Vaccine mRNA-1273/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Aged · Antibodies, Neutralizing/blood · COVID-19/immunology/prevention & control/virology · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Immunocompromised Host · Male · Middle Aged · Organ Transplantation · SARS-CoV-2 · Transplant Recipients
shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit) — for the antibody outcome the trial actually measured; the shelf claims nothing about infections prevented. The randomised, double-blind trial (Hall VG et al., PMID: 34379917; neutralisation analysis PMID: 34807716) assigned organ transplant recipients to a third dose of mRNA-1273 vaccine or placebo; 117 recipients were analysed (60 vaccine, 57 placebo), with sera before and 4–6 weeks after the third dose. After two doses, the proportion with positive neutralisation against all three variants was small compared with wild-type virus. After the third dose, positive neutralisation by the pseudovirus assay against the Delta variant was present in 33 of 60 (55%) vaccine recipients versus 10 of 57 (18%) on placebo — a difference of 37 percentage points (95% CI 19–53); differences were 36 points (17–51) for Alpha and 31 points (15–46) for Beta, with neutralisation values lower for variants than wild-type, especially Beta. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): a third dose clearly raised variant neutralisation in transplant recipients — with the analysis's own stated limitation printed on the shelf: there is no clear correlate of protection for neutralising antibody, and this was a secondary analysis of an immunogenicity trial.

cards.headline: Hall/Kumar trial, neutralisation analysis (n=117): Delta neutralisation positive in 55% after a third dose versus 18% on placebo (difference 37 points, 95% CI 19–53); Alpha +36, Beta +31
cards.summary: Hall/Kumar trial, neutralisation analysis (n=117): Delta neutralisation positive in 55% after a third dose versus 18% on placebo (difference 37 points, 95% CI 19–53); Alpha +36, Beta +31
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial — secondary neutralisation analysis (2022)
cards.people: 117 organ transplant recipients at a single-centre transplant programme (60 assigned mRNA-1273, 57 placebo for the third dose), analysed for neutralisation against wild-type virus and the Alpha, Beta and Delta variants by a surrogate virus neutralisation assay and a spike-pseudotyped lentivirus assay; sera collected before and 4–6 weeks after the third dose. The vaccine is named as published (mRNA-1273); the record names no manufacturer, so none is stated.
cards.result: After two doses, the proportion of patients with positive neutralisation for all three variants was small compared with wild-type virus. After the third dose of mRNA-1273, the proportion with a positive neutralisation response versus placebo improved for all three variants by both assays: by the pseudovirus assay against Delta, 33 of 60 (55%) were positive in the vaccine group versus 10 of 57 (18%) on placebo (difference 37 percentage points, 95% CI 19–53); differences were 36 points (17–51) for Alpha and 31 points (15–46) for Beta. In the vaccine group, neutralisation values were lower for variants than for wild-type virus, especially Beta. The authors' stated limitations: there is no clear correlate of protection for neutralising antibody, and this was a secondary analysis.
cards.watchOut: Antibodies are a surrogate: this trial was not sized or designed to count infections, hospitalisations or deaths, and the variants assayed (Alpha, Beta, Delta) have since been displaced — the durable lesson is that a third dose moves immunogenicity in transplant recipients, not a variant-specific promise.
cards.source: Hall VG et al. Neutralization of SARS-CoV-2 Variants in Transplant Recipients After Two and Three Doses of mRNA-1273. Annals of Internal Medicine. 2022. PMID: 34807716. Registry ID: NCT04885907. cards.people: One randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial in 117 organ transplant recipients, reported in a primary paper (2021) and a variant-neutralisation analysis (2022).
cards.result: Positive neutralisation after the third dose versus placebo: Delta 55% versus 18% (+37 points), Alpha +36 points, Beta +31 points; two-dose responses against variants were small. PROPOSED LIKELY for the immunogenicity claim, with the no-correlate-of-protection limitation carried on the face of the shelf.
cards.watchOut: This shelf answers an antibody question in transplant recipients; clinical-outcome questions (infections, severe disease) and later-variant or later-dose questions belong to other shelves and other evidence.
cards.source: Synthesis of Hall VG et al. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2021 (PMID: 34379917) and Annals of Internal Medicine. 2022 (PMID: 34807716).

shelves.title: Seasonal malaria chemoprevention in the Sahel: three large blinded trials cut clinical malaria by 70–86% and severe malaria sharply, on top of bednets — vomiting is the commonest side effect
shelves.question: In children in the Sahel, does seasonal malaria chemoprevention (sulfadoxine–pyrimethamine plus amodiaquine) reduce clinical malaria and severe malaria compared with no chemoprevention?
shelves.mesh: Antimalarials/therapeutic use · Artemisinins/therapeutic use · Artesunate · Bedding and Linens · Child, Preschool · Double-Blind Method · Drug Combinations · Drug Resistance/genetics · Humans · Infant · Malaria, Falciparum/epidemiology/prevention & control · Prevalence · Pyrimethamine/therapeutic use · Seasons · Senegal/epidemiology · Sesquiterpenes/therapeutic use · Sulfadoxine/therapeutic use
shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit) — the largest preventive effect in this band. Three large randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trials in Sahelian children aged 2–59 months agree: monthly chemoprevention during the transmission season cut clinical malaria by 86% (95% CI 80–90) in Senegal (Cissé B et al., PMID: 16503464), by 82% (78–85) in Mali (Dicko A et al., PMID: 21304923) and by 70% (66–74) in Burkina Faso (Konaté AT et al., PMID: 21304925). Severe malaria fell too — 2 versus 15 episodes in Mali (87% protective efficacy) and a 69% relative reduction in Burkina Faso — and in Mali and Burkina Faso the protection was on top of insecticide-treated bednets, which more than 93% of children slept under. The commonest harm is vomiting: children on chemoprevention were 2.8 times more likely to vomit in Burkina Faso, and vomiting was also increased in Senegal; no drug-related serious adverse event was recorded in any trial. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): seasonal chemoprevention is a large, consistent preventive win for Sahelian children, capped at POSSIBLE by this band's stamp cap — the trials themselves would support more.

cards.headline: Cissé 2006: artesunate plus sulfadoxine–pyrimethamine cut clinical malaria by 86% over 13 weeks — incidence 308 versus 2,250 episodes per 1,000 person-years
cards.summary: Cissé 2006: artesunate plus sulfadoxine–pyrimethamine cut clinical malaria by 86% over 13 weeks — incidence 308 versus 2,250 episodes per 1,000 person-years
cards.people: 1,136 children aged 2–59 months in Niakhar, rural Senegal, randomised to one dose of artesunate plus one dose of sulfadoxine–pyrimethamine or two placebos on three occasions during the malaria transmission season; primary outcome was a first or single episode of clinical malaria detected by active or passive case detection, over 13 weeks of follow-up.
cards.result: The intervention led to an 86% (95% CI 80–90) reduction in clinical episodes of malaria. Protective efficacy was 86% (77–92) with passive case detection and 86% (78–91) with active detection. The incidence of malaria was 308 episodes per 1,000 person-years at risk on active drugs versus 2,250 per 1,000 person-years on placebo — an absolute difference of 1,942 episodes per 1,000 person-years.
cards.watchOut: This trial used artesunate plus sulfadoxine–pyrimethamine, not the sulfadoxine–pyrimethamine plus amodiaquine pair the candidate question names — the SP+AQ pair is carried by the Dicko and Konaté trials below. Vomiting was increased on active drugs, though the intervention was generally well tolerated. Follow-up was only 13 weeks.
cards.source: Cissé B et al. Seasonal intermittent preventive treatment with artesunate and sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine for prevention of malaria in Senegalese children: a randomised, placebo-controlled, double-blind trial. Lancet. 2006. PMID: 16503464. Registry ID: NCT00132561. cards.headline: Dicko 2011 (Mali): sulfadoxine–pyrimethamine plus amodiaquine cut clinical malaria by 82% and severe malaria from 15 episodes to 2, on top of bednets
cards.summary: Dicko 2011 (Mali): sulfadoxine–pyrimethamine plus amodiaquine cut clinical malaria by 82% and severe malaria from 15 episodes to 2, on top of bednets
cards.people: 3,017 children aged 3–59 months in Kati, Mali, each given a long-lasting insecticide-treated bednet and randomised to three monthly rounds of sulfadoxine–pyrimethamine plus amodiaquine or placebo during the high transmission season (August–October 2008); 99.7% of control children and 99.3% of intervention children slept under a net.
cards.result: Clinical malaria occurred at 0.34 episodes per person-year on chemoprevention versus 1.90 on placebo — a protective efficacy of 82% (95% CI 78–85%, P<0.001), an absolute difference of 1.56 episodes per person-year. Severe malaria occurred in 2 children on chemoprevention versus 15 on placebo (protective efficacy 87%, 95% CI 42–99%, P=0.001). Malaria infection prevalence fell by 85% during the intervention period, and moderate anaemia (haemoglobin <8 g/dL) fell by 47% (95% CI 15–67%) by the end of the intervention period.
cards.watchOut: Adverse events were similar in both arms and there was no drug-related serious adverse event. The trial ran for a single transmission season, so it cannot speak to protection, resistance or tolerability over repeated annual seasons.
cards.source: Dicko A et al. Intermittent preventive treatment of malaria provides substantial protection against malaria in children already protected by an insecticide-treated bednet in Mali: a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial. PLoS Medicine. 2011. PMID: 21304923. Registry ID: NCT00738946. cards.headline: Konaté 2011 (Burkina Faso): same SP+AQ regimen cut clinical malaria by 70% and all-cause hospital admissions by 46%, on top of bednets — vomiting 2.8 times more likely
cards.summary: Konaté 2011 (Burkina Faso): same SP+AQ regimen cut clinical malaria by 70% and all-cause hospital admissions by 46%, on top of bednets — vomiting 2.8 times more likely
cards.people: 3,014 children aged 3–59 months in Burkina Faso, each given a long-lasting insecticide-treated bednet and randomised to three monthly rounds of sulfadoxine–pyrimethamine plus amodiaquine or placebo during the transmission season; 93% of children in both arms slept under a net.
cards.result: Malaria incidence was 0.87 per child during the intervention period on chemoprevention versus 2.88 on placebo — a protective efficacy of 70% (95% CI 66–74%, P<0.001), an absolute difference of 2.01 episodes per child. Severe malaria fell by 69% (95% CI 6–90%, P=0.04) and all-cause hospital admissions by 46% (95% CI 7–69%, P=0.03). Malaria infection prevalence at the end of the season fell by 73% and moderately severe anaemia by 56% (95% CI 36–70%).
cards.watchOut: Children on chemoprevention were 2.8 times more likely to vomit (95% CI 2.3–3.5, P<0.001), but no drug-related serious adverse event was recorded. As with the Mali trial, this is a single-season result; the effect of repeated annual chemoprevention on drug resistance is not answered here.
cards.source: Konaté AT et al. Intermittent preventive treatment of malaria provides substantial protection against malaria in children already protected by an insecticide-treated bednet in Burkina Faso: a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial. PLoS Medicine. 2011. PMID: 21304925. Registry ID: NCT00738946. cards.headline: Synthesis: three large trials, one direction — chemoprevention is the biggest preventive win in this part of the build
cards.summary: Synthesis: three large trials, one direction — chemoprevention is the biggest preventive win in this part of the build
cards.people: Three randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trials totalling 7,167 Sahelian children aged 2–59 months (Cissé 2006, Senegal, n=1,136; Dicko 2011, Mali, n=3,017; Konaté 2011, Burkina Faso, n=3,014), each giving three monthly rounds of chemoprevention during the transmission season.
cards.result: Clinical malaria: protective efficacy 86% (Cissé), 82% (Dicko), 70% (Konaté). Severe malaria: 2 versus 15 episodes (Dicko); 69% relative reduction (Konaté). Added benefits: all-cause hospital admissions down 46% (Konaté); moderate anaemia down 47% (Dicko) and 56% (Konaté). Harms: vomiting increased in all three trials (2.8 times more likely in Konaté); no drug-related serious adverse event in any trial. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — capped by this band's stamp cap; the trials would support more.
cards.watchOut: Boundary ruled: live shelf #968 homes chemoprevention combined with RTS,S vaccination and chemoprevention plus azithromycin — a different question about additions to chemoprevention. This shelf homes chemoprevention itself versus no chemoprevention. Regimen note: Cissé used artesunate plus sulfadoxine–pyrimethamine; Dicko and Konaté used the sulfadoxine–pyrimethamine plus amodiaquine pair the question names.
cards.source: Synthesis of Cissé B et al. Lancet. 2006 (PMID: 16503464); Dicko A et al. PLoS Medicine. 2011 (PMID: 21304923); Konaté AT et al. PLoS Medicine. 2011 (PMID: 21304925).

shelves.title: Screening women for abdominal aortic aneurysm: in the one randomised trial of 9,342 women, rupture rates were identical in screened and unscreened groups at 5 and 10 years — prevalence in women was a sixth of men's
shelves.question: In adults, does a one-time abdominal aortic aneurysm ultrasound screen reduce AAA mortality in women?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Aortic Aneurysm, Abdominal/diagnostic imaging/epidemiology/mortality · England/epidemiology · Female · Humans · Incidence · Male · Mass Screening/methods · Prevalence · Risk Factors · Sex Factors · Ultrasonography
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — for women, the screening benefit proven in men does not appear. The men's screening shelves rest on trials in men; the one randomised trial that screened women (Chichester, Scott RA et al., PMID: 11872050) randomised 9,342 women aged 65–80 to an invitation for a single ultrasound scan or control, found AAA prevalence of 1.3% in women versus 7.6% in men, and over 5- and 10-year follow-up the incidence of rupture was the same in the screened and control groups. A systematic review prepared for the Canadian Task Force (Ali MU et al., PMID: 27871502) put the women's estimate at RR 0.88 (95% CI 0.72–1.07) for up to 10 years — no significant difference — against a pooled 42% relative reduction in AAA-related mortality in men (RR 0.58, 95% CI 0.39–0.88). The original Chichester report (Scott RA et al., PMID: 7648155) had already shown the split: rupture incidence fell 55% relative in invited men, while rupture in women was low in both groups. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): one-time ultrasound screening of unselected women aged 65–80 does not reduce AAA rupture or mortality — a single-trial, sex-specific boundary on the men's screening evidence, held as Tier C.

cards.headline: Scott 2002 (Chichester, women): 9,342 women randomised — AAA prevalence 1.3% versus 7.6% in men, and rupture incidence the same in screened and control women at 5 and 10 years
cards.summary: Scott 2002 (Chichester, women): 9,342 women randomised — AAA prevalence 1.3% versus 7.6% in men, and rupture incidence the same in screened and control women at 5 and 10 years
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial (Scott 2002, Chichester women's trial)
cards.people: 9,342 women aged 65–80 years in the Chichester (England) programme, randomised to invitation for a single ultrasonographic AAA scan or to age-matched control; women with an AAA received follow-up scans and were considered for elective surgery if criteria were met. Follow-up 5 and 10 years.
cards.result: AAA prevalence was 1.3% in women — six times lower than the 7.6% found in men in the same programme. Over both the 5- and 10-year follow-up intervals, the incidence of rupture was the same in the screened and control groups of women. The authors concluded screening women for AAA is neither clinically indicated nor economically viable.
cards.watchOut: Single-trial shelf: this is the only randomised screening trial in women, and its abstract reports rupture incidence without a mortality split or confidence interval — the null is consistent but the precision comes from the systematic review card below. Women were unselected by smoking or family history, so a targeted high-risk women's strategy is not what was tested.
cards.source: Scott RA et al. Randomized clinical trial of screening for abdominal aortic aneurysm in women. The British Journal of Surgery. 2002. PMID: 11872050. cards.headline: Scott 1995 (Chichester, 5-year results): rupture incidence fell 55% relative in invited men — in women it was low in both groups
cards.summary: Scott 1995 (Chichester, 5-year results): rupture incidence fell 55% relative in invited men — in women it was low in both groups
cards.people: 15,775 men and women aged 65–80 years identified from family medical practices and randomised to invitation for ultrasonographic AAA screening or age- and sex-matched control; 5,394 of 7,887 invited (68.4%) accepted screening; AAA detected in 218 (4.0% overall, 7.6% of men).
cards.result: The incidence of rupture was reduced by 55% (relative) in men in the group invited for screening compared with controls. The incidence of rupture in women was low in both groups. No patient fit for operation who accepted elective treatment died from rupture.
cards.watchOut: The 55% figure is a relative reduction in rupture incidence in men only, reported without absolute rates in this record; it is the contrast that makes the women's null interpretable — the same programme, the same scan, a sixfold-lower prevalence and no measurable rupture dividend in women.
cards.source: Scott RA et al. Influence of screening on the incidence of ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm: 5-year results of a randomized controlled study. The British Journal of Surgery. 1995. PMID: 7648155. cards.headline: Ali 2016 (systematic review for the Canadian Task Force): women's screening estimate RR 0.88 (95% CI 0.72–1.07) — no benefit — versus RR 0.58 for AAA-related mortality in men
cards.summary: Ali 2016 (systematic review for the Canadian Task Force): women's screening estimate RR 0.88 (95% CI 0.72–1.07) — no benefit — versus RR 0.58 for AAA-related mortality in men
cards.people: Systematic review of one-time ultrasound AAA screening in asymptomatic adults, updating the USPSTF evidence base to April 2015; four randomised trials in men pooled, and the single Chichester trial reporting women separately, with follow-up to 10 years in women and 13–15 years in men.
cards.result: In men, pooled one-time screening reduced AAA-related mortality by 42% relative (RR 0.58, 95% CI 0.39–0.88; number needed to screen 212) and rupture by 38% relative (RR 0.62, 95% CI 0.45–0.86). The Chichester trial's women showed no significant difference between screening and control arms for up to 10 years of follow-up (RR 0.88, 95% CI 0.72–1.07). The review concluded the current evidence showed no benefit of one-time AAA screening in women.
cards.watchOut: The women's RR 0.88 rests on the same single Chichester dataset as the first card — the review adds precision and the male contrast, not an independent women's trial. A confidence interval reaching 0.72 leaves a modest benefit formally possible, which is why the stamp is POSSIBLE, not a stronger null.

systematic review (ali 2016) systematic review of one-time ultrasound aaa screening in asymptomatic adults, updating the uspstf evidence base to april 2015; four randomised trials in men pooled, and the single chichester trial reporting women separately, with follow-up to 10 years in women and 13–15 years in men. in men, pooled one-time screening reduced aaa-related mortality by 42% relative (rr 0.58, 95% ci 0.39–0.88; number needed to screen 212) and rupture by 38% relative (rr 0.62, 95% ci 0.45–0.86). the chichester trial's women showed no significant difference between screening and control arms for up to 10 years of follow-up (rr 0.88, 95% ci 0.72–1.07). the review concluded the current evidence showed no benefit of one-time aaa screening in women. the women's rr 0.88 rests on the same single chichester dataset as the first card — the review adds precision and the male contrast, not an independent women's trial. a confidence interval reaching 0.72 leaves a modest benefit formally possible, which is why the stamp is possible, not a stronger null. ali mu et al. screening for abdominal aortic aneurysm in asymptomatic adults. journal of vascular surgery. 2016. pmid: 27871502. mesh: age factors · aged · aged, 80 and over · aortic aneurysm, abdominal/diagnostic imaging/mortality/therapy · asymptomatic diseases · evidence-based medicine · female · humans · male · mass screening/methods · middle aged · odds ratio · patient selection · predictive value of tests · prognosis · risk factors · sex factors · time factors · ultrasonography · unnecessary procedures

cards.headline: Synthesis: one women's trial, one null — screening unselected women aged 65–80 does not reproduce the men's mortality benefit
cards.summary: Synthesis: one women's trial, one null — screening unselected women aged 65–80 does not reproduce the men's mortality benefit
cards.people: One randomised trial in women (Chichester, 9,342 women aged 65–80, single ultrasound invitation versus control, 5- and 10-year follow-up), the same programme's combined 5-year report (15,775 men and women), and a 2016 systematic review pooling the men's trials for contrast.
cards.result: Women: AAA prevalence 1.3% (versus 7.6% in men); rupture incidence identical in screened and control women at 5 and 10 years; review estimate RR 0.88 (95% CI 0.72–1.07). Men, for contrast: 55% relative reduction in rupture incidence in the Chichester 5-year report and a pooled 42% relative reduction in AAA-related mortality (RR 0.58, 95% CI 0.39–0.88). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) for screening unselected women; Tier C, single-trial.
cards.watchOut: Single-trial shelf — flagged on its face. The trial predates modern statin and smoking-cessation backgrounds and tested unselected women; it does not answer screening for women with a strong smoking history or family history, where prevalence — and any possible dividend — would be higher.

shelves.title: The mRNA RSV vaccine cut lower-respiratory disease by 83.7% relative in its first season in over-60s — one trial, a median of only 112 days watched, and a rougher two days after the jab
shelves.question: In older adults, does an mRNA RSV vaccine prevent RSV lower-respiratory disease compared with placebo (a platform boundary vs live #980's pregnancy question)?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Humans · Antibodies, Viral · Double-Blind Method · Respiratory Syncytial Virus Infections/epidemiology/prevention & control · Respiratory Syncytial Virus, Human/genetics · Respiratory Tract Diseases/diagnosis/epidemiology/prevention & control · Treatment Outcome · mRNA Vaccines/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Respiratory Syncytial Virus Vaccines/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Middle Aged
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — strong first-season protection from the mRNA platform, in a single trial that had watched participants for a median of only 112 days when the primary analysis was run. ConquerRSV randomised 35,541 adults aged 60 and over to one dose of mRNA-1345 (n=17,793) or placebo (n=17,748). Vaccine efficacy was 83.7% relative (95.88% CI 66.0 to 92.2) against RSV-associated lower respiratory tract disease with at least two signs or symptoms, 82.4% relative (96.36% CI 34.8 to 95.3) against disease with at least three signs or symptoms, and 68.4% relative (95% CI 50.9 to 79.7) against RSV-associated acute respiratory disease, with protection against both RSV subtypes A and B. The price was reactogenicity: solicited local reactions in 58.7% versus 16.2% and systemic reactions in 47.7% versus 32.9%, mostly mild to moderate and transient; serious adverse events occurred in 2.8% of each group. The protein-based RSV vaccines for this age group live on their own shelf (live #320); this shelf is the mRNA platform's separate record — and durability beyond one season is not in it. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a single dose of mRNA-1345 prevents RSV lower-respiratory disease in adults 60 and over, on one large trial with short median follow-up.

cards.headline: ConquerRSV (Wilson 2023): efficacy 83.7% relative against RSV lower-respiratory disease with ≥2 symptoms and 82.4% with ≥3 — local reactions 58.7% versus 16.2%
cards.summary: ConquerRSV (Wilson 2023): efficacy 83.7% relative against RSV lower-respiratory disease with ≥2 symptoms and 82.4% with ≥3 — local reactions 58.7% versus 16.2%
cards.people: 35,541 adults aged 60 years or older, randomised 1:1 to a single dose of mRNA-1345 50 μg (n=17,793) or placebo (n=17,748); median follow-up 112 days (range 1 to 379) at the primary analysis, conducted when at least 50% of anticipated lower-respiratory cases had occurred.
cards.result: Vaccine efficacy was 83.7% relative (95.88% CI 66.0 to 92.2) against RSV-associated lower respiratory tract disease with at least two signs or symptoms, and 82.4% relative (96.36% CI 34.8 to 95.3) against disease with at least three signs or symptoms. Efficacy against RSV-associated acute respiratory disease was 68.4% relative (95% CI 50.9 to 79.7). Protection was observed against both RSV subtypes (A and B) and was generally consistent across age and coexisting-condition subgroups. Solicited local adverse reactions: 58.7% versus 16.2%; systemic reactions 47.7% versus 32.9% — mostly mild to moderate and transient. Serious adverse events occurred in 2.8% of participants in each group.
cards.watchOut: Single-trial shelf, and an interim-shaped one: the primary analysis ran at a median follow-up of 112 days, so this record says nothing about second-season durability, revaccination, or rare harms (the Guillain-Barré signal tracked on the protein-vaccine shelf, live #320, cannot be excluded or confirmed at this exposure). Efficacy figures are relative; the abstract reports no absolute case rates, so none are printed here.
cards.source: Wilson E et al. Efficacy and Safety of an mRNA-Based RSV PreF Vaccine in Older Adults. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2023. PMID: 38091530. Registry ID: NCT05127434. shelves.title: Single-dose live oral cholera vaccine CVD 103-HgR (Vaxchora) for travellers: 90.3% efficacy at 10 days and 79.5% at 3 months in the human challenge trial — but 14% and not significant in the one large field trial
shelves.question: In adults travelling to cholera-risk areas, does the single-dose live oral cholera vaccine CVD 103-HgR (Vaxchora) prevent cholera, and by how much — and how does its challenge-trial record sit with its field record?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Antibodies, Bacterial/blood · Antibodies, Bacterial/immunology · Cholera/immunology · Cholera/prevention & control · Cholera Vaccines/administration & dosage · Cholera Vaccines/adverse effects · Cholera Vaccines/immunology · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Vibrio cholerae O1/immunology · Young Adult
shelves.balance: SPLIT — the answer depends on which test of the vaccine is being read. In the human challenge model the protection is large and replicated: in the randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled pivotal trial behind US licensure (Chen 2016, PMID: 27001804; 197 volunteers aged 18–45), moderate (≥3.0 L) to severe (≥5.0 L) diarrhoeal purge after ingesting wild-type Vibrio cholerae O1 El Tor occurred in 39 of 66 (59.1%) placebo recipients versus 2 of 35 (5.7%) vaccinees challenged at 10 days (vaccine efficacy 90.3%, a relative measure) and 4 of 33 (12.1%) vaccinees challenged at 3 months (efficacy 79.5%). An earlier randomised double-blind challenge trial found the same pattern at 3 months (Tacket 1999, PMID: 10569747: moderate or severe diarrhoea in 9 of 23 [39%] placebo recipients versus 1 of 28 [4%] vaccinees; protective efficacy 91%), and the earliest onset/duration studies reported 100% protection against diarrhoea on homologous challenge at 8 days and at 6 months (Tacket 1992, PMID: 1527420). In the field, the same vaccine did not reproduce this: in the randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial of 67,508 people aged 2–41 in North Jakarta (Richie 2000, PMID: 10738097), 93 evaluable cholera cases occurred over four years — 43 in vaccinees and 50 in placebo recipients — for an efficacy of 14%, not significant, and the authors concluded that single-dose CVD 103-HgR did not confer long-term protection in Jakarta; only seven cases occurred within six months, so short-term field efficacy could not be assessed. A Jakarta immunogenicity study hints at one reason the field is harder than the challenge ward: the dose that seroconverts over 90% of people in industrialised countries seroconverted only 16% of Indonesian children, and a ten-fold higher dose was needed for 75–87% seroconversion (Suharyono 1992, PMID: 1355798). The vaccine was licensed by the US FDA in 2016 for travellers (Saluja 2020, PMID: 31339792), and ACIP recommends it only for travellers aged 2–64 years going to an area with active cholera transmission (Collins 2022, PMID: 36173766) — cholera is rare in travellers, so this vaccine is rarely recommended for ordinary travellers. BOUNDARY: this shelf covers ONLY the live vaccine CVD 103-HgR (Vaxchora). The killed whole-cell oral cholera vaccines and their field efficacy in endemic settings (Kolkata two-dose 65% over 5 years; Bangladesh single-dose 40% / 63% against severe cholera) are homed on Shelf #1180 and are not re-carded here. PROPOSED SPLIT: strong, replicated protection in the volunteer challenge model at 10 days to 3 months; no significant protection shown in the one large field trial over four years.

cards.headline: Chen 2016 (the pivotal challenge trial behind licensure): moderate/severe cholera purge in 59.1% of placebo recipients versus 5.7% of vaccinees at 10 days (efficacy 90.3%) and 12.1% at 3 months (efficacy 79.5%)
cards.summary: Chen 2016 (the pivotal challenge trial behind licensure): moderate/severe cholera purge in 59.1% of placebo recipients versus 5.7% of vaccinees at 10 days (efficacy 90.3%) and 12.1% at 3 months (efficacy 79.5%)
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled human challenge trial (Chen 2016)
cards.people: 197 healthy adult volunteers aged 18–45 years at US sites (95 vaccinees, 102 placebo recipients for the safety set), randomly allocated 1:1 to a single oral dose of vaccine (PXVX0200, approximately 5 × 10^8 colony-forming units [CFU] of CVD 103-HgR) or placebo in double-blind fashion; challenged subsets ingested approximately 1 × 10^5 CFU of wild-type Vibrio cholerae O1 El Tor Inaba strain N16961 either 10 days or 3 months after vaccination and were observed on an inpatient research ward with stool output measurement.
cards.result: The primary endpoint — moderate (≥3.0 L) to severe (≥5.0 L) diarrhoeal purge — occurred in 39 of 66 (59.1%) placebo controls but in only 2 of 35 (5.7%) vaccinees challenged at 10 days (vaccine efficacy 90.3%, a relative measure; P < .0001) and 4 of 33 (12.1%) vaccinees challenged at 3 months (vaccine efficacy 79.5%; P < .0001). The absolute differences in attack rates were 53.4 percentage points at 10 days and 47.0 percentage points at 3 months, against the printed placebo attack rate of 59.1%. The vaccine was well tolerated, with no difference in adverse event frequency between vaccinees and placebo recipients. The authors concluded that the significant efficacy at 10 days and 3 months after one oral dose supports development as a single-dose cholera vaccine; this was the pivotal efficacy trial for FDA licensure.
cards.watchOut: A challenge trial is the most favourable possible stage: healthy young US volunteers with no prior cholera exposure, a single standardised inoculum of one El Tor Inaba strain, inpatient observation, and an endpoint of stool volume — not naturally acquired cholera on a trip, not other strains or serogroups, and no one over 45 was challenged. The 90.3% and 79.5% figures are relative efficacies; the absolute attack rates printed beside them (59.1% placebo) reflect a deliberate experimental infection that almost always takes, which no traveller's exposure resembles.
cards.source: Chen WH, Cohen MB, Kirkpatrick BD, Brady RC, Galloway D, Gurwith M, Hall RH, Kessler RA, Lock M, Haney D, Lyon CE, Pasetti MF, Simon JK, Szabo F, Tennant S, Levine MM. Single-dose Live Oral Cholera Vaccine CVD 103-HgR Protects Against Human Experimental Infection With Vibrio cholerae O1 El Tor. Clinical Infectious Diseases. 2016. PMID: 27001804. Registry ID: NCT01895855. cards.headline: Tacket 1999 (the earlier randomised challenge trial): at 3 months, moderate or severe diarrhoea in 39% of placebo recipients versus 4% of vaccinees — protective efficacy 91%; any diarrhoea 91% versus 18% — efficacy 80%
cards.summary: Tacket 1999 (the earlier randomised challenge trial): at 3 months, moderate or severe diarrhoea in 39% of placebo recipients versus 4% of vaccinees — protective efficacy 91%; any diarrhoea 91% versus 18% — efficacy 80%
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, multicenter volunteer challenge trial (Tacket 1999)
cards.people: 85 US volunteers recruited at the University of Maryland and Children's Hospital Medical Center/University of Cincinnati, randomised double-blind to a single oral dose of CVD 103-HgR (2 × 10^8 to 8 × 10^8 CFU) with buffer or placebo (killed Escherichia coli K-12); 51 of them (28 vaccinees, 23 placebo recipients) were orally challenged about 3 months after immunisation with 10^5 CFU of virulent Vibrio cholerae O1 El Tor Inaba strain N16961 from a standardised frozen inoculum.
cards.result: Ninety-one percent of vaccinees had a ≥4-fold rise in serum vibriocidal antibodies after vaccination. After challenge, 9 (39%) of the 23 placebo recipients and 1 (4%) of the 28 vaccinees had moderate or severe diarrhoea (≥3-litre diarrhoeal stool) (P < 0.01; protective efficacy 91%, a relative measure; absolute difference 35 percentage points). For diarrhoea of any severity, 21 (91%) of 23 placebo recipients and 5 (18%) of 28 vaccinees were affected (P < 0.001; protective efficacy 80%). Peak stool V. cholerae excretion was 1.1 × 10^7 CFU/g in placebo recipients versus 4.9 × 10^2 CFU/g in vaccinees (P < 0.001). The authors concluded the vaccine could be a safe and effective tool to prevent cholera in travellers.
cards.watchOut: Same challenge-model limits as Chen 2016, seventeen years earlier and with the older vaccine formulation: 51 challenged volunteers, one challenge strain, an artificial inoculum. Its value on this shelf is corroboration — the ~90% relative efficacy against moderate/severe disease at 3 months was found twice, in two randomised double-blind challenge trials, before it was found nowhere in the field.
cards.source: Tacket CO, Cohen MB, Wasserman SS, Losonsky G, Livio S, Kotloff K, Edelman R, Kaper JB, Cryz SJ, Giannella RA, Schiff G, Levine MM. Randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, multicentered trial of the efficacy of a single dose of live oral cholera vaccine CVD 103-HgR in preventing cholera following challenge with Vibrio cholerae O1 El tor inaba three months after vaccination. Infection and Immunity. 1999. PMID: 10569747. Registry ID: none in the record (pre-registration-era trial).
