cards.summary: Tacket 1992 (onset and duration): 100% protective against diarrhoea on homologous challenge at 8 days and at 6 months after a single dose
cards.type: Volunteer challenge studies of onset and duration of protection (Tacket 1992)
cards.people: North American adult volunteers in two challenge cohorts — one challenged 8 days after a single dose of CVD 103-HgR and one challenged 6 months after vaccination — with challenge by Vibrio cholerae classical Inaba strain 569B, the virulent parent strain of the vaccine; earlier challenge studies from the same programme, conducted 4–5 weeks after vaccination, had shown significant protection against both classical and El Tor V. cholerae O1.
cards.result: In both studies, CVD 103-HgR was 100% protective against diarrhoea (a relative efficacy of 100% as reported by the authors) and significantly reduced the rate of shedding of vibrios after challenge. Previously vaccinated subjects were less likely than naive controls to develop rises in vibriocidal antibody titre after challenge (P = .002), and their mean peak titre was lower than among controls. The authors concluded that CVD 103-HgR can provide homologous protective immunity as soon as 8 days after vaccination and that protection can persist for at least 6 months.
cards.watchOut: The abstract reports the 100% figure without printing the per-group denominators or the control attack rates, so no absolute rates are claimed on this card. The challenge was homologous — the vaccine's own parent strain — which is the easiest challenge the vaccine could face, and these were small early volunteer studies, not randomised efficacy trials of the Tacket 1999 / Chen 2016 size. Read it as the onset-and-duration claim (protection by ~8 days, still present at 6 months in the challenge model), not as a third independent efficacy estimate.
cards.source: Tacket CO, Losonsky G, Nataro JP, Cryz SJ, Edelman R, Kaper JB, Levine MM. Onset and duration of protective immunity in challenged volunteers after vaccination with live oral cholera vaccine CVD 103-HgR. The Journal of Infectious Diseases. 1992. PMID: 1527420. Registry ID: none in the record (pre-registration-era study). cards.headline: Suharyono 1992 (why the field is harder): the dose that seroconverts over 90% in industrialised countries seroconverted only 16% of Indonesian children; a ten-fold higher dose reached 75–87%
cards.summary: Suharyono 1992 (why the field is harder): the dose that seroconverts over 90% in industrialised countries seroconverted only 16% of Indonesian children; a ten-fold higher dose reached 75–87%
cards.type: Randomised dose-ranging safety and immunogenicity trial in an endemic-area population (Suharyono 1992)
cards.people: 412 children aged 5–9 years in north Jakarta, Indonesia, who received single doses of 5 × 10^6, 5 × 10^7, 5 × 10^8, 5 × 10^9, or 1 × 10^10 CFU of CVD 103-HgR, or placebo (5 × 10^8 inactivated Escherichia coli K-12), with buffer.
cards.result: All doses were well tolerated. The 5 × 10^8 CFU dose — highly immunogenic in subjects in industrialised countries, with greater than 90% seroconversion — elicited vibriocidal antibody seroconversion in only 16% of Indonesian children. A single 5 × 10^9 CFU dose produced seroconversion rates of 75% and 87% with two different batches of vaccine. The authors concluded that at the 5 × 10^9 CFU dose the vaccine is well tolerated and highly immunogenic in Indonesian children and should be further investigated as a one-dose live oral cholera vaccine in developing countries.
cards.watchOut: Immunogenicity, not clinical protection — seroconversion is the accepted correlate, but this card measures antibody response, not cholera prevented. It is carded because it is the fetched record that most directly explains the challenge-versus-field gap on this shelf: the same vaccine, at the traveller dose, immunologically under-performs in an endemic-area gut. Children in Jakarta are also not the shelf's traveller population; the point is the direction of the endemic-setting effect, not a number transferable to adult travellers.
cards.source: Suharyono, Simanjuntak C, Witham N, Punjabi N, Heppner DG, Losonsky G, Totosudirjo H, Rifai AR, Clemens J, Lim YL, et al. Safety and immunogenicity of single-dose live oral cholera vaccine CVD 103-HgR in 5-9-year-old Indonesian children. Lancet. 1992. PMID: 1355798. Registry ID: none in the record (pre-registration-era trial). cards.headline: Richie 2000 (the field trial — the counterweight): 67,508 people, four years, 43 vaccine versus 50 placebo cholera cases — efficacy 14%, not significant; single-dose CVD 103-HgR did not confer long-term protection in Jakarta
cards.summary: Richie 2000 (the field trial — the counterweight): 67,508 people, four years, 43 vaccine versus 50 placebo cholera cases — efficacy 14%, not significant; single-dose CVD 103-HgR did not confer long-term protection in Jakarta
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled field efficacy trial (Richie 2000)
cards.people: 67,508 persons aged 2–41 years in North Jakarta, Indonesia, a cholera-endemic area, who ingested one dose of CVD 103-HgR live oral cholera vaccine or placebo in a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial performed from 1993 to 1997 and were followed for four years, with cholera cases detected using hospital-based surveillance; a nested reactogenicity study (538 vaccinees, 535 controls) and a nested immunogenicity study (N=657) accompanied the trial.
cards.result: The nested reactogenicity study revealed no vaccine-attributable side effects, and the nested immunogenicity study showed vibriocidal seroresponses in 64–70% of vaccinees versus 1–2% of controls. Cholera incidence was lower than expected: 103 cases of Vibrio cholerae O1 El Tor diarrhoea were detected, of which 93 were evaluable for vaccine efficacy — 43 in the vaccine group and 50 in the placebo group — giving an efficacy of 14% (a relative measure), not significant. A suggestion of protection was observed among persons with blood group O (P=0.12). Only seven cases occurred within six months of vaccination, precluding assessment of short-term efficacy. The authors' conclusion, verbatim in substance: in Jakarta, single-dose CVD 103-HgR did not confer long-term protection; short-term protection from a single dose and long-term protection from two doses have yet to be studied.
cards.watchOut: This is the shelf's most important card and its easiest to misread in both directions. Against the vaccine: it is the only large field test, it was randomised and double-blind, and its point estimate is 14% with case counts (43 vs 50) that leave no room for a large hidden long-term effect. For the vaccine: cholera incidence was far lower than expected (103 cases in 67,508 people over four years), the trial was not designed to test the short window — the first months after vaccination — in which the challenge trials show protection and in which a traveller actually needs it, and only seven cases fell in that window. What the trial settles is long-term field protection from one dose in an endemic population: not shown. What it cannot settle is short-term protection of a non-immune traveller, which rests on the challenge evidence alone.
cards.source: Richie EE, Punjabi NH, Sidharta YY, Peetosutan KK, Sukandar MM, Wasserman SS, Lesmana MM, Wangsasaputra FF, Pandam SS, Levine MM, O'Hanley PP, Cryz SJ, Simanjuntak CH. Efficacy trial of single-dose live oral cholera vaccine CVD 103-HgR in North Jakarta, Indonesia, a cholera-endemic area. Vaccine. 2000. PMID: 10738097. Registry ID: none in the record (pre-registration-era trial). cards.headline: Saluja 2020 (overview): no cholera vaccine had been available to US travellers for decades until CVD 103-HgR (Vaxchora) was licensed by the FDA in 2016 — with no data in cholera-endemic populations and an 18–64 age restriction at licensure
cards.summary: Saluja 2020 (overview): no cholera vaccine had been available to US travellers for decades until CVD 103-HgR (Vaxchora) was licensed by the FDA in 2016 — with no data in cholera-endemic populations and an 18–64 age restriction at licensure
cards.people: Review of the licensed live attenuated oral cholera vaccine CVD 103-HgR (Vaxchora) and its place alongside the bivalent whole-cell killed oral cholera vaccines used in endemic and outbreak settings.
cards.result: No cholera vaccine had been available for United States travellers at risk for decades until 2016, when CVD 103-HgR (Vaxchora), an oral live attenuated vaccine, was licensed by the US FDA. A single dose protected US volunteers against experimental challenge 10 days and 3 months after vaccination. The review notes the constraints on wider use: the vaccine requires reconstitution, was age-restricted to 18 to 64 years, has no data in populations endemic for cholera, and faces challenges related to cold chain and cost in resource-poor settings.
cards.watchOut: A narrative overview, carded for the licensure frame (FDA, 2016, traveller indication) and for its plain statement that efficacy in endemic populations is untested — not as independent efficacy data; the trial cards above carry the numbers. Its 18–64 age statement reflects the licence at the time of writing; the ACIP card below records the later extension of the recommendation down to age 2.
cards.source: Saluja T, Mogasale VV, Excler JL, Kim JH, Mogasale V. An overview of VaxchoraTM, a live attenuated oral cholera vaccine. Human Vaccines & Immunotherapeutics. 2020. PMID: 31339792. Registry ID: none in the record (review). cards.headline: Collins 2022 (ACIP): CVD 103-HgR — the only cholera vaccine licensed in the United States — is recommended only for travellers aged 2–64 years to an area with active cholera transmission
cards.summary: Collins 2022 (ACIP): CVD 103-HgR — the only cholera vaccine licensed in the United States — is recommended only for travellers aged 2–64 years to an area with active cholera transmission
cards.people: Recommendations of the CDC's Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices for use of lyophilized CVD 103-HgR (Vaxchora, Emergent BioSolutions) in the United States, consolidating the earlier adult (18–64 years) recommendations and adding children and adolescents aged 2–17 years.
cards.result: ACIP recommends CVD 103-HgR, the only cholera vaccine licensed for use in the United States, for prevention of cholera among travellers aged 2–64 years to an area with active cholera transmission, given as a single dose. The report's framing of the underlying risk: cholera is rare in the United States, and cases occur among travellers to countries where cholera is endemic or epidemic and associated with unsafe water and inadequate sanitation; up to 10% of infections manifest as severe cholera (cholera gravis), and fluid replacement therapy can reduce the fatality rate to <1%. Travellers might be at increased risk of poor outcomes if they cannot readily access medical services or have a condition that dehydration would worsen, such as cardiovascular or kidney disease.
cards.watchOut: A recommendation is not an efficacy measurement — this card is the shelf's statement of how narrow the official indication is. The recommendation is keyed to areas with ACTIVE cholera transmission, not to cholera-endemic countries generally and not to travel at large: for the ordinary traveller, whose cholera risk is very low, this vaccine is rarely recommended, and nothing in the recommendation extends the challenge-trial efficacy beyond the populations and window in which it was measured.
cards.source: Collins JP, Ryan ET, Wong KK, Daley MF, Ratner AJ, Appiah GD, Sanchez PJ, Gutelius BJ. Cholera Vaccine: Recommendations of the Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices, 2022. MMWR Recommendations and Reports. 2022. PMID: 36173766. Registry ID: none in the record (recommendations report). cards.headline: Synthesis: near-complete protection in the challenge ward, none demonstrable in the field — and a recommendation deliberately narrowed to active-transmission travel
cards.summary: Synthesis: near-complete protection in the challenge ward, none demonstrable in the field — and a recommendation deliberately narrowed to active-transmission travel
cards.people: Seven sources: three volunteer challenge studies (Chen 2016, 197 volunteers, NCT01895855; Tacket 1999, 51 challenged; Tacket 1992, onset/duration cohorts), an endemic-area immunogenicity trial (Suharyono 1992, 412 children), the one large field efficacy trial (Richie 2000, 67,508 people), a licensure overview (Saluja 2020), and the ACIP recommendations (Collins 2022).
cards.result: Challenge model: a single dose of CVD 103-HgR prevented moderate/severe cholera after experimental Vibrio cholerae O1 El Tor challenge with vaccine efficacy (relative) of 90.3% at 10 days (attack rates 5.7% vaccine vs 59.1% placebo) and 79.5% at 3 months (12.1% vs 59.1%) in the pivotal randomised double-blind trial (Chen 2016); an earlier randomised double-blind challenge trial found 91% efficacy against moderate/severe diarrhoea at 3 months (4% vs 39%) and 80% against any diarrhoea (Tacket 1999); protection was reported as 100% against diarrhoea on homologous challenge by 8 days and still at 6 months (Tacket 1992). Field record: the only large field trial found efficacy of 14%, not significant (43 vaccine vs 50 placebo evaluable cases over four years in 67,508 people), with too few early cases (seven within six months) to test the short-term window (Richie 2000); in an endemic-area population the traveller dose seroconverted only 16% versus over 90% in industrialised-country subjects (Suharyono 1992). Licensure and recommendation: FDA-licensed in 2016 for travellers (Saluja 2020); ACIP recommends it only for travellers aged 2–64 to areas with active cholera transmission (Collins 2022). PROPOSED SPLIT — the challenge claim is strong, randomised, and replicated; the field claim for long-term protection from one dose is (the treatment made no difference) on the only large test, and short-term field protection of travellers has never been directly measured.
cards.watchOut: Tier C — the developer's personal verdict: the shelf's two halves point in different directions because they answer different questions, and collapsing them into one stamp would misstate one half or the other. Nothing here concerns the killed whole-cell oral cholera vaccines (Shelf #1180), cholera caused by V. cholerae O139 or non-O1 serogroups (not shown to be prevented by this vaccine), people living in cholera-affected areas (effectiveness not established), or travellers aged over 64. This vaccine is rarely recommended for ordinary travellers; the recommendation is confined to travel to areas with active cholera transmission.
cards.source: Synthesis of Chen WH et al. Clinical Infectious Diseases. 2016 (PMID: 27001804); Tacket CO et al. Infection and Immunity. 1999 (PMID: 10569747); Tacket CO et al. The Journal of Infectious Diseases. 1992 (PMID: 1527420); Suharyono et al. Lancet. 1992 (PMID: 1355798); Richie EE et al. Vaccine. 2000 (PMID: 10738097); Saluja T et al. Human Vaccines & Immunotherapeutics. 2020 (PMID: 31339792); Collins JP et al. MMWR Recommendations and Reports. 2022 (PMID: 36173766).

acip recommends it only for travellers aged 2–64 to areas with active cholera transmission (collins 2022). proposed split — the challenge claim is strong, randomised, and replicated; the field claim for long-term protection from one dose is (the treatment made no difference) on the only large test, and short-term field protection of travellers has never been directly measured. tier c — the developer's personal verdict: the shelf's two halves point in different directions because they answer different questions, and collapsing them into one stamp would misstate one half or the other. nothing here concerns the killed whole-cell oral cholera vaccines (shelf #1180), cholera caused by v. cholerae o139 or non-o1 serogroups (not shown to be prevented by this vaccine), people living in cholera-affected areas (effectiveness not established), or travellers aged over 64. this vaccine is rarely recommended for ordinary travellers; the recommendation is confined to travel to areas with active cholera transmission. synthesis of chen wh et al. clinical infectious diseases. 2016 (pmid: 27001804); tacket co et al. infection and immunity. 1999 (pmid: 10569747); shelves.title: Stronger social relationships predict survival: across 148 studies (308,849 people) stronger relationships carried 50% higher odds of survival (OR 1.50), and the most isolated Alameda County residents died at 2.3 times (men) and 2.8 times (women) the rate of the most connected over 9 years — observational evidence only
shelves.question: In adults, do stronger social relationships, and the absence of loneliness/social isolation, predict lower all-cause mortality?
shelves.mesh: Cardiovascular Diseases/mortality; Cause of Death; Humans; Interpersonal Relations; Mortality; Neoplasms/mortality; Risk; Social Support
shelves.balance: Observational evidence only — no randomised trial can assign social relationships, so this shelf caps at POSSIBLE and the face says so. Two Holt-Lunstad meta-analyses agree: across 148 studies (308,849 participants) stronger social relationships carried OR 1.50 (95% CI 1.42 to 1.59) for survival (PMID: 20668659), and loneliness (OR 1.26), social isolation (OR 1.29) and living alone (OR 1.32) each predicted higher mortality (PMID: 25910392). The founding cohort points the same way: in 6,928 Alameda County adults followed 9 years, the most isolated died at age-adjusted relative risks of 2.3 (men) and 2.8 (women) versus the most connected, independent of baseline health, socioeconomic status and health practices (PMID: 425958). Residual confounding and reverse causation (illness shrinking networks) cannot be excluded. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (harm) for social isolation/loneliness as a mortality risk marker — observational only.

cards.headline: Holt-Lunstad 2010: across 148 studies and 308,849 participants, stronger social relationships carried a 50% higher odds of survival (OR 1.50, 95% CI 1.42 to 1.59)
cards.summary: Holt-Lunstad 2010: across 148 studies and 308,849 participants, stronger social relationships carried a 50% higher odds of survival (OR 1.50, 95% CI 1.42 to 1.59)
cards.people: 148 studies with 308,849 participants in a meta-analytic review of social relationships and mortality risk; the association held across age, sex, initial health status, cause of death and follow-up period.
cards.result: The random-effects weighted average effect was OR 1.50 (95% CI 1.42 to 1.59) — a 50% relative increased likelihood of survival for participants with stronger social relationships. The association was strongest for complex measures of social integration (OR 1.91, 95% CI 1.63 to 2.23) and weakest for the binary living-alone indicator (OR 1.19, 95% CI 0.99 to 1.44). The authors judged the influence comparable with well-established mortality risk factors.
cards.watchOut: Observational only: pooled cohorts cannot prove that improving relationships extends life, and sicker people lose social ties (reverse causation). The living-alone estimate's confidence interval crosses 1.0, so that single indicator alone was not significant.
cards.source: Holt-Lunstad J, Smith TB, Layton JB. PLoS Medicine. 2010. PMID: 20668659. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: Cardiovascular Diseases/mortality; Cause of Death; Humans; Interpersonal Relations; Mortality; Neoplasms/mortality; Risk; Social Support

cards.headline: Holt-Lunstad 2015: loneliness (OR 1.26), social isolation (OR 1.29) and living alone (OR 1.32) each predicted higher mortality — 26%, 29% and 32% relative increases in the likelihood of death
cards.summary: Holt-Lunstad 2015: loneliness (OR 1.26), social isolation (OR 1.29) and living alone (OR 1.32) each predicted higher mortality — 26%, 29% and 32% relative increases in the likelihood of death
cards.people: Meta-analytic review of studies published January 1980 to February 2014 providing quantitative mortality data by loneliness, social isolation or living alone, in analyses that statistically controlled for several possible confounds.
cards.result: Weighted average effect sizes: social isolation OR 1.29, loneliness OR 1.26 and living alone OR 1.32 — corresponding to 29%, 26% and 32% relative increased likelihood of mortality. Objective and subjective isolation measures did not differ. Results were consistent across gender, follow-up length and world region, were stronger in samples with average age under 65 years, and were influenced by initial health status.
cards.watchOut: Observational only, and the effect sizes are odds ratios from adjusted observational models — they describe who dies sooner, not what any intervention changes. Initial health status moderated the findings, consistent with some reverse causation.
cards.source: Holt-Lunstad J, Smith TB, Baker M, Harris T, Stephenson D. Perspectives on Psychological Science. 2015. PMID: 25910392. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: Humans; Loneliness; Mortality; Risk Factors; Social Isolation

cards.headline: Berkman & Syme 1979 (Alameda County): over 9 years the most socially isolated residents died at 2.3 times the rate of the most connected men and 2.8 times the rate of the most connected women (age-adjusted relative risks)
cards.summary: Berkman & Syme 1979 (Alameda County): over 9 years the most socially isolated residents died at 2.3 times the rate of the most connected men and 2.8 times the rate of the most connected women (age-adjusted relative risks)
cards.people: A random sample of 6,928 adults in Alameda County, California, surveyed in 1965 (Human Population Laboratory) with 9-year mortality follow-up; social and community ties were measured by a Social Network Index (marriage, contacts with friends and relatives, church and group membership).
cards.result: People who lacked social and community ties were more likely to die during follow-up than those with more extensive contacts; age-adjusted relative risks for the most isolated versus the most connected were 2.3 for men and 2.8 for women. The association was independent of self-reported physical health at baseline, year of death, socioeconomic status, and health practices (smoking, alcohol use, obesity, physical activity, preventive-service use) and of a cumulative health-practices index.
cards.watchOut: A single 1965-era cohort with self-reported baseline health; adjustment cannot remove all confounding, and the relative risks compare extreme network categories, not the average person's risk.
cards.source: Berkman LF, Syme SL. American Journal of Epidemiology. 1979. PMID: 425958. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: two meta-analyses and the founding cohort agree that social deficits track with earlier death — survival odds 50% higher with stronger relationships, mortality odds 26–32% higher with loneliness, isolation or living alone — but all of it is observational
cards.summary: Synthesis: two meta-analyses and the founding cohort agree that social deficits track with earlier death — survival odds 50% higher with stronger relationships, mortality odds 26–32% higher with loneliness, isolation or living alone — but all of it is observational
cards.people: The carded evidence: two meta-analyses of observational studies (148 studies, 308,849 participants; and the 1980–2014 loneliness/isolation literature) plus one 9-year prospective cohort of 6,928 adults.
cards.result: Stronger social relationships: OR 1.50 (95% CI 1.42 to 1.59) for survival (PMID: 20668659). Loneliness OR 1.26, social isolation OR 1.29, living alone OR 1.32 for mortality (PMID: 25910392). Most isolated versus most connected in Alameda County: relative risk 2.3 in men and 2.8 in women over 9 years (PMID: 425958). Whether reducing loneliness reduces mortality is a separate, intervention question homed on the loneliness-intervention shelves (#5482, #5483), not answered here. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (harm) — observational evidence only.
cards.watchOut: Do not read these relative measures as treatment effects: no study here randomised anyone to more social contact, and absolute mortality rates by exposure group are not pooled in these records.

shelves.title: Women who attended religious services more than once a week had 33% relative lower all-cause mortality (HR 0.67, 95% CI 0.62–0.71) than never-attenders among 74,534 Nurses' Health Study women — observational, with healthy-attender confounding a standing concern
shelves.question: In women, is frequent religious-service attendance (a measurable form of community participation) associated with lower mortality?
shelves.mesh: Adult; Cardiovascular Diseases/mortality/*prevention & control; Depression/*prevention & control; Female; Health Status; Humans; Neoplasms/mortality/*prevention & control; Religion; Social Support; Spirituality
shelves.balance: Observational evidence only, so this shelf caps at POSSIBLE, and the healthy-attender effect (people well enough to attend differ from those who cannot) must be printed — the slate requires it and this balance prints it. In the Nurses' Health Study (74,534 women, 13,537 deaths), attending services more than once a week was associated with HR 0.67 (95% CI 0.62 to 0.71) for all-cause mortality versus never attending, with cardiovascular HR 0.73 and cancer HR 0.79; social support explained 23% of the association (PMID: 27183175). In the same cohort programme (89,708 women), weekly-or-more attendance was associated with an approximately five-fold lower suicide rate (HR 0.16, 95% CI 0.06 to 0.46) (PMID: 27367927). A modelling paper translating the attendance–mortality literature estimated 2–3 added life-years for weekly attendance (PMID: 16513898). None of this is randomised; attendance cannot be prescribed from this evidence. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only.

cards.headline: Li 2016 (Nurses' Health Study): among 74,534 women with 13,537 deaths, attending religious services more than once a week was associated with 33% relative lower all-cause mortality (HR 0.67, 95% CI 0.62–0.71) versus never attending; cardiovascular HR 0.73 and cancer HR 0.79
cards.summary: Li 2016 (Nurses' Health Study): among 74,534 women with 13,537 deaths, attending religious services more than once a week was associated with 33% relative lower all-cause mortality (HR 0.67, 95% CI 0.62–0.71) versus never attending; cardiovascular HR 0.73 and cancer HR 0.79
cards.type: Prospective cohort study (Li 2016, Nurses' Health Study)
cards.people: 74,534 women in the Nurses' Health Study, free of cardiovascular disease and cancer at baseline, with service attendance assessed from 1992 through June 2012; 13,537 deaths occurred, including 2,721 cardiovascular and 4,479 cancer deaths; Cox and marginal structural models adjusted for repeatedly measured demographic, lifestyle and medical covariates.
cards.result: Attending a religious service more than once per week was associated with 33% relative lower all-cause mortality compared with never attending (HR 0.67, 95% CI 0.62 to 0.71; P < .001 for trend). Cardiovascular mortality HR 0.73 (95% CI 0.62 to 0.85) and cancer mortality HR 0.79 (95% CI 0.70 to 0.89). Results were robust in sensitivity analyses. Potential mediators explained moderate shares: social support 23% (P = .003), smoking 22%, depressive symptoms 11% and optimism 9%.
cards.watchOut: Observational with a strong healthy-attender problem: women who are ill, depressed or disabled attend less, and adjustment plus sensitivity analyses cannot fully remove that. Women only, US nurses only — no men and no general-population estimate on this card.
cards.source: Li S, Stampfer MJ, Williams DR, VanderWeele TJ. JAMA Internal Medicine. 2016. PMID: 27183175. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: VanderWeele 2016 (Nurses' Health Study): among 89,708 women followed 1996–2010, attending services once a week or more was associated with an approximately 5-fold lower suicide rate (HR 0.16, 95% CI 0.06–0.46) versus never attending
cards.summary: VanderWeele 2016 (Nurses' Health Study): among 89,708 women followed 1996–2010, attending services once a week or more was associated with an approximately 5-fold lower suicide rate (HR 0.16, 95% CI 0.06–0.46) versus never attending
cards.type: Prospective cohort study (VanderWeele 2016, Nurses' Health Study)
cards.people: 89,708 women aged 30–55 in the Nurses' Health Study, with service attendance self-reported in 1992 and 1996 and suicide outcomes followed from 1996 through June 2010; models adjusted for demographic, lifestyle and medical covariates, depressive symptoms and social integration.
cards.result: Attendance at religious services once per week or more was associated with an approximately 5-fold lower rate of suicide compared with never attending (HR 0.16, 95% CI 0.06 to 0.46) — a relative measure based on a rare outcome. Versus less frequent attendance, the HR was 0.05 (95% CI 0.006 to 0.48) among Catholics and 0.34 (95% CI 0.10 to 1.10) among Protestants (P = .05 for heterogeneity). Results were robust to sensitivity analyses and to excluding women previously depressed or with cancer or cardiovascular history.
cards.watchOut: Suicide is rare, so the dramatic relative ratio rests on few events with a wide confidence interval; the same healthy-attender and confounding caveats as the mortality card apply, and the Protestant subgroup estimate was not significant.

cards.headline: Hall 2006 (actuarial modelling): weekly religious attendance was modelled as accounting for an additional 2 to 3 life-years — comparable with 2.5 to 3.5 years for statin-type agents and 3 to 5 years for regular exercise — at an estimated $3,000–$10,000 per life-year gained
cards.summary: Hall 2006 (actuarial modelling): weekly religious attendance was modelled as accounting for an additional 2 to 3 life-years — comparable with 2.5 to 3.5 years for statin-type agents and 3 to 5 years for regular exercise — at an estimated $3,000–$10,000 per life-year gained
cards.people: Modelling study (no new cohort): age-specific actuarial death rates were modified using published odds ratios for weekly religious attendance, regular physical exercise and statin-type lipid-lowering agents; secondary analyses estimated cost per life-year gained. N not documented as a primary sample in the record.
cards.result: Weekly attendance at religious services accounted for an additional 2 to 3 life-years, compared with 3 to 5 life-years for physical exercise and 2.5 to 3.5 life-years for statin-type agents. Approximate cost per life-year gained: $2,000–$6,000 for regular exercise, $3,000–$10,000 for regular religious attendance and $4,000–$14,000 for statin-type agents. The author stated attendance is not a mode of medical therapy and called for better research.
cards.watchOut: A model built on observational odds ratios, not new outcome data — it inherits every bias of the underlying attendance–mortality association and is carded only to show the size claim made for it, not as independent confirmation.

cards.headline: Synthesis: in US women, frequent service attendance tracks with one-third relative lower all-cause mortality and a much lower suicide rate, and modellers translate the association into 2–3 life-years — all observational, all vulnerable to the healthy-attender effect
cards.summary: Synthesis: in US women, frequent service attendance tracks with one-third relative lower all-cause mortality and a much lower suicide rate, and modellers translate the association into 2–3 life-years — all observational, all vulnerable to the healthy-attender effect
cards.people: The carded evidence: two Nurses' Health Study cohort analyses (74,534 women with 13,537 deaths; 89,708 women for suicide) and one actuarial modelling paper.
cards.result: All-cause mortality HR 0.67 (95% CI 0.62 to 0.71) for more-than-weekly versus never attendance (PMID: 27183175); suicide HR 0.16 (95% CI 0.06 to 0.46) for weekly-or-more versus never attendance (PMID: 27367927); modelled 2–3 added life-years for weekly attendance (PMID: 16513898). General social-relationship mortality evidence is homed on #5474 (PMID: 3399889 is homed on #5475) and not re-carded here. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational evidence only.

shelves.title: The widowhood effect survives its sharpest bias test: in over 1 million older Americans a current wife's death raised her husband's mortality while an ex-wife's death did not — arguing against homogamy bias — and a spouse's hospitalisation alone carried 16–22% as much mortality risk as a spouse's death
shelves.question: After a spouse's death, does the surviving spouse's mortality rise — and does the 'widowhood effect' survive homogamy controls?
shelves.mesh: Adaptation, Psychological; Aged; Bias; Causality; Family Characteristics; Female; Humans; Models, Statistical; Mortality/*trends; Probability
shelves.balance: Observational evidence only, so this shelf caps at POSSIBLE. Elwert & Christakis 2008 (over 1 million elderly Americans) ran the homogamy test: a current wife's death showed a strong effect on her husband's mortality across three empirical tests, while an ex-wife's death — which shares the similarity/shared-exposure history but cannot plausibly cause grief-driven mortality — showed no statistically significant effect, strengthening the causal interpretation (PMID: 19110901; the record reports the tests qualitatively, with no pooled hazard ratio printed). The companion Medicare study of 518,240 couples quantified the neighbouring exposure: a spouse's hospitalisation raised partner mortality by diagnosis (e.g., HR 1.22 for dementia, 1.19 for psychiatric disease in men), at 22% (men) and 16% (women) of the mortality risk associated with a spouse's death itself (PMID: 16481639). A pooled-panel review found a consistent survival advantage for the married but little mortality difference between widowed, divorced/separated and never-married statuses (PMID: 21526396) — a caution printed on the face. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (harm) — observational only.

cards.headline: Elwert & Christakis 2008: in over 1 million elderly Americans, a current wife's death showed strong evidence of raising her husband's mortality across three tests, while an ex-wife's death showed no statistically significant effect — discounting homogamy bias as the explanation
cards.summary: Elwert & Christakis 2008: in over 1 million elderly Americans, a current wife's death showed strong evidence of raising her husband's mortality across three tests, while an ex-wife's death showed no statistically significant effect — discounting homogamy bias as the explanation
cards.type: Longitudinal cohort study with bias tests (Elwert & Christakis 2008)
cards.people: Longitudinal sample of over 1 million elderly Americans, examining husbands, wives and ex-wives to separate causation from homogamy (spousal similarity) and shared-environment bias in the widowhood effect.
cards.result: Three empirical tests provided strong evidence for an effect of a current wife's death on her husband's mortality, yet no statistically significant evidence for an effect of an ex-wife's death on her husband's mortality. Because an ex-wife's death has no plausible causal (grief/exposure-loss) pathway but shares the homogamy history, the null ex-wife result argues the widowhood effect is not due to homogamy bias to any substantial degree. The record reports these tests qualitatively; no single pooled hazard ratio is printed in it.
cards.watchOut: The absence of a printed effect size in the record limits this card to the bias question it was designed for — it shows the widowhood effect is unlikely to be a similarity artefact, not how large the effect is. Shared-environment bias is only partly addressed (one type, per the authors).
cards.source: Elwert F, Christakis NA. Demography. 2008. PMID: 19110901. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: Adaptation, Psychological; Aged; Bias; Causality; Family Characteristics; Female; Humans; Models, Statistical; Mortality/*trends; Probability

cards.headline: Christakis & Allison 2006 (NEJM): among 518,240 Medicare couples followed 9 years, a spouse's hospitalisation raised the partner's death risk by diagnosis — in men HR 1.22 after a spouse's dementia hospitalisation and 1.19 after psychiatric hospitalisation — equalling 22% (men) and 16% (women) of the risk of a spouse's death itself
cards.summary: Christakis & Allison 2006 (NEJM): among 518,240 Medicare couples followed 9 years, a spouse's hospitalisation raised the partner's death risk by diagnosis — in men HR 1.22 after a spouse's dementia hospitalisation and 1.19 after psychiatric hospitalisation — equalling 22% (men) and 16% (women) of the risk of a spouse's death itself
cards.people: 518,240 couples enrolled in Medicare in 1993, followed 9 years; 383,480 husbands (74%) and 347,269 wives (67%) were hospitalised at least once, and 252,557 husbands (49%) and 156,004 wives (30%) died; Cox and fixed-effects (case-time-control) analyses.
cards.result: One-year mortality after a spouse's hospitalisation in men ranged from 6.4% (colon cancer) to 8.6% (dementia); in women from 3.0% (colon cancer) to 5.7% (psychiatric disease). Adjusted hazard ratios for men: stroke 1.06 (95% CI 1.03 to 1.09), congestive heart failure 1.12 (1.07 to 1.16), hip fracture 1.15 (1.11 to 1.18), psychiatric disease 1.19 (1.12 to 1.26), dementia 1.22 (1.12 to 1.32); colon cancer 1.02 (0.95 to 1.09) was not significant; women's risks were similar. Overall, a spouse's hospitalisation carried 22% (95% CI 17 to 27) of the mortality risk of a spouse's death in men and 16% (95% CI 8 to 24) in women.
cards.watchOut: The exposure here is a spouse's hospitalisation, not bereavement itself — carded because it quantifies, in the same research programme, how large the spouse-death association is relative to a measurable neighbouring exposure. Observational throughout.
cards.source: Christakis NA, Allison PD. New England Journal of Medicine. 2006. PMID: 16481639. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: Aged; Bereavement; Caregivers/psychology/*statistics & numerical data; Case-Control Studies; Female; Follow-Up Studies; Hospitalization; Humans; Male; Medicare

cards.headline: Rendall 2011 (marriage-and-survival review): pooled US panel data linked to death registrations found a consistent survival advantage for married over unmarried men and women — but little evidence of mortality differences between never-married, divorced/separated and widowed statuses
cards.summary: Rendall 2011 (marriage-and-survival review): pooled US panel data linked to death registrations found a consistent survival advantage for married over unmarried men and women — but little evidence of mortality differences between never-married, divorced/separated and widowed statuses
cards.people: Review and update using large-scale pooled panel survey data linked to death registrations and earnings histories for US men and women aged 25 and older, with formal contrast tests by gender, age and unmarried status. Pooled N not documented as a single figure in the record.
cards.result: A consistent survival advantage for married over unmarried men and women, with an additional survival 'premium' for married men. Little evidence of mortality differences between never-married, divorced/separated and widowed statuses — meaning the cross-sectional married-versus-widowed gap does not, in these data, isolate a widowhood-specific penalty beyond being unmarried. No pooled hazard ratio is printed in the record.
cards.watchOut: Status comparisons (widowed versus married at a point in time) are not the same as the within-person transition Elwert & Christakis tested; this card is the caution, not a refutation — but it is why this shelf's stamp stays at POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: Synthesis: a spouse's death is followed by raised mortality in the survivor, the ex-wife test says homogamy does not explain it, spousal hospitalisation carries a fifth or so of the death-associated risk — yet status-based pooling finds widowed people no worse off than other unmarried groups
cards.summary: Synthesis: a spouse's death is followed by raised mortality in the survivor, the ex-wife test says homogamy does not explain it, spousal hospitalisation carries a fifth or so of the death-associated risk — yet status-based pooling finds widowed people no worse off than other unmarried groups
cards.people: The carded evidence: one bias-test cohort of over 1 million older Americans, one cohort of 518,240 Medicare couples, and one pooled-panel review of US adults aged 25 and older.
cards.result: Current-wife death: strong effect on husbands' mortality; ex-wife death: no significant effect (PMID: 19110901). Spouse hospitalisation: adjusted HRs up to 1.22 (dementia) in men, equal to 22% of the spouse-death risk in men and 16% in women (PMID: 16481639). Married-versus-unmarried advantage consistent, but widowed ≈ divorced/separated ≈ never-married in pooled status contrasts (PMID: 21526396). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (harm) — observational evidence only.
cards.watchOut: Two of the three records print no pooled widowhood hazard ratio, so this shelf deliberately carries no headline widowhood effect size — any number would have to come from a record fetched for that purpose, not from these.

shelves.title: Social stress measurably slows healing and skews immune gene expression: high-hostile couples healed wounds at 60% of the rate of low-hostile couples, and perceived isolation showed the pro-inflammatory CTRA transcriptome pattern across 141 older adults — small mechanistic studies, not outcome trials
shelves.question: Do hostile marital interactions and perceived social isolation change inflammatory biology and wound healing?
shelves.mesh: Adult; Aged; Blister/etiology/immunology/physiopathology; Conflict, Psychological; Cross-Over Studies; Cytokines/*biosynthesis/immunology; Female; Hostility; Humans; Interpersonal Relations
shelves.balance: Mechanistic and small-study evidence, so this shelf caps at POSSIBLE and claims biology, not clinical outcomes. In a crossover experiment in 42 healthy married couples, blister wounds healed more slowly after a marital-conflict session than after a social-support session, with lower local cytokine production at wound sites; consistently high-hostile couples healed at 60% of the rate of low-hostile couples and showed larger next-morning rises in plasma interleukin-6 and tumour necrosis factor alpha after conflict (PMID: 16330726). In five longitudinal transcriptome surveys of 141 older adults, perceived social isolation showed the conserved transcriptional response to adversity — sympathetic up-regulation, classical-monocyte expansion, glucocorticoid desensitisation and down-regulated interferons — with the mechanism confirmed in a macaque isolation model (PMID: 26598672). The population-level check is weaker: a meta-analysis of 14 loneliness and 16 isolation papers found no loneliness association with C-reactive protein or fibrinogen and only analysis-dependent signals for interleukin-6 and fibrinogen (PMID: 32092313). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (harm) — mechanistic evidence only.

cards.headline: Kiecolt-Glaser 2005: in 42 married couples, blister wounds healed more slowly after marital conflict than after social support, and consistently high-hostile couples healed at 60% of the rate of low-hostile couples, with larger next-morning plasma IL-6 and TNF-alpha rises after conflict
cards.summary: Kiecolt-Glaser 2005: in 42 married couples, blister wounds healed more slowly after marital conflict than after social support, and consistently high-hostile couples healed at 60% of the rate of low-hostile couples, with larger next-morning plasma IL-6 and TNF-alpha rises after conflict
cards.people: 42 healthy married couples (aged 22–77 years, mean 37.04, SD 13.05; married a mean of 12.55 years), each admitted twice for 24 hours to a hospital research unit in a crossover design — once for a structured social-support interaction and once to discuss a marital disagreement — with standardised blister wounds and daily healing assessment after discharge.
cards.result: Blister wounds healed more slowly and local cytokine production (interleukin-6, tumour necrosis factor alpha, interleukin-1beta) was lower at wound sites following marital conflicts than after social-support interactions. Couples who consistently showed higher hostile behaviour across both interactions healed at 60% of the rate of low-hostile couples. High-hostile couples also produced relatively larger increases in plasma interleukin-6 and tumour necrosis factor alpha the morning after conflict than after support, compared with low-hostile couples.
cards.watchOut: N = 42 couples (84 people) with experimentally induced blister wounds — a healing model, not surgical or clinical wounds; the 60% figure compares habitually high- versus low-hostile couples, an observed grouping within a small sample.
cards.source: Kiecolt-Glaser JK, Loving TJ, Stowell JR, Malarkey WB, Lemeshow S, Dickinson SL, Glaser R. Archives of General Psychiatry. 2005. PMID: 16330726. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Cole 2015: across five longitudinal leukocyte transcriptome surveys in 141 older adults, perceived social isolation showed the CTRA pattern — sympathetic up-regulation, classical-monocyte expansion, glucocorticoid desensitisation and down-regulated type I/II interferons — with the myeloid mechanism confirmed in isolated macaques
cards.summary: Cole 2015: across five longitudinal leukocyte transcriptome surveys in 141 older adults, perceived social isolation showed the CTRA pattern — sympathetic up-regulation, classical-monocyte expansion, glucocorticoid desensitisation and down-regulated type I/II interferons — with the myeloid mechanism confirmed in isolated macaques
cards.type: Mechanistic human cohort programme with animal model (Cole 2015)
cards.people: 141 older adults in five longitudinal leukocyte transcriptome surveys of perceived social isolation (loneliness), plus mechanistic analyses in a rhesus macaque model of perceived social isolation, including simian immunodeficiency virus response.
cards.result: Perceived isolation was associated with up-regulation of the sympathetic nervous system, monocyte population expansion and the leukocyte conserved transcriptional response to adversity (CTRA). Macaque analyses confirmed CTRA activation and identified selective up-regulation of the CD14++/CD16− classical monocyte transcriptome, functional glucocorticoid desensitisation, down-regulation of type I and II interferons, and impaired response to simian immunodeficiency virus infection. The authors identify neuroendocrine-driven myeloid cell dynamics as a key mediator of the transcriptome skewing.
cards.watchOut: Gene-expression and cell-population outcomes, not infections or deaths in the human sample; the causal chain is supported by the animal model, and 141 human participants is a small base for a programme-level claim.
cards.source: Cole SW, Capitanio JP, Chun K, Arevalo JMG, Ma J, Cacioppo JT. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences USA. 2015. PMID: 26598672. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Smith 2020 (inflammation meta-analysis): across 14 loneliness and 16 social-isolation papers, loneliness showed no association with C-reactive protein or fibrinogen, an interleukin-6 association only in most-adjusted analyses, and isolation a fibrinogen association that survived adjustment — mixed, method-sensitive results
cards.summary: Smith 2020 (inflammation meta-analysis): across 14 loneliness and 16 social-isolation papers, loneliness showed no association with C-reactive protein or fibrinogen, an interleukin-6 association only in most-adjusted analyses, and isolation a fibrinogen association that survived adjustment — mixed, method-sensitive results
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of studies in adults aged 16 and over from the general population, drawn from 7,400 screened articles: 14 papers on loneliness and inflammation and 16 on social isolation and inflammation, synthesising C-reactive protein, fibrinogen and interleukin-6.
cards.result: There was no association between loneliness and C-reactive protein or fibrinogen, and a significant loneliness–interleukin-6 association in most-adjusted but not least-adjusted analyses. Social isolation showed a significant least-adjusted association with C-reactive protein and fibrinogen, which remained significant for fibrinogen in most-adjusted analyses; there was no association between social isolation and interleukin-6. Sensitivity analyses showed methodological heterogeneity affected the results. No pooled effect sizes are printed in the record.
cards.watchOut: This is the shelf's discordant card: at population level, standard inflammatory markers mostly do not move with loneliness — the strong mechanistic findings above have not been shown to translate into consistent circulating-marker differences.

cards.headline: Synthesis: controlled human experiments and transcriptomics say social stress changes healing and immune regulation; population marker meta-analysis says the circulating signal is weak and inconsistent — biology plausible, clinical meaning unproven
cards.summary: Synthesis: controlled human experiments and transcriptomics say social stress changes healing and immune regulation; population marker meta-analysis says the circulating signal is weak and inconsistent — biology plausible, clinical meaning unproven
cards.people: The carded evidence: one 42-couple crossover wound-healing experiment, one transcriptome programme in 141 older adults plus a macaque model, and one meta-analysis of 30 papers on circulating inflammatory markers.
cards.result: Wounds healed more slowly after conflict, at 60% of the low-hostile rate in high-hostile couples (PMID: 16330726). Perceived isolation tracked the CTRA pro-inflammatory/antiviral-suppressed programme with a myeloid mechanism (PMID: 26598672). Circulating markers: largely null for loneliness (C-reactive protein, fibrinogen), analysis-dependent for interleukin-6 and fibrinogen (PMID: 32092313). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (harm) — mechanistic/small-study evidence only; no clinical-outcome trial is carded here because none is in the fetched record set.

shelves.title: Volunteering and health: volunteers had 22% lower relative mortality in cohort meta-analysis (risk ratio 0.78) — observational evidence only, and the few experiments did not confirm it
shelves.question: Is volunteering associated with lower mortality and better health, and what do the cohort data actually support?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Mental Health · Public Health · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Social Capital · Volunteers/psychology
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational evidence only, and the face says so. Two meta-analyses of cohort data agree: Jenkinson 2013 (PMID: 23968220) found volunteers at lower mortality risk (risk ratio 0.78, a 22% relative risk reduction) with favourable depression, life-satisfaction and wellbeing findings in cohorts; Okun 2013 (PMID: 23421326) found a 24% lower relative mortality risk after adjustment (47% unadjusted — the shrinkage itself measures confounding). Anderson 2014 (PMID: 25150681) found the same directions across 73 papers with only one randomised trial among them. Crucially, Jenkinson's experimental studies did not confirm the cohort findings, and reverse causation (healthy people volunteer) is uncontrolled. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), capped by the observational base.

cards.headline: Jenkinson 2013: cohort studies linked volunteering to lower mortality (risk ratio 0.78) and better depression, life-satisfaction and wellbeing scores — but the experimental studies did not confirm the cohort findings
cards.summary: Jenkinson 2013: cohort studies linked volunteering to lower mortality (risk ratio 0.78) and better depression, life-satisfaction and wellbeing scores — but the experimental studies did not confirm the cohort findings
cards.people: 40 papers: five randomised controlled trials (seven papers), four non-randomised trials, and 17 cohort studies (29 papers) comparing volunteers with non-volunteers on physical and mental health and survival, identified from 12 databases to January 2013.
cards.result: Cohort studies showed volunteering had favourable effects on depression, life satisfaction and wellbeing, but not on physical health; these findings were not confirmed by experimental studies. Meta-analysis of five cohort studies found volunteers at lower risk of mortality (risk ratio 0.78, 95% CI 0.66 to 0.90) — a 22% relative risk reduction in observational data, with no absolute rates reported in the record. There was insufficient evidence that volunteering type or intensity consistently changed outcomes, and causal mechanisms remain unclear.
cards.watchOut: Observational evidence only for the mortality figure: healthier people are more able to volunteer (reverse causation and confounding), which is exactly why the unconfirmed experimental literature matters.
cards.source: Jenkinson CE, Dickens AP, Jones K et al. Is volunteering a public health intervention? A systematic review and meta-analysis of the health and survival of volunteers. BMC Public Health. 2013. PMID: 23968220. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: Humans · Mental Health · Public Health · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Social Capital · Volunteers/psychology

cards.headline: Okun 2013: in older adults, volunteering was associated with 24% lower relative mortality risk after adjustment (47% lower unadjusted) — a meta-analysis of cohort relations, not of trials
cards.summary: Okun 2013: in older adults, volunteering was associated with 24% lower relative mortality risk after adjustment (47% lower unadjusted) — a meta-analysis of cohort relations, not of trials
cards.people: Late-middle-aged and older adults (minimum age 55 years) in studies of organisational volunteering and mortality, meta-analysed as unadjusted (bivariate) effect sizes, adjusted effect sizes (controlling for variables such as health), and interaction effect sizes.
cards.result: On average, volunteering was associated with a 47% relative reduction in mortality risk unadjusted (95% CI 38% to 55%) and a 24% relative reduction after adjustment (95% CI 16% to 31%). Absolute mortality rates are not reported in the record, so these are relative associations only. Preliminary interaction evidence suggested the inverse association strengthens as public religiosity increases.
cards.watchOut: Adjustment shrinks the association by half (47% to 24%), showing how much confounding is present; residual confounding by baseline health and function cannot be removed by these adjustments.
cards.source: Okun MA, Yeung EW, Brown S. Volunteering by older adults and risk of mortality: a meta-analysis. Psychology and Aging. 2013. PMID: 23421326. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Anderson 2014: across 73 papers on volunteering in seniors, the most consistent findings were fewer depression symptoms, better self-reported health, fewer functional limitations and lower mortality — from mostly observational designs, with one randomised trial
cards.summary: Anderson 2014: across 73 papers on volunteering in seniors, the most consistent findings were fewer depression symptoms, better self-reported health, fewer functional limitations and lower mortality — from mostly observational designs, with one randomised trial
cards.people: 73 papers included from 113 identified on benefits of formal volunteering among older adults: descriptive, cross-sectional and prospective cohort studies, plus one randomised controlled trial.
cards.result: The most consistent associations were reduced symptoms of depression, better self-reported health, fewer functional limitations and lower mortality. The reviewers propose volunteering works by increasing social, physical and cognitive activity, and recommend objective outcome measures, prospective designs and direct study of dementia risk — none of which the existing literature yet supplies.
cards.watchOut: A narrative critical review without pooled estimates: useful for consistency of direction across designs, not for the size of any causal effect.

cards.headline: Synthesis: volunteers live longer and feel better in every cohort synthesis — but people well enough to volunteer differ from those who cannot, adjustment halves the association, and experiments have not confirmed it
cards.summary: Synthesis: volunteers live longer and feel better in every cohort synthesis — but people well enough to volunteer differ from those who cannot, adjustment halves the association, and experiments have not confirmed it
cards.people: The carded evidence: two meta-analyses of observational volunteering studies and one critical review of 73 papers (one randomised trial among them), all in older adults.
cards.result: Mortality associations are consistent: risk ratio 0.78 in five pooled cohorts (Jenkinson 2013); 24% lower relative risk after adjustment versus 47% unadjusted (Okun 2013). Depression, life satisfaction, wellbeing and functional limitation findings point the same way (Anderson 2014). But the only randomised evidence located by these reviews did not confirm the cohort results, so causality — and any prescription of volunteering as treatment — is unestablished. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), observational only.
cards.watchOut: The one structured volunteering programme with its own randomised programme of research, Experience Corps, is homed on its own shelf (#5489) and is not re-carded here; this shelf covers volunteering in general, where the evidence is cohort-based.
cards.source: Synthesis of Jenkinson CE et al. BMC Public Health. 2013 (PMID: 23968220); Okun MA, Yeung EW, Brown S. Psychology and Aging. 2013 (PMID: 23421326); Anderson ND et al. Psychological Bulletin. 2014 (PMID: 25150681).

shelves.title: Gardening and health: randomised horticultural-therapy trials pool to a medium mental-health benefit (effect size 0.55 across 18 trials) — community gardening evidence is weaker and observational data are publication-biased
shelves.question: Is regular gardening associated with better physical and mental health in meta-analysis?
shelves.mesh: Horticultural Therapy · Humans · Mental Health · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit). Three syntheses, three designs, one direction — with quality falling as the question widens. Tu 2022 (PMID: 35000249) pooled 18 randomised trials of horticultural therapy and found a medium mental-health effect (effect size 0.55). Briggs 2023 (PMID: 36151719), on group gardening in community adults (24 studies), found wellbeing may rise and depression symptoms may fall, with uncertain pooled effects. Soga 2017 (PMID: 27981022) pooled 22 largely observational studies (76 comparisons) with significant positive effects and detected publication bias. The randomised evidence covers delivered horticultural therapy, not gardening as a hobby. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).

cards.headline: Soga 2017: meta-analysis of 22 gardening studies (76 comparisons) found significant positive effects across depression, anxiety, body mass index, life satisfaction, quality of life and sense of community — with publication bias present
cards.summary: Soga 2017: meta-analysis of 22 gardening studies (76 comparisons) found significant positive effects across depression, anxiety, body mass index, life satisfaction, quality of life and sense of community — with publication bias present
cards.people: 22 case studies published after 2001 comparing health outcomes in gardeners or after gardening participation versus non-gardeners or before participation, mostly from the United States, then Europe, Asia and the Middle East; 76 comparisons between control and treatment groups. Total participant N not documented in the record.
cards.result: Meta-analytic estimates showed a significant positive effect of gardening on health outcomes overall and across subgroups, including reductions in depression, anxiety and body mass index and increases in life satisfaction, quality of life and sense of community. Egger's test indicated publication bias, but significant positive effects remained after trim-and-fill adjustment. The authors conclude a regular dose of gardening can improve public health.
cards.watchOut: Mostly before-and-after and gardener-versus-non-gardener comparisons, not randomised trials: healthier, wealthier people garden more, and the detected publication bias means the true average effect is likely smaller.
cards.source: Soga M, Gaston KJ, Yamaura Y. Gardening is beneficial for health: A meta-analysis. Preventive Medicine Reports. 2017. PMID: 27981022. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: Tu 2022: meta-analysis of 18 randomised trials found horticultural therapy improved mental health with a medium effect size (0.55), and no included trial reported a negative effect
cards.summary: Tu 2022: meta-analysis of 18 randomised trials found horticultural therapy improved mental health with a medium effect size (0.55), and no included trial reported a negative effect
cards.people: 18 eligible randomised controlled trials of horticultural therapy (indoor and outdoor plant activities, plant-related arts and crafts, typically at least eight sessions) with mental-health assessments, drawn from 1,056 records across Web of Science, PubMed, ProQuest and Cochrane. Total participant N not documented in the record.
cards.result: The meta-analysis showed the horticultural-therapy groups had a significant, positive impact on mental health versus control groups (effect size 0.55, a medium effect), with no statistical heterogeneity or publication bias detected among the included trials and no negative mental-health outcomes. The author recommends integrating horticultural therapy into healthcare settings, while noting concealed allocation and blinding need improvement in future trials.
cards.watchOut: Structured horticultural therapy delivered as treatment is not the same exposure as everyday gardening; trial quality (allocation concealment, blinding) was imperfect, and a single-author meta-analysis warrants the caution on this card.
cards.source: Tu HM. Effect of horticultural therapy on mental health: A meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials. Journal of Psychiatric and Mental Health Nursing. 2022. PMID: 35000249. cards.headline: Briggs 2023: 24 studies of group-based gardening interventions — meta-analyses suggest wellbeing may increase and depression symptoms may fall, but heterogeneity and unclear bias left the pooled effects uncertain
cards.summary: Briggs 2023: 24 studies of group-based gardening interventions — meta-analyses suggest wellbeing may increase and depression symptoms may fall, but heterogeneity and unclear bias left the pooled effects uncertain
cards.people: 24 studies (20 completed, 4 ongoing) of group-based gardening interventions in community-residing adults aged 18 and older reporting validated health and wellbeing outcomes, reviewed under a PROSPERO-registered protocol (CRD42020162187); poor reporting precluded meta-analysis for some studies.
cards.result: Meta-analyses suggest group gardening may increase wellbeing and may reduce symptoms of depression, but there was uncertainty in the pooled effects due to heterogeneity and unclear risk of bias for many studies; results for other outcomes were mixed. The reviewers describe the initial findings as promising and in need of corroboration in further studies.
cards.watchOut: The most cautious of the three syntheses on this shelf and the closest to the community-gardening question: its uncertainty, not the larger pooled effects elsewhere, is the right anchor for expectations.

cards.headline: Synthesis: gardening and horticultural therapy point consistently toward better mental health — a medium effect in randomised therapy trials, an uncertain one in community group gardening, and an inflated-looking one in observational comparisons
cards.summary: Synthesis: gardening and horticultural therapy point consistently toward better mental health — a medium effect in randomised therapy trials, an uncertain one in community group gardening, and an inflated-looking one in observational comparisons
cards.people: The carded evidence: one meta-analysis of 18 randomised horticultural-therapy trials, one systematic review and meta-analysis of 24 group-gardening studies, and one meta-analysis of 22 largely observational gardening studies (76 comparisons).
cards.result: Randomised horticultural therapy improved mental health with effect size 0.55 and no negative trial outcomes (Tu 2022). Community group gardening may improve wellbeing and depression symptoms, with heterogeneity and bias leaving pooled effects uncertain (Briggs 2023). Broader gardening comparisons are positive across depression, anxiety, body mass index, life satisfaction and quality of life, with publication bias detected (Soga 2017). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), strongest for structured horticultural therapy.
cards.watchOut: Exposure discipline matters: trials test prescribed, facilitated horticultural therapy (typically eight or more sessions). Extending their effect sizes to casual home gardening assumes the very thing the observational literature cannot prove.
cards.source: Synthesis of Soga M, Gaston KJ, Yamaura Y. Preventive Medicine Reports. 2017 (PMID: 27981022); Tu HM. Journal of Psychiatric and Mental Health Nursing. 2022 (PMID: 35000249); Briggs R, Morris PG, Rees K. Journal of Mental Health. 2023 (PMID: 36151719).

shelves.title: School-based HPV vaccination delivery and coverage (programme evidence only): school-based programmes achieved high coverage across 17 countries and 45 low- and middle-income countries in two reviews, and 75% at least-one-dose coverage in South Africa — with no head-to-head trial against clinic-based delivery
shelves.question: Does offering school-based HPV vaccination delivery increase adolescent vaccine coverage versus clinic-based delivery alone?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Female · Health Services Administration · Humans · Immunization Programs · Papillomavirus Infections · Papillomavirus Vaccines · Schools · Students · Vaccination
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — programme and review evidence only; no head-to-head trial of delivery settings is carded. A literature review of HPV delivery strategies (9 articles, 17 countries) found school-based programmes achieved high coverage in 9- to 13-year-old girls (PMID: 24295804). A systematic lessons synthesis from 45 low- and middle-income countries found school-based delivery supplemented by facility delivery for out-of-school girls attained high coverage, with limited data on facility-only strategies (PMID: 28575074). South Africa's national school-based programme reached 75% of 15-year-old girls with at least one dose and 61% with two doses by 2020, though coverage was declining (PMID: 35174123). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — school-based delivery is associated with higher adolescent HPV coverage in programme evidence; the comparison with clinic-based delivery alone is descriptive, not randomised.

cards.headline: Paul & Fabio 2014: across 17 countries, school-based HPV vaccination programmes achieved high coverage in 9- to 13-year-old girls, while facility-based programmes were the comparison experience
cards.summary: Paul & Fabio 2014: across 17 countries, school-based HPV vaccination programmes achieved high coverage in 9- to 13-year-old girls, while facility-based programmes were the comparison experience
cards.type: Literature review of delivery strategies (Paul & Fabio 2014)
cards.people: Nine articles representing seventeen countries, from a systematic search of PubMed in October 2012 for evaluations of national, regional, pilot or demonstration HPV immunisation programmes working within existing health systems; total participant N not documented in the record.
cards.result: School-based programmes achieved high HPV vaccination coverage rates in 9- to 13-year-old girls across the different studies and geographic locations, suggesting non-health-facility-based programmes are possible for HPV vaccine introduction. Grade-based eligibility criteria, compared with age-based criteria, may be easier to implement in school settings. The authors call for more work to standardise coverage estimates so programmes can be appropriately evaluated.
cards.watchOut: Nine programme reports, not a controlled comparison: countries that chose school-based delivery differ from countries that did not, and 'high coverage' is the review's qualitative summary — the record prints no pooled coverage figure for school-based versus clinic-based delivery.
cards.source: Paul P et al. Literature review of HPV vaccine delivery strategies: considerations for school- and non-school based immunization program. Vaccine. 2014. PMID: 24295804. cards.headline: Gallagher 2017: in 45 low- and middle-income countries, school-based delivery supplemented by facility delivery for out-of-school girls attained high coverage; facility-only strategies had limited data
cards.summary: Gallagher 2017: in 45 low- and middle-income countries, school-based delivery supplemented by facility delivery for out-of-school girls attained high coverage; facility-only strategies had limited data
cards.type: Systematic lessons synthesis of programmes and demonstration projects (Gallagher 2017)
cards.people: Evidence from 12 national programmes and 66 demonstration projects in 46 countries (45 low- and middle-income countries per the article title): 61 full texts from a systematic literature review (2,936 abstracts screened), 188 unpublished documents, and interviews with 56 key informants.
cards.result: School-based vaccine delivery supplemented with health facility-based delivery for out-of-school girls attained high coverage. There were limited data on facility-only strategies and little evaluation of strategies to reach out-of-school girls. Early engagement of teachers as partners in social mobilisation, consent, vaccination-day coordination, follow-up of non-completers and adverse events was considered invaluable, and micro-planning using school or facility registers enumerated target populations most effectively.
cards.watchOut: A lessons synthesis built substantially on programme documents and informant interviews: 'attained high coverage' is the consistent programme experience, not a measured effect of delivery setting against a randomised or matched clinic-based alternative.

cards.headline: Amponsah-Dacosta 2022: South Africa's school-based national programme, running since 2014, had reached 75% of 15-year-old girls with at least one dose by 2020 — but coverage was trending downward
cards.summary: Amponsah-Dacosta 2022: South Africa's school-based national programme, running since 2014, had reached 75% of 15-year-old girls with at least one dose by 2020 — but coverage was trending downward
cards.type: Narrative review of a national school-based programme (Amponsah-Dacosta 2022)
cards.people: South Africa's national school-based HPV vaccination programme from its inception in 2014 to 2020, reviewed narratively; coverage figures are for adolescent girls aged 15 years who had received vaccine at any time between ages 9 and 14 years. Total participant N not documented in the record.
cards.result: As of 2020, 75% of adolescent girls aged 15 years had received at least one dose of HPV vaccine between ages 9 and 14, and 61% had completed the full recommended two-dose schedule. Despite this reach, coverage and dose-completion rates followed a persistent downward trend. The review attributes declining demand in part to weakening social mobilisation, inadequate reminder and tracking systems, and vaccine hesitancy.
cards.watchOut: One country's programme with no clinic-based comparator arm: the 75% and 61% figures show what a mature school-based programme reached, and its downward trend shows delivery setting alone does not hold coverage over time.
cards.source: Amponsah-Dacosta E et al. Human Papillomavirus Vaccination in South Africa: Programmatic Challenges and Opportunities for Integration With Other Adolescent Health Services? cards.headline: Synthesis: school-based HPV delivery is consistently associated with high adolescent coverage across reviews of programmes in dozens of countries — but no carded record is a head-to-head trial against clinic-based delivery, and facility-only data are explicitly limited
cards.summary: Synthesis: school-based HPV delivery is consistently associated with high adolescent coverage across reviews of programmes in dozens of countries — but no carded record is a head-to-head trial against clinic-based delivery, and facility-only data are explicitly limited
cards.people: The carded evidence: one literature review of delivery strategies (9 articles, 17 countries), one systematic lessons synthesis (12 national programmes, 66 demonstration projects, 45 low- and middle-income countries) and one national programme review (South Africa, 2014–2020). No randomised or controlled head-to-head comparison of delivery settings is carded.
cards.result: School-based programmes achieved high coverage in 9- to 13-year-old girls across studies and geographies (Paul & Fabio 2014). School-based delivery supplemented by facility delivery for out-of-school girls attained high coverage, while facility-only strategies had limited data (Gallagher 2017). A mature national school-based programme reached 75% with at least one dose and 61% with a completed two-dose schedule, though coverage declined over time (Amponsah-Dacosta 2022). The slated question also asked about illness-related absence; no carded record reports that outcome for HPV delivery. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — programme and review evidence only.
cards.watchOut: Coverage achieved by a programme is jointly determined by consent systems, funding, vaccine supply and social mobilisation; attributing the whole difference between countries to the school setting alone would over-read every carded record.
cards.source: Synthesis of Paul P et al. Vaccine. 2014 (PMID: 24295804); Gallagher KE et al. PLoS One. 2017 (PMID: 28575074); Amponsah-Dacosta E et al. Frontiers in Public Health. 2022 (PMID: 35174123).

shelves.title: Split answer: prescribing gets inactive adults moving (benefit), but blood-pressure lowering at exactly 150 minutes/week is divided — 6 mmHg in one walking trial, non-significant in the exact-dose hypertensive trial
shelves.question: In adults who are inactive, does prescribing 150 minutes of moderate exercise per week improve blood pressure?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Blood Pressure · Energy Metabolism · Exercise Therapy · Female · Humans · Hypertension · Male · Middle Aged · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: SPLIT — the split is named in the stamp. As behaviour change, prescribing works: in the 878-patient Green Prescription cluster trial, counselling raised leisure exercise by 34 minutes/week and increased the share reaching 2.5 hours/week by 9.72 percentage points (Elley 2003, PMID: 12689976) — but that trial reports no blood-pressure effect size, only a trend. On blood pressure itself the two dose trials divide: walking 30 minutes five days a week for 12 weeks was followed by a 6 mmHg systolic fall with no change in controls (Tully 2007, PMID: 17699531), while the exact-dose trial in sedentary hypertensive adults — 30 minutes five days a week for 6 weeks — found a net −3.4/−2.8 mmHg that was not statistically significant (Cooper 2000, PMID: 11224966; the treatment made no demonstrated difference). PROPOSED SPLIT (prescription increases activity: benefit; blood-pressure lowering at exactly 150 minutes/week: divided): expect inactive adults to move more; expect, on this evidence, only a small and uncertain average blood-pressure fall from the prescription itself.

cards.headline: Cooper 2000: the exact guideline prescription — 30 minutes of moderate exercise five days a week (150 minutes/week) for 6 weeks — lowered daytime blood pressure by a net 3.4/2.8 mmHg, which was NOT statistically significant, in sedentary adults with unmedicated hypertension
cards.summary: Cooper 2000: the exact guideline prescription — 30 minutes of moderate exercise five days a week (150 minutes/week) for 6 weeks — lowered daytime blood pressure by a net 3.4/2.8 mmHg, which was NOT statistically significant, in sedentary adults with unmedicated hypertension
cards.people: Sedentary adults aged 25 to 63 years with unmedicated hypertension (office blood pressure 150–180 mmHg systolic and/or 91–110 mmHg diastolic), randomised to 30 minutes of moderate-intensity exercise (brisk walking or equivalent) five days per week for six weeks, or to control (maintaining existing activity levels); the participant N is not documented in the record. Outcome was daytime ambulatory blood pressure (10 am to 10 pm); compliance with the exercise programme was high.
cards.result: The reduction in mean daytime ambulatory blood pressure was greater in the intervention group than in controls, but the net effect was not statistically significant: systolic −3.4 mmHg (95% CI −7.4 to 0.6) and diastolic −2.8 mmHg (95% CI −5.8 to 0.2) — the treatment made no demonstrated difference at this sample size. Adjusting for baseline differences shrank the estimates further (systolic −1.9 mmHg, 95% CI −5.4 to 1.7; P = 0.31; diastolic −2.2 mmHg, 95% CI −4.9 to 0.5; P = 0.11). The authors conclude that expectations that a moderate-intensity exercise programme will produce a clinically important reduction in an individual's blood pressure are unlikely to be realised.
cards.watchOut: Six weeks is short and the confidence intervals include a clinically useful 7 mmHg systolic fall as well as zero — this trial does not prove the prescription does nothing; it proves the average short-term effect at exactly 150 minutes/week is smaller and less certain than guideline enthusiasm suggests. Participant N is not documented in the record, so no N is printed beyond that fact.
cards.source: Cooper AR et al. What is the magnitude of blood pressure response to a programme of moderate intensity exercise?
