cards.headline: Tully 2007: in 106 sedentary adults, walking 30 minutes five days a week (150 minutes/week) for 12 weeks was followed by a 6 mmHg fall in systolic and 3.4 mmHg fall in diastolic blood pressure, with no change in controls
cards.summary: Tully 2007: in 106 sedentary adults, walking 30 minutes five days a week (150 minutes/week) for 12 weeks was followed by a 6 mmHg fall in systolic and 3.4 mmHg fall in diastolic blood pressure, with no change in controls
cards.people: 106 healthy, sedentary adults aged 40 to 61 years (Northern Ireland Civil Service employees) randomised to a home-based walking programme of 30 minutes of brisk walking three days a week (n = 44), five days a week (n = 42), or a control group (n = 20), for 12 weeks; walking could be accumulated in bouts of at least 10 minutes and pedometers recorded steps. 89% (93 of 106) completed the study.
cards.result: Systolic blood pressure fell significantly in both walking groups — by 5 mmHg in the three-day group and 6 mmHg in the five-day (150 minutes/week) group (P < 0.05) — as did waist and hip circumferences, and functional capacity increased in both groups (15% and 11%). Diastolic blood pressure fell in the five-day group by 3.4 mmHg (P < 0.05). No changes occurred in the control group. The authors conclude there is evidence of benefit from exercising even at a level below that currently recommended in healthy sedentary adults.
cards.watchOut: The blood-pressure results are reported as within-group changes (with analysis of variance across groups), in healthy sedentary adults rather than hypertensive patients, over 12 weeks — a 6 mmHg within-group fall can include regression to the mean and measurement effects, and the record does not print a between-group blood-pressure effect size.
cards.source: Tully MA et al. Randomised controlled trial of home-based walking programmes at and below current recommended levels of exercise in sedentary adults. cards.headline: Elley 2003 (Green Prescription cluster trial, 878 sedentary patients): clinician counselling raised leisure exercise by 34 minutes/week and increased the share reaching 2.5 hours/week by 9.72 percentage points — but the record reports no blood-pressure effect size, only a trend
cards.summary: Elley 2003 (Green Prescription cluster trial, 878 sedentary patients): clinician counselling raised leisure exercise by 34 minutes/week and increased the share reaching 2.5 hours/week by 9.72 percentage points — but the record reports no blood-pressure effect size, only a trend
cards.people: Cluster randomised controlled trial in 42 rural and urban general practices in New Zealand: sedentary patients aged 40–79 years visiting their general practitioner (878 of 1,322 screened eligible patients participated; follow-up rate 85%, 750 of 878) received oral and written 'green prescription' physical-activity advice during usual consultations plus telephone and postal support from exercise specialists, or usual care, over 12 months.
cards.result: Mean leisure exercise increased by 2.7 kcal/kg/week (P = 0.02), or 34 minutes/week more, in the intervention group than in controls (P = 0.04), and total energy expenditure by 9.4 kcal/kg/week (P = 0.001). The proportion undertaking 2.5 hours/week of leisure exercise increased by 9.72% more in the intervention group than in controls (P = 0.003; number needed to treat 10.3). Several SF-36 quality-of-life measures improved significantly more in the intervention group. For blood pressure the record reports only that a trend towards decreasing blood pressure became apparent, and prints no effect size; there was no significant difference in four-year coronary heart disease risk. The authors conclude counselling in general practice is effective in increasing physical activity and improving quality of life over 12 months.
cards.watchOut: This is the real-world version of 'prescribing': most counselled patients did not reach 150 minutes/week (the average gain was 34 minutes/week), so the trial tests a prescription's effect on behaviour more than the physiological effect of 150 minutes actually performed — and on blood pressure it is silent beyond a trend.
cards.source: Elley CR et al. Effectiveness of counselling patients on physical activity in general practice: cluster randomised controlled trial. BMJ. 2003. PMID: 12689976. cards.headline: Synthesis: SPLIT — prescribing works as behaviour change (activity rises, quality of life improves), but at exactly 150 minutes/week the blood-pressure evidence divides: one walking trial shows a 6 mmHg systolic fall, the exact-dose hypertensive trial shows a non-significant 3.4 mmHg, and the large prescription trial reports no blood-pressure effect size
cards.summary: Synthesis: SPLIT — prescribing works as behaviour change (activity rises, quality of life improves), but at exactly 150 minutes/week the blood-pressure evidence divides: one walking trial shows a 6 mmHg systolic fall, the exact-dose hypertensive trial shows a non-significant 3.4 mmHg, and the large prescription trial reports no blood-pressure effect size
cards.people: The carded evidence: three randomised trials of prescribing or programming moderate exercise for inactive adults — Cooper 2000 (sedentary hypertensive adults, exactly 150 minutes/week for 6 weeks; participant N not documented in the record), Tully 2007 (106 sedentary adults, walking programmes for 12 weeks), and Elley 2003 (878 sedentary primary-care patients, 12 months of clinician counselling). Total documented participants exceed 900, so no small-N stamp labelling applies.
cards.result: At the exact guideline dose, Cooper 2000 found a net −3.4/−2.8 mmHg that was not statistically significant (the treatment made no demonstrated difference), while Tully 2007 found systolic falls of 6 mmHg in the 150-minutes/week walking group with no change in controls. Elley 2003 shows why the two can both be true: a prescription raises activity by only ~34 minutes/week on average, so population blood-pressure effects are diluted even if performed exercise lowers pressure. PROPOSED SPLIT (prescription increases activity: benefit; blood-pressure lowering at exactly 150 minutes/week: divided): prescribing 150 minutes of moderate exercise per week reliably gets inactive adults moving, but its average blood-pressure effect in these trials is small and inconsistently demonstrated.
cards.watchOut: Supervised exercise-training trials and their meta-analyses (a different question — exercise performed under supervision, often at higher intensity or in selected hypertensive volunteers) generally report larger blood-pressure falls; this shelf answers the prescription question as asked, in inactive adults, and should not be read as 'exercise does not lower blood pressure'.

shelves.title: Polypill in primary prevention: LDL cholesterol about 19 mg/dL lower and systolic blood pressure about 5.8 mm Hg lower than placebo, with fewer cardiovascular events in large randomised trials
shelves.question: Does a polypill improve blood pressure and cholesterol control in primary prevention?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Anticholesteremic Agents · Antihypertensive Agents · Aspirin · Atenolol · Blood Pressure · Cardiovascular Diseases · Cholesterol, LDL · Drug Combinations · Drug Therapy, Combination · Female · Humans · Hydrochlorothiazide · Incidence · Male · Medication Adherence · Middle Aged · Platelet Aggregation Inhibitors · Risk Factors · Simvastatin
shelves.balance: Yes on both control measures, and events fall too. In TIPS-3 (Yusuf 2021, PMID: 33186492; 5,713 people without cardiovascular disease at intermediate risk), the polypill lowered LDL cholesterol by approximately 19 mg/dL and systolic blood pressure by approximately 5.8 mm Hg versus placebo, with the primary event outcome at 4.4% vs 5.5% (HR 0.79, 95% CI 0.63 to 1.00). In PolyIran (Roshandel 2019, PMID: 31448738; 6,838 participants in a pragmatic cluster-randomised trial), major cardiovascular events occurred in 5.9% on the polypill vs 8.8% on minimal care (adjusted HR 0.66, 95% CI 0.55 to 0.80); the subgroup without pre-existing cardiovascular disease — the primary-prevention subgroup — had HR 0.80 (95% CI 0.51 to 1.12), not significant on its own. An individual-participant meta-analysis of the three large primary-prevention polypill trials (Joseph 2021, PMID: 34469765; 18,162 participants) found the primary outcome in 3.0% vs 4.9% (HR 0.62, 95% CI 0.53 to 0.73). Two or more large concordant randomised trials support the stamp. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit) — a polypill improves blood pressure and cholesterol control in primary prevention and reduces cardiovascular events.

cards.summary: TIPS-3 (Yusuf 2021): the polypill lowered LDL cholesterol by about 19 mg/dL and systolic blood pressure by about 5.8 mm Hg versus placebo in 5,713 people without cardiovascular disease, with events at 4.4% vs 5.5% (HR 0.79)
cards.people: 5,713 participants without cardiovascular disease who had an elevated INTERHEART Risk Score, randomised in a 2-by-2-by-2 factorial trial to a polypill (simvastatin 40 mg, atenolol 100 mg, hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg, ramipril 10 mg) or placebo, aspirin or placebo, and vitamin D or placebo; mean follow-up 4.6 years.
cards.result: LDL cholesterol was lower by approximately 19 mg/dL and systolic blood pressure lower by approximately 5.8 mm Hg with the polypill than with placebo. The primary outcome (cardiovascular death, myocardial infarction, stroke, resuscitated cardiac arrest, heart failure, or revascularisation) occurred in 126 participants (4.4%) in the polypill group and 157 (5.5%) in the placebo group (hazard ratio, 0.79; 95% CI, 0.63 to 1.00) — a 21% relative reduction. Polypill plus aspirin versus double placebo: 4.1% vs 5.8% (HR 0.69, 95% CI 0.50 to 0.97). Hypotension or dizziness was more frequent with the polypill.
cards.watchOut: The polypill-alone confidence interval reaches 1.00, so TIPS-3 alone is borderline for events; the control effects (LDL and blood pressure) are the direct answer to this shelf's question and are unambiguous in the record.

cards.headline: PolyIran (Roshandel 2019): major cardiovascular events 5.9% on the polypill vs 8.8% on minimal care (adjusted HR 0.66) in 6,838 participants; the no-prior-disease subgroup HR was 0.80 and not significant
cards.summary: PolyIran (Roshandel 2019): major cardiovascular events 5.9% on the polypill vs 8.8% on minimal care (adjusted HR 0.66) in 6,838 participants; the no-prior-disease subgroup HR was 0.80 and not significant
cards.people: 6,838 participants aged 40–75 years within the Golestan Cohort Study in Iran, cluster-randomised by village (236 clusters) to non-pharmacological preventive interventions alone (minimal care, n = 3,417) or the same plus a once-daily four-component polypill (n = 3,421; hydrochlorothiazide 12.5 mg, aspirin 81 mg, atorvastatin 20 mg, and enalapril 5 mg or valsartan 40 mg), followed for 60 months; the cohort included people with and without pre-existing cardiovascular disease.
cards.result: Major cardiovascular events occurred in 202 of 3,421 (5.9%) in the polypill group versus 301 of 3,417 (8.8%) in the minimal care group (adjusted hazard ratio 0.66, 95% CI 0.55 to 0.80) — a 34% relative reduction. There was no significant interaction by pre-existing cardiovascular disease: HR 0.61 (95% CI 0.49 to 0.75) with prior disease and 0.80 (95% CI 0.51 to 1.12) without it (P for interaction = 0.19). Median adherence was 80.5%, and adverse event frequency was similar between groups. Among high-adherence polypill participants the adjusted HR was 0.43 (95% CI 0.33 to 0.55).
cards.watchOut: PolyIran mixes primary and secondary prevention, and its primary-prevention subgroup estimate (HR 0.80) is imprecise; the shelf's primary-prevention claim rests mainly on TIPS-3 and the pooled analysis, with PolyIran concordant in direction.

cards.headline: Joseph 2021: pooling the three large primary-prevention polypill trials (18,162 participants), the primary outcome occurred in 3.0% vs 4.9% (HR 0.62), with reductions in infarction, stroke, revascularisation and cardiovascular death
cards.summary: Joseph 2021: pooling the three large primary-prevention polypill trials (18,162 participants), the primary outcome occurred in 3.0% vs 4.9% (HR 0.62), with reductions in infarction, stroke, revascularisation and cardiovascular death
cards.people: Individual participant data from the three large randomised primary-prevention trials of a fixed-dose combination (at least two blood-pressure-lowering agents plus a statin, with or without aspirin) versus placebo or usual care — TIPS-3, HOPE-3 and PolyIran — totalling 18,162 participants (mean age 63.0 years, 49.8% female), median follow-up 5 years.
cards.result: The primary outcome (cardiovascular death, myocardial infarction, stroke, or arterial revascularisation) occurred in 276 participants (3.0%) in the fixed-dose combination group versus 445 (4.9%) in the control group (hazard ratio 0.62, 95% CI 0.53 to 0.73, P < 0.0001) — a 38% relative reduction. Component hazard ratios: myocardial infarction 0.52 (0.38 to 0.70), revascularisation 0.54 (0.36 to 0.80), stroke 0.59 (0.45 to 0.78), cardiovascular death 0.65 (0.52 to 0.81). Effects were similar across lipid and blood pressure levels and with or without diabetes, smoking or obesity; gastrointestinal bleeding was slightly more frequent with aspirin-containing strategies (0.4% vs the control rate as printed in the record).
cards.watchOut: This meta-analysis re-uses the TIPS-3 and PolyIran participants carded above, so it is concordance and precision, not independent replication; the independent trial count for the stamp is the underlying trials themselves.

cards.headline: Synthesis: a polypill lowers LDL cholesterol by about 19 mg/dL and systolic pressure by about 5.8 mm Hg versus placebo, and large trials consistently show fewer cardiovascular events in primary prevention
cards.summary: Synthesis: a polypill lowers LDL cholesterol by about 19 mg/dL and systolic pressure by about 5.8 mm Hg versus placebo, and large trials consistently show fewer cardiovascular events in primary prevention
cards.people: The carded evidence: two large randomised trials (TIPS-3, 5,713 participants, pure primary prevention; PolyIran, 6,838 participants, mixed prevention with a primary-prevention subgroup) and an individual-participant meta-analysis of three trials (18,162 participants, overlapping the trials). Total unique participants exceed 12,000, so no small-N stamp labelling applies.
cards.result: Blood pressure and cholesterol control improve on the polypill (LDL −19 mg/dL, systolic −5.8 mm Hg in TIPS-3). Events: 4.4% vs 5.5% (HR 0.79) in TIPS-3; 5.9% vs 8.8% (adjusted HR 0.66) in PolyIran, with its primary-prevention subgroup at HR 0.80 (not significant alone); pooled primary-prevention estimate 3.0% vs 4.9% (HR 0.62). PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit).
cards.watchOut: The trials test a strategy (one pill, fixed doses) against placebo or minimal care, not against well-titrated separate prescriptions; how a polypill compares with good usual multi-pill care is a different question.
cards.source: Synthesis of Yusuf S et al. New England Journal of Medicine. 2021 (PMID: 33186492); Roshandel G et al. Lancet. 2019 (PMID: 31448738); Joseph P et al. Lancet. 2021 (PMID: 34469765).

shelves.title: COVID booster at ages 50–64 without major risk factors (observational only): relative hospitalisation risk falls by roughly half for the first weeks then wanes — but the absolute benefit is small, and no study isolates this exact subgroup
shelves.question: Does a COVID booster reduce hospitalization in adults aged 50 to 64 without major risk factors?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Humans · COVID-19 Vaccines · COVID-19 · COVID-19 Testing · Case-Control Studies · Vaccines · Hospitalization · Vaccines, Combined · ChAdOx1 nCoV-19 · England
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only, printed on the face: every carded estimate comes from test-negative or cohort designs, as no placebo-controlled booster trial exists in this age group. The relative benefit is consistent: the English test-negative study found the bivalent booster's incremental effectiveness against hospitalisation in people aged 50 and over peaked at 53.0% (relative) 2–4 weeks after the dose and waned to 35.9% after 10 or more weeks; the US networks found the updated 2023–2024 vaccine 52% and 43% effective (relative) against hospitalisation in immunocompetent adults. But the absolute benefit in a healthy 50–64-year-old is small, because baseline hospitalisation risk is low: in the US number-needed-to-vaccinate cohort of 1,285,032 adults, the median NNV to prevent one hospitalisation was 205 overall and was consistently lower (more favourable) in people aged 65 and over and in those with underlying conditions than in younger, healthier groups — the record does not print a separate NNV for 50–64-year-olds without risk factors, and none is invented here. No carded record isolates adults aged 50–64 without major risk factors as its own stratum; the age-specific claim is therefore an inference from the 50-and-over and all-adult estimates, printed as such. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only: a booster reduces the relative risk of COVID hospitalisation by roughly half in the first weeks, waning thereafter; for a 50–64-year-old without major risk factors the absolute number of hospitalisations prevented is small.

cards.headline: Kirsebom 2023 (England, test-negative): the bivalent BA.1 booster's incremental effectiveness against hospitalisation in people aged 50 and over peaked at 53.0% (relative) at 2–4 weeks and waned to 35.9% after 10 or more weeks
cards.summary: Kirsebom 2023 (England, test-negative): the bivalent BA.1 booster's incremental effectiveness against hospitalisation in people aged 50 and over peaked at 53.0% (relative) at 2–4 weeks and waned to 35.9% after 10 or more weeks
cards.people: Test-negative case-control study in England: 9,954 cases and 39,108 controls aged 50 years or older for the bivalent-booster analysis (people who had received at least two monovalent doses, the last at least 6 months earlier), tested in hospital settings between September 5, 2022 and February 5, 2023, during omicron circulation; analyses adjusted for week of test, sex, age, COVID-19 risk group, care-home residence, health or social care work, deprivation, ethnicity and recent positivity. A separate monovalent analysis included 19,841 cases and 43,410 controls.
cards.result: Incremental vaccine effectiveness of the bivalent BA.1 booster against hospitalisation peaked at 53.0% (95% CI 47.9 to 57.5) at 2–4 weeks after administration and waned to 35.9% (95% CI 31.4 to 40.1) after 10 or more weeks — relative effectiveness estimates; the record does not print absolute hospitalisation rates for the boosted and unboosted groups, and none are invented here. For context, effectiveness of three or more monovalent doses against hospitalisation plateaued from 6 months at around 30% in those aged 18–64 years (versus around 50% at age 65 and over). The record does not report a separate estimate for ages 50–64 without risk factors.
cards.watchOut: The 50-and-over estimate pools healthy 50–64-year-olds with older and clinically vulnerable people, whose higher baseline risk drives larger absolute benefit; the relative percentage cannot be read as the absolute gain for a healthy person in their fifties.
cards.source: Kirsebom FCM et al. Duration of protection of ancestral-strain monovalent vaccines and effectiveness of bivalent BA.1 boosters against COVID-19 hospitalisation in England: a test-negative case-control study. The Lancet. cards.headline: DeCuir 2024 (US VISION and IVY networks): the updated 2023–2024 (XBB.1.5) vaccine was 52% and 43% effective (relative) against COVID-associated hospitalisation in immunocompetent adults — estimates for all adults 18 and over, not split for ages 50–64 in the record
cards.summary: DeCuir 2024 (US VISION and IVY networks): the updated 2023–2024 (XBB.1.5) vaccine was 52% and 43% effective (relative) against COVID-associated hospitalisation in immunocompetent adults — estimates for all adults 18 and over, not split for ages 50–64 in the record
cards.people: Immunocompetent adults aged 18 years and over in two US vaccine-effectiveness networks, September 2023 to January 2024, analysed by test-negative case-control design for emergency-department/urgent-care encounters and for hospitalisation after an updated (monovalent XBB.1.5) dose. Median interval from the updated dose was 42 days (VISION) and 47 days (IVY) for the hospitalisation estimates.
cards.result: Vaccine effectiveness against COVID-associated hospitalisation was 52% (95% CI 47% to 57%) in one network and 43% (95% CI 27% to 56%) in the other — relative effectiveness; the record does not print absolute hospitalisation rates beside them. Effectiveness against emergency-department or urgent-care encounters was 51% (95% CI 47% to 54%) at 7–59 days after an updated dose and 39% (95% CI 33% to 45%) at 60–119 days. The record reports no age-stratified estimate for 50–64-year-olds and no estimate restricted to people without risk factors — printed plainly here rather than inferred on the card.
cards.watchOut: 'Immunocompetent adults' still includes older adults and people with major risk factors, so these percentages describe the average adult, not the low-risk 50–64 subgroup this shelf asks about; test-negative designs also carry the usual residual-confounding caveats.

cards.headline: Adams 2023 (VISION cohort, 1,285,032 adults): the median number needed to vaccinate with a booster to prevent one hospitalisation was 205 overall — and was lower (more favourable) in people 65 and over (110, 46 and 88 across study periods) and in those with underlying conditions (163, 69 and 131) than in younger, healthier adults
cards.summary: Adams 2023 (VISION cohort, 1,285,032 adults): the median number needed to vaccinate with a booster to prevent one hospitalisation was 205 overall — and was lower (more favourable) in people 65 and over (110, 46 and 88 across study periods) and in those with underlying conditions (163, 69 and 131) than in younger, healthier adults
cards.people: Retrospective cohort of 1,285,032 immunocompetent adults at five US health systems during omicron BA.1 predominance (December 2021–February 2022), all of whom had completed a primary mRNA series and were booster-eligible or boosted: 555,729 (43.2%) aged 18–49, 363,299 (28.3%) aged 50–64 and 366,004 (28.5%) aged 65 or over; 37.2% received a booster. There were 938 hospitalisations in total. Numbers needed to vaccinate were estimated from hazard ratios over three 25-day periods.
cards.result: The median estimated number needed to vaccinate to prevent one COVID-associated hospitalisation was 205 (range 44–615 across periods and sites), and 156 (range 75–592) to prevent one emergency-department encounter. NNV was lower across study periods for adults aged 65 and over (110, 46 and 88) and for those with underlying medical conditions (163, 69 and 131) — i.e., the absolute benefit per dose was smallest in younger adults without those conditions. The record does not print a separate NNV for the 50–64 group or for people without risk factors, and none is calculated here; the authors conclude NNV depends heavily on local incidence, outcome severity and patient risk factors.
cards.watchOut: NNV is incidence-dependent: these figures come from a high-incidence omicron wave, and in a low-incidence period the NNV for a healthy 50–64-year-old would be higher still. The study covers the first (monovalent) booster era, not the later bivalent or XBB formulations carded above.

cards.result: Relative effectiveness against hospitalisation: peak 53.0% waning to 35.9% after 10+ weeks (Kirsebom 2023); 52% and 43% at a median of about 6–7 weeks after an updated dose (DeCuir 2024). cards.watchOut: All three cards are observational — healthier-user bias can inflate vaccine-effectiveness estimates — and the exact population in the question (50–64, no major risk factors) appears as its own stratum in none of them; the shelf's answer is an inference from the 50-and-over and all-adult data, labelled as such.

shelves.title: MMR vaccine and autism (observational only): no association in over 1.9 million cohort children — adjusted HR 0.93 and RR 0.92, no clustering after vaccination, no risk in children with autistic siblings
shelves.question: In parents asking about timing, is the MMR vaccine associated with autism in children?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Autistic Disorder · Child · Child, Preschool · Cohort Studies · Denmark · Disease Susceptibility · Female · Humans · Infant · Male · Measles-Mumps-Rubella Vaccine · Proportional Hazards Models · Registries · Risk Factors · Siblings · Vaccination
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (no association) — observational only, printed on the face: this is an association question and every carded study is observational, so the house cap for observational evidence applies even though the cohorts are very large and closely concordant. Across more than 1.9 million children in the two Danish nationwide cohorts, MMR-vaccinated children were not more likely to be diagnosed with autism: adjusted hazard ratio 0.93 relative (Hviid 2019, 657,461 children) and relative risk 0.92 for autistic disorder and 0.83 for other autistic-spectrum disorders (Madsen 2002, 537,303 children), with no association by age at vaccination, time since vaccination, or calendar period, and no increased risk in subgroups with an autistic sibling or other risk factors. The meta-analysis (Taylor 2014; five cohort studies, 1,256,407 children) found the same: MMR and autism OR 0.84 relative (95% CI 0.70 to 1.01), vaccination and autism OR 0.99 relative. Every estimate sits at or below 1.0 with confidence intervals including 1.0 — there is no positive association to explain, and the timing pattern parents ask about (onset after vaccination) was specifically tested and not found. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (no association) — observational only: in nationwide cohorts totalling over 1.9 million children, MMR vaccination was not associated with autism (adjusted HR 0.93 relative; RR 0.92 relative), with no clustering after vaccination and no subgroup signal.

cards.headline: Hviid 2019: in 657,461 Danish children, MMR vaccination was not associated with autism — adjusted HR 0.93 relative — including in children with an autistic sibling and in the periods right after vaccination
cards.summary: Hviid 2019: in 657,461 Danish children, MMR vaccination was not associated with autism — adjusted HR 0.93 relative — including in children with an autistic sibling and in the periods right after vaccination
cards.people: Nationwide cohort of 657,461 children born in Denmark from 1999 through 31 December 2010, followed from 1 year of age through 31 August 2013 (5,025,754 person-years), linking MMR vaccination, autism diagnoses, other childhood vaccines, sibling history of autism and autism risk factors from Danish population registries.
cards.result: 6,517 children were diagnosed with autism (incidence 129.7 per 100,000 person-years). Comparing MMR-vaccinated with MMR-unvaccinated children gave a fully adjusted autism hazard ratio of 0.93 relative (95% CI 0.85 to 1.02). No increased risk after MMR vaccination was consistently observed in subgroups defined by sibling history of autism, autism risk factors (disease risk score) or other childhood vaccinations, or during specified time periods after vaccination. The authors conclude the study strongly supports that MMR vaccination does not increase autism risk, does not trigger autism in susceptible children, and is not associated with clustering of autism cases after vaccination. The record notes no individual medical charts were reviewed.
cards.watchOut: Observational registry data: vaccination was not randomised, diagnoses came from registries without chart review, and a hazard ratio of 0.93 is an absence of increased risk — it should not be read as the vaccine protecting against autism.
cards.source: Hviid A et al. Measles, Mumps, Rubella Vaccination and Autism: A Nationwide Cohort Study. Annals of internal medicine. 2019. PMID: 30831578. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Madsen 2002: in 537,303 Danish children (82% MMR-vaccinated), the relative risk of autistic disorder in vaccinated children was 0.92 — with no association by age at, time since, or date of vaccination
cards.summary: Madsen 2002: in 537,303 Danish children (82% MMR-vaccinated), the relative risk of autistic disorder in vaccinated children was 0.92 — with no association by age at, time since, or date of vaccination
cards.people: Retrospective cohort of all 537,303 children born in Denmark from January 1991 through December 1998 (2,129,864 person-years); 440,655 children (82.0%) received MMR vaccine. Autism status came from the Danish Psychiatric Central Register; 316 children were diagnosed with autistic disorder and 422 with other autistic-spectrum disorders.
cards.result: After adjustment for potential confounders, the relative risk of autistic disorder in vaccinated compared with unvaccinated children was 0.92 relative (95% CI 0.68 to 1.24), and the relative risk of another autistic-spectrum disorder was 0.83 relative (95% CI 0.65 to 1.07). There was no association between the age at the time of vaccination, the time since vaccination, or the date of vaccination and the development of autistic disorder. The authors conclude the study provides strong evidence against the hypothesis that MMR vaccination causes autism.
cards.watchOut: The confidence interval for autistic disorder (0.68 to 1.24) is wider than in the later, larger cohort because autism diagnoses were fewer (316) — this study excludes a large effect, and the tighter exclusion comes from Hviid 2019; both are observational.
cards.source: Madsen KM et al. A population-based study of measles, mumps, and rubella vaccination and autism. The New England journal of medicine. 2002. PMID: 12421889. cards.headline: Taylor 2014: meta-analysis of five cohort studies (1,256,407 children) — no relationship between MMR and autism (OR 0.84 relative) or between vaccination and autism overall (OR 0.99)
cards.summary: Taylor 2014: meta-analysis of five cohort studies (1,256,407 children) — no relationship between MMR and autism (OR 0.84 relative) or between vaccination and autism overall (OR 0.99)
cards.type: Meta-analysis of cohort and case-control studies (Taylor 2014)
cards.people: Evidence-based meta-analysis of case-control and cohort studies to April 2014: five cohort studies involving 1,256,407 children and five case-control studies involving 9,920 children, assessing vaccination, MMR, thimerosal and mercury exposure against subsequent autism or autism spectrum disorder.
cards.result: The cohort data revealed no relationship between vaccination and autism (OR 0.99 relative, 95% CI 0.92 to 1.06) or ASD (OR 0.91 relative, 95% CI 0.68 to 1.20), and no relationship between autism and MMR (OR 0.84 relative, 95% CI 0.70 to 1.01), thimerosal (OR 1.00 relative, 95% CI 0.77 to 1.31) or mercury (OR 1.00 relative, 95% CI 0.93 to 1.07). The case-control data likewise found no evidence of increased risk after MMR, mercury or thimerosal exposure. The authors conclude vaccinations are not associated with the development of autism or ASD.
cards.watchOut: The meta-analysis pools the same observational literature the other two cards sample — including the Danish cohorts — so its 1,256,407 children overlap with, and must not be added to, the cohort Ns. Pooling cannot remove a bias shared by all the underlying studies, though the consistency across countries, designs and eras narrows what such a bias could be.
cards.source: Taylor LE et al. Vaccines are not associated with autism: an evidence-based meta-analysis of case-control and cohort studies. Vaccine. 2014. PMID: 24814559. cards.people: The carded evidence: two Danish nationwide cohorts (657,461 and 537,303 children; over 7 million person-years combined) and one meta-analysis (five cohort studies, 1,256,407 children, overlapping with the cohorts and not additive). shelves.title: Varicella at 12 months, combined or separate — split: MMRV protects as well as separate MMR + varicella injections, but doubles the relative risk of febrile seizure in the second week (1 extra seizure per 2,300 first doses)
shelves.question: Should children receive the varicella vaccine at 12 months or as part of MMRV?
shelves.mesh: Age Distribution · Chickenpox Vaccine · Cohort Studies · Databases, Factual · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Humans · Incidence · Infant · Male · Measles-Mumps-Rubella Vaccine · Retrospective Studies · Seizures, Febrile · Severity of Illness Index · Sex Distribution · Time Factors · Vaccination · Vaccines, Combined
shelves.balance: SPLIT — both options give varicella at 12 months; the real choice is one combined injection (MMRV) versus two separate injections (MMR + varicella at the same visit), and the evidence splits cleanly between equal protection and unequal side effects. Protection is equal: in the immunogenicity trial (Lieberman 2006, 3,928 children), MMRV induced responses comparable to MMR + varicella for all four antigens, with 1-year antibody persistence above 95% for each. Fever and febrile seizure are not equal: fever of 38.9 °C or more was more frequent after MMRV in that trial (39.1% vs 33.1%), and in the large Vaccine Safety Datalink cohorts the risk of febrile seizure 7–10 days after the first dose was about double after MMRV (Klein 2010: RR 1.98 relative; excess 4.3 per 10,000 doses — one additional febrile seizure for every 2,300 doses instead of separate vaccines), a finding Klein 2015 confirmed while finding no significant difference in seven other serious outcomes. So the trade-off is convenience (one fewer injection) against a small absolute increase in febrile seizures, most of which are brief and benign but frightening; the carded evidence supports either choice and quantifies the difference rather than dictating it. PROPOSED SPLIT (protection: equal — comparable immunogenicity and persistence; safety: MMRV carries about twice the relative risk of febrile seizure 7–10 days after the first dose, an excess of 4.3 per 10,000 doses, versus separate MMR + varicella).

cards.headline: Klein 2010: febrile seizure risk 7–10 days after the first dose was about double after MMRV versus separate MMR + varicella (RR 1.98 relative) — an excess of 4.3 per 10,000 doses, or 1 extra seizure per 2,300 doses
cards.summary: Klein 2010: febrile seizure risk 7–10 days after the first dose was about double after MMRV versus separate MMR + varicella (RR 1.98 relative) — an excess of 4.3 per 10,000 doses, or 1 extra seizure per 2,300 doses
cards.type: Retrospective cohort study, Vaccine Safety Datalink (Klein 2010)
cards.people: Vaccine Safety Datalink cohort, children aged 12–23 months, 2000–2008: 83,107 MMRV recipients compared with 376,354 recipients of separate MMR and varicella vaccines, assessing seizures and fever visits after vaccination, with chart-review and self-controlled supplementary analyses.
cards.result: Seizure and fever clustered significantly 7 to 10 days after vaccination with all measles-containing vaccines, but not after varicella vaccination alone. Seizure risk during days 7 to 10 was higher after MMRV than after MMR + varicella vaccination (relative risk 1.98 relative, 95% CI 1.43 to 2.73); supplementary analyses gave similar results. The excess risk for febrile seizures 7 to 10 days after MMRV was 4.3 per 10,000 doses (95% CI 2.6 to 5.6) — 1 additional febrile seizure for every 2,300 doses given instead of separate MMR + varicella vaccines. The authors advise that providers recommending MMRV should tell parents it increases the risk of fever and seizure over that already associated with measles-containing vaccines.
cards.watchOut: Observational comparison within a health-care database: children given MMRV versus separate vaccines were not randomised, though the self-controlled analyses (each child as their own control) pointed the same way. The relative doubling sounds large; the absolute excess is 4.3 per 10,000 doses, and febrile seizures after measles-containing vaccines are typically brief — severity outcomes are not reported in this record.
cards.source: Klein NP et al. Measles-mumps-rubella-varicella combination vaccine and the risk of febrile seizures. Pediatrics. 2010. PMID: 20587679. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Klein 2015: across 123,200 MMRV and 584,987 MMR + varicella doses, seven other serious outcomes did not differ significantly — only seizure and fever at 7–10 days were higher after MMRV
cards.summary: Klein 2015: across 123,200 MMRV and 584,987 MMR + varicella doses, seven other serious outcomes did not differ significantly — only seizure and fever at 7–10 days were higher after MMRV
cards.type: Retrospective cohort study, Vaccine Safety Datalink (Klein 2015)
cards.people: Vaccine Safety Datalink, children aged 12–23 months, 2000–2012: 123,200 MMRV doses and 584,987 MMR + varicella doses, examining nine outcomes — anaphylaxis, immune thrombocytopenia purpura (ITP), ataxia, arthritis, meningitis/encephalitis, acute disseminated encephalomyelitis, Kawasaki disease, seizure, and fever.
cards.result: Comparing MMRV with MMR + V, risks for the seven main outcomes were not significantly different, and several outcomes had few or zero postvaccination events. Against comparison intervals, ITP risk was higher after both MMRV (odds ratio 11.3 relative, 95% CI 1.9 to 68.2) and MMR + V (OR 10 relative, 95% CI 4.5 to 22.5), and ataxia risk was lower after both. Compared with MMR + V, MMRV increased the risk of seizure and fever 7 to 10 days after vaccination (the record does not reprint the seizure effect size). The authors conclude the study identified no new safety concerns for either schedule.
cards.watchOut: Rare outcomes had few or zero events, so 'not significantly different' for outcomes like meningitis/encephalitis is a statement about very small numbers; the ITP signal applies to both schedules equally and is a property of measles-containing vaccines, not a point of difference between them.
cards.source: Klein NP et al. Safety of measles-containing vaccines in 1-year-old children. Pediatrics. 2015. PMID: 25560438. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Lieberman 2006: in 3,928 toddlers, MMRV was as immunogenic as separate MMR + varicella (1-year persistence above 95% for all four antigens) — but fever was more common after MMRV (39.1% vs 33.1%)
cards.summary: Lieberman 2006: in 3,928 toddlers, MMRV was as immunogenic as separate MMR + varicella (1-year persistence above 95% for all four antigens) — but fever was more common after MMRV (39.1% vs 33.1%)
cards.people: 3,928 healthy children aged 12–23 months at US and Canadian sites, receiving a single injection of one of three consistency lots of combined MMRV vaccine or MMR vaccine administered concomitantly with varicella vaccine at separate injection sites, with antibody persistence assessed 1 year postvaccination and tolerability followed for 42 days.
cards.result: Immune responses to measles, mumps, rubella and varicella for each MMRV lot were similar, and the combined MMRV response was comparable to the control (MMR + varicella) group; 1-year antibody persistence rates for all four viruses were each greater than 95% and comparable between groups. Overall adverse experience incidence was comparable, but fever (temperature 38.9 °C oral equivalent or tactile) was greater in MMRV recipients than in MMR + V recipients (39.1% versus 33.1%, P = 0.001); fevers were transient and there was no difference in the incidence of febrile seizures in this trial.
cards.watchOut: A trial of 3,928 children cannot detect a difference in an outcome occurring a few times per 10,000 doses — its 'no difference in febrile seizures' does not contradict the 459,461-child Datalink analysis on the previous cards; it measured immunogenicity and common reactions, which is what it was sized for.
cards.source: Lieberman JM et al. The safety and immunogenicity of a quadrivalent measles, mumps, rubella and varicella vaccine in healthy children: a study of manufacturing consistency and persistence of antibody. The Pediatric infectious disease journal. 2006. PMID: 16804432. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: give varicella at 12 months either way — MMRV and separate MMR + varicella protect equally; MMRV saves an injection and costs about 1 extra febrile seizure per 2,300 first doses
cards.summary: Synthesis: give varicella at 12 months either way — MMRV and separate MMR + varicella protect equally; MMRV saves an injection and costs about 1 extra febrile seizure per 2,300 first doses
cards.people: The carded evidence: two Vaccine Safety Datalink cohorts (83,107 MMRV versus 376,354 separate-vaccine recipients; and 123,200 versus 584,987 doses — overlapping Datalink populations across periods, not additive) and one randomised immunogenicity trial (3,928 children). All comparisons are of the first dose at 12–23 months.
cards.result: Immunogenicity and 1-year antibody persistence (over 95% for all four antigens) were comparable between MMRV and MMR + varicella. Febrile seizure risk 7–10 days post-vaccination was higher after MMRV (RR 1.98 relative; excess 4.3 per 10,000 doses; 1 additional seizure per 2,300 doses), fever was more frequent (39.1% vs 33.1%), and no significant difference was found in seven other serious outcomes. PROPOSED SPLIT (protection: equal — comparable immunogenicity and persistence; safety: MMRV carries about twice the relative risk of febrile seizure 7–10 days after the first dose, an excess of 4.3 per 10,000 doses, versus separate MMR + varicella).
cards.watchOut: This shelf covers the first dose at 12 months only. The second-dose (4–6 years) comparison is a different evidence base — the carded records here do not address it — and children with a personal or family history of febrile seizures are the subgroup for whom the seizure difference matters most in practice.
cards.source: Synthesis of Klein NP et al. Pediatrics. 2010 (PMID: 20587679); Klein NP et al. Pediatrics. 2015 (PMID: 25560438); Lieberman JM et al. The Pediatric infectious disease journal. 2006 (PMID: 16804432).

shelves.title: Brief clinician advice helps smokers quit: physician brief advice raised quitting by a relative 66% (about 1–3 extra quitters per 100 advised) across 17 trials, with concordant Cochrane evidence for nurses and motivational interviewing
shelves.question: Does a brief intervention from a primary care clinician help adults who smoke quit?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Patient Education as Topic · Physician's Role · Practice Patterns, Physicians' · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Smoking · Smoking Cessation · Smoking Prevention · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit) — three concordant Cochrane meta-analyses of randomised trials support it, which is the standard this library requires for LIKELY. The direct evidence is the physician-advice review (Stead 2013): brief advice versus no advice gave a relative risk of quitting of 1.66 (95% CI 1.42 to 1.94) across 17 trials — a relative measure that the reviewers translate honestly into about 1 to 3 extra quitters per 100 people advised, on an unassisted quit rate of 2 to 3%. The effect is a class effect of clinician intervention rather than one profession's trick: nurse-delivered interventions gave RR 1.29 (1.20 to 1.39; Rice 2013) and motivational interviewing beat even brief advice or usual care, RR 1.26 (1.16 to 1.36; Lindson-Hawley 2015). Intensity adds little — direct comparison of intensive versus minimal advice gave RR 1.37 — which is precisely why the brief form is worth doing. No mortality benefit is claimed: the one study that looked found no significant difference at 20 years. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit) — brief advice from a clinician increases quitting (relative risk 1.66; about 1–3 extra quitters per 100 advised).

cards.headline: Stead 2013 (Cochrane): brief physician advice versus no advice raised quitting (relative risk 1.66, 95% CI 1.42–1.94) across 17 trials — an absolute gain of about 1 to 3 extra quitters per 100 people advised
cards.summary: Stead 2013 (Cochrane): brief physician advice versus no advice raised quitting (relative risk 1.66, 95% CI 1.42–1.94) across 17 trials — an absolute gain of about 1 to 3 extra quitters per 100 people advised
cards.type: Cochrane systematic review of randomised trials (Stead 2013)
cards.people: 42 randomised trials conducted between 1972 and 2012 including over 31,000 smokers, mostly from unselected populations, with the most common delivery setting primary care; the brief-advice meta-analysis pooled 17 trials of brief advice versus no advice or usual care, with abstinence assessed at least six months after advice.
cards.result: Pooled brief advice significantly increased the rate of quitting (relative risk (RR) 1.66, 95% confidence interval (CI) 1.42 to 1.94) — a relative measure. Assuming an unassisted quit rate of 2 to 3%, a brief advice intervention can increase quitting by a further 1 to 3% (the review's own absolute translation). More intensive advice gave a higher point estimate (RR 1.84, 1.60 to 2.13) but direct comparison showed only a small advantage of intensive over minimal advice (RR 1.37, 1.20 to 1.56). Only one study examined mortality and found no statistically significant difference in death rates at 20 years.
cards.watchOut: The relative 66% increase sounds large against a 2–3% baseline: the honest clinical unit is the review's own 1–3 extra quitters per 100 advised, and most trials predate modern pharmacotherapy, so the estimate is for advice on the background care of its era.
cards.source: Stead LF et al. Physician advice for smoking cessation. The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2013. PMID: 23728631. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: Humans · Patient Education as Topic · Physician's Role · Practice Patterns, Physicians' · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Smoking · Smoking Cessation · Smoking Prevention · Treatment Outcome

cards.headline: Rice 2013 (Cochrane): nursing-delivered cessation interventions also raised quitting (relative risk 1.29, 95% CI 1.20–1.39) across 35 pooled studies with over 17,000 participants
cards.summary: Rice 2013 (Cochrane): nursing-delivered cessation interventions also raised quitting (relative risk 1.29, 95% CI 1.20–1.39) across 35 pooled studies with over 17,000 participants
cards.type: Cochrane systematic review of randomised trials (Rice 2013)
cards.people: 49 randomised trials of smoking cessation interventions delivered by nurses or health visitors with at least six months' follow-up; the main meta-analysis pooled 35 studies (over 17,000 participants) comparing a nursing intervention with a control or usual care.
cards.result: The nursing intervention increased the likelihood of quitting (relative risk (RR) 1.29, 95% CI 1.20 to 1.39) — a relative measure. The effect was similar in the low-intensity subgroup but with a wider confidence interval, and the reviewers note the evidence for an effect is weaker when interventions are brief and delivered by nurses whose main role is not health promotion or smoking cessation. Eleven studies comparing different nurse-delivered interventions detected no significant benefit from additional components.
cards.watchOut: Nurse interventions were often more than a single brief advice moment (counselling plus follow-up), so this card supports the clinician-advice class effect rather than isolating the briefest form; its smaller relative effect (1.29 versus 1.66) may reflect that mix.
cards.source: Rice VH et al. Nursing interventions for smoking cessation. The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2013. PMID: 23939719. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Lindson-Hawley 2015 (Cochrane): motivational interviewing — a brief clinician counselling style — beat brief advice or usual care (relative risk 1.26, 95% CI 1.16–1.36; 28 studies, N = 16,803), with the largest subgroup effect when delivered by primary care physicians
cards.summary: Lindson-Hawley 2015 (Cochrane): motivational interviewing — a brief clinician counselling style — beat brief advice or usual care (relative risk 1.26, 95% CI 1.16–1.36; 28 studies, N = 16,803), with the largest subgroup effect when delivered by primary care physicians
cards.type: Cochrane systematic review of randomised trials (Lindson-Hawley 2015)
cards.people: 28 randomised studies published between 1997 and 2014 involving over 16,000 participants; motivational interviewing was delivered in one to six sessions of 10 to 60 minutes by primary care physicians, hospital clinicians, nurses or counsellors, and compared with brief advice or usual care, with abstinence at least six months after the intervention.
cards.result: Motivational interviewing versus brief advice or usual care gave a modest but significant increase in quitting (relative risk (RR) 1.26, 95% CI 1.16 to 1.36; 28 studies; N = 16,803) — a relative measure. When delivered by primary care physicians the RR was 3.49 (95% CI 1.53 to 7.94; 2 trials; N = 736); by counsellors, 1.25 (1.15 to 1.63; 22 trials; N = 13,593). Shorter sessions (under 20 minutes) still showed benefit (RR 1.69, 1.34 to 2.12; 9 trials; N = 3,651). The reviewers caution about variation in study quality, treatment fidelity and heterogeneity.
cards.watchOut: The primary-care-physician subgroup (RR 3.49) rests on only two trials and 736 people, so it should not be quoted as the expected effect; the dependable figure is the overall 1.26 against a comparator that already includes brief advice — meaning MI adds a little over advice alone.
cards.source: Lindson-Hawley N et al. Motivational interviewing for smoking cessation. The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2015. PMID: 25726920. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: yes — brief clinician intervention helps adults who smoke quit, by a small absolute amount that is consistent across three independent Cochrane meta-analyses of randomised trials (relative risks 1.66, 1.29 and 1.26 against their respective comparators)
cards.summary: Synthesis: yes — brief clinician intervention helps adults who smoke quit, by a small absolute amount that is consistent across three independent Cochrane meta-analyses of randomised trials (relative risks 1.66, 1.29 and 1.26 against their respective comparators)
cards.people: The carded evidence: three Cochrane systematic reviews of randomised trials — physician advice (42 trials, over 31,000 smokers; brief-advice pool of 17 trials), nursing interventions (49 studies; main pool 35 studies, over 17,000 participants) and motivational interviewing (28 studies, N = 16,803). The reviews overlap in era but cover distinct deliverers and intervention styles; summed participants exceed 60,000, so no small-N stamp labelling applies.
cards.result: Brief physician advice versus no advice: RR 1.66 (1.42–1.94), translating to about 1–3 extra quitters per 100 advised on a 2–3% unassisted quit rate (Stead 2013). Nurse-delivered intervention versus control: RR 1.29 (1.20–1.39) (Rice 2013). Motivational interviewing versus brief advice or usual care: RR 1.26 (1.16–1.36) (Lindson-Hawley 2015). More intensive advice adds only a little over brief advice (direct RR 1.37). PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): a brief intervention from a primary care clinician helps adults who smoke quit — a real, replicated, but small absolute effect.
cards.watchOut: All three reviews rest on self-reported or biochemically validated abstinence at six months or more with losses counted as smokers; none shows a mortality effect (the single mortality study found no significant difference at 20 years), so the claim is about quitting, not yet about lives saved.
cards.source: Synthesis of Stead LF et al. The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2013 (PMID: 23728631); Rice VH et al. The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2013 (PMID: 23939719); Lindson-Hawley N et al. The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2015 (PMID: 25726920).

shelves.title: Stopping statins in primary prevention at the oldest ages (PARTIAL completion of live #3986's statin-benefit question): SPLIT — the completed SITE trial found stopping non-inferior on 3-year mortality, while French cohort data link stopping to more cardiovascular admissions
shelves.question: Should statins be stopped in adults over 80 without cardiovascular disease?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Hydroxymethylglutaryl-CoA Reductase Inhibitors · Female · Aged · Male · Atherosclerosis · Primary Prevention · Aged, 80 and over · Cardiovascular Diseases · Treatment Interruption
shelves.balance: SPLIT — the randomised stopping trial and the large observational cohort point in opposite directions, and the trial is the stronger design for the mortality question it asked. The SITE trial (published as SAGA/SITE) randomised 1,180 adults aged 75 and over (median age 80) who had taken a statin for at least a year for primary prevention and had no history of atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, to stop or continue, with 3 years of follow-up: mortality was 7.2% (35/484) in the stopping group versus 7.9% (48/604) on continuation, an absolute difference of -0.68 percentage points (95% CI -3.95 to 2.60), meeting the prespecified 5-point non-inferiority margin (Bonnet 2026). The trial's protocol records the design honestly: open-label, pragmatic, powered on mortality and cost-effectiveness, not on cardiovascular events (Bonnet 2020). Against it, the French nationwide cohort of 120,173 adherent 75-year-olds found statin discontinuation associated with a 33% relative increase in hospital admission for a cardiovascular event (adjusted HR 1.33), with coronary HR 1.46 and cerebrovascular HR 1.26 (Giral 2019) — observational data in which people stop statins for reasons (illness, frailty, end of life) that themselves predict events. PARTIAL completion: live shelf #3986 covers whether starting/continuing statins benefits over-75s without cardiovascular disease; this shelf covers the distinct stopping question in the over-80-centred population SITE actually enrolled (75 and over, median 80 — printed plainly, since no trial has enrolled over-80s only). SITE status, per the fetched records: the trial is completed and its results are now published (Lancet Healthy Longevity, 2026; NCT02547883 marked completed in the record) — it is no longer a protocol-only question. PROPOSED SPLIT (randomised: stopping non-inferior on 3-year mortality; observational: stopping associated with more cardiovascular admissions).

cards.headline: Bonnet 2026 (SAGA/SITE results): stopping statins was non-inferior to continuing for 3-year mortality in 1,160 analysed primary-prevention patients aged 75 and over (median 80) — deaths 7.2% stopping versus 7.9% continuing
cards.summary: Bonnet 2026 (SAGA/SITE results): stopping statins was non-inferior to continuing for 3-year mortality in 1,160 analysed primary-prevention patients aged 75 and over (median 80) — deaths 7.2% stopping versus 7.9% continuing
cards.people: Multicentre open-label pragmatic non-inferiority randomised trial in 297 French primary care offices: 1,180 participants aged 75 and over, prescribed any statin for at least 1 year for primary prevention, with no history of atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, randomised (5:4) to continue or stop; 1,160 were included in the primary-estimand analysis (639 continuation, 521 discontinuation randomised; mortality denominators 604 and 484 as printed in the record). Median age 80 years (IQR 78-84); 66.8% women; 29.5% had diabetes and 77.2% hypertension. Follow-up 36 months. Exclusions included dementia, progressive disease with life expectancy at most 3 months, and homozygous/double heterozygous familial hypercholesterolaemia.
cards.result: At 36 months, 35 of 484 participants (7.2%) in the discontinuation group and 48 of 604 (7.9%) in the continuation group had died. The absolute difference in all-cause mortality was -0.68 percentage points (95% CI -3.95 to 2.60): the upper bound did not exceed the prespecified 5-percentage-point non-inferiority margin, so discontinuation was non-inferior to continuation for 3-year all-cause mortality. Adverse events occurred in 74.0% (390/527) on discontinuation versus 73.1% (461/631) on continuation, with non-cardiovascular adverse events in 72.7% versus 72.3%. The authors conclude the findings support individualised decision-making about statin discontinuation in older adults. The record's abstract does not print a cardiovascular-event comparison, and none is invented here.
cards.watchOut: Non-inferior on mortality is not 'proven equal on cardiovascular events': the trial was powered for a 5-point mortality margin, was open-label, and enrolled 75-and-over (median 80) rather than over-80s only — and it excluded people with dementia and short life expectancy, two groups in whom stopping is most often considered.
cards.source: Bonnet F et al. cards.headline: Bonnet 2020 (SITE protocol): the stopping trial was designed as a 3-year, open-label, primary-care trial with mortality non-inferiority (5-point margin) and cost-effectiveness as its twin aims — the design record behind the 2026 result
cards.summary: Bonnet 2020 (SITE protocol): the stopping trial was designed as a 3-year, open-label, primary-care trial with mortality non-inferiority (5-point margin) and cost-effectiveness as its twin aims — the design record behind the 2026 result
cards.people: Study protocol for the SITE trial: people aged 75 and over treated with statins for primary prevention of cardiovascular events in outpatient primary care, randomised to statin cessation or continuation at the usual dosage, followed for 3 years. The protocol's planned sample size was 2,430 individuals, computed for 90% power on the mortality non-inferiority margin assuming a 15% 3-year mortality rate.
cards.result: No outcome results are reported — this is the design paper, carded so the shelf shows what the 2026 result was built to test. Its stated objectives were to assess the cost-effectiveness of statin cessation (incremental cost per quality-adjusted life year at 36 months, from the French healthcare system perspective) and the non-inferiority of cessation for overall mortality, the primary clinical endpoint. The protocol notes that trial data guide starting preventive medicines but do not define the timing, safety or risks of discontinuing them — the gap SITE was built to fill.
cards.watchOut: The executed trial randomised 1,180 people against a planned 2,430 — about half the planned sample — which is part of why its confidence interval (-3.95 to +2.60 points) is wide relative to its 5-point margin; the protocol card lets readers see that shortfall rather than discover it.
cards.source: Bonnet F et al. Discontinuing statins or not in the elderly? Study protocol for a randomized controlled trial. Trials. 2020. PMID: 32307005. Registry ID: NCT02547883. cards.headline: Giral 2019: in 120,173 adherent French 75-year-olds, stopping statins was associated with a 33% relative increase in cardiovascular hospital admission (adjusted HR 1.33) — the observational case against stopping
cards.summary: Giral 2019: in 120,173 adherent French 75-year-olds, stopping statins was associated with a 33% relative increase in cardiovascular hospital admission (adjusted HR 1.33) — the observational case against stopping
cards.people: Nationwide population-based cohort from French national healthcare databases: all subjects who turned 75 in 2012-2014 with no history of cardiovascular disease and a statin medication possession ratio of at least 80% in each of the previous 2 years — 120,173 subjects followed for an average of 2.4 years; 17,204 (14.3%) discontinued statins (defined as 3 consecutive months without exposure) and 5,396 (4.5%) were admitted for a cardiovascular event. Hazard ratios came from a marginal structural model adjusting for baseline and time-varying covariates including frailty indicators.
cards.result: Adjusted hazard ratios for statin discontinuation versus continuation were 1.33 (95% CI 1.18-1.50) for any cardiovascular event, 1.46 (1.21-1.75) for a coronary event, 1.26 (1.05-1.51) for a cerebrovascular event, and 1.02 (0.74-1.40) for other vascular events. The authors conclude discontinuation was associated with a 33% relative increase in admission for a cardiovascular event in 75-year-old primary-prevention patients and that randomised studies are needed to confirm the finding — the randomised study now exists (the SAGA/SITE card above) and did not confirm it on mortality.
cards.watchOut: In routine care, statins are often stopped because a patient is becoming ill, frail or near the end of life — reasons that raise event risk themselves. Adjustment including frailty indicators reduces but cannot remove that confounding, which is exactly the bias the randomised design exists to defeat.
cards.source: Giral P et al. Cardiovascular effect of discontinuing statins for primary prevention at the age of 75 years: a nationwide population-based cohort study in France. European Heart Journal. 2019. PMID: 31362307. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: stopping statins after 75 without cardiovascular disease was non-inferior on 3-year mortality in the randomised trial, while observational data link stopping to more cardiovascular admissions — a genuine design split
cards.summary: Synthesis: stopping statins after 75 without cardiovascular disease was non-inferior on 3-year mortality in the randomised trial, while observational data link stopping to more cardiovascular admissions — a genuine design split
cards.people: The carded evidence: one randomised non-inferiority trial (1,180 randomised, median age 80) with its protocol, and one nationwide cohort (120,173 people). Total carded participants exceed 120,000, so no small-N stamp labelling applies.
cards.result: Randomised: mortality 7.2% stopping versus 7.9% continuing, difference -0.68 points (95% CI -3.95 to 2.60), non-inferior at a 5-point margin (Bonnet 2026). Observational: cardiovascular admission adjusted HR 1.33 on discontinuation (Giral 2019). PROPOSED SPLIT (randomised: stopping non-inferior on mortality; observational: stopping associated with more cardiovascular admissions).
cards.watchOut: Neither source enrolled over-80s exclusively: SITE's median age was 80 within a 75-and-over trial, and the cohort turned 75 at entry. The shelf answers the stopping question for the oldest population actually studied and says so, rather than relabelling 75-plus evidence as 80-plus proof.

shelves.title: Daily multivitamins for cardiovascular disease and cancer prevention (PARTIAL completion of live #349): a consistent cardiovascular null, and one modest total-cancer signal in PHS II that COSMOS did not reproduce
shelves.question: Does taking a daily multivitamin prevent cardiovascular disease or cancer in generally healthy adults?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Cardiovascular Diseases · Double-Blind Method · Follow-Up Studies · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Myocardial Infarction · Physicians · Stroke · Treatment Outcome · Vitamins
shelves.balance: SPLIT (outcome) — this pack is a PARTIAL completion of live shelf #349, which homes the same trials' cognitive-ageing question; the slice built here is cardiovascular disease and cancer prevention. On cardiovascular disease the answer is uniform: no benefit in the Physicians' Health Study II over a median 11.2 years (major cardiovascular events HR 1.01) and none in COSMOS over 3.6 years (HR 0.98) — the treatment made no difference. On cancer the trials divide: PHS II found a modest, statistically significant 8% relative reduction in total cancer incidence (17.0 vs 18.3 per 1,000 person-years; HR 0.92, P = .04) with no significant effect on any site-specific cancer or on cancer mortality, while COSMOS found no reduction in total invasive cancer (HR 0.97). The older French SU.VI.MAX trial tested a single antioxidant capsule (not a broad multivitamin) and found a cancer benefit in men only (relative risk 0.69) with none in women (1.04). Product naming, per the supplement clarification rule: the PHS II and COSMOS records fetched describe the intervention only as a common daily multivitamin / daily multivitamin-multimineral and do not name the brand or manufacturer in the record; SU.VI.MAX's record gives the exact capsule contents, carded below. PROPOSED SPLIT (outcome): no cardiovascular prevention in any trial; a small total-cancer signal in one trial that the other large trial did not reproduce.

cards.headline: Physicians' Health Study II 2012 (cardiovascular): a daily multivitamin made no difference to major cardiovascular events over a median 11.2 years (HR 1.01)
cards.summary: Physicians' Health Study II 2012 (cardiovascular): a daily multivitamin made no difference to major cardiovascular events over a median 11.2 years (HR 1.01)
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial (Physicians' Health Study II)
cards.people: 14,641 US male physicians initially aged 50 years or older (mean 64.3 years), including 754 with a history of cardiovascular disease, randomised double-blind to a daily multivitamin or placebo from 1997, with treatment and follow-up through June 1, 2011. The record describes the intervention as a common daily multivitamin and does not name the brand or manufacturer.
cards.result: 1,732 confirmed major cardiovascular events occurred. A daily multivitamin had no significant effect on the composite of nonfatal myocardial infarction, nonfatal stroke and cardiovascular mortality: 11.0 vs 10.8 events per 1,000 person-years (hazard ratio 1.01, 95% CI 0.91–1.10; P = .91) — the treatment made no difference. Total myocardial infarction (HR 0.93, 95% CI 0.80–1.09), total stroke (HR 1.06, 95% CI 0.91–1.23), cardiovascular mortality (HR 0.95, 95% CI 0.83–1.09) and total mortality (HR 0.94, 95% CI 0.88–1.02) were likewise not significantly affected, with no difference between men with and without baseline cardiovascular disease (P = .62 for interaction).
cards.watchOut: Men only, and physicians — a well-nourished, health-literate population in whom a multivitamin has the least deficiency to correct; the null is strongest exactly here and is the population the question's 'generally healthy adults' most resembles.
cards.source: Sesso HD et al. Multivitamins in the prevention of cardiovascular disease in men: the Physicians' Health Study II randomized controlled trial. JAMA. 2012. PMID: 23117775. Registry ID: NCT00270647. cards.headline: Physicians' Health Study II 2012 (cancer): total cancer incidence was modestly lower on a daily multivitamin (17.0 vs 18.3 per 1,000 person-years; HR 0.92, P = .04) — an 8% relative reduction with no site-specific or mortality effect
cards.summary: Physicians' Health Study II 2012 (cancer): total cancer incidence was modestly lower on a daily multivitamin (17.0 vs 18.3 per 1,000 person-years; HR 0.92, P = .04) — an 8% relative reduction with no site-specific or mortality effect
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial (Physicians' Health Study II)
cards.people: The same Physicians' Health Study II cohort: 14,641 US male physicians aged 50 years or older, including 1,312 men with a history of cancer at randomisation, randomised to a daily multivitamin or placebo, followed a median 11.2 years. The record does not name the multivitamin brand or manufacturer.
cards.result: 2,669 men developed confirmed cancer, including 1,373 prostate and 210 colorectal cancers. Total cancer incidence was 17.0 per 1,000 person-years on multivitamin versus 18.3 on placebo (hazard ratio 0.92, 95% CI 0.86–0.998; P = .04) — an 8% relative reduction, about 1.3 fewer cancers per 1,000 person-years in absolute terms. There was no significant effect on prostate cancer (HR 0.98), colorectal cancer (HR 0.89) or other site-specific cancers, and no significant difference in cancer mortality (4.9 vs 5.6 per 1,000 person-years; HR 0.88, 95% CI 0.77–1.01; P = .07).
cards.watchOut: A borderline P value (.04) on one of many endpoints, with no supporting site-specific or mortality effect, in a trial whose participants were older male physicians — and the larger, later COSMOS trial on the next card did not reproduce the total-cancer reduction.
cards.source: Gaziano JM et al. Multivitamins in the prevention of cancer in men: the Physicians' Health Study II randomized controlled trial. JAMA. 2012. PMID: 23162860. Registry ID: NCT00270647. cards.headline: COSMOS 2022: a daily multivitamin made no difference to total invasive cancer (HR 0.97) or to cardiovascular events (HR 0.98) over a median 3.6 years
cards.summary: COSMOS 2022: a daily multivitamin made no difference to total invasive cancer (HR 0.97) or to cardiovascular events (HR 0.98) over a median 3.6 years
cards.people: 21,442 US adults (12,666 women aged 65 years or older and 8,776 men aged 60 years or older) free of major cardiovascular disease and recently diagnosed cancer, in a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled 2×2 factorial trial of a daily multivitamin-multimineral and cocoa extract, June 2015 to December 2020. The record describes the intervention as a daily multivitamin-multimineral and does not name the brand or manufacturer.
cards.result: Invasive cancer occurred in 518 participants on the multivitamin and 535 on placebo (hazard ratio 0.97, 95% CI 0.86–1.09; P = .57) — the treatment made no difference. There was no significant effect on breast cancer (HR 1.06) or colorectal cancer (HR 1.30); a protective association with lung cancer was observed (HR 0.62, 95% CI 0.42–0.92). The composite cardiovascular outcome occurred in 429 versus 437 participants (HR 0.98, 95% CI 0.86–1.12), and all-cause mortality was not significantly affected (HR 0.93, 95% CI 0.81–1.08). No safety concerns were identified.
cards.watchOut: Follow-up was a median 3.6 years — far shorter than PHS II's 11.2 years — so COSMOS cannot exclude a small cancer effect that takes a decade to appear; its lung-cancer signal is one secondary endpoint among many and should be read as hypothesis-generating.
cards.source: Sesso HD et al. Multivitamins in the prevention of cancer and cardiovascular disease: the COcoa Supplement and Multivitamin Outcomes Study (COSMOS) randomized clinical trial. The American journal of clinical nutrition. 2022. PMID: 35294969. Registry ID: NCT02422745. cards.headline: SU.VI.MAX 2004: a daily antioxidant capsule (vitamin C 120 mg, vitamin E 30 mg, beta carotene 6 mg, selenium 100 µg, zinc 20 mg) lowered total cancer in men (relative risk 0.69) but not women (1.04), and made no difference to ischemic cardiovascular disease
cards.summary: SU.VI.MAX 2004: a daily antioxidant capsule (vitamin C 120 mg, vitamin E 30 mg, beta carotene 6 mg, selenium 100 µg, zinc 20 mg) lowered total cancer in men (relative risk 0.69) but not women (1.04), and made no difference to ischemic cardiovascular disease
cards.people: 13,017 French adults (7,876 women aged 35–60 years and 5,141 men aged 45–60 years) in a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled primary-prevention trial; every participant took one daily capsule containing the stated nutritional doses of antioxidant vitamins and minerals, or placebo, for a median 7.5 years. No brand or manufacturer is named in the record; the exact formulation above is what the publication gives.
cards.result: Overall there were no major differences between groups in total cancer incidence (267 [4.1%] supplement vs 295 [4.5%] placebo), ischemic cardiovascular disease incidence (134 [2.1%] vs 137 [2.1%] — the treatment made no difference) or all-cause mortality (76 [1.2%] vs 98 [1.5%]). A significant sex interaction (P = .004) split the cancer result: relative risk 0.69 (95% CI 0.53–0.91) in men versus 1.04 (95% CI 0.85–1.29) in women, with a similar pattern for all-cause mortality (men 0.63, 95% CI 0.42–0.93; women 1.03, 95% CI 0.64–1.63). The authors suggest supplementation may work in men because of their lower baseline antioxidant status.
cards.watchOut: The tested product was a five-ingredient antioxidant capsule at nutritional doses — not a broad-spectrum multivitamin — so its male-only cancer signal cannot be transferred to the multivitamin products on the other cards; the sex split was a subgroup interaction, the design most prone to over-reading.
cards.source: Hercberg S et al. The SU.VI.MAX Study: a randomized, placebo-controlled trial of the health effects of antioxidant vitamins and minerals. Archives of internal medicine. 2004. PMID: 15557412. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: cardiovascular prevention is a consistent null across both large trials; the single modest total-cancer signal (PHS II, HR 0.92) was not reproduced by COSMOS — SPLIT (outcome)
cards.summary: Synthesis: cardiovascular prevention is a consistent null across both large trials; the single modest total-cancer signal (PHS II, HR 0.92) was not reproduced by COSMOS — SPLIT (outcome)
cards.people: The carded evidence: two reports from one randomised trial of 14,641 men followed 11.2 years (PHS II), one randomised trial of 21,442 older adults followed 3.6 years (COSMOS), and one randomised trial of a defined antioxidant capsule in 13,017 adults followed 7.5 years (SU.VI.MAX). Total carded participants exceed 49,000, so no small-N stamp labelling applies.
cards.result: Cardiovascular disease: HR 1.01 (PHS II) and HR 0.98 (COSMOS) — no effect in either trial. Cancer: total incidence HR 0.92 (P = .04) in PHS II with no site-specific or mortality benefit, HR 0.97 in COSMOS, and a men-only relative risk of 0.69 for a non-multivitamin antioxidant capsule in SU.VI.MAX. PROPOSED SPLIT (outcome): a daily multivitamin does not prevent cardiovascular disease; for cancer there is one modest, unreplicated total-incidence signal and no demonstrated mortality benefit. The cognitive-ageing question for these same trials stays homed on live shelf #349.
cards.watchOut: All three programmes enrolled generally healthy, largely well-nourished volunteers; none of this answers whether correcting an actual vitamin deficiency prevents disease — that is a different question with a different evidence base.
cards.source: Synthesis of Sesso HD et al. JAMA. 2012 (PMID: 23117775); Gaziano JM et al. JAMA. 2012 (PMID: 23162860); Sesso HD et al. The American journal of clinical nutrition. 2022 (PMID: 35294969); Hercberg S et al. Archives of internal medicine. 2004 (PMID: 15557412). Registry IDs: NCT00270647 (PHS II); NCT02422745 (COSMOS); none in the record (SU.VI.MAX).

shelves.title: Vimkunya (chikungunya VLP vaccine): 97.8% seroresponse at day 22 in ages 12–64 and 87% over 65 — an antibody surrogate, with no disease-efficacy trial
shelves.question: In adolescents, adults and older adults, does the chikungunya virus-like-particle vaccine (Vimkunya, PXVX0317) versus placebo produce seroprotective neutralising antibody responses with acceptable safety?
shelves.mesh: Chikungunya Fever · Chikungunya virus · Vaccines, Virus-Like Particle · Antibodies, Neutralizing · Immunogenicity, Vaccine
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: Vimkunya (chikungunya virus-like-particle vaccine, PXVX0317, Bavarian Nordic — named under the clarification exception) produced neutralising-antibody seroresponse in 97.8% of ages 12–64 at day 22 (versus 1.2% on placebo) and 87% of adults 65 and older (76% at day 183), with a mostly grade 1–2 safety profile across two phase 3 trials (n=3,258 and n=413). Every endpoint is an antibody surrogate — no efficacy-against-disease trial exists for any chikungunya vaccine — so the shelf caps at POSSIBLE. This is a different product from the live-attenuated vaccine homed at live shelf #1080.

cards.headline: Phase 3, ages 12–64 (2025): a single dose of Vimkunya produced a neutralising-antibody seroresponse in 97.8% at day 22 versus 1.2% on placebo (difference 96.6%)
cards.summary: Phase 3, ages 12–64 (2025): a single dose of Vimkunya produced a neutralising-antibody seroresponse in 97.8% at day 22 versus 1.2% on placebo (difference 96.6%)
cards.type: Phase 3 randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial, Lancet 2025
cards.people: 3,258 healthy adolescents and adults aged 12–64 at 47 US sites, randomised (2:2:2:1 across three manufacturing lots or placebo) to a single intramuscular dose of the chikungunya virus-like-particle vaccine Vimkunya (PXVX0317 — the tested product, Bavarian Nordic; named under the clarification exception for named vaccines) or placebo; 3,254 received vaccine (n=2,790) or placebo (n=464), and the immunogenicity-evaluable population was 2,983 (2,559 vaccine, 424 placebo).
cards.result: At day 22, seroresponse (serum neutralising antibody) was present in 2,503 of 2,559 (97.8%) vaccine recipients versus 5 of 424 (1.2%) on placebo — a difference of 96.6% (95% CI 95.0–97.5, P<0.0001); geometric mean titre was 1,618 versus 7.9. Lot-to-lot geometric-mean-titre ratios (0.95–0.98) met consistency criteria. The commonest adverse events on vaccine were injection-site pain (23.7%), fatigue (19.9%), headache (18.0%) and myalgia (17.6%), mostly grade 1–2 and self-limiting.
cards.watchOut: Seroresponse against a neutralising-antibody threshold is a surrogate: no participant was followed for prevention of actual chikungunya disease, here or in any chikungunya vaccine trial — protection is inferred, and this shelf says so on its face.
cards.source: Richardson JS, Anderson DM, Mendy J, et al. Chikungunya virus virus-like particle vaccine safety and immunogenicity in adolescents and adults in the USA: a phase 3, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial. The Lancet. 2025. PMID: 40158526. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT05072080. cards.headline: Phase 3, age 65 and older (2025): seroresponse was 87% at day 22 and 76% at day 183, with no vaccine-related serious adverse events
cards.summary: Phase 3, age 65 and older (2025): seroresponse was 87% at day 22 and 76% at day 183, with no vaccine-related serious adverse events
cards.type: Phase 3 randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial, Lancet 2025
cards.people: 413 adults aged 65 years and older at 10 US sites, randomised 1:1 to a single intramuscular dose of Vimkunya (n=206) or placebo (n=207), with neutralising antibody (NT80) measured to day 183 and safety assessed to 183 days; the day-22 immunogenicity population was 189 vaccine recipients.
cards.result: Seroprotective seroresponse (NT80 at least 100, the presumptive seroprotective threshold) on vaccine was 82% (149/181) at day 15, 87% (165/189, 95% CI 81.8–91.3) at day 22 and 76% (139/184) at day 183; responses at day 22 and 183 were similar in the 65–74 and 75-and-older groups. Both coprimary endpoints (superiority of titres over placebo, and geometric mean titre at day 22) were met. Adverse event rates did not notably differ between groups, most events were grade 1–2 and short-lived, and no vaccine-related serious adverse events or deaths occurred.
cards.watchOut: The older-adult seroresponse (87%) is lower than in the 12–64 trial (97.8%) and wanes to 76% by 6 months — the age group at highest risk of severe chikungunya is the one with the weakest surrogate response, printed rather than smoothed over.
cards.source: Tindale LC, Richardson JS, Anderson DM, et al. Chikungunya virus virus-like particle vaccine safety and immunogenicity in adults older than 65 years: a phase 3, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial. The Lancet. 2025. PMID: 40158524. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT05349617. cards.headline: CD4 T-cell report 2026: Vimkunya also induced antigen-specific CD4+ T cells, detectable by day 8 and stable to day 182 — in 30 vaccinated individuals
cards.summary: CD4 T-cell report 2026: Vimkunya also induced antigen-specific CD4+ T cells, detectable by day 8 and stable to day 182 — in 30 vaccinated individuals
cards.type: Immunology substudy report (longitudinal samples, N=30), Vaccine 2026
cards.people: Longitudinal clinical samples from 30 Vimkunya-vaccinated individuals, sampled before vaccination (day 1) and at days 8, 29, 57 and 182, assayed for chikungunya-specific CD4+ T cells by activation-induced marker assays; the record describes samples from the phase 3 programme, in which the vaccine (Bavarian Nordic) is an aluminium hydroxide-adjuvanted virus-like-particle vaccine approved in the USA, EU and UK for ages 12 and above.
cards.result: Chikungunya-specific CD4+ T cells were detected as early as day 8 after vaccination, rose in frequency over 57 days and remained stable to day 182, paralleling the antibody response. N=30 is printed on the face of this card: a mechanistic immunology report, supportive of the antibody story and nothing more.
cards.watchOut: Thirty people, no comparator arm and no clinical endpoint: cellular immunogenicity is a mechanism note, never efficacy evidence, and is graded that way here.
cards.source: Cortes FH, Agarwal R, Ha C, et al. Chikungunya virus virus-like particle vaccine (Vimkunya) induces a rapid and durable antigen-specific CD4+ T cell response. Vaccine. 2026. PMID: 42000146. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: Vimkunya gives near-universal seroresponse in ages 12–64 and a solid, waning response over 65 — against an antibody surrogate, with no efficacy-against-disease trial for any chikungunya vaccine
cards.summary: Synthesis: Vimkunya gives near-universal seroresponse in ages 12–64 and a solid, waning response over 65 — against an antibody surrogate, with no efficacy-against-disease trial for any chikungunya vaccine
cards.people: Synthesis of the three carded reports above (Richardson 2025, ages 12–64, n=3,258; Tindale 2025, age 65+, n=413; Cortes 2026, T-cell substudy, N=30).
cards.result: The virus-like-particle vaccine Vimkunya (PXVX0317, Bavarian Nordic — named under the clarification exception) is immunogenic by the regulator-accepted neutralising-antibody threshold: 97.8% seroresponse at day 22 in ages 12–64, 87% in adults 65 and older, with an acceptable, mostly grade 1–2 safety profile and early CD4+ T-cell responses. Every endpoint is a surrogate — no efficacy-against-disease trial exists for either chikungunya vaccine, so the stamp caps at POSSIBLE. Cross-point, in prose: the library's live shelf #1080 covers the other licensed product, the live-attenuated vaccine VLA1553 (IXCHIQ, Valneva), on its own trial base — a different product, differently made, whose age restrictions are what make this VLP vaccine's safety profile matter; its reports are not carded here.
cards.watchOut: Do not merge the two chikungunya vaccines: live-attenuated (shelf #1080) and virus-like-particle (this shelf) differ in construction, response rates and safety questions, and each shelf keeps to its own product.
